papers.abstract: World models and vision-language-action policy models are increasingly proposed as foundations for robot manipulation. They predict how scenes evolve and which actions to take, yet successful manipulation depends not solely on following observable trajectories but also on the hidden variable of interaction force. Neurophysiology has shown that humans possess a visual prior for this hidden variable, motivating us to ask the question: Do the representations of visual foundation models also capture the forces involved in an interaction? We define force awareness as the ability of representations to (1) indicate when contact force is applied, (2) track how it changes during an interaction, and (3) reflect how large it is. We probe frozen image, video, world- and policy model representations with a lightweight readout trained on synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets. Our experiments show that most models capture when contact occurs but not how much force is being applied. Surprisingly, robot post-training does not improve this either, highlighting an important gap in current models capabilities.
bullets: The study asks whether visual, world, and policy models encode hidden interaction forces important for robot manipulation.
Force awareness is defined as detecting contact, tracking force changes, and reflecting force magnitude.
Frozen model representations are evaluated with lightweight readouts using synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets.
Most models identify when contact occurs, but not how force changes or how large it is.
Robot post-training does not resolve this limitation, revealing a capability gap in current models.

papers.selection_reason: Probes force awareness in world-model and VLA representations for manipulation; directly relevant to embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: Can Visual World Models See Force?
papers.tldr: Visual foundation models can often detect contact but generally fail to represent the magnitude and changes of interaction force.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies with linearly composed scores have emerged as a promising approach to multitask robotic learning by combining separate factors to enable modular, task-wise adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretable functional decomposition. However, current training objectives do not encourage factor specialization, often resulting in uninterpretable denoisers whose composed prediction is an average over identical copies, undermining their architectural premise. To address this, we propose a drop-in score-decorrelation auxiliary loss, motivated by projective composition theory. Our approach encourages specialization by penalizing overlap directly between component noise predictions, with little architectural change or computational overhead. We demonstrate across multiple benchmarks that our decorrelation loss consistently reduces measurable double-counting between components, improves task decomposition, and produces behaviorally meaningful specialization without compromising multitask performance. Website: https://al3cl1.github.io/robotics-score-decorrelation.
bullets: Existing linearly composed diffusion policies often learn redundant components, undermining modular composition and interpretation.
The method adds a drop-in auxiliary loss that penalizes overlap between component noise predictions.
It requires little architectural change or computational overhead.
Across multiple benchmarks, it reduces component double-counting and improves task decomposition.
The resulting specialization is behaviorally meaningful while preserving multitask performance.

Without our loss (left), the four factors look identical; with it (right), factor 1 takes the base and factor 2 the gripper, with factors 0 and 3 sharing the arm.

Figure 2: Real-world cup flipping. Agent-view (top) and wrist-view (bottom) frames, left to right, on an ARX R5 arm. Over 25 trials, FDP with our loss succeeds 19 times, versus 15 for FDP and 10 for DP.
Figure 6: Action attribution across horizon and denoising steps. With our loss, factor 1 owns the base and factor 2 the gripper at every step.
Figure 4: Pairwise similarity between factors. Dark blocks mark redundant factors; only our loss removes them.

Table 7: Decorrelation objectives at 𝐾=8 on LIBERO-90. SR over 3 seeds × 500 rollouts. Ours gives the highest success and effective rank, keeping the factors distinct.
Table 5: Composite and subgoal success on LIBERO-10. Composite requires completing both subgoals, while subgoal gives credit for each: the best 𝜆 improves both.

Table 1: Success rates and decorrelation metrics across 𝜆. 2D is in-distribution; 1D and 3D are zero-shot (OOD). Higher 𝜆 lowers overlap and raises zero-shot success.

papers.abstract: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present ScaleEvals, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley-Terry model, while tag-stratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, ScaleEvals achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, ScaleEvals correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, rho=0.90, p=0.018), and remains internally consistent on a second embodiment, YAM (r=0.839, rho=0.80). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover three-policy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating ScaleEvals can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse.
bullets: Addresses evaluation bottlenecks caused by manual resets, human grading, and narrow fixed task suites.
Uses VLM-generated, scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags during continuous robot play.
Combines VLM grading, soft-win Bradley–Terry aggregation, and tag-stratified ANOVA for capability diagnostics.
Across 3,000+ rollouts, achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hour per station and reduces active human labor by 98%; VLM grading agrees with humans 90.7% of the time.
Ranks five generalist policies consistently with manual evaluations and predicts unseen-prompt ranking reversals through compositional behavioral evidence.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Deployment and aggregation architecture. Each evaluation cell runs policy streams through AutoPrompter and AutoGrader. PlayArena accumulates matched rollout evidence across cells to produce a global leaderboard and capability profiles.

Figure 6: Skill-tag-conditioned capability diagnostics. Per-tag mean task-progress profiles for each policy, from reset-free ScaleEvals and the held-out manual suite (up to 40 rollouts per policy). The panels use different radial ranges, shown on their grids; policy ordering within each panel is maintained. The tag decomposition localizes where policies differ, while coverage gaps in the small manual suite appear as axes the reset-free stream fills in.

Figure 8: Tag recomposition enables prospective policy-order prediction. Left: per-tag BT orderings for the active motion, skill, and object factors are combined using confidence- and supportweighted Borda aggregation. The predictor scores candidate tag sets, and a fixed template renders the selected composition as a natural-language prompt. The prompt and predicted policy order are frozen before execution. Right: prospective validation recovers 9/10 exact orders over 240 rollouts, with 96% pairwise concordance. Appendix Table 6 reports task-level results, and Appendix B.3 analyzes the Red 5 discrepancy.

Figure 4: ScaleEvals rank convergence (reset-free only). Bradley–Terry Elo per policy versus rollout budget B under per-tag-balanced sub-sampling, computed entirely from reset-free ScaleEvals play (no manual data). For this convergence visualization, every bootstrap fit is recentered to GR00T N1.7=1500; this additive shift does not change ordering and differs from the π0.5=1539 anchor used in the leaderboard. The policy ordering becomes stable by B=100 trajectories per policy, and subsequent estimates remain within approximately ±25 Elo.

Figure 10: Scene-aware skill tagging and difficulty. Both prompts require object transfer. In the second scene, the marker-to-cup alignment adds a precision demand, illustrating that skill tags depend on both instruction semantics and scene context. VLM-estimated difficulty, action verbs, and primary objects provide additional metadata for matched Bradley–Terry rankings and prospective prompt composition (Table 6).

Figure 9: Observed AutoPrompter skill-tag distribution. Across 2,486 accepted DROID rollouts, generated prompts contain 26 distinct action verbs and reference 32 objects. Tags are multi-label, so percentages sum to more than 100%. The distribution documents task coverage but is not a standardized semantic-diversity metric.

Right: ScaleEvals Bradley–Terry rating versus mean task progress for four anonymized policies (Policy A–D), with 250 rollouts per policy under four-policy alternation. Their correlation (Pearson r=0.839, Spearman ρ=0.800) supports internal consistency of the reset-free protocol on a second embodiment; YAM does not include an independent manualevaluation baseline.

DreamZero now leads on all eight tags (narrowest margins: precision 30 vs π0.5 29, reposing 35 vs GR00T N1.7 33); the previously reported precision/reposing inversions disappeared as more matched comparisons accrued. Caveat (radar). Radar charts encode value as radius but readers perceive area (∝ r2), which inflates apparent differences; the table is the quantitative source of record.

Per-policy ScaleEvals Bradley–Terry (left column) and raw mean task-progress (right column) plotted against the heldout manual eval suite’s mean TP. The manual suite contains n=198 observed rollouts (40 resetrequired rollouts for four policies and 38 for DreamZero), versus n=1750 ScaleEvals rollouts in the balanced subset (top row, 350 per policy) and n=2486 in the full corpus (bottom row); ScaleEvals therefore uses roughly 8.75× and 12.4× more rollouts than the manual suite, respectively. All four cells clear α=0.05; the BT correlation is uniformly tighter than the raw-TP correlation on both data slices, indicating that the soft-win Bradley–Terry aggregation removes some of the per-policy idiosyncratic noise present in the raw mean-TP. The manual panel (a) spans a [0, 100]% radial axis (its per-axisnormalized scores reach 100%; gridlines every 20%); the two ScaleEvals panels are normalized to [0, 60]% to resolve the AutoGrader task-progress spread (gridlines every 10%). Table 3: AutoPrompter difficulty calibration. Difficulty labels are grounded by few-shot examples and used for matching and aggregation rather than as a standalone measure of task quality.

Table 8: Bradley–Terry leaderboard on the balanced 1750 subset (n=350 rollouts per policy). Soft wins use raw task-progress score, pair weights track the matched-tag count. † Pi05 is the BT anchor (σθ=0 by construction). TP is mean task progress across the 350 rollouts; SR is the perfectrollout rate.

Table 5: End-to-end operational throughput and human involvement. Net throughput includes AutoPrompter VLM calls, failed task-generation retries, safety and visibility checks, policy execution, and rollout time. The manual baseline uses one operator per station for scene resets and grading. SCALEEVALS reduces active human involvement from 4 hours to 5 minutes per 100 rollouts (98%) and recorded five human interventions over the additional 530-rollout temporal-drift evaluation.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the dynamic real world requires understanding how the environment functions and evolves, and acting accordingly. Existing benchmarks, however, do not adequately address these needs. Physics-oriented benchmarks evaluate predictive fidelity but not closed-loop action. Dynamic robotic manipulation benchmarks often use simplified, physically implausible object motions, limiting evaluation of reasoning and action under realistic dynamics. Evaluation is also typically synchronized, freezing the environment during inference and making computation time irrelevant to task outcomes. To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark for evaluating the physical understanding and action capabilities of manipulation policies in dynamic scenes. RoboDyna comprises 20 conceptual dynamic tasks spanning five capability categories, with simple objects and minimal scene clutter, under a two-factor difficulty design, and 10 household tasks that instantiate the same capabilities in visually and semantically richer simulated real-world environments. RoboDyna provides 3,500 expert demonstrations, paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocols, metrics for task success and partial completion, and interactive tools for human baseline evaluation. Evaluating vision-language-action models and a world-action model across 5.4K episodes, we find that all policies achieve success rates below 20%, revealing substantial limitations in dynamic manipulation. The world-action model captures simple physical dynamics but struggles with complex interactions, and its prediction fidelity does not consistently align with task success. Sync-async comparisons show that inference latency flips 5-12% of episode outcomes while changing average success rates by at most 3%. Human baselines substantially outperform all policies under matched conditions. Project page: https://robodyna.github.io/robodyna/
bullets: Covers 20 conceptual dynamic tasks across five capabilities and 10 richer household tasks.
Includes 3,500 expert demonstrations, synchronous and asynchronous protocols, partial-completion metrics, and human-baseline tools.
Evaluations across 5.4K episodes show all tested policies achieve below 20% success, while humans substantially outperform them.
World-action models capture simple dynamics but struggle with complex interactions; prediction fidelity does not consistently predict task success.
Inference latency changes 5–12% of episode outcomes, though average success rates shift by at most 3%.

papers.abstract: Robots operating in the real world are inherently subject to partial observability, particularly in multi-robot collaboration, where individual observations may be insufficient for effective task execution. A key challenge is leveraging complementary observations from partner robots to support collaborative decision-making. We argue that information sharing should go beyond passively transmitting raw observations or generic visual features. Instead, robots should selectively encode task-relevant information according to task objectives and execution progress. To this end, we propose a task-oriented active context sharing framework that transforms robot observations into compact representations, preserving critical information under constrained communication budgets. The framework adopts a two-stage training paradigm. In the first stage, onboard observations and task instructions are jointly encoded into compact context representations. Task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning guide this collaboration-agnostic compression, preserving information about task objectives and execution progress. In the second stage, the learned representations are integrated into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, enabling bidirectional context exchange. Each robot combines complementary partner information with local observations to guide action generation. Action supervision jointly refines the context representations and policy, aligning information sharing with collaborative decision-making. Controlled experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains under constrained communication budgets, while three real-world experiments validate the framework in complex dual-robot tasks. These results highlight a shift from passive visual transmission toward active, task-oriented context sharing that directly supports collaborative decision-making.
bullets: Addresses partial observability in multi-robot tasks where each robot’s view is insufficient.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose ThinkLocoManip, an agentic harness for legged loco-manipulation designed to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments. Existing approaches typically follow either direct action generation or a plan-then-act paradigm, both of which can struggle with the generalization and error-recovery capabilities required for extended task execution. In contrast, ThinkLocoManip adopts an interleaved reasoning-and-acting paradigm, allowing the agent to continuously reason about its current state, execute actions, observe their outcomes, and adapt its strategy accordingly. Building on this paradigm, our agentic harness orchestrates a suite of specialized tools for perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion, enabling flexible composition of heterogeneous capabilities. Unlike existing robotic agentic harnesses, ThinkLocoManip explicitly incorporates locomotion as a tool domain for agent reasoning and execution. We further design a set of skills that explicitly account for both tool usage within each functional domain and coordination across domains, supporting effective execution of complex behaviors over long horizons. To tackle task failure during long-horizon interactions, we develop keyframe thinking mechanism to preserve critical execution context and support efficient error recovery. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that ThinkLocoManip substantially outperforms representative methods based on both direct action generation and plan-then-act paradigms across challenging long-horizon legged loco-manipulation tasks. Notably, ThinkLocoManip achieves a success rate of 77%, more than twice that of the strongest plan-then-act baseline (37.1%). Our experiments further validate the effectiveness of interleaved reasoning and acting, tool orchestration, and coordinated skill execution.
bullets: Targets the limited generalization and error recovery of direct-action and plan-then-act approaches.
Continuously reasons, acts, observes outcomes, and adapts its strategy during execution.

papers.abstract: Passive-wheel quadrupedal robots offer energy-efficient locomotion through leg-driven propulsion and momentum-driven gliding. However, navigation requires coordinating steering with intermittent propulsion and adapting push-glide timing to task demands. Velocity-tracking objectives may suppress the speed variations inherent in skating, discouraging efficient gliding. To address these challenges, we propose SkateNav, a unified skating-navigation framework based on reinforcement learning. A time-budgeted goal-reaching objective allows the policy to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their temporal allocation. An adaptive skating cycle structures gliding, pushing, and recovery, while frequency modulation at every control step adjusts phase durations to navigation demands. Simulation experiments demonstrate higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner-controller baselines, with ablations confirming the contributions of cycle structure and frequency adaptation. Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer from simulation to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah across cluttered indoor spaces, slopes, and paved outdoor surfaces. Supplementary videos are available on the project page: https://ktw1404.github.io/SkateNav/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of navigating with intermittent leg propulsion and momentum-driven gliding.
Uses a time-budgeted goal-reaching objective to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their timing.
Introduces an adaptive skating cycle with per-step frequency modulation for gliding, pushing, and recovery.
Simulation results show higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than evaluated planner-controller baselines.

papers.abstract: Dynamic object manipulation requires robots to anticipate target motion while replanning fast enough to avoid executing outdated actions. Existing approaches either rely on fast reactive control without an explicit future target state or encode anticipated motion only implicitly. World Action Models (WAMs) offer a promising alternative by coupling future visual prediction with action generation, but scene-level video objectives may underrepresent target dynamics that are critical for manipulation, while iterative video-action denoising introduces substantial latency. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model for efficient dynamic robotic manipulation. Our key insight is to explicitly ground future visual imagination in predicted target-object motion and use the resulting future representation to condition action generation, while preserving this anticipation pathway after acceleration. Given a short history of object masks, a history-conditioned motion predictor forecasts future masks encoding the target object's trajectory. A lightweight Trajectory ControlNet then steers a pretrained video model toward trajectory-consistent futures. The resulting future representation conditions an action expert to predict executable action chunks. To enable one-step inference without breaking this interface, we introduce a decoupled distillation scheme that combines distribution matching for the video backbone, Trajectory ControlNet realignment, and action rollout distillation to support accurate one-step action prediction conditioned on the compressed future representation. Comprehensive evaluations in simulation and the real world show that TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on dynamic object manipulation tasks while enabling efficient one-step video-action inference. Project page: https://kevingeng3.github.io/TrajWAM/.
bullets: Addresses the need to anticipate moving targets while replanning quickly enough to avoid stale actions.

Conditions an action expert on these representations to generate executable action chunks.
Introduces decoupled distillation for efficient one-step video-action inference, with strong simulation and real-world results reported.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing diverse dexterous manipulation policies is challenging: existing simulation-based approaches rely on human demonstrations which are difficult to scale, or use generic reward functions, which provide limited control over the hand-object interactions. We propose DexLink, which addresses these limitations by synthesizing diverse dexterous behaviors from sparse, reusable hand-object interaction templates. Given key task waypoints, DexLink retargets static interaction templates to target objects using an optimization that preserves spatial hand-object relationships. It then links the retargeted poses into an approximate reference trajectory and uses residual reinforcement learning to refine this reference into a closed-loop policy in simulation. Experiments spanning single-hand, bimanual, articulated, and dynamic tasks demonstrate that DexLink provides fine-grained control over task timing, grasp types, and high-level execution. The modular interaction templates transfer reliably across object scales, instances, and categories; without object-specific human demonstrations, the framework also matches the performance of dense reference-tracking methods. Finally, zero-shot deployment of policies trained purely in simulation shows promise for the simulation-based framework.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen {\pi}0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a {\pi}0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID {\pi}0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.

Also improves results on LIBERO-PRO and demonstrates simulated-prior guidance on a real Franka robot; scope includes scenarios where object motion and placement are constrained by obstacles or reachability.

papers.abstract: Dexterity is, at its core, finger-level control, yet existing dexterous manipulation and human-object interaction (HOI) generation methods rarely let one specify how an interaction is performed: five-fingered hands are often reduced to grippers, or finger usage is copied from individual human demonstrations. We present FineDex, a framework that makes finger-level intent both expressible and executable. FineDex learns coordinated human body, hand, and object motions that follow fine-grained instructions on hand selection, individual fingers, and contacts with articulated objects. To bridge generation and execution, FineDex leverages generated interactions as actionable priors for an agent that discovers physically feasible contact strategies through practice in a physics-based digital twin. By adapting at test time without per-instance retraining, FineDex generalizes across fine-grained instructions and object configurations. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art HOI generation quality and fine-grained controllability, substantial improvements in dexterous manipulation success, and successful deployment on a real dexterous humanoid robot.
authors: Yujia Zeng, Yuxin Chen, Yuzhen Song, Runhan Huang, Chensheng Peng, Yiyang Shao, Koushil Sreenath, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit control over hand choice, individual fingers, and contacts in existing HOI generation and manipulation methods.
Jointly generates coordinated human body, hand, and articulated-object motions conditioned on fine-grained interaction instructions.
Uses generated interactions as actionable priors for physics-based practice to discover feasible contact strategies.
Adapts at test time across instructions and object configurations without per-instance retraining.
Reports state-of-the-art HOI generation and controllability, improved manipulation success, and real humanoid-robot deployment.

papers.abstract: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.
authors: Insup Lee, Hojin Jeon, Sunguk Shin, Seoungbin Bae, Taekwan Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Dongsu Han
bullets: Targets slow VLA policies caused by the pace of human demonstrations.
Evaluates multiple speedup factors per successive motion window by comparing their retimed observation-action pairs.
Uses task instructions, visual context, and original motion with a pretrained language model to select an episode-level speed profile.
Outperforms baselines in overall task execution efficiency on LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen.
On three gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 tasks, matches or exceeds baseline success rates while completing successful trials faster.

papers.abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.
authors: Amirparsa Bahrami, Oliver Mortensen, Mohammad Sadegh Talebi
bullets: Studies finite discounted infinite-horizon MDPs under recursive entropic risk measures with parameter β ≠ 0.
Introduces the model-based ERM-VI-LCB algorithm for learning near-optimal policies from a fixed offline dataset.
Derives a PAC-type sample-complexity upper bound and a corresponding lower bound.
Shows that worst-case exponential dependence on |β|/(1−γ) is unavoidable.
Provides the first rigorous offline RL guarantees for recursive entropic risk across both risk regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Offline risk-sensitive RL with sample-complexity guarantees is transferable to safe robot policy learning from fixed datasets.
papers.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
papers.tldr: This work gives matching-style sample-complexity guarantees for offline RL with recursive entropic risk in both risk-averse and risk-seeking settings.

papers.abstract: Temporal difference (TD) learning is central to reinforcement learning. Many methods use semi-gradient TD, which may diverge, or develop algorithms with mean-squared Bellman or TD-error objectives that are difficult to analyze. Gradient TD algorithms overcome these challenges by using projection of the value function and present convergent off-policy algorithms. However, the algorithm for $\lambda$-return was limited to linear function approximation. Here, we extend the same to non-linear function approximation, which is desirable since many strong modern function approximators are complex and non-linear. Recent works have derived similar algorithms with a generalized projected Bellman error objective. Alternatively, we continue working with the projected Bellman error.
bullets: Semi-gradient TD methods can diverge, especially in off-policy settings.
Existing convergent gradient TD methods for $\lambda$-returns were limited to linear approximators.
The work develops a gradient TD($\lambda$) algorithm for non-linear function approximation.
It continues to optimize the projected Bellman error rather than adopting a generalized projected Bellman error objective.
The abstract does not report specific experiments or quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Gradient TD for nonlinear function approximation is a meaningful RL contribution transferable to robot policy learning.
papers.title: Gradient TD($\lambda$) for Non-Linear Function Approximation
papers.tldr: Extends gradient TD($\lambda$) learning from linear to non-linear function approximation while retaining a projected Bellman error objective.

papers.abstract: Collecting data from wireless sensors can be challenging when limited communication infrastructure prevents them from offloading their measurements. In such settings, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can exploit their mobility to harvest data locally, while coordinated UAV teams can provide efficient and redundant coverage of remote areas. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables such teams to learn decentralized coordination policies. However, training separate policies for different team and sensor populations is costly, and fixed-population policies may be vulnerable to agent failures. This work proposes F-MADDPG, a flexible variant of Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) that supports data harvesting with varying numbers of wireless sensors and UAVs. The framework also accommodates unexpected catastrophic failures that permanently remove agents during a mission. We compare F-MADDPG with a MADDPG baseline that uses multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and evaluate training strategies based on team-size sampling and exposure to agent terminations. The results show that F-MADDPG learns across the evaluated population sizes, completes missions faster than the baseline on average, benefits from inverse-cardinality team-size sampling compared with uniform sampling, remains effective after permanent agent losses, and gains no consistent benefit from exposure to failures during training.
authors: Thiago de Souza Lamenza, Bruno Jos\'e Olivieri de Souza, Markus Endler
bullets: Addresses the cost and fragility of training separate policies for fixed UAV and sensor populations.
Extends MADDPG to support variable numbers of UAVs and wireless sensors during missions.
Evaluates team-size sampling strategies and training with or without agent-failure exposure.
Learns across evaluated population sizes and completes missions faster on average than an MLP-based MADDPG baseline.
Inverse-cardinality sampling helps, while failure exposure provides no consistent training benefit.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.
authors: Boxuan Dong, Yupeng Qian, Ying Wu, Heshuai Li, Junhao Tan, Zhenxiong Tan, Weijia Wu, Weihao Yu
bullets: Addresses policy degradation caused by visual corruptions in jointly predictive world-action models.
Adds a training-only HOG diffusion transformer that predicts future image structure from RGB features via asymmetric attention.
Outperforms compared policies across four corruption types in RoboTwin-Plus, while maintaining comparable clean-scene performance.
Improves mixed-noise RoboTwin-Plus success from 78.86% to 82.86% and LIBERO Plus overall success from 74.49% to 75.26%.
Physical Franka-task gains are larger than simulated gains; an ablation favors combining RGB with HOG supervision rather than replacing RGB with HOG.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.
authors: Benjamin Fuhrer, Chen Tessler, Gal Dalal
bullets: Addresses locally conflicting objectives in constrained and offline RL, such as speed versus precision or imitation versus policy improvement.
Uses Gradient Boosting Trees to partition the state space and prevent contradictory updates from interfering.
Incorporates guidance from heuristics, sensor events, or rule-based systems while retaining a learned policy.
Theoretically characterizes information loss from early gradient aggregation and when its scoring isolates conflicting updates.
Across spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, meets episodic cost budgets and achieves near-expert offline performance across dataset sizes.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can act as robot-use agents that understand diverse scenes and control robots through policy code and tools. However, they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning, struggling with precise manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. Agentic robots therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA/WAM control through a policy harness. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same models. Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single design chosen from few alternatives. To guide harness design, we evaluate over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints. Seven controlled studies show effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM and VLA/WAM capabilities. Our findings specify what structure the VLM's policy code needs, where VLA manipulation needs help from tools and policy code, and when to involve the VLM at test time. The reference recipe X-Harness shows that these findings compose without weight updates, lifting base policies up to $+42.8$ points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts.
authors: Yuxiang Lai, Jike Zhong, Yu-Jhe Li, Lan Wang, Chengzhi Liu, Youbao Tang, Ming Li, Xi Xiao, Xiaofeng Yang, Liang Zhao, Zheda Mai, Ruixi Fan
bullets: VLMs provide broad perception and reasoning but struggle with precise 3D manipulation, while VLA/WAM models control trained tasks well but lack robustness and long-horizon reasoning.
Harness design can substantially change performance, making systematic evaluation important despite its high rollout and compute cost.
The study evaluates over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints.
Seven controlled studies identify how policy code, tools, and test-time VLM involvement should adapt to the capabilities of each model.
The proposed X-Harness combines these findings without weight updates and improves base policies by up to 42.8 points across memory, reasoning, and domain-shift settings.

papers.selection_reason: Large-scale study of policy harness design combining VLM reasoning with VLA/WAM control, directly relevant to vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Toward Agentic Robotics: A Large-Scale Study of Harness Design for Robot-Use Agents
papers.tldr: A large-scale study shows that carefully designed policy harnesses can effectively combine VLM reasoning with VLA/WAM control for more capable, robust robot-use agents.

papers.abstract: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.
authors: Xiang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Ya-Li Li, Tao Li, Rui Zhang, Junjie Lai, Weihua Zhang, Shengjin Wang
bullets: A multimodal LLM outputs a sparse sequence of end-effector keyposes, observes execution, and iteratively plans the next sequence.
A motion planner interpolates between keyposes, supporting both fast long-range movement and fine-grained manipulation.
The agent grounds keyposes using sparse, potentially noisy depth information and improves through execution feedback and task-specific rule distillation.
It achieves 74.5% on RoboDojo, 84.5% on RoboLab, and 88% success across 85 real-robot episodes, while costing $1.7 per episode on average.
The approach is training-free and targets lower inference cost than dense-control agent policies.

papers.selection_reason: Multimodal LLM agent for robot manipulation using sparse keyposes and execution feedback, directly fitting vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
papers.tldr: SOLVE makes LLM-based robot manipulation more efficient and versatile by planning sparse, ordered 6-DoF keyposes instead of dense step-by-step actions.

papers.abstract: Robot trajectories naturally decompose into variable-length phases with distinct semantic intents, such as reaching, grasping, and lifting. However, training policies to minimize MSE treats all actions as equal, obscuring their semantic structure. While latent action models attempt to create a structured prediction target by compressing action chunks into latent representations, existing approaches rely on two-stage training and context-blind decoders. Consequently, their representations are context-agnostic motion codes (e.g., "move down") which fail to capture behavioural intent (e.g., "pick up the block"). To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce the Emergent Latent-action MOdel (ELMO), an end-to-end framework that encodes robot trajectories as grounded semantic codes -- representations that ground task-level behavioural intent in the current environment. ELMO jointly trains a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder over dynamically chunked trajectories, learning a semantically grounded action space without separate pretraining. Across standard benchmarks, ELMO outperforms comparable prior methods by 9.6 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and by 0.75 in average task length on CALVIN. Furthermore, on Blocks -- our shortcut-free simulation and real-world generalization benchmark -- ELMO reaches a 38.6% success rate while all baselines remain below 5%, demonstrating its ability to capture the semantic structure of demonstrations. Website: https://uoft-isl.github.io/elmo.github.io/
authors: Jasper Gerigk, Yang Xu, Nicholas Rhinehart, Igor Gilitschenski

papers.abstract: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robotic palpation offers repeatable, quantitative estimates of tissue properties for stiff inclusion localization. However, existing methods often rely on prior mesh models or planar surface assumptions that do not generalize to complex human anatomy. We propose an ergodic palpation framework that operates directly on curved soft surfaces using point cloud data. Central to our approach is the Laplace--Beltrami operator, which grounds both online estimation and exploration in the surface intrinsic geometry. We estimate local viscoelastic parameters using an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) and fuse them into a surface-aware Gaussian Process (GP). This probabilistic model drives a diffusion-based ergodic motion planner, generating a continuous exploration trajectory that feeds the new informative samples back to the GP in a closed loop. Throughout this process, a hybrid force-impedance controller regulates interaction forces to maintain contact. We evaluate the approach against existing methods in simulation and validate it in physical experiments on tissue-mimicking silicone phantoms with varying geometries and viscoelastic properties, demonstrating geometry-consistent mapping and stiff inclusion localization under contact-rich conditions.
authors: Luca Beber, Cem Bilaloglu, Edoardo Lamon, Matteo Saveriano, Daniele Fontanelli, Luigi Palopoli, Sylvain Calinon

figures.caption: Figure 2. Detailed architecture of the proposed framework. During online operation, a tactile ergodic control policy generates desired end-effector trajectories and interaction forces based on the current ergodic information density (EID). A Cartesian force-impedance controller ensures stable and compliant physical interaction with the environment, while an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) estimates local viscoelastic parameters from measured end-effector states and contact forces. The GP model and the EID are continuously updated, closing the perception-action loop and enabling adaptive, information-driven exploration.

papers.abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.

Figure 2: Model diagram and objective. Our model comprises an encoder (CNN+GRU) that maps history (o≤t, a<t) to a stochastic latent s̃t; a dynamics model that predicts s̃t+1 from (s̃t, at); a reward model p(rt | s̃t, at); and an adversary network that predicts s̃t+1 from the history and current action, (o≤t, a≤t). Our objective has two parts: a reward sufficiency term, maximized when the latent state contains all information needed to predict the current reward, and a dynamics sufficiency term, maximized when the latent state is as informative as the full history for predicting the next latent state.

Figure 1: Side-by-side comparison of graphical model assumptions. Actions may be either fixed exogenously or depend on observations through a policy. Left (Dreamer): the observation at time t is conditionally independent of prior observations and actions given the current latent state, i.e., ot ⊥⊥ o<t, a<t | s̃t. Right (Ours): we allow ot to depend on the full history of observations (and, in general, on the history of states/actions). Under Dreamer’s assumption, any information in o<t needed to predict ot must be encoded into st; in our formulation this pressure is removed from st because past observations can inform ot directly.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots on deformable elastic terrains face a surface whose position and motion are coupled in space and time: deflection and rebound persist between contacts, and load at one foothold alters the support at others, so training must capture how each contact changes the support that follows. We present RIPPLE (Robust Interaction via Proprioceptive Policies on Large-deformation Elastic terrain), a simulation-to-real learning framework for humanoid control on such terrains. RIPPLE integrates ElasticMembrane, a pretensioned mass-spring mesh that models spatially coupled deflection, energy storage, and rebound, together with deformable contact into MJLab for GPU-parallel policy learning. Staged training then transfers rigid-ground skills to balance and jumping on these terrains using only proprioception, without vision or force sensing. Deployed zero-shot, the policies enable a MagicBot Z1 humanoid to balance, jump consecutively, and enter a trampoline from a rigid platform. In simulation, ElasticMembrane training holds standing success of at least 98.7% (mean over three seeds) on ElasticMembrane, IndependentSprings, and BouncyPlate under 0.3 m/s perturbations, whereas rigid-ground or contact-compliance training transfers poorly to the first two. A fixed policy tolerates stiffness from 0.35 to 2.8 times the training value, beds up to 7 m wide, and seven further simulated support scenarios, so transfer needs no calibration to the trampoline's stiffness. We plan to release the code soon. The interactive browser demo, videos, and scene configurations are available on the project page: https://fly-pigTH.github.io/wave_rider/

papers.abstract: Effective robotic manipulation calls for multimodal memory and rapid adaptation to shifts in contact dynamics. However, many existing policies, which retain either visual or wrench history, may miss key cues from the other modality. Moreover, even with wrench memory, fixed policies can struggle when contact conditions shift at deployment. To this end, we introduce M$^{2}$AdaptVLA, a vision-language-action model that integrates visual and wrench memories with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, the model uses test-time training (TTT) to encode observation history in fast weights. Each entry in the bounded TTT bank combines the corresponding frame's features with a readout from these weights, preserving cues that predate the oldest retained frame. For wrench memory, a context gate controls how much the action expert draws on wrench history as it jointly denoises future actions and wrenches. For predictive test-time adaptation, the auxiliary wrench prediction loss also provides online self-supervision. Using measured wrenches as targets, we update low-rank policy adapters by backpropagating only through the final denoising step. Real-world experiments show that the TTT bank outperforms visual memory baselines on progress tracking, scene recall, and demonstration following. On contact-sensitive tasks, the context gate yields higher success rates than direct injection or gated cross-attention. Predictive test-time adaptation improves robustness to shifts in contact dynamics. On eight tasks requiring visual and wrench memory, M$^{2}$AdaptVLA achieves a mean success rate of 82.71%, a 31.46% absolute gain over the strongest baseline. The project page is available at https://tlf-tlf.github.io/M2AdaptVLAPage/.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform well on fixed-instruction robotic manipulation benchmarks, but their ability to adapt to instruction changes during execution remains understudied. We introduce the Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench), evaluating 40 task revisions across seven update types and three execution stages using LIBERO, a simulated robotic manipulation benchmark. We compare performance when a new instruction is given before execution starts versus during execution, and examine whether the new task instructions are followed. Across 13 representative VLA configurations, average task success is 95.8% on the original object-manipulation tasks, compared with only 1.6% when the instruction changes which object to manipulate during execution. Controlled diagnostics show that policies often complete the original task before the updated one, and that their responses depend on the robot's physical state. We further test whether a simple scripted controller that releases the grasped object and moves the arm back helps robots respond to instruction changes. This improves success from 2% to 38% for {\pi}0.5 and from 8% to 48% for DM0.5, but can cause unwanted object motion. These findings reveal limitations that fixed-instruction benchmarks and task-success metrics alone can overlook in evaluating robotic manipulation. Project page: https://dtu-bench.github.io/

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model's own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM's success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.
authors: Syed Nazmus Sakib, Abdul Monaf Chowdhury, Peizhen Li, Nafiul Haque, Chandak Chakma, Md Mehedi Hasan, Zehong Cao, Shifat E. Arman

papers.abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.

papers.abstract: We present HoloBrain-0.5, a family of vision-language-action (VLA) models for manipulation across robot embodiments. The policies plan in a shared action space using robot state, kinematic structure, and calibrated camera observations. We standardize joint axes, coordinate frames, and tool-center points in robot descriptions (URDFs) and encode their kinematic graphs in a shared 3D representation. HoloBrain-0.5-Continuous generates action chunks by diffusion, while HoloBrain-0.5-Discrete uses residual finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and delayed autoregression. We pretrain both policies on over 10,000 hours of real-robot, simulation, and human-manipulation data spanning 15 embodiment categories. Across six closed-loop simulation settings, the discrete policy converges faster and reaches a higher mean success rate than the continuous policy (56.77% vs. 49.71%). On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves a mean progress score of 87.76% without task-specific post-training. After post-training, the continuous policy outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ on the seven-task benchmark (94.52% vs. 86.25%) and an 11-task dual-arm benchmark (79.07% vs. 69.41%). The discrete-initialized continuous policy transfers five tasks zero-shot from Piper to Piper-X, scoring 63.28% on average. With target-robot demonstrations, the continuous policy scores 89.2% on Franka Panda and 92.94% on a mobile dual-arm platform. Although pretraining includes no Unitree G1 data, post-training with limited G1 demonstrations yields a mean progress score of 70.24% across three humanoid tasks, compared with 11.00% for $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Xuewu Lin, Jiahao Wang, Jiawei Li, Mengdi Li, Zhengmao Sun, Yiwei Jin, Hongyu Xie, Zhengyang Feng, Kun Wu, Zihao Chen, Lianzhou Zhang, Lichao Huang, Zhizhong Su
bullets: Supports manipulation across 15 robot embodiment categories using standardized joint axes, coordinate frames, tool-center points, and shared 3D kinematic graphs.
Provides continuous diffusion-based action chunks and discrete residual-FSQ actions with delayed autoregression.
Pretrains on over 10,000 hours of real-robot, simulation, and human-manipulation data.

The discrete policy performs better in six closed-loop simulations, while the continuous policy achieves strong results after post-training across seven-task, dual-arm, cross-robot, and humanoid benchmarks.
Transfers to new robots with target-robot demonstrations and limited post-training, including zero-shot transfer from Piper to Piper-X.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.
authors: Qishuai Wen, Rui Chen, Haiwen Li, Zhiyuan Huang, Qiwen Gu, Bingjie Gao, Geng Li, Jing Tang, Xiangxiang Chu, Chun-Guang Li
bullets: Addresses the high rollout costs and sparse rewards of agentic reinforcement learning at test time.
Creates a closed loop where a supervisor provides natural-language feedback and a hypernetwork converts it into parameter updates.
Combines dense verbal supervision with in-parameter adaptation rather than relying only on in-context learning.
On ALFWorld and WebShop, Qwen3-4B vSFT achieves higher success rates than GRPO and Reflexion.
The approach is evaluated for self-improving agents, with scope limited to the reported benchmark tasks and comparisons.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of our proposed vSFT. Given a task, the hypernetwork first internalizes the system prompt and few-shot examples into an initial LoRA adapter, and then progressively incorporates the supervisor’s feedback through subsequent trial-and-error iterations, thereby adapting the agent over time.

This design trains the hypernetwork to convert verbal feedback into LoRA adapters that effectively steer the agent’s behavior (left panel).

The textual content to be internalized is first processed by the base model in a single forward pass to collect its key-value states in attention layers. The hypernetwork then uses these states to generate LoRA adapters, which are applied to the down-projection weight matrices of the FFN layers.

papers.abstract: Robots executing tasks in partially observed environments must resolve uncertainty while operating with incomplete skills. Inspired by human curiosity, we investigate how robots can formulate task-relevant hypotheses, seek evidence, and acquire missing skills during task execution. We propose CHASE, a Curiosity-guided Harness for Acquiring Skills from Evidence, which operationalizes curiosity as selecting investigations that resolve task uncertainty and expand executable capabilities. Four modules connect dynamic scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, on-demand skill acquisition, and verified execution. The planner balances information value, skill reuse, and acquisition/execution cost. Missing skills trigger bounded exploration, learning from verified segments, and held-out admission during acquisition; separate checks verify physical effects and acquired evidence. Newly admitted skills expand the executable investigation set, closing the loop between resolving uncertainty and acquiring capabilities. Simulation and real-robot experiments evaluate investigation, skill acquisition, and task execution. CHASE achieves 50-80% task success under combined information and capability gaps, with 70-90% evidence resolution.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Wei Zhang, Chenlei Zhu, Naiyu Chen, Xihua Wang, Jie Chen
bullets: Targets task execution when robots face both incomplete information and missing capabilities.
Combines scene understanding, hypothesis-driven planning, skill acquisition, and verified execution.
Selects investigations by balancing information value, skill reuse, and acquisition or execution cost.
Uses bounded exploration, verified learning segments, and checks for physical effects and evidence validity.
Simulation and real-robot experiments report 50–80% task success and 70–90% evidence resolution under combined gaps.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Retrieval instantiation of the CHASE pipeline. Acquisition enables learning; held-out reuse freezes the registry.

Figure 1. A retrieval example of task-directed curiosity. A visibility-only robot acts on current observations. A curious robot proposes locations, seeks evidence, identifies missing capabilities, and acquires validated skills to enable retrieval. The right branch illustrates acquisition mode.

Real: lift an occluding board, reveal and grasp a marker, and place it in a bin; wrist insets show the same video frame. Module bars indicate functional roles: planning (2) and composition/execution (4); other modules are muted.

papers.title: CHASE: Curiosity-Guided Skill Acquisition for Embodied Task Execution
papers.tldr: CHASE enables robots to resolve uncertainty and acquire missing skills on demand while executing tasks in partially observed environments.

papers.abstract: Robotic tasks combine object relations, logical dependencies, and temporal requirements, which robot planning and industrial control commonly specify in temporal logic (TL). We introduce TL-VLA, a vision--language--action framework that replaces natural-language task instructions with temporal logic, making this spatiotemporal structure explicit. A typed graph encoder and visual--logical fusion condition continuous actions on the task specification and the current observations. To prepare a general vision--language backbone for this interface, we develop TL-aware robot pretraining with separate semantic and structural readouts: a frozen language teacher aligns task semantics, the structural readout encodes TL syntax to support complex, long-horizon tasks, and autoregressive action prediction connects the graph representation to robot behavior. Downstream policies inherit the pretrained backbone and TL encoder and learn new fusion and action modules. On CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D, our TL-aware initializer reaches \textbf{3.800} average chain length and \textbf{62.3\%} five-task success, compared with 3.578 and 54.5\% for a FAST initializer pretrained on the same data and 3.485 average chain length for a Qwen+NL baseline. On LIBERO-10, TL-aware initialization improves success from \textbf{91.2\% to 95.8\%}. On LIBERO-Mem, our policy reaches \textbf{65.0\%} success without observation history, compared with 45.0\% for a Qwen+NL reference. On held-out Panda planning specifications, it reaches \textbf{59.6\%} at Success@256 over three generation seeds, versus 48.4\% for Qwen+TL and 37.0\% for Qwen+NL. These results support explicit logical task conditioning and transferable TL-aware representations for robot action learning.
authors: Zezhi Liu, Jingwen Sun, Hongjin Chen, Shaojie Ren, Peiyan Tu, Xin Jin, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Targets robotic tasks involving object relations, logical dependencies, and temporal requirements.
Encodes temporal-logic specifications with a typed graph encoder and fuses them with visual observations to condition continuous actions.
Pretrains a vision-language backbone with separate semantic and structural readouts, using a language teacher for task meaning and autoregressive action prediction for behavior.
Reports improvements across CALVIN, LIBERO-10, LIBERO-Mem, and held-out Panda planning specifications, including 95.8% success on LIBERO-10 and 65.0% on LIBERO-Mem without observation history.
The abstract supports the approach’s scope on the reported benchmarks and planning specifications; broader generalization is not established.

papers.selection_reason: Temporal logic as task language for VLA models with visual-logical fusion.
papers.title: Beyond Natural-Language Instructions: Temporal Logic as a Task Language for VLA Models with Visual-Logical Fusion
papers.tldr: TL-VLA uses temporal logic instead of natural-language instructions to give vision-language-action robots explicit spatiotemporal task structure, improving long-horizon and memory-dependent performance.

papers.abstract: Human videos are abundant and cheap to obtain, whereas robot trajectories remain scarce and costly, making zero-shot skill transfer from a single human demonstration an appealing route to scalable robot learning. Existing methods, however, either retarget human-specific geometry or match only static visual goals, and thus stumble over the cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch and the ungrounded action execution. We present the Co-World Model (CoWM), a predictive framework jointly optimized from paired yet unsynchronized human and robot streams. To bridge the cross-embodiment dynamics gap, CoWM disentangles each observation into a shared object-relation state and embodiment-specific context. It aligns latent actions across embodiments using effect-swap and action-sensitivity objectives,such that actions are matched by their predicted effects on the manipulated objects rather than by embodimentdependent kinematics. For grounded execution, a phase-aware receding-horizon controller estimates demonstration progress, projects the inferred human action prior onto the robot action-support density, and translates the resulting latent dynamics into executable robot commands. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CoWM, its cross-platform generalizability, and the contribution of each component. See the demo video in the supporting information for details.
authors: Xuetao Li, Xuan Jiang, Chen Liu, Zhongrui Rao, Yu Ling, Hui Wang, Sheng Liu, Miao Li
bullets: Addresses scarce robot data and cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch in human-video-to-robot transfer.
Jointly learns from paired but unsynchronized human and robot streams.
Disentangles shared object-relation states from embodiment-specific context.
Aligns actions by their predicted effects on manipulated objects, rather than kinematic similarity.
Experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms show effectiveness, cross-platform generalizability, and contributions from its components.
