papers.selection_reason: Addresses learning-based driving planners via critical-scenario generation, directly relevant to embodied navigation and robot learning.
papers.title: CriticalScenes: Scalable Photorealistic Critical-Scenario Generation for Closed-Loop Driving Adaptation
papers.tldr: CriticalScenes converts ordinary driving recordings into photorealistic hazardous interactions, improving critical-scenario planning and reducing collisions for some planners in closed-loop evaluation.

papers.abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.
authors: Burcu Kilic, David Drexel, Emre Ugur, Justus Piater
bullets: Existing clustering and reconstruction objectives may produce skills unrelated to current-state affordances or goal requirements.
The method quantizes action chunks by predicting their next-state effects conditioned on the current state and action.
Learned skills represent diverse outcomes reachable from a given state and can replace continuous actor outputs in offline RL.
A low-level controller converts selected discrete skills back into continuous actions for execution.
Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks show substantial, consistent improvements over continuous-actor and reconstruction-based baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Effect-driven skill abstractions for offline goal-conditioned RL, evaluated on robot navigation and manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: A state-effect-driven action quantization method learns discrete skills that better support long-horizon, goal-conditioned offline RL.

papers.abstract: Composing frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) skills under an agentic planner promises scalable long-horizon manipulation without long-horizon demonstrations, yet strong atomic skills routinely fail at seams even under a correct plan. Standard remedies reset the robot's pose or draft entry conditions in language, missing the physical cause we uncover via causal interventions: even after re-homing, a frozen VLA rigidly retraces its habitual trajectory and collides with displaced scene residue, whether or not it can see it. We propose the Skill Envelope, a policy-measured 3D geometric precondition capturing the volume a frozen skill sweeps during successful executions. Exploiting the insight that the rigidity making a frozen skill fragile at seams also makes its trajectory predictable in advance, we expose each envelope as two classical 3D tools (CHECK to detect blocking residue and FREE to locate safe placement regions), establishing a division of labor where VLAs execute in-distribution manipulation and code repairs out-of-distribution states. On LIBERO-Goal with frozen $π_{0.5}$, our zero-failure envelope predicts collisions at 0.946 AUROC (0.944 from one RGB-D view) and beats frontier VLMs on seam readiness (0.902 vs. 0.793); using it for skill ordering and code repair lifts success from 82.8% to 92.3% on two-step seams and from 29.7% to 93.8% on drawer-bearing 3-4 step chains, matching privileged world reset. Together, these results show that reliable VLA composition hinges on measuring a policy's physical workspace rather than guessing preconditions in language. Ongoing work closes the loop with autonomous LLM orchestration, synthesized free-object recovery, and cross-policy evaluation on cluttered benchmarks and real hardware.
bullets: Frozen VLAs can collide with residual objects because they rigidly retrace habitual trajectories, even after re-homing or when residue is not visible.
The method models each skill’s swept volume as a 3D geometric precondition and exposes it through CHECK for collision detection and FREE for safe placement.
On LIBERO-Goal with frozen π₀.₅, envelope-based collision prediction achieved 0.946 AUROC, or 0.944 from one RGB-D view.
Using envelope-guided ordering and code repair improved two-step seam success from 82.8% to 92.3% and 3–4-step drawer chains from 29.7% to 93.8%.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and remains limited by ongoing work on autonomous orchestration, cluttered benchmarks, and real hardware.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Geometric tools detect collisions from depth, outperform VLMs, and repair multi-step chains. (a) Real handoff (push the plate→ cheese in the bowl): top, CHECK flags the displaced plate (red) intersecting the next skill’s 3D envelope Ek (teal); bottom, FREE marks a safe zone outside both Ek and the following skill’s envelope Ek+1 (indigo: wine to rack) so moving the plate will not block the upcoming step (amber arrow illustrates planned free-object repair, Q2, Table II). (b) Pre-execution collision detection across 640 handoffs using only nominal-rollout overlap (no failure data): geometry detects collisions with both drawers (0.986) and free objects (0.847), and a single RGB-D camera nearly matches simulator state (0.944 vs. 0.946 AUROC). (c) Top: predicting whether the next skill will succeed on 429 handoffs, our envelope-based readiness model (0.902 AUROC) beats frontier VLMs prompted with images (Img) or BATON-style text rules (Text) by at least +0.110. Bottom: on 128 drawer-bearing 3–4 step chains, envelope-guided skill ordering and code repair (Plan+Fix) lifts full-chain success from 29.7% (Random+Home) to 93.8% (+64.1 pts), matching simulator World Reset (90.6%).

Fig. 2. Seam failures are primarily physical and policy-specific. (a) Comparing three interventions on the exact same transition and random seed of open middle drawer → push the plate (totals over 10 trials): returning the arm home (Re-homed) still collides 10 of 10 times; erasing the drawer from the policy’s camera input (View Reset, inset) leaves the physical collision unchanged (0/10 success, 10 of 10 collisions); only physically closing the drawer (World Reset) succeeds (10/10). (b) Top: on the same open drawer, push the plate’s 3D envelope intersects the drawer (red, 0/10), whereas turn on the stove sweeps clear (no overlap, 10/10). Bottom: across all nine skills that can follow open middle drawer (dashed green line: World Reset 9–10/10), our 3D overlap cleanly separates the six colliding skills (breaking five) from the three clear ones, whereas frontier VLM Qwen4-Max flags nearly every skill as blocked across 7 held-out trials per pair, even the completely unaffected turn on the stove.

papers.selection_reason: 3D geometric skill envelopes for composing frozen VLA skills in long-horizon manipulation, using policy-measured spatial preconditions and code-based repair.
papers.title: VLAs Execute, Code Recovers: 3D Skill Envelopes Bridge the Compositional Gap in Agentic Manipulation
papers.tldr: Skill Envelopes measure the 3D workspace swept by frozen VLA skills, enabling code to detect and repair physical seam failures in long-horizon manipulation.

papers.abstract: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.
bullets: A controlled study finds spatially structured semantic features improve generalization under visual perturbations and preserve recoverable motion information.
PreWAM represents future supervision through source-relative changes and resulting future states in pretrained DINO feature space.
Residual World Prediction emphasizes dynamic information while retaining future-state semantics.
Temporal-Scale Prediction models both short-term motion and longer-horizon state evolution.
Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation show strong performance and improved robustness under diverse shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PreWAM overview. A shared Qwen VLM processes current observations and language instructions to provide features for the action expert and world predictor. The predictive branch uses paired-frame features from frozen DINOv3 as visual states, learning source-to-future changes through Residual World Prediction across short, medium, and long horizons through Temporal-Scale Prediction. Joint supervision of changes and future states trains the VLM alongside action learning; deployment uses only the VLM and action expert.

papers.selection_reason: World-action model with latent future prediction (DINO-feature prediction space, residual and temporal-scale prediction) for robot manipulation policy learning.
papers.title: PreWAM: Exploring the Design of Latent Future Prediction for World-Action Modeling
papers.tldr: PreWAM improves robotic manipulation by predicting future state changes in a structured DINO-feature space, strengthening generalization and robustness to visual distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Mid-execution instruction changes expose trajectory hijacking: policies remain influenced by non-target task trajectories after a switch.
Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS) queries the same policy with interfering alternative instructions and uses target–counterfactual action differences to redirect behavior.
CAS is training-free, model-agnostic, and evaluated across five VLA/WAM policies, two benchmarks, and real-robot settings.
On CALVIN-Custom-Switch for switching times 15–21, CAS raises π₀.₅ from 5.8% to 54.6%.
CAS-guided successful rollouts provide stronger self-training supervision and improve generalization to unseen later switches.

figures.caption: Figure 5 provides an overview of our approach. CAS is a training-free, model-agnostic inferencetime method for mitigating trajectory hijacking during mid-execution instruction switching. Beyond inference, successful CAS-guided rollouts can be used for self-training, providing de-hijacking supervision and enabling iterative improvement of the underlying policy.

Figure 4: Visualization of trajectory hijacking and instruction-conditioned action contrast. Colors denote four tasks: put the wine bottle on top of the cabinet, put the bowl on top of the cabinet, put the cream cheese in the bowl, and turn on the stove. Colored curves show demonstration trajectories, and same-colored arrows show the corresponding 3D end-effector translational actions projected onto the 2D camera plane. Panels (a,b) show two forms of trajectory hijacking in bowl-tostove switching rollouts, with the first frame at ts and subsequent frames after the switch. In (a), the policy completes the non-target bowl task; in (b), it partially drifts toward the bowl trajectory. Panels (c,d) show instruction-conditioned actions predicted from the same observation under the four task instructions: they nearly overlap in (c) but remain clearly distinguishable in (d).

Figure 1: Illustration of trajectory hijacking and the intuition behind CAS. The robot is first instructed to pick up the red block and starts moving toward it. The instruction is then changed to pick up the blue block. Without CAS, the policy may fail to redirect sufficiently toward the blue block; instead, its post-switch behavior can remain drawn toward the red-block trajectory, a failure mode we refer to as trajectory hijacking. In (c), the dashed red arrow denotes the action predicted under the red-block instruction, and the dashed blue arrow denotes the action predicted under the blue-block instruction. CAS contrasts these two actions, and their difference provides a corrective direction, producing the green corrected action that steers the robot away from the interfering trajectory prior and toward the switched target.
Figure 2: Success rates of OpenVLA-OFT, π0, π0.5, Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA at different switching steps. Performance generally degrades with later switches.

Figure 6: Real-world comparison of mid-execution instruction switching. The instruction switches from picking up the red block to picking up the blue block. Without CAS, insufficient redirection leads to an empty grasp; with CAS, the robot successfully picks up the blue block.

Figure 3: Visualization of attention persistence after instruction switching. We visualize actionto-vision attention in OpenVLA-OFT at the last language-backbone layer (layer 31), averaged over attention heads and action-token positions. At an intermediate execution state, we switch only the instruction while keeping the visual observation unchanged. In both examples, attention remains concentrated on the gripper and the previous target object (red), rather than shifting toward the new target (green), suggesting that visual attention can remain biased toward previously relevant objects despite instruction changes.

Figure 5: Overview of CAS. (a) Under mid-execution instruction switching, strong visual priors can cause the policy to remain drawn toward a non-target trajectory, resulting in trajectory hijacking. (b) Inference-time CAS identifies interfering non-target tasks, uses target–counterfactual action differences to determine where to steer, and trajectory proximity to determine how much to steer. In the red-to-blue block example, the hijacking task happens to coincide with the source task, but this need not hold in general. For clarity, the arrows show a single action from the predicted action chunk. (c) Successful CAS-guided rollouts can be used for self-training (CAS-ST), and this process can be applied iteratively. The blue-boxed comparison illustrates the effect of CAS-ST: given the same observation, the policy produces more task-distinct actions after self-training.

Figure 10: Representative rollout sequences for π0.5. Under instruction intervention, the first grasp attempt is slightly misaligned, but the policy still approaches and interacts with the correct target. Under vision intervention, the policy instead exhibits erratic motion without a clear taskdirected manipulation pattern.

Figure 8: Representative rollout sequences for OpenVLA-OFT. Under instruction intervention, the policy behaves similarly to clean inference and successfully grasps the correct object, whereas under vision intervention the gripper repeatedly translates toward the right without exhibiting a recognizable manipulation behavior.

Figure 9: Representative rollout sequences for π0. Under instruction intervention, the policy still reaches and grasps the correct object, although it does not complete the lift. Under vision intervention, the gripper moves slowly toward the right with substantially reduced motion magnitude.

Figure 12: Representative rollout sequences for LingBot-VA. Under instruction intervention, the policy still executes a coherent manipulation behavior but grasps an object corresponding to a different task. Under vision intervention, the gripper instead drifts toward the right and slightly downward without exhibiting comparable task-like structure.

Figure 11: Representative rollout sequences for Fast-WAM. Under instruction intervention, the first grasp attempt is misaligned, but the policy continues to approach the correct target. Under vision intervention, the robot repeatedly moves toward the basket while rotating, substantially degrading the recognizable task-like manipulation behavior.

Figure 13: Representative mid-execution stop failure after explicit training on the “remain still” instruction. The source instruction is “put the bowl on the plate.” At the switching state, the instruction is changed to “remain still” (left). Despite the updated instruction, the robot continues to move substantially over the following 100 environment steps (right), resulting in a cumulative end-effector path length of 30.74 cm and a final displacement of 23.81 cm from the switching state.

Figure 21: Successful rollouts for a switch from put the bowl on the stove to push the plate to the front of the stove. Both rollouts ultimately complete the target task. Without CAS, the policy remains more affected by the source-task trajectory prior and approaches the plate from a less suitable interaction position. As a result, one side of the plate lifts during the push, making the manipulation less smooth. With CAS, the gripper redirects toward a more suitable position for interacting with the plate and pushes it more smoothly toward the target location. Thus, although both rollouts succeed, CAS yields a cleaner post-switch manipulation trajectory.

Figure 22: Successful rollouts for a switch from push the plate to the front of the stove to put the cream cheese in the bowl. Both rollouts eventually complete the target task. Without CAS, the initial post-switch redirection toward the cream cheese is insufficient, causing the first grasp attempt to miss. The policy must then re-approach the object and perform additional corrective motions before succeeding. With CAS, the gripper redirects more effectively toward the cream cheese and succeeds on the first grasp attempt, yielding a cleaner trajectory with fewer unnecessary intermediate actions.

Figure 23: Successful rollouts for a switch from push the plate to the front of the stove to put the bowl on the stove. Both rollouts ultimately succeed. Without CAS, the policy does not redirect sufficiently toward a favorable grasp configuration and awkwardly catches the front edge of the bowl before lifting it. With CAS, the gripper is redirected toward a more suitable grasp pose and stably grasps the side of the bowl, resulting in more direct progress toward the updated task. Despite identical binary success outcomes, the two rollouts therefore exhibit clearly different post-switch manipulation quality.

papers.abstract: A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.
bullets: Reconstructed the Robotic World Model (RWM) and its uncertainty variant, evaluating many trained, compressed, and alternative-architecture simulators.
Training on the simulator’s own rollouts outperformed one-step training over long horizons, despite worse one-step accuracy.
Pruning preserved much more short-horizon than 2-second performance, showing that one-step evaluations can misjudge design choices.
Ensemble disagreement correlated with rollout error but was severely miscalibrated, covering far fewer outcomes than expected.
Simulator accuracy did not reliably predict policy success: most fine-tuned models produced failing walking policies, though a secondary policy-in-simulator test ranked models well.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies inherit the operator's pace, and re-timing the demonstrations to run faster works only until success collapses at two to three times demonstration speed. Recent methods attribute that collapse to distribution shift and answer it with finer rules for which segments may be sped up; we show it has a mechanical cause that segment selection cannot address. A low-level controller realises only a bounded displacement per control period, so merging consecutive commands produces sums outside that bound: training pairs that promise a transition the plant cannot deliver. The share of such pairs in the re-timed data, which we call the exceed share, tracks where the retrained policy collapses. The rule that follows has a single parameter: merge greedily while the sum stays realisable. Every command is then realisable by construction, the demonstrated geometry is preserved, and the speed-up lands only where the demonstrator left slack. On four simulated robomimic tasks, 200 held-out seeds per cell, a merge cap of two is at or above the frozen policy's success on all four, by 14 points on Square, and shortens the successful episodes. At matched tempo, uniform re-timing loses 9 and 16 points on Can and ToolHang, is within noise on the other two, and reaches zero on the hardest at 2x. Placement also matters: no shuffled, entropy-guided or speed-conditioned alternative beats the rule on three of the four tasks, by margins the exceed share alone does not explain; on the fourth, at a tempo the task absorbs, every placement lands in the same band. The same principle carries to a simulated humanoid whole-body tracker: re-timing 429 reference motions within its velocity envelope succeeds on 71% of clips at 2.3x, against 51% for uniform time scaling at 2x.
bullets: The study identifies a mechanical failure mode: merging commands can exceed the low-level controller’s per-period displacement bound.
It introduces exceed share, the fraction of unrealizable re-timed training pairs, which tracks where policy success collapses.
A one-parameter greedy rule merges commands only while their summed displacement remains realizable, preserving demonstration geometry and using available slack.
Across four simulated robomimic tasks, a merge cap of two matches or exceeds frozen-policy success, improves Square by 14 points, and shortens successful episodes.
The approach also transfers to simulated humanoid tracking, achieving 71% clip success at 2.3× speed versus 51% for uniform scaling at 2×.

papers.abstract: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.
bullets: Naively adapting diffusion guidance to flow matching can break the coupling distribution used during training, weakening control and causing instability.
The proposed method derives guidance geometrically from flow matching’s inherent coupling structure.
It is evaluated on robotic collision avoidance, dexterous manipulation, inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring tasks.
Experiments across robotics and image generation show improved sample quality and guidance stability without additional overhead.

papers.abstract: We investigate how humanoid robots can learn a series of motor skills defined by human infant motor development scales, and we evaluate which scales are comprehensive enough to serve as self-contained guides for developing gross motor skills up to standing and walking. We represent each motor development scale as a developmental graph that guides the training of a humanoid robot. We then apply this graph within a reinforcement learning framework so that the robot learns skills following the natural phases of human motor development described by the scale. Our work demonstrates that graphs derived from three out of four popular pediatric motor scales can successfully guide humanoid robots to develop these skills. The fourth scale misses some intermediate milestones that the other scales have, which causes some failures. After adding a missing milestone in its graph, it also enables the robot to develop those skills successfully.
bullets: Evaluates whether pediatric motor-development scales can serve as complete guides for robot learning through standing and walking.
Converts each scale into a developmental graph and integrates it with reinforcement learning.
Three of four evaluated scales successfully guide skill development.
The fourth scale fails because it omits intermediate milestones; adding one enables successful learning.
Scope is limited to gross motor development up to standing and walking.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-scene interaction requires coordinated spatial reasoning, physical feasibility, and the ability to recover from compounding execution errors. Text-driven motion models are largely scene-agnostic and lack closed-loop correction, while geometry-conditioned approaches depend on paired scene-motion training or explicit 3D preprocessing that limits generalization to novel layouts and open-vocabulary goals. We present InteractAgent, an agentic multimodal LLM system for long-horizon human-scene interaction that plans, executes, observes, and reflects in a closed loop, using a single MLLM as both planner and evaluator and a frozen MotionLLM as the executor. InteractAgent integrates Online Observation for step-wise recovery decisions (continue/redo/replan) and Memory-Augmented Reflection for multi-round plan refinement with adaptive stopping. On UniHSI, InteractAgent improves task success and reduces penetration compared with training-free baselines. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/InteractAgent.
bullets: Addresses scene-agnostic text-driven motion generation and error accumulation in long-horizon interactions.
Uses one multimodal LLM as planner and evaluator, with a frozen MotionLLM executing motions.
Performs step-wise recovery via continue, redo, or replan decisions.
Refines plans across multiple rounds with memory-augmented reflection and adaptive stopping.
On UniHSI, improves task success and reduces penetration versus training-free baselines.

Together, these mechanisms form a dual-layer reflective loop that progressively improves motion quality and scene consistency.

papers.abstract: This work demonstrates the use of a fast simulation-based training framework to learn control policies using reinforcement learning. The hardware requirements are minimal and the simulation-learned policies transfer reliably to the real world. With this setup, we show that a quadruped robot can learn to traverse diverse real-world terrains reliably---including in a lunar-analog facility---after less than 20 minutes of training on a single consumer-grade GPU. These results provide a glimpse of a future where reinforcement learning is a crucial tool in developing more capable and robust space robotic systems. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/vUFJiZdJaQ0.
bullets: Motivation: make reinforcement learning practical for capable, robust space robotics.
Method: train control policies in fast simulation with minimal hardware requirements, then deploy them on a real quadruped.
Result: the robot traverses diverse real-world terrains reliably, including a lunar-analog facility.
Training uses less than 20 minutes on a single consumer-grade GPU.
Scope: demonstrates promising real-world transfer for quadruped locomotion in space-robotics-relevant environments.

papers.abstract: Real-world egocentric videos capture multi-step household procedures, but their recorded trajectories leave alternative actions and recovery from the learner's own mistakes largely unexplored. We introduce EgoVine, a post-training framework that turns a fixed demonstration set into interactive experience for long-horizon planning. EgoVine operates in executable symbolic environments compiled from real-world video annotations, where an agent must coordinate object manipulations under partial observation and account for delayed consequences. Restoring a decision state allows the learner to explore alternative actions and compare their eventual outcomes. Union jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction in one model, using the same executions to supervise candidate comparison and recovery. Verified repairs add recovery targets from failed attempts, while comparisons among sampled continuations guide policy updates. The updated planner then returns to the environments, with its own decisions and mistakes shaping the next round of experience. On a shared benchmark, EgoVine-1.5B achieves 81.8% success on Main planning tasks and 66.7% on longer task compositions, outperforming all evaluated Flash LLM baselines on both. EgoVine connects real demonstrations to an iterative learning process that trains compact planners on choices and futures beyond the recorded trajectories.
bullets: Converts annotated egocentric videos into executable symbolic environments with partial observation and delayed consequences.
Restores decision states to compare alternative actions and their eventual outcomes beyond recorded trajectories.
Jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction, while verified repairs provide recovery targets from failures.
Iteratively feeds the planner’s own decisions and mistakes back into subsequent experience.
EgoVine-1.5B reaches 81.8% success on main tasks and 66.7% on longer compositions, outperforming evaluated Flash LLM baselines.

papers.abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. authors: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang, Wisdom Oluchi Ikezogwo, Ainaz Eftekhar, Max Argus, Jason Ren, Jiafei Duan, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting one manipulation policy to robots with different morphologies and capabilities.
Conditions on a scene-linked kinematic graph encoding joint positions, motion axes, connectivity, and visual context.
Uses flow matching to predict relative joint motions across varying degrees of freedom and configurations.
Trained with procedurally generated, physically feasible embodiments and simulated trajectories across diverse tasks.
Achieves 63.0% success on held-out simulated evaluations and nearly twice the success of the next-best method on an unseen real-world robot.

papers.abstract: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.
authors: Feixiang Ruan, Guodong Lv, Kewei Zhang, Wenbo Huang, Yintianrun Zhang, Qiang Wang, Ruiyang Si, Shunyu Yang, Shulong Jiang, Weicheng Duan, Rui Ni, Jianxin Bi, Lekai Wang, Yuze Fan, Haobo Li, Zeliang Fu, Jiankun Zhang, Duomin Wang, Enze Xie, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and limited scalability of high-quality dexterous-manipulation demonstrations.

Refines programs across randomized layouts to improve robustness and execution efficiency.
Reports leading simulated benchmark performance, including a 72.9 Bench2Dex score and 81.0% DexJoCo success under full randomization.
Demonstrates real-world learning on a bimanual 22-DoF-hand platform, including piano playing and calligraphy; new sheet-music pieces can be learned in as little as 30 minutes.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of PyRUA-Dex. All learning takes place in simulation. Stage 2 (refinement): one agent finds the program’s bottleneck stage by a stage-wise failure analysis, refines it on randomized layouts and selects the version with the best held-out record. The resulting program runs frozen, without a language model. For the real world, the simulation is built from the real scene (real-to-sim), the frozen program is transferred (sim-to-real), and real-world feedback updates the simulation for the next round of refinement.

papers.abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.

Introduces a mobile manipulation benchmark for vision-language-action models, scoring both pick-and-place success and grasp location.
The dataset is intended for public release to support research in visual and embodied AI.

papers.abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $\beta$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.
authors: Kshitiz, Zheyuan Hu, Robyn Wu, Yizhou Li, Yunchu Zhang, Vattanary Tevy, Kavya Tayal, Shawn Yin, Aykut Onol, Kushal Arora, Dhruv Shah, Abhishek Gupta, Zackory Erickson, Aviral Kumar

The authors define “connected behavioral coverage” as behaviors linking challenging robot-environment states to states that enable further progress.
They introduce β-Data, collected through adversarial teleoperation with reversible perturbations and no resets, then relabel trajectory segments with local natural-language outcomes.
A pretrained policy is finetuned on these trajectories while conditioning on recent action history.

In simulation and across three real-robot platforms, the approach shows better zero-shot generalization, more favorable data scaling, and more effective online finetuning than standard demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Scaling embodied simulation requires diverse objects with executable physical representations. We present RFW-W, a physical asset universe connecting rigid, articulated, and deformable asset sources to task-conditioned scene composition. Its reported inventories comprise 1,010,386 asset records: 524,611 rigid assets in 1,212 categories (RFW-R), 402,410 articulated assets in 531 categories (RFW-A), and 83,365 jointly verified deformables in 485 categories (RFW-S). These taxonomies contribute 2,228 dataset--category entries. RFW-R couples category-guided generation with collision geometry, composed physical properties, and interaction annotations; RFW-A uses reusable agent-authored procedural generators with explicit part and joint structure; RFW-S uses structure-aware simulation representations, calibration, and independent testing. A common interface preserves physical requirements specific to each asset type for retrieval and scene assembly. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that RFW-R provides broader asset coverage and stronger scene-fulfillment capabilities than existing datasets. Across five RoboTwin tasks, using 100 demonstrations per task for each asset source, policies trained on RFW-R achieve macro success rates of 71.2% in clean settings and 41.8% under randomization, exceeding the strongest baseline by 15.8 and 10.6 percentage points, respectively. RFW-W provides a scalable and unified asset foundation for generating physically grounded, task-conditioned embodied worlds.

On five RoboTwin tasks, RFW-R policies achieved 71.2% clean and 41.8% randomized macro success, outperforming the strongest baseline by 15.8 and 10.6 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Physics-based soccer characters must perform diverse motor skills and transition smoothly between them, such as dribbling into a shot. However, skills that perform well in isolation may fail when executed sequentially, as preceding behaviors can leave the character and ball in unfamiliar states. We present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework that enables multiple soccer skill transitions through shared adaptation while preserving the original skill policy outside transitions. MESSI first trains eight task-competent experts using motion priors and task rewards, then distills them into a unified, skill-conditioned Transformer. Rather than retraining individual experts for different transitions, we train a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student through online reinforcement learning. Activated upon skill switching, the adapter helps the target skill handle unfamiliar entry states, while a learned exit mechanism determines when to return control to the original student. By disabling the adapter during native skill execution, MESSI preserves the original student policy by construction. Experiments across individual skills, skill transitions, and continuous skill chains demonstrate substantial improvements over direct switching, including an increase in dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8%.
authors: Xiaogang Peng, Jiaqi Zou, Lei Zhong, Sirui Xu, Huaizu Jiang
bullets: Trains eight task-specific experts, then distills them into a skill-conditioned Transformer.
Uses a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter trained with online reinforcement learning to handle unfamiliar transition states.
A learned exit mechanism returns control to the original policy after the transition.
Preserves native skill behavior by disabling the adapter outside transitions.
Improves dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8% and benefits broader skill chains.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Overview of MESSI. (i) Skill-specific expert learning: each of the eight skills is trained with a motion prior and its own task reward. (ii) Multi-skill distillation: the experts are distilled into one skill-conditioned student over a unified observation space, by behavior cloning followed by DAgger. (iii) Unified transition adaptation: a shared conditional LoRA adapter on the frozen student acts only after a skill switch and is trained online on predecessor-generated states.

papers.abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $\pi_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.
authors: Xuanchen Liu, Hejun Zhang, Boxuan Dong, Ying Wu, Heshuai Li, Wen Gao, Yonghong Tian, Weihao Yu
bullets: Introduces RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark comparing mirror-free tasks with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions.
Across five policy types, all mirror settings reduce success; average drops range from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points, reaching 62.5 points on mirrored tabletops.
Matched non-reflective panels show that collisions alone do not explain failures: 50–88% of mirror-specific failures involve no recorded robot–panel contact.
Analyses indicate phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real objects, with additional diagnostics for grasping, pushing, and occlusion.
Real-robot tests with π₀.₅ and FastWAM also show reduced success, motivating reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) used in robot task planning to derive assembly procedures from existing manuals may correctly interpret individual assembly actions yet confuse exact part identities, predict unsupported Part IDs, or produce inconsistent parts across assembly steps. Thus, we propose CAPER (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement), a manual-guided robotic assembly framework that enables VLMs to generate assembly procedures with two modules--PartGround and PlanRefine. PartGround aligns step-level manual evidence with product-specific inventory and part-reference information to identify exact Part IDs and quantities, transforming free-form hardware prediction into evidence-guided assignments represented in a shared Assembly Intermediate Representation (Assembly IR). PlanRefine audits PartGround assignments against finite inventory by removing the lowest-confidence assignments. Uncertain identity cases remain marked for review in the Assembly IR. We evaluate CAPER on the IKEA Assembly in the Wild (IAW) dataset. Experiment results show that CAPER reaches a Finite-inventory Consistency Rate of 83.33% and produces zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences. At the plan level, PlanRefine removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 -> 0) and excess units (51 -> 0). Overall, the results indicate that PartGround and PlanRefine improve part reliability, while also enhancing finite-inventory consistency and local prediction accuracy. Project page and video: https://xhzzzz123.github.io/CAPER/
authors: Hanzhao Xi, Zhonghao Li, Suxuan Liu, Shanghan Zhou, Zesheng Chen, Qiufeng Wang, Yaran Chen

On the IAW dataset, CAPER achieved 83.33% finite-inventory consistency with zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences.
It reduced inventory-overuse pairs from 9 to 0 and excess units from 51 to 0.

papers.abstract: People can anticipate how an object moves and the effort an interaction may require by watching others. How can embodied agents acquire this understanding from video? Force measurements provide direct sensory supervision, but require specialized equipment and remain limited in quantity. We introduce VidForce, which estimates an interaction trajectory together with a force profile from a third-person RGB video; 2D contact clicks and textual object-action prompts are optional. Our approach makes limited instrumented measurements useful for interpreting human interactions through learned physical prototypes as a prior. The prototypes share learned force levels and temporal profiles across interactions of comparable effort, with visual and semantic cues determining their contribution to each observation. Geometric and vision-language features adapt this prior to the observed interaction, while a joint conditional flow refines an initial tracked trajectory together with the force profile. Paired human and instrumented-gripper recordings provide measured force references for supervising human video, and a separately trained torque model demonstrates that the formulation extends to other sensory quantities. We evaluate trajectory recovery and force estimation through baseline comparisons and controlled ablations on held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset. On this evaluation subset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE and RMSE of 4.81 N and 5.92 N, respectively, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N. On real-world videos, VidForce infers motion and force reliably and consistently despite the variability in human execution. We further deploy VidForce on a Spot robot, where trajectories and force profiles estimated from human demonstrations drive real-world articulated-object manipulation, and report success rates across repeated trials. Project page: https://rafaymhddn.github.io/vidforce
authors: Rafay Mohiuddin, Jiaqi Chen, Marc Pollefeys, Hermann Blum
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of force-measured interaction data for learning physical understanding from video.
Uses learned physical prototypes capturing shared force levels and temporal profiles across similarly effortful interactions.
Combines visual, semantic, geometric, and optional 2D contact cues, then jointly refines trajectories and force profiles with a conditional flow model.
Evaluated on held-out Hoi! interactions, achieving 6.6 cm trajectory ATE and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N, with peak-force MAE/RMSE of 4.81/5.92 N.
Demonstrates transfer to torque prediction and deploys video-derived trajectories and forces for Spot robot manipulation; performance is evaluated across repeated trials.

papers.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking enables humanoid robots to reproduce diverse skills from human demonstrations. Existing model-free reinforcement learning methods either distill motion specialists into a single policy at the cost of performance or train a generalist policy directly using cluster-scale computation. SuperMimic reduces this computational cost through a differentiable world model that implicitly learns the physics shared across motions by predicting the next state from the current state and action. However, this implicit formulation may not fully capture the underlying physical processes. Errors around changes of support can accumulate over imagined rollouts used to train the tracking policy. To address this challenge, we introduce DynaMimic, a differentiable world model that explicitly incorporates shared physics into state prediction. Specifically, its network predicts a contact wrench at each candidate support link and a residual generalized force. DynaMimic then uses these predictions to compute the next state through closed-form Lagrangian forward dynamics. Across 60 full LAFAN1 motions, DynaMimic reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 18.6% relative to SuperMimic. For terrain tracking, we give both methods the same local height maps. Relative to terrain-conditioned SuperMimic, DynaMimic reduces MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour (66.15 to 56.28~mm) and by 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips (141.88 to 126.57~mm). On a real A3 humanoid, the learned policies can perform diverse skills, such as floor recovery, cartwheel and a box vault.
authors: Chaoyue Xing, Linyi Huang, Yiting He, Yixuan Yin, Siqi Hou, Yi Zhang, Liyuan Pan, Miaomiao Liu, Daqi Liu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation near support transitions in imagined rollouts for whole-body motion tracking.
Predicts contact wrenches and residual generalized forces, then computes state updates using closed-form Lagrangian dynamics.
Reduces MPJPE by 18.6% across 60 LAFAN1 motions compared with SuperMimic.
With terrain conditioning, lowers MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour and 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips.

At each substep, the integrator maps each link’s mean wrench λ̄ (i) b,t to generalized forces, adds the residual, actuator, and passive forces, and advances the state. papers.abstract: World models support embodied decision-making by predicting future environment states. In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes jointly affect visual observations, making future-state prediction challenging. We propose Motion-Conditioned World Modeling, which incorporates predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions. A Geometry--Progress module jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances through shared motion modes and path-conditioned progress distributions. This formulation captures uncertainty in route selection and motion progress while preserving their dependence. Action-induced coordinate transformations express predicted paths in the next robot frame, providing geometrically grounded conditions for future visual-state prediction. Future visual feature reconstruction supervises the motion predictor through the conditioned transition branch, linking explicit motion representations to subsequent observations. The model is jointly optimized with motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision, enabling the tracking policy to combine visual context with predictive motion cues.Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks demonstrate improved tracking performance and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight $0.5$B backbone.
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Xuan Yao, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses uncertainty from target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes in embodied visual tracking.
Uses predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion in latent state transitions.
Geometry–Progress jointly models geometric paths and travel distance while preserving their dependence.

Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks show improved tracking and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight 0.5B backbone.

papers.abstract: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.
authors: Maximilian Xiling Li, Nils Blank, Paul Mattes, Pankhuri Vanjani, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Discrete skill policies can fail because of their vocabulary, selector, or execution, but joint training makes these causes hard to separate.
MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with a nearest demonstrated motion, then boundedly corrects it toward the prediction without training new parameters.
Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped reference policy is statistically equivalent to the original.
On LIBERO-90, quantization has no measurable cost and skill choice costs at most 2 points; selector placement and correction explain nearly all remaining gaps, up to 12 points.
Offline reconstruction fails to predict these effects or reliably assess library size, design, and transfer across benchmark suites.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to translate task intent into physical interactions as the scene changes. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. A common phase-level interface supports specialized policies and generalist action models. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show how Atomic Policy improves task following and supports recovery in complex, long-horizon manipulation. Project page: https://aaronzkd.github.io/atomic-policy/
authors: Kaidi Zhang, Pengyuan Guo, Zhengtong Xu, Caiyi Zhang, Huayi Gou, Guanlin Huang, Aaron Lim, Anas Rafei, Yu She
bullets: Targets the challenge of translating ambiguous task goals into changing physical interactions.
Uses a VLM for symbolic state and goal estimation, followed by PDDL-based skill planning.
Steers atomic manipulation skills with language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies outcomes for replanning.
Provides a common phase-level interface for specialized policies and generalist action models.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show improved task following and recovery in complex long-horizon tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Atomic Policy architecture, shown with point-steered skills for Tabletop Manipulation. The planner combines VLM state and goal estimation with PDDL planning. For the active pick blue cube phase, the grounder (MolmoPoint) supplies a 2D image point pk. The selected skill generates an action chunk At using a diffusion U-Net conditioned on images, proprioception qt, and pk. The VLM checker evaluates the outcome against a phase-specific checklist: done advances the plan, not_done continues the phase, and replan requests a new plan. Blue arrows indicate execution and phase transitions; the red arrow indicates replanning.

Figure 5. Real-robot trial outcomes. Top: in-distribution (ID); bottom: out-of-distribution (OOD). Boxes show the interquartile range (IQR), dark lines mark medians, and whiskers extend to the outermost observations within 1.5 IQR of the box edges. White diamonds mark means, and dots show individual trials (n = 10 per method, task, and condition). Tasks are arranged by increasing language-grounding and compositional demands, from Multi-drawer to Stacking to Crossword. The language-only end-to-end baselines show wide trial-to-trial variation on Stacking and poor performance on Crossword, suggesting limited steerability as language-conditioning demands increase. Atomic + MolmoBot improves over fine-tuned MolmoBot on OOD Stacking and Crossword, supporting the combined benefit of point guidance and atomic-phase execution. Atomic + π0.5 also improves on these tasks without point inputs, showing that high-level planning and checker-controlled execution can improve OOD performance through language-based phase guidance alone.

Figure 6. Completion time of successful real-robot trials. Top: ID; bottom: OOD. Only trials with a task score of 1 are included. Large dots show the mean completion time, vertical lines show ± one sample standard deviation, and faint dots show individual trials; n is the number of successful trials for each method. Fine-tuned MolmoBot completes no Crossword trial, and fine-tuned π0.5 completes a single ID Crossword trial. Completion time for Atomic Policy includes planning, verification, and replanning by the VLM, so successful Atomic Policy trials take longer than successful end-to-end trials; for example, Atomic + π0.5 averages 128.6 s on ID Stacking versus 61.6 s for fine-tuned π0.5. Means based on few successes, such as n ≤ 2, should be interpreted with caution.

Figure 3. Task instructions and phase execution. Each row pairs an instruction with selected observations from execution. Bold labels name atomic phases, and the text after each colon identifies the point target; n/a denotes a phase without point conditioning. Blue boxes mark replanning after a detected failure or uncertain task state, such as a fallen cube in Stacking. The checker uses phase-specific completion criteria to continue execution, advance the phase, or request a new plan. Ellipses omit repeated or previously illustrated phases.

Figure 7. Failure modes on Multi-drawer. Each panel traces the 20 trials of one method (10 ID and 10 OOD) from execution to outcome. Trials either proceed without a recorded failure or encounter an error that is recovered through replanning or remains unresolved. Outcomes are SUCCESS (task score 1), PARTIAL (0 < task score < 1), and FAIL (task score 0). Failure types are wrong object or order (incorrect object, sequence, word, target recognition, or plan), reach or stuck (target or receptacle not reached, drawer not opened, or robot motion stalls), grasp, and place. Recovery is counted only when explicitly recorded in the evaluation notes. No method produces a zero-score trial on Multi-drawer. The Atomic Policy variants fail mainly through grasp and place errors, with one planning error for Atomic + MolmoBot. For fine-tuned MolmoBot, 7 of its 11 unsuccessful trials involve failure to reach the OOD receptacle during placement: the policy fails to guide the grasped object to the white bowl, suggesting difficulty grounding the unfamiliar receptacle’s location.

Figure 4. Learning curves on MolmoSpaces PnP Next-To. MolmoBot and π0.5 are evaluated during task-specific fine-tuning. Solid curves show success averaged over the ten most recent checkpoint evaluations. For the first nine checkpoints, the average uses all checkpoints evaluated so far. Dashed horizontal lines indicate each model’s zero-shot success rate.

Figure 8. Failure modes on Stacking. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. All 17 unrecovered failures of Atomic + DP and 9 of 10 of Atomic + MolmoBot are grasp or place errors, while Atomic + π0.5 fails in only 3 of 20 trials. Atomic + DP struggles with the fine-grained alignment required for stacking, suggesting that its low-level visuomotor policy has not learned sufficient placement precision from the available demonstrations. High-level replanning can retry these actions but cannot ensure accurate execution. In contrast, wrong object or order accounts for 8 of 11 failed trials of fine-tuned MolmoBot and 3 of 4 of fine-tuned π0.5, which together produce 11 zero-score trials.

Figure 9. Failure modes on Crossword. Panels and failure types follow Fig. 7. Wrong object, order, or place accounts for 36 of 39 unsuccessful trials of the fine-tuned baselines, whose rollouts often follow the training word or misorder letters. In contrast, 25 of 31 unrecovered failures across the Atomic Policy variants are grasp or place errors, and four trials succeed after recovery. Together with Tab. 4, these results support the benefit of explicit guidance and closed-loop planning for both ID execution and OOD generalization: Atomic + MolmoBot raises task score from 30.0 to 82.5 on ID trials and from 0.0 to 72.5 on OOD trials. papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. However, successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. The same task may require different teams as robot capabilities change, resources become unavailable, or objects replace robotic support. We argue that reliable multi-robot manipulation requires physical necessity reasoning: understanding what a task demands, which resources can fulfill those demands, and which are truly necessary. We introduce MRBench, a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. It comprises eight tasks with distinct concurrency and reach constraints, each evaluated under five configurations that change the required resources while preserving the task goal. Our evaluation reveals that existing coordination agents perform well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support. To address this gap, we propose MRScissors, which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and identifies minimal feasible teams through constrained search. Across two model backbones, MRScissors achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points, respectively. Together, these findings expose a critical gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity.
authors: Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Ruihe An, Chang Gong, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Existing coordination success with a reference team does not ensure agents understand which robots are necessary.
MRBench covers eight tasks with varying concurrency and reach constraints across five resource configurations.
Agents struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support.
MRScissors separates task requirements from measured capabilities and searches for minimal feasible teams.
It achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy across two backbones, outperforming baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MRBench and MRScissors for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation, addressing a critical gap in understanding robot team requirements.
papers.title: MRBench: Benchmarking Physical Necessity Reasoning in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Manipulation

papers.abstract: We present the Screw Attention Policy, a geometry-centric manipulation framework that supplies task geometry explicitly and learns only execution. The policy operates on object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes provided by perception and robot models. The policy requires only 30K learned parameters. Trained entirely in simulation on a single robot arm, the policy generalises to new scene layouts, transfers zero-shot across robot embodiments, and deploys directly on a real robot, without adaptation or fine-tuning. It achieves 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen robot arms, and 21 of 24 trials on a real robot. These results suggest that much of what manipulation policies learn at scale is geometric structure that can instead be supplied.
bullets: Uses object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes as explicit geometric inputs.
Learns execution rather than reconstructing task geometry from data.
Trained on a single simulated robot arm with no adaptation or fine-tuning for transfer.
Reports 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen arms, and 21/24 real-robot trials.
Scope: performance depends on accurate perception and robot-model geometry supplied to the policy.

papers.abstract: Most imitation policies that predict chunks of future actions use the dense action representation, in which the chunk holds one control target per step. In stage-structured manipulation, where a task can be divided into stages with definable endpoints, the keypose action representation instead sets each step of the chunk to the endpoint of the stage that step belongs to, and a speed-capped servo supplies the motion. We compare the two in several simulated manipulation tasks and on a real robot, with the same chunk length and matched demonstrations, observations, policy architectures and update budgets; in simulation, each one's execution rule is selected on tuning scenes. When the simulated demonstrations are slowed, paused and rerouted, dense success falls sharply while keypose stays roughly level, across three policy architectures and with endpoints extracted from the recorded demonstrations; keypose also leads under object-size and position shift. With clean demonstrations, keypose leads only when they are scarce and is otherwise close to or behind dense across the simulated tasks, provided that the demonstrations and execution rule suit its executor; when they do not, it falls far below dense. The same dependence on the executor appeared on a real robot learning to open a drawer from human demonstrations: dense succeeded more often, and keypose improved substantially only after its executor's rotation and forward speed were adjusted to the demonstrations. These results suggest that keypose trades sensitivity to such variation in the demonstrations for sensitivity to execution that departs from them.
authors: Haizhou Ge, Mengshuo Wang, Zhixing Chen, Lei Han, Chen Wang, Lu Shi, Guyue Zhou, Ruqi Huang
bullets: The study compares dense action chunks with stage-endpoint-based keypose chunks for stage-structured manipulation.
Experiments use matched policies, demonstrations, observations, chunk lengths, and update budgets in simulation and on a real robot.
With slowed, paused, or rerouted demonstrations, dense performance drops sharply while keypose remains roughly stable; keypose also handles object and position shifts better.
With clean demonstrations, keypose helps mainly when demonstrations are scarce and can perform much worse when its executor is mismatched.
In a real drawer-opening task, dense succeeds more often, while tuning keypose's executor substantially improves it.
