papers.abstract: Recent studies of embodied agents based on frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) develop harness engineering around the MLLM, such as harnesses with post-trained policies and recursive self-improvement loops. Yet whether these additions exceed the native capability of the MLLM remains unexplored. We introduce SimplEvo to explore how far an MLLM can improve under direct control when it retains its execution experience in self-written text memories. It requires no weight updates, post-trained policies, or privileged information. The MLLM writes a coordinate-free task memory once from a single demonstration. Under a strict train-test protocol, it then creates a bounded working memory on training episodes only and refines it after each episode with lessons on procedure, completion, and recovery. Both memories stay fixed at test time. On EBench, SimplEvo lifts the success rate (SR) of GPT-6-Astra under direct control from 46.7% to 81.7%, and tops the RoboDojo leaderboard with 69.63% SR and a score of 75.32. Compared with memories that also store past visual frames, SimplEvo reaches a similar SR with text memory alone while using fewer tokens. With its memories fixed, SimplEvo also generalizes to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations. Moreover, the working memory transfers across models: written by GPT-6-Astra, it can be reused as is by weaker MLLMs and improve their performance without any adaptation of their own.
bullets: Addresses whether harness engineering can surpass an MLLM’s native capability through direct, experience-based memory evolution.
Creates a coordinate-free task memory from one demonstration and refines bounded working memory after training episodes with procedural, completion, and recovery lessons.
Keeps both memories fixed at test time, while generalizing to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations.
Raises GPT-6-Astra’s EBench success rate from 46.7% to 81.7% and achieves 69.63% success on RoboDojo.
Text-only memory matches visual-frame memory success with fewer tokens and can transfer across models without adaptation.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies can handle many robot manipulation tasks, but understanding their failures remains difficult. Unfamiliar conditions and small action errors can lead to failure, yet watching the robot alone tells us little about what went wrong inside the policy. We introduce MIND (Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Diagnosis), a method that looks inside a trained policy to detect failures during execution and identify the internal concepts involved. MIND uses a sparse autoencoder to break down the policy's internal activations into features that can be studied individually. We give meaning to these features by linking their activity to the robot's position, movement, and surroundings, and by steering their activations to examine how they affect the robot's actions. From successful and failed executions, we learn how the features behave on the way to a failure. During execution, MIND flags deviations from these patterns and uses the meaningful features contributing most to the change to describe the problem. Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot show that changes in these internal features help detect and explain failures. By using the same features for detection and diagnosis, MIND connects failure signals to understandable changes inside the policy.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of diagnosing failures caused by unfamiliar conditions or small action errors from robot behavior alone.
Uses a sparse autoencoder to decompose policy activations into individually analyzable features.
Links feature activity to the robot’s position, motion, and surroundings, and probes their effects by steering activations.
Learns feature patterns from successful and failed executions, then flags deviations and identifies features driving the change.
Simulation and physical-robot experiments show that internal-feature changes can support both failure detection and explanation.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.
authors: Zexin He, Rui Li, Yushi Lan, Chengkai Jin, Zhi Hou, Xingang Pan
bullets: Organizes one robot as persistent agents, each controlling a configurable group such as an arm, gripper, torso, or chassis.
A hyper-agent assigns tasks, coordinates physical dependencies, and dynamically reallocates control between lead and member agents.
Supports concurrent execution for independent subtasks and coordination for tightly coupled manipulation.
Across 72 real-world rollouts in 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduced task-balanced time cost by 28.2% versus a single-agent Direct Policy.
Provides a 90-rollout evaluation and a real-world dataset of observations, programs, actions, and feedback; it also demonstrates mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.
authors: Xiao-Ming Wu, Kang Liao, Yuexiao Ma, Taolin Zhang, Mingqian Zhou, Nuo Chen, Ziming Li, Yihang Luo, Rui Li, Zhonghua Wu, Tianyu Xie, Xiawu Zheng, Zhongang Cai, Zhi Hou, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Analyzes prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use in frontier-model robotic harnesses.
Finds that interfaces leveraging native visual reasoning and tool use outperform reliance on handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors.
Provides guidance on action representation and chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement.
Achieves 83.3% success on RoboLab-120 and succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot real-world manipulation trials.
Interventions suggest performance depends more on accurate spatial target estimation than explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the Robotic Agentic Loop. A robotic harness consists of four key dimensions: 1) Prompting, including task instructions and visual observations; 2) Planning, including context management, planning strategies, and model and reasoning effort selection; 3) Tool Use, including acting tools and policy models; and 4) Action Execution, including action formats, action chunking, and asynchronous execution. These dimensions operate within a closed-loop framework and form the design space systematically explored in Embo-Harness.

Figure 4. Overview of Embo-Harness. Embo-Harness is designed to leverage the model’s native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, failure-derived skills, or action priors. The harness takes task instructions and high-resolution visual observations as inputs to GPT-6-Astra with xhigh reasoning effort. The frontier model produces short, fixed-length chunks of absolute end-effector (EEF) actions. Short multi-action sequences and VLA refinement are further integrated as tools to enhance manipulation performance. Zoom in for best view of the demos.

Figure 2. Typical Robotic Harness Paradigms. (1) Tool/code-aspolicy harnesses leverage frontier models for high-level planning while relying on predefined tools or generated code for action execution. (2) Model-as-policy harnesses delegate action generation to specialized policy models. (3) Frontier-model-as-policy harnesses directly generate robot actions using frontier models. All three paradigms operate within a closed-loop framework, differing primarily in how robot actions are generated.

papers.abstract: World action model (WAM) is a promising paradigm for visuomotor control by jointly modeling world dynamics and actions. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large generative models and iterative sampling which incur substantial latency for action generation, limiting real-time deployment. In particular, there are two root causes of inefficiency in conventional flow matching or diffusion based action models in WAMs: 1) transporting uninformative Gaussian noise into precise actions necessitating multiple ODE steps, and 2) repeatedly injecting task context through expensive cross-attention modules. Our key insight is that jointly learning and aligning the source and action manifolds streamlines the transport between them, substantially accelerating action generation. Building on this insight, we introduce VITA-WAM, a WAM architecture with manifold-aligned flow-matching (VITA flow matching) that directly transports latent observation representations containing visual, language, and proprioceptive information into latent actions. More specifically, a flow latent alignment (FLA) mechanism is employed to facilitate manifold alignment between latent observation and action representations, enabling accurate generation with few ODE steps. The resulting architecture also eliminates costly attention for observation conditioning during repeated denoising steps. Notably, with a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and by 1.65 pp on LIBERO, achieving these gains through the FLA objective without distillation, while inferring at 55.67~ms latency, a $2.10\times$ speedup compared to FastWAM.
authors: Boqi Zhao, Dechen Gao, Hanchu Zhou, Hang Wang, Junshan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency of conventional diffusion- or flow-matching-based world-action models caused by noise-to-action transport and repeated cross-attention.
Directly transports latent visual, language, and proprioceptive observation representations into latent actions.
Uses flow latent alignment (FLA) to align observation and action manifolds and support accurate generation with few ODE steps.
With one ODE step, it outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and 1.65 points on LIBERO.
Achieves 55.67 ms inference latency, a 2.10× speedup over FastWAM, without distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustration of VITA-WAM architecture. 1) During training (top), a Q-Former fuses visual, language and proprioception into a latent source z0, where the visual signal is the output of the video DiT supervised by video flow matching. The action encoder maps the action chunk into a target latent z1. The source and target representations are jointly learned with VITA flow matching through FM, AE and FLA objectives, with FLA supervising the action chunk decoded from the ODE-generated latent. 2) During inference (bottom), a single video DiT forward pass extracts current-observation features, which are fused with language and proprioception by the Q-Former to construct the source latent z0. The action DiT then performs conditioningfree ODE integration starting from z0 to generate the action latent ẑ1, which is decoded into an action chunk.

Figure 6: Training and inference architecture of VITA-WAM (visual conditioning). The Q-Former constructs the source latent from visual observations, language, and proprioception. During ODE integration, the action DiT additionally uses mixed video–action attention with cached video K/V. The action decoder converts the generated latent into an action chunk.

Figure 1: Comparing conventional flow matching (left) vs. VITA flow matching (right). Conventional flow matching learns to transport Gaussian noise to the target manifold, necessitating multiple ODE steps. VITA flow matching (right) jointly learns and aligns the source and target representation manifolds with the Flow Latent Alignment (FLA) mechanism, thus enabling generation with simplified transport paths and fewer ODE steps. VITA-WAM employs VITA flow matching, significantly improving the efficiency of WAM action generation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3\% and 90.6\% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2\% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3\% vs. 93.7\% success).

Achieves 91.3% and 90.6% average success on RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, while reducing VLM calls by 74.2% versus chunkwise monitoring.

papers.abstract: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.
authors: Nicolas Bolouri, Gaya Mehenni, Daniel Toyama
bullets: Maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every reward via a cross-fitness matrix.
A Planner selects parent rewards and generates targeted mutation directives; a separate Mutator converts them into validated executable reward programs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Habitats evolutionary lifecycle. At generation t, the population Pt contains executable reward–policy pairs. (1) Policies for newly synthesized rewards are trained from scratch, while inherited survivor policies remain fixed. (2) Every policy is evaluated under every population reward to construct the cross-fitness matrix Ft. (3) Normalized cross-fitness profiles are used to compute Specialist Quality (SQ), Behavioral Diversity (BD), and Grounded Behavioral Profile Coverage (GC). (4) Individuals whose policies dominate their own reward niches and outperform the random-policy baseline form the survivor set Vt. (5) The Planner determines the offspring count, selects parents, and proposes mutation directives, while the Mutator generates and validates executable reward programs. Valid offspring join the survivors to form Pt+1 = Vt ∪ Ot; invalid candidates receive up to three replacement attempts before their offspring slot is discarded.

Figure 2: Population quality, diversity, grounded coverage, and downstream adaptation. (A–B) SQ and BD are equal-weight macro-averages across environments, shown as their means across generations and their values in the final population. (C) GCAUC is reported separately for each environment on a logarithmic scale. (D) Downstream adaptation is measured by paired win rate against task-specific Scratch policies trained for 20,000 episodes. Meta-policies route among sizematched, frozen libraries produced by Habitats, Direct Mutation, or Independent Generation and are trained for 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000, or 20,000 episodes; the dashed line denotes parity. Error bars in (C–D) indicate ±1 standard deviation over three seeds.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Neil He, Qinglong Zheng, Changyi Yang, Tong Wei, Andy Mao, Zetian Li, Chaoran Cheng, Hui Ren, Ruihan Guo, Xianrui Zhong, Xizheng Yu, Jingyuan Li, Xi Zhu, Kaiqu Liang, Chang Xu, Zun Qian, Zidi Xiong, Yuezhu Zhao, Xu Huang, Ge Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that fixed model weights cannot adapt lifelong without costly or temporary methods such as reflection, memory, search, or prompting.
The agent analyzes its own task records, identifies an inefficient hidden-state behavior, and rewrites a single weight tensor overnight.
It evaluates each edit against the unchanged agent on practice tasks and retains only changes that do not degrade performance.
Across thousands of held-out episodes, the retained edit improves task completion while reducing steps, wasted actions, and token use at the same per-step cost.
Improvement remains stable over multiple rounds; among four model sizes, only the 27B agent exhibits this behavior, within the described household setting.

figures.caption: Figure 6 The same night at four sizes: the 2B model cannot start, the 4B agent measures and withdraws, the 9B agent waits for a test it never asks for, and only the 27B agent measures its way to an edit that holds. Figure 1 The self-upgrading loop: the agent works by day and rewrites its own weights at night. Top: its life on the job, as a schematic. By day the agent works with the weights it has; at night it turns to itself, edits its own weights and tests the edit. An edit that holds is kept, and the next day starts from it (θ1 = θ0 ⊕∆1); an edit that fails is withdrawn, and the agent stays as it was (the middle night). How well it works climbs only when a night keeps its edit, and the loop does not end. A day is any stretch of work, a night the time between two days; nothing depends on the clock. In our experiments the 27B agent kept one edit in the four nights of Fig. 22; what that edit gave it, measured on held-out tasks, is in Fig. 2. Bottom: one night. The agent reads its own record, traces a failure to its cause inside its network, writes an edit to its weights, and examines its edited self against last night’s self on the same tasks and seeds. The edit is kept only if it holds in a confirmation on practice tasks that were reserved from it all night; otherwise it is withdrawn.

Figure 3 The night that kept its edit, step by step: the agent diagnoses its own work, rewrites one tensor, examines the edit against its unchanged self, and keeps it only if a confirmation on reserved tasks holds. Diagnose: its own sentence; 1,366 of the 4,418 steps of its 128 opening episodes end without an action. Examine: its 13 paired tests, in order: the change in the share of steps without an action, edited minus unchanged, on the same practice tasks and seeds; a bar is a test beyond two standard errors. papers.abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation learning remains challenging due to the high cost of collecting real-world interaction data. Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) offers a promising route by enabling policy learning in simulation grounded in real-world observations, yet scaling this paradigm across diverse tasks and physical interactions remains difficult. We introduce Real2Worlds2Real, a self-improving agentic framework that integrates scalable simulation-world construction with policy development. Given limited visual observations and task descriptions, its tool-orchestration harness constructs faithful digital twins and expands them into diverse, physically executable digital cousins. The agent adaptively selects tools and revisits construction decisions, using visual and execution feedback to refine geometry and physical behavior. Building on these worlds, the agent orchestrates policy development by coordinating data generation, policy learning, and refinement based on task requirements and simulation rollout feedback. Across both stages, the agent distills validated procedures into reusable skills that guide subsequent tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved world fidelity and successful real-world policy transfer, with performance gains from increasing world diversity and interaction-data volume. Skill reuse further improves world-building efficiency and long-horizon task success.

papers.abstract: A generalist manipulation policy should perform new tasks, operate in unfamiliar scenes, and transfer skills across robot embodiments. We present Wrist Video Policy (WVP), a closed-loop manipulation framework that learns how manipulation unfolds through video prediction and recovers executable motion through geometric estimation. Our key idea is to represent robot motion through wrist-camera trajectories, which determine the corresponding end-effector poses through a fixed hand-eye transformation. We pair a video generator that predicts future wrist views with a pose estimator adapted from a pretrained 3D model to recover the corresponding camera trajectories. Model stitching maps the generator's predicted latents directly into the estimator's intermediate feature space, bypassing RGB decoding. This decomposition allows task knowledge to expand through broad human and robot video data while reusing geometric motion estimation across tasks and embodiments. The resulting pose estimator transfers across Franka Panda, PiPER-X, and Galaxea R1 Pro without further fine-tuning. Across tabletop and laundry-room settings, WVP generalizes to tasks ranging from precise grasping and inserting to handling deformable objects, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluations. Our project page is at https://wrist-video-policy.github.io.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves $\pi_{0.5}$ across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.
authors: Hengzhi Jiang, Haixu Liu, Jindou Jia, Tinglan Wang, Shaobo Chen, Yiren Zhao, Ziyang Rao, Laiyuan Cui, Jiaxin Dong, Yin Ma, Hai Wei, Jiaqi Bai, Tuo An, Xinyu Zhou, Hao Ban, Hongdong Zhu, Yanqi Wang, Jiaqi Dou, Nuo Qian, Qi Liu, Bin Jin, Chang Wu, Qingfeng Li, Hui Yang, Weiyu Guo, Dicong Qiu, Qi Gao, Jianwei Niu, Kai Wen, Jianfei Yang

Uses a conditional Boltzmann machine to assign energies to binary source states, trained with an offline listwise objective based on resulting action quality.
Decodes the learned energy landscape through an Ising solver into continuous noise, followed by standard flow integration; the base VLA remains unchanged.
Improves π₀.₅ across three benchmarks, outperforming compared baselines and noise-optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, and ranking second to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus.
Also shows gains with noise-adapted fine-tuning, action-to-action warm starts, and the SmolVLA backbone.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Boltz-Flow. Right. A conditioning module replaces the Gaussian source of a frozen flow-matching policy. It maps the robot observation and instruction to a flow source, which the frozen flow heads integrate into an action chunk for the robot. Left. Inside the conditioning module, a Transformer encoder on the GPU turns the observation and instruction tokens into energy tokens, which clamp the visible layer of a conditional BM. papers.abstract: We present SurgeCount, a system for auditable robotic surgical sponge counting that composes learned skills under a written procedural protocol. Retained sponges cause preventable harm, and surgical teams count every sponge before closure to reduce that risk. The robot repeatedly isolates one deformable sponge from a tangled pile and places it in the next numbered counting-tray slot, requiring handling of occluded grasp threads while preserving step order. We train one subtask-conditioned policy on eleven short skills and learn when each skill ends. At each learned boundary, a stateful vision-language model selects the next skill from an operator-authored specification of step order, visual verification, and recovery. This creates temporal commitment to each subtask and enables failures to be recovered by recomposing existing skills rather than using a dedicated recovery policy. We evaluate five methods across 100 real-robot trials using 20 matched layouts. SurgeCount fills 47 of 60 ordered slots and completes 12 of 20 procedures, compared with 27 of 60 and 3 of 20 for the strongest of four end-to-end policies trained on the same data. Replacing the detailed protocol prompt with a minimal prompt reduces performance to 29 of 60 slots and 5 of 20 completed procedures. These results show that long-horizon performance depends not only on visuomotor capacity, but also on how learned skills are committed, verified, and composed. This tabletop proof of concept motivates further evaluation of protocol-guided robotic sponge counting in clinically representative settings.
authors: Sung Eun Kim, Xiaoman Zhang, Xucheng Wang, Pranav Rajpurkar
bullets: Targets retained-sponge risk by repeatedly isolating tangled, deformable sponges and placing them into ordered tray slots.
Uses one policy spanning 11 short skills, with learned skill boundaries and a stateful vision-language model selecting the next protocol-specified action.
Supports recovery by recomposing existing skills rather than relying on a dedicated recovery policy.
Across 100 real-robot trials, filled 47/60 slots and completed 12/20 procedures, versus 27/60 slots and 3/20 procedures for the strongest end-to-end baseline.
A minimal protocol prompt reduced performance to 29/60 slots and 5/20 completed procedures; the study is a tabletop proof of concept requiring clinical evaluation.

papers.abstract: Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, 10,807 interactive, resettable, and verifiable physics environments built from real-world videos via an automated Real2Sim and quality assurance pipeline. Each runs in an isolated, Harbor-compatible harness that hides privileged states and grading logic to mirror real-world sensing. From the same pipeline, we hold out 500 unseen tasks to establish RoboUniverse-Verified, an expert-verified zero-shot benchmark. Evaluating 11 closed- and open-source models reveals a huge gap: frontier models reach 85.8\% success, while open-source baselines lag at 2.6\% to 10.0\%, bottlenecked by low-level grasping, deformable-object manipulation, and post-contact physical control. Finally, we collect about 17K multi-turn trajectories totaling 0.79B tokens with GPT-6 Astra and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, yielding RoboUniverse-35B-A3B. Our model achieves substantial zero-shot gains on RoboUniverse-Verified, lifting the success rate from 0.8\% to 21.2\%, while achieving zero-shot task completions across LIBERO-MAX, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, and a real Franka arm. We open-source the RL-ready environments and model to lay the foundation for large-scale reinforcement learning in Agentic Robotics.

papers.abstract: Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.

papers.abstract: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce \textbf{WorldLeague}, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of \textbf{60 simulated robot tasks} by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in \textbf{WorldSeek}, rearrange objects in \textbf{WorldShape}, and adapt to changes in \textbf{WorldShift}. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's \emph{Physical Agency Profile}. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing ($\mathcal{F}^{2}$), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. papers.abstract: Personalization of powered prosthesis control to individual user needs remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, policy iteration with constraint embedded (PICE), a reinforcement learning (RL) tuning approach, has been developed and validated. This feasibility study investigated whether the developed approach can personalize a commercial powered knee prosthesis under clinically realistic conditions. To reduce the time for personalization, tuning was initialized with a policy learned offline from one non-disabled participant walking on a treadmill and was then applied to three other non-disabled participants walking with the knee through a bypass adapter on a 5-meter walkway. All participants reached the goal within 8-18 tuning steps (1.7-4.2 minutes of walking), reducing the knee-kinematic feature error by 64-90% on average. These results support the feasibility of implementing the RL-based tuning approach in clinically realistic conditions with space and equipment constraints.

papers.abstract: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.

papers.abstract: Can foundation models pretrained for generic numerical prediction serve as in-context robot learners? We investigate this question through tabular foundation models (TFMs), which are pretrained to infer input-output relationships from labeled examples in context. We introduce TabAct, which casts visual imitation as numerical prediction: frozen visual features and robot proprioception form the inputs, future action chunks form the targets, and each demonstration time step provides one labeled example that conditions a frozen TFM for closed-loop control. The predictor receives no robot-specific training or target-task fine-tuning. With one target-task demonstration available to each method, TabAct with TabICLv2 achieves the highest average success among all evaluated methods on both LIBERO and Meta-World, exceeding the strongest baseline by 20.9 and 5.8 percentage points, respectively. Additional demonstrations improve control without updating model weights: with five demonstrations, success reaches 94.2% on LIBERO-Object. These results demonstrate that generic numerical pretraining can provide an effective foundation for in-context robot learning.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.
authors: Qiwei Liang, Zhengtu Liang, Minghao Lai, Yikeng Chen, Yiming Wang, Boyang Cai, Yuetong Fang, Taowen Wang, Baiqiao Yin, Tianxing Chen, Yue Chen, Jiaming Liang, Guangyu Chen, Shaolong Zhu, Daolin Ma, Renjing Xu

An inverse-dynamics readout is among the strongest pre-policy measurements of representation quality.
Recognition, depth, correspondence, and other statistics are not sufficiently reliable to replace rollout evaluation; fine-tuning can affect metrics inconsistently.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies are often trained with static domain randomization for real-world deployment. However, real-world environments often exhibit unmodeled dynamic variations, such as payload changes or friction shifts, that lie outside the randomization distribution, leading to performance degradation upon deployment. We propose a framework that moves beyond static domain randomization by adapting a learned dynamics model to the deployed target conditions, with a concurrent teacher-student paradigm applied to both the policy and dynamics model. This framework integrates the dynamics model into an on-policy reinforcement learning pipeline, letting the performance of the policy align with the empirical target dynamics. Experimental validations on bipedal locomotion tasks demonstrate competitive adaptability under extreme physical variations, including a payload reaching 80% of self-weight and an oil-lubricated low-friction surface.
authors: Rui Dai, Shunpeng Yang, Zhen Fu, Maolin Lei, Jiaqi Song, Hua Chen, Nikos Tsagarakis
bullets: Static domain randomization can fail under unseen payload and friction changes.
The method adapts a learned dynamics model to deployed target conditions.
A concurrent teacher–student scheme updates both the policy and dynamics model.
The adapted dynamics model is integrated into on-policy reinforcement learning.
Bipedal experiments show adaptability under payloads up to 80% of self-weight and oil-lubricated low-friction surfaces.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.
authors: Paul Mattes, Ayman Abdeldayem, Denis Shcherba, Wojciech Samek, Marc Toussaint
bullets: Addresses policy degradation and changing state dimensions as object counts exceed training ranges.

Trains only the selection and warping policies with PPO, treating the pretrained skill as a black box.
Evaluated on cube arrangement with gantry and Franka Panda robots; training with at most nine cubes generalized to up to thirty on the gantry.
Compared approaches—including fine-tuning, local-view learning without warping, and an entity transformer—collapsed within their training counts under the same budget.

papers.abstract: We introduce EgoDepth-Bench, comprising 941,233 synchronized samples collected across 37 distinct physical environments. Each sample combines six calibrated RGB views with metric depth in the native fisheye view, reconstructed from five active-infrared stereo modules. A calibrated ball-bar confirms millimeter-level geometric accuracy, with a median error of 1.27 mm on a known sphere spacing. Environment-held-out splits enable evaluation of generalization to unseen environments. Across monocular, stereo, and multi-view models, the benchmark measures both depth accuracy and prediction coverage, including on hands and objects. Fine-tuning MapAnything on EgoDepth-Bench reduces metric AbsRel from 0.708 to 0.091 and scale-aligned AbsRel from 0.327 to 0.072 on unseen environments. These results demonstrate that EgoDepth-Bench provides effective supervision and enables rigorous evaluation of metric and relative depth estimation in egocentric manipulation. The project page provides the evaluation code and interactive RGB-depth sequences.

Evaluates depth on hands and objects, targeting egocentric manipulation scenarios.
Fine-tuning MapAnything substantially improves metric and scale-aligned AbsRel on unseen environments, from 0.708 to 0.091 and 0.327 to 0.072, respectively.

papers.abstract: General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub- network in a Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration.
authors: Nilay Kushawaha, Abdalla Swikir, Fares Abu-Dakka
bullets: Represents each skill as a dedicated expert in a Progressive Neural Network, preserving previously learned skills.
Uses LoRA-based lateral connections with learnable gates to selectively transfer knowledge while reducing dense-lateral parameter costs.
A frozen local LLM decomposes natural-language instructions, routes subtasks to experts, and requests new experts when needed.
Evaluated on twelve MetaWorld tasks and cross-embodiment Sawyer, Panda, and UR5e transfer, with improved success over learning from scratch under limited demonstrations.
Real-robot experiments demonstrate compositional manipulation and expert orchestration.

papers.abstract: Robust visual servoing during robotic grasping remains challenging, as approach-phase occlusion frequently disrupts closed-loop control. To address this, we present an active observation framework in which one arm of an existing dual-arm platform carries an RGB-D camera as an active observer while the other executes grasping. The observer repositions to maintain or recover a shared target-gripper view within the feasible shared-view workspace. Occlusion during the final approach is particularly acute: fixed eye-to-hand lacks an active recovery mechanism once the target is hidden, while eye-in-hand can suffer from self-occlusion and sensitivity to hand-eye calibration. The observer first uses an active two-phase viewpoint strategy to align high-precision RGB-D axes with task-relevant error components. If visibility later degrades, an occlusion-triggered exploration module pauses the worker arm and scores candidate viewpoints by observation quality to recover a shared target-gripper view. Because both objects are detected in a single RGB-D image, the resulting Relative Servo Error avoids differencing two independently transformed target and gripper estimates. We evaluate the system on a dual 6-DoF Piper platform using an open-vocabulary detector with text prompts, without task-specific fine-tuning or demonstrations. Across 50 randomized trials per object, the system achieves 94% grasp success versus 76% for a reactive viewpoint baseline and 64% for a fixed camera. On triggered severe-occlusion trials, recovery takes $1.8 \pm 0.6$ s on average.
authors: Zhilun Hu, Yuqi Cheng, Yuxiang Tan, Wenpan Li, Weiming Shen
bullets: Occlusion during final grasp approach can disrupt closed-loop control, especially for fixed or eye-in-hand cameras.
A dual-arm setup uses one arm to reposition an RGB-D camera while the other performs the grasp.
A two-phase viewpoint strategy aligns observations with task-relevant errors, while occlusion-triggered exploration searches for recovery views.
A shared RGB-D image directly estimates relative servo error, avoiding differences between independently transformed detections.
In 50 randomized trials per object, grasp success reached 94%, compared with 76% for a reactive viewpoint baseline and 64% for a fixed camera; severe-occlusion recovery averaged 1.8 ± 0.6 seconds.

papers.abstract: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench
authors: Hiroaki Honda, Koya Sakamoto, Shu Morikuni, Yusuke Iwasawa, Taiki Miyanishi
bullets: Benchmarks 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks across 16 skills and 13 speeds from 0.10–0.40 m/s, with matched static counterparts and randomized scenes.
Fine-tunes eight vision-language-action and world-action models using demonstrations covering the full speed range, comparing single-frame and three-frame observations.
Six models peak at intermediate speeds and often act for the average training speed rather than the observed belt speed.
Past frames improve success by 10–40 percentage points for three models; ground-truth or image-estimated speed improves all tested models.
Temporal context helps mainly when speed is more linearly decodable, including in models pretrained on multiple frames.

papers.title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?
papers.tldr: SWEEP-Bench reveals that embodied policies often fail to adapt actions to an object’s actual motion speed, while temporal observations or explicit speed estimates can improve performance.

papers.abstract: Behavior-cloning policies show strong ability in sequential control by generating coherent multi-step action chunks, yet their purely imitative objective limits zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks. While offline reinforcement learning offers principled policy improvement, existing methods either require task-specific reward supervision or remain tied to a specific actor during critic training or policy deployment, inflating training cost and restricting cross-policy generalization. We observe that evaluating actions under the data-collecting behavior largely preserves their relative value ordering across target policies, offering a way around actor coupling. Combining this property with reward-free successor prediction, we propose Actor-Free Behavior-Induced Representations (ABI) to learn multi-horizon action-chunk representations from unlabeled trajectories without reward supervision or actor training. At test time, pairing the frozen representation with lightweight task readouts forms a chunk critic that guides target policies without parameter updates and transfers directly across distinct unseen policies. Our analysis establishes when the value ordering is preserved across policies and when selecting among proposed chunks improves closed-loop return. Across 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, ABI's chunk critic guides weak imitation policies to match or surpass zero-shot RL baselines with high sample efficiency, outperforms existing zero-shot critics on identical proposals, and improves externally trained RL actors without retraining. From raw pixels, ABI delivers substantial guidance gains and surpasses prior zero-shot RL baselines on visual manipulation, highlighting its potential for visuomotor control.
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Jianming Ma, Xing Gao, Chunhua Shen
bullets: Addresses limited zero-shot generalization in behavior-cloning policies and actor-coupled offline RL critics.
Uses behavior-induced value ordering and reward-free successor prediction to learn multi-horizon action-chunk representations.
Combines a frozen representation with lightweight task readouts to form chunk critics that transfer across policies.
Guides target policies through action selection without policy parameter updates or task-specific reward supervision.
Across 65 locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks, improves weak imitation and externally trained RL policies, including from raw pixels for visual manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at individual robotic skills, yet integrating heterogeneous skills into a single policy remains a key challenge for general-purpose robotic control, especially in whole-body tasks with differing manipulation and locomotion requirements. Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations.
authors: Le Yang, Haoyang Lyu, Honglei Jin, Wenshuo Chen, Jiawei Liang, Wenqiang Wang, Yutao Yue, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Multi-skill integration is difficult because joint fine-tuning and parameter merging can degrade individual skills during closed-loop control.
The method analyzes task-conditioned expert updates and identifies dominant, sometimes opposing directions in a shared response subspace.
GeoMerge-OPD combines response-space regularization via G-isometry, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation from independently fine-tuned task experts.
Experiments across two VLA backbones show balanced skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, including under perturbations.
The approach is evaluated on the reported benchmarks and focuses on mitigating behavioral interference during skill integration.

papers.abstract: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.
authors: Shuxun Wang, Xiaonan Jiang, Zhaoyu Wang, Ziyuan Chu, Xihang Yue, Pengfei Liu, Haodong Zhu, Shiqi Liu, Mingzhi Zheng, Liang Su, Linchao Zhu
bullets: Addresses the cost of real-world data and limited realism in visuo-tactile simulation.

VeriIDM infers actions from verified videos using scene context, gripper details, and frame-to-frame motion.
Across five real-world tasks, synthetic data improved all four evaluated policies, with more trajectories yielding further gains.

papers.abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
authors: Jiawei Guo, Yu Huang, Dijiang Dong, Yue Liu, Peiran Ren, Wei Shen
bullets: Evaluates instruction fidelity across eight manipulation tasks with 6–12 instruction branches per task, while keeping the initial scene and robot state fixed.
Branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation details to isolate behavioral adaptation to language changes.
Task-specific checkers assess terminal outcomes and execution compliance using trajectories, contacts, and event sequences.
RoboInF-4K contains 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived motion and contact annotations.
Evaluations of four manipulation or inference-only agents reveal a gap between task success and faithful instruction execution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and preserves \textbf{\color{blue}90.4\%} of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.
authors: Yihao Shen, Yuxuan Chen, Xuantong Liu, Jun Gao, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Addresses multi-skill task failures caused by wrong target selection and lost progress tracking.

On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, success increased from 57.5% to 70.5%, preserving 90.4% of standalone successes and rescuing 37 of 85 failures.
The same fixed supervision rules improved four other frozen policies by 8–10 percentage points on a shared 50-scene subset.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | How RoboHarness-Zero divides control between a frozen VLA and a supervising VLM. Execution loop: the VLA receives the full task instruction and controls the robot by default. VLM supervisor: at each checkpoint, the VLM checks progress on the current substage. After two verified physical failures, the VLM can take over for a bounded number of steps before handing control back. papers.title: Body and Soul: Decoupling Robotic Brain and Policy with RoboHarness-Zero

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
authors: Hyeonjae Kim, Jeongsol Kim, Sunwoo Park, Chanyu Moon, Yoojin Oh, Youngjun Jun, Kyumin Choi, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Asynchronous action generation reduces latency but stale observations cause performance degradation, especially during failed policy rollouts.
DelayOPSD compares a synchronous teacher using the current observation with a delayed student using an earlier observation and in-progress actions.
The student imitates the teacher throughout the iterative denoising process, with training performed on the policy’s own delayed rollouts.
With a 10-step delay, SmolVLA success rises from 70.2% with demonstration training to 78.7% with DelayOPSD, versus 70.4% for naive asynchronous execution.
DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among compared methods across LIBERO and Kinetix and improves real-robot success from 46% to 62%, without extra deployment modules.

(b) Training. (1) Student states from delayed rollout and denoising: a step t of its own delayed rollout, and an intermediate state aτ of its own denoising at that step. (2) Distillation from the synchronous teacher at these states: the student sees ot and the committed actions pt, and the teacher, the same policy run without delay, sees ot+K . papers.abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.
authors: Tingjun Dai, Jianxiang He, Mingfei Han, Qihao Yu, Longtao Jiang, Changlin Li, Minghao Jin, Zhihui Li, Xiaojun Chang

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/
authors: Haoran Zhang, Haokai Ding, Han Zhou, Zuxing Lu, Heng Zhang, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses failures of object-only trajectory tracking, such as incorrect contacts and finger sliding.
Uses interaction rewards to preserve demonstrated hand-object configurations and contacts.
Factorizes the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies conditioned on each other’s states.
Introduces assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum for difficult manipulation phases.
Across four benchmarks, three simulators, and five robot embodiments, it improves tracking and contact preservation over baselines; contact preservation is better in 117 of 122 comparable runs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DexDuet. (a) A human demonstration provides the object trajectory, which gives the policy πθ the next object pose, and the hand motion, which is retargeted to a reference motion that the robot hands imitate. Inside πθ , two per-hand policies share one network, and each maps its own observation o and the partner observation z to an action a. (b) Two interaction rewards compare each robot hand with the human hand relative to the object. The hand graph reward compares the palm and finger directions and the fingertip gaps, and the hand-object contact reward compares the distance and the closest point of each hand region to the object. (c) A-RSI gives each segment b of the demonstration its own assistance level hb, which it lowers (green) or raises (red), never above a ceiling h̄(u) that decreases over the updates u. Episodes start from states that the policy has reached, and their start segment is drawn from p(b), which favors the segments with a high failure rate fb.
