papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.
authors: Haoxiang Zhan, Haoqin Hong, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen
bullets: Existing manipulation benchmarks only partially test time-sensitive everyday tasks.
AWAIT is a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion under explicit action windows.
Agents must identify when an intervention window opens and coordinate decisions with physical movements.
Results show difficulty detecting window onset and that repeated actions can exhaust the window, even when individual decisions are shorter than it.

papers.abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.
authors: Kevin Qiu, Zhao Yang, Marek Cygan
bullets: The study evaluates 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with PPO under Standard, Strict, and Reset-free torso-fall reset rules, using a shared evaluator.
Morphology rankings differ sharply: Strict versus Reset-free rankings correlate only 0.21, compared with about 0.89 expected from seed noise alone.
Removing fall resets hurts flat-ground-evolved bodies more (45% lower per-step reward) than variable-terrain bodies (16%).
The pattern is supported by permutation tests and also appears with SAC on a 24-body subset.
Selecting bodies by worst-case reward across protocols preserves at least 91% of each protocol’s best-body reward in-sample and over 80% across held-out seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how training protocol (reset rule) changes morphology rankings in robot co-design, directly relevant to learned robot control and co-optimization.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
authors: Rongze Tang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianjie Fang, Ziming Liu, Zhaolu Wang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen

Expands a single-agent world action model across an agent dimension using shared weights and an agent-axis curriculum.
Uses joint self-attention, hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks to coordinate agent-specific behavior.
Introduces MA-Task Harness and MA-Bench, covering seven tasks with joint success, role, and collaboration metrics.
Achieves 82.7% mean joint success on MA-Bench and real-time closed-loop collaboration on a heterogeneous robot team.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

papers.abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $\pi_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.
authors: Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen, Hexin Wang, Hanyu Zhou, Zhenglin Wan, Wangbo Zhao, Pengfei Zhou
bullets: Across 14 vision encoders and 16 manipulation tasks, off-the-shelf teachers provided little clean-task benefit and substantially reduced robustness to perturbations.
Common teacher-selection criteria such as global semantics and spatial structure did not predict VLA performance.
Behavioral Structure Metric (BSM) measures whether nearby teacher representations lead to similar expert actions and strongly correlates with perturbation success.
Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA) selects teachers with higher BSM than the student and ends alignment based on the student’s BSM.
On SmolVLA, BAVA matched continuous alignment using one-third of the alignment budget and improved average success by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
authors: Jiaxi You, Yiwei Shi, Yanlin Li, Rihui Song, Weibing Li, Kai Huang, Weiru Liu
bullets: Addresses action-semantic shifts when fixed-dimensional policy outputs change meaning across procedure phases.
Uses phase-specific proposal heads followed by deterministic filtering, state-dependent bounds, and phase-dependent task-space decoding.
Adds local repair for failures and a read-only provenance trace for command replay and rule-level auditing.
Across three held-out retinal-injection blocks, achieves 94.27±0.64% completion, 64.40±2.43% success within 35 μm, and no hard violations.
On the same frozen Correction network, contract-based decoding raises completion from 12.27% to 90.47%; all 1,996 binding interventions matched their declared effects.

papers.abstract: World models support robotic manipulation by predicting how the scene evolves under a planned action. For garments this prediction is notoriously difficult: deformations are complex, and self-occlusion leaves much of the cloth unobserved. Planned gripper trajectories provide a useful motion prior because cloth held by a gripper moves with it, while the remaining deformation must be predicted. We introduce ClothCast, a world model that applies this prior to the cloth's points and learns the residual motion. ClothCast takes one RGB-D observation, the camera pose, the robot's own model and the planned gripper trajectories, with no cloth mesh or material parameters. It lifts the observation to a layered point set that includes hypothesized occluded layers, carries the points with a blended rigid prior derived from the gripper poses, and predicts the residual motion with a video-diffusion point-flow model. Over entire 4- to 11-second episodes at 10 Hz, the moved points are rendered into depth, from which a geometry-conditioned completion model synthesizes RGB; after release, a hand-designed settling step replaces the learned motion. We further release ClothCastBench, 10,000 simulated dual-arm cloth-manipulation episodes with the ground-truth cloth mesh, including occluded layers, at every frame. On 492 held-out episodes, ClothCast achieves 2.5x lower sequence-averaged visible-surface Chamfer distance than Flex-{\pi}, the strongest baseline in geometry (14.0 mm vs. 35.6 mm), and 3.7 dB higher cloth-region PSNR than Cosmos-Predict2.5, the strongest baseline in cloth PSNR. On a 50-episode ablation subset, the rigid prior alone, applied to ClothCast's learned initial geometry with the same post-processing, already outperforms both geometry-capable baselines, and the learned residual lowers its error by about a third.
authors: Yushen Hu, Yilong Song, Zhen Zhou, Apurv Kushwaha, Harshvardhan Chandirasekar, Zhu-Tian Chen
bullets: Addresses cloth world modeling from a single RGB-D observation despite complex deformation and self-occlusion.
Uses camera pose, robot model, and planned gripper trajectories without requiring a cloth mesh or material parameters.
Lifts observations into layered point sets, applies a blended gripper-motion prior, and predicts residual motion with a video-diffusion point-flow model.
ClothCastBench provides 10,000 simulated dual-arm cloth-manipulation episodes with ground-truth meshes and occluded layers.

On 492 held-out episodes, it reports 14.0 mm visible-surface Chamfer distance and higher cloth-region PSNR than the cited baselines; a rigid prior alone already outperforms geometry-capable baselines, while residual learning further reduces error.

papers.abstract: Deep learning has shown promise for estimating human pose with multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar through walls. Building paired radar and pose datasets demands considerable time and manual effort, while large visual pose datasets provide no corresponding radar echoes. Physical simulation can supply synthetic signals, but requires expertise in scattering models and can leave a gap between simulated and real data. To address this challenge, we introduce MIMORPHEUS, a framework that generates radar echoes from 3D human poses through conditional diffusion. To prepare echo and pose representations, MIMO-VAE compresses the echoes according to their channel and fast time sample structure, while SkeleCoder learns pose features through contrastive alignment with echo features. These pose features then guide diffusion in the MIMO-VAE latent space, and the VAE decoder reconstructs echoes from the generated latents. Once trained, the generator augments radar data by producing different echoes for a recorded pose and supplies the radar modality for pose annotations in existing visual datasets. In data augmentation experiments, our method reduces MPJPE by 6.8%-11.2% across four radar pose estimators. Transfer experiments with three public pose datasets also show that visual pose annotations can supply useful radar training data. Code will be made publicly available on GitHub.
authors: Shizhao Zhang, Yanyan Zhang, Deshui Yu, Jun Pan, Guangyou Fang
bullets: Addresses the cost of collecting paired radar–pose data and the simulation-to-real gap.
Compresses radar echoes with MIMO-VAE and learns pose features via contrastive alignment in SkeleCoder.
Generates radar echoes conditioned on 3D poses through diffusion in the VAE latent space.
Augmentation reduces MPJPE by 6.8%–11.2% across four radar pose estimators.
Transfer experiments indicate that visual pose annotations can provide useful radar training data.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yushuo Hou, Anqi Zhao, Moyun Liu, Xingwei Zhao, Bo Tao, Jiawei Du, Joey Tianyi Zhou
bullets: Visual foresight is important for action prediction, but frame-aligned latents overfit to training-scene appearance.
The method separates semantic latents, which determine what and how to accomplish, from motion-oriented latents that predict future interactions.
Motion reasoning progresses from the global scene to the object–destination interaction region and then to the robot state.
Compared with LaST₀, it improves success across simulated and real dual-arm settings, including out-of-distribution environments.
The approach targets scene-change robustness; its scope is demonstrated on the reported SimplerEnv-WidowX and AgileX Piper tasks.

Each latent is conditioned on all its predecessors, and the action expert generates an action chunk conditioned on the observation, the instruction, and the latents. The inset (Motion over steps) overlays the interaction regions at t+8, t+16, and t+24 with the end-effector path: the regions contract toward the destination and trace how the robot moves rather than what the scene looks like. papers.selection_reason: Motion-oriented latent reasoning for VLA robot manipulation; directly fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning improves VLA robot manipulation by modeling how scenes evolve during an action rather than predicting isolated future-frame appearances, boosting generalization under environmental changes.

papers.abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.
authors: Meng-Hao Guo, Yi Zhang, Zhe-Han Mo, Han-Zheng Wang, Jia-Jun Wang, Xin-Sheng Chen, Jiaxi Song, Yi-Xuan Deng, Jia-Ning Li, Xuanyu Chu, Hengrui Zhang, Huan-ang Gao, Yongming Rao, Shi-Min Hu
bullets: Addresses the limited transparency of how broadly generalizable robot-control models can be trained.
Represents behavior as semantic steps built from reusable, parameterized action primitives with explicit progress descriptions.
Uses CP-SFT and a robot-specific system prompt to constrain outputs while preserving broader pretrained capabilities.
Trained with over 5,000 hours of robot data plus general VQA data; nanoAstra-9B reaches 17.8% zero-shot success on RoboTwin 2.0’s randomized benchmark.
Streaming inference overlaps computation with motion, reducing robot idle time from 35.0% to 6.9% on a single H20 GPU.

papers.title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: nanoAstra trains VLMs for generalizable robotic manipulation by combining semantic action modeling with capability-preserving fine-tuning, achieving strong zero-shot performance and efficient streaming execution.

papers.abstract: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.
authors: Kun Dai, Tianqi Wang, Haibo Lei, Chaoyang Li, Kai Zhang, Fuyuan Qiu, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li, Chuqing Cao, Tao Xie, Wenming Tan
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic visual-language features and physical force-tactile measurements.
Uses a two-stage design: semantic-physical alignment and subsequent VLA integration.
Learns hierarchical multimodal physical representations with cross-modal alignment, future wrench prediction, and action prediction.
Employs a gated cross-attention bridge to incorporate physical features into action generation.
Outperforms the PI05 baseline across three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks.

papers.tldr: A2I-VLA improves contact-rich manipulation by aligning force-tactile signals with visual-language semantics before integrating them into a VLA model, raising success from 70% to 95% in real-world tests.

papers.abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.
authors: Qiwei Wu, Xiangyu Chen, Xin Xiang, Rui Zhang, Yihang Kang, Weiran Chen, Zikang Xie, Yangfan Li, Tao Wang, Xiangzheng Wang, Tianyi Bi, Zhiyan Zhang, Xianpeng Wang, Mingqian Zhou, Yan Yu, Chuanyu Li, Wenjie Zhang, Tao Li, Weihua Zhang, Renjing Xu, Junjie Lai

A model fine-tuned only on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks.
Simulation and real-robot success rates are highly aligned across eight policy variants (Pearson r=0.998; MMRV=0.010).
Combining teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data improves randomized-task success from 20% to 60% versus teleoperation alone.

papers.title: Tacinf: A Unified Tactile Infrastructure for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: Tacinf is an open-source, low-cost infrastructure that unifies tactile data, simulation, multimodal policy learning, and sim-to-real deployment for force-aware robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to regulate the force it applies, not only where it moves. Existing force-aware policies learn this force from demonstrations and therefore reproduce the force levels they were trained on, which fails once the interaction demands more force than any demonstration. We present Force2Act, a hybrid force-position policy built on two complementary mechanisms. A global force policy plans the motion and the interaction force once per action chunk, with force represented relative to the measured interaction, so that the planned force scales with the load. Between planning steps, a reactive compliance policy, termed Mixture of Force Experts, identifies at every control step the force expert that governs the interaction and regulates the force through it, so that the contact holds when it changes within a chunk. We further introduce Force2Act-Bench, a simulation benchmark of five contact-rich tasks that gives the community a common and repeatable way to test force-aware policies and measure how well they regulate the interaction force. Force2Act achieves an overall success rate of 93.8%, compared with 77.0% for the strongest baseline, and its reactive regulation reduces the failures on block pivoting from 30 to 10 of 150 trials. On a real robot, Force2Act reaches an average success rate of 94.2% over four tasks, against at most 27.5% for the baselines.
authors: Keerthi Vasan Murugan, Fangguo Zhao, Jiafei Duan
bullets: Problem: Demonstration-trained force policies may fail when tasks require forces beyond those seen during training.
Method: A global force-position policy plans motion and load-relative force per action chunk, while Mixture of Force Experts reactively regulates contact between plans.
Contribution: Introduces Force2Act-Bench, a five-task simulation benchmark for evaluating force-aware manipulation.
Results: Achieves 93.8% overall simulation success versus 77.0% for the strongest baseline, and 94.2% average real-robot success across four tasks versus at most 27.5% for baselines.
Scope: Evaluations focus on five simulated contact-rich tasks and four real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Dexterous functional grasping is critical for robotic tool use, yet current dexterous hands exhibit substantial morphological diversity. This hardware heterogeneity makes cross-embodiment functional grasping a fundamental but largely unexplored problem. Existing functional grasping methods use retargeted hand poses as guidance, tying task representation to a specific embodiment and failing to explicitly capture object-centric functional contact intent, limiting generalization across hands. To address this, we propose FunGrasp-Zero, a reinforcement learning framework for zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping. Instead of relying on embodiment-specific joint configuration, FunGrasp-Zero captures functional intent via an object-centric, cross-embodiment-consistent contact map, adapted to heterogeneous hands through morphological mapping. We construct a hand-object potential field from mapped contact regions, yielding attractive and repulsive guidance vectors. A Field-Conditioned Graph Attention Network (FC-GAT) leverages these vectors to coordinate multi-finger motion across hands, while a potential field reward guides fingers toward target regions and penalizes non-target collisions to enforce functional alignment and stability. We further establish X-FunBench for cross-embodiment functional grasping, evaluating both physical grasp success and functional intent preservation across hands. Evaluated on X-FunBench, our unified policy, co-trained on four embodiments, achieves 86% average grasp success rate across five unseen hands on novel objects. Deployed on four unseen physical hands (Leap, Inspire, Sharpa, Wuji) for novel object grasping, the policy achieves 80% average success rate without fine-tuning. To our knowledge, FunGrasp-Zero is the first RL-based framework to achieve zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping across unseen hands in both simulation and the real world.
authors: Yanhan Lin, Yuliang Wu, Yihao Guo, Wei-Jin Huang, Jianwen Li, Jiawei Tang, Xiaolong Huang, Yuquan Wang, Ancong Wu, Wei-Shi Zheng

Introduces X-FunBench to evaluate grasp success and preservation of functional intent across embodiments.
Achieves 86% average simulated success on five unseen hands and 80% average real-world success on four unseen hands without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Many deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms store agent-environment interactions in a replay buffer and later learn by sampling transitions from it. However, this approach can be memory-inefficient and can delay learning because the agent can learn from a transition only when the buffer samples it. Additionally, most of these methods use one-step or short multi-step temporal-difference (TD) updates, which are slow at credit assignment. An alternative approach is to learn from the stream of observations as they arrive without relying on a buffer. Eligibility-trace algorithms allow these incremental updates and can also assign credit over many steps. These algorithms were common with linear function approximation but have only recently been used in deep RL. Basic questions, such as how to use vector step sizes with eligibility traces in the deep RL setting, remain open. In this work, we first show that adaptive vector step sizes must be part of the eligibility trace to keep the equivalence between the forward and backward views. We then show that the step sizes of common optimizers, such as Adam, do not have an online backward view. We introduce a new optimizer, Function-Space Distance (FSD), that maintains the forward-backward equivalence. We test four eligibility-trace algorithms covering semi-gradient and gradient TD updates, as well as value-based and actor-critic methods. We show that FSD performs better than SGD or naively applied Adam. The resulting algorithms outperform or match other streaming methods and are comparable to or better than PPO, which uses a buffer, in most environments. Code available at https://github.com/esraaelelimy/ada_traces
bullets: Replay-buffer methods delay learning and often use short-horizon TD updates, limiting fast credit assignment.
The work shows that vector-valued adaptive step sizes must be included in eligibility traces to maintain forward–backward equivalence.
Common optimizers such as Adam lack an online backward view when combined with eligibility traces.
The proposed Function-Space Distance (FSD) optimizer preserves this equivalence and is evaluated across four streaming eligibility-trace algorithms.
FSD outperforms SGD and naively applied Adam, while the resulting methods match or exceed other streaming approaches and are comparable to or better than PPO in most tested environments.

papers.abstract: Hand pose estimation aims to recover the spatial configuration of hand joints from visual observations and serves as a fundamental perception module for downstream systems that rely on complete and topologically consistent hand representations. Most existing methods are developed under the assumption of fully articulated hand structures and tend to produce unstable or implausible predictions when parts of the kinematic structure are persistently absent, resulting in degraded performance or even system failure despite available partial observations. To study this challenge, we construct IncNYU, a physiologically constrained benchmark that simulates structural incompleteness through morphological modification of complete hand models and retains reference locations for both intact and synthetically removed regions. Based on this benchmark, we propose InsHaPE, an Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation framework designed to remain robust under structural incompleteness while preserving performance on standard, fully articulated hands. Built on hierarchical kinematic modeling, InsHaPE introduces two complementary components. First, a topology-aware distillation strategy transfers joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hand representations, providing anatomically consistent initialization under missing structures. Second, a progressive kinematic reasoning module performs structured inference along the kinematic chain, enabling complete and anatomically consistent pose estimation under severe structural variations. Extensive experiments on NYU/IncNYU, together with external validation on MSRA, demonstrate that InsHaPE improves robustness under structural incompleteness while maintaining competitive performance on complete hands. System-level evaluations further show that InsHaPE improves robustness for downstream applications that require fixed-topology hand pose representations.
authors: Kanglei Zhou, Zikai Hao, Liyuan Wang, Xiaohui Liang
bullets: Introduces IncNYU, a benchmark simulating physiologically constrained structural incompleteness with reference locations for intact and removed regions.
Uses topology-aware distillation to transfer joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hands.
Applies progressive kinematic reasoning to infer complete poses along the hand’s kinematic chain.
Experiments on NYU/IncNYU and external validation on MSRA show improved robustness under structural variation and competitive results on complete hands.
System evaluations indicate benefits for downstream applications requiring fixed-topology hand representations.

papers.abstract: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/
authors: Mingxi Jia, Patton Jiyang Yin, Haojie Huang, Ivy Xiao He, Xuanru Liu, Gefei Liu, Dian Wang, Stefanie Tellex

The approach handles moderate embodiment error and generalizes beyond robot-data scene layouts.
It improves average success over the strongest baseline by 12.9 points in simulation and 51.7 points in real-world tasks, while matching robot-only training with 2.75× less collection time.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.
authors: Jingxiang Qu, Tian Xie, Youngjin Hong, Changhyun Choi, Yang Katie Zhao, Yi Liu

papers.abstract: Image policies are scalable but remain brittle to camera viewpoint changes. On LIBERO, we identify proprioception as an input shortcut: masking robot states sharply degrades several policies, while retraining from images alone recovers much of the loss. We introduce ViewPACT, an image policy trained with privileged geometric supervision. Auxiliary objectives recover end-effector and task-relevant object poses in the camera frame, while deployment requires only RGB observations. Joint geometric supervision improves mean simulation success from 37.4% to 78.4% under unseen external-camera viewpoints, with more modest gains under separately evaluated object, scene, and camera-intrinsic shifts. Across four real-robot tasks, combining simulated and real-image geometric supervision achieves 68.1% mean success, versus 3.1% for fixed-view behavior cloning and 30.6% for the strongest evaluated alternative. These results support geometric supervision for viewpoint robustness in the evaluated fixed-view demonstration setting.

papers.abstract: Min-of-K (MoK) training is widely used to train models that produce diverse outputs from random noise. For each target, it draws K outputs from the model and backpropagates only through the one closest to the target. However, MoK generally does not make the generated distribution match the data distribution. In this paper, we analyze the MoK bias across all values of K and show that tuning K shifts between failure modes, from mode dropping at small K to distribution flattening at large K. We further prove that every nontrivial loss based only on target-candidate distances fails to recover some data distribution, since these distances do not reveal how the candidates are placed relative to each other. Based on these analyses, we propose mirrored MoK (MMoK), a drop-in modification of MoK training that draws one extra sample from the model, applies the closest-candidate selection rule against it, and subtracts the resulting distance. Since this distance is measured between samples of the model, it provides additional information about how the candidates are placed relative to each other. We prove that MMoK can in principle recover data distributions that MoK cannot. We empirically validate MMoK on five scenarios, namely synthetic mixtures, pedestrian and vehicle trajectory prediction, tropical cyclone forecasting, robotic policy learning, and ambiguous medical image segmentation. The results confirm the effectiveness and generality of MMoK in both distribution learning and task performance.
authors: Jiaru Zhang, Zeyun Deng, Hyunsoo Yun, Yupeng Zhou, Bingyao Du, Juntong Peng, Zichong Yang, Can Cui, Chuheng Wei, Ruqi Zhang, Ziran Wang

Experiments across five synthetic and real-world scenarios support its effectiveness for distribution learning and task performance.

papers.abstract: Accurate material identification is important for robotic manipulation, yet vision-based methods face challenges when materials have similar appearances. Herein, we report T-Tac, a soft, thin, active thermal tactile sensor that identifies materials through their transient thermal responses. T-Tac integrates a polyimide film heater with an ionic conductive film temperature sensor, providing controlled thermal excitation and resistance-based temperature measurement in a film assembly suitable for mounting on robotic grippers. Single-sided transient plane source modeling and finite element simulations relate the thermal response to material thermal properties, while calibration and repeated measurements characterize the heating and sensing performance. Loading experiments at room and elevated temperatures further characterize the sensor response under an applied force. A hybrid classification framework concatenates extracted thermal descriptors with multiscale convolutional neural network features and uses an ExtraTrees classifier for material prediction. Experiments on 12 materials achieve a mean classification accuracy of 92.69\% using a 3 s heating pulse and a 10 s observation window. These results support T-Tac as a compact approach to integrating active thermal material sensing into robotic end effectors. This work shed a light on the new approach for robotic material identification.

papers.abstract: 3D affordance grounding aims to localize 3D regions specified by an interaction query. Existing methods predict a single affordance mask, overlooking the inherent diversity of human-object interactions. We introduce diverse 3D affordance grounding, a new task that requires predicting multiple plausible regions for a given object and affordance query. We then propose Div3DAffordNet, a transformer-based set prediction model capable of generating diverse affordance regions. To address the scarcity of diverse 3D affordance data, we develop an automated pipeline leveraging 2D generative models and 3D reconstruction techniques to synthesize 3D affordances, followed by lightweight human verification (reducing the annotation time by 72X), yielding the Div3DAfford benchmark. Extensive experiments show Div3DAffordNet effectively captures multi-mask affordance regions. Our method achieves the SOTA affordance grounding performance in the multi-mask setting, reducing GED-SIM from 0.745 to 0.492, while maintaining competitive single-mask performance on the standard benchmark of 19.0 mIoU.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of single-mask methods, which miss diverse human–object interactions.
Proposes Div3DAffordNet, a transformer-based set prediction model for generating multiple affordance regions.
Builds the Div3DAfford benchmark using 2D generative models, 3D reconstruction, and lightweight human verification.
The automated annotation pipeline reduces annotation time by 72×.
Achieves state-of-the-art multi-mask performance, reducing GED-SIM from 0.745 to 0.492, while retaining 19.0 mIoU on single-mask grounding.

papers.abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.

bullets: Trained on 49k hours spanning real robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and human motion.

Improves vision-language-action models over FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot.
Human-hand-motion-only training performs close to robot-data-trained tokenizers, suggesting robot data may not be essential.

papers.abstract: Existing surgical world models often leave implicit how instrument motion drives localized tissue responses and how interaction history informs subsequent actions. We introduce KineState-SWAM, a surgical world-action model coupling action prediction and video generation through a persistent interaction state, separating kinematically determined instrument motion from learned scene evolution. A flow-matching policy predicts joint trajectories conditioned on interaction state, robot configuration, and task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning converts these trajectories into surface-motion tokens and spatially aligned instrument renderings using calibrated URDF kinematics. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently updates the state through geometry-guided attention and motion-aligned feature transport, carrying interaction history into subsequent action predictions without intermediate video synthesis. The State-Geometry Adapter combines state-dependent spatial modulation with localized geometric residuals to guide video generation. Interaction-aware supervision emphasizes tissue responses near instrument working regions. We introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines within matched action-conditioning settings. Ablations support preserving and transporting interaction states for long-horizon prediction.
authors: Rulin Zhou, Yujie Ma, Rui Tang, Qiujie Song, Wanhao Liu, Guoheng Ma, Liangjing Shao, An Wang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the missing link between instrument motion, localized tissue response, and interaction history in surgical world models.

Maintains interaction history through recurrent geometry-guided dynamics and guides video generation with state and geometric residuals.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings.
authors: Qihang Chen, Tengjie Li, Hongwei Lu, Jason Wu, Chyna Qu, Shikui Tu, Lei Xu
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-aware perception and predictive action selection in precise manipulation.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.
authors: Chendong Xiang, Chengwen Zhang, Ruowen Zhao, Zeyuan Wang, Shuhe Huang, Rongxu Cui, Min Zhao, Fan Bao, Hengkai Tan, Jun Zhu

Achieves 83.5/100 across six unseen Astribot S1 tasks and 69.5% success on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, surpassing Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points.
Transfers context-specified behaviors to rearranged layouts and substituted tools despite training only on scene-aligned pairs.

papers.abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $\eta=1/H$ requires $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.
bullets: Studies tabular finite-horizon MDPs with known rewards, unknown horizon-dependent transitions, and access to a generative model.
Introduces sample-based NPG algorithms using backward policy updates without explicitly estimating transition probabilities.
Establishes last-iterate sample complexity of $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ under three batch-size and step-size schedules.
Proves a matching lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, even for adaptively selected queries, showing the $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable.
For known transition kernels, exact NPG with step size $1/H$ may require $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case.

For Klein et al. [2024], we compute the total number of transition queries by summing, over all updates, the number of rollouts at each update times their length. Their guarantees hold with probability at least 1−δ. Our NPG methods return a last iterate πT that is ε-optimal in expectation under the fixed initial state distribution ρ.

Table 1: Sample-complexity bounds for model-free policy optimization in γ-discounted infinitehorizon MDPs under generative access. Each rollout step counts as one transition query. The gap is the optimality gap. For guarantees with an additive approximation error, ε denotes the allowable gap above that error. A check mark indicates that the guarantee applies to the last iterate.

papers.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)
authors: Jiangtao Kong, Yuchen Wang, Yandong Luo, Rongchao Xu, Guang Wang, Yanbing Mao, Lu Gan, Tianyi Zhou, Huajie Shao
bullets: Targets the latency of iterative MPPI planning and the limitations of action-level planner imitation.
Represents complete H-step proposals using k-MPPI and a mixture of factor analyzers to model multimodality and temporal/action correlations.
Introduces Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization, which uses MPPI evaluations and advantage estimates to improve policy targets while maintaining planner alignment.
Improves control performance and sample efficiency across 31 continuous-control tasks while reducing MPPI refinement iterations by 50%.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go2 for stable, high-frequency velocity-tracking locomotion.

papers.title: Fast World Planner: Advantage-Aware Action-Chunk Policy for Online Planning

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
authors: Tamoghno Das, Keyon Jazayeri, Yerin Cho, Nazmul Takbir, Arshia Aravinthan, Nikil Dutt
bullets: Addresses reliability failures when objects move during robot execution and policy switching causes stalls or stale observations.
Uses a learned trigger to selectively escalate from a lightweight policy to a higher-compute policy based on recovery potential and intervention risk.
Runs the incoming policy asynchronously alongside outgoing actions and aligns its context with the expected takeover state.
On LIBERO-Long, perturbed-task success rises from 69.5% to 77.1%, with 84.9% overall success—comparable to synchronous switching at 84.5%.
Reduces median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms and generalizes to unseen perturbations without retraining or recalibration.

State alignment predicts the robot state at handoff, while vision alignment projects the visual context into aligned visual tokens. The aligned state, visual tokens, and language instruction then form the takeover context for OpenVLA-OFT.

papers.abstract: Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.
authors: Yicheng Zhu, Linfeng Tian, Yang Chen, Tao Li, Zilin Bian
bullets: Liquid payloads can continue sloshing after maneuvers, making rigid-payload and simple slosh assumptions unsafe near rollover limits.
PLiMB is a GPU-parallel, high-fidelity simulator coupling FLIP fluid dynamics with many multibody vehicles to generate training data and references.
The proposed model combines modal slosh and roll physics, history-based hidden-state estimation, and a learned correction without requiring tank sensors.
It evaluates thousands of candidate plans in one GPU-batched pass within a 20 Hz control cycle.

Near rollover limits, it never selected an unsafe plan in the standard tank and made about half as many unsafe choices in a wide tank; history-based state estimation halved near-limit prediction error there.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The physics-anchored response model. Once per tick, the liquid ROM (Fig. 3) is stepped on the vehicle’s on-board signals to estimate the hidden liquid state ξ̂g , and a recurrent latent z summarizes the same history. For all candidate plans in one GPU batch, the physics prior rolls vehicle and liquid forward together, and a second ROM copy, started from ξ̂g , feeds its roll moment Mx back into roll (green). The fitted constants are ca, cM , ωr , ζr , amax and ky . A learned correction, one head per label source, refines the prior’s response series, and a peak head predicts ℓ̂ and ê (and an uncertainty σ that Eq. (1) does not use).

Figure 6. Scaling on one GPU (pre-registered). Left: median time per call against the number of candidate plans per call. Below the dashed line, a call fits one 20 Hz tick. Right: peak GPU memory. Our deployed model fits the tick up to 4,096 plans, while its as-scored implementation, the physics-only planners and every simulator in the loop miss it at every batch size. FLIP stops at 256 plans (median call over 300 s). In memory, B, K and Q coincide, as do R and E and the two implementations of ours.

papers.title: Knowing What You Carry: Scalable Physics-Anchored World Models for Robotic Planning with Liquid Payloads
papers.tldr: A physics-anchored world model infers hidden liquid motion from driving history and enables fast, safer robotic planning with liquid payloads.

papers.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
authors: Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas
bullets: Learns from 61,773 automatically labeled production picks using pre-pick heightmaps, actions, food, and utensil information.
Predicts post-pick heightmaps and picked mass with uncertainty; mass is evaluated on 12,294 held-out picks across nine foods.
Achieves 10.93 g RMSE, outperforming commanded-target/per-food-mean baselines and the controller’s internal estimate.
Rejecting the most uncertain picks yields 89.4% coverage with 10.28 g RMSE.
Performance is weakly sensitive to commanded volume/depth and can fail without warning on unseen target weights; broader food and utensil coverage is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Learns an action-conditioned food-picking world model from production data for robot planning and mass prediction.
papers.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
papers.tldr: A production-trained food-picking world model predicts both the next pan state and picked mass, enabling uncertainty-aware planning for assembly robots.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) are increasingly deployed on robots whose cameras and controllers differ from those used to collect their training data. Such deployment introduces two kinds of shifts. Visual shifts, such as a moved camera, change the observed images; actuation shifts, such as a retuned controller, latency or an added payload, change only how commanded actions translate into robot motion. Invisible to the policy, actuation shifts sharply degrade its success, even under domain randomization. In this work, we propose PEA, a test-time calibration method that identifies actuation shifts through active probing before task execution. Specifically, before each episode, the robot executes a short probe that moves one arm axis at a time with known commands, so that gain, delay and drift leave separable traces. A closed-form identifier estimates them from the response, and PEA compensates every subsequent command so that the robot executes the motion the policy intends. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts. Experiments on LIBERO with a WAM and a VLA show that, without any policy training, the identifier of PEA recovers most of the success lost to actuation shifts and generalizes to shifts unseen during training (e.g., from 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy).
authors: Jie Liu, Hui Xie, Qinfeng Feng, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Actuation changes such as controller retuning, latency, payload, or drift can severely reduce robot success without altering camera observations.
Before each episode, the robot performs short, axis-wise probes with known commands to reveal gain, delay, and drift.
A closed-form identifier estimates these effects, and PEA compensates subsequent commands without retraining the policy.
For combined visual and actuation shifts, a removable low-rank adapter adjusts the frozen policy to visible visual changes.
On LIBERO with a WAM and VLA, PEA recovered much of the lost performance and generalized to unseen actuation shifts, including 61.0% to 89.7% on LIBERO-Spatial with Cosmos-Policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PEA. Actuation shifts are invisible in images but revealed by motion, so PEA moves before it acts. (1) Probe: before each episode, the robot executes a 30-step probe that pushes one arm axis at a time with zero-sum commands, so that each gain, the delay and a constant drift leave separable traces. (2) Estimate: a closed-form identifier (orange), calibrated once offline and requiring no policy training, reads per-axis gain ĝ, delay d̂ and drift correction b̂ from the response (curves: logged x motion under gain 1.6 and a 1-step delay). (3) Act: every command of the frozen policy (gray) is rescaled and offset, and the arm holds for d̂ steps after each chunk; a lightweight LoRA adapter (blue) on the frozen weights, conditioned on the probe, handles visual shifts such as a moved camera.

Figure 4. Rollouts from the same initial state (Cosmos-Policy; last frame of each episode with the end-effector path, dot: start). Left, coupled camera and gain shift: the identifier alone corrects the gains but not the view, and the adapter completes the task. Middle, 30 N payload: the released model presses the gripper down; the identifier’s drift term lifts it. Right, 3× stiffer controller: each command moves the arm too far and the released model overshoots; the identifier reads effective gains of 1.5–1.9 and scales the commands down.

Figure 3. Identification accuracy on unseen probes. (a) Estimated vs. true per-axis gain on 360 probes not used for calibration: 120 in the training range, 120 with a 15 or 30 N load and 120 outside the range. (b) Mean gain error; the noise bar adds 0.5 mm Gaussian noise per step. The delay is exact for all probes.
Figure 6. Probe design at equal budget. Gain error of four 30- step probes under the diagnostic identifier of Table S3.

Figure 5. Real-robot rollouts on a PiPER arm (final top-down frame of one rollout each). Under a 200 g payload, π0.5 carries the cube too low and pushes the target aside; with PEA, it places the cube as without payload.

papers.title: Probing Invisible Actuation Shifts for Test-time Calibration of Visuomotor Policies
papers.tldr: PEA calibrates frozen visuomotor policies at test time by probing the robot to identify and compensate for invisible actuation shifts before task execution.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.
authors: Tzu-Yuan Huang, Shao-Hsuan Chang, Dai-Jie Wu, Ralf R\"omer, Yung-Hui Li, Stefan Sosnowski, Angela P. Schoellig, Kenneth Marino, Sandra Hirche
bullets: Safety filters can prevent unsafe actions but may push robots into states poorly represented in training data, reducing task performance.
InteR-VLA broadens task-relevant state coverage with diverse demonstrations under the same data budget.
The framework aligns training data with safety-filtered deployment to mitigate intervention-induced distribution shift.
Real-world experiments cover in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings across two evaluated VLAs.
InteR-VLA maintains safety and raises Safe Success Rate up to 90%, compared with 0% for nominal policies.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Standard VLA fine-tuning covers only nominal states (white band) and can produce unsafe trajectories (red). Learning safety from data requires extensive safety-critical coverage, while safety filters may drive execution into out-ofdistribution (OOD) states (grey), degrading task competence. papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real gaps caused by imperfect physics, perception errors, and unmodeled dynamics.
Uses conditional flow matching to infer physical parameters and residual fidelity domains in a latent space.
Samples realistic environments from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning.
Triggers adaptation only after detected anomalies, with sequential proposals and uncertainty-modulated exploration.
Across five robots, it achieves accurate posterior inference; on a damaged wheeled robot, rough-terrain success increases from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk decreases by 88%.

papers.abstract: A policy that transfers from simulation to a lab robot often fails in the field. Calibrating a simulator from real-world data typically targets only a few hand-picked parameters, and even calibrated simulators fail to capture unmodeled dynamics, while environments reconstructed via onboard perception inherit sensing noise and artifacts. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a framework based on conditional flow matching that infers online, directly from a robot's execution data, both simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity - the remaining dynamics discrepancy and the gap between perceived and true environment geometry. A simulation-trained anomaly detector determines when recalibration or fine-tuning is required using onboard sensory signals alone, while an exploration policy actively modulates posterior uncertainty using optimism in the face of uncertainty. Across five robot platforms with up to 39 calibrated parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain map, NFC achieves the most accurate posterior distributions compared to established simulation-based inference baselines. In physical outdoor experiments with a wheeled robot suffering an axle failure across snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC increases rough-terrain navigation success from 26% to 70% while reducing orientation jerk by 88%.
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real failures caused by incomplete dynamics models and noisy environment reconstruction.
Uses conditional flow matching to estimate physical parameters plus residual fidelity, including dynamics discrepancies and geometry errors.
A simulation-trained anomaly detector triggers recalibration, while uncertainty-driven exploration improves information gathering.
Across five robot platforms, NFC produced the most accurate posterior distributions among evaluated simulation-based inference baselines.
In outdoor tests with an axle failure, rough-terrain success rose from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk fell by 88%.
