papers.abstract: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.
authors: Jinlin Gan, Mingzhe Li, Junsheng Zhang, Zhibo Zhou, Jiahan Geng, Yuhua Luo, Changwang Zhang, Chenglu Wen, Lan Xu, Siqi Shen, Cheng Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between human pose estimation and conventional robot pose estimation for humanoid robots.
Introduces Humanoids, combining synthetic 3D supervision, real-world 2D annotations, and RGB sequences paired with robot states.
Combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding.
Shows strong articulation and 3D pose recovery on Humanoids and DHRP-H1, including zero-shot transfer to real-world evaluation.
Public release of the dataset and code is planned to support further research.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.
authors: Ye Mao, Jinhui Xiong, Egor Larionov, Shiyang Lu, Krystian Mikolajczyk, Wei Ye
bullets: Addresses the limitation of models tied to fixed camera counts, placements, or layouts.

Uses curriculum training and Cross-View Slot Agreement to align geometrically and semantically similar regions.
Achieves the best evaluated generation quality on RoboView-Bench and improves cross-view consistency over independent view generation.
Transfers gains to world-action models, robot benchmarks, and a real Franka robot, including better generalization across camera settings and scenes.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/
authors: Zhiyuan Li, Charles Eret, Dingsheng Liu, Xuan Zhao, Joshua Choi, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Amir Rasouli
bullets: Covers 80 bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished environments, with 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K language instructions.
Varies distractor density from clean scenes to dense visual and operational clutter.
Introduces safety-aware metrics for collisions with the environment and non-target objects, beyond task success rate.
Evaluates visual, linguistic, and object-level perturbations through per-factor analysis.
Experiments show clutter reduces success and increases non-target collisions, while perturbation type and training-data composition affect performance.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video is the most scalable source of manipulation data for robot learning, but its difficulty lies in producing high-quality supervision. Existing large corpora lack metric 3D labels or rely on heterogeneous devices, motion-capture labs, or a headset's built-in real-time tracker, whose accuracy is not reported for the released data. We introduce RoboCap-10k: 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation recorded during workers' paid shifts in 11 countries, spanning 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks. Every hour is captured on one device, the RoboCap, a 250 g hat with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. Online calibration brings every device below 1 px of epipolar error, visual-inertial SLAM yields gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories, and a multi-view hand tracker yields metric cm-precise hand poses. Each episode is annotated with task and sub-task language captions. Project page: https://robocap10k.com
authors: Kheri Hughes, Qasim Ali, Nikash Bhardwaj, Owen Akhibi, Niresh Dravin, Vivek Sharma, Sam Cho, Ethan Lee, Paul Luo, Sunny Yu, Jonathan Victor, Amanda Young, Michael Cho, Ademi Adeniji, Vincent Liu
bullets: Contains 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation across 11 countries, 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks.
Uses a lightweight 250 g hat equipped with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs.
Provides gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories and centimeter-precise metric hand poses.
Includes task- and sub-task-level language captions for each episode.

papers.abstract: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.
authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Mailhe, Hang Yu, Yikang Liu, Xiao Chen, Ankush Mukherjee, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, safe interactive environments for robotic ultrasound learning.
Conditions a causal ultrasound generator on CT-derived anatomy and probe-controlled anatomical and acoustic visibility.
Combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion, and long-rollout alignment; inference reaches 81.2 FPS.
Introduces the Action-Following Index to evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity.
On 40 held-out volumes, it improves liver and macro-organ AFI, reduces long-rollout brightness drift, and raises simulated key-plane success from 48.2% to 81.2%.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for surgical robots is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. Meanwhile, many robot-assisted procedures are recorded as stereo video, yet policies cannot learn from them directly; clinical video carries no action labels. We present FlowScope, which pretrains a surgical policy network on unlabeled clinical video by forecasting scene flow, the metric 3D motion of scene points, with labels computed by off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models. We pretrain the trunk of an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) on a dataset of 1,149 clinical procedures (1.35M clips) and discard the flow head afterward, so the deployed policy is a standard ACT with no added inference cost. On a real surgical robotic system, FlowScope raises needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and first-handover success on needle regrasp from 4% to 52% (full task: 2% to 14%) over training from scratch (n=50 trials each), and retains its gains with a generative flow-matching action head. Ablations indicate that metric 3D motion is the strongest pretraining signal among those tested; kinematics, 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow, each paired with kinematics, yield smaller or no gains. Representation analyses suggest that scene-flow pretraining encodes metric needle depth more accurately, that kinematics pretraining increases reliance on the robot state, and that needle-depth probes follow the ordering of real-robot success where offline validation error does not.
authors: John J. Han, Adam Schmidt, Jingpei Lu, Zooey He, Muhammad Abdullah Jamal, Jie Ying Wu, Omid Mohareri
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of labeled robot demonstrations by learning from action-free stereo surgical video.
Pretrains an Action Chunking Transformer trunk to forecast metric 3D scene motion, using pseudo-labels from stereo depth and optical flow.
Uses 1,149 procedures and 1.35M clips; the auxiliary flow head is discarded before deployment.
Improves needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and full needle-regrasp success from 2% to 14% in 50-trial evaluations.
Metric 3D motion outperforms the other tested pretraining signals; analyses link gains to more accurate needle-depth representations.

papers.abstract: Flow matching policies underpin the state-of-the-art in robot learning, with impressive results ranging from long-horizon planning to dexterous manipulation. However, they provide no measure of whether their predicted commands can be trusted, particularly in novel situations outside their training set. Epistemic uncertainty reflects uncertainty about the model's weights and quantifies this ignorance, but calculating it at inference time from a flow matching policy is not trivial. Actions are produced by an ODE solver, requiring uncertainty to be propagated through the entire integration process. BayesDiff addresses this problem for diffusion models by propagating the mean and variance of the state through the denoising chain under a last-layer Laplace posterior approximation, but it severely underestimates the epistemic uncertainty. In this paper we: i) prove that, for flow matching and diffusion ODEs, BayesDiff's total variance decays at rate $O(1/T)$ as the number of Euler steps $T$ used by the solver increases; ii) introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters that fix this problem by carrying the cross-covariance between state and weights; and iii) widen the last-layer posterior with observation embeddings the policy already computes, improving uncertainty estimates without retraining for CoMP and several test-time estimators alike. We demonstrate these benefits on three manipulation benchmarks with applications in failure detection and demonstration selection for fine-tuning, where CoMP corrects BayesDiff's variance collapse while matching or outperforming several uncertainty estimators.
authors: Miguel Saavedra-Ruiz, Anqi Li, Claudia D'Arpino, Alperen Degirmenci, Tucker Hermans, Fabio Ramos
bullets: Targets unreliable confidence estimates for pre-trained policies in novel situations.
Proves BayesDiff’s propagated variance decays as O(1/T) with more Euler solver steps.
Introduces two extended/unscented-Kalman-inspired recursions that propagate state–weight cross-covariance.
Improves last-layer uncertainty estimates using observation embeddings already computed by the policy, without retraining.
On three manipulation benchmarks, supports failure detection and demonstration selection while matching or outperforming several estimators.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Variance collapse in moment propagation. (a) The reference is the empirical covariance of 4000 trajectories, one per posterior draw θ(m) ∼ N (θMAP,Σθ). (b) BayesDiff returns 1/46 of it, consistent with Theorem 1. (c) Our estimators CoMP-EKF and CoMP-UKF carry the cross-covariance between the state and the weights and recover the reference to within 1%. (d) The total variance trPT at the same seed for every estimator re-run on each grid from T = 10 to 400 Euler steps. BayesDiff halves with every doubling of T , while our methods track the reference regardless of the number of Euler steps.

BayesDiff ranks at most 40% of these observations correctly and reorders them at every evaluated step count, whereas CoMP ranks 77 to 93% correctly with a stable ordering across different numbers of integration steps.

Figure 6: Calibration with the augmented head on robomimic. All estimators use the augmented last-layer Laplace posterior. Bars show medians over 150 observation windows per task with bootstrap 95% intervals; dashed lines mark reference values estimated from the augmented posterior. Both BayesDiff variants have expert-action NLLs above 108.

papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty estimation for flow-matching robot policies; directly relevant to learned robot control and manipulation.
papers.title: Coherent Moment Propagation: Epistemic Uncertainty for Pre-trained Robot Policies
papers.tldr: Coherent Moment Propagation estimates epistemic uncertainty in flow-matching robot policies by preserving state–weight dependencies during ODE integration, avoiding BayesDiff’s variance collapse.

papers.abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
bullets: Uses newly observed frames for label-free test-time training while preserving a short input history.
Accumulates updates within an episode and resets them between episodes, retaining information beyond the observation window.
Improves task success across four simulation benchmarks and two world-action models.
On RoboCasa GR-1, 2.4 seconds of history matches a 9.6-second model; 4.8 seconds exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points.
Adaptation improves predicted future frames and increasingly influences actions as episodes progress.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.
authors: Guangyu Zhao, Yongchang Zhang, Ruizhang Jiang, Zhihong Yu, Yuhao Zhang, Tao Wu, Qimin Zhou, Kunsong Shi, Haoran Wen, Zeyu Zhang, Yin Li, Kun Zhan, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Introduces VMBench, a benchmark for manipulation tasks requiring memory of locations, appearances, and their associations.
Uses a hierarchical design: a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes, while an executor predicts actions from selected memories.
Achieves 49.9% average success on VMBench, 31.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.
Transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances and reaches 43.7% success on an unseen task with a few memory annotations, near 44.3% with full supervision.
Also reports competitive RMBench results and improvements in real-robot manipulation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MomentMem. (a) The memorizer uses recent observations and existing memory to decide whether to store the current frame. The executor predicts actions from the updated memory and current input. (b) Each epoch, we sample an anchor from each key segment. Under a teacher-forced history, the anchor is positive. Earlier frames in the segment remain in the observation context but are excluded from the loss. Later frames are negative because the event has been stored.

Figure 3. Few-shot memorizer transfer on VMBench. After training on the other VMBench tasks, the memorizer adapts to Flash Beacon from five annotated demonstrations. It reaches 43.7% closed-loop success. This is close to 44.3% with full memory supervision and above 29.0% when adapting pretrained Qwen3-VL with the same data.

Figure 4. Real-world experiments. Top: Similar to Placement Imitation. A human places the cube at a target and then moves it back. The robot must place the cube at that target. Bottom: Similar to Explore Cube. The robot must find the cube under one of three cups without revisiting any cup.

Image sequences illustrate how evidence is acquired and used after it is no longer visible. The final column shows each task’s visual OOD variant.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.
authors: Junde Li, Wei-Han Yu, Xiangyi Chu, Yaoxin Li, Jiawei Xu, Ka-Fai Un, Pui-In Mak
bullets: Addresses three grounding failures: lost contact geometry, misaligned token-level gradients, and optimization collapse from discrete indicators.
Uses a forward-only tactile encoder, token-parallel zeroth-order activation updates, and SlipGuard for continuous incipient-slip verification.
On an elasto-plastic shell, its closed-loop gate reached 29× lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp and avoided permanent deformation.
Achieved 97.6% average success across three evaluated LIBERO suites while reducing peak activation memory 7.12× versus a backpropagated step.
Scope is limited to the reported structural-shell and LIBERO evaluations.

papers.abstract: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch where identical joint values yield different spatial configurations across robot embodiments.
Uses a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that reconstructs both joint angles and link poses.
Generates scalable kinematic supervision with MorphGen and pretrains on 40 million morphology-state pairs.
Evaluated with a frozen tokenizer in a vision-language-action policy on RoboTwin 2.0 and the ten-task EmbodiBench benchmark.
Link-pose supervision is important: removing it lowers EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting to hidden, changing physical conditions that make identical robot states respond differently to the same action.
Re-infers a latent context from recent interactions and uses it to condition a fixed network modeling inertia and potential energy.
Requires neither retraining nor a hand-specified robot model to adapt to new conditions.
In Isaac Sim experiments with a Franka Panda arm, it predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing unseen-payload error by 1.6–3.8× over baselines.
The learned context captures payload properties and changes, supports counterfactual torque queries, and produces physically valid gravity and inertia components.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality, safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. Observations suggest that RCPI provides the closest estimation to the exact solution and has the most stable training curve; however, it is data-intensive and requires the largest volume of data. D-DDPG is the most data-efficient one, but at the price of the training stability. Based on the observations, we provide suggestions for the algorithm selection for AV decision making.
bullets: Evaluates FVI, RCPI, DQN, and discrete-action D-DDPG on the same AV decision-making problem.
Compares optimality, safety, training stability, and training and decision costs.
RCPI most closely matches the exact solution and shows the most stable training.
D-DDPG is the most data-efficient but has less stable training.
The findings inform algorithm selection for AV decision-making.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.
bullets: Studies offline Q-learning in tabular, finite-horizon MDPs with KL regularization.
Introduces KLQ, a simple KL-regularized variant of classical Q-learning.
Proves KLQ achieves a fast sample complexity of \(\widetilde{O}(1/\epsilon)\) without explicit pessimism, but with exponential parameter and horizon dependence.
Introduces KLPQ, adding pessimism to retain the fast rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence.
Claims the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.
papers.selection_reason: Fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning with KL regularization, relevant to RL-based robot learning.
papers.title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization
papers.tldr: KL-regularized Q-learning achieves fast O(1/) offline sample complexity, with pessimism removing its exponential dependence on regularization and horizon.

papers.abstract: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.
bullets: Behavioral diversity can support role specialization, but the ideal level depends on the task and is difficult to tune.
ADiCo uses fast-timescale Diversity Control to track a target diversity level and a slower Extremum Seeking Controller to adjust that target from mean episodic returns alone.
Across six configurations and two cooperative MARL tasks, it maintained low diversity when homogeneous behavior helped and higher diversity when heterogeneous behavior was needed.
ADiCo matched or exceeded DiCo with the best grid-searched target and unconstrained DiCo.
The method provides a model-free, gradient-free alternative to manually selecting diversity targets.

papers.abstract: A robot must choose an action before it can see the outcome. In a recorded demonstration, later camera frames show what happened after the robot moved. Hindsight Self-Distillation (HSD) uses these later frames to teach a policy what to extract from current images. During training, a teacher sees both the current and later frames, while a student sees the current frames. They share a visual encoder and an action predictor. Each branch summarizes its images with a small set of feature vectors. These visual summaries supply all visual input to the action predictor. The teacher learns from demonstrated actions. For each noisy action sequence, the student learns from either the demonstration or the teacher's denoising prediction. It also learns to match the teacher's visual summaries. We analyze which aspects of the teacher's predictions the student can recover from its inputs. At deployment, the student encodes the current images once and reuses its summaries at every denoising step. HSD achieves average success rates of 98.50\% on LIBERO and 92.31\% on RoboTwin 2.0.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing actions before their outcomes are visible.
A teacher sees current and later frames, while a student sees only current frames; both share visual and action components.
The student learns from demonstrated actions or the teacher’s denoising predictions and matches the teacher’s visual summaries.
At deployment, the student computes current-image features once and reuses them throughout denoising.
Reports average success rates of 98.50% on LIBERO and 92.31% on RoboTwin 2.0.

papers.abstract: Scaling embodied interaction data requires a broad collection of usable tasks, yet specifying and validating each task instance remains costly. We present AgenticTask, an agent-based framework that expands existing task collections under human intent. Its central representation links interaction requirements to object and part bindings, scene and robot configurations, initial conditions, and completion criteria. A task-generation agent reuses interaction structure to construct supported variations and revises incompatible configurations using validation feedback. A task-execution agent uses the same bindings and geometric records to select robot-supported skills and check completion against the original task criteria. On RoboCasa, the framework builds the AgenticTask collection, saving 16,450 task instances from 20,323 construction attempts at a throughput of 166.97 saved instances per elapsed hour, with 62.26% of construction attempts passing the configured physical checks. The execution agent completes approximately 38% of evaluated tasks, with successful cases spanning object placement, articulated manipulation, and sequential arrangement. Diagnostic analysis identifies improvement priorities in construction reliability, action selection, task-robot compatibility, and runtime integration. Together, these results demonstrate task-collection expansion with measured construction productivity and concrete execution evidence, providing a foundation for subsequent interaction-data collection for embodied AI.

papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) acquire diverse skills through large-scale motion imitation and massively parallel reinforcement learning, yet broad behavioral capability does not ensure precise execution across physical conditions. Without distinguishing the underlying dynamics, policies may favor conservative compromises over environment-specific precision. We introduce ECHO, an in-context BFM that turns interaction experience into environment-specific control, separating general behavioral capability from dynamics-specific execution. Mixed and Annealed Sampling first establishes a behavior prior in a single pretraining stage by balancing targeted practice with broad motion coverage. Building on this prior, Context Representation and Residual Adaptation learns structured dynamics representations from interaction histories to guide residual corrections to the frozen prior, enabling adaptation without test-time parameter updates. Extensive experiments show that ECHO outperforms all baseline methods across diverse motions and physical conditions. Moreover, deployment on the Unitree G1 demonstrates whole-body teleoperation spanning extreme acrobatics and terrain interaction, alongside payload adaptation in manipulation and whole-body control. Page is available at https://mwondering.github.io/echo-bfm/
bullets: Addresses the gap between broad skill coverage and reliable execution under changing physical conditions.

Experiments report better performance than all baselines across diverse motions and physical conditions.

papers.abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.
authors: Thomas Mousseau, Tyler Kastner, Davide Baldelli, Amir-massoud Farahmand
bullets: Addresses the limited distribution families supported by existing distributional RL algorithms.
Computes the learning loss in the frequency domain using characteristic functions.
Unifies quantile and categorical distributional RL approaches.
Can represent previously inaccessible distributions, including mixtures of continuous distributions.
Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments show potential performance gains from greater distributional flexibility.

papers.abstract: We study active exploration for minimax transition estimation in unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). Frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer~\citep{gu2026kappa} addresses this problem through a parameterized family of exploration objectives, but requires confidence-bound constructions and joint optimization over plausible transition kernels and occupancy measures, introducing a computational burden that limits its practical applicability. We develop Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer, which simplifies this procedure by placing Dirichlet priors on the transition distributions. Under the posterior mean estimator, the posterior expected squared $\ell_2$ error equals the total posterior variance, providing a closed-form exploration signal. The algorithm plans under the posterior mean model, eliminating confidence-set optimization. Under the stated assumptions, this simpler planning procedure retains the $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/3})$ surrogate convergence rate of frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer. We further bound the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experiments on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi demonstrate lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than the tested baselines.
authors: Xihe Gu, Urbashi Mitra, Tara Javidi
bullets: Targets active exploration for minimizing worst-case transition-estimation error in MDPs.
Uses Dirichlet priors; posterior expected squared ℓ2 error becomes a closed-form total posterior-variance signal.
Plans under the posterior-mean transition model, avoiding confidence-set and joint occupancy optimization.
Retains a stated \widetilde{O}(T^{-1/3}) surrogate convergence rate and bounds posterior variance against an asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark.
Experiments on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi report lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than tested baselines.

papers.abstract: Policy representations in reinforcement learning have expanded beyond Gaussian policies to diffusion and flow-matching based generative policies. However, existing RL methods remain representation-specific, lacking a unified optimization interface for emerging generative policies. In particular, extending likelihood-based objectives to multi-step generative policies couples optimization to their internal generation process, where accumulated likelihood ratios can weaken the update signal. Meanwhile, generative-policy-specific methods often rely on multi-candidate generation and critic-based selection, improving overall return while providing limited improvement to the policy itself. We introduce DR-APO (Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization), which decouples policy improvement from policy representation through advantage-guided target improvement and representation-compatible direct action fitting, providing a shared optimization principle for Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies. Across five MuJoCo-v5 tasks, DR-APO remains competitive with SAC for Gaussian policies and achieves the best aggregate policy-only performance for both diffusion and flow-matching policies. NavDP post-training improves the Success Rate (SR) from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% in real-world navigation. These results demonstrate a unified policy-improvement principle across Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies, from continuous-control learning to embodied-policy post-training.
bullets: Addresses weakened update signals and representation-specific objectives in multi-step generative policies.
Uses advantage-guided target improvement with representation-compatible direct action fitting.
Matches SAC competitively for Gaussian policies and achieves the best aggregate policy-only performance for diffusion and flow policies across five MuJoCo-v5 tasks.
Post-training NavDP raises navigation success from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% in real-world navigation.
Demonstrates applicability from continuous control to embodied-policy post-training.

papers.abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.
authors: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu, Lvmin Zhang, Ivor Tsang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning action representations and dynamics without action labels, often requiring dynamics to be learned from scratch.
Uses one pretrained video prior for two roles: inverse dynamics via a transition encoder with learnable action queries, and forward dynamics via a causal action-conditioned generator.
Trains both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck to discover actions transferable across visual contexts and embodiments.
Achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and stronger zero-shot transfer in navigation and robotic manipulation, according to the abstract.
The framework also works with predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, suggesting applicability beyond generative video models.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.
authors: Yiyang Du, Yuxuan Kuang, Qitao Zhao, Yixuan Wang, Zhanqiu Guo, Yi Xu, Xin Li, Wenbin He, Liu Ren, Chenyan Xiong
bullets: Analyzes direct low-level robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks, beyond episode-level success rates.
Pairs each policy action with a stated local intent, then uses a critic to assess outcomes and failure modes.
Finds closed-loop recovery, reliable semantic grounding, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation.
Identifies bottlenecks in grasping and alignment, with uneven recovery across failure types.
Releases 12,844 annotated actions and a fine-tuned open-source critic; failure-mode accuracy improves from 32.58% to 74.24% on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark.

papers.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx
authors: Kai Lu, Chenyang Ma, Ioannis Havoutis
bullets: Targets failures caused by tightly coupled temporal structure, skill execution, and precision in monolithic VLA models.

Applies world-coordinate locking for base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and anchored contact targets.
Experiments on three simulated tasks and one real Unitree G1 task show improved stage progression and task success rates.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.
authors: Hao Vo, Taisei Hanyu, Yuki Ikebe, Pham Tri Quang, Sreevenkata Anjani Tishita Godavarthi, Nghi D. Q. Bui, Daniel Sonntag, Chase Rainwater, Duy Minh Ho Nguyen, Anh Nguyen, Ngan Le
bullets: Evaluates dynamic extrinsic dexterity involving gravity, friction, inertia, mass, and center of mass—not just gripper–object contact.
Introduces nine throwing tasks across 100 scenes, with uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects and varied destinations.
Uses 35K trajectories generated by an automatic pipeline combining grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization.

papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features. Taking the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation as a design principle, we build this basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a fixed reference policy. With such a basis, the successor features at a state-action pair are a linear combination of the base features at that same pair, which is not true in general, and the coefficients are known in closed form: each successor feature is its base feature multiplied by $\theta_i = 1/(1-\gamma\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is its eigenvalue. The long-term return is thus predicted from the same features as the immediate reward, no successor-feature network or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a new task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. The agent acts greedily on the action values of the reference policy, which is one step of policy improvement over it and suffices to reach a single goal. In a two-goal gridworld, with the uniform random walk as reference policy, whose eigenvectors are the low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, agents built this way maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal, whereas SimpleSF and DQN lose most of their return at each change.
bullets: Uses eigenvectors of a reference-policy transition matrix as reusable base features.
Successor features have closed-form coefficients, eliminating a successor-feature network and replay buffer.
Adapting to a new reward or goal requires only linear regression on the reward.
Greedy action selection provides one-step policy improvement and can reach a single goal.
In a two-goal gridworld, performance remains near maximal across goal changes, unlike SimpleSF and DQN.

papers.abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.
authors: Shibo Zhou, Tianqi Hong, Zheng Yan, He Yang
bullets: Addresses the human-intensive design–build–test–iterate workflow in power-electronics hardware development.
Uses workspace scanning, machine-specific constraints, and an executable digital twin to rehearse robot actions, fabrication, and circuit behavior before fabrication.
Coordinates a robot arm, PCB printer, pick-and-place machine, cameras, sensors, an OPAL-RT simulator, and an oscilloscope from a single text instruction.
In a 60 Hz notch-filter demonstration, it completed a first-run experiment without human intervention in 2 h 39 min and achieved 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz.
The rehearsal identified five pre-fabrication issues, while the agent also diagnosed and resolved faults during execution.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Architecture of JARVIS. The agent reads and writes the records, its long-term memory, and acts through two channels. In the twin, the agent asks questions and rehearses. The twin’s four layers (geometry, behavior, physics, provenance) mirror the bench. Through the accountable execution layer, the agent runs programs on the real machines. This layer logs every attempt, enforces every safety limit in code and holds the machine skills. The bench consists of unmodified machines. Scans and the machines’ live states keep the twin in step with the bench. Two screens show people what the bench does and what the agent thinks. A person states the need in plain language and agrees to the agent’s plan; once the run starts, no person intervenes.

Fig. 10. What people in the lab see during a run, as recorded in the run of Sec. VII-A. (a) The live display, here as the arm carries the carrier to the pick-and-place machine. The bench overview is the live 3D twin. The device at work is shown large: here the arm, with its pose and joint angles, its place on the bench seen from above, and what its gripper holds. Every other device stays live in the row below: the printed board and the bed’s temperature, the board waiting for its parts, the simulator and the oscilloscope waiting for the test, and the 3D scanner after its survey. The run’s steps appear along the bottom once the agent has worked them out, and the current step is highlighted. (b) The thinking screen at the end of the run. A person types one request in plain language at the start. The agent shows its reasoning as it works (what it observes, checks and compares) and states its conclusions and decisions in its own voice; here, the verdict’s explanation, the next design, and the improvements it proposes from the run itself.

Fig. 4. How the bench is connected. Machines are shown by their role. Line styles show the type of each link. The agent and its twin run on the control computer; the agent’s reasoning comes from a language model in the cloud.

Fig. 7. Physics in the twin. (a) Heat transfer. The heated bed warms the aluminium carrier and the board by conduction; the board loses heat to the air, and the carrier to the arm. The twin runs the cure’s own heating program on a simulated bed and, from the heat path between the bed and the board, predicts the temperature at the board’s surface: it holds at the ink’s cure temperature. The twin also predicts when the carrier is cool enough for the arm to grip. (b) Thermal expansion. Aluminium grows more than the board and more than the cold frame around the carrier. Up to 240 ◦C, a gap stays open around the carrier, and the board stays held. (c) Bending of the aluminium flexures. Two beams, clamped at both ends, hold the carrier in place. As the carrier grows, the beams bend further and push harder; their deflection stays inside the slot behind them. Schematics not to scale; curves computed by the twin’s models.

Fig. 6. From scans to the twin, and a rehearsal in it. (a) The 3D scanner on the arm’s wrist views the bench from several directions; each cone is one view. (b) The agent fuses the views into one panorama of the bench, a point cloud in the arm’s frame, coloured by height above the surface below. (c) The agent places the complete CAD model of every machine, fixture and tool where the scan found it. The result is the executable digital twin. (d) Before anything moves, the agent rehearses the experiment in the twin. It checks motion, heat, time, the circuit and its test, and the machine files.

Fig. 2. The JARVIS bench and the agent’s twin of it. (a) The physical bench. (b) The twin of the same bench at the start of a run. Every machine and fixture is placed where the bench scan found it: the robot arm with its gripper, the printer, the pick-and-place machine with its dock and tape feeders, the tool rack, the test nest holding the carrier, the test head on its stand, the push-out pin, the next blank board, the simulator and the oscilloscope. (c) Close-ups of the twin. Left: the tool rack holds the printer’s probe, paste dispenser and ink dispenser. Middle: in the carrier, the board sits in an adapter and the adapter sits in a base. Right: at the end of a run, the tested board is pushed out of the adapter on the push-out pin, and the empty adapter is set onto the next blank board.

Fig. 5. How a board travels through the bench, and how boards are exchanged. (a) The board clips into an adapter, an open frame. The adapter sits in a base. Through the opening, the board rests directly on the base, and its top stays below the adapter’s rim. The adapter and the base each have a grip tab, by which the arm holds them. A board of another size uses another adapter. (b) Board exchange at the end of a run. The base stays in the test nest, and the arm moves only the adapter. (1) The arm lowers the adapter over a push-out pin, which pushes the tested board out near one edge; the board drops onto the table. (2) The arm lowers the empty adapter onto the next blank board, which clips in. (c) The route of one board. The arm carries the whole carrier from machine to machine, and the whole carrier is heated on the printer’s bed. After the test, the exchange loads the next blank board, and the next run starts again in the test nest. Schematic, not to scale.

Fig. 8. The build, step by step. The board is the agent’s own layout, shown as it is after each step. (a) Before the run, the 3D scanner on the arm’s wrist scans every machine and fixture that the run uses, and the agent matches each scan to its place in the twin; a place that does not match stops the run. (b) The printer’s carriage waits at its tool-change position. A printed marker, found by the 3D scanner, locates the tool rack, and the arm moves a tool head from the rack onto the carriage. (c) The probe touches the bare board at many points. The result is a height map (unevenness exaggerated), so the nozzle can follow the surface. The nozzle follows the map, so an uneven board is printed at a constant gap; the agent decides how large a step between neighbouring points each stage may have, small on a bare board and larger once printed pads stand higher. (d) The ink dispenser draws the traces in ink, at a constant gap above the uneven surface (inset: a section along one trace). (e) The whole carrier stays on the heated bed while the ink cures, then cools until the arm can grip it safely. (f) The probe finds two features of the printed circuit (1, 2), and the paste layer is aligned to them; the paste dispenser sets a dot of solder paste on each pad. (g) The down-looking camera finds the board’s three fiducials. The nozzle picks each part from a tape feeder, the up-looking camera checks it, and the part is set on its paste. (h) The bed heats the whole carrier again; the paste melts and forms the joints (inset: one joint before and after). Schematic, not to scale.
Fig. 12. The board built and tested by JARVIS. The traces printed in ink, the 14 parts placed and reflowed, and the gold discs on the test pads, as the board came out of the run.

Fig. 9. The hardware-in-the-loop test. The board, still in its adapter and base, sits in the test nest. The arm places the test head on the board and holds it there through the sweep; the arm’s gripper holds the head by a fin on its top, and the head’s six contact tips touch the board’s six test pads, each wired out. A and B are not used by this board. An analog output of the simulator drives the board’s input (IN) with a sine wave. Two analog inputs record IN and OUT, and the gain OUT/IN is measured at every frequency. An oscilloscope also measures IN and OUT, as a second instrument. Inset: the twin’s prediction of the gain. Schematic, not to scale.

Fig. 14. The next design. (a) The board that the agent proposed from the measured data, as drawn in KiCad (copper and silkscreen): the same layout, every resistance divided by ten and every capacitance multiplied by ten. (b) The measured board, the twin recalibrated on it, and the next board predicted by the recalibrated twin. (c) The passband near 1 Hz enlarged: the next board meets the limit that the built board missed.

Fig. 13. The requirement as code, the twin’s prediction and the measured board. Red: the acceptance limits derived from the requirement. Green: the twin’s predicted response of the notch board, for nominal parts and for 300 virtual boards with random part values within their tolerances. Orange: the board measured by the simulator; open circles: the oscilloscope’s readings.

Fig. 15. A defect found by simulation in the twin, and the agent’s own redesign. The printer draws its ink-start pattern at the center of the rectangle that encloses the circuit. Simulated in the twin, the pattern on the first layout, v1, would cross the traces (red strokes). No person pointed this out: the agent found it in the rehearsal and changed the design itself, adding two marks that move the center. On the revised layout, v1b, whose marks the built board keeps, the pattern lands on bare board.

The arm carries the board, changes the printer’s tool heads eight times, holds the test head and exchanges the board. papers.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
papers.tldr: JARVIS autonomously designs, fabricates, tests, diagnoses, and improves circuit boards by coordinating laboratory equipment through a rehearsed digital twin.

papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

bullets: Introduces 30 simulated manipulation tasks across five application domains, with three difficulty levels and Clean/Random scenes, totaling 180 configurations.
Separates evaluation into Mind (history-based decisions), Act (precise and timely execution), and Mind2Act (closed-loop reasoning and action).
Includes a diagnosis harness that attributes failures to Mind, Act, or their composition and produces system profile cards.
Evaluations show that strength in isolated reasoning or execution does not transfer to combined tasks; the strongest agent achieves 52.7% on Mind, 39.0% on Act, but only 12.0% on Mind2Act.
Identifies reasoning–execution composition through environmental feedback as the primary open challenge.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of Mind2Act World. Mind2Act World is a diagnostic benchmark for embodied mind, physical action and their composition in robotic manipulation. Mind tasks test history-based reasoning, Act tasks test precise and timely physical execution, and Mind2Act tasks test their closed-loop composition, where action outcomes guide subsequent decisions. The 30 tasks come from 5 real-world application domains and cover 12 capability categories. Each runs at 3 difficulty levels in Clean and Random scenes (180 configurations), with 4,500 expert demonstrations for training end-to-end policies. Agents and end-to-end policies share the same tasks, information contract and evaluator, and are ranked on separate leaderboards. A diagnosis loop then attributes the failed episodes of a system to Mind, Act or their composition and summarizes them in a model profile card that points to its next improvement. Top: the three views of Mind2Act World. Middle: the application domains, capability categories, tasks and diagnosis loop. Bottom: the open-source ecosystem, the evaluated models and the continuously updated leaderboards.

Fig. 6. Training, evaluation and diagnosis pipeline. Training: end-to-end policies are fine-tuned on 4,500 demonstrations generated by scripted experts. Evaluation: the policies predict action chunks and the agents call motion tools, while the evaluator decides success from simulator state hidden from both. Diagnosis: episode logs feed a model profile card, which records where each failed episode first breaks down and whether the failure lies in Mind, Act or their composition (Section 6.1). Dashed elements are the next stage of the loop. The failure codes on a card become concrete changes (Table 7), and the improved model is evaluated again (Section 7). The evaluation and diagnosis panels trace one recorded GPT-6 Astra episode on S1 Medium, and the card panel is illustrative.

Fig. 10. Overview of the model profile card. The card reads from top to bottom, as on the project website. Results by view gives the success rate in each view. Where failures break and Which side failed give the step at which failed episodes first break down and whether Mind, Act or their composition failed. First failures and Where tasks break give the most frequent failure codes and where typical tasks stop. Model gives a four-letter behavioral profile (Appendix E.6). Capability profile and Under pressure give the success of each task at Easy, Medium and Hard, grouped by capability and view, and the success rate by difficulty. What could help turns the codes into directions for improvement. The numbers are an illustrative example; the measured cards of three representative systems are given in Appendix E.4.

Fig. 2. All 30 tasks, grouped by view and capability. Mind tasks emphasize decisions based on historical observation, Act tasks precise and timely physical execution, and Mind2Act tasks the closed-loop composition of the two, in which action outcomes guide subsequent decisions. Each view has ten tasks, and together they cover twelve capability categories and five application domains. The central wheel groups the capability categories by view; the surrounding tiles show each task’s ID and scene, framed by view. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), giving 180 configurations.

Fig. 3. Difficult steps inside eight Hard-level tasks. Each panel follows one Hard-level demonstration through four intermediate steps and shows what makes each step hard: the bold label under a frame names the operation, and the italic line the demand that makes it difficult. A failure at any of these steps blocks the stages after it. The color of the task ID gives its view, and the tag beside the task name the Hard-level setting; Fig. 4 compares the levels themselves.

Fig. 4. Easy, Medium and Hard levels of twelve tasks. Four tasks per view at Easy, Medium and Hard. A harder level keeps the goal and raises one or more task demands: Mind tasks add more to remember or infer, Act tasks require more spatial accuracy and physical stability, and Mind2Act tasks lengthen the workflow or shorten the response window. The label under each frame gives the parameter that changes, and the icon beside each task name gives the kind of demand (key below the panels; its counts cover all 30 tasks).

Fig. 7. Task setups grouped by application domain. Nineteen of the thirty tasks are shown with the objects and equipment each one uses. All thirty tasks are performed by the same two-arm ARX X5 robot.

Fig. 9. Failure diagnosis on an example profile card. An illustrative example, the same as in Fig. 10 and on the project website; the measured cards of three representative systems are in Appendix E.4. (a) Three-layer diagnosis. The workflow as a funnel: in this example, the rule layer settles about a third of the failed episodes, and the rest pass to the LLM judge and, where it is uncertain, to the human check. (b) Beyond the success rate. The example end-to-end policy rarely completes these three tasks, and most of its failures on each task occur at a single early step. (c) Across all failures. The card follows the failed episodes from the step at which each first breaks to its failure code.

Fig. 11. Planned work beyond this report. Top: Outcome feedback, matched runs with and without it; Coverage and cost, broader and repeated evaluation with its cost; Transfer, the analysis carried to other simulators. Bottom: Diagnosis, sharper profile cards for more models and the planned loop from a card to a better model that is evaluated again. The small drawings are schematic.

Fig. 8. Success rates by view, and Random versus Clean successes. (a) Success rate by view. Final success rate on Mind, Act and Mind2Act, with 95% Wilson intervals. (b) Random vs. Clean successes. For the six end-to-end policies, the ratio of successful Random episodes to successful Clean episodes on the same instances.

Fig. 13. Model profile card of G0.5 (VLA). Panels as in Fig. 10. Other in the side panel collects failures with an episode-level code, such as stalls and cases the evidence cannot decide. The memory and lifestyle letters of the behavioral profile (N, P) are weak leans (Appendix E.6).
Fig. 14. Model profile card of InternW0 (WAM). Panels as in Fig. 13.
Fig. 15. Model profile card of GPT-6 Astra (agent). Panels as in Fig. 13. Each task and level has ten episodes, and the difficulty bars run to 70%.

Fig. 12. Demonstration collection and quality control. A scripted expert executes each task instance at 120 Hz while the robot state, contacts and camera readbacks are logged on every physics tick. An episode is kept only if the test-time scorer gives it full score, timing-critical tasks keep the required margin, the arms make no selfor cross-arm contact, and the recording is gap-free and clock-aligned. Otherwise it is discarded and collected again. Kept episodes are stored as 30 Hz HDF5 files.

Table 1. Comparison with existing benchmarks. Among the compared benchmarks, only Mind2Act World assesses the same task demands both in isolation and in composition, and attributes each failure to reasoning, execution or their composition, with per-model summaries in profile cards. Scale: # Tasks in each benchmark’s own unit; Avg. demo, mean length of a training demonstration. Task design: Workflow, tasks derived from real-world requirements. Capability: Composition, decisions conditioned on realized outcomes are tested; Iso.+Comp., the same task semantics are assessed in isolation and in composition. Systems: VLA includes other end-to-end policies. Diagnosis: Stage loc., failures are localized to the stage at which the episode broke down; Attribution, failures are attributed to reasoning, execution or their composition; Harness, a dedicated tool analyses episode logs beyond success and score; Profile card, a model receives a card summarizing where it fails and its behavioral tendencies. stated focus, or evaluated in the original paper or on the official leaderboard; × not; “-” not reported or not applicable.

Table 5. Final success rate (%) on every task, grouped by application domain. Each block lists the tasks of one domain of Table 2 and closes with the domain mean, the mean of its task rates. In each block, the first three columns are the agents and the other six the end-to-end policies; task IDs are colored by view (Mind, Act, Mind2Act) and named in Table 20. Each cell pools the Clean and Random settings and the three difficulty levels: 30 episodes per task for an agent and 300 for an end-to-end policy. Shading, in the view’s color, deepens with the success rate, and a gray 0 marks a task that the system never completes. M1, DR4, PR5, PR6, CP03, CP04, CP07 and CP09 have no success in any of the 56,700 episodes. Appendix Table 13 gives task scores and the two settings separately.

Table 3. Evaluation episodes per system. Every system runs the same 180 configurations: thirty tasks at three difficulty levels, each in a Clean and a Random scene setting. An end-to-end policy runs ten times as many episodes per configuration as an agent. Counts are per system. The primary result combines the Clean and Random configurations of each task and difficulty with equal weight.

Table 13. Task scores and setting-level success rates. For each task and system, the first number is the mean task score (0–100) over both settings and the gray pair the success rate (%) in the Clean / Random setting. Each setting has 15 episodes per task for an agent and 150 for an end-to-end policy.

Table 4. Mind2Act World leaderboards. Each cell reports task score (0–100) / success rate (%) for one view. For each model, the first row pools the three difficulty levels, and All is the mean of the Clean and Random settings. The Overall score is 0.25 Mind+ 0.25 Act+ 0.50 Mind2Act, which gives Mind2Act as much weight as the two single views together (Section 4.3). The Overall success rate pools all episodes.
