Table 6. Evaluation time and cost per system. Time per call is the mean duration of one API request of an agent or one action prediction of an end-to-end policy, run locally on one GPU; episode time is the mean wall-clock time of an episode, over all tasks and by view. API cost is the mean cost of an agent episode at the providers’ list prices and the cost per successful episode.

Table 8. Training dataset statistics by benchmark view and difficulty level. Statistics cover all 30 tasks, with 50 episodes per task at each difficulty level. Frames count synchronized samples per camera; durations use the recorded sampling frequency of 30 Hz.

Intervals treat episodes as independent draws and therefore describe sampling over the fixed instance lists; they do not include variation between tasks or between repeated runs.

Table 14. Successful episodes by difficulty level. Counts out of 100 episodes per level (50 Clean and 50 Random) for two end-to-end policies, on the tasks where at least one of them succeeds repeatedly. The level totals equal the task counts of the release.
Table 16. Completed Mind2Act episodes by task. Each task has 30 episodes per agent and 300 per end-to-end policy, pooled over the three difficulty levels and both settings.

Table 15. Failure codes used in episode diagnosis. The table groups 18 codes by the stage at which the failure occurs. Three episode-level codes cover an exhausted budget, stalled or repeated actions, and insufficient evidence.
Table 11. Outcomes by setting. Overall scores (0.25 Mind+ 0.25 Act+ 0.50 Mind2Act) and numbers of successful episodes in each setting.
Table 18. Stop reasons of agent episodes. Number of episodes by stop reason in the Clean and Random settings, 450 episodes each.
Table 9. System interfaces. What each system family receives and returns under the shared protocol.

Table 19. Definition of the four profile letters. Each dimension keeps the question that MBTI asks about a person and answers it with two task groups of the benchmark. The system takes the letter of the group on which it does better. Letter 1 compares the two single-capability views, and letters 2–4 each compare two task groups within one view (column Measured on).

Table 17. Failures settled by each diagnosis layer. Top: failed episodes settled by the rule layer and passed to the LLM judge. Bottom: share of failures attributed to each side, among the failures the rules settle and among all failures. The remainder carry episode-level codes.
Table 10. Run budgets. 𝐵 denotes the task- and level-specific end-to-end budget in physics steps.

Table 7. Directions for improvement by failure group. Grouped as on the profile card (Mind, Act and Composition). The directions concern the training data of end-to-end policies and the harness of agents. Evidence is from the measured cards of Appendix E.4 and the results of Section 5.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark for robotic manipulation that evaluates the composition of reasoning and execution, providing a crucial tool for assessing embodied intelligence capabilities.
papers.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: Mind2Act World diagnoses whether robotic manipulation failures arise from reasoning, physical execution, or composing both through feedback.

papers.abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.
bullets: Awaken-Human pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body motion across more than 100 skills.
Awaken-HI jointly predicts human motion and retargeted robot actions using a shared action expert in a vision-language-action model.
Direct human-motion supervision improves transfer of loco-manipulation skills to humanoid robots.
More human pretraining data lowers held-out robot action prediction error and improves downstream real-robot success.
After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, the policy reaches a 93.75% mean success rate across eight tasks and generalizes to unseen objects and object–destination pairings.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Effect of auxiliary depth supervision on visual representations. The left panel shows the RGB inputs and the ℓ2-norm maps of the final-layer image features for both models. We train a separate DPT probe on each frozen backbone under identical settings. The model trained with depth supervision better recovers the relative depths of the arms, supporting surfaces, and background shown in the stereo-derived targets.

Figure 2: Object and skill coverage in Awaken-Human. The dataset contains 17.02 million episodes spanning more than 100 skills. The left panels show the distribution of object categories (top) and episode counts for selected skills (bottom). The right panel shows representative egocentric frames.

Figure 3: Visual diversity in Awaken-Human. Each point represents a video sample in a two-dimensional t-SNE projection of V-JEPA 2 features. Selected clusters appear in color and the remaining samples in gray. Dashed lines link the example frames on either side to their corresponding clusters.

Figure 4: Two-stage training of Awaken-HI. We pretrain Awaken-HI on Awaken-Human, using a shared action expert to jointly predict human motion, wrist poses, and retargeted robot actions, with auxiliary depth and subtask supervision. We then retain the shared expert and robot action branch and fine-tune the policy on real-robot demonstrations.

Figure 5: Eight whole-body loco-manipulation tasks on the EngineAI T800. Each row shows the key stages of one task from left to right. For long-horizon evaluation, we chain the tasks in rows 2–5 to form the industrial stocking task and those in rows 6–8 to form the household tidying task.

Figure 6: Scaling whole-body egocentric pretraining improves action prediction and real-robot success. From left to right, the panels show inference MSE, validation loss, empirical power-law fits for both metrics, and real-robot success rates after post-training. Stars mark the lowest plotted value on each curve in the first two panels. In the final panel, □, △, and ♢ denote Bimanual Object Storage, Garment Hanging, and Laundry Basket Relocation, respectively. The solid orange line shows their mean success rate, which rises from 56.7% to 90.0% as pretraining data increases from 5,000 to 50,000 hours.

Table 2: Real-robot task success on the EngineAI T800. We evaluate each method in ten trials per task and report success rates as percentages. The mean is computed over the eight individual tasks. Long-horizon success requires completing all stages in order without resetting the robot or the scene.

Table 3: Generalization to new instruction combinations and unseen objects. For each of four new pairings of familiar objects and destinations, we report the placement success rate over ten trials per method. Tissues and a medicine bottle, both unseen during robot post-training, appear together in ten additional trials per method. We report a separate completion rate for each object.
Table 1: Comparison with existing egocentric human datasets. Hours and episodes are those released by the original source, and – denotes a value the source does not report.

Table 4: Ablation of human motion, wrist pose, and depth supervision. We pretrain all variants on the same 5,000 hours of Awaken-Human data. Before robot post-training, we report MSE on normalized actions, mean 3D Euclidean position errors for the root and each wrist, and joint-angle MAE for the whole body and legs. After post-training, we report success rates for three household tasks and their mean, with ten real-robot trials per task for each variant.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Awaken-HI, a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation, paired with a large-scale egocentric video dataset (Awaken-Human), directly advancing embodied AI and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
papers.tldr: Awaken-HI scales humanoid loco-manipulation by learning from synchronized human video and whole-body motion, achieving strong transfer to real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Weile Li, Yunfan Lou, Muqing Shi, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Zhibo Pang
bullets: Addresses inconsistent benefits from adding tactile sensing to vision-language-action models.
A tokenizer conditioned on visual observations and executed actions compresses future tactile changes into discrete innovation codes.
TacInno-VLA predicts these codes as an auxiliary training target, adding no deployment-time tactile module.
Achieves 87.5% average success across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks.
Outperforms the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively; ablations support visual/action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of the TacInno tokenizer. The encoder compresses the tactile observations from t to t+15 into the 16-bit code ct, and the decoder reconstructs the future tactile change from Xt and ct. The encoder and the decoder are both conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, so that ct retains tactile innovation (lower left).

Figure 3. Architecture of TacInno-VLA. Tactile tokens and four learnable code queries are inserted into the action expert of π0.5. During training, two auxiliary heads predict the tactile innovation code from the code queries and the current contact state from the tactile tokens. The attention mask (left) prevents all other tokens from attending to the code queries. At deployment (top left), the TacInno tokenizer and both auxiliary heads are removed.

Figure 4. Temporal distribution of tactile innovation on a held-out Lift Can demonstration. The left panel shows, at five time steps, the head-camera image, the tactile change over the next 15 steps, and the components explained by visual observations and executed actions (blue) and by the code (orange). The right panel shows the magnitude of the tactile change (gray), the fraction explained by the code (orange), and the can tilt angle (dashed). The fraction explained by the code peaks before contact onset (a) and at incipient slip (c).

Table 4. Real-world experiments. All policies are trained on the same demonstrations of each task, and we report success rates (%). The visuo-tactile baselines are listed separately from the ablated settings and our method.

Table 1. Comparison of TacInno-VLA and baselines on UniVTAC. All policies are trained on the same 50 demonstrations per task. We report closed-loop success rates (%), with rows sorted by average success rate in ascending order. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results, respectively.

Table 3. Tactile-off test on the two lifting tasks. The first two columns report the relative drop in closed-loop success rate, computed on the same seeds with and without tactile input (100 seeds on Lift Can and 25 on Lift Bottle, except 25 on both tasks for UniVTAC-ACT and 100 on both for N0-VTLA). The last two columns report the relative change in the error of the predicted arm and gripper actions on held-out Lift Can demonstrations. Positive values indicate reliance on tactile input.
Table 2. Ablation study on the two lifting tasks. We report success rates (%). The variant w/o tactile input is the π0.5 of Tab. 1, and every other variant differs from TacInno-VLA in one design.

papers.selection_reason: Tactile-innovation supervision for VLA models in contact-rich manipulation.
papers.title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
papers.tldr: TacInno improves contact-rich manipulation by training VLA models to predict only tactile changes that vision and actions cannot explain, without requiring tactile processing at deployment.

papers.abstract: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output. We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one $\pi_{0.5}$ checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks. The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network. The endpoints do not fit the sink profile. Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers. On 250 paired episodes, masking them or zeroing their values changes success by less than 4 points, and replacing their value directions with those of another observation lowers it by 3.2 to 7.2 points across three donors, whereas the same replacement on two non-endpoint tokens in the executed prefix lowers it by 28.4 points. The token that does fit the sink profile on mass and value norm is the prefix BOS; on this checkpoint, zeroing its value raises success in two paired runs, by +13.2 points (95% CI [+7.0, +19.4]) and +6.0 points ([+0.2, +11.8]). Inside the action chunk, a relative-offset routing profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75% of action-token spread and keeps closed-loop success on three held-out tasks (42.7% against a 38.7% baseline), while uniform or shuffled routing drops success to 3-4%. High attention mass alone does not tell what a token does.
authors: Yuxi Zheng, Yueqian Lin, Yudong Liu, Zijia Tang, Junyu Pan, Yiheng Wang, Hai Helen Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: The study tests the sink interpretation of the first and last action tokens in one π₀.₅ checkpoint, without evaluating the horizon-selection rule.
The endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key attention mass, with excess linked to rotary positional encoding across network depth.
Their value norms remain near the action-token average, and masking or value zeroing changes success by less than 4 percentage points.
Replacing endpoint value directions has a modest effect, while analogous replacement for non-endpoint executed-prefix tokens causes much larger losses.
Relative-offset routing preserves performance on three held-out tasks, whereas uniform or shuffled routing reduces success to 3–4%; prefix BOS more closely matches the sink profile.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes attention structure in flow-based VLA policies for robot manipulation.
papers.title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Endpoint action tokens in a flow-based VLA policy attract slightly elevated attention but do not behave like attention sinks; their functional role is better explained by positional routing.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains. However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging. Heterogeneity in robot embodiments, task formulations, geometric conventions, and action interfaces fragments interaction experience across benchmarks and hardware. We rethink robot skill learning through alignment: Can heterogeneous interactions across benchmarks and embodiments jointly improve one shared skillset for robot manipulation? We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation skills by aligning heterogeneous settings. Specifically, UniCraft represents observed scene geometry using consistent coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots. It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing interaction feedback to jointly refine shared skills and the orchestration policy that guides their selection and composition, without any demonstrations or model weight updates. We interleave tasks from 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments, collecting 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model. During training, UniCraft improves pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks by 9-28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8-13.3 on RoboTwin 2.0, and 3.1-14.4 on RoboCasa365 (Epochs 1-3). After training, with the learned skills frozen, UniCraft demonstrates zero-shot transfer across 4 new robot embodiments and 5 additional agent models on robosuite and RoboDojo.
authors: Ziyue Wang, Yaopeng Yang, Liyi Zhou
bullets: Addresses fragmented robot-learning experience caused by differing embodiments, task formats, geometry conventions, and action interfaces.
Uses consistent scene coordinates, aligned sensing/control interfaces, and a canonical task format to combine interactions across benchmarks.
Jointly refines reusable skills and an orchestration policy without demonstrations or model-weight updates.
Training across 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments improves unseen-task performance across LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365.
Frozen learned skills transfer zero-shot to 4 new embodiments and 5 additional agent models on robosuite and RoboDojo.

(a) Stacked bars show outcome percentages at 1,000–4,000 environment steps, pooling 30 cases with five repeats (150 rollouts) per condition. papers.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.
authors: Zilang Cen, Chao Tang, Fangcheng Liu, Weishi Mi, Wei Hao, JiaYu Xu, Dehao Huang, Yehui Tang, Xiaohui Cui, Tingguang Li, Xiaoyuan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency and token costs of frequent multimodal-model calls during long-horizon manipulation.
Coordinates a low-level policy with a high-level reasoning agent using an online monitor of visual progress and interaction history.
Triggers agent review to repair execution, revise subtasks, or coordinate both, while verified outcomes update memory and transitions.
On RMBench, improves task success by 24.0 percentage points over the strongest agent-based baseline while reducing token use by 65.3%.
Improves task success by 15.1 percentage points over the strongest policy-based baseline and is validated on three real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: One fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is enforcing temporal safety constraints, such as satisfying formal specifications. Existing methods often transform logic formulas into automata for state augmentation and reward shaping. However, this approach assumes that automaton construction is both feasible and tractable, which limits its applicability to small specifications and linear temporal logic (LTL). This paper proposes Actor-Predictor, a framework that learns a surrogate representation of logic progress without explicitly constructing an automaton. The predictor continuously estimates whether a partial trajectory will satisfy the formal specification in a later step, and its learned features are provided as auxiliary inputs to the actor, which is then optimized using GRPO and RWR. We show theoretically that, under sufficient predictive accuracy, the learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state. Experiments on grid world and robotic tasks in Isaac Lab demonstrate that Actor-Predictor outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks. It also performs well on non-regular formal specifications, such as $(a^n b^n)$, for which finite-automaton-based approaches are not applicable.
authors: Josef Brozovich, Qining Zhang, Lei Ying
bullets: Targets temporal safety constraints and the scalability limits of automata-based reward shaping, especially beyond small LTL specifications.
A predictor estimates whether a partial trajectory will eventually satisfy the specification; its features guide an actor trained with GRPO and RWR.
Theoretically, sufficiently accurate predictions yield a representation equivalent to the corresponding automaton state.
Experiments in grid worlds and Isaac Lab robotic tasks show improved performance over automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks.
The framework also handles non-regular specifications such as $(a^n b^n)$, which finite-automaton methods cannot represent.

papers.abstract: LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) on whole-body control. The library couples MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API, exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1. A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while compact JAX implementations of many RL and IL algorithms provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design, the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT at https://github.com/robfiras/loco-mujoco.
authors: Firas Al-Hafez, Davide Tateo, Oleg Kaidanov, Aditya Bhatt, Artur Zelik, Zhengyi Luo, Jan Peters
bullets: Supports 9 humanoid, 3 musculoskeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments in a unified MuJoCo, MJX, and MjWarp API.
Includes curated native motion-capture data for humanoids and supports retargeting from AMASS and LAFAN1.
Provides interchangeable observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization through a plug-in architecture.
Offers compact JAX implementations of RL and IL algorithms with JIT-compiled end-to-end training.
Includes SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting, plus a companion repository for sim-to-real deployment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.
authors: Zheyuan Liu, Chuhan Wang, Jinduo Guo, Yue Huang, Xiangchi Yuan, Ningshan Ma, Meng Jiang
bullets: Initial-state refusal may fail after takeover during task execution, and simply failing to complete a task can still cause physical incidents such as dropping objects.

Joint policy adaptation learns these fallback targets while preserving actions for retained tasks.
On evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduced post-takeover target success to 1.3% with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while maintaining high retained-task success.
The method targets settings where holding is an appropriate fallback response and is evaluated with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid agents in everyday environments are expected to react to diverse cues as humans do, with semantically appropriate and physically executable behaviors. Existing cue-driven reaction generation methods support only a narrow range of cue modalities and are limited to purely kinematic generation, leaving the resulting reactions susceptible to physical artifacts. To this end, we present MixReact, the first unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from text, audio, and video cues, integrating a Discrete--Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT) for state prediction with a History-aware Action Transformer (HAT) for physical execution. DisCo-MoT couples a discrete masked-modeling branch with a continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way mixture attention within a MoT architecture. Guidance from discrete context mitigates collapse into averaged behaviors in one-to-many reaction generation, while direct prediction in continuous state space bypasses the decoding bottleneck of discrete representations. HAT then maps the predicted next state and observed execution history to executable actions, enabling robust closed-loop control in physics-based simulation. Experiments across all three modalities demonstrate consistent improvements over the baselines in fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency, while ablations validate the complementary contributions of the components. Our code will be released to facilitate future research. Project page: https://binlee26.github.io/MixReact_Page/
authors: Bin Li, Xing Zhu, Jingya Wang
bullets: Addresses limited cue modalities and physically implausible artifacts in existing reactive humanoid generation methods.
Uses DisCo-MoT to combine discrete masked modeling with continuous autoregressive diffusion for multimodal next-state prediction.
Employs HAT to convert predicted states and execution history into actions for robust closed-loop physics-based control.
Experiments across text, audio, and video show improved fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency over baselines.
Ablations support the complementary roles of the framework’s components.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MixReact. MCA maps a text, audio, or video cue to the semantic memory C. Within DisCo-MoT, discrete masked modeling samples a complete reaction once, providing cached intermediate keys and values that guide history-conditioned autoregressive diffusion through one-way mixture attention. HAT converts each predicted next state and observed execution history into an executable action, while simulator feedback updates both prediction and control histories.

Figure 7. User study interface. Participants view the input cue alongside generated reactions from different methods and rate each reaction on a five-point scale, ranging from 1 (very poor) to 5 (very good).

papers.abstract: Active urban sensing orchestrates a mobile sensor fleet to proactively inspect a dynamic road network and gather critical information for system management. This problem simultaneously requires understanding the complex spatio-temporal evolution and making decisions with partial observations. In this work, we focus on active sensing in a large-scale urban road network with utilities grounded in dynamic traffic states, while prior work has rarely considered these factors jointly. We propose \emph{SenseAlign}, a Reinforcement Learning-based (RL) framework that learns decision-aligned predictive representations for coordinating an urban sensing drone fleet. SenseAlign first trains a privileged teacher agent that exploits future ground-truth traffic for optimal sensing choices. The student agent has an auxiliary branch that learns to predict future traffic with partial observations, in addition to the RL-trained actor and critic branches. During student learning, our framework matches the action distributions of the teacher under ground-truth and student-predicted future traffic, while keeping the teacher's observations unchanged. Such a design shapes the latent space for decision-making instead of prediction alone. At inference time, the student agent has no overhead as all this learning is done in training. We conduct comprehensive experiments with the real road network of central Barcelona containing 1570 road segments, and demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the baselines on multiple utility formulations. The codebase will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.
bullets: Addresses active sensing in dynamic, large-scale urban road networks where decisions must be made from partial observations.
Uses a privileged RL teacher with future traffic information and a student with prediction, actor, and critic branches.

At inference, the student incurs no additional prediction overhead.
Experiments on central Barcelona’s 1,570-road-segment network show consistent gains over baselines across multiple utility formulations.

papers.abstract: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution. Effective action generation therefore requires not only modeling object dynamics but also anticipating how future interactions will shape task progress. To this end, we propose \textbf{PhysVAM}, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model that represents anticipated interactions through their effects on future task progress. This value-based formulation provides task-directed foresight without reconstructing future visual states. Conditioned on current observations and historical object and robot motion, PhysVAM jointly learns action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch learns horizon-specific latent representations through future task-value prediction from successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that facilitate task success. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior task success, with absolute success-rate improvements of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines in simulation and real-world tasks, respectively. Project page: https://metarobo.github.io/physvam.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.
authors: Zhengtu Liang, Qiwei Liang, Tao Lin, Shihang Weng, Boyang Cai, Xiangyu Chen, Yikeng Chen, Jiaming Liang, Bohan Tan, Yu Yan, Renjing Xu
bullets: Flow-matching policies face different challenges when recovering noisy actions versus refining nearly clean ones.
Endpoint prediction is more stable at high noise, while velocity prediction provides more accurate corrections near clean actions.
UniVEP jointly trains both targets with consistency supervision and switches between them during inference, using one network run per step.
It improves success and efficiency in simulated and real-world manipulation; on RoboTwin, one StarVLA run reaches 61.36% success versus 59.96% for the best single-target baseline using 16 runs.
With LiLa-WAM, two UniVEP runs outperform the best 16-step single-target baseline while reducing inference latency by 77.1%.

papers.abstract: Artificial Spiking Neural Networks have gained remarkable attention in the last few years due to their proven ability in simulating biological neural cultures and producing similar activity and trends. Nevertheless, whether they can be trained for humanoid locomotion while retaining biological plausibility and robust performance at once remains an open question. We study this problem by proposing a biologically inspired spiking network, trained by different learning schemes and tested on the H1-2 Unitree Humanoid. These schemes differ in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear readout is trained, the same network but with its synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and finally backpropagation through time as a non biological baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. We show that e-prop reached 100% survival rate matching backpropagation through time, whereas both the fixed reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We explore in further detail which trends a real culture could and could not produce until now. Finally we demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on a full size humanoid H1-2.
authors: Fatima Atwi (LAAS-GEPETTO, Nantes Univ - ECN), Constant Roux (LAAS-GEPETTO), Christian Bergaud (LAAS-MEMS), Olivier Stasse (LAAS-GEPETTO)

E-prop achieved 100% survival, matching backpropagation through time; the fixed reservoir and reward-modulated STDP reached about 43.7% and 11%.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but \emph {object-mediated} locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot--board locomotion.
authors: Ganeshvar Soenessardien, Michael Przystupa, Kevin Sebastian Luck
bullets: Addresses object-mediated locomotion requiring coordination with both the ground and a passive skateboard.

The changing prevalence of terminations implicitly progresses learning from stance control to sustained robot–board locomotion.
Demonstrated on a K1 humanoid, with no specific quantitative results reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson's ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young's modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.
authors: Haoqin Hong, Ding Fan, Fubin Dou, Tianyu Huang, Yuzhuo Chen, Zhemeng Zhang, Hanxiao Jiang, Congcong Zhu, Gerhard Petrus Hancke, Jingrun Chen, Rynson WH Lau
bullets: Addresses the limitation that matching observed video motion may not yield correct responses to new forces, especially in spring-based models coupling volume and shape changes.
Enriches local deformation modes while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation.
Uses offline calibration to translate shared relative response edits into stiffness updates for interpretable material editing and transfer.
On synthetic scenes, reduces Poisson’s-ratio error by 75.8% and Young’s-modulus relative error by 22.1% versus PhysTwin.
A new egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark and real-world tests show improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error at interactive speeds.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MorphTwin, a method for reconstructing interactive physical twins from video by enriching local deformation modes, which is relevant to simulation-based manipulation and 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: MorphTwin: Enriching Deformable Material Responses from Videos for Morphable and Interactive Physical Twins
papers.tldr: MorphTwin reconstructs deformable physical twins from video with independently controllable deformation responses, improving material accuracy and future-motion prediction over PhysTwin.

papers.abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.
authors: Dong An, Tianyu Liu, Haoran Ding, Wen Yang, Anqing Duan, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Problem: Video world models often follow robot actions but predict inconsistent or collapsed object motion because scene dynamics and appearance are inferred together.
Method: Lift the initial frame into 3D points, predict their response to robot motion with a learned dynamics model, then render the simulated points into pixel-aligned videos for a video model.
Results: Object-motion error decreases by 8.6% and 6.2% with two DROID video renderers, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot, without reducing image quality.
The rendered video tracks the simulated dynamics: better point predictions produce better object motion, while editing points can steer the generated video.
Scope: Results are demonstrated in controlled DROID experiments and on a real bimanual robot.

papers.selection_reason: Separates dynamics prediction from visual rendering in robotic world models by using 3D point dynamics as a proxy, significantly improving object motion accuracy in simulation and real-world manipulation.
papers.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: A 3D point-dynamics proxy separates robot interaction modeling from video rendering, improving manipulated-object motion while preserving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.
authors: Nico Leuze, Samed Dogan, Maximilian Hoh, Henry Schaub, Alfred Sch\"ottl
bullets: Reconstructs millimeter-precision 3D space and uses staged heatmaps to remove background points.
Predicts object classes, translation offsets, and rotations at high resolution for multiple objects in one pass.
Uses canonical-coordinate voting with confidence-weighted, symmetry-aware Procrustes pose recovery, avoiding costly post-processing.
Introduces attention-gated knowledge distillation guided by task-supervised heatmap priors.
Reports 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene on IPD, 96.1 ADD-S on MV-YCB, and competitive performance on densely packed ROBI bins.

The translation votes uj naturally form clusters. Along class predictions, these gate a FiLM-conditioned canonical-coordinate head, and one single batched symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve returns 6D poses [(R̂k, t̂k)].

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on 6D pose estimation for robotic bin picking, a core manipulation task in embodied AI, utilizing sparse multi-view RGB-D data.
papers.title: SCCV-6D: Sparse Canonical Coordinate Voting for Holistic Multi-View RGB-D 6D Pose Estimation in Robotic Bin Picking

papers.abstract: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: https://www.jinkuncao.com/FAB.
bullets: Predicts dense 2D/3D body points and an MHR representation, then fits SMPL with one learned pass and two Gauss–Newton steps.
FAB-L runs from detection to fitted body 4.6× faster than SAM 3D Body’s eager-PyTorch body-only path on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks.
Estimates foot, hand, and knee contacts to align the body with static scene geometry and support world-space motion recovery.
FAB-Retarget transfers motion to a Unitree G1 using dense points or fitted meshes, producing closer-following references than several specialized retargeters and an IK-based SAM 3D Body pipeline.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.

papers.abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.

State-indexed targets enable cross-episode context-goal composition.
Achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach on 1,000 TEST Cube trials; predictive ranking improves matched PushT success from 4.7% to 44.9% and TwoRoom from 33.8% to 77.7%.

papers.abstract: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.

bullets: Addresses the problem of physical properties becoming unobservable in later frames while still affecting future actions.

On distracted Two-Stage PushT, improves terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA.
Achieves the lowest mean physical readout error across six models and two seeds, reducing distractor-induced along-push MAE by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA.

papers.abstract: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Chenyuan Zhou, Chaoyi Huang, Zibo Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Yong-Lu Li
bullets: Addresses cross-tool manipulation by identifying geometric features shared across tools with similar functions.
Uses an embodied agent to reconstruct demonstrations in simulation, form and test affordance hypotheses, and refine extraction skills.
Encodes discovered functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone for training and inference.
Builds a reusable affordance-extraction skill library for unseen tools.
Achieves 86.1% simulated cross-tool trajectory-retargeting success and improves real-robot task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$ across three tasks.

(b) Encoded functional-region features join image, language, and robot-state tokens to condition the π0.5 action expert. It iteratively denoises action tokens, decoded into robot actions and an auxiliary affordance trajectory.

(a) The initial region on the target tool misses the ring. (b) The agent tests alternative contact locations and orientations. In Test 1, the selected region fails to enter the ring; in Test 2, the forward-tilted hook region allows the ring to slide off during lifting; Test 3 retains the ring. (c) The refined skill selects a flat or gently concave hook region near the tool tip and keeps it nearly horizontal throughout the lift.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD)}, a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by $3.5$ points on NavTest and $5.0$ points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.
authors: Chengkai Xu, Yicheng Guo, Jiaqi Liu, Yiming Cui, Shiyu Fang, Peng Hang, Hao Zhang, Jian Sun
bullets: Addresses the problem that more demonstrations may be redundant or harmful, and that data value differs across planners.

Controlled group-removal experiments support the directional fidelity of PAD’s valuations.
Candidate rankings vary substantially across planner families, highlighting the need for policy-aware curation.
Policy-specific curation improves EPDMS and consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across multiple planner types while reducing scene-level regressions.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
authors: Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: WAMs are costly because they combine video generation with action prediction using large transformers.
A shared six-block core is recurrently applied to execute 30 layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert; video and action experts use different depths.
Elastic self-distillation trains one checkpoint to support varied action-depth and sampling-step budgets.
The 0.58B-parameter model reports 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, with 7.4× lower peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched measurements.
On real hardware, it achieved 71.3% success over 80 trials; performance degrades when action depth is aggressively reduced without budget-aware training.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities. Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution: parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy. Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation. To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block's input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert's computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts' linear outputs. A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers. The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four $\pi_{0.5}$ specialists and achieves 77.83% success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Wenshuo Chen, Honglei Jin, Le Yang, Jianfei Song, Shaofeng Liang, Lei Wang, Junze Zhu, Kailong Wang, Zhengxi Jin, Haozhe Jia, Honglin Chu, Songning Lai, Xiucheng Wang, Yutao Yue

On LIBERO, merging four π₀.₅ specialists achieves 77.83% success over 1,200 episodes, outperforming prior baselines reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses the failure of robot policies to compose reliable atomic skills over long-horizon tasks.
A VLM observes camera images and provides the next step in the policy’s instruction format; successful rollouts are relabeled and used for fine-tuning.
On stalled states, next-step coaching increases subgoal completion by 4.6× over the original task instruction.
Unassisted success on unseen long-horizon scenes improves from 47.4% to 59.3%, outperforming human-demonstration and self-collected-success fine-tuning at equal data budgets.
The action backbone remains frozen; the approach is scoped to leveraging existing skills through language guidance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CoachSI. (a) Coached collection. The policy weights are fixed and every action is the policy’s own. (b) Hindsight relabeling and fine-tuning. Successful rollouts keep their observations and actions, and ℓt is replaced by g. Fine-tuning mixes them with human demonstrations and updates only the video backbone. (c) Deployment. The fine-tuned policy receives observations and g alone, with no coach. Each square is one action chunk, colored by the instruction the policy receives; ticks mark completed subgoals. The example is one long-horizon task: alone, the pretrained policy completes the first subgoal and stalls; with the coach, it completes the task; after fine-tuning, it completes the task in an unseen scene without the coach.

papers.abstract: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSEPose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerancedilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.
authors: Junghoon Seo, Hakjin Lee, Jaehoon Sim
bullets: Addresses mesh-dependent reconstruction targets for unseen object instances from partial RGB-D observations.

On REAL275 and HouseCat6D, closely matches surface-based supervision and remains stable across boundary perturbations and viewpoints.
Supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across both benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Deficits in reactive balance can increase fall risk among older adults and individuals with neuromuscular impairments, motivating the need for interventions that improve balance recovery. Wearable robotic exoskeletons offer a promising approach to addressing this need by augmenting balance control. However, developing controllers that deliver appropriately timed and scaled assistance remains challenging, as evaluating each candidate strategy requires repeated exposure to destabilizing perturbations. We propose a simulation-to-real framework that combines motion imitation and reinforcement learning to develop balance-assistive ankle exoskeleton control. A muscle-driven neuromusculoskeletal model was trained using a small set of motion-capture data from a single subject to reproduce kinematic and kinetic responses to backward-translation perturbations. This model served as a virtual human for training a reinforcement-learning exoskeleton controller. The resulting controller generated bilateral ankle assistance using only inertial sensor measurements, without explicit perturbation detection. We implemented the controller on-board a bilateral ankle exoskeleton and evaluated it in five healthy subjects whose data were not used for training. Assistance increased the perturbation magnitude that subjects could withstand without stepping by 11.8% and reduced peak center-of-mass displacement and velocity by 13.5% and 28.2%, respectively. Individual benefits varied with baseline recovery strategy and body mass. These results indicate that a single virtual human can yield transferable balance assistance, and that more diverse virtual humans could further improve its effectiveness.
bullets: Targets fall risk caused by impaired reactive balance and the challenge of tuning assistance without repeated physical perturbations.
Combines motion imitation with reinforcement learning in a muscle-driven neuromusculoskeletal simulation.
Uses only inertial sensors and requires no explicit perturbation detection to generate bilateral ankle assistance.
In five untrained healthy subjects, assistance increased no-step perturbation tolerance by 11.8% and reduced peak center-of-mass displacement and velocity by 13.5% and 28.2%.
Benefits varied with individuals’ baseline recovery strategies and body mass; broader virtual-human diversity may improve effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Physical AI requires models that understand spatial relationships and dynamic environments and translate observations into actions under limited onboard compute. We present TuringPAI, a family of models for on-device Physical AI comprising TuringPAI-VL for shared vision-language understanding, TuringPAI-Drive for autonomous driving, and TuringPAI-Embodied for robotic manipulation. TuringPAI-VL is a 0.65B model built on HybridViT-MLQ, which combines convolutional local aggregation with Transformer-based global modeling. Multi-scale Latent Queries integrate spatial features and observation history within the same visual Transformer, providing a compact, structured interface to the language model. Training combines general vision-language data with geometric, cross-view, and temporal supervision. TuringPAI-VL supports general multimodal understanding and improves quantitative geometric perception over Qwen2-VL-2B, while providing a shared initialization for the two downstream VLA models. For autonomous driving, TuringPAI-Drive maintains all evaluated ADE/FDE metrics within 1.2\% of a full-token HybridViT baseline using the MLQ interface and achieves comparable aggregate scores in an in-house simulation evaluation. Using XPeng Native Runtime (XNRT) on a single NVIDIA Orin-X SoC, TuringPAI-Drive generates trajectories at 12\,Hz in on-vehicle operation. For robotic manipulation, TuringPAI-Embodied achieves a 96.8\% average success rate across the four LIBERO suites. These results demonstrate a shared vision-language foundation for driving and robotic manipulation under practical on-device constraints.
authors: Qiman Wu, Hanlin Chen, Yuhua Wei, Mingyuan Wang, Shaman Tang, Minghao Li, Rui Xin, Xingye Liu, Zhichao Yang, Yiqi Yu, Hongyan Pei, Xiaowen Tian, YingYing Liu, Shiwen Liu, Jiahui Hu, Yizhao Wang, Yuheng Zhang, Anhua Liu, Yue He, Shuang Su, Da Zhu, Hua Zhou, Pengfei Diao, Haojie Yang, Weichao Huang, Hang Zhang, Honggou Yang, Xianming Liu

papers.abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
authors: Linfeng Dong, Jianwei Niu, Jiuyi Zhao, Ruibing Feng, Xinghao Wu, Wu Yang, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu, Mu Li

A flow-matching action expert uses the latent memory while Perception Attention directly grounds actions in the current view.
Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions to reduce inference cost for long histories.
Achieves strong simulated and real-world performance, including 68.8% average success on real-world memory tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ActMem. (b) Inside the backbone, the subtask tokens that form Memory CoT follow the history and the current view in the sequence, so under the causal mask they read both, and their hidden states become Ct; the action expert receives only Ct, not the history tokens. (c) Efficient Memory CoT Inference. Consecutive decisions usually share the same subtask, so the previous subtask is reused as a draft and verified against the updated context in a single parallel pass. If it is accepted, its hidden states are recomputed to give the new Ct, with no token-by-token decoding.
