papers.abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and fragmented, model-specific training stacks of embodied models.
Uses a common abstraction layer to share infrastructure without restricting model architectures or execution requirements.
Combines reusable and hardware-aware optimizations spanning computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8 communication for DDP/FSDP.
Also provides unified data infrastructure, egocentric-to-robot data synthesis, and concurrent simulator evaluation.
Reports 1.47×–4.38× higher training throughput and 4.1×–23.2× faster evaluation than corresponding open-source baselines.

papers.abstract: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.
authors: Xinzhe Fu, Qi Shao, Yuanfei Xie, Taoyu Wu, Zhihao Cao, Long Hu, Hong Liang, Xianzhi Li, Anh Nguyen, Baoru Huang, Rongsheng Li
bullets: Addresses missing and corrupted depth caused by specular reflection and refraction in transparent-object RGB-D images.
Builds coordinate-aware global and local multi-range inverse-depth hypotheses around a prior-guided prediction.
Uses recurrent refinement with out-of-bounds masking and validity-aware fusion, followed by spatially gated residual correction.
Reportedly achieves lower error than several prior methods across five datasets.
Real-robot evaluations show improved surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of MIR-Depth. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model provides the relative-depth prior. Transformer and CNN encoders extract RGB-mask, relative-depth, and raw-depth features, which are summed at each scale. The summed features provide multi-scale context, while a decoder and depth head predict initial depth D0. Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses construct one shared global inverse-depth volume aggregated by a 3D hourglass alongside medium and fine pixel-wise local volumes filtered by depth-axis convolutions. Selective Recurrent Refinement queries these volumes, encodes lookup features together with per-offset validity indicators, and fuses active ranges to update inverse depth through a multi-scale ConvGRU. Spatially Gated Correction weights the full-resolution residual relative to D0 to produce completed depth for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Dongheon Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: At least 96% of observed failures are stalls: the object remains stationary while the model predicts progress.
Stalls arise both with and without distribution shift, challenging the attribution of failures solely to model error.
Unstick combines on-policy fine-tuning with a fixed-weight loop breaker: prediction-error memory or random re-initialization at each replan.
Residual memory recovers most adaptation gains on pushing tasks; re-initialization works well for shape shifts but less for visual shifts.
The findings identify planning-loop fixed points as a major limitation of warm-started gradient-descent planners.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor
authors: Zexun Lin, Yuan Feng, Xike Xie
bullets: WAMs incur high latency from multi-step denoising during robotic control.
The method addresses dual nonuniformity: velocity residuals vary sharply across denoising stages, and integration step sizes unevenly amplify state errors.
It derives a trajectory error tolerance bound linking velocity residuals and integration steps to final action-distribution error.
WAMotor selects reliable anchor velocities, delays speculation when needed, and uses integration-step-aware verification thresholds.
Evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show 2.86×–4.28× speedups with maintained success rates.

papers.title: WAMotor: Accelerating World Action Models via Speculative Inference under Dual Nonuniform Denoising Dynamics

papers.abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to handle distribution shifts during deployment without source-domain retraining. However, backpropagation-based adaptation incurs heavy memory overhead on resource-constrained robots, whereas zeroth-order (ZO) methods suffer from high estimation variance under limited perturbation budgets. We observe that while ZO estimation enables low-memory adaptation with rapid initial gains, it often stalls or degrades over long-horizon updates due to noisy gradient estimates. To address these limitations, we propose Dune, a zeroth-order optimizer that stabilizes long-horizon adaptation by coupling online historical error prediction with current perturbation observations. Specifically, Dune learns a lightweight, time-conditioned error predictor from past optimization dynamics and fuses its predictions with instantaneous ZO estimates, achieving effective variance reduction without backpropagation or extra forward passes. Additionally, we theoretically characterize how estimation variance restricts convergence in high-dimensional, small-population regimes, motivating the use of historical statistics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO and real-world robots demonstrate that Dune achieves superior success rates under a low memory footprint, with ablations confirming improved closed-loop stability and post-disturbance recovery.
authors: Chengyang Dong, Ze Chen, Kai Ye, Chutian Wang, Heng Xu, Wei Mo, Maomao Li, Jiayan Xu, Jiayuan Wu, Yihao Xiao, Linhua Ye, Zhonghua Peng, Ruize Han, Jialong Sun
bullets: Targets VLA adaptation under deployment distribution shifts without source-domain retraining.
Addresses zeroth-order estimation noise, which can cause long-horizon adaptation to stall or degrade.
Uses a lightweight online historical error predictor fused with instantaneous zeroth-order estimates, without backpropagation or extra forward passes.
Theory links estimation variance to convergence limits in high-dimensional, small-population settings.
Experiments on LIBERO and real robots report higher success rates, improved closed-loop stability, and better post-disturbance recovery under low memory.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window's value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.
authors: Dijia Zhan, Jinyi Li, Xuemiao Xu, Yan Zhou, Yu Liu, Shaoshan Liu, Jie Tang
bullets: Demonstration windows differ in supervision value, and that value changes during training.
Periodically scores temporal windows with five policy-native signals and updates sampling weights.
Prioritizes informative, learnable windows without changing the policy architecture, objective, or inference cost.
Across ten LIBERO-Plus tasks, reaches 76.1% success under visual perturbations and 81.3% in clean scenes, outperforming the reported Uniform and FAKTUAL baselines.
Scope: evaluated on LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks and focused on adaptive data sampling.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a lightweight policy model to mitigate the difficulty of handling higher-dimensional action spaces in reinforcement learning (RL), alongside an algorithm to effectively train it. To address this, we focus on drifting models, which can implicitly represent complex distributions and infer actions in a single forward pass. However, while drifting models can be straightforwardly trained via backpropagation of the Q-gradient, this alone cannot be expected to appropriately capture the desired action coordination. Therefore, this paper constructs a three-step learning algorithm to encourage the action coordination. First, the source distribution of the drifting model is co-optimized as a diagonal policy model. This conditions the drifting model to attach the coordination, which cannot be expressed by a diagonal distribution, as residuals. Second, a discriminator model before and after drifting is introduced with adversarial training for a regularization term. This actively promotes the extraction of the coordination that fundamentally separates the two distributions. Third, best-of-N sampling is applied for action selection during rollouts in order to give directionality toward/beyond the regions where the coordination is insufficiently extracted/sufficiently discovered. The proposed method consistently improves the sample efficiency and the final control performance over the conventional diagonal distribution modeling across three locomotion tasks with high-dimensional action spaces. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that this improvement is achieved by reducing variance in certain action dimensions, effectively coupling them with other actions as action coordination.
bullets: High-dimensional actions are difficult to coordinate when modeled with conventional diagonal distributions.
The method uses a drifting model that represents complex action distributions and generates actions in one forward pass.
Training combines co-optimization of a diagonal source policy, adversarial discrimination before and after drifting, and best-of-N rollout sampling.
Across three high-dimensional locomotion tasks, it consistently improves sample efficiency and final control performance over diagonal modeling.
Analysis attributes the gains to reduced variance in some action dimensions and stronger coupling among actions.

papers.abstract: The success of manipulation policies is closely tied to the spatial relationship between the robot and the target object, as well as the task being performed, making the ability to adjust the robot's pose critical for successful execution. When the robot starts away from the task, such adjustments require coordinating navigation with local manipulation. Jointly training these capabilities incurs substantial computational and data costs, while navigating toward a predefined goal pose limits the flexibility needed to adapt to task-specific manipulation requirements. To address these challenges, we propose Learning to Move from and for Manipulation Policies (M4M), a framework that learns manipulation-aware mobility directly from pretrained manipulation policies. By leveraging the hidden representations of the policy's action-generating network as dense supervision, together with a limited number of manipulation execution outcomes, we learn a spatially conditioned embedding that captures task-dependent manipulation success across candidate robot poses. From the robot's current stereo observations, this representation estimates manipulation success at unvisited poses without rolling out the manipulation policy at each location. It is further integrated into navigation policy training, while a learned handoff policy decides when to transition from navigation to manipulation, enabling the robot to move and manipulate in a unified, task-aware manner. Across eight articulated-object tasks in unseen RoboCasa kitchens, M4M achieves 47.0% mean task success, compared with 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation execution, and refrigerator-closing experiments show consistent improvements across four frozen manipulation policies.
authors: Siyuan Zheng, Zhong Cao, Henry X. Liu
bullets: Addresses the need to coordinate navigation and manipulation when the robot starts away from the task, while reducing the cost of jointly training both capabilities.
Uses hidden action-policy representations and limited manipulation outcomes to learn a spatially conditioned embedding of manipulation success across robot poses.
Predicts success at unvisited poses from stereo observations without executing the manipulation policy at every location.
Integrates the learned representation into navigation and uses a handoff policy to decide when to switch to manipulation.

Achieves 47.0% mean success across eight unseen RoboCasa kitchen tasks, versus 26.5% for the strongest baseline and 19.2% for direct manipulation; refrigerator-closing tests improve across four frozen policies.

papers.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Shaowei Liu, Albert J. Zhai, Henry Che, Wei-Chiu Ma, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling heterogeneous physical interactions in robotics.
Assigns distinct motion experts to rigid, deformable, and prehensile physical regimes.
Trains on mixed simulation and real-world data and integrates with Model Predictive Control.
Improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes and strengthens real-world MPC performance.

Figure 4: Model Predictive Control (MPC) performance. (a) Box pushing and (b) toy manipulation results. Each section details the prediction error across planning steps (left) and success rate vs. error threshold (right). MoRE achieves lower error and higher success than the baselines.

papers.abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.
authors: Clinton Enwerem, Saleh Kemal, John S. Baras, Calin Belta
bullets: Residual reinforcement learning adapts an imitation policy under a limited environment-interaction budget.
The method separates a phase’s failure frequency from its impact on full-task completion by estimating completion gain from paired episodes.
Positive gain estimates select which action components to correct and how to distribute training episodes across phases.
In docking and bimanual assembly simulations, gain-based allocation targeted phases that were not always the most failure-prone and improved completion.
A release-phase residual policy improved held-out completion from release-start states by 16.9% in one assembly configuration.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.
authors: Qianzhong Chen, Muyuan Lin, Yuyin Sun, Mac Schwager, Cheng-Hao Kuo, Roberto Mart\'in-Mart\'in
bullets: Addresses unsafe real-world exploration and simulator exploitation of residual sim-to-real gaps.
Uses simulated play data to improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction in an action-conditioned video world model.
Aligns the world model with deployment observations using 20 autonomous real-robot rollouts per task, without teleoperation.
Forms a closed-loop RL environment from the VLA, whole-body controller, and video world model with dense progress rewards.
Across three real-robot tasks, video-world-model RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, versus 48.3% for real-robot RL.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
bullets: Addresses the lack of grounded scene-change reasoning in VLM-generated multi-step manipulation plans and the inefficiency and drift of pixel-level world models.
Imagines candidate plans in DINOv2 feature space using a flow-matching world model with action cross-attention and causal temporal history.
A dual-head critic evaluates imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before robot execution.
On six language-conditioned tasks, it achieved 83.3% success, outperforming the reported latent-world-model, VLM-only, and pixel-diffusion baselines.

All executed plans were verified successfully; remaining failures came from low-level grasp or placement slips, while simulation results showed strong CALVIN and cluttered nut-assembly performance with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Verify2Act overview. Stage 1: a VLM proposes candidate multi-step plans from the camera observation and the language instruction. Stage 2: V2A-WM rolls out each candidate in the frozen DINOv2 latent space (St → St+k), conditioned on CLIP action tokens. Stage 3: a goal head scores the terminal latent state against the goal, and a temporal consistency head checks consecutive imagined states; the best verified plan is executed.

Fig. 4. Results on the robot. (a) Task success per task and averaged over tasks. (b) Outcome of the episodes of each method: success, execution failure (the plan was correct but a skill failed), or planning failure (the executed plan could not satisfy the goal).

Fig. 2. V2A-WM training and inference. Inference: a single Euler step integrates from noise z0 to z1 = z0 + v̂, and the delta decoder reconstructs Ŝt+1 = St + fdec(z1).

papers.abstract: Ferrofluids are liquids containing magnetic nanoparticles, enabling shape control through external magnetic fields. This deformability supports their use as soft robotic bodies that can navigate confined spaces and manipulate objects. Their nonlinear continuum dynamics, however, make reliable control challenging. Existing work shows how spatial magnetic fields from electromagnet arrays can establish and maintain desired ferrofluid configurations. A complementary objective is to exploit the fluid's dynamics under limited actuation to reach prescribed shapes that may not be sustainable at equilibrium. Here, we use deep model-based reinforcement learning to control these transient shapes. Learning directly through physical interaction, our policies select current commands for a single fixed electromagnet based on visual observations, guiding the moving ferrofluid toward prescribed geometries. The learned policies repeatedly attain a variety of shapes spanning polygons, asterisks and pentominoes. These results demonstrate that learning directly from physical interaction enables reliable fluid shaping, opening new possibilities for controlling ferrofluid-based soft robots.

papers.abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/
authors: Arthur Bucker, Pramod Anantharam, Jonathan Francis, Jean Oh
bullets: Addresses OOD failures caused by scarce, multimodal robotics data and policy overfitting to small distribution shifts.
Combines LVM/VLM semantic reasoning with object-relational distance pairs along meaningful geometric axes to form task-specific guidance.
Transfers motion patterns from successful in-distribution rollouts without retraining the policy.
Works in simulation for pose and task-goal shifts and on a real robot for cable placement and unseen-object steering.
In reported experiments, it more than doubled success one grid step outside training positions and nearly eliminated object confusion when steering toward unseen objects.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our visual-geometric policy steering framework. Offline analysis (at task initialization, once per episode): (1) we retrieve the most relevant successful in-distribution rollout τ∗ by weighted image (DINOv2) and text (CLIP) similarity; (2) a VLM selects the task-relevant object-relational distance pairs per motion phase (e.g., gripper–cube distance d1, cube–table distance d2, gripper orientation θ), evaluated per timestep into the reference trends Φ; (3) a VLM with SAM2 matches the demonstration objects to the live OOD scene (e.g., the cylinder takes the cube’s role), re-targeting each pair. Online steering (every action chunk): (4) perception projects the live scene into the same distance space and aligns each pair to Φ within a window, giving the reference d∗. At every denoising step, a differentiable dynamics model F forecasts the features d(A) of a candidate chunk A, and a line-searched gradient step on the trajectory loss corrects the frozen policy’s velocity field, yielding the steered chunk A′.

papers.abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

papers.abstract: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.
authors: Zirui Song, Jiadong Zhang, Zheng Lu, Xiaosong Ma, Xiaojun Chang, Xiuying Chen

The study recommends testing both incomplete executions and valid task completions that differ from expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Long-horizon planning suffers from compounding prediction errors and weak guidance from distant goal similarity.

Across manipulation, navigation, and reaching tasks, GEMS achieves success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World.
The method outperforms evaluated world-model planning baselines, while relying on a frozen world model.

papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

Ablations show cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision are important for coordination.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce \textbf{HINT-WAM}, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline expert-trajectory training and reliable execution on a model’s self-generated states.
Uses the demonstration’s future video as privileged hindsight for a teacher, while the student receives only deployment-time observations.
Applies on-policy self-distillation along the student’s denoising trajectories to provide dense action targets.
Uses an energy-score, distribution-level objective to transfer the teacher’s action distribution to a flow-matching action expert.
The abstract presents the framework and motivation but reports no quantitative experimental results or explicit limitations.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human recordings are far cheaper than dexterous robot demonstrations, promising stronger pretraining and direct skill learning without task-specific robot data. Yet humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics, so human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies, providing only retargeted end-effector (EEF) actions. This raises two questions: how human data should supervise the policy, and how a dexterous robot should read out actions at deployment. We address both in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), a vision-language-action (VLA) model whose backbone predicts discrete action tokens of EEF chunks as an auxiliary task, while a shared flow-matching expert outputs two executable streams, EEF and joint. On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, a matched study shows that discrete supervision helps learn from human data, driving backbone gradients and shaping action-informative representations across domains. Under standard control pipelines at deployment, direct joint readout excels at fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, scoring 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for π0.5, whereas IK-based EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE learns new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.
bullets: Human recordings provide useful visual and action information but lack robot joint positions and actuator commands.
A VLA backbone predicts discrete EEF action chunks, while a shared flow-matching expert produces executable EEF and joint streams.
Discrete supervision drives informative cross-domain representations and improves learning from human data.
Joint readout is effective for fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, while IK-based EEF readout better supports human-to-robot transfer.
The method can learn new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.

papers.abstract: Freely swiveling casters are widely adopted in industrial AMRs/SDVs for their mechanical simplicity and load capacity. However, caster misalignment during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers induces strong contact nonlinearities, widening the planning-execution gap between commanded $(v, ω)$ and realized motion. Existing caster-aware strategies are highly sensitive to state-estimation reliability, causing unstable execution in uncertain transition regimes. To address this, we present Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control (MSC), a planning-execution integrated hierarchical framework featuring two core mechanisms. First, an uncertainty-aware NMPC (CU-MPC) dynamically schedules caster-aware costs and input regularization using predictive uncertainty to suppress overly aggressive maneuvers. Second, a reinforcement learning-based execution layer estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability, transforming high-level velocity commands into physically executable wheel speeds adapted to current contact conditions. Validations in Isaac Sim and real robots demonstrate that MSC offers a clear comparative advantage over existing decoupled compensation approaches by significantly improving caster-state estimation accuracy, minimizing misalignment, and enhancing tracking robustness in caster-sensitive maneuvers.
bullets: Addresses planning–execution gaps caused by caster misalignment and nonlinear contact effects during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers.
Uses predictive uncertainty to adapt caster-aware costs and input regularization, discouraging overly aggressive commands.
Employs an RL execution layer to estimate and predict caster states under partial observability and convert velocity commands into executable wheel speeds.
Validated in Isaac Sim and on real robots, with improved caster-state estimation, reduced misalignment, and more robust tracking than decoupled compensation approaches.

This hierarchical integration mitigates the planning–execution gap arising from caster-induced contact nonlinearities.

papers.abstract: Haptic shared control in surgical robotics combines human-side and robot-side forces at a shared end effector while preserving operator involvement. However, the effects of geometric safety choices on task execution and force coordination remain unclear. We model the interaction as a two-agent cooperative Markov game under centralized training and decentralized execution, comparing learned human control with a task-tuned fixed-impedance baseline. This model-free multi-agent reinforcement learning framework supports joint policy adaptation without requiring a complete analytical interaction model. It compares MADDPG and rMAPPO with an epigraph-constrained approach under common geometric task definitions. In simulation, rMAPPO generally achieved the highest return and tracking performance, whereas the epigraph approach produced more conservative motions and lower geometric exposure, including no observed collision or dangerous-region exposure after geometry transfer. With real operator input, fixed-impedance-trained policies were faster and successful in all recorded trials. Policies trained with a learned partner exhibited greater command opposition, while the fixed epigraph condition produced the most aligned commands. This work provides a benchmark for studying human-control representation and constraint-handling trade-offs in haptic shared control.
bullets: Models human–robot interaction as a cooperative Markov game with centralized training and decentralized execution.
Compares MADDPG, rMAPPO, and an epigraph-constrained method against a fixed-impedance baseline.
In simulation, rMAPPO generally delivered the best return and tracking, while the epigraph method produced more conservative, lower-exposure motions.
With real operator input, fixed-impedance-trained policies were fastest and succeeded in all recorded trials; fixed epigraph control yielded the most aligned commands.
Provides a benchmark for studying human-control representations and constraint handling in haptic shared control.

papers.abstract: Training humanoid robots to learn human behaviors requires expensive data collection, and human-robot interaction data can be even more difficult and costly to collect. Training a specialized reaction model for each humanoid embodiment can also be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Human-to-humanoid motion retargeting provides a more scalable alternative, allowing human-human reaction data to serve as a common motion representation for different humanoid embodiments. However, due to morphological and kinematic differences between humans and humanoid robots, a reaction preferred in human motion space may not be the most suitable one for execution on a particular robot embodiment. In this work, we propose an inference-time reaction search framework that leverages stochastic sampling from a generative reaction model and jointly considers reaction quality and humanoid embodiment feasibility. Given the observed interaction, our framework generates multiple plausible reaction candidates. Each candidate is retargeted to the target humanoid and evaluated using complementary interaction and embodiment-specific feasibility criteria, allowing candidate selection under the physical constraints of the target embodiment. Since the reaction generator remains frozen, the framework can adapt to different humanoid embodiments at inference time without retraining. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework maintains overall human reaction quality while improving the feasibility of retargeted humanoid reactions across different embodiments. The proposed pipeline improves humanoid retargeting feasibility by 1.61%. Moreover, human-space and G1 best-candidate selections disagree in 78.98% of samples, demonstrating substantial embodiment dependence. Code will be released.
bullets: Human-preferred reactions may be unsuitable after retargeting because humanoids differ in morphology and kinematics.
The framework samples multiple reactions from a frozen generative model, retargets them, and scores interaction quality alongside embodiment-specific feasibility.
It adapts reaction selection to different humanoid embodiments entirely at inference time.
Experiments report a 1.61% improvement in retargeting feasibility while maintaining overall human reaction quality.
Human-space and G1-specific best choices disagree in 78.98% of samples, highlighting strong embodiment dependence.

papers.abstract: Reliable manipulation requires policies that generalize across tasks, layouts, and object interactions. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained multimodal understanding with learned control, but their performance remains limited on unfamiliar task compositions. We present Axiom-0, a VLA policy that addresses both the quality of its representations and their use in action generation through hierarchical self-refinement. Intra-VLM Representation Refinement (IVRR) strengthens selected intermediate features through consistency supervision with learned feature projections during training. VLM-Action Interface Refinement (VAIR) recursively updates the resulting conditioning before action generation. Joint optimization of the supervised VLM layers, VAIR, and the action generator connects the two components. On RoboCasa365, Axiom-0 achieves 62.32% overall success in our evaluation, exceeding the highest published leaderboard score (Paimon-0, 58.1%) by 4.22 percentage points and the Xiaomi-Robotics-1 reference by 4.92 points. Under the evaluated profiling setup, mean action-chunk generation latency increases by 1.7% over Xiaomi-Robotics-1. These results demonstrate improved task completion with modest inference overhead.
bullets: Targets poor generalization to unfamiliar task compositions, layouts, and object interactions.
Uses Intra-VLM Representation Refinement to improve selected intermediate features through consistency supervision.
Uses recursive VLM-Action Interface Refinement before action generation, jointly optimized with supervised VLM layers and the action generator.
Achieves 62.32% overall success on RoboCasa365, with 1.7% higher mean action-chunk latency than Xiaomi-Robotics-1 under the evaluated setup.
Scope: results are reported for RoboCasa365 and the specified profiling configuration.

papers.abstract: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from large-scale vision-language pretraining, but tend to memorize training trajectories, limiting their ability to adapt learned interactions to new task and scene configurations. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{Region-Aware Interaction Networks (RAIN)}, which formulates a task as a sequence of goal-conditioned subtasks, each specified by an action type and a target-region mask. This formulation allows learned skills to be reused across different objects and scene layouts and composed into task sequences not seen during training. Its Target-adaptive Cross-View Encoder (TCE) conditions multi-view features on target masks and exchanges information across views, while PlanDiT predicts target-directed trajectories and actions. A Transition Head estimates subtask completion to enable automatic transitions. We also introduce a \textbf{Reference-based Retargeting Strategy (RRS)}, which uses recorded trajectories to synthesize smooth approaches to reference interactions with alternative target regions, without collecting additional data. Experiments on \textbf{LIBERO-Analogy}, our new benchmark for robotic task generalization, and real-world tabletop tasks demonstrate that RAIN generalizes more robustly than existing VLA baselines.
bullets: Addresses VLA models’ limited adaptation to new objects, layouts, and unseen task compositions.
Decomposes tasks into subtasks defined by an action type and target-region mask.
Uses a target-adaptive cross-view encoder, PlanDiT for target-directed actions, and a transition head for automatic subtask sequencing.
Reference-based retargeting synthesizes smooth approaches to new target regions from recorded trajectories without additional data.
Evaluations on LIBERO-Analogy and real tabletop tasks show more robust generalization than existing VLA baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture of RAIN. For each subtask, RAIN receives an action type and target masks. The Target-adaptive Cross-view Encoder (TCE) conditions multi-stage features from the third-person and wrist views on the target masks. The PlanDiT uses these stage-wise features to jointly predict future waypoints and action chunks. The Transition Head pools target-region features and fuses the views to predict subtask completion.

Fig. 5. VLM-based goal-mask prediction. The VLM decomposes the instruction into action–target pairs. papers.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.
authors: Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Muchen Xu, Celina Shiyu Wang, Hao Dong, Ruohai Ge, Rong Xue, Benjamin J Kolligs, Aditya Dutt, Sasanka Nagavalli, Nassim A. Samad, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh, Yue Wang, Yuliang Guo

Uses a mixture-of-transformers that couples the VLM with foresight and continuous action experts.
Predicts future spatial tokens directly in the VLM’s native visual-token space.
Trained on human videos and robot trajectories, it reports 81.9% success on SIMPLE and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks at 110 ms per chunk.
Also remains competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

Jointly predicts scene-structure latents, appearance latents, and robot actions to model scene evolution and action generation.
Pretrained with approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot-manipulation data; achieves strong results across simulated and real-robot, single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous benchmarks.
Shows robustness to perturbations, improved scaling with more data than a video-VAE-only baseline, cross-embodiment transfer, and effective few-shot adaptation.

papers.abstract: Robot reward modeling faces two challenges: generalizing across tasks and accurately tracking progress in long-horizon manipulation. General-purpose reward models demonstrate broad task transfer, but transfer from short-task pretraining to long-horizon tasks remains underexplored. Long-horizon progress models often rely on task-specific subtask classifiers or fixed action vocabularies, limiting the reuse of learned progress knowledge when adapting to new tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce Grana, a vision-language robot reward model that learns to identify unfinished subtasks and estimate their continuous progress using open-vocabulary subtask descriptions. We train a language-conditioned model to estimate progress in short-horizon tasks and individual subtasks of long-horizon tasks. For long-horizon tasks, we combine the selected subtask's predicted progress with credit for preceding completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress. General progress prediction requires training the model across diverse tasks with progress supervision that accounts for imperfect execution. Elapsed-time proxies can misrepresent progress when relative subtask durations vary, or failures reverse local progress. We therefore introduce an annotation protocol that converts sparse subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations into dense progress targets, without requiring annotators to assign numerical progress scores. Pretraining with this supervision on 200 diverse, mostly short-horizon manipulation tasks enables zero-shot reward prediction on unseen tasks and improves progress prediction after adaptation to multi-minute, long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate (i) generalizable reward prediction, including adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, (ii) benefits from pretraining and composing subtask progress estimates, and (iii) improved downstream policy performance.
authors: Zi-ang Cao, Kaiyuan Zheng, Yinzhen Xu, Haonan Duan, Jiasheng Gu, Fengyuan Hu, Nan Zhu, Kun Lei, Kevin Lin, Ruijie Zheng, Shenyuan Gao, Fangqi Zhu, Zhe Zhang, Radha Poovendran, Linxi Fan, Guanzhi Wang, Yuke Zhu

Pretraining on 200 diverse manipulation tasks supports zero-shot unseen-task reward prediction, improves adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, and boosts downstream policy performance.

papers.abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.
authors: Hengguang Zhou, I-Hung Hsu, Li Chen, Priyanshi Shrivastava, Anastasios Angelopoulos, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ion Stoica, Cho-Jui Hsieh

Across 351 real multi-turn sessions involving 348 users, 23 languages, and six simulators, population-level measures sometimes missed wrong goals, ignored constraints, and out-of-character behavior.

papers.tldr: Existing user-simulator metrics often miss meaningful behavioral failures, motivating an evaluation suite that tests agent-utility and fidelity at both population and individual-trace levels.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

Benchmarking 11 models finds that stronger hand-pose control does not reliably produce coherent object-state evolution or persistence.

papers.abstract: LLM-based artificial societies exhibit rich behavior but often lack scientific grounding: personas and environments are assumed, interaction networks are synthetic, and simulators are generated as free-form code, making results difficult to tie to real populations and sensitive to the backbone model. We argue that simulated worlds should be sampled from observed data, while simulation logic should be implemented by composing operations from a shared, task-independent vocabulary. In this paper, we introduce ABSClaw, a zero-code agent that compiles natural-language requests into executable, reality-grounded social simulations. ABSClaw grounds who acts, where they act, and with whom they interact in survey and census data, geospatial sources, and real networks. It expresses state transitions through 26 atomic operations. To support an open and extensible ecosystem, ABSClaw further allows capabilities to be added as lifecycle-scoped skills without modifying its core. Furthermore, we propose ABSBench, a benchmark of 193 real-world social-simulation tasks. On ABSBench, ABSClaw achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated social simulators. Three real-world case studies show that grounding personas, environments, and interaction networks each improves agreement with observed outcomes. With one runtime skill, ABSClaw executes 13 population-scale simulations, collectively involving 25 million agents. Together, these results demonstrate ABSClaw's real-world fidelity, extensibility, and scalability.

Case studies link grounding to improved agreement with observed outcomes, while one skill enables 13 simulations involving 25 million agents.

papers.abstract: Robot learning systems require synchronized, high-quality demonstrations that combine visual, proprioceptive, and action data. However, collecting such datasets with mobile manipulators is often slowed down by fragmented teleoperation interfaces and manual post-processing workflows. This paper presents an integrated framework for teleoperated multimodal data collection on a Clearpath Dingo-O mobile base equipped with a Kinova Gen3 Lite manipulator and an Intel RealSense RGB-D camera. The framework combines single-controller operation of the base, arm, and recording process with an automated ROS-based pipeline for data capture, image-quality filtering, temporal synchronization, visualization, and export to machine-learning-ready Zarr datasets. We validate the system on a pick-and-place mobile-manipulation task in which the robot transports a bottle between two surfaces. The results show that the unified controller supports complete task execution and recording without external commands, while the data pipeline produces synchronized datasets for short demonstrations and identifies corrupted visual frames. The proposed framework provides a practical basis for producing structured demonstrations for robot-learning research.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.

Revalidates and updates defenses as embodied actions change the observed scene.
Evaluated across four attack methods and multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control.
Succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of evaluated tasks, improving LIBERO-Object success from 0% to 70.0%, with 548.9 ms mean decision time per control step.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) learn control representations from action-free video, but existing pipelines typically train latent policies with behavioral cloning, without an explicit policy improvement objective. Although offline RL offers a natural approach to policy improvement, standard methods do not transfer directly to learned latent action spaces. We find that the structure of learned latent actions makes naive offline RL unreliable: directly maximizing value over latent actions or fitting a unimodal policy can produce latent actions that cannot be realized by physical execution, while the latent representation can merge physical controls that receive different rewards. To understand when latent-space optimization remains valid, we derive conditions under which policy improvement transfers to decoded execution and under which latent and physical optima align. Building on these insights, we propose LAPIS for goal-conditioned latent policy improvement, grounding value-based policy improvement in observed state-latent transitions and using a conditional flow policy to capture their multimodal structure. LAPIS outperforms baselines on most tasks, with the clearest gains in visual manipulation, and remains effective even with only 1% action labels, where competing methods largely collapse.
authors: Donghyeon Ki, Xiaoyu Chen, Jun Ho Seo, Hayeong Lee, Kyungyoon Kim, Byung-Jun Lee, Li Zhao
bullets: Latent Action Models usually use behavioral cloning, lacking an explicit policy-improvement objective.

papers.abstract: Many multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods handle policy mismatch through products of per-step trace coefficients, leading to a trade-off between variance control and long-horizon signal. The maximum trace length consequently becomes a sensitive hyperparameter. We propose MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation), which replaces these products with a binary stopping indicator: one until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet, zero thereafter. At the true value function, the indicator's idempotence yields a variance bound governed by meeting-time survival. For practical implementation, a single sampled action provides a model-free surrogate for the stopping rule, requiring no transition model or mixing-time estimate. We derive separate sufficient conditions for contraction of the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control tasks, MINT outperforms the reported multi-step baselines; the main MuJoCo comparison uses a common cap without per-task cap-length tuning. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of MINT on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench experiments; MINT adapts the backup horizon to reduce target variability relative to long fixed-horizon backups across tasks and dynamics.
authors: Seungyub Han, Taehyun Cho, Dohyeong Kim, Kyungjae Lee, Jungwoo Lee
bullets: Addresses the variance–long-horizon trade-off caused by products of per-step trace coefficients and sensitive trace-length tuning.

Shows effectiveness across MuJoCo, DeepMind Control, Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench, including reduced target variability versus long fixed-horizon backups.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.
authors: Wenhao Li, Zhongyi Han, Yuhao Wei, Liang Han, Yilong Yin, Liqiang Nie
bullets: Problem: Standard few-shot VLA policies memorize camera-to-robot geometry and fail after camera bumps or robot re-docking.
Method: Uses the robot arm via forward kinematics as a metric calibration target and static scene geometry as a world anchor.
Canonicalization: Corrects the image, robot state, actions, and start pose to the original calibration frame without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data.
Evaluation: Introduces LIBERO-PoseShift and evaluates simulation plus four real-world UR5e tasks under camera, base, and compound shifts.
Results: Improves shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and 36.7 points on the real robot, without perturbed training data or test-time calibration.

papers.abstract: Interactive imitation learning enables robots to learn from human interventions during deployment. These interactions naturally produce sparse human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Yet existing methods either leave this experience unused for action supervision or imitate historical robot actions, which can reinforce suboptimal behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA), a framework that learns from autonomous robot experience through set-valued supervision of policy relabels. Later policy checkpoints relabel this experience, and agreement across checkpoints filters the relabels. Since agreement does not guarantee correctness, SeRA constructs desired action sets around accepted relabels. Following Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), it trains an action-chunking diffusion policy to increase the probability of actions within these sets. A step-masked denoising loss combines accepted relabels with available human corrections in partially supervised chunks. Experiments across five simulated manipulation tasks in online and offline settings show that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms baselines that imitate historical robot actions or exact relabels. On a real-robot tomato-picking task, SeRA achieves 80% success, compared with 40% for SDP, using the same human feedback and training budget. These results demonstrate that relabeled autonomous robot experience can complement human corrections to improve policy performance.
authors: Zhaoting Li, Cosimo Della Santina, Jens Kober
bullets: Interactive imitation learning produces abundant autonomous experience but sparse human action labels.
SeRA uses later policy checkpoints to relabel autonomous rollouts and filters labels where checkpoints agree.
It represents accepted relabels as desired action sets rather than assuming exact correctness.
An action-chunking diffusion policy is trained with a step-masked denoising loss over relabels and human corrections.
Across simulated manipulation tasks and a real tomato-picking task, SeRA improves performance, reaching 80% success versus 40% for SDP on the real robot.

papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound-guided needle interventions have primarily focused on target localization and accurate needle placement, while the subsequent acquisition of diagnostic material remains comparatively underexplored. Moreover, pleural fluid aspiration and tissue biopsy are typically addressed as separate procedures, despite sharing common requirements for ultrasound guidance, safe access, and sample transport. This work presents a unified robotic framework for ultrasound-guided fluid and tissue extraction using a single vacuum-assisted end effector. The proposed system combines force controlled ultrasound scanning, semantic target identification, automated needle deployment, and procedure specific material acquisition. A coaxial needle assembly and shared pump assisted pathway enable direct pleural fluid aspiration, while controlled cannula actuation provides the additional cutting action required for solid-tissue acquisition. End-to-end evaluation using a Franka Emika Panda robot over 50 phantom trials achieved successful extraction in 23/25 pleural fluid aspiration trials (92\%) and 22/25 tissue acquisition trials (88\%). Following successful tissue-target access, acquisition and transport were completed in all 22 trials.

In 50 phantom trials, fluid aspiration succeeded in 23/25 cases (92%) and tissue acquisition in 22/25 cases (88%).

papers.abstract: Intuitive robot programming approaches, such as Programming by Demonstration, enable non-experts to teach robots tasks through hand-guided demonstrations. However, for in-contact tasks requiring force control for parts of the motion, automated segmentation of motion types is crucial for improving usability. Considering the related work, this work proposes a neural network-based segmentation method categorizing motion into three fundamental types using input data of cartesian twists and wrenches at the end effector. We collect demonstration data using a 7-axis robot with a wrist-mounted force torque sensor and generate ground truth labeling by hand. While still in development, our research direction aims to enable non-experts to program in-contact tasks more intuitively.
authors: Johannes Hartwig, Marcello K\"ogler, Dominik Henrich
bullets: Targets Programming by Demonstration for non-expert robot users.
Addresses the need to distinguish motion types when force control is required.
Uses end-effector Cartesian twists and wrenches as neural-network inputs.
Considers three fundamental motion categories.
Demonstrations are collected with a 7-axis robot and wrist-mounted force-torque sensor, with labels assigned by hand.
