papers.abstract: 3D affordance acts as a critical link between perception and action, providing priors for robotic manipulation. While existing approaches predominantly leverage human priors as direct references, they often overlook that affordance is not an object-intrinsic property but is inherently coupled with the agent's embodiment. Due to the structural and morphological disparities between human hands and robot end-effectors, directly applying human priors causes severe incompatibility for robotic execution. Motivated by this, we introduce a novel task setting, 3D Human-to-Robot Affordance Transfer, which addresses the affordance misalignment arising from distinct embodiment structures. To support this task, we construct the Human-Robot Paired Affordance Dataset (HPAD), the first large-scale 3D affordance benchmark in which every object is annotated with both human-prior and simulation-validated robot labels. HPAD covers 2,137 objects across 80 categories and 13 atomic action primitives, yielding over 27,000 object-action pairs. On top of HPAD, we propose the 3D Affordance tRansfer neTwork (ART). ART first filters geometric false positives in the human prior via a reliability gating stream, then reconstructs the prior into a robot-actionable distribution through hierarchical reconstruction and a graph-diffusion refinement that resolves the topological mismatch between human and robot affordances. Experiments on HPAD demonstrate the reliability of the proposed task and the superiority of ART. We further validate ART on a 6-DoF arm with a parallel-jaw gripper in a 2,400-execution benchmark across 12 objects and 4 action categories; ART attains the best success rate (86.5% over its 480 trials), confirming the practicality of the transfer paradigm. papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.

Performs favorably across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, combining task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency.

papers.abstract: Embodied models depend on real interaction data, yet collecting it on physical robots is slow and labor-intensive. Recent ego-to-robot pipelines retarget first-person view human videos to robot data via transferring hand and arm motion. They judge fidelity mainly by visual appearance. However, trajectories often fail in terms of physics: fingers hover beside objects, and grippers close on empty space. We argue that how the object moves and the contacts that drive the motion count. Thus, we present Ego2X, an object-centric framework that converts monocular egocentric video into physically executable robot data across dexterous hands and parallel grippers. Ego2X centers on CORE (Contact-centric Object-interaction REpresentation), which records each contact on the object by its surface anchor, as well as relative force, grasp mode, and interaction state. Throughout the pipeline, CORE corrects hand-object drift via object-relative constraints, steers inverse kinematics toward contacts the robot must realize, and preserves held objects during arm erasure and robot compositing. On HOT3D, contact-driven correction reduces in-contact hand depth error by 33.7%, while on EgoDex, contact-driven retargeting realizes 62.9% of annotated contacts, surpassing the official HuRo pipeline (27.9%). In RoboTwin 2.0, post-training X-VLA on Ego2X episodes alone, without simulator demonstrations, raises task success rate from 40.5% zero-shot to 67.0% across 200 paired scenes. We will publicly release our conversion pipeline and CORE-annotated dataset for dexterous hands and parallel grippers.

papers.abstract: Efficient use of expert demonstrations is essential for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, directly imitating expert trajectories couples nominal intention, which specifies where the vehicle should go, with multimodal driving styles, which determine how that intention is executed. Different combinations of these factors can yield similar expert trajectories, obscuring their respective causal contributions and forcing the policy to learn both from a single entangled target. This ambiguity limits how effectively the policy can exploit expert demonstrations. We propose CausalDrive, a causal decomposition framework for data-efficient driving policy learning that separates deterministic nominal intention prediction from probabilistic driving style modeling. Specifically, we construct counterfactual nominal trajectories from navigation command, map topology, and ego state by removing style dependent effects, providing a Nominal Intention Planner with supervision independent of expert trajectories. Conditioned on the predicted nominal intention and surrounding agents, a diffusion-based Style Execution Policy models diverse driving styles as a multimodal distribution over residuals between nominal and expert trajectories. This causally structured supervision reduces redundant learning of shared nominal behavior in routine scenarios, directing expert supervision toward informative execution variations and improving data utilization. CausalDrive achieves 91.2 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance. Further experiments demonstrate strong performance with limited expert data and clear advantages in challenging interactive scenarios.
authors: Xiaobao Wei, Jingxian Wu, Lirong Yang, Qing Han, Yuan Gao, Ziwei Yang, Shuai Yang, Weiwei Liu, Chang Huang
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of learning intention and execution style from entangled expert trajectories.

Uses a diffusion-based policy to model diverse style residuals conditioned on nominal intention and surrounding agents.
Achieves 91.2 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.5 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with strong results under limited data and in interactive scenarios.

papers.abstract: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.
bullets: The study evaluates two LIBERO-Spatial tasks that differ only in the landmark word identifying one of two bowls.
Unseen synonyms often direct the policy to the named bowl, unlike made-up words, but one task’s closed-loop completion falls to 67.6% versus 100% for the original wording.
Token-pasting tests suggest landmark information affects object choice before the connector, while coordinated information from landmark, instruction, and image tokens affects behavior after it.
Diversified landmark-word finetuning—and even connector-only training—can repair synonym completion; original-instruction finetuning does not.
Closed-loop evaluation should separately measure object choice and completion, with interventions on both sides of the connector; open-loop starting-frame scores can miss part of the repair.

papers.abstract: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it. However, as the controller maintains balance under contact constraints, the executed motion can depart from the reference in ways that change the action it conveys. Our central insight is that semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the complete motion the robot physically executes. Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{SemPhys}, a framework that trains motion generators using semantic feedback from simulated executions. A differentiable world model and a fixed tracking controller predict a short segment of a recorded execution. SemPhys inserts this prediction at its original position, scores the complete trajectory against the instruction, and backpropagates through the predicted segment. A paired anchoring loss stabilizes adaptation by keeping each generated reference close to its counterpart from the initial generator. On BONES-SEED, SemPhys largely preserves instruction retrieval accuracy from reference to execution and achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on executed motions among the evaluated methods.
authors: Zejian Kang, Yeqiang Wang, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Bingqian Wu, Fan Zhou, Jianjie Zhang, Chentao Shen, Wentao Yang, Rui Qian, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language-conditioned reference motions and controller-executed motions under balance and contact constraints.
Uses a differentiable world model with a fixed tracking controller to predict execution segments and assess the complete resulting trajectory against the instruction.
Backpropagates semantic feedback through inserted predicted segments to adapt the motion generator.
Adds an anchoring loss to keep adapted references close to those from the initial generator.
On BONES-SEED, it largely preserves reference-to-execution instruction retrieval accuracy and achieves the highest executed-motion retrieval accuracy among evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.

papers.abstract: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models couple action learning with future prediction, enabling robotic policies to capture environmental dynamics for robust control. However, prevailing methods take a reconstruction-oriented approach to model future videos, allocating substantial capacity to appearance details that are incidental to control. In this work, we reformulate world modeling for manipulation as control-centric future prediction in latent space, and present LaST1.0, a unified latent World-Action Model. Rather than modeling an observation-complete video future, LaST1.0 predicts compact, geometry-aware latent targets derived from future wrist views, focusing the supervision on the evolving robot-object interactions required for fine-grained manipulation. To better support this control-centric paradigm, LaST1.0 revisits the visual input interface and attention mechanism of its unified architecture. It adopts a vision-encoder-free design with a lightweight patch embedder, exposing fine-grained visual cues directly to the backbone, and introduces LaST-Attention for structured spatiotemporal interactions across modalities. Evaluations across two robot embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks---RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus---demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art success rates and generalizes to novel scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of control-centric latent world modeling for robust manipulation.
authors: Hao Chen, Xuheng Zhang, Zhuangzhe Wu, Jiaming Liu, Shaobo Zhang, Jialin Gao, Zhonghao Yan, Di Wu, Sixiang Chen, Peng Jia, Chi-Wing Fu, Shanghang Zhang, Pheng-Ann Heng

papers.abstract: In precision manipulation, small errors in alignment or force can cause jamming or deformation, making contact feedback essential for adapting pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models to these tasks. A single tactile observation leaves the response to recent actions ambiguous. Direct tactile fusion during post-training can also disperse the action expert's visual attention and reduce the share it allocates to contact regions. To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA augments pretrained VLAs with lightweight tactile modules. A queryable action-response memory retrieves recent contact responses so that the action expert can combine them with immediate tactile feedback. Contact-guided gaze supervision concentrates the visual attention of the tactile semantic token on image regions corresponding to fingertip contact. CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33% mean success across three MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50% for direct tactile fusion with the same sensor inputs. It also achieves 67% success on an optical-tactile task from the public UniVTAC benchmark and 66.7% mean success across three real-robot tasks. These results show that tactile post-training helps pretrained VLAs adjust to changing contact.

papers.abstract: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states. We propose 3DTouch, a tactile-geometric conditioning approach for vision-language-action (VLA) models. 3DTouch constructs a shared 3D visuo-tactile representation by expressing RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile measurements in the robot-base frame, preserving each taxel's spatial location and force vector. Hand-object and object-object relations derived from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces explicitly describe the relative arrangement of interacting entities. Together, these representations condition the VLA action expert on spatially localized contact forces and relative surface geometry, providing explicit cues for contact adjustment and object alignment. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and by 20 percentage points over the strongest evaluated alternative. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with further gains from shared spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations.
authors: Xin Zhang, Shiqi Zhang, Siyuan Cao, Juncheng Cai, Yedong Shen, Yuxuan Gao, Dianlong Wen, Kaixue Long, Lu Zhang, Yao Li, Jiajun Deng, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and visually ambiguous contact states that make local geometry and object relations difficult to infer from vision alone.

Adds hand-object and object-object relations from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces to guide contact adjustment and object alignment.
Evaluated on five real-world tasks with a UR7e and XHand, improving average success by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and 20 points over the strongest alternative.
Ablations show complementary benefits from scene geometry, spatial tactile feedback, shared spatial grounding, and explicit geometric relations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of 3DTouch. (a) 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG) back-projects RGB-D observations into scene point clouds and transforms taxel positions and force vectors into a shared robot-base frame using forward kinematics (FK). Separate encoders produce scene tokens and finger-level tactile tokens. (b) Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM) aligns reference object meshes using estimated poses and encodes relative displacements and distances between hand landmarks and nearby object surface points, and between representative regions of interacting objects, into hand–object (HO) and object–object (OO) tokens. The scene, tactile, and relation tokens jointly condition the action expert, while the original vision-language pathway and flow-matching objective are preserved.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+$\pi_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots must recover from falls and resume commanded motion to sustain locomotion. Learning these behaviors in one policy requires supervision that accommodates both upright movement and ground-contact recovery. We present ReLoco, a framework that uses behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors to learn locomotion, get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and command resumption within one proprioceptive policy. During training, robot posture selects the expert pool and conditions a shared discriminator with two behavior-specific outputs. Task rewards and shared regularization support command tracking and recovery, while temporary assistance facilitates exploration. A simulation-based refinement stage supplies robot-executed motion references for this supervision. Ablations examine conditional supervision, output separation, and reference quality under matched settings. At a common training iteration, the full policy achieves $96.80\%$ independent get-up success and $96.96\%$ push-recovery success, including command resumption. Its torso planar velocity root-mean-square error is $0.1266$~m/s, $14.7\%$ lower than the conditional single-output variant, with similar joint-angle discrepancy measured by dynamic time warping. Deployment on the 64.5-kg Tiangong~3.0 humanoid demonstrates walking, running, get-up, and locomotion resumption after falls using one proprioceptive actor, without controller switching or on-robot policy fine-tuning.

Task rewards, regularization, temporary assistance, and simulation-refined robot motion references support learning and exploration.
The full policy reports 96.80% independent get-up success and 96.96% push-recovery success, including command resumption.
Deployment on the 64.5-kg Tiangong 3.0 demonstrates walking, running, fall recovery, and resumed locomotion.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing hand-object interactions is an important task, and achieving it with a single camera makes large-scale capture practical but challenging due to heavy occlusions. We introduce HOForce to track hands and objects, and further recover interaction forces from single-view RGB-D video and known object properties. For two-hand manipulation, we jointly model fingertip forces of both hands and the contact forces between objects when two objects are presented. The reconstructed forces also improve motion tracking by giving pose constraints in the occluded regions. HOForce recovers hand and object motion more accurately on DexYCB and TACO and produces less hand-object penetration than interaction baselines on DexYCB. On our dataset of fingertip forces recorded with tactile sensors, HOForce reduces normal-force MAE by 24.5% relative to the strongest baseline. The recovered forces reproduce object motion in MuJoCo and transfer to other engines after adaptation.
authors: Jiahui Wang, Wanqing Du, Yuanbin Zou, Zhefeng Xu, Feng Xu
bullets: Targets single-camera hand–object reconstruction, where severe occlusions make motion and force estimation difficult.
Models fingertip forces for both hands and contact forces between objects during two-hand manipulation.
Uses reconstructed forces as pose constraints in occluded regions, reducing hand–object penetration.
Improves motion accuracy on DexYCB and TACO and achieves lower penetration than interaction baselines on DexYCB.
Reduces normal-force MAE by 24.5% versus the strongest baseline on a tactile-sensor dataset; recovered forces reproduce object motion in MuJoCo and transfer to other engines after adaptation.

papers.abstract: Native mobile GUI agents require large-scale training trajectories covering both individual app functions and multi-goal workflows within and across apps, which makes automatic task synthesis a promising way to scale training data. Existing synthesis pipelines, however, produce each task as free-form text, leaving implicit how its subgoals depend on one another. This matters because composition is a skill in its own right: a policy may complete each subtask of a workflow on its own, yet fail to chain these subtasks into the complete workflow. We present MobileWeave, which instead synthesizes every task as an executable program derived from the app implementations of a controllable simulator. MobileWeave abstracts each app into a typed capability graph with semantic types shared across apps, composes atomic programs into single- and cross-app composite programs through explicit value and object dependencies, and verifies each program by native execution, deriving both its instruction and its completion check from the same program. Trained on teacher trajectories collected for these tasks and on recovery supervision at the policy's own stalls, MobileWeave-8B improves its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld, with comparable gains at 4B. Beyond these gains, we find that composition is learnable from task structure: explicit dependencies between subgoals act as a training signal that teaches a policy to compose skills it already masters. We release data, model, and code at https://maxxnotmarx.github.io/MobileWeave/ .
authors: Ziyi He, Xian Wu, Qiyuan Chen, Haitao Li, Cehao Yang, Yinghao Zhu, Xichen Zhang, Xiao Chen, Yushi Feng, Lequan Yu
bullets: Targets a limitation of free-form task synthesis: implicit subgoal dependencies can cause agents to complete subtasks individually but fail to chain them.
Represents apps as typed capability graphs and composes atomic programs using explicit value and object dependencies across apps.
Verifies tasks through native execution, deriving both instructions and completion checks from the same executable program.
Training includes teacher trajectories and recovery supervision at policy stalls.
MobileWeave-8B improves its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld; comparable gains occur at 4B.

Right: successful teacher rollouts form the SFT trajectories, and one-step teacher interventions in the policy’s action loops yield the recovery SFT data.

papers.abstract: Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.
authors: Manav Kulshrestha, Shreyans Jain, Apoorva Vashisth, Ankush Gupta, Damon Conover, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the need to choose grasps that are both physically feasible and suitable for the downstream task.
Introduces a dataset with 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations across 100,911 image-task pairs and 17 object categories.
Generates task-independent grasp proposals, then uses a language-conditioned re-ranker to jointly evaluate them.
Outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points and is validated on real objects with a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of LAGR. Given multimodal visual observations, a task-independent proposal generator extracts fused visual features and predicts physically plausible grasp candidates with associated confidence scores. A language-conditioned re-ranker combines proposal geometry, multi-scale visual features, and task instruction embeddings, then applies a proposal-context transformer to jointly evaluate candidate suitability. The final grasp is selected by combining task-compatibility predictions with physical confidence, without modifying the proposed grasp geometry.
Figure 2. Comparison of representative grasp annotations from existing datasets and LAGR.

Figure 1. Examples of LAGR generating distinct task-specific grasps for the same real-world objects. Functional tasks favor grasps that enable effective tool use, whereas handover tasks favor grasps that leave the handles accessible to the recipient.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison of task-conditioned grasp prediction and grasp stability. SR denotes grasp success rate, IoU denotes intersection-over-union with ground-truth grasp rectangles, and Angle Err. is grasp orientation error. Table 2. Ablation studies on the design components of our approach. Accuracy requires IoU ≥ 0.25 and angular error ≤ 30◦. Angle statistics use positive-overlap matches. Best mean results are bold.

papers.abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/
authors: Ghadi Nehme, Dahyun Nam, Akshay Govind Srinivasan, Faez Ahmed
bullets: Agents co-design robots from standard components plus a custom 3D-printed part, with simulated designs physically built and tested.
The benchmark includes 10 obstacles across three difficulty levels and evaluates four frontier coding agents.
Across 16,427 simulations and 135 physical robots, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and discover mechanisms beyond search baselines.
Only 66% of simulated passes transfer to the real world across all levels, and performance drops on harder tasks and universal-robot requirements.
Real-failure videos enable redesigns that sometimes correct the simulator and remove 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.
authors: Apoorva Vashisth, Manav Kulshrestha, Damon Conover, Zachary Kingston, Aniket Bera
bullets: Targets performance degradation in long-horizon tasks involving interdependent manipulations.
Uses an execution-aware, VLA-agnostic framework that evaluates motion progress and revises future plans from observed outcomes.
Leaves the underlying VLA policy unchanged and requires no additional fine-tuning.
Improves success rates by 21.9% on RoboCasa365 and 10.4% on CALVIN over the next strongest baseline.
Also demonstrates real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RePlan-VLA. Given a long-horizon language instruction and visually grounded scene observations, the planner decomposes the task into executable short-horizon subtasks, which are sequentially executed by a frozen VLA policy. A separate progress estimator monitors execution at the manipulation-primitive level, detects deviations from the intended subtask, and generates naturallanguage failure feedback. Upon failure, the planner uses the updated scene observations and diagnostic feedback to revise the remaining subtask sequence. The bottom panel illustrates this closed-loop process: after successfully placing a croissant on the cutting board, the robot approaches an incorrect object while retrieving a jam jar. RePlan-VLA detects the mismatch and replans, enabling the robot to recover and complete the remaining manipulation.

The examples illustrate recovery from an incorrect object grasp, restoration of a missing manipulation prerequisite, and completion of previously omitted actions. All three executions ultimately succeed.

papers.abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

papers.abstract: Tactile feedback helps visual manipulation policies respond to local contact, but changes in tactile observations do not always require corrective motion, and sustained corrections do not always require new tactile features. We introduce TacPilot, a tactile residual framework that separates representation updates from action intervention around a frozen visual policy. TacPilot uses a perception gate to determine when tactile features need refreshing and updates only affected regions while reusing unchanged features. A separate intervention gate determines whether bounded Cartesian and gripper residuals modify the nominal visual action. This separation allows tactile perception and action correction to follow different spatial and temporal demands during manipulation. In offline expert-trajectory replay, local feature reuse reduces encoded regions by 56.4% relative to periodic full encoding, with essentially unchanged action predictions. In an exploratory simulation evaluation spanning two cylinder sizes, TacPilot succeeds in 26 of 30 trials (86.7%). We further validate TacPilot on OpenArm v2 equipped with Paxini tactile sensors across four contact-rich manipulation tasks.
authors: Yunzhen Zhang, Yuxiao Zhu, Jie Yang, Yufeng Miao, Bing Luo
bullets: Avoids unnecessary tactile updates and corrective motions during contact-rich manipulation.
Uses a perception gate for selective local feature refresh and an intervention gate for bounded Cartesian and gripper residuals.
Reuses unchanged tactile features, reducing encoded regions by 56.4% with essentially unchanged action predictions in offline replay.
Achieves 26/30 successes (86.7%) in simulation across two cylinder sizes and is validated on OpenArm v2 across four manipulation tasks.
Scope: evaluations cover limited simulated object sizes and four real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.
authors: Jinhao Zhang, Yushen Zuo, Ke Rui, Weitao Zhou, Haibao Yu, Honglong Tian, Xiaoheng Ma, Jie Mei, Jiawei Wang, Minglei Li

Reports leading performance across LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro, and improved long-horizon planning on RoboCasa365.
Real-world experiments support the method’s practical effectiveness.

papers.abstract: When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video-action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning. We find that the way video predictive training is supervised affects subsequent action learning. In our experiments, adapting at many noise levels yields a large gain, while adapting only at the noise level used at deployment yields none. Weight-transfer experiments further show that the gain stays with the adapted weights when they remain in the video generation model and disappears when they are used only to initialize the action policy. Initial loss and gradient measurements at the start of joint training indicate that target-domain predictive training gives the video model a better starting state, making subsequent joint learning of prediction and action easier. Under matched data and training budgets, predictive adaptation improves control. We evaluate the complete policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks.
authors: Chenxi Han, Ruby, Epoch, Orion, Luke, Bin, Dusk, Lyra, Cal, Alvin, Hubert, Alex, Jiahe Han, Tao Zhang, Hang Liu, Shoujie Li, Yizhe Li, Bokui Chen, Houde Liu, Guoping Pan, Yi Cheng

Evaluates the resulting policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks under matched data and training budgets.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
authors: Xuji Zhang, Qilin Zhong, Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Jian Di, Kun Li, Yang Cao, Wenjun Lv
bullets: Addresses unreliable decisions when policies must retrieve relevant information from long, redundant observation histories.
Uses Recall-Relocalization to connect episodic memories to the current view through a small number of recall slots.
Converts recall slots into Gaussian source components via Recall Anchors, guiding flow-policy generation toward intended actions.
The transport network completes actions from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy.
Reports 80.4% average success on MIKASA-Robo, with gains of 20.3 and 18.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline on simulated and real-robot task suites, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RecallFlow. The present observation is encoded into tokens Zt. Recall Anchors turns each slot into a Gaussian anchor in action space; with a standard Gaussian, the anchors form the source p0. A transport network conditioned only on Zt carries x0 ∼ p0 to the action chunk, so memory reaches the action solely through the source.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
authors: Artur Kuramshin, Charlotte Cloutier, Michael Przystupa, Kirsty Ellis, Mohammad S. Akhter, Glen Berseth
bullets: Dexterous manipulation is difficult because most VLA training data targets parallel-jaw grippers, while multi-finger teleoperation data is scarce.
The study combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL) for adapting VLAs to a LEAP hand.
Across five fine-tuning recipes and two simulation tasks, SFT rollout success poorly predicts post-DSRL performance.
Freezing the VLM and tuning only the action expert yields the most steerable policy, including for out-of-distribution placements.
LoRA is reported as the least steerable adaptation approach.

papers.abstract: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.
authors: Wei Liu, Abrar Anwar, Huihua Zhao, Soha Pouya, Yan Chang
bullets: World-action policies are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise useful for steering.
LoRN uses a small actor to choose directions in a fixed low-rank projection of high-dimensional noise.
A norm-controlled construction keeps steered noise near the typical scale of Gaussian samples.
Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy.
Simulation-trained steering transfers to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks without additional real-world training.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LoRN enables low-rank noise steering of large generative robot policies. Existing noise steering methods improve frozen policies by steering the initial noise used to generate an action chunk. However, extending noise steering to the much higher-dimensional outputs of vision-language-action models and world-action models is challenging. Left: LoRN learns a small set of coefficients that selects a noise direction within a fixed low-rank subspace, keeping the actor’s output dimension small regardless of the full noise dimension. Middle: This formulation allows LoRN to steer either action noise or video noise in world-action models. We find that steering the video noise is surprisingly expressive for denoising actions, thus LoRN enables a new way to steer a world-action model’s actions. Right: Mean final success per policy family, averaged over its tasks, for the base policy, DSRL action-noise steering, and LoRN. Video-noise steering produces large gains on the evaluated world-action models; on action policies, LoRN achieves comparable final success to DSRL while generally improving early-training success (Table 11). The DSRL bars use the same variants as Figure 6, with its full-dimensional form on Cosmos3-Edge.

Figure 7: Action-noise steering across robot policies. Learning curves of LoRN (green), DSRL (gray dashed), and LP-DS (dark gray dash-dotted) on twelve tasks: the mean over five seeds with a band of one standard deviation across seeds. Dotted horizontal lines mark base-policy success. The 𝜋0 tasks use LIBERO and ALOHA, 𝜋0.5 uses YAM, and Diffusion Policy uses Robomimic. Horizontal axes show gradient updates for 𝜋0 and environment steps for the other policies, in millions; several panels end before the full training budgets of Table 4 to show the phase in which the methods separate, so training budgets should be compared within each task. The 𝜋0 and 𝜋0.5 curves are five-evaluation running means of 10- and 16-episode evaluations; the Robomimic curves are raw 200-episode evaluations. Diffusion Policy uses full-rank LoRN (𝑟 = 𝑁 = 28).

Figure 9: LoRN enables stronger steering while maintaining the noise norm. Steering-rule comparisons on Cosmos3-Edge using a rank-32 video projection. Bars show mean success with standard errors over three training seeds; dotted lines mark base-policy success. Increasing the steering strength 𝛼 improves LoRN’s performance, whereas additive steering increases the noise norm and loses task success. The LP-DS adaptation [24] and the PSS-related control [17] retain approximately the original noise norm but yield limited gains. Here, 𝛼 caps the steering strength while 𝛽 sets the LP-DS correction’s target norm limit √ 𝛽𝑁 . The relative noise norms are measured in units of √ 𝑁 . Both use our adaptations of the published steering rules within the shared setup, rather than reproductions of the complete methods.

Figure 6: Video-noise steering improves success across world-action models. Base-policy success, DSRL action-noise steering, and LoRN action- or video-noise steering on RoboLab and LIBERO. DSRL steers all 256 action-noise entries on Cosmos3-Edge, the stronger of its two forms there (Table 7); on DreamZero-14B it tiles a 32-dimensional latent over the chunk, and on DreamZero-5B it replaces the action noise with its latent. Bars show means; error bars show standard errors over three training seeds. Base-policy references have no training-seed error bars. Labels round means to whole percentages. Video steering achieves the highest mean on nine of ten model–task pairs; DSRL performs best on DreamZero-5B Moka pot. Evaluation protocols and retained training budgets differ across models and some configurations; see the appendix.

Figure 3: LoRN steers frozen generative robot policies through a low-dimensional noise subspace. (a) High-dimensional Gaussian noise concentrates near a thin shell. We find that moving far from its typical norm can degrade the policy’s actions. (b) A fixed random orthonormal projection 𝑃 maps 𝑟 actor coefficients into the full 𝑁 -dimensional noise space, with 𝑟 ≪ 𝑁 . The plane and its intersection with the sphere illustrate the low-rank subspace. (c) Given observation 𝑜, the actor learns coefficients 𝑢 through reinforcement learning to produce noise inputs that improve the policy’s actions. The projected output 𝑃𝑢 is normalized to √ 𝑁 and mixed with an independent Gaussian sample 𝜀 at strength 𝑠, using weights that preserve the expected squared noise norm. The colors illustrate advantage relative to the base policy, implying that our low-rank subspace captures high-advantage regions for policy improvement. The projection 𝑃 and pretrained model remain fixed while the steering actor is trained. (d) This construction enables LoRN to steer video or action noise in a world-action model. Algorithm 1 provides more details about LoRN.

Figure 13: Sample efficiency of action-noise steering across twelve robot tasks. Horizontal bars show the mean training steps to sustained target success for DSRL (gray), LP-DS (dark gray), and LoRN (green); lower is better. Whiskers show one sample standard deviation across the seeds contributing to each bar. The success target is 80% on ten tasks, 50% on Load dishwasher, and 20% on Pack container, as indicated in the panel labels. Means and standard deviations are computed over attaining seeds only, out of five training seeds per method; the label on each bar gives the number of attaining seeds 𝑛, and bars with different 𝑛 are not directly comparable. Horizontal axes use thousands of gradient updates for 𝜋0 and thousands of environment steps for the other policies, with a separate scale for each task; attainment times use discrete evaluation checkpoints without interpolation or smoothing. LoRN reaches the target first on six of the twelve tasks, including all three Robomimic tasks; DSRL is first on Moka pot, Alphabet soup, and Butter, and LP-DS on Cream cheese, Transfer Cube, and Load dishwasher.

(a) The bound (1 − 𝑝𝜏 )𝑟 on the probability that a random subspace misses the good region at one state, for three shares 𝑝𝜏 ; the dashed line marks rank 32. (b) Simulation in which a single fixed subspace serves 4,000 states, each with its own linear advantage field. (c) The best advantage reachable in 𝒮𝑃 grows with rank, while its average advantage remains zero.

Arrow labels show the average root-mean-square (RMS) change from the reference action chunk; arrow widths show relative sensitivity within each model. (a) “Pick up the cube and place it in the bowl.” (b) “Pick up the black marker and put it into the red cup.” (c) “Pick up the black cube with the left arm, hand it to the right arm, and place it in the blue bowl.” The steering actors are trained only in an Isaac Lab reconstruction of the station and deployed unchanged.

A fixed projection 𝑃 restricts the actor to the same subspace at every decision; its intersection with the sphere is shown here as a great circle. (a) Six decisions illustrate how the useful noise inputs change with the observation, while green points mark the actor’s choices. papers.abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.
authors: Nidhi Parayil, Benjamin Greenland, Thierry Peynot, Chris Lehnert
bullets: Addresses contact-rich agricultural tasks where foliage blocks vision and contact observations are intermittent.

Achieved 95% branch-manoeuvring success and 87.5% zero-shot success on unseen tomato and lime plants across reported trials.
Outperformed tactile and reactive baselines and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned policy failed.

papers.abstract: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.
bullets: Frozen DINO and V-JEPA feature distances poorly reflect object-to-goal distance, with rank correlation at most 0.11 versus 0.87 for object-mask centroids.
The learned representation reduces interference from background and robot-arm patches by separating object identity, spatial displacement, and dynamics.
DOCK uses forward kinematics from joint angles as annotation-free supervision for grasped-object motion.
In 21 simulated kitchen tasks, DOCK places the object in 15 tasks, matching an oracle using true object position and outperforming mask geometry (10) and frozen features (9).
Its task ranking transfers to unseen layouts, object instances, and categories, including scenes where an unseen robot arm is visible.

papers.abstract: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile over a gripper. To solve this problem, we present LuxTac, a flexible, scalable optical taxel array, about 3.5 mm thick and built from off-the-shelf parts. Each taxel is a digital RGBC light-to-digital converter under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, so the back-scattered LED light falls monotonically with local indentation depth. The same board accepts two interchangeable gel cartridges: a plain one for normal sensing, and one with colored walls that encodes the local shear in the color of the returned light, with no camera, magnets, or bump overlay, making LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array to resolve shear at individual taxels. Characterized with an automated CNC indenter and a six-axis force/torque sensor, the normal cartridge responds linearly to force ($R^2$ = 0.999) from 104 mN to at least 5.8 N, with 2.0% repeatability, 5.9% hysteresis, and a taxel-to-taxel variation of 6-10% after normalization. With the shear cartridge, per-taxel models estimate the three-axis force at every taxel; across three indenter shapes and nine held-out sessions, the summed estimates reach $R^2$ = 0.96/0.96/0.92 in x/y/z, each taxel's estimate 0.92/0.93/0.94, and the median shear-direction error is 4.8 degrees. Adding LuxTac pressure readings to an Action Chunking Transformer policy substantially improves peg-in-hole success over a vision-only baseline. Design files, code, and videos are available at https://luxtac.github.io.
authors: Md Rakibul Islam Prince, John Pelan, Zhiyuan Zhang, Adyaa Khera, Katherine Pesetski, Adeesh Desai, Akimizu Sugiyama, Minwoo Ki, Benjamin Alan Capelle, Temitope Ibrahim Amosa, Zijie Xu, Yihan Huang, Taehun Chung, Long Wang, Wei Li, Shaoting Lin, Yu She
bullets: Uses digital RGBC light sensors beneath interchangeable silicone gel cartridges to infer indentation and shear without cameras, magnets, or bump overlays.
The approximately 3.5-mm-thick array is flexible, scalable, and built from off-the-shelf components.
Normal-force sensing is highly linear, while per-taxel models estimate three-axis forces and shear direction across held-out sessions.
Adding LuxTac pressure sensing substantially improves peg-in-hole success for an Action Chunking Transformer over vision alone.
Design files, code, and videos are publicly available; results are demonstrated within the tested force range, cartridges, and robot-learning task.

papers.abstract: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions. Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose $\Phi$-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics. The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $\Phi$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $\Phi$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.
authors: Iv\'an L\'opez-Broce\~no, Maximilian St\"olzle, Daniel Feliu-Talegon, Daniela Rus, Cosimo Della Santina
bullets: Targets the limitation of deformation models that ignore dynamic and mechanical effects, especially for stiff, heavy, or fast-moving objects.
Combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network with a learned affine mapping from observed DLO positions to latent coordinates.
Its Lagrangian structure provides explicit energy expressions and supports a model-based PD controller with closed-loop stability and convergence guarantees.
Across simulated and real bimanual experiments, the approach improves prediction efficiency and substantially reduces endpoint regulation error versus model-free PD control.
The evaluation covers four simulated DLOs and one real robotic setup; broader conditions beyond these experiments are not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $\pi_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.
bullets: LIBERO-trained VLA policies often fail on LIBERO-PRO when objects move or instructions change.
The method augments demonstrations by relocating and rotating objects, transferring tasks across environments and surfaces, and paraphrasing instructions.
A perception module using frozen DINOv3 features provides object positions and gripper-state information alongside TinyCLIP image and instruction embeddings.
A from-scratch flow-matching diffusion transformer predicts actions from this decoupled representation.
RageVLA achieves 0.72 on LIBERO-PRO, compared with 0.53 for the best published model; performance remains strong under object displacement tests.

papers.abstract: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.
authors: Xuanwei Liu, Guipu Cao, Zhongyi Luo, Jiafei Duan
bullets: Existing tokenizers concatenate both arms’ actions, leaving shared motions and cross-arm dependencies for the policy to learn implicitly.

papers.abstract: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.
authors: Nikhil X. Bhattasali, Jaron Cui, Lerrel Pinto, Grace W. Lindsay
bullets: Introduces Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical rat body for embodied simulation.

The model learns multiple locomotion speeds and gait transitions, with behavior, kinematics, and neural activity consistent with experiments.
Cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict responses to graded perturbations; interface design strongly affects trainability and gait quality.

papers.abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.
bullets: Taylor reachability is limited by complex-plane singularities, especially in rational terms and sigmoid-like controller gates.
The proposed Chebyshev abstraction uses the full reachable set and avoids Taylor’s degree-dependent width cap, improving geometrically with polynomial degree.
The work derives closed-form rigorous remainders, including the first polynomial softmax-transformer abstraction.
In closed-loop systems and MNIST classifiers, Chebyshev certificates remain valid in cases where Taylor certificates diverge or become unknown.
Measured width limits agree with theory to 89–94%, and certified claims passed Monte Carlo checks with zero observed violations.

papers.abstract: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of formally identifying safe initial states through scalable backward reachability analysis.
Refines an input-space cover by analyzing activation patterns and splitting where the relaxation gap is predicted to be largest.
Produces certified inner and outer approximations rather than relying on a single convex bound.
Evaluated on high-dimensional models, including a linearized Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein Transformer block.
Also examines how model-level reachability guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT systems.
