papers.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).
authors: Hang Zhang, Qijian Tian, Yuan Xie, Xuhong Wang, Xin Tan

Verification: A Meta-Reviewer replays the generated model and construction process, diagnoses failures, and routes bounded repairs.
Contribution: The system produces models and instructions suitable for both human builders and robot assembly.
Results: Experiments report better performance than recent agentic systems and demonstrate downstream robot-manipulation utility.

papers.abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.
authors: R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy
bullets: Addresses the limitation of pairwise latent-action learning, which may miss how physical transitions evolve over time.
Uses a shared inverse dynamics model for compact latent actions and a recurrent latent world model for multi-step JEPA feature prediction.
Transfers the learned representation to a vision-language model through latent distillation and recurrent future-feature prediction, then adapts it with action flow matching.
At deployment, removes the auxiliary latent-action and world-model branches so the VLM directly predicts robot actions.
Achieves 97.9% on LIBERO, 70.0% on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations, and ranks second on both LARY metrics among compared methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of ReLAP. Stage 1 learns temporally coherent latent actions from unlabeled human and robot video through local and recurrent prediction in frozen JEPA features. Stage 2 trains a vision-language model to predict the latent sequence from the current image and instruction under the frozen Stage-1 models. Stage 3 adds a flow-matching action expert of alternating DiT blocks conditioned on the VLM context, the predicted latent actions, and the current and predicted future JEPA features; the forward model stays trainable under the terminal feature loss.

papers.abstract: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves $O(\log^2 T)$ expected regret over $T$ interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.
authors: Luca Vignola, Melanie Zeilinger, Bruce D. Lee
bullets: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system.

With positive definite input penalties, certainty-equivalence polylogarithmic regret requires restrictive identifiability of all unknown parameters under optimal feedback; singular penalties relax this requirement.
A certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves O(log^2 T) expected regret whenever controller identifiability holds.
An Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound is established for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails.

For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker condition than knowing the full input matrix and applicable to underactuated systems such as a cart-pole.

papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/
authors: John Hua Yao. Qi Wu, Yihuai Gao, Chelsea Finn, Zipeng Fu
bullets: Collects natural, near-human-speed demonstrations through kinesthetic teaching on a backdrivable bimanual platform.
Uses test-time action smoothing for smoother high-speed policy execution.
Applies masking to align visual data during demonstration collection and deployment.
With 50 demonstrations per task, achieves over 80% success on tasks including ball catching, clothing folding, battery insertion, and table bussing.
Demonstrates performance close to human speed across these bimanual tasks.

papers.abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.
authors: Yanghong Liu, Yang Chen, Kailang Xu, Bang Du, Feiyang Yang, Jiawei Xia, Zhengtao Yao, Yubiao Zhang, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Ruihai Wu, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses costly robot demonstration collection and the embodiment gap between humans and bimanual dexterous robots.
Uses human-object interactions to select task-relevant robot grasps from geometry-based candidates.
Combines object trajectories with relative bimanual wrist trajectories to preserve task structure and coordinated motion.
Adaptively weights object- versus wrist-level guidance according to confidence in video-derived object motion, then refines behavior under robot constraints in simulation.
Evaluates simulation data generation and downstream vision-based diffusion-policy learning on pouring, sweeping, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate-cleaning tasks.

The PPO policy then refines these priors in simulation: reliable object motion provides task-level guidance, while lower-confidence segments allow greater residual adaptation and increased wristmotion guidance. Successful full-episode rollouts under perturbed initial conditions are retained as robot demonstrations and distilled into a vision-based Diffusion Policy for real-robot deployment.

papers.abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.
bullets: Fixed-gain PD control cannot simultaneously optimize motion and contact-force tracking across swing and contact phases.
A reinforcement-learning policy predicts per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements during training.
The policy uses inertia-scaled impedance priors, enabling control across subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric inputs.
Across 129 participants and six activities, it improves kinematic and force fidelity over fixed-gain PD, torque-based, muscle-actuated, and existing imitation controllers.
The learned impedance representation transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot, and generalizes to withheld activities.

papers.abstract: The goal of Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) is to find a population of high-performing policies that solve a decision-making problem in diverse ways. Despite recent progress, QD-RL methods predominantly rely on evolutionary operators--including black-box optimizers, mutations, and crossovers--to facilitate exploration and induce diversity. Scaling these methods becomes increasingly costly as policies and behavior spaces grow larger. Building on the Soft QD view of quality-diversity optimization, we introduce \textbf{Re}pulsive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (\textbf{RePPO}), which adapts PPO to jointly optimize a compact population of diverse, high-quality policies using a population-dependent, dynamically shaped reward. On standard continuous-control tasks, RePPO achieves a strong quality-diversity tradeoff compared with state-of-the-art QD-RL methods. Ablations further characterize this tradeoff by examining how each component affects individual quality and collective diversity. To assess RePPO's scalability, we extend our evaluation to learning from pixels and fine-tuning large language models. In pixel-based tasks, where large policies make most traditional QD-RL methods infeasible, RePPO maintains quality on par with standard PPO while achieving substantially higher diversity. Its successful application to language model fine-tuning further demonstrates, for the first time, that QD-RL methods can scale to this domain. Together, these results show that directly optimizing compact populations with RePPO provides a scalable approach to QD-RL across increasingly complex domains.
bullets: Targets the scalability and exploration costs of evolutionary Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning.
Adapts PPO with a dynamically shaped, population-dependent reward inspired by the Soft QD framework.
Jointly optimizes a compact policy population for both individual performance and collective behavioral diversity.
Matches standard PPO quality while achieving substantially higher diversity in pixel-based tasks.
Also scales QD-RL to large-language-model fine-tuning, extending evaluation beyond conventional control settings.

papers.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
authors: Ruixi Yu, Dairu Liu, Xuchuan Chen, Zekun Qi, Zekai Li, Zhuo Cao, Luyang Niu, Yingsheng Zhang, Sikai Liang, Ke Fan, He Wang, Li Yi

papers.abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.
authors: Minjae Kwon, Amir Moeini, Shangtong Zhang, Lu Feng
bullets: Safe ICRL requires fixed-parameter policies to learn unseen constrained tasks from interaction histories while respecting a cost budget.
The revised Safe AD teacher explores according to remaining budget, then switches to an expert policy after observing reward or cost.
Training with dynamic budgets increases the diversity of return-and-budget histories and improves return while reducing cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah.
A-Lag reweights actions using predicted cost and an adaptive Lagrange multiplier updated from observed costs.
Across all five environments, A-Lag lowers mean episode cost but also lowers mean final return in four.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models trained on dynamic-budget histories (Dynamic) and on fixed-budget histories (Fixed), on the test tasks. Each curve shows the mean episode return or cost over three seeds, with a shaded band of ±2 standard errors. With dynamic budgets, A-Lag has a lower cost in four of the five environments, all but PointGoal, and Safe AD has a higher return in all five, compared with fixed budgets.

Figure 2: In-context adaptation on the test tasks. Each curve shows the mean episode return or cost over three seeds, with a shaded band of ±2 standard errors. A-Lag starts every deployment at λ = 0, and λ is adjusted during test time by Eq. (9). In DarkRoom, PointGoal and CarGoal the return of A-Lag and Safe AD rises over the episodes while their cost falls. In HalfCheetah and Ant their cost drops sharply after the first episode, and in HalfCheetah the return falls with it. A-Lag’s Ant return also declines across episodes. A-Lag has a lower cost than Safe AD in DarkRoom, CarGoal and Ant, at a lower return. The mean costs are also slightly lower in PointGoal, at a slightly lower return, and in HalfCheetah, where it ends with a higher return. CDT has a higher cost than both in the navigation and velocity tasks and does not find the goal in DarkRoom.

papers.selection_reason: Safe in-context RL for embodied navigation and locomotion tasks, with deployment-time adaptation from interaction history.
papers.title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Safe Algorithm Distillation improves safe in-context RL by training on budget-aware teachers and adjusting actions online to control cost, reducing costs across five environments.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.
authors: Itamar Mishani, Mukund Krishnakumar, Oren Salzman, Maxim Likhachev
bullets: Targets the costly search over skill sequences and parameters in multi-skill manipulation tasks.
Uses a fast learned world model to predict skill feasibility and resulting world states.
Repairs only affected search regions when predictions are invalidated, while simulating every skill in the final plan.
Evaluated on increasingly difficult cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks and demonstrated on a physical robot.
Plans faster with fewer simulator queries while matching or exceeding baseline success rates across settings.

An ensemble of M models provides the uncertainty from prediction disagreement.

From left to right: Task 1, cluttered object retrieval; Task 2, retrieval requiring manipulation of the containing bin; and Task 3, wrench retrieval requiring the wrench to first be repositioned. Easy and medium variants progressively remove clutter while preserving the task objective. The green region denotes the goal region.

papers.tldr: Lazy-MOSAIC speeds up long-horizon robot manipulation planning by using learned skill-effect predictions to limit expensive simulation to promising candidates.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk may fail to reflect the changes that the proposed actions would induce in visual representations, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal-rethink-refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.
authors: Haoyun Tang, Baqiao Deng, Enjin Zhou, Songwen Tian, Keyao Xu, Bowen Jing, Kun Wang, Ke Ma, Zhandong Mei, Huibin Li
bullets: Addresses the limitation of future predictions that ignore how proposed actions alter visual representations.
Uses a proposal–rethink–refine loop with latent multi-horizon predictions and residual corrections.
Adds affordance-guided observation–action memory plus near-fine, far-coarse prediction granularity.
Reports strong results across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa24, and three real-world OOD conditions.
Diagnostics and ablations support complementary benefits from rethinking and affordance guidance, with two-pass latency reported across platforms.

papers.abstract: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.
authors: Lucas Schulze, Sucheth Shenoy, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Addresses uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics while limiting sensitivity to measurement disturbances.
Uses a gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network with stable linear filtering to encode context across frequencies.
Provides guarantees for exponential forgetting and finite-horizon, frequency-weighted context perturbation bounds.
In simulated and real manipulation tasks, it reduces high-frequency sensitivity and residual torque error, produces smoother motion, and degrades less under injected disturbances.
Evaluation includes model predictive control and real-robot frequency-sensitivity analysis; results are scoped to the tested low-pass realization.

papers.abstract: Cooperative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate their motions while ensuring whole-body collision avoidance and preserving task-relevant behaviors. We propose CALDS (Cooperative Adaptation of Learned Dynamical Systems), a framework that enables mobile manipulators to adapt learned single-agent behaviors for coordinated execution. Building on individual dynamical systems (DSs) learned from demonstrations, CALDS enables cooperative adaptation through two key components: Cooperative Policy Selection, which identifies compatible combinations of learned policies, and Temporal Adaptation, which ensures collision-free cooperation while preserving the spatial structure and convergence properties of the original behaviors. We evaluate CALDS across three diverse scenarios: assistive dressing, restaurant cleaning and serving, and drawer opening and object placement. Quantitative results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving task success and enabling safe, coordinated simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrated behaviors.
authors: Saray Bakker, Wendelin B\"ohmer, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: Addresses coordination, whole-body collision avoidance, and behavior preservation in cooperative mobile manipulation.
Uses learned dynamical systems from demonstrations as the basis for adaptation.
Combines Cooperative Policy Selection with Temporal Adaptation to select compatible behaviors and avoid collisions.
Evaluated in assistive dressing, restaurant cleaning and serving, and drawer opening with object placement.
Reports improved task success and safe simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CALDS for cooperative multi-agent adaptation in a restaurant scenario, where one robot cleans a table while the other places a cup on the cleaned area. Firstly, we generate a set of learned single-agent DSs for each task. In the multi-agent context, Cooperative Policy Selection ranks and selects the most promising combination, which Temporal Adaptation then adjusts to satisfy task constraints while ensuring whole-body collision-free trajectories, selecting the next-best combination if unsuccessful.

Figure 3: Results over 200 randomized runs per scenario, reporting the overall success rate, the individual metrics, i.e. goal reaching, collision avoidance, and task ordering (restaurant scenario), and path deviation.

papers.abstract: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. papers.abstract: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.
authors: Ke Sun, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Yike Zhang, Yanzhe Chen, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fast-evolving contact forces and slow API-only model decisions.
Uses calibrated force sensing or joint torques with self-terminating force primitives that return on contact events.
Converts force traces into physical quantities with uncertainty for model reasoning instead of exposing raw force streams.
Introduces HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables.
Reports large gains in real and simulated zero-shot success, with performance matching expert controllers on HiddenPhys.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ForceHarness, illustrated with one logged call. Blue marks the command path and teal the force path. The frozen model reads its inputs and returns one tool call, here a search during a USB-plug insertion. The inset sketches how search presses with Fd and follows a spiral until the plug drops into the hole, while the photo and the force trace come from this call. Beneath the primitive, the robot’s stock impedance controller turns the lead into force, and the bottom layer of ForceHarness estimates and re-zeros the hand force with Eq. (1). The same harness drives a real arm and two simulators, and a fixed guard bounds what any primitive can do. Fixed estimators turn the trace into physical quantities with uncertainties and flags, which return to the model as the tool result.

papers.abstract: Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

papers.abstract: Egocentric hand motion provides physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation and vision-language-action pretraining. Reliable use of this supervision requires accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. Existing methods typically lift framewise estimates produced under weak perspective into world coordinates. By ignoring joint-dependent depth variation at close range, this approximation couples errors in translation, orientation, and articulation that persist after world lifting and worsen under occlusion. We present MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local spatial structure and metric scale. Fused with visual features, this geometry guides coarse metric estimation and conditions every step of temporal generation. The model jointly recovers world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and shape, while structural priors and temporal context support estimation under partial occlusion. MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, and wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9% relative to HaWoR, respectively. World-space acceleration error decreases by 44.2% and 64.3%, demonstrating improved temporal fidelity alongside more accurate absolute localization.

Reports substantial reductions in camera-space and world-space MPJPE, wrist error, and acceleration error relative to HaWoR.

The resulting conditions are supplied to every flow-matching step to jointly recover world-space wrist translation, global orientation, articulation, and shape. Camera motion defines the metric world reference.

papers.abstract: Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties. Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives. Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge. We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour. The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure. We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics. We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments. In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine. For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE's 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings. Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations. Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.

papers.abstract: Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target. Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations. We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation. Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation. Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task-contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similar contacts.Project page: https://wrist-informed-tactile-representations.github.io/.
authors: Haotian He, Yiyang Chen, Congsheng Xu, Wenchao Yue, Mingze Ye, Shuai Chen, Yi Yang, Yaping Li, Haonan Wang, Weinan E, Wenzhao Lian, Zhijie Deng
bullets: Motivation: Similar tactile contacts may require different actions depending on hand, object, and target configuration.
Method: Deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views before downstream policy action generation.
Pretraining: Learns from nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data.
Results: Improves average task success over vision-only policies by 28.8% and 15.0% for GR00T N1.7 and π0.5, respectively, across four tasks.

papers.abstract: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.
authors: Ruizhe Wang, Rui Liu, Hongliang Chen, Junyi Guo, Fangyu Wu, Yaran Chen
bullets: Targets assembly hierarchy inference from individual parts and target illustrations.
Fuses a dedicated SVG encoder with representations from a pretrained vision-language model.
Uses RHPO to reward hierarchy-preserving equivalent solutions rather than only matching one reference tree.
Adds repair-cost feedback to prefer decisions requiring fewer downstream corrections.
Achieves the best Equivalent-Hard F1 among evaluated methods, including a 17.69-point gain over GPT6-Astra on an IKEA-derived test set, with strong independent-dataset performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Assembly architecture and RHPO training (a–c) The indexed parts and target drawing illustrate four assembly steps. Each resulting subassembly maps to an internal node of the reference tree, also shown in nested JSON. (d) For a fixed goal or action, unassisted rollouts estimate full success (Q) and tree quality (V). Separate repair rollouts estimate the mean number of subsequent repairs (C). At the first certified downstream error, the verifier rolls back, replaces the erroneous merge using the annotated graph and reference tree, and resumes the frozen policy. GRPO uses Q and V at both decision levels and favors lower repair cost among eligible candidates with near-best quality and a certified paired cost gap. Action-only distillation transfers probability mass from verified invalid actions to verified valid actions while preserving the mass on unknown actions.

papers.abstract: Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations.
authors: Yongji Fu, Yijiong Lin, Yi Zhou, Yi Qi, Guanqun Cao
bullets: Addresses sensor-dependent differences that hinder transferring representations and combining multi-sensor tactile data.
Uses multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training to learn shared spatiotemporal features.
Jointly trains on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction using paired videos from matched contact events.
Experiments show cross-sensor translation and transferability to downstream perception tasks.
Scope: applies to optical tactile videos and relies on paired cross-sensor observations of corresponding contacts.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of TacBridge. Multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training and event-paired cross-sensor learning yield a shared spatiotemporal tactile representation. The learned representation supports controllable tactile video generation conditioned on source-video features and target-sensor information. We further evaluate the learned representation on downstream tactile perception tasks and new real-world tactile data.

Fig. 3: Tactile attribute classification on a real robot. A robot arm presses a GelSight sensor on two fabrics and records one tactile reading per fabric. Each column requests one target sensor: GelSight Mini, GelSlim, DIGIT, and GelSight. The cell outlined in orange is the recorded source frame and always lies in the column of that row’s own sensor, so it falls on the diagonal for the first three rows and returns to the GelSight Mini column for the fourth. Every other cell in a row is a decoding of the same latent under the target-sensor condition of its column. papers.abstract: Training and verifying neural network-based control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) can be computationally demanding. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that jointly learns a CLF and a stabilizing controller using structured neural networks and a projection-based parameterization. Specifically, we employ Polyak-Lojasiewicz networks (PLNets), which parameterize nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates, and construct a stable-by-design surrogate of the closed-loop dynamics that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by construction. The controller combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction term resembling Sontag's universal formula and is trained to align the resulting closed-loop dynamics with the stable-by-design surrogate. Unlike classical approaches based on Sontag's formula, our framework does not require a known CLF; instead, it learns the CLF and controller simultaneously. We establish local and global stability guarantees for the learned controller and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through numerical examples.
bullets: Addresses the computational difficulty of training and verifying neural control Lyapunov functions (CLFs).
Uses Polyak–Lojasiewicz networks to represent nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates.
Constructs a surrogate closed-loop system that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by design.
Combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction inspired by Sontag’s universal formula.
Provides local and global stability guarantees and demonstrates effectiveness through numerical examples.

papers.abstract: Achieving human-like behavior on humanoid robots has advanced rapidly by leveraging motion-capture demonstrations rather than hand-crafted cost functions. Adversarial imitation supplies a style signal that lets a policy fulfill a task while adhering to a desired style, but is difficult to transfer to hardware. Whole-body tracking through reinforcement learning instead deploys reliably and imitates demonstrations faithfully, but the resulting policies are conditioned on the future reference, so they require a reference trajectory at runtime and can fail when the motion differs from the training data. We train a humanoid policy directly with whole-body tracking rewards while restricting its actor to compact locomotion commands and robot observations. Reference motion supervises the reward and privileged critic, without supplying reference joint trajectories to the actor or requiring teacher distillation. The demonstrated style is thereby encoded in the policy through the tracking reward, so the robot reproduces the whole-body style under commanded velocities. Trained on a single random-walk motion and commanded with velocity profiles from held-out motions, our policy reaches at least 98\% success in simulation and completes every trial on the Unitree G1. On held-out slow walking, whole-body tracking drops to 2\% success and command-conditioned distillation to 56\%, and both fail on the real robot. On the trained motions, the joint position error of our policy stays within 8\% of whole-body tracking, and it has a higher style coverage than adversarial motion priors (AMP), which fell on the real robot without a safety crane.
authors: Murad Dawood, Oezge Drama Berkenkamp, Antonio Gonzales Marin, Nutan Chen
bullets: Addresses the need for reference trajectories at runtime and poor transferability in conventional whole-body imitation.
Trains with whole-body tracking rewards and a privileged critic, while withholding reference joint trajectories from the actor and avoiding teacher distillation.
Encodes demonstrated style directly into a velocity-conditioned policy from a single random-walk motion.
Achieves at least 98% simulated success and completes every Unitree G1 trial under held-out velocity profiles.
Scope: performance degrades substantially on held-out slow walking, where competing tracking and distillation methods also fail on hardware.

papers.abstract: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.
authors: Biwen Yang, Zhe Cao, Jin Zhang, Haoyang Sun, Zonglu Hu, Jintao Zhao, Zhehao Zhang, Kaizheng Chen, Chengyi Liu, Chengyu Wei, Siyuan Wu, Ruiheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the problem that retained, transported, or subsurface heat can affect later contact outcomes.
Tracks spatial and depth-resolved thermal state for both contact partners through contact, transport, and separation.
Produces synchronized RGB-thermal observations, states, actions, and event-level task checks on one execution clock.
Provides a paired six-task benchmark with 4,448 trajectories and integrations for MuJoCo and Isaac Sim.
Reported studies show improved contact-site selection with visible thermal history and higher transfer completion when training uses dynamic histories.

papers.abstract: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10\%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.
authors: Markus Peschl, Dana Kianfar, Daniel Dijkman
bullets: High-fidelity generalization to unseen motions is compute-intensive due to interference across diverse motion tasks.
Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP) introduces a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state–reference pairs.
It outperforms on-policy and off-policy RL baselines in simulation and real-world tracking across multiple datasets, by up to 10%.
The work establishes a QTOP scaling law and reports limited dataset-size impact in moderately sized GPU-hour regimes.

papers.abstract: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.
authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Shangchen Zhou, Wenzheng Zeng, Yanzhe Chen, Zechen Bai, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Organizes 114 robotic reward-model methods into five families: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone pi_0-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.
authors: Haixiang Wu, Zhihao Guan, Yang Yang
bullets: Equal fusion can overwhelm proprioception despite its rich dynamic information; inter-joint coupling is identified as the key action-determining structure.

Inverted Action Chunking independently decodes per-joint trajectories.
ACiT improves success on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, especially those requiring dynamics and coordination; the design also improves pi_0 execution efficiency.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation, yet heterogeneous sensing mechanisms and observation formats hinder cross-hardware transfer. Since physical contact is governed by Newtonian mechanics, we ground tactile representations in six-dimensional wrenches, establishing a common physical reference across sensing mechanisms. Specifically, we pair tactile observations from all sensors with wrench measurements, enabling shared physical supervision without requiring direct tactile-to-tactile pairing between sensors. To support learning at scale, we develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million paired tactile observations and wrench measurements from 24 sensors spanning four families of sensing principles. Building on this dataset, our framework combines sensor-specific input adaptation with a shared tactile encoder. By learning to reconstruct wrenches, the encoder maps observations from different sensors into a shared, continuous feature space grounded in contact physics. To leverage these representations for manipulation, we introduce TaF-Policy, which integrates tactile features with visual observations and robot states to generate action chunks. We evaluate the learned representations through wrench estimation, cross-sensor retrieval, few-shot adaptation to unseen sensors, and robotic manipulation. On the core benchmark, our method reduces single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baseline. In manipulation experiments, TaF-Policy achieves average success rates of 51.33% across three simulated tasks and 46.25% across four real-world tasks, compared with 47.33% and 23.75%, respectively, for the strongest baselines evaluated on the same task sets. Project page: https://mrjiangjm.github.io/TaF-Foundation/.
authors: Jiaming Jiang, Yuzhe Huang, Baokun Yang, Hao Liang, Li Gao, Haoran Guo, Pei Lin, Shengcheng Luo, Chenxi Xiao, Wanlin Li, Ziyuan Jiao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of transferring tactile models across sensors with different mechanisms and observation formats.
Pairs observations from 24 sensors across four sensing families with wrench measurements, avoiding direct tactile-to-tactile pairing.
Uses sensor-specific input adaptation and a shared encoder trained to reconstruct wrenches, producing a common physical feature space.
Improves single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baselines.
TaF-Policy combines tactile features with vision and robot states, achieving higher average success on the reported simulated and real-world task sets.

(a) Sensorspecific input adapters and family-specific projections map heterogeneous tactile observations into tokens for a shared Transformer. A learnable physical query aggregates the encoded tokens into a 768-dimensional continuous tactile representation. (b) Six-dimensional wrench reconstruction and alignment with EMA wrench embeddings provide shared physical supervision. The learned representations are evaluated on single-frame wrench estimation, temporal wrench estimation with historical wrench inputs, cross-sensor retrieval, and robotic manipulation using TaF-Policy in simulation and the real world.

papers.abstract: Many everyday objects, such as storage boxes, baskets, and chairs, are too large or heavy for a gripper to grasp, yet a single arm can still pick them up by wrapping around and supporting them. Such grasps are hard to learn: wrapping motions are difficult to teleoperate, and existing datasets contain little whole-arm pickup data. We introduce WAG (Whole-Arm Grasp Dataset), the first large-scale dataset for single-arm pickup of large objects, with 1.7~million joint configurations across 793 objects. We sample configurations directly in joint space, execute each through squeeze and lift primitives in simulation, and stress-test survivors under active shaking and external forces. To demonstrate the utility of WAG and accomplish the whole-arm pickup task, we develop ARMFUL, a whole-arm pickup pipeline that pairs a diffusion model trained on WAG, generating whole-arm grasps from the object's point cloud, with a motion planner that reaches them collision-free before the same squeeze-and-lift execution. In simulation, ARMFUL reaches 85.4\% lift success on training and 69.9\% on held-out objects, and it lifts the object in 70 of 100 trials on a physical Franka arm across 10 IKEA objects.
authors: Xinyi Yu, Yunshuang Li, Daniel Seita, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
bullets: Addresses the lack of whole-arm grasp data and the difficulty of teleoperating wrapping motions for large-object pickup.

Uses a diffusion model to generate whole-arm grasps from object point clouds, combined with collision-free motion planning and squeeze-and-lift execution.
Achieves 85.4% lift success on training objects and 69.9% on held-out objects in simulation.
On a physical Franka arm, successfully lifts objects in 70 of 100 trials across 10 IKEA objects.

(b) Motion planning. The arm follows an RRT-Connect path to the selected arm grasp configuration, and the same squeeze-and-lift execution completes the pickup.

papers.abstract: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: https://asymeef.vercel.app/.

papers.abstract: When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module. We argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations: a policy can retain the required information yet fail to read it out as the correct action. To test this view, we propose ReRead: with the backbone frozen, a corrector re-reads the current and two previous caches to predict an action residual. The corrector sees no images, is trained solely on offline demonstrations from all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and adds only 4.17% latency. Ablations and interventions show that the correction relies on the backbone's own representations: none of four external visual encoders adds further gain, and swapping in past caches from other trajectories sharply increases action error. On the 11 hardest RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, ReRead improves the success rates of LingBot-VLA, $\pi_{0.5}$, and Fast-WAM by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, it raises Fast-WAM's average success rate from 90.73% to 92.66%. On a Flexiv dual-arm robot, it raises success on a phase-ambiguous task from 0% to 36%.

Gains depend on trajectory-consistent internal representations: external visual encoders add no further benefit, while mismatched caches increase error; scope includes RoboTwin 2.0 and one Flexiv task.

papers.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler's limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the $\pi_0$ VLA reduces the action head's forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.
authors: Jingru Guo, Alessandra Russo, Joey Bose, Christos Ziakas
bullets: Flow-based VLAs are difficult to fine-tune with on-policy RL because multi-step ODE sampling is slow and rollout groups have low variance.
VLA-SSD conditions a single-jump generator on a Brownian path to create a stochastic one-step action policy.
The method provides a conditional action density for likelihood-ratio RL algorithms.
On LIBERO, distillation reduces action-head forward-pass time by 7.7× with a 5.5% relative success-rate decrease.
Using its greater sample diversity, GRPO post-training improves a π₀.₅ VLA’s success rate by 20.6% relative.

papers.abstract: We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training. Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model. Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another. XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs. We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator. For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet. It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic. On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU. XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma's tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.
bullets: They build on SuperMimic, using a learned robot world model and analytic policy gradients through imagined short rollouts.
The training loop, including MuJoCo Warp simulation, is compiled with JAX and parallelized across up to four GPUs.
XMimic tracks all 40 LAFAN1 clips with a Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes on four H100 GPUs.
XSoma learns rough-terrain locomotion with a one-second horizon, no critic, and exact computation of non-dynamics quantities such as foot terrain height.
The reported speedups are 3.7× over BlinkMimic and 12.3× over FastSAC, with XSoma using one-eighth as many environment steps as FastSAC.

papers.abstract: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Meanwhile, explainable reinforcement learning aims to learn meaningful behavioral representations through policy interaction. However, these objectives are inherently conflicting, as continual learning emphasizes policy stability whereas explainable behavior learning requires adaptive exploration. Existing methods rarely address both simultaneously. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes a Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FECHRL) method. A two-stage behavior cloning strategy is introduced to balance rapid policy adaptation and explainable behavior evolution by progressively transitioning from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a fuzzy critic based on a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy inference system is proposed to alleviate value extrapolation errors during the transition between imitation-guided learning and autonomous exploration, thereby improving continual training stability. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.
bullets: Addresses the conflict between stable knowledge retention and adaptive, explainable exploration in continual robot navigation.
Uses two-stage behavior cloning to transition from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning.
Introduces a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy critic to reduce value extrapolation errors during this transition.
Experiments on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks show stable retention and meaningful behavioral explanations.
The abstract reports effectiveness in the tested sequential navigation setting, without specifying broader generalization limits.

papers.abstract: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.
bullets: Standard Koopman controllers can stabilize the learned latent model while leaving the deployed nonlinear plant locally unstable.
Stability transfers when learned and true closed-loop dynamics match to first order on the embedding’s tangent space; approximate matching yields a robustness margin.
TIK estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces this tangent-space matching, while using a bilinear predictor for state-dependent actuation.
Across four unstable benchmarks, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilized the nonlinear plants, unlike all 40 Standard Koopman controllers.
TIK achieved 88% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with 0.25 ms planning and controlled simulated seven-joint arms in 1–5 ms per step; stability testing was inconclusive under high noise.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive normalizing flows (NFs) provide a tractable density for learning and sampling continuous robot actions. We show that a single maximum-likelihood objective can train vision--language--action (VLA) policies competitive with leading methods on manipulation benchmarks. We present NF-VLA, which combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement. Its deep--shallow architecture concentrates visual, language, and proprioceptive prefix conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while unconditioned shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation. The vision--language backbone and flow are jointly trained by exact maximum likelihood on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks. The same learned density supplies a single score-based correction at inference, refining generated actions to account for training-time smoothing without a separately trained denoiser. Trained on LIBERO from a pretrained vision--language backbone without robot pretraining, NF-VLA achieves 98.35\% success across the four standard suites and 72.6\% on LIBERO-Plus using the same checkpoint without further fine-tuning. Ablations show that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement both improve closed-loop success. Together, these results establish carefully structured autoregressive flows as a competitive approach to VLA control, with one learned density supporting policy training, action generation, and refinement.
authors: Ruichen Deng, Qinyu Zhao, Yong-Hyun Park, Mutian Tong, Liang Zheng, Jiatao Gu
bullets: Targets vision-language-action control with tractable action densities and a single maximum-likelihood training objective.
Combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks.
Uses a deep–shallow design: deep blocks process multimodal conditioning, while shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation.
Reports 98.35% success across LIBERO’s four standard suites and 72.6% on LIBERO-Plus without further fine-tuning.
Ablations indicate that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement improve closed-loop success.
