papers.abstract: Safety filters for heterogeneous robot teams fail because of missing constraints, overestimated braking capabilities and conflicts between individually satisfiable constraints. We present OntoCBF, which compiles a domain ontology with a class taxonomy, typed relations, safety axioms and a dynamics profile per robot class into a control barrier function filter with one quadratic program per agent. Description-logic entailment supplies the constraints of any team online, including those that follow from chains of relations and from classes defined by what a robot carries, so the existing safety axioms cover new robot classes, payload classes and combinations. We prove that a subclass may reuse the braking capability of its parent whenever it can produce every velocity of the parent, a property separate from subsumption. For box-bounded double integrators this property is also necessary, and every loss of safety then begins with a conflict. Once three robots interact, the safe set of pairwise barriers contains states from which a collision is unavoidable, and such states persist in larger teams under any fixed capability reduction. In a simulated warehouse where humans ignore the robots, a filter written for the design classes violates safety in 89-100 % of the episodes with unseen classes. In all scenarios, including one with 32 robots, OntoCBF violates safety in 20-70 % of the episodes, each time after a conflict, with a median deepest intrusion of 10-17 % of the keep-out distance. A multi-agent PPO policy trained with the filter in the loop lowers the rate of infeasible quadratic programs, nearly all of them conflicts, by 18-41 %.
authors: Peng Wu, Seyede Fatemeh Ghoreishi, Nathan Bastian, Mohsen Imani, Tian Lan, Mahdi Imani
bullets: Motivation: Existing safety filters miss derived constraints, overestimate braking capabilities, and fail when individually valid constraints conflict.
Method: Compile class taxonomies, typed relations, safety axioms, and robot-specific dynamics into one control-barrier-function quadratic program per agent.
Contribution: Description-logic entailment supports unseen robot, payload, and combined classes; the work also characterizes when subclasses can reuse parent braking capabilities.
Results: In warehouse simulations, design-class filters violated safety in 89–100% of episodes with unseen classes, while OntoCBF violations occurred in 20–70% of episodes and followed conflicts.
Scope/limitation: With three or more robots, pairwise-safe states can still lead unavoidably to collisions; policy training reduced infeasible programs by 18–41% but did not eliminate conflicts.

papers.abstract: Dexterous grasping policies are usually trained for one arm paired with one hand. Every new pairing then needs its own policy, and the number of policies grows with every arm and hand added. We ask whether a single policy can control many arm-hand combinations and transfer to pairings and hands it has never seen. This is hard because robots differ in the number, layout, and dynamics of their joints, so their observations and actions share no common interface. We present DexFormer 2.0, a single reinforcement learning policy for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping. It maps every robot to a canonical joint interface with validity masks, encodes each joint's morphology with attention biased by the kinematic tree, and uses a Transformer-XL memory to infer embodiment-dependent dynamics from recent interaction. Trained on 18 combinations of four arms and six hands, it reaches 89% stable success on seen combinations and 51% on six held-out arm-hand pairs, outperforming GRU and DexFormer 1.0 baselines. Without fine-tuning, it also grasps with four new hand types and, through retargeting, with parallel grippers. Ablations show that memory, the kinematic-tree bias, and broader pairing coverage each matter for transfer. On a physical Flexiv arm, distilled students transfer zero-shot from simulation with two hands, including a held-out pair. Project website: https://davidlxu.github.io/dexformer2-web/.
authors: Lixin Xu, Ke Zhang, Xinyu Liu, Jie Tan, Senming Tan, Jiaju Yin, Yating Feng, Xiaoyi Lin, Xiyue Dong, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses the need to train a separate grasping policy for each arm–hand pairing with incompatible joint interfaces.
Canonicalizes robot joints using validity masks, morphology-aware attention over kinematic trees, and Transformer-XL memory for embodiment-dependent dynamics.
Trained on 18 combinations of four arms and six hands; achieves 89% stable success on seen pairings and 51% on six held-out pairs.
Transfers without fine-tuning to four new hand types and, via retargeting, to parallel grippers; ablations identify memory, kinematic bias, and pairing coverage as important.
A distilled policy transfers zero-shot from simulation to a physical Flexiv arm with two hands, including a held-out pairing.

MorphNode encodes the canonical joint state, Transformer-XL adds a 16-step key/value memory, and a task encoder feeds the current task observations directly to the actor head, which outputs a masked Gaussian over 29 actions. The critic, used only in training, has the same structure with its own weights and memory. Bottom: MorphNode. A body encoder (arm, hand, and mount MLPs) gives bt; MorphAttention attends over joint and context tokens with topology biases and pools them to rt; gated fusion gives the spatial code st = LN(bt + αrt).

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are capable of producing desired robotic behaviors in ideal settings. However, they often fail when the robot's actuation changes at deployment. For example, remounting, mechanical wear, or command latency changes can lead to failed tasks and unsafe behaviors. To address the inevitable actuation shift, we propose ReGround, an inference-time method that keeps the VLA frozen and re-grounds its intended motion. ReGround learns the deployed robot's dynamics from task-agnostic motor babbling, and then tracks the policy's intended motion while staying close to the policy's own plan. ReGround activates only upon detecting a shift, and needs no rewards, demonstrations, or retraining. We show via two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings that ReGround can restore near-oracle success, such as raising $\pi_{0.5}$'s success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency, while remaining safer than a linear-calibration baseline. Project website and open-source code: https://umersiddique94.github.io/ReGround/.
authors: Umer Siddique, Peilang Li, Yongcan Cao
bullets: Actuation shifts from remounting, wear, or latency can cause VLA policies to fail or behave unsafely.
The method learns deployed-robot dynamics through task-agnostic motor babbling and re-grounds the VLA’s intended motion.
It activates only when a shift is detected, while staying close to the policy’s original plan.
Across two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings, ReGround restored near-oracle success and was safer than linear calibration.
For example, it improved π₀.₅ success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency.

papers.tldr: ReGround adapts frozen vision-language-action models to changed robot actuation at inference time, restoring performance without retraining, rewards, or demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Agents that call tools and robots that execute tasks are challenged by two shortcomings: they repeat what failed before, and they learn from runs that they only believe succeeded. We describe the construction of a memory that addresses both, built for a production agent platform. Every run is recorded as an episode, and only an outcome confirmed by an external check, a test, a tool result or a person counts; the agent's own claim never does. What is learned from episodes is kept in a memory with two parts: an associative matrix, written with the delta rule, which finds the procedure that applies to a situation; and a section of ordered, addressable step records that answers what comes after a given step, where a step is a goal of the agent, not a motion. Because the matrix sums its associations, it keeps no order and cannot return or delete a single one; it serves as the finder, and order, outcome counts and deletion live in the records. We describe how execution outcomes are stored, how episodes are recalled and used for solving tasks, and the file format that stores the memory. In simulation, a robot that judged its own success and stopped when it believed it was done reported $96\%$ of its tasks as done and solved $35\%$; with external verification it solved $79%$. In a store of $100000$ synthetic episodes ($457$MB on disk), the oldest episode was still found first, no episode from another person's memory was returned, and a success vouched for only by the model was never recalled; a lookup took $16$ms on a laptop and $40$ms on a server node (median). Task outcomes were measured up to about $10000$ confirmed records, where the exact records solved every revisit at the first attempt.
authors: J\"urgen Paulhart ([core] Informationstechnologie / Eldric), Peter Sch\"uller (NeuraMix AI GmbH,Technische Universit\"at Wien)
bullets: Addresses repeated failures and unreliable self-reported success in agent and robot task execution.
Uses a delta-rule associative matrix to find relevant procedures, plus ordered step records to retrieve subsequent goals, outcomes, and deletions.
Stores episodes only when success is confirmed by tests, tool results, external checks, or people—not by the agent’s own claim.
In simulation, external verification increased solved tasks from 35% to 79%, compared with 96% self-reported completion.
On 100,000 synthetic episodes, retrieval preserved episode ordering and memory isolation; median lookup took 16 ms on a laptop and 40 ms on a server node.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a specific episodic and procedural memory architecture for tool-using agents and robots, fitting the subtopic of robot learning and manipulation by providing a method for skill acquisition and interaction history retention.
papers.title: A Matrix with Steps: An Episodic and Procedural Memory Method for Tool-Using Agents and Robots
papers.tldr: A two-part episodic and procedural memory lets tool-using agents and robots learn only from externally verified outcomes while retrieving applicable procedures and ordered next steps.

papers.abstract: Sim-to-real RL has achieved impressive results in dexterous manipulation but remains limited to tasks with accurate rigid-body simulation. However, these methods cannot be applied to skills that involve deformable and particles, with which the simulation speed will become too slow for large-scale RL learning. We present DAPPT, a sim-to-real framework for end-to-end dexterous tool-use manipulation skills, e.g., sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, without simulating non-rigid materials. Our method learns a domain-aware RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain parameters, and distills it into an end-to-end domain-aware sensorimotor policy. Furthermore, explicit domain represen-tation enables fast selection of domain parameters that can maximize downstream task performance. We evaluate DAPPT end-to-end on six dexterous manipulation tasks, including sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, sand scraping, mouse-wheel scrolling, dispenser pressing, and spray triggering. Our method achieves 1.5-3.8x in task metrics through the best domain parameter and transfers zero-shot to the real world.
bullets: Targets non-rigid manipulation tasks that are too slow or difficult to model accurately in simulation.
Learns a domain-aware RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain variables.
Distills the learned policy into an end-to-end domain-aware sensorimotor controller.
Uses explicit domain representations to select parameters that improve downstream task performance.
Evaluated on six tasks, achieving 1.5–3.8× task-metric gains with optimized parameters and zero-shot real-world transfer.

papers.abstract: Continuous and accurate estimation of human hand kinematics is important not only for intuitive human-machine interaction, but also for capturing fine-grained human manipulation demonstrations that can provide action supervision for embodied-intelligence datasets and dexterous robot learning. However, individual sensing modalities may be insufficient for reliable estimation under varying operating conditions. We present a finger-unencumbered multimodal framework for continuous regression of 20 hand joint angles from egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG). The framework combines a Vision Transformer-based visual encoder, a Transformer-based EMG encoder, and a degree of freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder. To account for the varying informativeness of visual and EMG cues across joint DoFs and input conditions, the decoder assigns a separate learnable query to each DoF, enabling DoF-specific and context-adaptive fusion of the two modalities. The framework was evaluated on synchronized multimodal data from 10 participants. Averaged across participants, the proposed fusion model achieved a mean coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of $0.88$ and a mean absolute error (MAE) of $2.80^\circ$, compared with $0.82$ and $3.21^\circ$ for the vision-only model and $0.68$ and $5.13^\circ$ for the EMG-only model. It also outperformed the evaluated representative unimodal baselines and alternative fusion designs. DoF-wise analyses showed larger fusion gains for visually ambiguous joints and viewing conditions, while synthetic visual occlusion demonstrated greater robustness than vision-only estimation. These results highlight the complementary value of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for capturing fine-grained human hand kinematics, with potential applications in human demonstration acquisition and dexterous robot learning.
authors: Jiahang Liu, Wenbo Zhang, Junsong Wang, Zhenzhi Ying, Siqi Hou, Naohiko Sugita, Liming Shu
bullets: Addresses unreliable hand-kinematics estimation from any single modality under changing conditions.
Uses Vision and EMG Transformers with one learnable query per joint degree of freedom for context-adaptive multimodal fusion.
Evaluated on synchronized data from 10 participants, achieving mean R²=0.88 and MAE=2.80°.
Outperformed vision-only, EMG-only, and alternative fusion baselines; gains were strongest for visually ambiguous joints and conditions.
Synthetic occlusion tests indicated greater robustness than vision-only estimation, supporting demonstration capture and dexterous robot learning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed multimodal fusion framework. The framework takes synchronized egocentric RGB images and forearm HD-sEMG signals as inputs. The vision branch extracts spatial hand-region tokens from cropped RGB patches using a ViT backbone, while the EMG branch converts windowed hand-crafted sEMG features into temporal EMG tokens using a Transformer encoder. After adding modality embeddings, tokens from both modalities are concatenated and fused by a query-based Transformer decoder, in which each hand DoF is represented by an independent learnable query and mapped to its corresponding joint angle through a shared multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression head for continuous estimation of 20 hand joint angles.

Fig. 2. Experimental setup for multimodal data acquisition. (A) An RGB camera was set on the forehead of the participant. 10 motion-capture cameras were arranged around the experimental area to record the hand movements of the participant. The red, blue, and yellow boxes indicate the egocentric RGB camera, motion-capture cameras, and the hand–forearm sensing setup, respectively. (B) Functional schematic of the wireless HD-sEMG acquisition unit. The unit comprises three main functional parts. The power-management unit (PMU) supplies power to the acquisition and processing circuits. The EMG signal-processing path receives the differential signals generated between the electrode-array channels and the wrist-mounted common reference electrode, and performs amplification, band-pass filtering, analog-to-digital conversion, and onboard signal processing. The microprocessor controls signal modulation and demodulation and communicates with the host computer through the radio-frequency wireless interface. (C) Placement of motion-capture markers and the HD-sEMG acquisition system. Reflective markers were attached to anatomical landmarks on the dorsal hand to record hand kinematics, with three palm markers defining the palm reference frame. Two 64-channel HD-sEMG electrode arrays were placed over the forearm flexor and extensor regions, respectively. Each array was connected to a wireless acquisition unit, and a wrist-mounted reference electrode provided the common reference for differential recording.

Fig. 4. Temporal trajectories of predicted angles for 20 hand joint DoFs under different input modalities with the palm facing down. The fusion model follows the ground truth more closely and stably than the EMG-only and vision-only models.
Fig. 3. Overall comparison of fusion, vision-only, and EMG-only models using R² and MAE (°) metrics.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of reconstructed hand meshes under different input modalities. From left to right, the columns show the egocentric image, ground-truth hand pose, fusion result, vision-only result, and EMG-only result. The fusion model produces hand poses that are closer to the ground truth.

Fig. 6. DoF-specific modality attention patterns and representative temporal analyses of the proposed fusion model. (A, B) EMG and visual attention mass for individual hand DoFs, together with the relative MAE changes of the proposed DoF-query Transformer and the global-query variant with respect to the vision-only and EMG-only baselines, under the palm-facing-down and palm-facing-side conditions, respectively. Vision attention mass is displayed downward for visual comparison. (C)–(G) Ground-truth joint angles, EMG-only, vision-only, and fusion model predictions, and EMG attention mass for the thumb, index, middle, ring, and pinky finger, respectively, under representative motions. These examples illustrate that modality-attention patterns vary across DoFs and adapt dynamically to the temporal context.

Fig. 7. Robustness evaluation under synthetic visual occlusion. Average performance of visiononly, EMG-only, and the fusion models is compared across increasing occlusion ratios from 0% to 70%, using R² and MAE as evaluation metrics.

Bold values indicate the best performance within each comparison.

papers.abstract: We present RoboKit, a high-performance, general-purpose toolkit for parallel differentiable optimization in robotics, built on three principles: (i) Performance and flexibility: GPU-parallel multi-seed solvers pair sampling with versatile optimizers, running 2-60$\times$ faster than task-specific baselines across seven tasks; (ii) Geometry, rendering and physics: hybrid and coarse-to-fine representations accelerate collision, differentiable rendering and simulation, optimizing 4096 grasps in 2.97 s; (iii) Integration with learning: costs are differentiable and simulation is parallel, so RoboKit both distills optimization into policies and trains RL; distilled policies run 9-240$\times$ faster at comparable accuracy, and RL reaches a GPU baseline's scores up to 2.1$\times$ sooner on the same simulator.
authors: Jianglong Ye, Xuanbin Peng, Conor Mc Gartoll, Changwei Jing, Lai Wei, Jiali Chen, Xueyan Zou, Xiaolong Wang
bullets: Uses multi-seed, GPU-parallel solvers combining sampling with flexible optimizers.
Employs hybrid and coarse-to-fine geometry, rendering, and physics representations for faster computation.
Reports 2–60× speedups over task-specific baselines across seven tasks.
Optimizes 4,096 grasps in 2.97 seconds and enables distilled policies to run 9–240× faster at comparable accuracy.
Accelerates reinforcement-learning progress to baseline scores by up to 2.1× on the same simulator.

papers.tldr: RoboKit is a GPU-parallel toolkit that accelerates differentiable robot optimization and integrates it with policy distillation and reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Learning manipulation tasks from few demonstrations requires abstractions that capture the changes relevant to task completion, such as object poses in rigid-body manipulation. However, tasks such as cleaning are defined by changes in visual state rather than object pose, making the choice of task representation less clear. In this work, we propose Cleanly-DINO to learn visual task spaces from few demonstrations. Given a mask of a task-relevant region and frozen ViT features, Cleanly-DINO fits a projection to isolate a task space and fit a progression metric to it. We train the model on diverse cleaning examples and evaluate its ability to localize incomplete task regions and transfer across visual domains. We also study its utility for robot learning by using it as an observation encoder and reward signal in a reinforcement learning setting. Finally, we deploy our fitted model within a real-world robotic wiping pipeline to evaluate its use in guiding task execution.
authors: Adrian R\"ofer, Melika Shekarriz, Jos\'e Arce y de la Borbolla, Iman Nematollahi, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses cleaning tasks where success depends on visual-state changes rather than object poses.
Uses task-relevant region masks and frozen ViT features to learn a projected task space and progression metric.
Trained on diverse cleaning examples to localize incomplete regions and transfer across visual domains.
Evaluated as an observation encoder and reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Deployed in a real-world robotic wiping pipeline to guide task execution.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Cleanly-DINO approach for learning visual task spaces. We train our model from video sequences with masks for the task-relevant region. We embed the images and train a projection layer under a self-supervised contrastive objective to separate the initial from the final task state. In the projected task space, we select anchor points to measure task progress as movement between these. In deployment, we use our model trained on cleaning tasks to identify dirty regions in an unseen setting in order to drive a robotic wiping pipeline and to serve as the observation space and reward for a reinforcement learning agent.

Figure 4: Impression of our real robotic setup and the robot’s observation, and before and after examples. The robot is tasked with wiping the table in front of it in places it identifies as dirty. It does so competently on the regularly patterned tablecloths, as well as the plain wooden table. The method fails to generalize to the irregularly patterned tablecloth in the bottom right.
Figure 2: Impression of the six tasks in our dataset. We use a combination of self-recorded and internet videos. Each second row shows the hand-crafted labels we use for evaluation.

Figure 3: Cross-domain study: Left: Providing training data from the target domain (k) always works best, but training on up to three foreign domains also boosts performance. Importantly, adding out-of-domain data has almost no negative impact. Right: Training on one source task and then adding demonstrations for another target task benefits the target without costing the source. The gain is greater for the Linear head, but this is due to its lower starting point. These gains are limited without the abstention filter.
Figure 5: Appearance variations we apply to robosuite’s wipe env to evaluate the observation space’s sensitivity to the specific observations it encountered during training.

Table 3: Stroke policies trained with the learned progression as their reward, in simulation. Peak and Final are the evaluated wiped fraction at its maximum and at the end of training; Rollout is training-episode performance over the last 25% of training. Mean ± standard deviation over three seeds.

Table 1: Within-frame AUROC on held-out demonstrations, all tasks used for training. plain is the grouping of Sec. 3.1 alone, abstain filters by Sec. 3.2. Raw DINOv2 (no head) performs better than any plain condition and also than DINOv3. Meanwhile, abstain enables Cleanly-DINO to exceed this baseline performance.

Table 2: Comparison of Cleanly-DINO and raw DINOv2’s success transfer under shifting visual appearance. Starting at the same performance in the training scene, both observation spaces perform worse under changed visual appearance. The decline is ≈ 2x as large for DINOv2 as for Cleanly-DINO with a widening deviation.

papers.selection_reason: Directly contributes to robot learning and manipulation with a method for learning visual task spaces.
papers.title: Cleanly-DINO: Efficiently Learning Visual Task Spaces for Robotics
papers.tldr: Cleanly-DINO learns a visual task representation from few demonstrations to recognize cleaning progress and guide robotic wiping.

papers.abstract: Advancing from individual embodied intelligence to swarm embodied intelligence is a key step toward scalable, general-purpose embodied intelligence. Complex tasks often require multiple agents to divide responsibilities, coordinate handovers, and manipulate shared objects collaboratively. However, existing robot learning methods rely primarily on individual demonstrations, which provide limited supervision for modeling dependencies among agent actions, while collecting multi-robot demonstrations at scale remains difficult. Human egocentric demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, yet distributed observations from multiple participants cannot directly supervise decentralized policies. We introduce EgoSwarm, the first robot learning framework for learning decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. EgoSwarm collects more than 50 hours of collaborative experience using a robot-free multi-person egocentric system. We introduce the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP) and Swarm Interaction Token (SIT) to recover cross-agent interaction relations from distributed observations and transform this experience into local supervision consistent with deployment-time information constraints. We further propose SwarmVLA, which transfers knowledge of swarm behavior to decentralized policies conditioned on local observations, local history, and limited neighbor messages. SwarmVLA achieves a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks. Project page:https://xitong-c.github.io/EgoSwarm_Page/.
authors: Ziqiang Liu, Xitong Chen, Min Li, Yiqun Li, Zhuoping Yin
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable multi-robot demonstrations and the difficulty of learning dependencies among agents’ actions.
Collects over 50 hours of collaborative experience with a robot-free, multi-person egocentric system.
Introduces Swarm Interaction Packets and Tokens to recover cross-agent relations and create deployment-consistent local supervision.
Proposes SwarmVLA, a decentralized policy conditioned on local observations, history, and limited neighbor messages.
Reports a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EgoSwarm. EgoSwarm is the first robot learning framework for decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. It reconstructs cross-agent interaction in the form of the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP), encodes deployment-available interaction information into the Swarm Interaction Token (SIT), and learns locally executable collaboration policies through SwarmVLA.

Figure 3: EgoSwarm pipeline for decentralized multi-robot collaboration. (a) Multimodal egocentric recordings are temporally aligned and reconstructed into quality-annotated Swarm Interaction Packets (SIPs). (b) A causal CTDE teacher learns coordination representations and action flow fields from collective interaction supervision, which are distilled into the decentralized student policy. (c) During deployment, each robot constructs local Swarm Interaction Tokens (SITs), aggregates quality-aware neighbor information, and generates future actions from the resulting Action Context.

Figure 5: Real-world multi-robot collaborative task execution. The figure illustrates representative execution sequences of the three evaluation tasks: Multi-Robot Flexible Handover (MRFH, top), Dynamic Collaborative Transport (DCT, middle), and Large-Scale Deformable Object Manipulation (LSDOM, bottom). Frames progress from left to right; red arrows indicate robot motion directions, and dashed circles highlight key interaction regions.

Figure 2: EgoSwarm Capture and shared human–robot sensing interface. Human participants wear SwarmEgo sensing heads to record synchronized multi-person egocentric demonstrations. Each sensing head integrates task and scene cameras, infrared cameras, an IMU, and UWB sensing. The robot platform reuses the same sensing interface and UWB infrastructure, reducing the perception gap between human demonstrations and decentralized robot deployment.

Figure 6: Evaluation of SIP relative-geometry reconstruction. (a) Optical motion capture provides reference poses for ground-truth evaluation. (b) Translation and rotation error distributions over 30 independent multi-person interaction segments. SIP achieves a translation RMSE of 4.8 mm and a rotation RMSE of 2.6◦.

Figure 4: Composition of the SwarmVLA training data. The dataset consists of three complementary sources for decentralized multi-robot learning: human swarm data for cross-agent interaction experience, robot adaptation data for embodiment alignment, and joint robot teleoperation data for task-specific collaborative action supervision.

Table 1: Success rates (%) across three swarm manipulation tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Learning decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human egocentric demonstrations, fitting learning from human videos and robot learning.
papers.title: EgoSwarm: Learning Decentralized Robot Swarm Intelligence from Human Swarm Demonstrations
papers.tldr: EgoSwarm learns decentralized multi-robot collaboration from scalable human egocentric swarm demonstrations by converting distributed observations into local training signals.

papers.abstract: Visual reinforcement learning (RL) policies that land a drone on a moving platform can fail when the landing pad looks different from the one used in training. Using binary target masks as the visual input removes most pixel-level appearance information while preserving the spatial representation of the target, and lets a text prompt specify the target. In simulation, we test whether a frozen (fixed-weight) mask-based DrQ-v2 policy can handle a new pad when only the prompt of its fine-tuned SAM 3 detector changes. A banana-themed pad lowered landing success from 75.6% to 12.0%, and SAM 3 rarely detected it under the original prompt. A revised prompt, chosen after testing several candidates, restored success to 68.4% with no weight updates. In a separate experiment with a policy trained on ground-truth masks, filling in masks that were missing while the pad was visible helped landing far more than the tested mask-centroid and area corrections. Tracking the pad over time supplied masks more often and also kept producing them after the pad was confirmed absent from the rendered image, but it did not establish a reliable improvement in landing success. Whether a usable mask reaches the policy at all thus appears to be an important limiting factor for this approach.
bullets: Binary target masks preserve target location while reducing sensitivity to pad appearance, with prompts specifying the target.
A novel banana-themed pad reduced success from 75.6% to 12.0% because the original SAM 3 prompt rarely detected it.
Selecting a revised prompt restored success to 68.4% without updating the policy weights.
For missing masks, mask filling improved landing more than the tested centroid or area corrections.
Temporal tracking produced masks more often but also hallucinated masks after the pad disappeared, without reliably improving landing success.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the shared perception, policy, and control pipeline. Direct SAM 3 masks take precedence and temporal predictions provide fallback observations. The evaluated frontends differ in their temporal anchoring (Section VI). CLIP similarity is part of the perception metadata and does not reject masks.

papers.tldr: Prompt changes can substantially improve frozen mask-based visual RL landing on novel moving platforms, but reliable target-mask availability remains a key bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents learn from mistakes, yet their decisions can be difficult to trace back to those experiences. We investigate whether a tabular agent's decisions can be explained by its bad experiences, defined as the training transitions associated with safety or task events. A fixed training log is replayed from the same initial Q-table under three conditions. FULL retains all updates, SKIP omits bad-experience updates, and NEUTRALIZE retains those updates without their event penalties. We illustrate the method on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluate it in closed-loop driving in CARLA. On the full driving task, FULL reached the goal from 33 of 40 test starts, whereas SKIP and NEUTRALIZE reached it from none, indicating that the bad experiences carry decision-relevant information. At the local level, for 47 decisions shortly before a failure of SKIP or NEUTRALIZE, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences, with a median size of one, caused the trained agent to select the failing policy's action in 46 cases. For this agent, the results indicate that its decisions can be explained by its bad experiences.
authors: Ahmad Alfan Alfian Irfan, Nur Ahmad Khatim, Mansur Arief
bullets: Replays one fixed training log from the same Q-table under three conditions: all updates, skipped bad-experience updates, or neutralized penalties.
Demonstrated on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluated in closed-loop CARLA driving.
In CARLA, the full agent reached the goal from 33/40 starts, while skipping or neutralizing bad experiences succeeded from none.
For 46 of 47 decisions preceding failures, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences—median size one—reproduced the failing action.
The conclusion is scoped to the evaluated tabular agent and environments.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies by drawing several action candidates and executing the best one. We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The plans are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.
authors: Hanbo Zhang, Lianlei Shan, Liuhaichen Yang, Zezhi Tang
bullets: Standard candidate resampling quickly saturates because candidates differ mainly by noise, not by distinct plans.
A lightweight planner proposes latent plan hypotheses, while a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan in a single backbone pass.
Plans are learned from demonstrations without plan labels or rewards; the policy selects the highest-likelihood action chunk.
On CALVIN ABC→D, eight plan-conditioned candidates achieve 69.9% success versus at most 64.9% for matched plan-free or same-plan baselines.
Benefits are strongest when tasks have multiple solutions: PlanDiv removes more failures on LIBERO-Long and reaches 51/54 real-arm trials on two multi-solution tasks.

One shared masked-diffusion executor decodes a candidate chunk Âk under each plan in S=4 unmasking steps, so the candidates come from K different plans instead of K samples under one condition. The policy executes the candidate with the highest score, by default the mean log-probability of its tokens. (b) Training. papers.tldr: PlanDiv improves VLA test-time scaling by generating diverse latent plans rather than noisy resampled actions, substantially increasing success on tasks with multiple valid solutions.

papers.abstract: Real-time whole-body imitation from monocular video requires both a robust universal tracker and high-quality real-time reconstruction. We present MoViC, a framework that uses live RGB video as a control signal for humanoid robots without wearable tracking devices. The framework combines monocular human motion reconstruction, robot retargeting, and a transformer-based behavior foundation model. The policy receives proprioceptive history, a single explicit next-step reference, and a compact frequency-domain motion representation that supplies temporal context without explicitly stacking future reference frames, which reduces the input dimension and network size. During deployment, our extrapolation method bridges the 10-Hz visual estimation with 50-Hz controller, enabling asynchronous visual processing and policy execution. Hardware experiments further demonstrate highly dynamic motion tracking and device-free teleoperation of bimanual and single-arm manipulation tasks from live monocular RGB input. Project page: https://movicproject.github.io/ .
authors: Yimin Han, Jiahui Zhang, Wanyue Li, Zeren Luo, Yeke Chen, Liu Zhao, Peizhuo Li, Xiaoyu Ji, Shihao Dong, Xuechao Chen, Zhangguo Yu, Annan Tang, Peng Lu
bullets: Combines monocular human-motion reconstruction, robot retargeting, and a transformer-based behavior foundation model.
Uses proprioceptive history, one explicit next-step reference, and a compact frequency-domain motion representation for temporal context.
Extrapolates visual estimates from 10 Hz to support a 50 Hz controller with asynchronous perception and policy execution.
Hardware experiments demonstrate dynamic motion tracking and bimanual and single-arm manipulation from live RGB input.

papers.abstract: When a robot practices without human resets, every attempt still costs wall-clock time, actuator wear, and sometimes a person's attention, yet the schedulers that decide what to practice next treat attempts as free. We present an open, low-cost testbed for measuring these costs: a self-built SO-101 arm runs two demonstration-trained ACT policies that reset each other, with a vision-based success detector and a ledger that records the time, joint travel, and human interventions of every attempt. We formulate cost-aware practice scheduling, in which task selection is rewarded by measured competence gain net of embodied cost, and specify in advance the comparison that will test it. Its first two conditions, run on hardware for 51 minutes of robot time, show that a fixed retry limit did not reduce the share of execution time lost to failures (36%, against 27% for a feasibility rule; not significant) and saved no robot time. The logs suggest why: failures showed no sign of clustering, so a retry right after a failure was as likely to succeed as any other attempt. The ledger also shows that most of the retry rule's extra human time came from cubes knocked out of reach rather than from the rule itself, and a cost-aware rule replayed on the logs recovers the sensible choice without a hand-set limit. We also report lessons from building the system, including a coverage effect in which concentrating demonstrations in a smaller workspace raised success there from 8/20 to 10/10.
bullets: Robot attempts incur measurable wall-clock time, joint travel, actuator wear, and human intervention costs.
The testbed uses a self-built SO-101 arm, two demonstration-trained ACT policies, vision-based success detection, and per-attempt cost logging.
Across 51 minutes of hardware operation, a fixed retry limit lost 36% of execution time to failures versus 27% for a feasibility rule; the difference was not significant and saved no robot time.
Failures did not cluster, so immediately retrying after failure was no more likely to succeed than other attempts.
Log replay suggests cost-aware scheduling can recover sensible choices without a hand-set retry limit; concentrated demonstrations also improved local success from 8/20 to 10/10.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: The practice loop, drawn with real frames from one unattended cycle. (1) The scene camera sees the cube, and the detector marks it as on the table. (2) The scheduler turns that into the next attempt: place from the table, retrieve from the tray, a call for help if the cube is out of reach. (3) The chosen ACT policy drives the arm. (4) The detector scores the result; here the cube has settled in the tray. (5) The ledger writes one row for the attempt; the values shown are a real row from our logs. (6) The arm returns to the pose every demonstration started from, and the loop repeats. The dashed arrow is what this paper adds: today’s scheduler records the cost but never reads it, and the proposed scheduler decides with it.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) decisions at intersections affect the delay, braking, and motion smoothness of surrounding human-driven vehicles (HDVs). Learning socially compatible behavior requires connecting imagined interaction outcomes with feedback from executed actions. We propose a world-model reinforcement learning framework combines imagined policy improvement with direct value and policy calibration from finalized interactions, balancing AV progress with HDV interaction burden. An interaction-aware latent model supports imagination, while off-policy correction and replay updates enable observed rewards and transitions to supervise both the critic and actor. Simulation experiments at an unsignalized intersection achieve a 100% success and reductions in following-HDV acceleration variation of 65.5% and 44.0% relative to PIWM and DreamerV3, respectively. Ablations identify complementary roles for value calibration in reducing HDV burden and policy calibration in improving passage efficiency. Tests under out-of-distribution traffic shifts further show lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.
authors: Sen Shen, Ning Liu, Xiangrui Kong, Yingwei Li, Dongkun Han
bullets: Targets socially compatible AV behavior at unsignalized intersections by balancing passage efficiency with HDV interaction burden.
Uses an interaction-aware latent world model for imagined policy improvement, plus off-policy replay to calibrate both value and policy from finalized interactions.
Simulation achieved 100% intersection success and reduced following-HDV acceleration variation by 65.5% versus PIWM and 44.0% versus DreamerV3.
Ablations associate value calibration with lower HDV burden and policy calibration with improved passage efficiency.
Under out-of-distribution traffic shifts, the method produced lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.

papers.selection_reason: World-model RL framework with imagined interaction and value/policy calibration for autonomous driving, fitting interactive world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Value and Policy Calibration from Execution Feedback for Socially Compatible Driving
papers.tldr: A world-model RL approach calibrates imagined driving policies with real execution feedback to improve AV progress while reducing disruption to surrounding human drivers.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as an important paradigm in robot learning, jointly predicting future scene states and robot actions from current observations and instructions. However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model's ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model (DiffWAM), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. DiffWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Xinheng Zhang, Haoyu Xiong, Chao Jing, Xiaohan Zhang, Linshan Li, Hongbang Fan, Xingyu Chen
bullets: WAMs can be distracted by task-irrelevant future-state content, such as static backgrounds.
DiffWAM jointly predicts future frames, robot actions, and latent differences between consecutive observations.
Its Mixture-of-Experts design uses World, Action, and Diff Experts with attention masking to isolate their roles.
The World and Diff Experts are removed at inference, so the method adds no inference overhead.
It reports state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Framework of DiffWAM. The Observation Encoder provides current-observation representations to the World, Diff, and Action Experts. The World and Diff Experts receive the same noised future-frame latents, share their first N −M layers, and use independent final M layers for state generation through denoising and latent-difference prediction through regression, respectively. Structured unidirectional attention separates the expert pathways. At inference, both visual prediction experts are removed, retaining only the Observation Encoder and Action Expert without additional inference overhead.

Figure 5. Real-world setup, task execution sequences, and success rates. Left: the robot workspace and camera placement. Right: example executions of Place Pens, Store Block, and Stack Cups. Bottom: success rates of FastWAM and DiffWAM-S across the three tasks.

Figure 4. Training configurations and shared inference pathway of DiffWAM. DiffWAM-S freezes the independent LDB while retaining difference prediction during small-scale training. DiffWAM-L first trains the independent Diff Expert parameters with the remaining modules frozen, then jointly trains all modules. Orange denotes trainable modules, and blue with snowflake symbols denotes frozen modules; in DiffWAM-S, the shared World–Diff layers remain trainable. Both configurations retain only the Observation Encoder and Action Expert at inference.

Figure 3. Structured attention masks in DiffWAM. (a) Attention in the first N −M layers, where the World and Diff Experts share visual processing layers. (b) Attention in the last M layers, with independent state and diff prediction pathways. (c) Observation and action pathways retained at inference. papers.abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.
authors: Zhanjiang Yang, Lijun Sun, Yueming Li, Meng Li, Yijun Yang
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization of existing MORL methods beyond task- or objective-specific policies.
Uses a multimodal diffusion transformer with likelihood-free flow matching to model diverse trade-off trajectories.
Trains in three stages: large-scale pre-training, curated-data mid-training, and few-shot post-training on new tasks and trade-offs.
Outperforms prior methods on most D4MORL tasks, including zero-shot interpolation/extrapolation and few-shot adaptation in continuous control.

papers.abstract: We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.
authors: Mohammad Al-Jarrah, Yuhang Mei, Karen Leung, Bamdad Hosseini, Amirhossein Taghvaei
bullets: Frames imitation learning as conditional sampling of action chunks given observation histories.
Introduces three variants: optimal transport policy (OTP), flow matching policy (FMP), and stochastic interpolant policy (SIP).
Unlike Diffusion Policy, uses the empirical demonstration distribution rather than a fixed Gaussian reference.
On Push-T and robomimic Square, the methods are competitive with Diffusion and Consistency Policies while requiring smaller networks and shorter training.
OTP minimizes inference cost with one evaluation; SIP achieves the strongest scores among the proposed methods at higher cost.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical high-speed legged locomotion requires motion planners to balance safety foresight with online computational efficiency. Although short prediction horizons reduce rollout costs, they provide limited safety foresight, and strict safety constraints severely restrict the feasible trajectory space. We propose a recovery-guided model-based diffusion (MBD) framework for safety-critical legged locomotion. It incorporates a learned terminal recovery critic into short-horizon trajectory optimization. Specifically, the critic approximates the worst-case future clearance margin along rollouts of a designated recovery policy. We introduce a feasibility-guided refinement strategy that combines within-horizon constraints and terminal recoverability at each sampling stage, while retaining feasible elites to mitigate sampling-support loss. Across 50 paired randomized Unitree Go2 obstacle-avoidance trials, our approach achieves zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success, while requiring substantially less computation than long-horizon MBD baselines. A project page is available at https://zack4417.github.io/rg-mbd/.
authors: Lei Zheng, Shivam Sood, Mithun Vanniasinghe, Guillaume Sartoretti, Armin Lederer
bullets: Short prediction horizons reduce computation but offer limited foresight, while strict safety constraints shrink feasible trajectories.
The method adds a learned terminal recovery critic that estimates worst-case future clearance under a recovery policy.
Feasibility-guided refinement enforces current-horizon constraints, terminal recoverability, and preserves feasible elite samples.
In 50 paired randomized Unitree Go2 obstacle-avoidance trials, it achieved zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success.
The approach required substantially less computation than long-horizon model-based diffusion baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations, robot states, and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but their multimodal interfaces introduce new security risks. Existing VLA backdoor attacks primarily study trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored. We investigate suppression-aware backdoors, which combine conjunctive trigger activation with instruction-conditioned suppression. We instantiate this design through three variants: Cross-Modal Trigger, combining robot-state and spatially separated visual triggers; Self-Suppressing Trigger, requiring a state trigger and a [DISRUPT] instruction token for activation, with [RESTORE] token suppressing the attack; and Multi-Trigger, additionally requiring a visual trigger while retaining suppression even when physical triggers persist. We evaluate these attacks using SmolVLA on two SO-100 manipulation datasets against four baselines: State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, and SilentDrift. Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger reduce Isolation Forest detection from 96--98% to 1--18% and action-space l divergence by 10--14X, achieving 63--71% attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance. Experiments with OpenVLA on LIBERO further show that the attacks transfer to a 7B-parameter policy, evading STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection. Our findings establish conditional suppression as an important dimension for evaluating backdoor threats in VLA policies.
bullets: Targets security gaps in vision-language-action models, especially conditional suppression of backdoor behavior.
Proposes three designs: Cross-Modal Trigger, Self-Suppressing Trigger, and Multi-Trigger.
Evaluations on SmolVLA and OpenVLA show reduced detectability, 63–71% attack success, and preserved clean-task performance.
The attacks also evade STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection, highlighting suppression as a key threat dimension.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space. Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning. We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning. A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps. Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%. Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.
authors: Jiarui Dong, Zhiheng Liang, Yanjun Li, Zeyu Zhang, Heejeong Nam, Haoyu Chen, Hao Tang
bullets: Uses single-depth-camera point clouds to preserve metric geometry for manipulation.
Predicts future point-cloud embeddings and plans in latent space with a policy head on frozen representations.
A decoder visualizes imagined 4D point clouds, achieving mean point error under 1.1 cm over 200 steps.
Outperforms pixel-based JEPA models on reported OGBench tasks and leads MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate results.
Policies trained only in a digital twin transfer zero-shot to a real arm with gripper and dexterous hand.

papers.abstract: A distributed multi-robot object transportation strategy is proposed for objects of unknown shape, size, geometry, mass and mass distribution without any prior knowledge about the object or number of robots involved in the transportation process. Robots follow the boundary of the object and dynamically determine viable pushing points. A novel object-model-free heading-error-driven pushing effort regulation method is proposed to promote goal-directed object motion; robots regulate their pushing effort using individual and collective heading errors. Robots dynamically relocate around the object boundary if a pushing point is lost or the required pushing effort exceeds its capability to correct its heading. The proposed method is validated using simple and complex shapes with convex and non-convex boundary regions and dynamically changing weight distribution of objects. Detailed analysis on the effects of robot distribution and initial object pose on the transportation performance in terms of required time and path efficiency is also presented. Scalability analysis revealed that object transportation time is dependent on the number of pushing surfaces available which in turn depends on the object size, shape, and set inter-robot safety distance. The proposed system yielded highly efficient object paths with consistent elapsed transport times over several trials robust to external disturbances such as non-uniform friction between contacting surfaces and robot wheel slip.
authors: Tamzidul Mina, Shyam S. Kannan, Wonse Jo, Shaocheng Luo, Galen B. King, Byung-Cheol Min
bullets: Robots track an object’s boundary and dynamically identify viable pushing locations without a prior object model.
Individual and collective heading errors guide each robot’s pushing effort toward the goal.
Robots relocate when a pushing point is lost or when their available effort cannot correct the object’s heading.
Validation covers convex and non-convex shapes, complex geometries, changing weight distributions, friction variation, and wheel slip.
Transport paths were highly efficient with consistent elapsed times across trials; scalability depends on available pushing surfaces, object properties, and inter-robot safety distance.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.
bullets: The study compares computation reuse across replanning calls with simply reducing denoising steps on LIBERO-Goal.
Two uncached steps were non-inferior to ten on 500 initial states for one checkpoint and noise seed.
Latency fell from 202 ms to 92 ms per replanning call on an RTX A6000 under PyTorch’s default compile mode.
Caching offers limited speedups when fresh steps and image/video processing remain necessary; estimated savings were at most 11–14% in one setup.
Cache performance degraded when cached steps covered more of the flow path or noise was resampled, motivating evaluation under deployed sampler settings.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates a flow-matching world action model and denoising-step caching, directly relevant to interactive world models and robot policy learning.
papers.title: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model
papers.tldr: For Fast-WAM, using two uncached denoising steps preserves ten-step success while halving latency, leaving limited benefit and notable fragility for cross-cycle caching.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation missions must satisfy timed and conditional requirements that can be expressed in signal temporal logic (STL). While a practical means of monitoring these requirements is from camera images, this is challenging because STL robustness depends on physical margins, such as distances and clearances, that are not directly observed. Rather than learning a separate visual monitor for each formula, we learn a shared latent representation from multi-view images and decode physically meaningful margins for individual predicates. Co-training the encoder with predicate decoders increases the certification rate from 58.7% to 96.3% compared with a frozen encoder, despite nearly unchanged predicate sign accuracy. STL semantics then compose these margins into robustness estimates for any bounded formula over the trained predicates, without retraining. We further calibrate the decoding errors of selected STL clauses using conformal prediction, yielding two-sided intervals that certify both satisfaction and violation and propagate through interval STL to any formula composed from the clauses. In simulated kitchen missions (LIBERO), our monitor correctly predicts satisfaction or violation in 98.9% of 4662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas. For missions lasting up to 17 min, calibrated bounds establish satisfaction or violation for 96.9% of missions without incorrect conclusions. A single calibration also provides simultaneous 91.0% coverage across all 255 conjunctions of eight clauses, allowing new formulas without recalibration.
authors: Xinpei Ni, Glen Chou, Samuel Coogan
bullets: Targets timed and conditional robotic manipulation requirements that are difficult to monitor from images because STL robustness depends on unobserved physical margins.
Learns a shared multi-view latent representation with predicate-specific decoders, then composes decoded margins using STL semantics without retraining per formula.
Conformal calibration produces two-sided robustness intervals and propagates guarantees through interval STL to certify both satisfaction and violation.
In simulated LIBERO kitchen missions, it achieved 98.9% correct decisions over 4,662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas.
Scope: results are demonstrated in simulation and for trained predicates; calibration is needed for selected STL clauses, though one calibration supports new formula conjunctions.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the challenge of monitoring physical constraints (STL) in robotic manipulation using a shared latent visual representation to decode physical margins, bridging perception and physical safety.
papers.title: Physics-Grounded STL Monitoring from Image Observations
papers.tldr: A shared vision model decodes physics-grounded margins from images to monitor arbitrary STL formulas, with calibrated intervals that reliably certify satisfaction or violation.

papers.abstract: Physics-based control is central to robot learning, but differentiating through implicit physics steps typically requires Hessian or Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) linear solves; we ask whether gradient steps suffice. Each simulation step minimizes an energy under many contact and collision constraints. Without constraints, we view control over $K$ steps as $K$-level optimization with strongly convex lower levels, recast as one min--max problem. Our Penalized Single-loop $K$-level method (PSK) uses only gradients and a projection, updates all levels in parallel, and reaches an $\epsilon$-stationary control in $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ iterations, with a $K$-independent exponent but a $K$-dependent constant. Contact-rich constraints, however, typically violate a constraint qualification (CQ). We replace each constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width. Under mild assumptions that need no CQ, every exact solution of the banded lower levels is then feasible and banded Fritz--John, and PSK keeps the $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ complexity. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the $K$-independent exponent: with width $\epsilon$ and fixed $K\geq2$, deterministic zero-respecting methods need $\Omega(\epsilon^{-(K+3)/4})$ calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with $1/\epsilon$. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.
bullets: Recasts unconstrained K-step control as a single min–max problem with strongly convex lower levels.
Uses only gradients and projection, updating all levels in parallel without Hessian or KKT solves.
Achieves an $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ iteration bound, with an exponent independent of the number of levels $K$.
Smooths contact constraints using fixed-width bands to avoid requiring constraint qualifications; shrinking bands can worsen complexity.
In navigation experiments, PSK reached all goals with 16 levels and had lower equal-time loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation was better in 10.

papers.selection_reason: Matrix-free method for physics-based control, relevant to robot learning and control optimization.
papers.title: PSK: A Matrix-Free Single-Loop Method for K-Level Physics-Based Control
papers.tldr: PSK is a matrix-free, gradient-only method for multilevel physics-based control that handles contact constraints without constraint qualifications, with provable complexity and competitive navigation results.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to acquire complex skills, but standard RL formulations do not guarantee that learned policies satisfy safety constraints, which limits their use in safety-critical settings. Existing safe RL methods with provable guarantees typically support only restricted classes of constraints and require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions, which prevents their direct integration with state-of-the-art algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). In this paper, we extend the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework to overcome these limitations. Our formulation accommodates a general class of trajectory-level safety constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability, and our analysis allows for biased value and gradient estimators. We show that, with high probability, the constraint violation throughout training is bounded by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as the number of rollouts grows, and decays to this level if the initial policy is unsafe. We also establish the convergence properties of the iterates to approximate KKT points of the original safe RL problem. Finally, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with PPO-style estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body control policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.
authors: Pol Mestres, Varun Gabbita, Jason H. K. Siu, Sergio A. Esteban, Hampus Serneke, Joel W. Burdick, Aaron D. Ames
bullets: Handles general trajectory-level constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability.
Permits biased value and gradient estimators, enabling integration with PPO-style methods.
Bounds constraint violations with high probability by estimator bias plus a term that vanishes with more rollouts.
Proves convergence toward approximate KKT points and decay of violations from unsafe initial policies.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real whole-body control on a Unitree G1 and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.

papers.title: Towards Probabilistically Safe Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Deployment on Humanoid and Aerial Robots
papers.tldr: An extended robust safe RL framework provides probabilistic safety guarantees with biased PPO-style estimates and supports zero-shot deployment on humanoid and aerial robots.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7-4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0-1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0% over $\pi_{0.5}$) at 92.7 ms latency.
authors: Chongyu Fan, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella, Jason Corso, Sijia Liu
bullets: Existing world-action models waste capacity reconstructing mostly static backgrounds instead of modeling robot and object motion.
The method learns residual feature changes between current and future frames in frozen DINOv3 space, emphasizing manipulated regions.
A lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT jointly models actions and visual residuals using conditional flow matching.
Without robot pretraining, ResWAM reports strong results across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot tasks, with 92.7 ms latency.
Scope: results target action-conditioned visual prediction and manipulation; the abstract does not establish broader settings beyond these evaluations.

papers.selection_reason: Residual world-action model with action-conditioned future prediction, fitting interactive world models and VLA/robot learning.
papers.title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
papers.tldr: ResWAM improves vision-language-action policies by predicting only task-relevant visual changes, enabling strong robot manipulation performance with lower compute.

papers.abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.
authors: Yinghao Li, WeiHsien Lee, Zeyu Zhang, Canyang Zhao, Ke Fang, Xing Li, Bing Liu
bullets: Addresses whether brain activity can provide task-level intent without symbolic commands or hand-designed skills.
Uses a hierarchical framework: neural activity is read once as intent, then a learned visuomotor policy closes the control loop.
In counterfactual grasping, changing the neural intent changed which object the robot grasped, even when vision alone could not determine the target.
Representing the full neural population latent improved grasp completion from 69% to 81% across 132 held-out scenes; direction-only decoding did not help.
Intent effectiveness depended on neural location and timing: preparatory PMd signals supported grasping, with PMd outperforming M1 in one dual-array session.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The NI-ACT framework. (A) Control division. Conventional BCIs decode continuous velocity commands at every time step and keep the user inside the fast control loop. In NI-ACT, cortical activity supplies a task-level intent token once per task, sent at task start, and an embodied policy closes the fast perception–action loop with the robot and its environment. (B) Network architecture. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) maps binned PMd and M1 spikes to a 128-D population latent, a 2-D goal direction, and 7-class direction logits; an intent interface (Hard-7, Soft-2D, or Full-Latent) passes one of these to an action-chunking transformer (ACT) that also observes two cameras and the joint state, and the policy predicts 32 future joint targets. Fig. 3a gives how each interface enters the policy.

Figure 3: Architecture and data protocol of NI-ACT. (a) The frozen temporal convolutional encoder maps a window of binned spikes to a 128-D population latent z, from which a direction head reads a unit goal direction v̂ and a class head reads 7-way logits ℓ. The interface G selects one output: Hard-7 (one-hot of arg max ℓ) and Soft-2D (v̂) are appended to the 9-D joint state, giving 16-D and 11-D state inputs; Full-Latent (z) is kept separate from the joint state, projected from 128 to 512 dimensions, and enters the transformer encoder as its own intent token. The interfaces therefore differ in content, dimensionality, and injection pathway. Both camera images pass through one shared ImageNet-initialized ResNet-18, giving 7 × 7 feature maps (49 tokens per camera). With the VAE disabled, the latent token is constant. The encoder (4 layers) attends over all tokens; the decoder (1 layer, 32 learned queries) and a linear head predict 32 future 9-D joint targets. (b) Neural trials are split into training and held-out sets before any pairing. Each of the 207 counterfactual demonstrations is paired with a training trial of the same target direction, and the resulting intent is held constant over every frame; ACT is trained by behavior cloning, one policy per interface and neural source. At deployment, each of the 132 held-out scenes receives a held-out trial of its target direction; the intent is read once and held fixed while the policy replans every 32 steps. No neural trial is shared between training and evaluation. Trial counts refer to the monkey-J recording.
