papers.selection_reason: Neural intent interface for brain-embodied robotic manipulation; directly fits learned visuomotor control and manipulation.
papers.title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: NI-ACT shows that a brief intracortical neural signal can specify a persistent manipulation goal while a vision-and-proprioception policy autonomously executes the task.

papers.abstract: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.
authors: Akhil S. Anand, Xun Shen, Marc Peter Deisenroth, Sebastien Gros
bullets: Co-design couples system design with the policy operating it, since each affects the other.
The design gradient separates direct design effects from indirect effects through the design-dependent optimal policy.
Policy sensitivity is computed with the implicit function theorem applied to the policy-gradient stationarity condition.
A proof-of-concept algorithm combines this sensitivity with stochastic value gradient policy optimization.

On a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional designs, it consistently outperforms Bayesian optimization and evolution strategies; convergence to an approximately stationary design is proved.

papers.selection_reason: Gradient-based co-design of systems and RL policies is transferable to robot morphology and control co-optimization.
papers.title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
papers.tldr: A differentiable-simulator method jointly optimizes system designs and RL policies by computing how the converged policy changes with the design, avoiding costly black-box design search.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.
authors: Zequan Zeng, Junqin Yang, Kai Wang
bullets: Targets critical stages such as grasping, alignment, and insertion, where generalist VLA control may be imprecise or unstable.
Trains specialized atomic-skill policies with a shared RL Token state representation and the VLA policy’s reference action.
Uses a Mamba-based router with temporal history and semantic attention to select skills based on evolving task state.
Achieves 90.47% average Macro-F1 across four LIBERO task suites, 7.08 percentage points above an MLP router.
Raises Tube Transport full-task success from 20.04% to 85.67% in simulation.

The dynamic router then combines historical state information and skill semantics to coordinate policy selection and switching during multi-stage manipulation.

Fig. 2. Architecture of the dynamic skill router. The dynamic skill router combines Mamba-based temporal encoding with a historical feature window to capture temporal context. Candidate skill descriptions form semantic queries, which interact through self-attention and extract skill-relevant historical features via cross-attention. papers.abstract: We address tracking a moving object on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, despite an imprecise digital twin, measurement errors, and noise. Our novel approach augments a loop-shaped inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a residual policy learned via Soft Actor-Critic in the digital twin. A delay-compensated Kalman filter fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to provide latency-aware moving target position estimates. We compare the achieved performance to a performance bound for a class of model-based controllers derived from a frequency-domain sensitivity analysis, quantifying the minimum achievable error imposed by uncertain kinematic model mismatch. Simulation and hardware experiments indicate that our residual policy drives tracking error below the bound. Across conveyor speeds (27.9-41.8 mm/s), our method reduces mean tracking errors from 1.1-1.4 mm (baseline inverse-Jacobian PI) to 0.3-0.7 mm. These results show that learning residual corrections in a limited-fidelity simulator, combined with delay compensation, can substantially improve model-based control under modeling and measurement uncertainties while maintaining reliable sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Mahdi Nobar, Alisa Rupenyan, John Lygeros, J\"urg Keller
bullets: Targets conveyor-borne object tracking despite model mismatch, camera delays, measurement errors, and noise.
Combines an inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a Soft Actor-Critic residual policy trained in a digital twin.
Uses a delay-compensated Kalman filter to fuse out-of-sequence camera measurements and estimate target position.
Simulation and hardware tests show mean tracking error decreasing from 1.1–1.4 mm to 0.3–0.7 mm across the tested conveyor speeds.
The approach achieves errors below a frequency-domain performance bound for the evaluated controller class.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.
authors: Gaytri Jena, Kapil Wanaskar, Aman Chadha, Vasu Sharma, Vinija Jain, Amitava Das
bullets: Benchmarks 10 hospital chores in Isaac Sim, each with five scored sub-tasks linked by persistent state.
Tracks chain-break locations, post-failure behavior, and drift between estimated and true position.
Uses a scripted robot as a solvability check and evaluates agents through image-based, skill-level tools.
In 15 preliminary runs, 2 completed all five sub-tasks; only three chores had scripted-robot proofs.
Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by another call and 111 by a non-failing call; results are not yet a full benchmark.

papers.abstract: In simulation, Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs pick-and-place in robot cells with gripper or base-frame changes without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. It uses pre-trained vision-language and language models for interpretation, measures the command map and camera geometry from its own motion and fingertips, estimates lens distortion, and plans grasps from measured object depth. A controlled study of eight public LIBERO-fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs) varies robot hardware, camera geometry, appearance, and base frame. Gripper and frame changes dominate their losses in the tested fractional design. Across 18 cells with these changes, frozen VAA achieves 230/360 successes (64%), the refined VAA 268/360 (74%), and the strongest released VLA on this subset 76/360 (21%). Paired ablations support the self-calibration bundle, lens estimation under compounded changes, and the measured-depth pipeline. On a two-step LIBERO-Goal chain with object state carried between instructions, VAA completes 54/60 chains in changed cells, while four evaluated VLAs complete none.
authors: Jae Hun Hwang, Yechan Seo, Hong-In Won
bullets: Targets deployment failures caused by changes in grippers, base frames, cameras, and appearance.
Uses pretrained vision-language and language models with self-measured command maps, camera geometry, lens distortion, and object depth for grasp planning.
Across 18 changed cells, frozen VAA succeeds in 64% of trials and refined VAA in 74%, versus 21% for the strongest evaluated VLA.
A two-step task chain succeeds in 54/60 changed-cell chains, while the four evaluated VLAs complete none.
Results and ablations support the combined self-calibration, lens-estimation, and measured-depth components.

papers.title: Self-Calibrating Vision-Agent-Action: Deploying Pick-and-Place to New Robot Cells without Demonstrations or Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Self-calibrating Vision-Agent-Action enables zero-demonstration, zero-fine-tuning pick-and-place across changed robot cells by measuring scene and robot geometry from its own motion.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for visuomotor policies typically relies on teleoperated robot demonstrations, which are costly because every episode requires a trained operator controlling a physical robot in real time through teleoperation interfaces and wearable body-tracking hardware. Egocentric glasses capture human demonstrations without a robot or handheld grippers, yet they track only the head and in-view human hands, and directly copying human motion to a robot with different stature, arm reach and hand morphology fails to produce feasible contacts. \method{} converts egocentric glasses recordings into physically verified robot training trajectories. An agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs collision and textured visual assets from the recorded RGB-D and head streams, completes unseen surfaces when needed, and predicts target contact bands on the manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, a grasp planner turns each contact band into a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, bilevel stance optimization plans collision-free standing postures that keep hand targets reachable, and a whole-body motion generator synthesizes lower-body locomotion and out-of-view arm motion. Two-stage motion correction then blends visibility transitions kinematically and trains a reinforcement-learning tracking policy in physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards, completing manipulation phases even when the object leaves the camera view. Rendering the reconstructed scene through the robot's onboard camera along the optimized rollout yields synchronized robot-view images, proprioception and verified action labels. Fine-tuned exclusively on this converted dataset, without real-robot demonstrations, GR00T N1.7 performed loco-manipulation tasks autonomously on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://robonana.github.io/ego2sim2humanoid/

Produces synchronized robot-view observations, proprioception, and verified action labels for policy training.
A GR00T N1.7 policy trained exclusively on the converted data autonomously performed loco-manipulation tasks on a Unitree G1.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Architecture of E2S2H, illustrated on a bottle-lift recording. From egocentric video and tracked hand landmarks, agentic real-to-sim masks objects and builds a textured visual scene with simplified collision geometry. Each object pairs a visual mesh with a collision model marked by target contact regions. Along the human (orange) and adapted robot (green) camera paths, the robot poses trace adaptation and correction. During the approach with hands out of view (cyan), the whole-body motion generator drives locomotion and unseen arm motion, then begins blending arm targets prior to visibility. Once hands enter the camera view (blue), tracked human landmarks take over arm guidance. Placing the robot directly on the projected human head path (red) does not guarantee a collision-free stance. Stance adaptation is therefore required to keep clear of the table while holding targets within reach in a comfortable posture. Directly copying the human palm onto the robot hand likewise fails, causing finger penetration or missed contact in the grasp comparison above. The final pose (grey) combines bilevel stance adjustment with contact-band Dex3 grasp planning. Kinematic optimization and reinforcement learning in physics simulation refine this plan into a dynamically feasible rollout. E2S2H then renders the robot camera view from the reconstructed scene along the rollout path to produce synchronized training data.

papers.abstract: JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement. Jointly learned from offline demonstrations, this process iteratively updates the same plan before execution, making future predictions directly participate in action generation without candidate-action search. We evaluate short-horizon goal reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution. The results show that goal-aware predictive feedback supports competitive task performance while maintaining a compact model and low online computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Dovisya/WA-JEPA.
authors: Tao An, Weihang Liang, Tianqi Wang, Chuqing Cao, Wenming Tan, Kai Zhang, Haibo Lei, Tao Xie, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li
bullets: Addresses the high online cost of repeatedly evaluating candidate action sequences in JEPA-based world models.
Generates an action proposal, predicts future scenes and proprioceptive states, then iteratively refines the same plan using the task goal.
Combines goal-discrepancy residual feedback with future-scene context feedback for chunk-wise action refinement.
Learns the action generation and predictive feedback process from offline demonstrations.
Evaluated on short-horizon reaching, long-horizon tasks, and full-task execution, achieving competitive performance with a compact model and low online computation.

papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.
bullets: Targets the cost of re-solving HJ reachability whenever obstacles change and the false-safe errors of a single conditioned network.
Caps the obstacle margin to make the value function provably local, enabling body-frame window inputs, small-scene training, and scene-size transfer.
Uses an output structure that enforces conservative value bounds and counterexample mining to expand the learned safe set under the HJ inequality.
Reports recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach with near-zero rollout collisions across tested obstacle settings.
Extends to a 10D quadrotor, achieving markedly lower collision rates than baselines.

papers.abstract: Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds.
authors: Ran Qi, Yixin Xiao, Dawei Wang, Zhiyuan Li, Jinbang Huang, Xuan Zhao, Yintao Ma, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited gains from improving robot agents and models independently.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RoboCoEvo. The co-evolution framework of agent and policy improving each other over successive rounds. (a) Policy-Guided Agent Evolution: the agent locates failures in the policy’s failed rollouts and groups recurring failures into failure modes (FMs), shown at the top for each round. For each FM, it writes a detector that identifies the failure state in a rollout (red) and a recovery program that completes the failed subtask from this state in simulation (green). As the policy improves, its rollouts expose FMs that did not occur in earlier rounds. In each subsequent round, the agent writes detectors and recovery programs for the newly identified FMs and refines those of persisting FMs to improve detection accuracy and recovery success. (b) Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion: the policy is fine-tuned on the corrective experience together with the original demonstrations, which enables the policy itself to avoid or recover from the targeted failures. The rollouts of the updated policy initiate the next round, and its task success increases over successive rounds. The scores compare the base policy with the policy after RoboCoEvo.

Figure 2: The RoboCoEvo pipeline. Each round proceeds clockwise, starting with rollouts of the current policy πi. Policy-Guided Agent Evolution (right): the agent identifies failure modes (FMs) from K sampled failures and writes a detector dm for each FM. The detectors localize failure states in all failed rollouts, from which the agent writes a recovery program ρm for each FM. Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion (left): failure-conditioned augmentation perturbs each localized state s into J states s̃j of the same FM, and ρm completes the failed subtask from both the original and the perturbed states, which yields the corrective experience Ri. The policy is then post-trained on D0 and the accumulated corrective experience to obtain πi+1, whose rollouts start the next round. Steps marked with circular arrows are updated in every round.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of the base policy and RoboCoEvo on targeted failure modes. Each row shows one failure mode on one benchmark. Left: the base policy π0 enters the failure mode and fails to recover. Right: after RoboCoEvo, π1 enters the same failure mode and recovers without the agent. Frames are aligned by stage.

Figure 3: Failure-conditioned augmentation on two BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. From an observed failure state s (left), the agent edits the robot and object states in the simulator to obtain perturbed states s̃1, s̃2, . . . (right) that preserve the same FM. Each perturbed state serves as an additional initial state for the recovery program, so a single observed failure yields multiple recovery runs.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.
bullets: Addresses deployment-time constraints not present in demonstrations without retraining the policy.
Samples several action chunks, certifies them with a barrier condition, then selects the highest-valued certified chunk.
Certification guarantees safety independently of the critic and bounds deviation from the policy conditioned on feasibility.
CAST-V estimates policy-conditioned viability to preserve future safe control authority; CAST-VL learns it from controller logs.
Across manipulation, quadrotor, humanoid, and unicycle tasks, CAST generally improves joint task-and-constraint success over output filtering.

(a) A safety filter keeps the robot in the safe set h ≥ 0 (shading: the barrier), but its rollouts on the blocked route stall at the zone: the policy never learned to continue from there (40 rollouts, with counts). (b) Viability v of the policy’s certified chunks, by simulation: the probability that it keeps sampling certified chunks over the next 8 decisions. Certified chunks exist in the red region too, but lead to a dead end; of the N = 8 drawn at one decision four head into it, and CAST-V executes a viable one. (c) The same map from a network trained on the controller’s logs, without model rollouts (CAST-VL): its boundary v = 0.5 (black) follows the simulated one (white) where the rollouts pass. Figure 10: Two diagnostics. (a) Viability or success as the learning target? Both networks are trained on the same logged episodes of the critic-free controller, with the same features, architecture and recipe; only the label differs (viability of the executed chunk, or the episode’s joint success). Unicycle, unseen zones, three policies × 500 scored scenarios; bands: 95 % intervals, and at 100 episodes the range of three disjoint subsets, in each of which viability is ahead. With 300 episodes the two are level (+0.01 [−0.00, +0.03]), with 1000 the success critic is slightly ahead (−0.01 [−0.03, −0.00]), and with 3000 by 0.02. Viability is the cheaper label to learn and needs no task outcome; a success critic can replace it when logs are plentiful. (b) Where violations come from. Square, new requests, learned predictor (1 200 scored episodes per controller): share of violating episodes among those that executed at least one fallback chunk failing the certificate (an uncertified correction, or the hold backup, which is accepted without margins) and among those whose chunks were all certified. Theorem 1 covers the second group; none of its episodes violated.

papers.abstract: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.
bullets: Studies deployment-time compute allocation for a frozen chunked robot policy: more denoising per call versus more frequent replanning.
Evaluates both nominal compute rate and total compute per completed attempt, using discovery and held-out task comparisons.

In synchronous LIBERO simulation with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint and chunk length K=50, d=2 with h=2 achieved 139/160 successes versus 122/160 for d=5, while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step.
Increasing replanning from h=2 to h=5 at d=2 used 60.7% less arithmetic per attempt but produced nearly identical successes; equivalence was not established.
Findings are a scoped case study, not a universal deployment recommendation; arithmetic and latency characterize costs differently.

papers.abstract: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.
authors: Yiting Chen, Kelin Yu, Sarthak Kaingade, Bryan Trinh, Kaiyu Hang, Roberto Martin-martin, Nima Fazeli, X. Alice Wu
bullets: Addresses forceful multi-finger manipulation under uncertain contact and interaction dynamics, beyond geometry-based interaction.
Uses tactile-observable interaction representations with cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contacts.
Adapts motor behavior from tactile history while coordinating an upper-body manipulation policy with a pretrained locomotion controller.
Trained entirely in simulation and transferred zero-shot to a Unitree G1 with multi-fingered hands.
Substantially outperforms standard RMA and reactive tactile-policy baselines across four real-world commercial round doorknobs.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation. (a) The upper-body manipulation policy commands the right arm and hand, while a pretrained locomotion controller commands the leg and waist joints to maintain whole-body balance under interaction-induced disturbances. The two policies share whole-body proprioceptive feedback, coupling manipulation and balance within an integrated control system. (b) Each fingertip contact force is parameterized in cone coordinates by the normal load n, force cone angle α , and circularly encoded shear direction (sinφ ,cosφ). This formulation separates the uncertainty source while preserving the contact mechanics. (c) The policy learning proceeds in two stages. First, the privileged encoder and tactile-centric policy are optimized jointly end-to-end under the task objective, forming an oracle policy and yielding a task-relevant interaction latent. Both modules are then frozen, and the adaptation encoder is trained through latent regression to estimate the interaction latent from a 2s history of deployable observations. (d) During real-world deployment, the adaptation encoder updates the interaction latent online from tactile interaction history and conditions the frozen tactile-centric policy to generate manipulation motor commands.

papers.abstract: Robots in homes, warehouses and farms must pick up objects they have never seen, usually without a 3D model or a category label. A grasping policy that works directly on the point cloud from a depth sensor needs only the geometry the robot observes, so it applies to any new object. Offline grasp generators such as Contact-GraspNet work this way, but they rank grasps by learned plausibility rather than by whether the grasp actually lifts the object. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize for that directly and make a point-cloud grasping policy much better on average, yet it leaves specific grasps persistently unsolved. We present a human-in-the-loop failure loop that targets those grasps: situations an RL policy keeps failing are mined automatically, sent to a virtual-reality application where a person picks the object up with their own hands, and returned to training as two grasp points. The person contributes only where to grasp; the robot chooses its own approach. In simulation, RL raises success on unseen objects from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%. Adding 58 human demonstrations nearly doubles success on the hard cases RL kept failing, from 24% to 45%, and recovers performance that RL alone loses on similar cases that were never demonstrated, without reducing success on unseen objects.
authors: Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Karthik Rengarajan, Bharath Narasimhan, Chris von Csefalvay
bullets: Targets objects and grasps that an RL policy repeatedly fails to lift, without requiring object models or category labels.

papers.abstract: Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object's initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9-2.2x for each of five decoders, and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020-0.021 regret at 1.6-1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported. Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3-29x lower latency.
bullets: Evaluated decoders, losses, geometric projections, and coordinate frames on simulated and human PushT tasks.
Representing inputs and outputs in the object’s initial SE(2) frame reduced decision regret by 1.9–2.2× across five decoders.
Single-pass decoding achieved 0.020–0.021 regret in 1.6–1.8 ms, outperforming 10-step diffusion and cached autoregression in both speed and regret.
Soft-token expectation with end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection produced the lowest trajectory error and exact rigid-body consistency.
Decoder-head choice had no measurable regret effect; the preregistered claim that frame effects exceed decoder differences was not supported.

papers.abstract: Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.
bullets: Targets “Agentic Sleeper” attacks that appear legitimate initially, accumulate across sessions and agents, then activate across memory, logic, and infrastructure.

Warns at least three sessions before visible degradation and achieves 0.69 top-1 trace-back accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 across 24 variants.
Live LangGraph and AutoGen evaluations show posterior-guided defense reduces propagation below the self-sustaining regime; removing only visibly compromised agents does not.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process. By conditioning reward signals on the currently active subgoal, Skill-LR produces stage-specific credit that evolves with the hierarchical plan, reducing temporal variance and improving sample efficiency. On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks, including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and strong credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe, demonstrating that subgoal-aligned latent rewards offer a principled path toward stable, interpretable credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.
bullets: Targets sparse, delayed feedback and the limitations of transition-level return decomposition.
A vision-language model identifies the active subgoal at each timestep.
A two-stage LLM prompting process generates a matching latent reward formulation.

This suggests that subgoal-conditioned latent reward decomposition yields a more stable and learnable return-modeling objective in more challenging hierarchical tasks.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.
bullets: Addresses robot learning from human videos without action supervision.
Builds on a pretrained VLM with a mixture-of-training architecture for shared action and representation prediction.
Uses future visual-state prediction as an independent, complementary signal to action prediction.

The generation expert is removed at inference.

papers.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

papers.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
papers.tldr: Simulation-only reinforcement learning trains an open-weight reasoning model to control real robots natively, with strong transfer to unseen robots, tasks, and the physical world.

papers.abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
bullets: Addresses the heuristic assumptions and sensitive hyperparameters used by existing self-supervised movement-representation methods.
Predicts in latent space rather than reconstructing precise joint configurations, aligning with semantic anticipation of actions.
Uses forward and backward autoregressive prediction to exploit temporal ordering and combine past and future context at inference.
Separates prediction targets into global sequence semantics and local context-independent movement to prevent representation collapse.
Performs strongly on motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most reported metrics.

papers.abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
authors: Tony H. Zhang, Connor Mattson, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting demonstrations for multiple agents simultaneously.
Uses Round-Robin Behavior Cloning to train initial per-agent imitation policies.
At each step, centralized critics choose among imitation- and RL-proposed actions for each agent.
A gated, Q-filtered cloning penalty regularizes RL toward imitation only when imitation actions are judged better.

Across four cooperative benchmarks, IBMARL improves beyond imitation faster than demonstration-based baselines and can exceed demonstrator performance; it also outpaces imitation learning with real human demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.
authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Mike Degany, Deyuan Qu, Qing Yang, Matyas Szanto
bullets: Self-play handover succeeds with the trained partner but fails with unfamiliar scripted partners.
The learned giver always offers immediately, causing the receiver to rely on one fixed rendezvous timing.
A one-second delay sharply reduces success, confirming timing overfitting as the main failure mode.
Hidden start-delay randomisation improves unseen-partner success to 80% in both seeds, versus 35–41% for a matched control.
The improvement generalises to new scenarios and held-out partners, reduces high-force contact, and requires no partner retraining.

papers.abstract: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.
authors: Guangxi Feng, Philip Yasskin, Wei Yan
bullets: Motivation: AR-Classroom requires robust alignment between virtual overlays and a physical manipulative during spatial-learning activities.
Method: A compact YOLO model predicts 20 airplane keypoints from 128×128 RGB crops, and a perspective-n-point solver estimates 6DoF pose from corresponding 3D landmarks.
Synthetic evaluation: Ground-truth-guided cropping improved detection on annotated images from 32.5% to 46.2% and mean keypoint F1 from 42.9% to 44.6%, while reducing keypoint precision.
On-device demonstration: The application sustained approximately 72 FPS with a tested tracking target of 2 Hz and showed overlay alignment before and after manual rotation.
Scope/limitation: Results are preliminary; quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage remains future work.

papers.abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that \ac{RL} in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that \ac{RL} and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors. Videos: https://sites.google.com/leggedrobotics.com/heavy-metal-acrobatics This is the author's version of the work. It is posted here by permission of the AAAS for personal use, not for redistribution. The definitive version was published in Science Robotics on 11 November 2026, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.aef0894
authors: Pierre-Jean Lorentz, Pascal Egli, Edo Jelavic, Cliff Li, Ramitha Sundar, Harikrishnan Suresh, Paul Montgomery, Lee Redden, Matthias M\"uller, Ozan Sener, Vladlen Koltun, Marco Hutter
bullets: Heavy machinery is difficult to automate because of complex hydraulic dynamics, nonlinear delays, and the risks of physical experimentation.
The approach trains reinforcement-learning policies in simulation and transfers them to a John Deere 332G skid-steer loader.
The loader autonomously performs two-wheel balancing, rough-terrain driving, trajectory tracing, spinning, bucket swinging, and safe four-wheel landings.
The work demonstrates sim-to-real reinforcement learning for dynamic control of heavy construction equipment.
The demonstrated scope focuses on specific high-dynamic acrobatic maneuvers and does not establish general-purpose autonomy.

papers.title: Heavy Metal Acrobatics: Learning Dynamic Control for Skid-Steer Loaders
papers.tldr: Simulation-trained reinforcement learning policies can transfer to a real 5-tonne skid-steer loader, enabling autonomous acrobatic maneuvers near the limits of its actuation.

papers.abstract: Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions. In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances. Our method adopts a two-stage teacher-student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs. We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains. Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.
authors: Siyuan Wang, Dongjie Zhu, Jinxuan Lu, Wenjun Xu, Jiankun Wang

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in 3D environments. Recently, connecting VLMs with model-predictive controllers (MPC) has emerged as a paradigm for combining strong semantic reasoning with physics-based planning. However, connecting these two for contact-rich robotic manipulation requires a task representation that bridges the two and captures how physical interactions can be reasoned by VLMs. In this work, we introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that connects a pretrained VLM to a shared sampling-based MPC through an editable objective program. Each program specifies a sequence of stages for completing a task, combining running and terminal costs from a cost library with stage completion conditions. Given a natural-language task instruction and scene observation, we build a simulation-based digital twin through real-to-sim, and the VLM generates an objective program that is executed by the MPC in the simulation. The program is iteratively updated by the VLM based on MPC rollouts, before being deployed in the real world. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and the real world on four tabletop manipulation tasks, and show that it outperforms strong baselines. Additional videos and examples are available on the project website: https://zihaolu001.github.io/oap-project/
authors: Zihao Lu, Trong Gia Hung Nguyen, Fuquan Wang, Yifan Zhu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing physical interactions in a form that VLMs can reason about and MPC can execute.
Uses stage-based objective programs combining running and terminal costs with completion conditions.
Builds a real-to-sim digital twin; the VLM generates and iteratively revises programs using MPC rollouts before real-world deployment.
Evaluated in simulation and on four real-world tabletop manipulation tasks, outperforming strong baselines.
Scope is demonstrated on tabletop manipulation tasks and relies on simulation-based planning with iterative VLM updates.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Method Overview. Given the task specification in the form of a scene observation and a language description, we generate a digital twin through real-to-sim. VLM then generates objective programs given the task specification, the digital twin, and a predefined cost library. The objective program describes the running and terminal objective terms for the MPC, on a potentially multi-stage task, along with completion conditions for every stage. The VLM iteratively improves the objective programs based on the rollouts in the digital twin, with an MPC that optimizes controls based on the objective program. A stage verifier decides when to advance to the next stage when all completion conditions are met. Finally, the object program is deployed in the real world with the same MPC while the digital twin is synced to the real world execution.

papers.abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.
authors: Xianxu Wu, Shang-Ching Liu, Zhaocong Liang, Hengxiang Chen, Yujian Ma, Shenwen Deng, Qiang Li, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that tabletop manipulation safety constraints are scene-dependent and often absent from instructions.
Stores reusable textual safety rules in an explicit Constraint Space rather than relying only on semantic retrieval.
Uses a lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model to select applicable constraints from the task and environment context.
Employs a multimodal Safety Inspector to detect incorrect selections and unseen hazards, then provide corrective planning feedback.
Uses validated feedback for test-time adaptation and adds newly identified constraints to the knowledge base.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust humanoid locomotion, yet training recipes (rewards, architectures, hyperparameters) remain hard to reuse across robots with different native joint coordinates, since policies output native joint angles while action scales, bounds, gains, and penalties are defined in those robot-specific coordinates. Existing transmission models convert native targets into actuator commands but do not standardize the coordinate interface exposed to the policy. We introduce a body-aligned virtual joint space upstream of this mapping: policy actions and observations follow a common anatomical convention, and a deterministic kinematic layer maps virtual targets to native ones, leaving the existing transmission and low-level control stack unchanged. Under a single unmodified recipe on three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts, it is the only interface that tracks accurately, keeps the feet aligned with the travel direction, and trains stably on all three, and on Unitree G1 hardware it reduces heading drift by nearly a factor of six.
authors: Sol Choi, Mingon Kim, Seokin Seo, Jongeun Choi, Donghyeon Kim, Yisoo Lee
bullets: Native joint coordinates make rewards, action bounds, gains, and penalties robot-specific, hindering recipe reuse.
The method exposes policy actions and observations in a common anatomical space.
A deterministic kinematic mapping converts virtual joint targets to each robot’s native coordinates while preserving the existing control stack.
Across three humanoids, it tracked accurately, maintained foot alignment, and trained stably with one unmodified recipe.
On Unitree G1 hardware, it reduced heading drift by nearly sixfold.

papers.abstract: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.
bullets: The study isolates cross-view coupling effects while preserving per-camera perturbation distributions, trajectories, and action labels.
Global appearance, ghost injection, and target-color changes have small average effects for late-fusion Diffusion Policy.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.
bullets: Policies weight noisy object observations by α = V/(V + s²), where V is the learned proprioceptive anchor’s error variance.
A single measurement of V predicted 10 held-out sensitivities far better than classical errors-in-variables regression (MAE 0.025 vs. 0.37).
In deployment, persistent observation offsets produced closed-loop sensitivities greater than α in all 15 tested policies; full offset following occurred in 8.
Lower α was associated with lower success, especially for diffusion policies; a prospective test predicted success within 0.03.
All results used simulated manipulation, synthetic Gaussian noise, and preregistered evaluations; some findings were post hoc.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Who drives the robot decides what its state says about the object. (1) In training, a human demonstrator who sees the true position W drives the robot, and each episode is recorded with the robot state C, a reading Y with added noise s, and the action a. (2) Because the demonstrator steers toward W , a demonstration state points at it. (3) A policy trained by imitation learns this anchor, m(C) = E[W |C] with error variance V , and moves its estimate Ŵ only a fraction α =V/(V + s2) of the way toward the reading. (4) In deployment the policy drives, so its state points where it is going, and until contact a persistent reading offset δ is indistinguishable from a moved can. Ghost cans mark beliefs about the can’s position: blue, the anchor; orange, the reading; black, the estimate. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how imitation policies discount perception noise via a proprioceptive anchor, relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.tldr: Imitation policies learn to combine proprioception with noisy object readings in a predictable way, but this noise discounting does not reliably transfer to closed-loop deployment.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor imitation learning has become a predominant paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, yet it remains data-inefficient and brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by distilling priors from internet-scale data, but the ``right'' representation for robotics remains unresolved: existing studies span broad but sparse task distributions and reach conclusions that vary and even conflict, pointing to strong task and setting dependence. We examine this question by bringing a magnifying glass to a common contact-rich manipulation task: insertion. We compare representations from widely used vision foundation models against an explicit contact-centric representation on two closely related insertion tasks, perturb each along controlled axes of occlusion and physical tolerance, and test whether conclusions transfer to the real world. Task dependence proves to be more subtle than previous, broadly scoped evaluations revealed: the best representation differs even between our near-identical tasks, and small changes shift trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, results across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the distinct value of spatially-grounded, and in particular, contact-centric information for contact-rich policy learning, while underscoring how difficult it is to estimate such cues reliably under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise. We hope these findings motivate further study of representations in contact-rich manipulation, along with advances in contact perception and its integration into visuomotor policy learning.
authors: Leon Kim, Dinesh Jayaraman, Michael Posa
bullets: Evaluates vision foundation-model representations against an explicit contact-centric representation for two closely related insertion tasks.
Tests controlled changes in occlusion and physical tolerance in simulation, then examines transfer to real-world settings.
Finds that small task or condition changes can unpredictably alter which representation performs best.
Across experiments, contact-centric and spatially grounded cues provide distinct benefits for contact-rich manipulation.
Reliable contact estimation remains difficult under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31x the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55x. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99x the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.
authors: Huiwen Han, Nuo Chen, Ziyao Zeng, Dayou Li, Hao Wang, Amir Hossein Rahmati, Xiaoning Qian, Bangya Liu, Zhiwen Fan
bullets: Vision-based replays miss finger contact timing and force, creating a force gap in simulated demonstrations.
The system combines RGB-D views with an 880-taxel glove and reconstructs interactions in MuJoCo using subject-specific tactile hands.

papers.abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io
authors: Mariana Sosa Guzm\'an, Yide Song, Amin Abyaneh, Gregory Dudek, Hsiu-Chin Lin

Evaluated in simulation and the real world on preventable hazards, rejection-required tasks, and safe task variants.

papers.abstract: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $\pi_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.
authors: Gongyue Teng, Yuqing Xie, Yixian Zhang, Feng Gao, Shu'ang Yu, Jiaji Rao, Sukai Wang, Guanghui Ren, Ya Zhang, Maoqing Yao, Yu Wang, Chao Yu, Xinlei Chen
