papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising capabilities for robot manipulation, but their performance on accessible mobile bimanual platforms remains underexplored. We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual platform integrating two LeRobot SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot 4 and a LeRobot-ROS 2 software stack. Using long-horizon toilet cleaning as a case study, we collect 250 real-world demonstrations and evaluate $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, and GR00T under the same embodiment and task conditions. We further evaluate variants using SARM-derived task-progress signals and short-term MEM observation history. Among the evaluated models, $\pi_0$ performs best, achieving 60% strict and 70% relaxed autonomous success, increasing to 90% with limited human intervention. In contrast, the evaluated progress- and memory-augmented variants do not improve their corresponding baselines. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of long-horizon mobile bimanual manipulation on accessible hardware while highlighting remaining challenges in reliable VLA deployment. papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bring multimodal understanding and world knowledge to end-to-end autonomous driving. To further improve the quality of predicted trajectories, existing studies introduce candidate refinement, residual denoising, and token correction. However, these methods typically focus on unified refinement of the entire trajectory, paying limited attention to the distinct physical quantities and their interactions. We further investigate physical specialization and coordination in trajectory refinement, centering on position and heading for simpler and more intuitive correction modeling. To this end, we propose CARE-Drive (Coupled Alternating Refinement for Ego-trajectories), which decomposes trajectory refinement into waypoint residual correction and position-conditioned heading generation. Through imitation learning and a future-token auxiliary task, the backbone provides predictive representations and a base trajectory. The position expert predicts bounded metric waypoint residuals, while the heading expert reconstructs vehicle orientation from adjacent angular increments conditioned on the corrected path. With the backbone frozen, the two experts are optimized alternately through supervised initialization and reinforcement fine-tuning. This design simplifies refinement through clear physical specialization while preserving conditional coupling during prediction and optimization. On NAVSIM v1, CARE-Drive achieves 88.8 PDMS, improving by 2.4 points over the unrefined base trajectories generated by the same backbone. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of specialized experts and staged training.

papers.abstract: Granular materials exhibit complex and highly variable interaction dynamics, making their reliable manipulation challenging without knowledge of their physical properties. We present an interactive perception framework that infers granular material properties directly from force-torque measurements acquired during scooping. The proposed Latent Filter++ combines a bio-inspired frequency-temporal filter-bank representation with a causal latent dynamical model, allowing the representation to evolve as interaction observations become available while avoiding hand-crafted signal preprocessing. The learned latent representation captures physically meaningful variation in granular materials and supports estimation of properties including grain size and bulk density. Evaluated on 26 diverse granular materials, the approach generalizes to materials excluded from training and enables few-shot adaptation of property-specific mappings using a small number of additional interaction samples. Finally, we demonstrate the relevance of the inferred properties to downstream manipulation by examining their correlation with the maximum acceleration the materials can withstand without spilling from the spoon during transport.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robotic manipulation is versatile, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills and a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. We propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end to end on the real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. papers.abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.
authors: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets world-model failures when robot dynamics change unexpectedly, such as after grasping an unknown payload.
Uses a fast correction for prompt adaptation and a slow correction for retained dynamics, with prediction errors driving both.
Dynamically reweights pretrained experts without modifying their parameters.
Evaluated on five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, achieving lower multi-step mean error than ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task.
Reported gains cover early adaptation, transient disturbances, and long-horizon retention; code and datasets are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Quadrupedal mobile manipulators can extend their manipulation workspace by coordinating the mounted arm with the mobile base. At the task level, short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories provide an interface for specifying the desired manipulation motion without prescribing how it should be realized by the arm and base. However, executing such trajectories remains challenging because the controller must determine when and how the base should move, and this decision depends on the mounted-arm morphology. We therefore present PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that takes an EE trajectory as the sole task-level motion command and generates coordinated arm--base motions across four families of 6-DoF mounted arms, with extended-reach trajectories beyond the initial fixed-base reach. Within PolyMorphWBC, a trajectory-conditioned coordinator determines the base motion from previewed EE targets, while arm-specific Inverse Kinematics (IK) tracks the current target, and a frozen locomotion backend executes the resulting motion. Cross-arm reuse is enabled by a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)-derived morphology conditioning, together with online residual-wrench feedback. We train PolyMorphWBC on procedurally generated arms and structured trajectories within and beyond fixed-base reach. In IsaacLab, it achieves 93.95% completion with 2.30cm position error and 4.81{\deg} orientation error on held-out trajectories and arm morphologies. In MuJoCo evaluation against UMI-on-Legs, PolyMorphWBC reduces EE position error by 69--72% and orientation error by 91--97% across four within- and extended-reach trajectories. On a physical Go2--ARX5 system, we demonstrate language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using EE trajectories from pi_0 without vision-language-action (VLA)-generated base commands.

papers.abstract: When robots interact with elastic surfaces such as mattresses and trampolines, changes in loading cause the surfaces to deform and rebound, altering subsequent contact locations and forces. We present Elastra, a simulation framework for modeling this interaction and supporting the training and evaluation of robot control policies. Elastra represents each surface using elements that move only vertically, with elastic connections and damping to model deformation and recovery. Contact forces drive surface motion, and the updated surface geometry is used to compute subsequent contact forces. We systematically validate our simulations against an independent implementation and a real mattress load curve. We further use Elastra to train the Unitree G1 humanoid to stand up on mattresses and trampolines. Using the pretrained HoST policy and ProtoMotions motion tracker as original controllers, we train residual policies through reinforcement learning to add corrections to their joint targets. Adding these residual policies increases the success rate with HoST from 44.1\% to 72.5\%, and from 55\% to 89\% on the trampoline. With ProtoMotions, the success rate increases from 19.0\% to 45.0\% for initial poses not encountered during training. The code and video are available on https://github.com/yichg/elastra.

papers.abstract: Real-world robot imitation learning is often limited by the cost of collecting physical demonstrations, which typically yield only one action label per visited state. We present CrowdMAPS, a web-based crowdsourcing paradigm for augmenting real-robot datasets with Multiple Actions per State (MAPS). After or during standard robot data collection, CrowdMAPS distributes visited robot states to remote annotators through a web-based 3D interface, where they specify alternative valid actions without requiring access to physical robot hardware. This expands robot datasets along a complementary "width" dimension--by increasing the number of actions per visited state--rather than only by collecting more trajectories. We evaluate CrowdMAPS using keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations supplied by non-expert annotators and train imitation policies on the resulting MAPS data. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing MAPS width from one to ten actions per state improves sample efficiency and increases average success rates by 35.6 percentage points for keypose policies and 33.0 percentage points for trajectory policies. These results show that software-mediated human annotations can augment physical robot data to afford denser supervision, establishing CrowdMAPS as a scalable digital layer for real-robot data collection.

papers.abstract: Safe trajectory tracking (STT) aims to enable autonomous vehicles to follow a reference trajectory accurately while avoiding collisions. This problem is particularly challenging for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) in highly dynamic environments. Existing non-learning-based STT methods often use simplified vehicle and interaction models to meet real-time requirements, which may result in suboptimal tracking accuracy. Although Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) can help address this limitation, widely used Lagrangian DRL methods often suffer from unstable training because increasing Lagrange multipliers amplify policy-gradient magnitudes. To address these issues, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for STT, called STT Control Epigraph Form RL (STTC-EFRL). In this framework, the STT problem is formulated as an epigraph-form min-max optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we develop a learning mechanism that uses a decreasing scalar related to the epigraph to adjust the policy gradient descent direction without increasing the gradient magnitude, thereby improving training stability. We also develop a computationally efficient ray-casting method to compute a polyhedron scaling factor for safety quantification. Experimental results, including Vehicle-in-the-Loop tests, show that STTC-EFRL achieves higher tracking accuracy than the considered non-learning-based baseline and more stable training than widely used Lagrangian DRL methods, while satisfying safety requirements in connected environments.

papers.abstract: Embodied continual learning requires controllers to infer changing situations, retain prior behavior and reuse motor skills without task labels or known boundaries. The challenge is deciding when to recover earlier behavior and which skills can support new learning. We introduce Situation-guided Primitive Integration for Recurrent Embodiment (SPIRE), a recurrent-spiking system that infers latent contexts from action-outcome evidence and learns context-specific motor actors online. Mature actors become protected sources that combine with a target-context residual to drive recurrent-spiking motor populations. Across coordinate, three-joint and hidden-force control, SPIRE maintained control, autonomously inferred situations, retained prior behavior and accelerated acquisition of an unseen source composition, reducing mean interactions to criterion by approximately 40% relative to matched fresh controllers. Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early acquisition in every matched intervention, demonstrating causal reuse. Against seven recurrent continual-learning and modular-control comparators, SPIRE achieved 2.4 times the mean prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible task-free alternative selected for each paired stream. These results demonstrate autonomous recovery and causal reuse of motor skills for new learning in continuous embodied control.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.

At inference, the verifier scores candidate actions and selects the highest-scoring one for execution.

papers.abstract: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the task goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space; these actions form a graph policy that is defined only where the required transitions have been observed. StructRL transfers these actions to model-free learners: as action preferences for a DQN Q-model and as target directions along shortest observed paths for a SAC actor. For DQN on three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, final success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 (DoorKey), 0.10 to 0.80 (KeyCorridor) and 0 to 0.50 (ObstructedMaze); plain DQN does not catch up with three times the budget. For SAC on continuous PointMaze, graph-derived direction labels raise final success from 0.17 to 1.0 on seven matched runs that reached the goal. Distilling the graph policy into a fresh Q-model gives a DoorKey 6x6 controller that reaches the goal from 91% of reachable states, against 38% for plain DQN. Scaling experiments identify three bottlenecks: incomplete graph support, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional inputs.
bullets: Builds an explicit graph from collected experience and uses dynamic programming to derive policies over observed states.
Transfers graph guidance to DQN through action preferences and to SAC through shortest-path direction targets.
On three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, DQN success improves to 0.90, 0.80, and 0.50, versus 0.10, 0.10, and 0 for baseline DQN.
On PointMaze, graph-derived SAC guidance raises final success from 0.17 to 1.0 across seven matched runs that reached the goal.
Key limitations are incomplete graph coverage, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional observations.

papers.abstract: Learning safe policies that generalize to unseen environments is difficult under bounded actuation, where an unsafe decision may become unrecoverable. Conventional control barrier function (CBF) filters enforce only instantaneous safety and ignore future recoverability. We propose SAFTER (Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability), which embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter into Soft Actor-Critic training. SAFTER unifies current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input admissibility into a single differentiable certificate. Its CBF condition yields an exact minimum-intervention projection without iterative online optimization. In quadruped navigation, SAFTER reaches 90% training success with 30.6% fewer transitions than Vanilla SAC and 34.1-35.1% fewer than current-state CBF-filtered SAC baselines. Across unseen simulated environments, SAFTER improves success by up to 42.4 and 61.4 percentage points over the state-of-the-art methods CBF-RL and SEA-Nav, respectively, and achieves 73.3% and 76.7% success on two real-world navigation maps. Ablations identify accurate differentiation through the safety filter as a key contributor to robustness, in which replacing the projection Jacobian with the identity approximation reduces success rate in a High-Shift environment from 61.4% to 6.2%. These results show that recoverability-aware filtering serves as both a runtime safety mechanism and a learning mechanism for sample-efficient, robust policies.
bullets: Addresses unsafe, potentially unrecoverable actions under bounded actuation and unseen environments.
Integrates current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input limits into one differentiable certificate.
Uses a closed-form backup-CBF filter with exact minimum-intervention projection, avoiding iterative online optimization.
In quadruped navigation, reaches 90% training success with fewer transitions and substantially improves success in unseen simulated environments and two real-world maps.
Accurate differentiation through the safety projection is critical; an identity Jacobian approximation sharply reduces performance in a high-shift setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SAFTER. During training, the critic evaluates the executed action and the actor differentiates through the same safety map.

papers.abstract: GAMBIT is an opening chess move in which a player sacrifices a piece, typically a pawn, to gain a positional advantage later in the game. Analogously, in multi-robot coordination, individual robots may need to forgo locally reward-maximising behaviours to improve overall team performance. Such self-sacrificial behaviours are difficult to capture with manually designed heuristics, particularly in dense, interaction-rich environments. Focusing on double-integrator continuous dynamics, this work studies how to learn such coordinated heuristics over motion primitives for multi-robot trajectory execution. Our framework, GAMBIT, first learns coordinated motion-primitive selection through imitation learning and subsequently fine-tunes the policy through reinforcement learning. We further introduce a safeguarded rollout mechanism with backup trajectories that guarantees collision-free execution at all times. Experiments demonstrate that GAMBIT substantially outperforms a range of baselines, including centralised motion planners and decentralised reactive planners, while exhibiting strong scalability. In particular, it coordinates over a thousand robots with planning latency below a few hundred milliseconds in continuous domains.
bullets: Addresses coordination in dense, interaction-rich environments where locally optimal robot actions can harm team performance.
Uses imitation learning to initialize coordinated motion-primitive selection, followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning.
Introduces safeguarded rollouts with backup trajectories to guarantee collision-free execution.
Outperforms centralized and decentralized planning baselines and scales to over a thousand robots with sub-second planning latency.
Scope: multi-robot systems with continuous double-integrator dynamics; the abstract does not specify experimental datasets or detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. GAMBIT framework overview. We aim to learn a coordination-aware GNN policy that provides heuristic preferences over motion primitives. The framework consists of (a) imitation pretraining and (b) RL fine-tuning. The former step learns from demonstration trajectories by treating motion-primitive selection as a classification task. The latter uses multi-agent RL to maximise multi-robot navigation performance through our safeguarded rollout mechanism. The resulting policy, combined with the safeguarded rollout, enables collision-free execution while retaining high scalability.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation. They act by first predicting how a task should be performed and then decoding the actions from that future. However, the remaining actions are invalid once execution drifts from the prediction. Simply replanning from the already out of distribution state rarely restores what the task still requires; existing execution monitors decide when to stop, but not what to restore. We observe that the answer is already in hand: the future the WAM predicted before acting depicts exactly the states it intended to pass through. We introduce FAVOR (Future Anchored Verification and Online Recovery), a lightweight framework that keeps these predicted frames as anchors and uses them for verification and recovery. An Anchor Verifier compares each observation with its anchor, together with the executed actions, to flag deviations that break the task. Anchor-Guided Recovery uses a vision-language model to turn the flagged anchor into a short corrective instruction. Under strengthened instruction guidance, the WAM executes this instruction to return to the intended future. It then resumes the task. FAVOR raises the task success of the base WAM from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without modifying the policy.
bullets: Addresses the problem that execution drift invalidates remaining actions and replanning from the deviated state may not restore task progress.
Stores the WAM’s predicted future frames as anchors for monitoring and recovery.
An Anchor Verifier compares observations and executed actions against anchors to identify task-breaking deviations.
A vision-language model converts flagged anchors into corrective instructions, after which the WAM resumes execution.
Improves success from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without changing the policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FAVOR. (a) The frozen WAM predicts future frames and the IDM decodes an action chunk; the predicted frames are retained as anchors. Every ∆ steps, the verifier compares the observation with its anchor: a pass continues execution, and the failure interrupts the remaining actions and triggers recovery. (b) The Anchor Verifier encodes the prediction–observation pair with DINO, fuses it with action and horizon embeddings, and outputs a failure score through a causal GRU; an alarm is raised when the score exceeds τ . (c) Anchor-Guided Recovery: a VLM reads the alarmed anchor, the current observation, and the task, and issues a corrective instruction.
Figure 3: Effect of the guidance scale on recovery predictions. All branches start from the same trigger state and the corrective instruction “pick up the cup”.

Figure 4: Qualitative examples of Anchor-Guided Recovery on LIBERO. In each case, the top row shows the observed execution and the bottom row the WAM’s retained prediction up to the alarm (orange frame); red circles mark where the observation departs from its anchor. Right of the alarm, native continuation under the original instruction fails (top), while the corrective instruction issued by the VLM (green) restores the anchored condition and the task succeeds (bottom). Both branches start from the same simulator state at the alarm.
Figure 5: Distribution of the maximum episode score for successful and failed LIBERO episodes under each detector, on its native scale (higher indicates failure); each point is one episode.

papers.abstract: Human videos offer scalable manipulation data, but the embodiment gap between human hands and robot manipulators limits their direct use. Existing video-editing methods replace hands with rendered robots, yet inaccurate interaction reconstruction and compositing can produce inconsistent grasps and implausible robot-object occlusions. We address these failures from two complementary physical aspects: interaction geometry and scene visibility. First, an interaction-aware contact reconstruction module combines hand-object segmentation with mesh-level contact prediction to recover dense 3D contacts, then converts them into temporally stabilized grasps for parallel-jaw grippers. Second, a depth-aware compositing module uses scene and robot depth to enforce physically consistent robot-object occlusions. The resulting videos preserve the interaction structure of human demonstrations in a robot-compatible form and are co-trained with robot demonstrations. Using identical human videos and robot data, we compare against robot-only training and the original Masquerade pipeline. Across four RoboTwin tasks and two Diffusion Policy visual encoders, our method achieves the highest average success rates, with especially strong gains under out-of-distribution scene variation. Real-world deployment further shows that the proposed co-training approach improves robustness to visual distractors when the task geometry is observable, while performance on depth-sensitive grasps remains limited by the single-camera setup.
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human hands and robot manipulators in using human videos for robot learning.
Reconstructs dense 3D hand-object contacts and temporally stabilized grasps for parallel-jaw grippers.
Uses scene and robot depth to produce physically consistent robot-object occlusions during compositing.
Co-training with robot demonstrations achieves the best average success across four RoboTwin tasks and two visual encoders, with strong gains under out-of-distribution scene changes.
Real-world robustness improves with visual distractors when task geometry is observable; depth-sensitive grasps remain limited by the single-camera setup.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our framework. (a) Interaction-aware contact reconstruction combines hand–object segmentation and mesh-level contact prediction to recover temporally stable opposing contacts for robot grasp retargeting. (b) Depth-consistent compositing compares scene and rendered-robot depth to enforce physically correct robot–object occlusions. The resulting robotized videos are co-trained with real robot demonstrations for policy learning.

papers.abstract: Feedback controllers for flows are expensive to design, since each candidate must be evaluated with a high-fidelity solver. Differentiable surrogates reduce that cost, but they also introduce a failure mode that prediction error cannot detect. Policy optimization uses the derivative of the objective with respect to the action, which we call the action gradient and which can be computed either through the surrogate or through the high-fidelity solver. Optimization through the surrogate uses only its action gradient, and a surrogate can follow the flow trajectory closely while misestimating this derivative. The surrogate action gradient is compared against a central finite-difference estimate from the high-fidelity solver on held-out states, under acceptance criteria fixed before the comparison, and we call that comparison an audit. A low-dimensional feedback law is then fitted to the surrogate action gradient when the surrogate passes the audit, and to the solver estimate when it does not. This law initializes a neural policy, and a quadratic penalty holds the policy near it during optimization. The proposed approach is validated on four test cases. The resulting controllers outperform or match a model-free baseline, while using 3 to 156 times fewer high-fidelity solver interactions across the four test cases. One surrogate predicts the objective at correlation 0.9996 but its action gradient at only 0.459, so prediction accuracy does not identify a usable surrogate. Another surrogate, whose action gradient agrees with the solver estimate at correlation 0.996, makes the objective 0.52% worse when the policy is optimized through it without the anchor penalty, so an accurate gradient alone does not provide a working controller. Finally, a surrogate that passes the audit at one fixed action fails it around the actions the deployed controller applies, so a pass is local.
bullets: Surrogate prediction accuracy alone can hide unusable action gradients for policy optimization.
The method audits surrogate gradients against high-fidelity finite-difference estimates on held-out states using pre-set criteria.
A low-dimensional gradient-based feedback law initializes the neural policy, which is regularized to remain near this anchor.
Across four test cases, controllers match or outperform a model-free baseline while using 3–156× fewer solver interactions.
Audit validity is local: gradients must be checked near the actions used by the deployed controller.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The extracted law reduces the objective almost as much as model-free PPO, the anchored controller built from it improves this reduction, and the released controller loses almost half of it. Panel d reports the reduction of the objective against paired uncontrolled rollouts from the same initial states, for matched model-free PPO over three training seeds, the anchored controller over four training seeds, the extracted law over eight initial conditions, and the released controller over four training seeds.

Panel a shows the uncontrolled vorticity field and panel b the controlled field from the same initial state. Panel c shows their difference so that the regions of the wake changed by the control are visible. Panel d compares the lift coefficient over time in the two cases. Panel e reports the reduction of the objective against a paired uncontrolled rollout from the same initial state, for matched model-free PPO over 12 paired rollouts, the released controller over 32 paired rollouts, and the extracted law over eight initial conditions. The dashed line marks zero reduction, and a point to its right is a controller that improves the objective. Panel f applies the extracted law obtained at Re = 100 at Reynolds numbers 150, 200 and 250 with no refitting, and the shaded band marks the condition at which it was fitted.

Figure 1: Surrogate action gradients are compared with high-fidelity central differences on held-out states under fixed acceptance criteria. After a pass, the extracted law is fitted to the surrogate gradient, which is inexpensive to evaluate. After a failure instead, it is fitted to the measured gradient, unless a replacement surrogate passes a new audit. The extracted law is transferred to the neural policy by law projection, and used as the reference of the anchor penalty, which a cone around the law replaces in the case of a failure. The law, the anchored controller and the released controller are each evaluated in the solver. Black boxes refer to the audit, green and orange paths to its two outcomes, and purple boxes to the controller construction.

Panel b compares the field surrogate with a phase polynomial at two audit horizons against the threshold τ1 = 0.70, on 18 states from the closed-loop trajectories of each surrogate’s own controller, a different set from the eight-state audit of Section 4.1 of the main paper. In panel c the audited phase is the one the measured gradient selects, and the unsupported phase is the one unregularized optimization selected.

Figure 5: The controller weakens the vortices and reduces enstrophy for every training seed. Panel a shows the uncontrolled final vorticity field, panel b the controlled field from the same initial state, and panel c their difference on a separate scale. Panel d shows enstrophy over time for one initial condition, with and without control, from the first step onward. The shaded interval marks the final 10 control steps, over which enstrophy is averaged to evaluate a controller. Over this interval enstrophy is 82.5% lower with the proposed controller. This value comes from a single trajectory, so it differs slightly from the 82.01% averaged over all seeds and evaluation conditions in the text. Panel e shows the held-out enstrophy reduction, whose upper row holds one value for each of the eight controller training seeds and whose lower row holds one value for each of the four PPO training seeds, each the mean over the same eight evaluation conditions.

Figure 6: The surrogate-based controller weakens the field at both forcing amplitudes, at a cost close to that of matched TD3 and below that of matched polynomial TD3. Panels a to c show the uncontrolled field, controlled field, and their difference at µ = 0.225. Panels e to g show the corresponding fields for the controller with observer at µ = 0.121. Each controlled field and its uncontrolled pair start from the same initial field. Panels d and h compare the controller with matched TD3 and matched polynomial TD3 on the eight held-out initial fields. The row labeled controller in panel d is the surrogate-based controller at µ = 0.225, and the row labeled observer in panel h is the controller with observer at µ = 0.121. Lower accumulated state cost is better.

Figure 13: The extracted law separates from every trained controller within the first 50 control steps and holds that separation to the end of the horizon, at Reynolds number 100. Panel a shows the objective under the uncontrolled flow and under seven controllers, including the phase polynomial and neural ordinary differential equation pathwise controllers. Each curve is a mean over the paired restart states available to that controller, smoothed over 15 control steps. The uncontrolled objective, PPO, and the extracted law are drawn heavier because they carry the comparison, and the remaining diagnostics are drawn lighter. Panel b divides the running paired reduction by the running uncontrolled objective, so each curve ends near the full horizon reduction reported for that controller, except PPO, whose 300-step rollouts from four other restart states are truncated here at 200 steps. The model-free baseline draws from four restart states, while every other controller draws from the same bank of eight. Therefore, it is matched in objective and solver, and unmatched in initial state.

papers.selection_reason: Model-based RL with action-gradient auditing and anchored policies is directly transferable to learned robot control.
papers.title: Audited Gradients, Anchored Policies: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Flow Control
papers.tldr: Auditing surrogate action gradients and anchoring policy optimization enables efficient flow control with far fewer high-fidelity solver interactions.

papers.abstract: Many applications of multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) require policies that balance conflicting objectives while satisfying safety constraints. We study safe MORL with zero constraint violation throughout learning, covering both cumulative and stepwise constraints. A key challenge is to explore sufficiently under unknown dynamics and constraint costs without violating the constraints. For a given preference over objectives, we develop an algorithm to learn a safe Pareto optimal policy by combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds. With high probability, every policy executed over $T$ episodes incurs zero constraint violation. The algorithm returns a safe Markov policy induced by the averaged occupancy measure and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization. We further develop a preference-free algorithm that first explores safely without a prespecified preference and then computes a safe policy for any given preference without further interaction. Over $T$ exploration episodes and $K$ planning iterations, it retains the same safety guarantee and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T}+1/\sqrt{K})$ suboptimality gap. Both algorithms require knowledge of a policy that strictly satisfies the constraints and its costs. We then relax these requirements, incurring at most constant cumulative violation. To our knowledge, we provide the first sample-efficient MORL algorithms that guarantee safety for every executed policy.
bullets: Addresses MORL with conflicting objectives and cumulative or stepwise safety constraints under unknown dynamics and costs.
Combines optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds to enable safe exploration for a specified objective preference.
Guarantees, with high probability, zero constraint violation for every policy executed over T episodes.
Achieves an approximately O(1/√T) suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization; preference-free learning adds an approximately O(1/√K) planning term.
Requires a strictly feasible policy and its costs for zero-violation guarantees; relaxing this requirement permits constant cumulative violation.
papers.selection_reason: Safe multi-objective RL with zero-violation guarantees is transferable to robot learning and control.
papers.title: Safe Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning: Zero Constraint Violation and Primal-Averaging Convergence
papers.tldr: The paper develops safe multi-objective reinforcement-learning algorithms that guarantee zero constraint violation during learning while converging to safe Pareto-optimal policies.

papers.abstract: In micromanipulation, erroneous hand motion limits unaided manipulation accuracy, which can affect task performance and safety in critical applications like microsurgery. Handheld robots (micromanipulators) enable motion accuracy beyond human limits by providing robotic assistance in a low-cost, compact, intuitive form factor. Particularly, active constraints are an effective form of robotic assistance, which aids the operator by restricting the robot's permissible motion based on task-specific requirements or objectives, thereby providing task guidance and enforcing safety. However, existing formulations of active constraints for handheld systems are limited, most notably because of the inability to provide guidance and enforce safety simultaneously. Implementing active constraints with optimization-based methods can address these limitations, but existing implementations are designed for free-standing robots, and neglect that handheld robots actuate relative to the operator's hand with a limited workspace. In this work, we propose an optimization-based active constraint framework for handheld micromanipulation that enables simultaneous guidance and safety enforcement. The formulation was implemented in a handheld robot and demonstrated on a medically relevant artificial task. Results show that the proposed formulation reduced safety violation rate by more than two orders of magnitude relative to baselines, while recovering the threefold accuracy loss from enforcing safety alone.
bullets: Hand motion errors limit accuracy and safety in critical micromanipulation tasks such as microsurgery.
Existing handheld active-constraint methods cannot provide task guidance and safety enforcement at the same time.
The framework accounts for handheld actuation relative to the operator’s hand and the robot’s limited workspace.
Implemented on a handheld robot and demonstrated in a medically relevant artificial task.
It reduced safety violations by more than two orders of magnitude versus baselines and recovered the threefold accuracy loss caused by enforcing safety alone.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models currently demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of real-world robotics tasks. However, they often still lack the generalization ability to handle large visual out-of-distribution shifts. Post-training of VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to benefit robustness, but significant room for improvement remains. In this work, we systematically study the effect of image augmentation on VLA post-training. We find that it is crucial to augment only the critic module during RL updates, while leaving the actor's input clean during both rollouts and updates. For $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 this raises out-of-distribution success on LIBERO-Plus by $7.8$ and $10.0$ points respectively, while augmenting the actor collapses training entirely. We investigate a range of augmentation types and strengths, and provide practical recommendations for improving generalization in VLA post-training.
bullets: VLA models still struggle with large visual out-of-distribution shifts despite strong task performance.
Image augmentation should be applied exclusively to the critic during RL updates; the actor should receive clean inputs during rollouts and updates.
For π₀.₅ and GR00T N1.5, this improves LIBERO-Plus out-of-distribution success by 7.8 and 10.0 points, respectively.
Augmenting the actor causes training to collapse in the studied setting.
The study evaluates augmentation types and strengths and offers practical recommendations for VLA post-training.

papers.abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $\pi_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
authors: Ilia Larchenko, Gleb Zarin, Atindra Nair, Keerti Manney, Vitaly Kleban, Mirko Kiefer, Anjana Yodaiken
bullets: Targets long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge.
Uses one π₀.₅-based vision-language-action checkpoint across all 100 tasks, with extended training and variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching.
Expanded from 50 to 100 tasks using semantic stages, warm-started task and stage embeddings, and a 21-dimensional teleoperation-aligned action space.
Routes 14 tasks to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent, whose mean Q was 0.639 versus 0.108 for the learned policy on those tasks.
The team placed 9th overall and was the only independent team in the top 10; the public submission scored 0.446 Q.

papers.abstract: Small, holonomic Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) enable close-range inspection of underwater structures from arbitrary viewpoints, requiring accurate position and attitude tracking under state and input constraints. Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) naturally handles these requirements, but relies on an accurate dynamics model, which is difficult to obtain underwater. In this paper, we present a nonlinear MPCC in all six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) for a holonomic AUV and alleviate the inaccuracies in the dynamics by augmenting the nominal model employed with residual dynamics learned via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. The learned residual is embedded in the optimal control problem through a zero-order robust optimization scheme, which keeps the controller real-time capable at 25 Hz. A simulation ablation shows that residual selection is essential when designing the controller, and simulation and in-water experiments with the Multimodality, Observing, Low-cost, Agile (MOLA) AUV validate the resulting controllers against a nominal MPCC and a field proven Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller.
authors: David D\"orner, Giancarlo Troni, Ignacio Torroba, Ivan Stenius
bullets: Targets accurate position and attitude tracking for close-range underwater inspection under state and input constraints.
Uses a nonlinear six-DoF MPCC with Gaussian Process regression to learn residual dynamics beyond a nominal model.
Embeds the learned residual through zero-order robust optimization, enabling control at 25 Hz.
Ablation results show that selecting appropriate residual dynamics is essential for controller design.
Simulation and in-water MOLA AUV experiments validate the controllers against nominal MPCC and PID baselines.

papers.tldr: A GP-augmented nonlinear MPCC improves six-DoF trajectory tracking for a holonomic AUV while remaining real-time capable under model uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM

bullets: Frames signal injection as a distribution-alignment problem rather than a formatting choice.
Uses frozen-denoiser reconstruction error to show frequency-domain encodings better match the pretrained video latent prior than conventional spatial encodings.
Packs proprioception, actions, and values into disjoint frequency bands, lifted by inverse DCT without adding modules or changing architecture.
Supports policy, world-model, and value prediction through a fixed band layout and slot-aware routing.
Reports 68.9% success on RoboCasa with 39% lower inference latency, and 85.0% success across three real-world Franka tasks.

papers.abstract: A representation that accurately predicts a deformable object's response is not necessarily the one most useful for choosing manipulation actions. We study this distinction between predictive utility and decision utility in planar single-grasp shape control of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs). As a common decision backbone, we introduce Geometry-Pointer-Flow (GPF), a geometry-grounded policy that separates grasp-location selection from grasp-conditioned motion generation. Its geometry-only variant reduces one-step executed shape error by 32.8% relative to a DLO-specific diffusion policy, while using 18.7 times fewer parameters and achieving approximately 193 times faster inference. On this backbone, we compare physical context represented by ground-truth parameters, estimated parameters, and learned interaction-history representations, for both forward prediction and executed control. For prediction, ground-truth physical parameters reduce next-shape error by 15.8% over geometry alone, and estimated parameters are slightly more predictive than interaction history. This ordering does not carry over to control: estimated parameters provide no detectable one-step control gain, whereas history-conditioned GPF reduces executed error by 9.9% relative to geometry-only GPF across 470 paired simulation trials. In closed loop, interaction history improves strict-threshold attainment in simulation and yields the strongest zero-shot performance on hardware. All policies are trained exclusively in simulation and transferred to the physical robot without real-world training or fine-tuning. These results show that physical context should be evaluated by the decisions it supports rather than by predictive accuracy alone. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Chengxiao Dong, Alessio Caporali, Hongyu Lan, Gianluca Palli
bullets: Studies planar single-grasp shape control of deformable linear objects (DLOs), distinguishing predictive utility from decision utility.
Introduces Geometry-Pointer-Flow (GPF), which separates grasp-location selection from grasp-conditioned motion generation.
Geometry-only GPF reduces one-step executed shape error by 32.8% versus a DLO-specific diffusion policy, with far fewer parameters and faster inference.
Although ground-truth and estimated physical parameters improve forward prediction, estimated parameters provide no detectable control gain.
History-conditioned GPF reduces executed error by 9.9% across 470 paired simulation trials and transfers zero-shot to hardware, with all training done in simulation.

papers.abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.
authors: Vikram Ramavarapu, Himanshu Udupi, Ashish Gautam
bullets: Addresses how functional modularity can emerge in recurrent spiking networks for reinforcement learning.
Introduces CoRe SNNs with controller, action-specific, and latent-state communities; actions are selected by the community reached by a spike walk.
Proposes Map-STDP, a local three-factor rule that encourages modular structure during learning, alongside partial and full modularity regimes.

On CartPole, Map-STDP improves learning over unstructured networks and can match sealed modularity; recurrent action communities improve or match feed-forward actors across CartPole, LunarLander, and Acrobot.
The best modularity strength is task-dependent: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while regimes perform similarly on LunarLander.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.
bullets: Formalizes self-evolving multimodal agents using four criteria plus self-reference.
Analyzes a three-stage loop: experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation.
Compares self-evolving and fixed loops to separate scenario-specific limits from design-inherent limits.
Frames mechanism transfer as trade-offs dependent on resources such as output equivalence and checkable outcomes.
Classifies mechanisms as portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant, and proposes matched-budget tests for unresolved judgments.

papers.abstract: We propose a Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm for controlling nonlinear robotic systems with unknown dynamics. The K-MBRL learns a control policy by minimizing an approximate policy objective that combines the analytical immediate cost with an estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step predicted state. To this end, we develop a stochastic Koopman operator-based learning method to approximate the unknown nonlinear dynamics in a linear representation, while a critic function estimates the remaining future cost. This formulation offers two key advantages. First, the linear Koopman dynamics simplify the model-dependent policy gradient computation to a constant matrix product, enabling computationally efficient policy improvement. Second, one-step model propagation mitigates the accumulation of prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts while retaining long-term cost information through the critic. The learned policy enables real-time control through feedforward evaluation without online optimization. We establish policy learning convergence guarantees under standard stochastic approximation assumptions. Simulations on HalfCheetah and quadruped four-legged locomotion tasks demonstrate strong sample efficiency and improved performance compared with classical model-free and model-based reinforcement learning baselines. A pendulum swing-up task is used to assess policy gradient approximation accuracy and conduct ablation studies on the learning mechanism and key hyperparameters. The proposed K-MBRL is further validated on a physical quadruped robot performing a challenging sequence of maneuvers: rising to an upright posture supported by two rounded rear feet, maintaining balance during bipedal walking, and safely returning to the ground, as shown in Fig.1.
authors: Wenjian Hao, Paulo C. Heredia, Shaoshuai Mou
bullets: Learns a linear Koopman representation of unknown nonlinear dynamics and estimates future cost with a critic.
Uses one-step model prediction to reduce error accumulation while retaining long-term cost information.
Simplifies policy-gradient computation to a constant matrix product, enabling efficient policy improvement and feedforward real-time control.
Provides convergence guarantees under standard stochastic approximation assumptions.
Demonstrates strong sample efficiency and performance in simulations, plus maneuvers on a physical quadruped robot.

papers.abstract: Temporal-difference critics regress onto a bootstrapped target and usually need a target network. Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) instead expresses the in-sample optimal values of offline RL as the solution to a linear program over the dataset. Its neural solver ALBUM relaxes the constraints into hinge penalties with fixed coefficients, and its guarantees are conditions on coefficients chosen in advance. We solve the same program with the method of multipliers: the coefficients become multipliers learned by dual ascent, with one penalty parameter $\rho$. In the convex case the fixed points are the KKT pairs of LBLP, and at every stationary point the applied constraint weights balance the objective exactly. The critic can serve a Gaussian actor, a flow actor, and best-of-N sampling, and for the Gaussian actor we propose an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective. With a single $Q$ and $V$ and no target network, our AL-LBLP with best-of-N reaches 60.1\% average success on the 50 state-based OGBench tasks. On long-horizon tasks, it reaches 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant and 79.8% on antmaze-giant. It does not collapse up to batch size 8192.
authors: Jongchan Park, Hyukjun Yang, Narim Jeong, Donghwan Lee
bullets: Motivation: LBLP avoids bootstrapped critics’ target networks, but prior ALBUM uses fixed constraint coefficients with restrictive guarantees.
Method: Apply the method of multipliers to LBLP, learning constraint weights through dual ascent with a single penalty parameter ρ.
Theory: In the convex case, fixed points are LBLP’s KKT pairs, and stationary-point constraint weights exactly balance the objective.
Deployment: The critic supports Gaussian and flow actors as well as best-of-N sampling; an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective is proposed for Gaussian policies.

Results: With one Q and V and no target network, AL-LBLP with best-of-N achieves 60.1% average success across 50 OGBench tasks, including 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant and 79.8% on antmaze-giant, without collapse at batch size 8192.

papers.abstract: Deliberation costs are commonly used in hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) to prevent options from collapsing to primitive actions. Existing approaches rely on fixed penalties or duration-based adaptations, both of which are indirect proxies for an option's utility. This paper argues that option persistence should instead depend on the opportunity cost of abandoning the current behavior. We propose the Opportunity-Cost Option-Critic ($OC^2$) framework, which defines a state-dependent deliberation cost using the positive value gap between the active option and its best alternative. This encourages persistence when the current option is clearly preferable and allows rapid switching when a better option emerges. We show that directly learning such costs leads to a degenerate zero-cost solution and introduces an auxiliary objective that aligns the learned cost with the value-gap target. The approach is evaluated in Four Rooms and Pinball domains under stationary, goal-shift, and geometry-shift conditions. In the Pinball goal-shift task, the $OC^2$ framework achieves a 52\% first-ten-episode success rate compared with 18\% for a fixed-cost baseline. The results suggest that opportunity-cost-based persistence improves adaptation in non-stationary environments.
authors: Khaled Ammoura, Aya Kayal, Naseem Daher
bullets: Fixed or duration-based deliberation costs indirectly control option persistence and may hinder adaptation.
OC² defines a state-dependent cost from the positive value gap between the active option and its best alternative.
An auxiliary objective prevents learning from collapsing to a degenerate zero-cost solution.
Across Four Rooms and Pinball conditions, OC² supports persistence when useful and rapid switching when alternatives improve.
In Pinball goal-shift tasks, OC² reached a 52% first-ten-episode success rate versus 18% for a fixed-cost baseline.

papers.abstract: We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions. Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations. To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand--object interactions. Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation. Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions. InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand--object relationships. An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories. Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA. Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DexSeed/.
authors: Huaijin Pi, Zehong Shen, Yong Wang, Kechun Xu, Changpeng Wang, Dingkun Wei, Xueyang Wang, Wenjia Wang, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Taku Komura

Uses InteractionMesh-based retargeting, arm trajectory augmentation, physics simulation, and RL-based finger control to generate executable rollouts.
Pairs successful simulated observations and actions with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA policy.
Experiments report better contact fidelity and whole-arm execution than evaluated baselines, with simulation and real-world demonstrations of language-specified grasps.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion interfaces should accommodate application-specific movement constraints while retaining useful reference behavior. Local content redaction requires a controller to replace selected movements even when it continues to receive the original reference. Removing the tracking incentive for those movements leaves their replacement unspecified. We introduce RedirectMimic, which separates the reference observed by the actor from the target used to train its execution. A rule-generated edited reference guides tracking rewards during proximal policy optimization, while the deployed observation and action interfaces remain unchanged. We evaluate pose- and speed-defined arm editing in Unitree G1 simulation using a tracker pretrained on 7,509 motion clips. On the overhead-arm task, RedirectMimic reduces core-window content occurrence to 2.7%, compared with 58.9% for reward zeroing and 32.8% for anti-tracking. It achieves 94.2% core-window joint success, combining content suppression, fall-free execution, and local retention. On the speed-defined task, fast outward arm movements occurred at similarly low rates under all three local editing methods. Across both tasks, RedirectMimic achieved the lowest replacement error among these methods and tracked unedited motions with accuracy comparable to that of the pretrained controller. Project page: https://xiaopeng-whu.github.io/RedirectMimic/.
bullets: Addresses local motion redaction when the controller still observes the original reference and replacement behavior is otherwise unspecified.
Separates the actor’s observed reference from its training target; a rule-generated edited reference supplies tracking rewards during PPO.
In Unitree G1 simulation, overhead-arm content fell to 2.7%, with 94.2% core-window joint success and fall-free execution.
Outperformed reward zeroing and anti-tracking on overhead-arm suppression and replacement error; unedited-motion tracking remained comparable to the pretrained controller.
For speed-defined editing, all methods achieved similarly low rates of fast outward arm movements, indicating task-dependent differences in method effectiveness.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, endowing policies with strong capabilities for modeling temporal and physical dynamics. Existing WAMs, encompassing both video-first action prediction and joint video-action modeling, directly transfer global physical representations from world models to action generation. However, global scene representations may underemphasize local robot-object interactions, creating a mismatch between representations optimized for world evolution and those required for manipulation. To bridge this gap, we propose LaST0.5, a novel WAM that introduces an interaction-centric physical representation between world modeling and action generation. Specifically, LaST0.5 learns a compact interaction-centric latent space under the supervision of visual interaction cues between the robot and the environment. This reasoning space is instantiated as a latent expert that bridges the world expert and the action expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Furthermore, LaST0.5 performs adaptive world-to-action transfer by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, using progress consistency to adjust action execution and trigger future resampling. Finally, we pretrain LaST0.5 on a large-scale robotic data corpus comprising over 14k hours of data, establishing interaction-centric physical reasoning as a scalable and effective paradigm. LaST0.5 achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, surpasses the previous state of the art on ten evaluated RLBench tasks, and demonstrates robust long-horizon execution and precise dexterous manipulation in real-world experiments.
authors: Xuheng Zhang, Yiming Zhang, Jialin Gao, Hao Chen, Jiaming Liu, Ji Li, Runzhong Huang, Yinxi Wang, Chenyang Gu, Zihan Yang, Yaowei Liu, Zhonghao Yan, Ziyu Guo, Renrui Zhang, Peng Jia, Pheng-Ann Heng, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between global world representations and the local robot–object interactions needed for manipulation.
Uses a latent expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers to connect world and action experts through interaction-focused physical reasoning.
Adaptively transfers world predictions to actions by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, enabling execution adjustment and future resampling.

Pretrained on over 14k hours of robotic data; achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, exceeds prior state of the art on ten RLBench tasks, and performs robustly in real-world long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
Scope: evaluated across benchmark and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, with the abstract not specifying broader domains.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The LaST0.5 Framework. (a) LaST0.5 unifies a World Expert, Latent Expert, and Action Expert within a Mixtureof-Transformers (MoT) architecture. To bridge global scene dynamics and precise local control, the Latent Expert distills future frames into compact, interaction-centric representations. (b) The Adaptive World-to-Action Transfer (AWAT) mechanism predicts progress values to assess task-progress consistency in imagined futures. Figure 1: Overview. Existing WAMs directly transfer representations of global scene dynamics to action prediction, potentially overlooking the localized robot–environment interactions required for manipulation. LaST0.5 bridges this gap through Interaction-Centric Latent Reasoning (ICLR), which learns a compact latent space supervised by visual motion and objectaffordance cues, establishing a hierarchical reasoning paradigm that progressively transforms global world representations into interaction-centric abstractions and ultimately into robot actions. LaST0.5 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RLBench simulation benchmarks and demonstrates robust long-horizon and precise manipulation in real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from formal specifications often separates task definition, reward shaping, curriculum design, and policy diagnostics into different mathematical objects. This fragmentation requires additional conversion steps and discards structure already present in the specification, such as subtask boundaries, ordering constraints, and quantitative measures. We introduce TBTCL (Temporal Behavior Tree Centric Learning), a framework that uses Temporal Behavior Trees (TBTs) as a unified interface for specification-guided reinforcement learning. A single TBT specifies the task, induces dense robustness-based rewards, defines a curriculum, and supports better understanding of learned policies. By adapting TBT syntax and semantics for specification-guided reinforcement learning, we provide a formalism that is more expressive than popular specification languages such as LTL and inherently hierarchical. We present algorithms to automatically extract a curriculum DAG and derive dense, robustness-based rewards directly from TBT semantics. Furthermore, we utilize TBT trace segmentation to build understandable competence profiles and automatically adapt the reward toward bottlenecks. We evaluate TBTCL on six specifications across discrete and continuous domains and show that Temporal Behavior Trees can serve as a specification, a reward, a curriculum, and a diagnostic.
bullets: Addresses fragmentation between task definitions, rewards, curricula, and diagnostics in formal-specification-based RL.
Uses one Temporal Behavior Tree to encode hierarchical subtasks, ordering constraints, and quantitative robustness measures.
Automatically derives dense robustness-based rewards and a curriculum represented as a DAG from TBT semantics.
Segments execution traces to produce competence profiles and adapt rewards toward learning bottlenecks.
Evaluated on six specifications across discrete and continuous domains, demonstrating TBTs’ use as specifications, rewards, curricula, and diagnostics.

papers.abstract: In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has progressed to whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination, which depends on the locomotion controller accurately executing velocity commands from the navigation policy. However, carrying an object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking. Persistent tracking biases can accumulate into position and heading deviations, increasing the risk of collisions and navigation failure. To address this problem, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under asymmetric upper-body loads. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to modulate actor features for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations. Cross-load tracking consistency training compares loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to promote consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads. Real-world experiments demonstrate collision-free goal reaching in all 40 tested navigation trials under unilateral hand loads with a fixed mapless navigation policy.
authors: Xianghui Wang, Aoran Fu, Liyou Luo, Shanze Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses persistent velocity-tracking and directional biases caused by carrying an object in one hand.
Uses estimated-wrench modulation of actor features to compensate for asymmetric loads while preserving reflected-action correspondence.
Trains consistency between loaded and unloaded conditions under identical velocity commands.
Simulation results show improved tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads.
Real-world tests achieved collision-free goal reaching in all 40 navigation trials with unilateral hand loads and a fixed mapless policy.

papers.abstract: Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model. Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors. After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points. Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes. The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.
