papers.abstract: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.

papers.abstract: Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated. Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and pi0.5) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5x reduction. Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of -2.5 percentage points (95% CI -23 to +19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p = 0.86). The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera. Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance. We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.
bullets: Four imitation-learning policies were evaluated on the same 50-demonstration pick-and-place task using an SO-101 arm.
Across 40 rollouts per lighting condition, success was 20/40 at ~520 lux and 19/40 at ~45 lux.
There was no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity to the lighting change.
Image brightness fell only 3% on the front camera and 19% on the wrist camera, likely due to automatic camera adjustments.
The study argues that camera settings and image statistics—not room lux alone—should be reported and controlled; exposure was not locked.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $\pi_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.
authors: Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Jingye Zhang, Zhifang Liu, Siyao Xiao, Zirong Ding, Yuhong Zhang, Kangjie Chen, Dongbin Zhang, Guorui Song, Guocun Wang, Peng Jiao, Haoqian Wang
bullets: Aligns robot actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a common behavioral-intent space.
Uses an embodiment-conditioned decoder to translate shared intent into robot-specific actions and control interfaces.
Adapts to a new robot from a single recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only embodiment embeddings.
With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO reaches 76.7% average success on real SO-101 and Piper robots, versus 70.0% for fully finetuned π₀.
Reports 97.3% success on LIBERO, 52.7% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 80.8% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CIALLO. (A) During pretraining, three encoders map an action chunk with proprioception, a pair of current and future frames, and an instruction grounded in the current frame into a shared intent space. We align their outputs with contrastive losses and train a shared decoder to reconstruct the demonstrated actions from each intent, conditioned on the robot’s embodiment parameters. (B) To learn a policy, Qwen-CIALLO predicts intent from observations and instructions, using the frozen action encoder as a teacher and the demonstrated actions to supervise the decoder output. CS denotes cosine similarity loss. (C) To transfer the codec to a new robot, we first calibrate its essential vector and arm and axis embeddings while keeping the shared weights fixed, then train the policy with the calibrated codec frozen.

Figure 2. The action codec. The action encoder (middle) uses the essential vector E to map control signals into shared intent, incorporating context from the proprioceptive encoder (top). The decoder (bottom) combines this intent with the target action schema and current proprioception, remodulates the result for the target embodiment, and uses the TransConv Head to predict each control scalar on a shared basis of 256 ordered bins. The decoded action is the softmax expectation over the bin centers.

Figure 4. Evolution of bin weights under scalar supervision. Bars show the softmax weights at six training steps. The blue line indicates the predicted scalar, computed as their expectation, and the red cross marks the nominal target of 0.75. The prediction approaches the target as the weights change, although no loss is applied directly to the bin weights.

Figure 3. Vision and text paths. The vision encoder compares current and future observations with a shared frozen DINOv2 backbone and an E-conditioned local interaction encoder, then pools valid tokens from multiple cameras into chunk-level intent. The text codec compresses the instruction into a task-level intent, grounds it using features reused from the current frame to form the same K ×D intent interface, and reconstructs masked instruction tokens from the task-level intent.

A shared three-dimensional t-SNE embedding is fitted after reducing the flattened intents to 50 dimensions with PCA. papers.abstract: Reliable state feedback of excavator front-end mechanisms is essential for autonomous excavation, yet retrofitting existing machines with dedicated joint sensors, external cameras, or visual markers can increase deployment and maintenance burdens. This paper proposes a closed-loop autonomous excavation framework for continuous inference of excavator joint states using onboard visual observations and control-related temporal information. The framework encodes structural cues from the current cab-view image, models short-term motion trends from historical joystick commands, and introduces a rolling state buffer for the bucket joint to preserve temporal continuity under severe occlusion. Mechanical joint-range constraints are incorporated into the learning objective to suppress infeasible estimates. The current cab-view image and inferred states are supplied to an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)-based control policy for online action generation. Experiments in an AGX Dynamics for Unity simulation environment under diverse operating conditions evaluate joint-state inference and end-to-end task execution. Across 20 autonomous excavation trials, the framework achieved a 95% task-completion rate, with an average joint-state-inference-and-control latency of 10.11 ms per step. The bucket-joint inference achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.965 degrees. These results demonstrate a sensor-light and computationally efficient joint-state-inference approach that can support closed-loop autonomous excavation with reduced dependence on additional sensing infrastructure.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.
authors: Yi Wang, Jingqiu Wu, Lei Yao, Zhaoshuo Li, Haoyu Zhu, Yirui Zhou, Huaiyuan Xu, Ying Zheng, Chuang Yang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Organizes Ego2Robot learning into four paradigms: embodiment transfer, action/task supervision, representation pretraining, and latent action/dynamics modeling.
Analyzes what information each paradigm extracts from human video and how robots use it for policy learning.
Reviews benchmarks spanning egocentric videos, robot demonstrations, and synthetic or simulated resources.
Highlights open challenges in physical feasibility, human–robot coordination, in-context adaptation, evaluation, and predictive control.

papers.abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
authors: Xu Luo, Jiaying Yang, Hao Wu, Junlin Xie, Zijin Hong, Ji Zhang, Lianli Gao, Jingkuan Song
bullets: Long action chunks create high-dimensional optimization problems for online RL, making real-world adaptation costly.
ExRL adds a lightweight adapter that predicts each chunk’s execution length.
The adapter is trained with off-policy RL in a low-dimensional space whose expressivity increases with chunk size.
Experiments in simulation and on real robotic tasks show sample-efficient adaptation across diverse long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific tuning.

papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
authors: Rumi Loghmani, Bozhang Song, Victor Alvarado, Aliyah Redding, Amir Barati Farimani
bullets: Reads experiment steps from a photo of a printed protocol.
Identifies identical containers by reading labels from multiple camera views, without fixed positions or fiducial markers.

Completed 5/5 runs of one protocol and 4/5 of another without human intervention; correctly identified all containers in 160 localization trials.
Demonstrated on a Franka Panda arm and two children’s chemistry-kit protocols, so scope is limited to the tested setup and procedures.

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Mingzhe Li, Bruno Castro da Silva
bullets: Addresses the failure of local safety filters when constraints invalidate an entire behavior mode.
Steers the generator’s behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margins.
Uses a path-space control-barrier-function quadratic program to correct only residual violations.
Provides finite-time recovery guarantees and reduces the burden on path-level correction.
Experiments in navigation and robot end-effector planning show preserved safety, better goal reaching, and less correction than path-level filters.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Experimental domains and test-time safety constraints. Each row shows one planning domain: 2D point-navigation, Maze2D, and Franka 3D end-effector planning. The first column visualizes the original scene and multimodal demonstration dataset, where multiple behaviors can reach the same goal. The remaining columns show three test-time safety constraints imposed on the same pretrained planner. Green circles denote starts, orange stars denote goals, and red shaded regions denote unsafe sets. These constraints test whether a method can preserve safety and goal reaching when certification requires more than local path repair.

Figure 3: Latent steering provides the warm start needed for path-space repair. Stage I performs behavior-level selection by steering the latent and changing the decoded rollout before certification; Stage II then applies path-level CBF repair to remove residual violations. The second row removes Stage I and applies the same path-space correction directly, corresponding to SAFEFLOWMATCHER. Without the latent-steered warm start, the local corrector remains tied to the original rollout and fails to produce a goal-reaching safe path. With Stage I, the corrected trajectory starts from a better behavior and Stage II only needs to repair the remaining local violation.

Figure 1: Latent Barrier Steering separates behavior selection from path repair. A vanilla flow-matching planner may generate a goal-reaching but unsafe rollout under a new constraint. A path-space CBF corrector such as SAFEFLOWMATCHER can enforce safety locally, but may produce a trajectory that is safe while no longer reaching the goal when the selected behavior mode is blocked. LBS first steers the behavior latent from z0 to z+ toward a safer rollout, then applies path-level CBF repair only for residual violations, yielding a trajectory that is both safe and goal-reaching.

papers.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.
bullets: Addresses the lack of team-level coordination in language-guided RL for partially observable search-and-rescue environments.
Uses an LLM to convert human instructions into semantic cues for strategy selection and agent role assignment.
Introduces the LG-MAHDP formalism to model language grounding, hierarchical decisions, and distributed coordination.
In simulated disaster scenarios, the system reports faster learning, stronger coordination, improved subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance, and 20–30% higher victim rescue rates.
Ablations identify language grounding and the shared cognitive workspace as critical components; results are limited to simulated SAR settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework for Language-Grounded Hierarchical Decision-Making. Left: Verbal input 𝑣from the human operator is processed by the LLM-driven Context Extractor to produce contextual features 𝐶. These features, together with observations 𝑠from the Environment and information priorities 𝑀from the Information Space, are integrated within the Strategic Decision Engine (SDE). The Attention Space refines strategy selection by mapping semantic cues and priority information via Ψ(𝐶,𝑀). The SDE outputs high-level strategies 𝜔, which the Worker modules translate into low-level actions 𝛼executed within the Environment. The resulting observations are fed back into the shared workspace, enabling continuous learning and adaptation. Right: Comparison of LLM outputs with and without retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in simulated SAR operations, showing that RAG enhances contextual precision, hazard annotation, and task-specific semantic structure in generated outputs.

Fig. 5. Coverage-efficiency comparison across models. Grouped bar chart showing (from left to right) coverage ratio, revisit index, and dead-zone ratio for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL. LG-HRL attains the highest coverage and lowest dead-zone ratio while also reducing redundant revisits, demonstrating the most efficient spatial exploration among all methods.

Fig. 7. Ablation results for core components. Normalized system performance under removal of key architectural elements. Removing any component reduces performance, with language grounding and the shared cognitive workspace contributing most strongly to mission success.

Fig. 8. Agent Trajectories Under LG-HRL Control. The plot above shows how UAV and UGV agents behave when guided by the proposed Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LGHRL) system. UAV trajectories (blue) exhibit broad-area scouting patterns characteristic of airborne reconnaissance, while UGV trajectories (green) remain grounded and focus on directed paths suitable for close-range navigation and victim retrieval. Hazard zones are denoted by red “X” markers, and both agents demonstrate safe, deliberate navigation around these areas.

Fig. 3. Coordination Entropy Reduction Across Training. Coordination entropy trajectories for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL across 2000 training episodes. LG-HRL exhibits the fastest decline in entropy and stabilizes at the lowest value, indicating efficient division of labor and emergent cooperative behavior. HRL shows moderate improvements, while Flat RL continues to exhibit high entropy due to the absence of semantic grounding and hierarchical structure.

Fig. 6. Victim rescue performance across models. Comparison of rescue success rates for Flat RL, HRL, and LG-HRL across five disaster scenarios. LG-HRL consistently achieves the highest rescue rates (88–92%), surpassing HRL and Flat RL by a substantial margin.

Fig. 4. Impact of language grounding on strategic accuracy. Comparison of HRL without language grounding (yellow bars) and LG-HRL with language grounding (blue bars) across three metrics: subgoal-selection accuracy, hazard-avoidance success, and responsiveness to natural-language mission updates. Language grounding yields substantial gains in all three dimensions, highlighting the value of LLM-based semantic guidance for safe and aligned multi-agent decision-making.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
authors: Denis Grachev, Damien LaRocque, Omar Moured

papers.abstract: Reliable medical laboratory automation requires robots to complete entire workflows in protocol order while handling changes during execution. A robot may execute each motion correctly yet fail the workflow by confusing visually similar stages or stalling after human intervention. We present Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework that couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision--language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation. A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision--language--action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates it with the monitor. We evaluate Robo-MLT against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82\% and 70\%, exceeding $\pi_{0.5}$ by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively. After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. These results indicate that, under the evaluated conditions, explicit workflow monitoring makes long-horizon laboratory manipulation more reliable and recoverable.
authors: Zequan Zeng, Kai Wang, Delvin Ce Zhang, Huaping Liu, Zhipeng Yuan, Junqin Yang, YunLong Zhang
bullets: Targets failures from confusing similar workflow stages and stalling after human intervention.
Uses a vision–language planner to create ordered atomic skills from the protocol and workspace view.
A multiframe monitor detects skill completion or infeasibility, triggering progression or replanning.
A skill-conditioned vision–language–action policy generates trajectories, coordinated asynchronously with monitoring.
Achieves 82% success in blood gas analysis and 70% in tube sorting; it also replans after sample removal and continues processing.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of Robo-MLT. A frozen Qwen3.7-Max planner maps a user command, the instrument protocol, and an initial scene observation to an ordered sequence of atomic skills. System 2 tracks the plan with a dual-head execution monitor and invokes replanning once the active skill can no longer be completed; System 1 executes the active skill with a Qwen3-VL-conditioned flow-matching policy.

Fig. 3. Architecture of the System 2 execution monitor. Frozen SigLIP2 encoders embed a sliding window of M multiview observations and the active skill instruction lt; a causal temporal encoder and cross-attention blocks ground the observation history in the instruction to form the feature vt, from which two MLP heads predict the completion and recovery probabilities γ̂t and β̂t.

(Top) In a reversible workflow, visually similar observations can require opposite actions; a policy without explicit workflow state may therefore act at the wrong stage. (Bottom) System 2 tracks the active skill from temporal observations; System 1 maps that skill and the current observation to fine-grained trajectories.

papers.abstract: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.
authors: Delin Zhao, Zhengrong Yue, Junlin He, Yali Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed practice sources, which may fail to expose new weaknesses as capabilities change.
Alternates updates to a curriculum harness that proposes informative challenges and an execution harness that develops reusable revisions.
Uses admitted challenge snapshots to compare execution revisions while keeping the other component fixed.
Starting from compact LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting deployment outperformed evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels.

On LIBERO-PRO, it achieved 74.0% success, improving over the initial deployment and direct VLA-controller execution; case studies cover practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.
authors: Daniel Campa, Spandan Das, Srinjoy Das
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency and inflexibility of monolithic diffusion models for offline RL transition synthesis.
Uses a chain-rule factorization into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, with estimators suited to each factor.
Matches the SynthER baseline across 12 D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks while substantially reducing generation cost.
Best-of-10 targeted action synthesis improves over real-data training on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings, averaging +8.9 D4RL points.
Performance degrades on expert mixtures because of inaccurate advantage estimates, not the synthesis mechanisms themselves.

papers.abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.
authors: Ruimeng Liu, Denan Liang, Ruofei Bai, Fuming Zhang, Kuan Xu, Shenghai Yuan, Lihua Xie
bullets: Targets slow, discontinuous discrete coordinate decoding and inadequate point regression for multi-contact or irregular affordances.
Shares lower multimodal layers while routing upper layers to specialized spatial and linguistic experts to reduce gradient interference.
Represents each coordinate as one token using visual positional embeddings, aligning coordinates with image features.
Uses differentiable Signed Distance Field supervision without requiring costly mask decoders.
Reports a 15.7% average gain and 8.31× throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-grounding benchmarks, while preserving performance across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

(e) Region-based Mask-SDF supervision for continuous point prediction, penalizing exterior predictions while accommodating multi-peak affordance regions without mode averaging. papers.abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.
authors: Yihang Che, Zhongwei Yu, Yang Li, Xingyu Lu, Hongxia Yu, Jun Wang
bullets: Current self-driving laboratories often separate language-based planning from robotic execution, limiting physical grounding and embodied intuition.
ESA combines a memory-based reasoning and Bayesian-optimisation Digital Agent, a generalisable instrument-controlling Embodied Agent, and a unified coordination interface.
In autonomous wastewater-treatment experiments, ESA explored more than 200 million possible conditions over 15 continuous rounds.
Solution transmittance improved from 82% to 99.7%, with a reported 98.5% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation.
Learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, supporting broader autonomous laboratory operation.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Illustration of the Bayesian Optimisation framework as a central component of the ESA architecture. BO receives initial experimental configurations and objectives from the Principal Investigator (PI) Agent. As experiments are conducted by the Embodied Agent, the outcomes are relayed back to BO, providing essential data for refining its surrogate model. BO utilises this feedback to update its predictions and identify the next optimal configuration for experimentation. The Scheduler facilitates the execution of these configurations by coordinating between BO and the Embodied Agent. Ultimately, the best decision obtained during BO is recommended to the Reporter.

Figure 1: The Evolution of Self-Driving Laboratories. This timeline traces the development of autonomous experimentation systems from initial concepts in the 1940s to foundation model integration in recent years, spanning three eras: Early Era (1940s–2009, bottom) establishing foundational principles from design of experiments to closed-loop robot scientist; Modern Era (2009–2022, middle) deploying specialised robotic platforms across scientific domains; and LLMs Era (2022–present, top) integrating foundation models for high-level reasoning.

Figure 2: The architecture of the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), a hybrid cognitive–embodied paradigm for self-driving laboratories with three components. The Digital Agent, the cognitive core and central novelty of ESA, evolves open-endedly by integrating online knowledge, embodied experimentation, and past experience for reasoning, planning, and decision-making. The Embodied Agent orchestrates diverse robots and scientific instruments through multiple control modules for generalised, reliable, and adaptive operation. The Embodied Unified Interface connects digital intelligence with heterogeneous laboratory devices via standardised, low-latency, and safe protocols. Together, they close the loop between perception, reasoning, and embodied execution for autonomous scientific discovery.

Figure 3: Overview of the robotic platform. The dual-arm robot comprises two 6-DoF robotic arms equipped with 1-DoF grippers, a 2-DoF articulated head, an omnidirectional AMR base offering 2 planar DoFs for holonomic motion, and a 1-DoF lift for vertical adjustment. These degrees of freedom are highlighted in the blue box. The platform also integrates a synchronised multi-camera sensing suite consisting of one RGB and one depth camera mounted on the head, two RGB cameras on each wrist, and one RGB camera on the chest, as indicated in the orange box. Together, these components provide rich proprioceptive and multi-view visual feedback to support both global perception and fine-grained manipulation.
Figure 4: Transmittance results across 15 experimental rounds.

papers.abstract: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.
bullets: Targets the challenge of handling objects with different materials, deformation, and contact dynamics.
Estimates physical parameters by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation.
Conditions a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy on the recovered physical properties.
Uses a physics memory bank for efficient retrieval without online simulation optimization.
Experiments in simulation and the real world report improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed training framework. Given multi-view images, we first estimate the physical properties of the manipulated object by combining feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF-3DGS) with MPM via a differentiable physical simulation. The simulator is coupled with a differentiable rasterizer and optimized under video guidance, where gradients are back-propagated through the simulation. Physics-based constraints, including Dirichlet boundary conditions for manipulation events and geometric consistency via temporal Chamfer distance, further regularize the estimated physical parameters by aligning simulated particle dynamics with demonstration videos. The learned physical parameters are then injected into a physical-aware diffusion policy as physics conditions, together with language instructions and visual observations, enabling the policy to predict physics-consistent robot actions and gripper states.

Fig. 3. Object preservation results on fragile objects. Among successful pick-and-place trials, the methods differ in their ability to preserve object integrity. We evaluate object preservation by measuring grape rupture and irreversible deformation of paper cups over 30 successful pick-andplace trials. A trial is considered successful only if the object remains intact, exhibiting neither grape rupture nor irreversible deformation. Our method achieves the highest object preservation success rate on both object categories.

Fig. 4. Visualization of learned material-aware routing weights in our MoE policy. Each row represents an object and each column corresponds to a physical-property expert. The bubble size and color indicate the routing weight assigned to each expert. The learned router discovers clear expert specialization, where objects with different physical characteristics are preferentially routed to their corresponding experts while maintaining adaptive soft assignments across experts.

papers.abstract: Human-level dexterity remains a central open problem in robotics, yet few simulation frameworks cover the full workflow of dexterous manipulation, from setting up a robot to collecting dexterous demonstrations and evaluating policies. We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator. DexSuite provides 30 tasks and assembles its 10 arms and 12 end-effectors, from parallel-jaw grippers to dexterous hands, into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. It also ships a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. Moreover, we define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs spanning diverse contact complexities and horizons, and release a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes in simulation from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policies. We release DexSuite as open source and hope others will build on it. Videos and datasets are available at https://dexsuiteorg.github.io

papers.abstract: We introduce DreamFormer, a model-based agent that acquires language-conditioned, multi-task skills by imitating expert demonstrations within the latent imagination of a learned world model. DreamFormer first learns a task-agnostic Transformer world model from unstructured play data, then acquires task-specific behaviors by optimizing an intrinsic reward that aligns agent-generated rollouts with expert demonstrations in latent space. Since the policy is trained on-policy inside imagination, it is exposed to its own errors during training, mitigating the covariate shift inherent to offline behavioral cloning. To make long-horizon imagination affordable, DreamFormer encodes a high-resolution multi-view robotic observation into a single input token, avoiding both spatial downsampling and the multi-token representations used by prior Transformer world models. On the long-horizon CALVIN benchmark, DreamFormer outperforms LUMOS, the comparable model-based agent, on single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs 2.34 average tasks completed per chain of five) while keeping imagination rollouts tractable. Against HULC, the behavior cloning baseline, it nearly doubles performance on zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment (1.30 vs 0.67), indicating that dynamics learned by the world model transfer more readily than a directly cloned policy. This is consistent with the role attributed to internal models in biological agents, where a model of environment dynamics supports behavior in situations not previously encountered.
bullets: Learns a task-agnostic world model from unstructured play data, then optimizes task behavior in imagined rollouts aligned with expert demonstrations.
On-policy training within imagination exposes the policy to its own errors, reducing offline behavioral-cloning covariate shift.
Compresses high-resolution multi-view observations into a single token to keep long-horizon Transformer imagination tractable.
On CALVIN, completes more tasks than LUMOS in single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs. 2.34) and nearly doubles HULC’s zero-shot transfer performance (1.30 vs. 0.67).

papers.abstract: We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual fea- tures together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp- transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask- support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D- to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment- specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.
bullets: Uses locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D templates aligned with the target camera, robot, gripper, and workspace.
Combines DINOv2 features, appearance, and depth cues to guide SAM2 object segmentation.
Retrieves templates through a two-stage geometry-semantic cascade and selects between two grasp-transfer estimators via confidence gating.
Refines transferred grasps using mask-support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D-to-3D conversion.
Demonstrates adaptation without end-to-end retraining and tolerance to the evaluated viewpoint and illumination changes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies may predict a transferable manipulation strategy yet fail to realize it reliably on the encountered object: objects compatible with the same grasp differ in geometry and compliance, and visual feedback degrades under closure occlusion. AgenticTactileVLA is presented as an execution-time supervisor that shifts part of object-specific adaptation from prediction to physical interaction. A fixed VLA provides the approach and hand targets; the supervisor decides whether to remain transparent, refine finger flexion, retain or release the corrected configuration, return control to the VLA for retry, or select a compliant hand-control regime. It uses finger-position and motor-effort feedback as proprioceptive contact evidence and requires neither tactile sensors nor VLA retraining. On a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand, a randomized matched-block evaluation on five objects held out from VLA training yields 61.3% completion for the base VLA, 72.0% for unconditional close-to-stall control, and 84.0% for the supervisor under a shared budget; the gain is positive on every object and persists under moderate pose perturbations. Ablations show the gain is not explained by extended closure alone, and that selective triggering reduces correction episodes by 65.7% with no detected change in completion. A retention audit shows acceptance predicts retention in 88.9% of held-out cases, while compliant objects expose conservative false rejection. A thin-walled-cup study demonstrates contextual routing to compliant control, matching an always-compliant reference. These results suggest that contact-guided execution-time adaptation can improve the object-level generalization of a fixed VLA to held-out objects by adapting physical realization without object-specific retraining.
bullets: Addresses failures caused by object-specific geometry, compliance, and visual occlusion during grasp execution.
Supervises a fixed VLA by selectively refining finger flexion, retaining or releasing corrections, retrying with VLA control, or routing to compliant hand control.
Uses finger position and motor-effort feedback as contact evidence, requiring no tactile sensors or VLA retraining.
On five held-out objects, completion improved from 61.3% for the base VLA to 84.0% with the supervisor under a shared budget; gains persisted under moderate pose perturbations.
Selective triggering reduced correction episodes by 65.7% without detected completion loss, while compliant objects revealed conservative false rejection as a limitation.

papers.abstract: Transferring visual representations pretrained on human videos to robot manipulation requires learning reliable correspondences between human and robot demonstrations. However, paired demonstrations can differ in execution rate and in the proportion of non-key frames that do not directly reflect task progress. Frames at the same relative timestamp may therefore represent different task stages, which can cause correspondence learning to fail. To address these issues, we propose Frame-Level Temporal Alignment (FLTA), a framework that uses two temporal priors to adapt visual encoders pretrained on human videos for robot manipulation. It learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations, allowing frames at different relative temporal positions to match. A global progress prior combines normalized temporal positions with visual similarity to construct a soft correspondence target. A local temporal order prior penalizes backward transitions while allowing stays and varying forward rates to accommodate execution-rate differences. With ResNet-50 and ViT encoders, our method achieves relative improvements of 46.93% and 65.96%, respectively, over the best baselines in average simulation success rates and achieves higher task success rates on real-world manipulation tasks. These results also suggest that effective human-robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected. Our project page is available at https://rtx5090ultra.github.io/FLTA-Project-Page/.
bullets: Addresses mismatched execution rates and irrelevant non-key frames in human–robot demonstrations.
Learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations.
Uses a global progress prior for soft correspondences and a local temporal-order prior that permits stays and variable forward rates.
Reports relative average simulation success improvements of 46.93% with ResNet-50 and 65.96% with ViT over the best baselines, plus higher real-world task success.
Suggests that selecting which encoder parameters to update may matter more than updating more parameters.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a conformal-seeded hybrid strategy for solving inverse kinematics of offset, redundant 7-DoF robot arms of the humanoid class. Analytical inverse kinematics (AIK) provides closed-form solutions with very low computational cost. However, for offset kinematic structures, the exact closed-form solution is generally unavailable, and practical AIK must rely on an approximate or simplified kinematic model. In contrast, numerical inverse kinematics (NIK) can achieve high-precision solutions on the full kinematic model. However, its convergence is highly sensitive to initialization. To overcome these limitations, we propose a two-stage hybrid inverse kinematics framework with conformal-calibrated seed selection. First, an approximate analytical model efficiently enumerates a finite set of candidate joint solutions. Second, we rank these candidates using a lightweight learned predictor of post-refinement difficulty, wrapped by split-conformal prediction into a calibrated upper bound that serves as the selection score. The best-ranked seed is then refined using a Levenberg-Marquardt solver on the full kinematic model. The proposed method combines fast candidate generation, learned seed ranking with a calibrated difficulty bound, and accurate numerical refinement, achieving real-time performance of less than 40us and a success rate of 100% in our evaluation on reachable targets. We validate the approach through large-scale stochastic simulation across the workspace and experimental demonstrations with motion planning on a humanoid robot arm. Demonstration videos are available at https://youtu.be/aeiBmw1XRbw.
bullets: Targets offset, redundant 7-DoF humanoid-class arms where exact analytical IK is unavailable and numerical IK is initialization-sensitive.
Generates candidate joint solutions from an approximate analytical model, then ranks them with a learned predictor wrapped in split-conformal calibration.
Refines the selected seed using a Levenberg–Marquardt solver on the full kinematic model.
Reports under 40 μs runtime and 100% success on reachable targets in evaluation, with simulation and humanoid-arm demonstrations.
Scope is limited to reachable targets and the evaluation setting described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript
bullets: Addresses the limitation that demonstrations from other scenes lack feedback about the robot’s current world.
RoboScript implements WICL by combining one demonstration with simulated rehearsal, reflection, and frozen Task Memory.
Achieves 83.4% mean success across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks using one demonstration per task and no gradient updates.
The approach generalizes across visual distributions, benefits from larger foundation models, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment adaptation.
Scope: performance is demonstrated for agentic manipulation, with deployment inputs isolated to information available on the real robot.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces World In-Context Learning (WICL) for robot manipulation, fitting Robot Learning and Manipulation. The paradigm of learning world dynamics/context rather than weights fits Latent Action Models.
papers.title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: World In-Context Learning lets a frozen robot model rehearse a demonstrated task in simulation, store feedback in context, and transfer the resulting task memory to new scenes without gradient updates.

papers.abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.
bullets: Studies linear-function-approximation policy evaluation when TD updates must cross a rate-limited channel.
Batches updates to reduce transmission variance and adaptively quantizes innovations.
Provides a high-probability finite-time error bound for the proposed method.
Above a finite channel-capacity threshold, matches unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors.
Uses O(d log T) transmitted bits over horizon T to attain the order-optimal Õ(1/T) rate, improving communication complexity over prior work.

papers.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
bullets: Problem: Action learning can weaken pretrained language–video alignment, but guidance on data and supervision design is limited.
Method: Systematically evaluates language–video, language–video–action, and joint supervision using about 47,000 hours of general, egocentric, UMI, and robot videos.

Key findings: Egocentric video mixed with UMI demonstrations improves control generalization under a fixed training budget; architecture and joint-training choices affect how well these data are used.
Scaling the selected pretraining setup and post-training on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations yields 88.10% success in Easy and 61.56% in Hard conditions.
The model reaches 40.00% success across three real-world tasks, versus 23.33% for the strongest baseline, and the authors release data, code, and weights.

papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.
bullets: Targets soft powered descent, where limited fuel demands efficient guidance trajectories and control.
Uses model-based reinforcement learning built on DreamerV3 for the entry-descent-landing problem.
Operates from state sensor observations, advancing toward end-to-end landing solutions.
Reportedly lands within 2 m of the designated zone with velocity norm below 0.3 m/s.
Designed to be sample-efficient and generalizable across landing scenarios.

papers.abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.
bullets: Robot probe pressure alters vascular anatomy, motivating fast biomechanical simulation for autonomous access.
The simulator used Stable Neo-Hookean tissue and a Vertex Block Descent solver on one GPU.
In a cylindrical phantom, artery predictions stayed within 5 percentage points and vein predictions within 3 points through 11 mm of compression.
A selected setting reduced solver time from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms per frame while staying within 1.03 points of the finest reference; the full stack ran at 56.4 ms per frame.
A realistic digital leg reproduced the expected clinical signal: the vein collapsed more than the artery.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining heterogeneous tactile data despite sensor-specific physics and limitations.
Supports piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors, with extensibility to new sensor types.
Produces plug-and-play tactile tokens compatible with diffusion policies and VLA models, including π₀.₅ and LingBot-VLA.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots across multiple hardware platforms show benefits for complex manipulation while retaining computational efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of LingBot-Touch. Top: what tactile data look like at scale. Our 5,000-hour corpus is multi-source, pooling egocentric recordings from human tactile gloves with teleoperated robot hands across piezoresistive, magnetic, and optical sensing (left); heterogeneous in taxel geometry, resolution, and channels, which we reconcile in a canonical fingertip space (middle); and sparse, with most taxels silent most of the time (right). Bottom: what one encoder trained on this corpus enables. Frozen features recover contact force, location, extent, and dynamics and align with vision (left); the same tokens plug into imitation-learning and VLA policies on real dual-arm hands (middle) and into reinforcement learning in simulation (right). LingBot-Touch transfers to a sensor model unseen in pretraining without retraining, and its 5.46M-parameter Tiny variant adds under 0.2% to the parameters of the policies it augments.

Figure 3. Overview of LingBot-Touch. LingBot-Touch learns unified tactile representations through self-supervised prediction in latent space. Heterogeneous spatiotemporal signals from magnetic, piezoresistive, and visuotactile sensors are mapped to a canonical spherical space and incorporated into pretraining through weighted sampling. Modality-specific tokenizers convert these signals into tokens for a shared Transformer backbone equipped with 5D rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). The context encoder processes only visible tokens, and its outputs are concatenated with mask tokens before being passed to the corresponding modality-specific predictor. The target encoder processes the unmasked input, providing latent targets for the context loss on visible positions and the prediction loss on masked positions. Its parameters are updated through an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the context encoder, with gradients stopped through the target branch.

Figure 7. Scaling with pretraining data and model size. Frozen-encoder probing on Sharpa Wave (top) and XHand1 (bottom) for Tiny and Small encoders pretrained on 1K to 5K hours with fixed source proportions. Small improves or holds on every task with every increment of data on both hands; Tiny saturates at about 4K hours and loses retrieval recall at 5K.

Figure 8. Single-source versus multi-source pretraining. Blue: probed on Sharpa Wave. Orange: probed on XHand1. Top: adding 441 hours of piezoresistive data and the other sensor’s data to a fixed 331 or 228 hours of a sensor’s own data improves seven of eight sensor-task pairs. Bottom: at a fixed 1,000-hour budget, a single-source model beats the three-source mixture on its own sensor on seven of eight pairs, by the widest margins on the spatial tasks. Bold marks the better of each pair. LingBot-Touch uses the HaT-Tiny backbone.

Figure 2. Composition and diversity of the LingBot-Touch pretraining dataset. Our dataset comprises 4,983 hours of tactile recordings, spanning 464K episodes and 1.33 billion frames across piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensing modalities. To support representation learning for downstream understanding of contact physics and robotic dexterous manipulation, it covers diverse real-world human and robot manipulation tasks, encompassing varied sensing principles, spatial resolutions, sampling frequencies, and physical taxel layouts.

Figure 6. Comparison with FTP-1 using frozen pretrained backbones. Results on Sharpa Wave (top) and XHand1 (bottom). Gray bars show FTP-1 with sensor-specific adapters trained for each platform. Colored bars show LingBot-Touch with the HaT-Small backbone, pretrained on 5K hours of tactile data and evaluated without sensor-specific encoder adaptation. Arrows indicate whether lower or higher values are better.

Figure 5. Contact-physics probing tasks. Five frozen-encoder probing tasks on two dexterous hands, Sharpa Wave and XHand1: fingertip force recovery, contact center and coverage estimation, future force prediction, and tactile-to-video retrieval. They test contact intensity, spatial structure, short-term dynamics, and cross-modal correspondence. Each task trains its own attentive probe on the multi-level features of the frozen EMA target encoder. For fingertip force recovery, labels are obtained by averaging the per-finger resultant force vectors over each pair of consecutive frames and then computing their magnitudes. Contact centers are computed as contact-strength-weighted centroids of valid taxels above the activation threshold, while contact coverage is the fraction of valid taxels that are active. Future force labels represent per-finger changes in force magnitude at each of the next four frames relative to the final history frame. Contact centers are supervised only when contact is present.

papers.abstract: A challenging bottleneck in manipulation research is reproducibility and comparability of methods in real-world environments. Since manipulation is an interactive task, it cannot be evaluated on a static dataset of observations. Benchmarking in simulation is a common remedy, but cannot cover the whole complexity of real-world tests. This paper proposes a new paradigm of stochastic challenges. Like the well-known YCB objects, it is based on reproducible real-world scenes and therefore allows system-level innovation and comparability between different platforms. Due to their stochastic nature, our challenges however, mimic the rigor and surprise of hidden test sets. To this end, we show how different robots in different labs can be compared based on their success rate over different random task samples, if these samples come from the same distribution. We propose stochastic challenges as a general paradigm for robot benchmarking and implement this paradigm in a novel benchmark for mobile manipulation, on which we compare two robots tested in two different labs.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating interactive manipulation using static datasets or simulation alone.
Uses reproducible real-world scenes with randomized task samples to emulate hidden-test-set rigor and variability.
Enables comparison across platforms when task samples are drawn from the same distribution.
Implements the paradigm in a mobile-manipulation benchmark and compares two robots tested in two labs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Stochastic Challenges target several desired aspects of robotic benchmarking: (i) systemlevel innovation, i.e. not restricting evaluation to specific hardware; (ii) local evaluation, avoiding the effort to transport systems and reducing the chance of errors when trying to reproduce methods; (iii) reduced overfitting, testing true generalization instead of pre-known tasks.

Figure 2: Concept overview. Seeded randomization generates reproducible KALLAX manipulation scenes; robots across labs (Stretch 3 and Spot) execute sampled configurations, with outcomes statistically aggregated for robust comparison.
Figure 3: Experimental setup. Our KALLAX benchmark draws sample configs from the same distribution, which are then recreated in two different labs to evaluate the two different robotic systems.
Table 1: Testing on same vs. different shelf configurations. Averaged success rates vary substantially with the selected scene subset when few seeds are used.
Table 2: Observed robot success rates and detectable margins. Margins are computed for α = 0.10 and 80% power. Partial successes are counted as failures, and all configuration labels are included.
