papers.abstract: Robots are typically evaluated in episodes that begin from a reset, while industrial work consists of repeated jobs whose outcomes affect subsequent operations. Evaluating such work at scale requires simulation of task-critical physical interactions, construction of industrial environments, and measurements of performance as scene state persists. We present HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0, a framework for simulating, generating, and evaluating industrial robot work. Given a human-specified workplace and task, the framework defines a world pairing a scenario of scene variants and process logic with an evaluation defining a job, metrics, and a rubric. HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0 comprises three components. HOLIDAY-SIM extends Newton's SDF-based hydroelastic contact with additional constitutive laws and a semi-implicit primal-dual solver, couples stateful actuator dynamics to articulated motion, and derives tactile and joint observations from simulated states. Agentic world construction generates simulation-ready assets and scene variants using geometric and interaction checks, and proposes task-conditioned evaluations for human confirmation and executable checks. 24/7-BENCH introduces seven industrial tasks in which jobs are evaluated without resetting the scene, measuring completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy. Controlled studies characterize the proposed contact, actuator, and tactile models and examine the effectiveness of verification-guided world construction. Experiments on scene and evaluation generation further reveal the limitations of model critics and the difficulty of ensuring that generated evaluations faithfully capture task requirements. We examine job-level evaluations with scripted trajectories (e.g., code-as-policy) but have not yet compared policies over persistent runs.
bullets: Targets the gap between reset-based robot benchmarks and real industrial workflows, where each job changes the state for subsequent jobs.
Combines HOLIDAY-SIM for contact, actuator, articulated-motion, tactile, and joint-state simulation with agentic construction of verified workplace assets and scene variants.
Introduces 24/7-BENCH with seven industrial tasks evaluated using completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy.
Controlled studies assess the simulation models and verification-guided world construction, while generation experiments expose weaknesses in model critics and evaluation fidelity.
Evaluations currently use scripted trajectories; policies have not yet been compared over persistent runs.

papers.abstract: Generative models can support both state estimation and control in robotics. For control, a common approach is to use the model as a policy that directly samples actions conditioned on observation histories. However, models that jointly represent states, actions, and observations can also predict how the robot state and its environment evolve. We investigate whether these predictions can improve state estimation and control through a change in inference procedure, without modifying the pretrained model. To this end, we use particle filtering to maintain competing hypotheses about state histories. A single pretrained diffusion model generates these hypotheses along with their predicted observations and associated action proposals. As new measurements arrive, particles are reweighted according to how well their predicted observations match the measurements. While particle filtering conventionally uses these weights only for state estimation, we also use them to guide action selection, favoring proposals associated with hypotheses that better explain the observations. Simulation experiments in partially observed navigation and vision-based manipulation demonstrate improvements in both state estimation and task performance compared to action generation without filtering, using the same pretrained model and no additional test-time information.
bullets: Addresses partially observed robotics, where uncertainty about state can hinder control.
Maintains competing state-history hypotheses using particles generated by one pretrained diffusion model.
Reweights particles by agreement between predicted and observed measurements.
Uses these weights for both state estimation and action selection, without modifying the model or adding test-time information.
Simulation results in navigation and vision-based manipulation show improved estimation and task performance over unfiltered action generation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.
bullets: Soft-robot RL is hindered by costly hardware interactions and unreliable or unavailable simulators.
A time-scale separation reduces the robot dynamics to a low-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM).
A 6,924-parameter polynomial ODE learned from pre-collected data provides the RL training environment.
On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, the policy trained in 3 hours deployed without fine-tuning and achieved 40% lower tracking error than comparable RNN- and transformer-based approaches.
The approach remains demonstrated on one soft-arm trajectory-tracking task and depends on the validity of the aSSM reduction.

papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.
bullets: Learns a nonlinear reduced-order ODE directly from hardware data.
Integrates the learned model into a model predictive control scheme.
Demonstrates closed-loop tracking with static and dynamic constraints.
Reports improved accuracy and precision over data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning.
The hardware-data-based approach is intended to generalize to other soft robotic systems.

papers.abstract: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.
bullets: Latent-action assignments vary drastically across training runs and numerical precision, despite similar robot motion inputs.
The method adds a straight-through similarity loss to align a video-trained tokenizer’s code geometry with macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv) activity.
On held-out shape categories, PMv alignment reaches 0.52 versus 0.20–0.26 for released or no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for random kinematic encoders.
Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer, but a hand-designed initial-stroke-direction descriptor scores higher (0.65).
A shuffled-PMv control still scores 0.41, and downstream manipulation effects are specified for future testing rather than reported.

papers.abstract: Large-scale pretraining is reducing the amount of adaptation required to deploy embodied foundation models, but it is not guaranteed that a pretrained model already provide the level of performance required in every deployment. Practitioners therefore need to understand how well a pretrained model matches a target deployment and how much adaptation data is left to be collected. We study whether a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations can reveal whether and how much target-domain data will be required before any adaptation. We introduce FlowEval, a set of training-free metrics that use the flow-matching objective to probe an embodied foundation model with a set of demonstrations. FlowEval quantifies predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations to assess how well a pretrained model fits a target deployment. Across four embodied foundation model families: Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, FlowEval distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across real-world and simulated manipulation. Further, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we showed that FlowEval correlates with how success rate improves as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that FlowEval can serve as a lightweight, training-free diagnostic of how much model--deployment adaptation may be required.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of assessing pretrained model fit to a new deployment and estimating remaining adaptation-data needs.
Introduces training-free metrics based on the flow-matching objective and predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations.
Distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across four embodied foundation model families in real and simulated manipulation.
On 17 RoboCasa365 tasks, FlowEval correlates with success-rate gains from additional adaptation data for Pi-0.5 and GR00T.
Provides a lightweight diagnostic, though its demonstrated scope is manipulation deployments and the evaluated model families.

papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum reinforcement learning has been explored for robotic decision-making, but evaluations often emphasize task success, return, or convergence, leaving unresolved whether quantum circuit outputs influence constrained actions and remain traceable through robot execution. We present \texttt{Qubit-to-Motion}, an evidence-centered framework for support-constrained sequencing and simulated robotic placement. Four Pauli-$Z$ readouts provide the sole learned input to the actor and critic, while a support mask enforces admissible object selection. Each decision is recorded and linked via step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints to a sealed route, deterministic Cartesian and inverse-kinematics waypoints, prescribed joint motion, and MuJoCo contact replay. A frozen checkpoint is evaluated across five deterministic 30-object scene variants. All 150 placements satisfy support, containment, and settling criteria. A fixed-state zero-readout intervention changes $90.0\pm0.0\%$ of decisions, demonstrating dependence on the joint circuit representation. Mean macro travel is $34.537\pm0.206$~m, inference requires $8.60\pm1.27$~ms per route, and replay achieves $8.764\pm0.220~μ$m mean final position error with 0.356~mm maximum interpenetration. These results establish reproducible decision-to-contact traceability. The implementation is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Qubit-to-Motion-Quantum-Reinforcement-Learning-F7DC}{\textcolor{linkpink}{the anonymous repository}}.
bullets: Addresses whether quantum circuit outputs truly influence constrained actions and remain traceable during execution.
Uses four Pauli-Z readouts as the actor–critic input, with a support mask enforcing admissible object choices.
Links each decision to sealed routes, deterministic waypoints, joint motions, and MuJoCo contact replay using step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints.
Across five deterministic 30-object scenes, all 150 placements met support, containment, and settling criteria.
A zero-readout intervention changed 90.0% of decisions, while replay achieved 8.764 μm mean final-position error and 0.356 mm maximum interpenetration.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
bullets: Problem: Existing vision-language-action and world-action priors may not adequately capture humanoid robot motion structure.
Method: Kinematic Action Models pretrain directly on whole-body motion and condition generation on tasks, visual observations, and execution feedback.
Architecture: Kimodo-Policy combines a frozen text-to-motion backbone, lightweight ControlNet visual conditioning, hierarchical root-body-hand coordination, and motion-history-based action chunks.
Results: It reports 72.14% overall success on HumanoidArena, competitive SIMPLE performance, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks.
Scope: Results provide initial evidence that motion generation can complement foundation models for humanoid action learning.

papers.abstract: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.
bullets: Targets eight bimanual tasks scored on safe, efficient, coordinated execution against human demonstrations.
Uses AWR and RECAP to train a π₀.₅-based policy/value function on advantages from the official score.
Treats each rollout as a Thompson-sampling trial over roughly 20 inference parameters.
Adds generated full-reward demonstrations and recovery episodes from the policy’s failures to address exploration gaps.
The generic method reached 0.85 RDS in two days but remained far from convergence; the submitted system improved substantially.

papers.abstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
bullets: Zero-shot, end-to-end robot control gives coding agents capabilities beyond earlier VLA and WAM systems.
Digital threats such as indirect prompt injection can propagate from webpages or emails to physical robot behavior.
ArmedAgent evaluates robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios.
The benchmark is tested in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm across several frontier models and agent frameworks.
Results indicate substantial safety risks in current coding-agent robot-control systems.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/
bullets: Learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from depth, hand geometry, and demonstrations.
Predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, including occluded finger dynamics and scene changes.
Aligns policy queries with world-model predictions, then freezes the world model and transfers its dynamics into policy latents.
At deployment, the policy uses only RGB observations, language, and robot state.
Improves success from 49.4% to 60.5% on 11 DexJoCo tasks and achieves 58.3% versus 50.0% for the strongest baseline on three real-robot tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2 DexForesight architecture and query alignment. The spatial world model learns action-conditioned hand motion and visual changes from RGB, offline scene depth, hand geometry, and language. Demonstrated controls condition the world queries through the query adapter and are also supplied to both prediction experts. Queries from the frozen world model supervise policy queries, which condition the action expert.

Figure 1 Learning and transferring spatial foresight. Demonstrations spanning 60 tasks and five spatial categories train an action-conditioned spatial world model to predict visual dynamics and 3D hand flow. The learned spatial foresight is transferred into a low-level policy, enabling action generation without world-model execution or future decoding at deployment. DexForesight outperforms prior world-action models in both simulation and real-robot evaluations.

papers.abstract: We present a pipeline for transferring Awa Odori, a traditional Japanese festival dance, from monocular video to a commercial Unitree G1 EDU humanoid. The pipeline combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, reinforcement learning for motion tracking in simulation, and onboard deployment via ONNX. Training ran on a single RTX 5070 GPU. An eleven-version deployment ladder evaluated on hardware examines three interventions. We detect and repair silent corruption of deployment artifacts, model state-estimator drift during training, and edit the reference motion to support stable execution and a controlled ending. The final policies achieved three consecutive rope-free completions of a 43-second routine, a 46-second performance with automatic handoff, and a continuous 9.7-minute rope-free performance composed from the captured motion. In a live handover, a single remote request let the robot start from and return to the manufacturer's walking controller on stage, with a measured torque-free window of 45-140 ms. We report the training dynamics and hardware outcomes and discuss failure boundaries involving compliant flooring and occlusion in monocular capture.
bullets: Combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, simulated reinforcement-learning motion tracking, and ONNX onboard deployment.
An eleven-version hardware ladder addresses deployment-artifact corruption, state-estimator drift, and reference-motion edits for stable completion.
The robot completed the routine three consecutive times without a rope, performed a 46-second automatic-handoff demonstration, and sustained a 9.7-minute composed performance.
A live remote handoff returned control between the dance policy and the manufacturer's walking controller, with a measured torque-free window of 45–140 ms.
Failure boundaries include compliant flooring and occlusions in monocular video capture.
papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real humanoid dance learning from monocular human video via RL and retargeting; directly fits embodied robot learning and human-video transfer.
papers.title: From Festival Video to the Stage: A Sim-to-Real Ladder for Long-Horizon Expressive Whole-Body Dance on a Commercial Humanoid
papers.tldr: A sim-to-real pipeline transfers a 43-second Awa Odori dance from monocular video to a Unitree G1 EDU, enabling repeated and extended hardware performances with automatic controller handoff.

papers.abstract: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/harp.
bullets: Models human activity as part of the manipulation task rather than background variation.
Covers four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence, with paired human-present task variants.
Includes a demonstration-generation pipeline and evaluates VLA, imitation-learning, and heuristic policies.
Human presence challenges current policies; manipulation and recovery are the dominant failure sources, and success does not consistently imply better safety.
HARP-Bench demonstrations improve simulated performance and help on real-world human contribution, but transfer to interruption remains limited.

papers.abstract: Learning-based safety certification offers a promising route for verifying complex dynamical systems when explicit models are unavailable, but existing data-driven methods often scale poorly: they treat the system as a black box, rely on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, and consequently suffer from sample complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. This paper shows that a common structural property of dynamical systems--monotonicity--can be used to break this curse of dimensionality. We develop a data-driven framework for robust safety verification and safe controller synthesis for unknown monotone systems using only simulator queries. Our main theoretical result proves that, for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is completely characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. This structure reduces certificate verification over continuous state spaces to localized boundary checks over finitely many cells. To learn such certificates, we introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone neural architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions. We then propose a training and refinement algorithm that, upon successful termination, returns formally valid neural barrier certificates and, under mild partition assumptions, requires only $O(n)$ simulator queries. Across high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to $13{,}659$ states and traffic networks with $1{,}000$ states, our method certifies safety in regimes where prior approaches either do not converge or exceed memory limits. These results demonstrate that exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound.
bullets: Addresses the exponential sample complexity of black-box safety certification methods for complex systems.
Uses monotone inductive barrier certificates to characterize safety when unsafe sets are upper-closed.
Reduces continuous-space certificate verification to localized checks on finitely many boundary cells.
Introduces Max-Monotone Networks, which universally approximate monotone functions, plus a training and refinement procedure.
The method can require only O(n) simulator queries under mild partition assumptions and certifies systems with up to 13,659 states in reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), only a small fraction of an offline dataset can be labeled with rewards, and the central question is which samples should be labeled to learn a high-performing policy from the resulting partially labeled dataset. Prior work formalized this as a reward-selection problem by focusing on the selection stage while treating downstream policy learning as a black box, in a regime where queried rewards are not retained for reward-model training. We instead study the retained-label setting, where queried rewards can be stored and used to fit a reward model before policy learning. We bound the suboptimality of the learned policy in terms of two sources of error: one arising from offline RL on a fixed, offline dataset, and the other from uncertainty in the reward model. Since reward selection cannot change the offline dataset, the limited labeling budget must be used to strategically reduce reward uncertainty. Motivated by RLLF's observation that useful rewards tend to keep the agent on high-return trajectories, we introduce Successor-Guided Uncertainty REduction (SURE), a novel method that uses successor features to select rewards that are both uncertain and associated with states from which high-valued states are reachable. We formally derive SURE from a bound-induced design objective and characterize its exact one-step marginal gain. Empirically, SURE reaches near full-feedback performance with few reward labels across a variety of domains and offline-RL backbones, yielding an effective method for feedback-efficient reinforcement learning.
bullets: Addresses reward selection in retained-label reinforcement learning from limited feedback, where queried rewards train a reward model.
Decomposes policy suboptimality into offline-RL error and reward-model uncertainty.
Uses successor features to prioritize samples that are both uncertain and connected to reachable high-value states.
Derives SURE from a bound-based objective and characterizes its exact one-step marginal gain.
Empirically achieves near full-feedback performance across multiple domains and offline-RL backbones with few labels.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Ablation of the SURE score on representative maze rounds. Each row shows a different stage of selection. From left to right: acquired feedback locations, exact one-step gain ∆(s, a;Y[b], ρb), Reach-only score, Uncertainty-only score, and SURE score. Red boxes mark the highest-scoring cells under each criterion, and the green star denotes the goal region.

Figure 1: Illustrative retained-label reward-selection example in a navigation task. The agent must reach the goal while avoiding a central obstacle. With the initial reward labels, the policy learned from the current reward model takes a long detour, while a more direct path remains possible. Uncertainty-only selection chooses a state where the reward model is uncertain, but the selected state may be far from trajectories that lead to high return. Reachability-only selection chooses a state that can lead toward regions assigned high value by the current reward model, but this estimate can be misleading when the reward model is inaccurate. SURE combines both signals, selecting for labeling a reward that is uncertain under the current reward model and lies on a reachable path toward currently high-value states, yielding a better policy with fewer reward labels.

papers.abstract: Vision-based control policies, including vision-language-action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process. We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots. We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the high action-inference cost that slows vision-based robot execution.
Generates continuous target positions from discontinuous predictions using a tracking-control formulation.
Uses asynchronous inference and variance-based adaptive action skipping to improve execution speed.
Evaluated with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot.
Reports substantial speedups while maintaining high task success rates.

papers.abstract: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.
bullets: Introduces 3D full-object flow: dense trajectories over an object’s complete surface, including occluded regions, for rigid and deformable objects.
Provides a 1210-hour dataset combining real-world videos and physical simulations to supervise complete 3D object motion.
Develops a scalable annotation pipeline and quality metrics for recovering and evaluating full-object flow from observations.
Trains a world model that predicts full-object flow from an image and task description over reconstructed object geometry.
Reports reliable annotations, scalable flow prediction, and effective manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Object-centric full-object flow prediction framework. Given an initial RGB-D observation and task instruction, Qwen2.5-VL [39] extracts task-conditioned visual-language features, while a joint PointTransformer V3 [40] (PTv3) encodes reconstructed object and scene geometry. These features are fused into object tokens and refined by self-attention. The object queries attend to scene and language context through a cross-attention decoder, conditioned on noisy flow and time t, before a flow head predicts dense trajectories over the complete object surface.

Fig. 7: Visualization of real-world full-object flow annotations. Examples from AgiBot World [31], EPIC-KITCHENS [22], and Something-Something V2 [25]. Colored trajectories represent the estimated motion of points on the reconstructed complete object surface, with colors progressing from red at earlier timesteps to blue at later timesteps. Each example corresponds to a different manipulation clip processed by our automatic annotation pipeline.

Fig. 2: Automatic data annotation pipeline. Given an in-the-wild manipulation video, a VLM identifies the target object, describes the task, and segments the video into atomic action clips. For each clip, our pipeline extracts the target-object masks, reconstructs the complete object mesh and the point clouds, and aligns the mesh with the point clouds across frames to recover the object motion. The motion is propagated over the complete object surface to produce 3D full-object flow.

papers.abstract: In offline reinforcement learning, diffusion models fill two roles with complementary strengths. Typically guided by a critic, a diffusion policy is value-aware and favors high-return, behavior-supported actions, but it is short-sighted: it never lays out the states it intends to visit. A diffusion planner is far-sighted, synthesizing such a long-horizon trajectory, but it is only behavior-driven at execution, realizing each planned transition using only offline behavior.Each is strong exactly where the other is weak. We introduce DPDP to bring them together at the planner's execution step, where a planned transition becomes an action. Reading the planner's inverse-dynamics executor as a posterior over actions: the environment's transition likelihood relates an action to the planned next state, while the behavioral prior determines its weight under the offline data. Replacing this prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy preserves the planned transition likelihood and favors valuable actions that can serve the plan. We target the resulting clean-action distribution in two ways. A training-free sampler composes policy and inverse-dynamics scores at matched action noise levels and applies Langevin correction; this route uses a shared action noise schedule and an approximately common terminal prior. A preference objective instead amortizes the transfer into a single diffusion executor. Across D4RL, DPDP improves the planner it builds on, staying competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion and leading on long-horizon navigation.
bullets: Addresses the short-horizon nature of critic-guided diffusion policies and the behavior-only execution of diffusion planners.
Reinterprets the planner’s inverse-dynamics executor as an action posterior and replaces its behavioral prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy.
Provides a training-free score-composition sampler with Langevin correction and a preference-based objective for a single amortized executor.
Across D4RL, improves its underlying planner, remains competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion, and leads on long-horizon navigation.

figures.caption: Table 1: Long-horizon navigation on D4RL. Normalized return averaged over five seeds. The blue DQL+ (value policy) and DV+ (planner) are our reimplemented schedule-matched base models; the purple DPDP-inf and DPDP-ft are the two realizations of the transfer, each annotated with its gain over the base planner DV+. On both suites, the policy and the planner are individually comparable, and unifying them exceeds both on the suite average.

Table 2: Gym-MuJoCo locomotion on D4RL. Normalized return averaged over five seeds; columns as in Table 1. The blue DQL+ (value policy) and DV+ (planner) are our reimplemented schedulematched base models. These are dense-reward, reactive tasks with no goal to reach: every step is scored on the spot, so they reward immediate control rather than foresight. The value policy DQL+ therefore leads and planning is unnecessary, yet the transfer still improves the base planner DV+ on nearly every task, narrowing the gap to the reactive frontier.

papers.selection_reason: Combines a diffusion policy and a diffusion planner for offline RL, creating an interactive world model for long-horizon planning and robot control.
papers.title: DPDP: Diffusion Policy-Steered Diffusion Planner for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: DPDP combines long-horizon diffusion planning with value-aware diffusion policies to select high-value actions that still realize planned transitions in offline RL.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation with world action models (WAMs) relies on hand configuration and contact information, yet joint-state and whole-hand tactile observations may be partially or entirely missing. RGB images provide scene context and hand-object geometry but are insufficient to reliably recover these missing modalities. We further observe a correlation between hand state and tactile information. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BAT-WAM, a framework that bridges visual, joint-state, and tactile representations for WAMs. BAT-WAM learns separate codebooks and decoders for the tactile and action streams. An RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge connects the two streams for bidirectional learning, while visual information serves as continuous context. Under the HTBench evaluation protocol, BAT-WAM reduces the root mean squared error (RMSE) of tactile reconstruction by 34.73% under fully masked conditions and 38.84% under partially masked conditions, relative to an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint. For future tactile prediction conditioned on target-time RGB and historical actions, it reduces mean RMSE by 85.56% relative to OpenWAM with HandTouch. Real-robot experiments further show that BAT-WAM consistently outperforms related WAM baselines in dexterous manipulation. Generalization experiments on unseen objects and scenes also demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline models. These findings support joint modeling of visual context, hand state, and touch as a representation approach for multimodal WAMs.
bullets: Addresses missing or incomplete hand-state and whole-hand tactile observations, which RGB alone cannot reliably reconstruct.
Uses separate tactile and action codebooks/decoders connected by an RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge for bidirectional learning.
Reduces tactile reconstruction RMSE by 34.73% under fully masked and 38.84% under partially masked conditions versus an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint.
Improves future tactile prediction mean RMSE by 85.56% versus OpenWAM with HandTouch.
Outperforms related baselines in real-robot manipulation and generalizes better to unseen objects and scenes.

papers.abstract: The diversity of a distilled diffusion policy's outputs matters beyond how it impacts the policy's success rate. In particular, downstream applications like test-time search and policy improvement require exploration. Thus, we want to distill multi-modal demonstrators into diffusion policies which reproduce their conditional action distributions. Standard data collection for behavior cloning applies a sliding window to demonstration episodes, which pairs unique observation histories with actions. These datasets can be fit by a policy that is either multi-modal, or unimodal with high Lipschitz constant to capture a diversity of actions seen at nearby observation samples. Prior work finds that diffusion policies trained on sparse data learn the latter, memorizing one action per observation. We adapt vine sampling to behavior cloning data collection to resolve this ambiguity: at some states the demonstrator visits, query it $k$ times from exactly the same observation. On a synthetic task, we study how the number of actions per observation, $k$, affects the learned policy, and find that larger $k$ yields a policy that better matches the demonstrator's conditional distribution, including its multi-modality and diversity. On a 2D truck unloading task, vine sampling likewise leads to a policy closer to the demonstrator and substantially improves both best-of-$N$ and expert iteration performance.
bullets: Behavior-cloning datasets typically pair each observation history with one action, leaving action-distribution ambiguity unresolved.
The method queries the demonstrator multiple times from exactly the same observation, collecting $k$ actions via vine sampling.
On a synthetic task, increasing $k$ improves the learned policy’s match to the demonstrator’s conditional distribution, including multi-modality and diversity.
On a 2D truck-unloading task, vine sampling improves similarity to the demonstrator and boosts best-of-$N$ and expert-iteration performance.

papers.abstract: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io
bullets: Addresses VLA failures under shifts in viewpoint, background, object identity, and robot morphology.
Uses geometric calibration to warp source demonstrations toward the target setup.
Applies coarse-to-fine retrieval to select trajectories compatible with the base VLA.
Guides flow-matching inference without retraining the VLA or enlarging its context window.
Evaluated across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation; it outperforms related baselines in simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RAGu pipeline. (a) We filter real-world datasets using semantic keywords for broad task categories with similar kinematic profiles, such as pick-and-place via language instruction labels in the datasets. (b) Task-relevant objects in the target scene are identified using semantic bounding box detection to extract target waypoints W ′, allowing the source trajectories to be smoothly adapted despite visual shifts. (c) Retrieval candidates i are coarsely pruned to the top-N using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based matching. We then select the optimal trajectory i⋆ from pruned trajectories i ′ ∈ [N ] that minimizes the guidance gradient norm (||∇A0 Ci∗(Xt)||2), retrieving the demonstration best aligned with the VLA’s expected Cartesian trajectory Xt. (d) At test time, the chosen reference i⋆ defines an energy field (Lwarp ≈ ||Xt − i⋆||2), steering diffusion denoising for zero-shot adaptation.

Figure 4: Real-World Success Rates. Comparing RAGu against the base flow-matching policy (π0.5), retrieval-based in-context learning baseline (RICL) and a VLM-based goal steering baseline (Omniguide). We evaluate the models across 5 diverse manipulation tasks: Open Drawer, Open Cabinet, Close Microwave, Towel to Plate, & Wipe Table.

Figure 2: RAGu enables zero-shot adaptation across domains and embodiments. RAGu transfers manipulation knowledge across four settings: Real→Real, Real→Sim, Sim→Real with different morphologies with the base VLA’s weights completely frozen without any parameter update.

Scene correspondence errors (10.4%) are target-side: triangulation failure, cross-view inconsistency, or out-of-bounds projection of the detected waypoints. These percentages describe warping outcomes, not task success rates, which are reported in Table VII.

Figure 5: Execution rollout comparison on the Wipe Table task. RAGu continuously guides the end-effector along the table surface to execute a successful wipe. In contrast, Omniguide lifts the towel off the surface when transporting it toward the next discrete waypoint, failing to maintain contact with the table. RICL fails. (videos on website)

Figure 3: Real-to-Sim Cross-Embodiment Warping. Real-world DROID demonstrations are warped to provide structural priors in simulated environments. The background streams visualize the distribution of candidate trajectories retrieved via coarse-grained DTW filtering.

Values in brackets are 95% Wilson confidence intervals. Each ∆ column shows the absolute improvement over π0.5. Multi-stage retrieval is required both to cover large domain gaps and to meet real-time constraints. Shrinking the retrieval pool to a single trajectory reduces mean RoboLab success from 36.4% to 28.4%.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging. To address this, we propose DreamVLA, which uses generated motion trajectories to guide reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, converting them into reliable task execution trajectories. These trajectories train VLA models in simulation without new task-specific teleoperation data. Our central contribution is a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure: after a failed learner rollout, we restart the RL expert from a sampled learner state with the same reference suffix and aggregate successful corrective trajectories, addressing the distribution shift left by offline imitation. We evaluate picking from a platform, opening a drawer, pressing a button, and walking and picking from a platform, with ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated dataset scale. Project website: ember-center-berkeley.github.io/DreamVLA.
bullets: Targets the bottleneck of collecting extensive whole-body humanoid demonstrations and designing task-specific RL rewards.
Uses generated motion trajectories as references to guide reinforcement learning toward reliable task execution.
Introduces reference-conditioned DAgger distillation: failed learner rollouts are corrected by restarting an RL expert from sampled learner states with the same reference suffix.
Evaluates platform picking, drawer opening, button pressing, and walking-plus-picking tasks, with ablations on DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated-data scale.

Our DAgger loop restarts the privileged expert from a sampled state of a failed VLA rollout, follows the same reference suffix, and aggregates successful recoveries. The final VLA is evaluated on four simulated tasks. Motion and simulation reference images are adapted from DreamControl [3].

papers.abstract: Iterative neural policies usually spend the same computation on every decision, although the benefit of additional processing varies across states. We introduce Adaptive Internal Computation (AIC), an iterative policy that learns when to stop refining its latent representation and act. In AIC, we train action selection and stopping jointly, an expected-depth penalty values computation and intermediate value predictions provide auxiliary supervision. We show that when only some states benefit from further refinement, an ideal state-dependent allocator outperforms every state-independent stopping schedule at the same expected depth. With at most eight refinement steps per decision, AIC executes 3.3 steps on average across twelve benchmark tasks and lowers per-decision latency by 31--44% relative to a fixed eight-step policy on four control and robotics tasks. Its mean reward exceeds the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four. Ablating adaptive stopping and value supervision separately shows that stopping accounts for most of the reward gain on PickCube and AntMaze, where it also executes more refinement steps and that supervision accounts for most of it on RareEvent.
bullets: The work addresses the inefficiency of using the same number of iterative computations for every decision.
AIC jointly learns action selection and when to stop refining, using an expected-depth penalty and intermediate value predictions.
With up to eight refinement steps, it averages 3.3 steps across twelve benchmark tasks.
On four control and robotics tasks, AIC reduces per-decision latency by 31–44% versus a fixed eight-step policy.
AIC beats the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four; stopping and value supervision contribute differently across tasks.

papers.tldr: Adaptive Internal Computation lets reinforcement-learning policies spend more reasoning on difficult states and less on easy ones, reducing latency while often preserving or improving reward.

papers.abstract: Variable impedance control enhances the interaction capability of robot manipulators by adapting impedance parameters online. However, time-varying impedance parameters may inject energy into the system and violate passivity, particularly when tasks demand rapid stiffness changes. Existing methods address this by increasing damping or limiting the stiffness profile, which often degrades the dynamic response. In this work, we propose a quadratic programming-based parameter optimization framework that guarantees passivity by modulating the desired inertia to compensate for energy injected by stiffness variations, while preserving a critically damped system. For the case of diagonal impedance matrices, we optimize the rates of change of inertia and stiffness subject to a passivity constraint formulated as a convex quadratic program. We extend the framework to compliance control, where the desired inertia is coupled to the robot's configuration-dependent inertia matrix. We use an eigendecomposition based on Cholesky factorization to optimize the spectral weights while maintaining passivity. Experiments on the Kinova Gen3 7-degree-of-freedom manipulator validate both methods with human interaction perturbations. Comparisons with an energy tank approach and a nonpassivity-based method demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves less conservative stiffness tracking without requiring an energy reservoir or damping overhead.
bullets: Addresses energy injection and passivity violations caused by rapidly changing impedance parameters.
Optimizes inertia and stiffness change rates under a convex passivity constraint while maintaining critical damping.
Extends the approach to compliance control by optimizing spectral weights coupled to configuration-dependent robot inertia.
Validated on a Kinova Gen3 7-DoF manipulator during human interaction perturbations.
Achieves less conservative stiffness tracking than energy-tank and nonpassivity-based methods without an energy reservoir or added damping overhead.

papers.abstract: Search allows a robotic policy to evaluate candidate futures before committing to an action. Motivated by test-time planning for vision-language action (VLA) models, we study selective search over action chunks in PushT using a frozen Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy. Beam search generates perturbed alternatives around the policy prediction and scores them through rollouts from cloned simulator states. Across 50 evaluation episodes, beam search raises task success from 0% to 18% and increases average cumulative reward from 39.44 to 103.2. We introduce One Step Ahead (OSA), a gate that simulates the nominal policy chunk and invokes full search only when its predicted coverage drop exceeds a threshold. In the reported ablations, OSA preserves or improves success while reducing runtime by approximately 3x relative to full beam search. Ablations over tree depth, branching factor, beam width, and replanning frequency show that larger search budgets do not consistently improve performance. The results support selective test-time search for action-chunking policies; evaluation on language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots remains future work.
bullets: Beam search evaluates perturbed action-chunk candidates using rollouts from cloned simulator states.
Across 50 episodes, success increases from 0% to 18%, and average cumulative reward rises from 39.44 to 103.2.
One Step Ahead (OSA) triggers full search only when the nominal policy predicts a coverage drop.
Search-budget ablations show that larger tree depth, branching, beam width, or replanning frequency do not consistently help.
The study is limited to simulated PushT; language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots are not evaluated.

papers.abstract: Learning whole-body musculoskeletal control from human motion is important for developing human-like robots, assistive devices, and rehabilitation systems. This task presents two main challenges, namely reference trajectories that are kinematically plausible but difficult to reproduce through muscle-driven dynamics, and a highly redundant 700-dimensional action space in which unstructured exploration can easily disrupt the target motion. In this paper, we propose a motion-to-policy pipeline that exploits muscle redundancy in two complementary stages. First, muscle-aware retargeting (MAR) performs bounded adaptation of kinematic trajectories subject to hard semantic, anatomical, and contact constraints. We motivate the constraint bounds by analyzing how reference-trajectory artifacts affect muscle-driven tracking. Second, null-space exploration (NSE) estimates a one-control-frame mapping from muscle excitations to generalized forces and injects bounded, anatomically structured perturbations along its null space into the actions of a value-guided flow policy. On a 24-clip motion-capture benchmark, MAR and NSE together solve every reference, reach the full horizon with half the samples of the baseline pipeline, and lower joint-center error by 44% without late collapse. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end pipeline that transforms monocular video into a trained whole-body imitation policy controlling 700 muscles.
bullets: Addresses kinematically plausible references that are difficult to reproduce with muscle-driven dynamics and exploration in a 700-dimensional action space.
Muscle-aware retargeting adapts trajectories within semantic, anatomical, and contact constraints.
Null-space exploration adds bounded, anatomically structured perturbations that preserve generalized forces while guiding policy learning.
On 24 motion-capture clips, the combined method solved every reference, used half the baseline samples, and reduced joint-center error by 44%.
Scope: whole-body musculoskeletal control with 700 muscles; the abstract does not report broader settings beyond this benchmark.

papers.abstract: Safe offline reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to learn policies that maximize return while satisfying safety constraints, using a static dataset. To characterize state-wise safety, reachability analysis identifies the feasible region, defined as the set of states from which constraints can be satisfied at every future step. Policies are commonly extracted from learned value functions with advantage-weighted regression (AWR). However, AWR relies on exponentiated weights that amplify value estimation errors, whereas behavior-regularized policy gradient methods directly utilize the action gradient of the value function and often make more effective use of learned critics. We propose Feasibility-Optimized Conditional Actor Learning (FOCAL), a method that incorporates behavior-regularized policy gradients into a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) actor. FOCAL optimizes this policy using a first-order objective partitioned by feasibility, updating the actor to increase return on transitions estimated to be feasible and to reduce constraint violations on transitions estimated to be infeasible. During inference, FOCAL dynamically adjusts the scale of the latent prior according to the estimated feasibility of the state to adjust the conservatism of action sampling. Theoretically, we show that for AWR, the policy update variance depends exponentially on the advantage error, whereas for FOCAL it scales linearly with the variance of the value estimation error. Across the DSRL benchmark, FOCAL satisfies the constraints on all evaluated tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns compared to baselines.
bullets: Targets offline policy learning under state-wise safety constraints using a static dataset.
Uses behavior-regularized policy gradients in a CVAE actor instead of AWR’s error-sensitive exponentiated weights.
Partitions learning by estimated feasibility: improves return in feasible regions and reduces violations in infeasible regions.
Adjusts latent-prior scale during inference to control action-sampling conservatism based on state feasibility.
Provides a variance analysis and satisfies constraints on all evaluated DSRL benchmark tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns.

papers.abstract: This paper presents enhancements to the DINOBot framework for imitation learning of object-object interactions. We introduce two key contributions aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of alignment in imitation-based robotic tasks. First, we integrate RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) for outlier rejection during the alignment phase, effectively mitigating the impact of noisy depth data and spurious feature matches. This improves robustness when transferring demonstrations to real-world applications. Second, we refine the semantic correspondence process by focusing on task-relevant interaction regions, ensuring that the learned representation prioritizes critical object features that influence successful manipulation. We evaluated our approach in a range of real-world manipulation tasks, including picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring, using a robotic system. The experimental results demonstrate an overall improvement of 13.8% in task success rates compared to the baseline, along with faster convergence in the alignment process. These results highlight the effectiveness of our enhancements in improving precision and efficiency for object-object interaction imitation in robotics.
bullets: Targets noisy depth data, spurious feature matches, and irrelevant object regions in imitation-based manipulation.
Uses RANSAC to reject alignment outliers and improve robustness during demonstration transfer.
Prioritizes semantic correspondences in task-relevant interaction regions.
Evaluated on real-world picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring tasks.
Reports a 13.8% overall task-success improvement over the baseline and faster alignment convergence.

papers.abstract: Policies for dexterous manipulation depend on design choices made before training: which sensors enter the observation, where they are placed, and how their readings are arranged for the encoder. These choices are rarely examined. For tactile sensing, simulation studies place taxels uniformly over the hand, and this placement has become a default without being tested. We test this default under a single controlled protocol. The protocol holds the teacher, the training procedure, and the candidate taxels fixed and varies only the sensor configuration and the representation. We evaluate it on in-palm rotation and grasping with three robot hands. A small set of taxels selected from contact statistics matches a far larger uniform set. Taxels at rarely contacted sites are equivalent to no tactile input. With all candidate taxels, their layout in the input tensor does not affect performance, even for a convolutional encoder. Uniform placement therefore overestimates the number of taxels a task requires. We distill these results into lessons for designing tactile policies and into a minimal set of design choices that a tactile policy study should report.
bullets: Uniform taxel placement is tested under a controlled protocol rather than assumed effective.
A small set of taxels chosen from contact statistics matches the performance of a much larger uniform set.
Taxels in rarely contacted locations perform like providing no tactile input.
With all candidate taxels, arranging them in the input tensor does not affect performance, including with convolutional encoders.
Results from in-palm rotation and grasping across three robot hands motivate reporting a minimal set of tactile-policy design choices.

papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.
bullets: Meta-RL typically needs diverse training environments and reward functions, while BFMs enable zero-shot adaptation from reward-free data.
The work identifies four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and mixed reward supervision.
MetaBFM combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning during training.
At test time, it balances exploration, exploitation, and zero-shot reward inference.
It matches supervised meta-RL performance in-distribution while generalizing to reward functions absent from training.

papers.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.
bullets: Addresses off-policy evaluation for hierarchical policies composed of temporally extended options.
Avoids requiring annotations identifying which option generated each action in the logged data.
Introduces an intra-option fitted Q-evaluation method based on value estimation over state-option pairs.
Develops two continuous-action variants and evaluates them on AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation.
Eliminates the bias of naive FQE and achieves substantially lower mean squared error than option-level importance sampling in the reported tasks.

papers.abstract: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.
bullets: Builds an object-centric task graph from instructions and a skill library, then uses execution records to identify capability gaps.
Improves task organization, hand-offs, recovery routes, and repeatedly failing perception, motion, manipulation, or verification skills.
Adopts revisions only after full-task evaluation and paired comparisons, enabling validated local changes to accumulate.
On ten RoboDojo development tasks, average success increased from 30.0% to 86.2%; across eight real-world tasks, it succeeded in 62 of 80 real-robot trials.

papers.abstract: Learned manipulation policies often rely on wrist-mounted cameras for close-range visual feedback that complements external views of the workspace. However, contact-rich manipulation requires establishing and maintaining contacts that can remain hidden even from wrist cameras. Tactile sensors mounted on fingers can reliably and directly measure contact, without needing visual access. In this work, we show that this feedback enables policies to recover the performance advantage of wrist cameras using scene and egocentric vision together with touch. Our approach incorporates two low-cost tactile arrays into a visuotactile ACT policy, without wrist images during training or deployment. We evaluate six real-world task families spanning placement, insertion, occluded retrieval, and sustained-contact tool use. On three contact-rich tasks, we independently vary wrist-camera and tactile availability while keeping the demonstrations, policy architecture, and optimization settings fixed. Adding wrist cameras improves success by 18.3-28.3 percentage points over vision without wrist images. Adding tactile sensing instead improves success by 31.7-60.0 percentage points and yields higher observed success than vision-only policies with wrist cameras on all three tasks, with significant advantages on two under Holm-corrected tests. These results support finger-mounted tactile sensing as an effective alternative to wrist cameras in the evaluated contact-rich settings.
bullets: Wrist cameras may still fail to observe contacts hidden by objects or the robot hand.

Evaluation covers six real-world task families, including placement, insertion, occluded retrieval, and sustained-contact tool use.

The findings are scoped to the evaluated real-world contact-rich settings.

papers.abstract: Most robotic handwriting rigidly mounts the pen and reduces writing to trajectory tracking. A freely held pen instead couples grasp stability, tip motion, and contact force. We present Grip, Trace, Write, a force-aware simulation environment and learning framework for high-DoF handwriting. A two-branch actor separates pen retention from arm-wrist writing while preserving their closed-loop coupling. Training learns a grasp controller, initializes writing from inverse-kinematics demonstrations by behavior cloning, and improves writing through reinforcement learning with rewards on ink, force, time, and retention. Across diverse tasks, the policy improves completion, precision, force regulation, and efficiency over behavior cloning and inverse kinematics, and generalizes without fine-tuning to unseen English and Chinese content. These results establish force-aware handwriting as a testbed for dexterous tool use.
bullets: Addresses the coupled challenges of grasp stability, pen-tip motion, and contact force in robotic handwriting.
Uses a force-aware simulation environment with separate but closed-loop coupled branches for pen retention and arm-wrist writing.
Combines grasp control, inverse-kinematics demonstrations with behavior cloning, and reinforcement learning guided by ink, force, time, and retention rewards.
Outperforms behavior cloning and inverse kinematics across completion, precision, force regulation, and efficiency metrics.
Generalizes without fine-tuning to unseen English and Chinese writing content; positioned as a testbed for dexterous tool use.

papers.abstract: In this work, we train agents to act under uncertainty according to specified, belief-dependent rules. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can in theory train agents to follow rules if encoded into well-designed rewards, but in practice, RL fails to perfectly optimize these rewards, leading to ineffective or noncompliant agent behavior. Belief-space planners by construction produce behavior in line with developer specification, but require hand-programming online planners and belief-state estimators, adding significant engineering complexity at scale. We combine the two: we plan offline to generate a dataset of sample trajectories and then distill the plans into a policy that acts on raw observations. We propose two changes to planner distillation that address problems specific to history-based policies: Dual Averaging, a loss that combines per-timestep predictive loss and average loss on task changes, and $ρ$-Optimal Reinforcement, a feedback mechanism that reinforces the policy's own successful rollouts when these are near-optimal. We provide a sufficient condition under which static search problems with noiseless observation models is complete, and show that maximum-likelihood-observation planning implies this condition in static search with continuous beliefs. We create a challenging new domain, Scavenger, where an agent needs to gain information in order to succeed. We evaluate our distilled policy in two versions of Scavenger, one where information is provided visually and one where it is provided as a command in natural language. In either case, the learned policy attains a success rate above 90% in Scavenger, compared with at most 5% for RL. We also find that distilled planners transfer with greater than 60% success to following unseen and intentionally vague commands and greater than 75% success to following floorplans larger than those seen in training.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of making RL agents reliably comply with specified, belief-dependent behavior and the engineering cost of hand-coded belief-space planners.
Distills offline belief-space task-and-motion-planning trajectories into a history-based policy operating on raw observations.
Introduces Dual Averaging for combining timestep and task-change losses, plus ρ-Optimal Reinforcement to reinforce near-optimal successful rollouts.
In the new Scavenger domain, the distilled policy exceeds 90% success in both visual- and language-guided settings, versus at most 5% for RL.
Transfers to unseen vague commands with over 60% success and larger-than-training floorplans with over 75% success.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: An overview of the Scavenger domain. (b) The robot must search among possible locations for a hint, either represented visually or as a command in natural language. (c) It succeeds when it approaches the marker hinted at, and then takes a relevant “guess” action when it is sufficiently close to that marker.
