papers.abstract: We present RevoSim, a scalable and high-fidelity multimodal tactile simulator for the BrainCo Revo3 hand that jointly models 285 piezoresistive taxels and five visuotactile fingertips. RevoSim efficiently generates synchronized pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement observations; on a single RTX 5090, its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration supports up to 4,096 parallel environments. We train in-hand manipulation and grasping policies entirely in simulation, establishing a foundation for future sim-to-real transfer. Project page: https://braincotech.github.io/RevoSim-web/.
authors: Ke Zhang, Lixin Xu, Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Dong, Jie Tan, Lianghu Shao, Xianpeng Wang, Chuanyu Li, Renjing Xu
bullets: Models 285 piezoresistive taxels and five visuotactile fingertips.
Generates synchronized pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement data.
Supports up to 4,096 parallel environments on a single RTX 5090 in its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration.
Enables fully simulation-trained in-hand manipulation and grasping policies.
Establishes a foundation for future sim-to-real transfer; real-world transfer is not demonstrated in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.
bullets: Fixed PPO clipping does not distinguish harmful extreme ratios from large but tolerable policy changes.
OPO sorts minibatch importance ratios and identifies those most likely to affect the update.
It assigns selected ratios adaptive, sample-wise clipping radii based on a prescribed tail profile.
The method retains a first-order objective and requires only minibatch sorting plus a modified policy loss.
Experiments on MuJoCo and Atari show strong performance relative to established baselines.

Figure 1: Overview of OPO. A minibatch of importance ratios is ordered, and the empirical tails are assigned teacher targets induced by a prescribed generalized Pareto tail profile. This yields adaptive sample-wise proximal targets, thereby replacing scalar clipping with order-based tail control. In contrast, PPO imposes the same scalar clipping boundary across ratios.

Figure 4: Overview of the OPO algorithm. OPO generates the target r⋆t from the GPD teacher profile, then assigns each target to the corresponding order statistic: the t-th ordered ratio r(t) is assigned the corresponding r⋆t . This process encourages the empirical tail ratios to follow the prescribed shape.

papers.tldr: Ordered Policy Optimization improves PPO by adaptively clipping the most extreme importance ratios in each minibatch instead of applying one fixed range to every sample.

papers.abstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.
authors: Hongkun Yu, Francisco M. L\'opez, Francisco Cruz
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting human object-manipulation videos into motion cues for robots.
Combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand–object association and contact localization.
Supports count-aware contact detection in untrimmed videos and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers.
Improves contact-count accuracy and localization distance over an adapted VRB2 baseline on a 30-task benchmark, with further gains in RGB-D rollouts.
Produces more feasible trajectories and successful tasks than adapted baselines in six robot evaluation sequences; evaluation focuses on single-hand scenes and selected multi-hand scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HOC2R inference architecture. Shared outputs comprise contact-region proposal boxes, per-box touch scores, an enclosing-region contact-count prediction, and a whole-image contact-likelihood heatmap. Count-aware automation reranks heatmap candidates using touch scores and emits the predicted number of points. Fixed-two localization filters candidates through proposal boxes, progressively examines more heatmap maxima until two eligible candidates are found, applies touch reranking, and returns two points for a known active contact segment. Their midpoint is lifted with aligned depth and camera calibration into a robot-base trajectory.

Figure 1: HOC2R training architecture. The proposal head uses frozen DINOv3 features and patch labels to predict candidate contact-region boxes. The proposalbox touch head uses each proposal’s SAM feature crop and box label to predict whether the box contains contact. The enclosing-region count head uses the SAM feature crop covering the top-ten proposal boxes and frame-level labels to predict contact presence and count. The whole-image heatmap head uses SAM features and Gaussian targets to predict pixel-wise contact likelihood.
Figure 6: In-domain contact-count confusion over 210 held-out frames. Rows show ground truth, and columns show predictions.

Figure 4: Comparison on seven external RGB-D rollouts. In (a), points show aggregate F1@10, and thin bars show task-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. In (b), points show mean localization distance, thin bars show its 95% confidence interval, and wide stems span the median-to-90th-percentile error. Shorter stems indicate more consistent localization.

Figure 5: External multi-hand diagnostics. VRB2 associates its prediction with the resting hand. EgoHOS responds to the resting hand and the clothing sleeve beside the manipulating arm, and its point adapter retains these unrelated boundaries. In contrast, HOC2R proposal boxes focus on the manipulating hand, and the fixed-two decoder localizes the pencil contact. The assignment errors are 156.11 px for VRB2, 126.00 px for EgoHOS-Point, and 17.81 px for HOC2R.

Figure 3: Robot evaluation workflow illustrated on the pen-motion demonstration. HOC2R extracts two image contacts (a), whose midpoint forms a 2D trajectory (b). Aligned depth and camera calibration map the trajectory into the robot base frame (c). Shared filtering and waypoint resampling are applied before inversekinematics execution (d).

papers.selection_reason: Extracts hand-object contact trajectories from human videos for robot motion transfer, fitting human-video learning and manipulation.
papers.title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
papers.tldr: HOC2R extracts robot-usable hand–object contact trajectories from human videos using frozen vision features and learned localization heads, improving contact detection and robot task success in evaluated scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $\pi_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.
authors: Jiachen Tao, Gengyu Zhang, Haoxuan Wang, Bing Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses skill retention and phase-dependent skill composition in vision-language-action policies.
Finds that per-skill low-rank updates occupy a distinguishable low-dimensional parameter subspace.
Stores each skill as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter, augmented with trainable residuals.
Uses a VLM-conditioned per-chunk router supervised by an action-derived oracle to select primitives based on task progress.
On RoboCasa365, reports 56.43% atomic-skill and 20.00% composite success, versus 17.86% and 17.50% for a two-stage π₀.₅-LoRA baseline; also validates on a real AgileX PIPER robot.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the PRISM framework. (1) Skill primitive learning (§4): each atomic skill is fitted with its own rank-r action-expert LoRA (Bi, Ai), yielding a primitive bank of disjoint slots, frozen after atomic training. (2) Router learning from composite demonstrations: a prefixconditioned router rθ reads the VLM prefix ht and emits a per-chunk mixture α(t) over the bank, supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic action-derived oracle A. (3) Chunk-wise routed execution (inference): each LoRA-injected action-expert layer applies the routed mixture at the activation level (Eq. 5), producing an action chunk.

Figure 1: Within-skill LoRAs concentrate; across-skill LoRAs spread across N . (a) Cumulative singular energy ρ≤k vs k/T : within-PP saturates at the first component, while cross-skill rises along the uniform null ρ≤k=k/T (dashed). (b) Top-1 energy ρ1: 0.948 vs 0.265. (c) PR/T (1.0=maximal spread, 1/T=collapse): 0.37 vs 0.93. (d) Effective rank/T : 0.42 vs 0.97. Across all metrics, withinskill LoRAs are more concentrated than across-skill LoRAs.

Figure 3: Per-skill update tensors span an effectively N -dim subspace. Normalized spectra overlap across N=6 and N=11; PR=5.59 at N=6 and PR=10.78 at N=11.

Figure 6: Real-robot training data: fisheye observations. Representative frames from the wristmounted fisheye RGB stream used for teleoperated training, sampled left-to-right along each trajectory. Top: Cup→Table (Atomic 1) – the red cup is lifted off the doll and placed on the table. Middle: Doll→Plate (Atomic 2) – the doll is picked up and placed on the patterned plate. Bottom: the Composite chains the two atomic skills in sequence.

A successful inference on the Cup→Table→Doll→Plate composite task: the robot first lifts the cup off the doll (t0–t4), then picks up the doll and places it on the plate (t5–t9). The router supplies a per-chunk mixture α(t) over the bank that switches from the Cup→Table primitive to the Doll→ Plate primitive mid-trajectory.

papers.title: PRISM: Primitive Routing via In-context Skill Mixing for Retentive VLA Adaptation
papers.tldr: PRISM preserves reusable VLA skills as frozen low-rank primitives and routes among them in context to execute long-horizon composite tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.
authors: Ramy ElMallah, Marc Bishara, Hyegang Kim, Yuxi Zhang, Chongyu Zhu, Chi-Guhn Lee
bullets: Simulates robots, cameras, IoT devices, wearables, residents, visitors, faulty sensors, and time-evolving hazards in Isaac Sim.
Includes 20 tasks across five household-assistance and safety families, where identical alerts may have different causes.
Scores outcomes and action sequences using temporal-logic checks and predefined action costs.
Across six VLMs, the best family-balanced score is 61.9%; models over-reacted, with prohibited interventions occurring more than twice as often as missed required interventions.
Designed as an extensible platform for studying coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy–safety trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under "not X" and "X". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.
bullets: On LIBERO-Goal, negated instructions did not change the executed task: the forbidden task occurred in 79% of negated rollouts, versus 78% completion for plain tasks.
A goal probe produced similar representations for “not X” and “X,” indicating weak encoding of negation in the executed goal.
The first action depends mainly on instruction tokens before layer 12 and the final prompt token from layer 16 onward.
Steering instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12/18 rollouts; later prefill interventions failed, while patching every decoded action token at layer 24 redirected 15/18.
Layer-32 goal read-outs detected non-compliance during changing instructions, supporting external enforcement and monitoring of safety constraints.

papers.abstract: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
authors: Onur Beker, Andreas Ren\'e Geist, Georg Martius
bullets: Addresses the throughput bottleneck caused by replacing coarse collision primitives with precise mesh-mesh collisions.
Introduces new broadphase and narrowphase collision-detection routines, plus contact-dynamics computation.
Designed for massively parallelized robotics workloads, including reinforcement learning and trajectory optimization.
Experiments show physical faithfulness comparable to established simulators and approximately an order-of-magnitude higher throughput for detailed mesh-mesh collisions.
Source code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.title: Lodos: A Lightweight Simulator Designed for Contact-Rich Interactions with Detailed Meshes
papers.tldr: Lodos is a lightweight rigid-body simulator optimized for fast, physically faithful contact-rich simulation with detailed mesh-mesh collisions.

papers.abstract: Lodos-v2 is a GPU-based simulation framework for massively parallel rigid-body dynamics with contact. It is specifically designed to achieve high throughput in scenes involving collisions among large numbers of detailed meshes. Its predecessor, Lodos-v1, had two main limitations. First, it solved the standard convex relaxation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, thereby inheriting well-known physical artifacts, including lift-off and artificial compliance in the normal direction, as well as creep in the tangential direction. Second, its contact-group reparameterization scheme, which rescales spring-damper forces using a single factor per collision pair, could not be integrated with other constraints required by a full-fledged simulator, such as joint limits and welds. Lodos-v2 addresses both limitations through two main contributions. First, it introduces an efficient algorithm for solving the exact frictional contact problem by sequentially solving a cascade of convex relaxations in primal form within an outer proximal minimization loop. Second, it extends the contact-group reparameterization scheme of Lodos-v1 to the primal formulation of cone-complementarity-based contact dynamics, enabling its integration with the other constraints of a full-fledged simulator. Experiments demonstrate that these contributions result in throughput improvements over established rigid-body simulation frameworks. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
authors: Onur Beker, Andreas Ren\'e Geist, Georg Martius
bullets: Targets high-throughput GPU simulation of collisions among large numbers of detailed meshes.
Solves the exact frictional contact problem via a cascade of primal convex relaxations inside an outer proximal minimization loop.
Extends contact-group reparameterization to support integration with constraints such as joint limits and welds.
Addresses lift-off, artificial normal compliance, and tangential creep inherited from Lodos-v1’s convex relaxation.
Experiments report throughput improvements over established rigid-body simulation frameworks; source code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator. This is why we introduce \method{}, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile. To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples. Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.
bullets: Addresses the need for motion-capture systems or calibrated state estimators in direct robot locomotion learning.
Rewards following a commanded acceleration profile, using measurements available from the onboard IMU.
Combines off-policy XQC reinforcement learning with high-gain joint control and left-right symmetry augmentation.
In simulation, learns walking on Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples.
The added control and augmentation components reduce training falls by 81%; without them, learning takes over an hour.

papers.abstract: Geometric assembly requires fine spatiotemporal coordination to place parts without causing collisions or deadlocks under tight clearances. To address this, we present an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that treats each part as an agent and learns a shared policy for continuous assembly control. A graph neural network represents the pieces, their target poses, and their spatial relationships, and predicts translational and angular velocities for each component. Per-agent proximal policy optimization with a centralized graph critic directly learns motion and temporal coordination within a single feedback policy. We study this formulation through planar Tangram assembly, where pieces must slide and rotate into a given configuration while remaining on the assembly surface. Procedural generation of target configurations and randomized initial arrangements support training and evaluation across diverse assembly problems. Our experiments isolate the roles of relational structure and multi-agent optimization, and compare learned control with sampling-based planning. We demonstrate concurrent assembly in simulation and transfer the policy to sequential execution on a real robot, as our object-centric formulation decouples learned assembly coordination from low-level physical control. Project page: https://tangrambench.org/
authors: Paul Knau{\ss}t, Kay Pompetzki, Nico Bohlinger, Niklas Funk, Cristiana de Farias, Rolf Findeisen, Jan Peters
bullets: Models each assembly piece as an agent with a shared policy for continuous translation and rotation.
Uses a graph neural network to encode pieces, target poses, and spatial relationships.
Combines per-agent PPO with a centralized graph critic to learn motion and temporal coordination.
Evaluates planar Tangram assembly across procedurally generated targets and randomized starting arrangements.
Demonstrates concurrent simulated assembly and transfer to sequential execution on a real robot; comparisons include sampling-based planning.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Policy ablations. On the top row, we show the architecture ablation on TangramBench-Trio. papers.abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approaches train reinforcement learning (RL) agents on diverse curricula that may evolve with their capabilities. While prior work has largely focused on how these curricula are constructed, we study whether their students remain trainable under the resulting distributions. Across multiple UED mechanisms, environment complexities, and extended training horizons, we identify recurring learner-side pathologies, including parameter growth, degraded value--outcome ordering, and loss of representational diversity, that accompany stagnation and performance degradation. These findings connect limitations in UED to optimization failures previously identified in conventional deep RL, while showing how adaptive curricula couple the learner's optimization state to its future training distribution. Controlled interventions show that mitigating selected pathologies improves learning. Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or increasing environment interaction. Our results establish learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED. Effective curricula require students that remain capable of learning from the distributions they produce.
authors: Johan Obando-Ceron, Walter Mayor, Michael Dennis, Aaron Courville, Pablo Samuel Castro
bullets: Across multiple UED mechanisms and environment complexities, learner pathologies recur during stagnation and performance decline.
Observed issues include parameter growth, degraded value–outcome ordering, and reduced representational diversity.
Adaptive curricula couple the learner’s optimization state to the distributions it encounters in the future.
Targeted interventions that mitigate selected pathologies improve learning, long-horizon performance, and zero-shot generalization.
The findings support learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture. We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress. By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training. VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation. On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%. Project page with code, data and videos: https://ai4ce.github.io/VICTR/
authors: Luca Macesanu, Tianluo Zhang, Aditya Patil, Archit Sharma, Kevin Angers, Christopher M. Clark, Chen Feng, Juexiao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting demonstrations that match the robot’s current execution stage during in-context learning.
Introduces an In-Context Value Function Estimator that estimates task-relative progress from a reference video, instruction, and current observation.
Uses progress-aligned demonstration chunks with a post-trained π₀.₅ policy for in-context action generation.
On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, success rises from 6.2% to 23.8%, while task progress increases from 28.9% to 55.5%.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are expected to take over strenuous material handling in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, where operating existing wheeled carts would let them move heavy loads without modifying the workplace. However, humanoid cart pushing remains challenging because the bimanual grasp closes a force-coupled loop in which the contact wrenches that drive the cart also disturb the robot's balance, and payload changes alter the coupled dynamics. We propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that regulates cart velocity through two-stage reinforcement learning. A locomotion prior is first trained under varied hand loads and upper-body postures to provide balance support. A force latent and a state latent are then inferred from onboard observations, without external force sensors, and fed to a residual policy that coordinates bounded arm, waist, and leg adjustments with base-velocity commands. Multi-objective rewards penalize bimanual internal opposition, grasp slip, and actuator saturation, encouraging the policy to apply contact force on demand without human demonstrations. Sim-to-sim experiments show that ForPC reduces cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% relative to a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only) and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% on the multi-bend route. Trained solely in simulation, the policy also transfers to a physical Unitree G1 without real-world training or fine-tuning and, with no payload-specific adjustment, pushes a cart carrying up to 30 kg at 0.5 m/s. These results suggest that humanoid robots could eventually replace humans for efficient material handling in daily life.

Trains a locomotion prior, then a residual policy using inferred force and state latents from onboard observations without external force sensors.
Coordinates arm, waist, leg, and base-velocity commands while discouraging internal force opposition, grasp slip, and actuator saturation.
In simulation, reduces cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% versus locomotion-only control.
Transfers from simulation to a physical Unitree G1, pushing carts up to 30 kg at 0.5 m/s without real-world training or payload-specific adjustment.

papers.abstract: A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint that was absent from its demonstrations, such as avoiding an obstacle it has never seen. Retraining for every new constraint is impractical, so the constraint must be enforced at inference time. Enforcing it must not discard what the policy learned: an action the policy would rarely sample may avoid the obstacle yet fail the task. We therefore want actions that are both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy. Gradient guidance, the most common approach, steers noisy states, so it must evaluate its cost on the policy's running estimate of the clean action; when the policy is uncertain between passing left or right of an obstacle, this estimate is their average and can pass straight through it. We instead build on rejection and projection. Rejection redraws actions until one is safe: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare. Projection moves an action to the nearest safe one: it is efficient, but the result need not be plausible. Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection's efficiency and rejection's plausibility. CS-Pi, our draw-project-renoise sampler, projects each draw to the nearest safe action, adds noise back scaled to how far the projection moved it, and re-runs the unmodified policy until a draw is safe. Replacing only the projection step extends CS-Pi to continuous costs. Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, an orientation preference, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi reaches 81% safe success on the shelf and 55% on hardware, against 55% and 40% for projection, while staying plausible.
authors: Soumojit Bhattacharya, Oliver Kroemer, Shubham Tulsiani
bullets: Addresses the conflict between safe actions and actions likely under the learned policy.
Combines rejection and projection through draw-project-renoise sampling.
Projects each draw to safety, restores noise based on projection distance, and reruns the unchanged policy until safe.
Extends to continuous costs by replacing the projection step.
Evaluated in simulations and zero-shot hardware deployment, achieving higher reported safe success than projection while remaining plausible.

papers.abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark

bullets: Contains approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 Halifax buildings across four seasons, day/night conditions, and varied weather.

Benchmarks point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer models.
Finds semantic segmentation difficult under class imbalance, while repetitive-structure instance separation and geometry-based functional reasoning are harder.

papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
authors: Zuhao Liu, Melih Darcan, Zhengdi Yu, Riza Alp Guler, Tolga Birdal
bullets: Addresses the need for hand-pose priors that account for the interacted object, beyond unconditional pose models.

Uses Riemannian geometry to project poses onto the plausible field and optimize for the interacting object.
Evaluations show utility for pose refinement, occluded-hand reconstruction, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

papers.abstract: We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. MR0 combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. A three-stage training recipe aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior through discrete action-token pre-training, transfers these priors to continuous cross-embodiment control through flow-matching mid-training, and adapts the policy through real-world post-training. We introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections to provide positive and negative supervision for CFG-DAgger without value learning or advantage labeling. A unified end-effector interface supports heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. An event-driven agent maintains persistent task events and reassesses plans when progress or feasibility changes, enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than $\pi_{0.5}$ across three real-robot tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90. Qualitative agent deployments demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions.

papers.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations is a reliable way to teach robots new tasks, but the gains from each additional demonstration shrink as the policy improves. Continued improvement can instead come from supervised deployment, where an operator places the objects and intervenes when the policy fails. We ask how to maximize improvement from a fixed budget of supervised episodes on high-precision manipulation tasks with wide ranges of object placements. We observe that failures can concentrate in a small subset of initial states, so uniform collection spends much of the operator's time on states the policy already handles. Mulligan makes the initial-state distribution a decision, starting each round's episodes at observed failures and untried states. To further improve data efficiency, we augment interactive imitation learning with a value function trained on all data, including failures that imitation discards. Across three real-world tasks evaluated on 2,550 held-out, blinded episodes and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform initial-state sampling at matched collection budgets, and combined with value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+Mulligan, improves final real-task success by 10-34 percentage points. With operator interventions, the human-robot team completes 98% of collection episodes, remaining productive while the policy learns. Videos, code, and data are available at https://mulligan.page/.
bullets: Uniform data collection becomes inefficient as policies improve because many sampled states are already solved.
Mulligan treats the initial-state distribution as a decision, prioritizing observed failures and untried states each round.
It also trains a value function on all collected data, including failures omitted by standard imitation learning.
Across three real-world and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform sampling at matched collection budgets.
With value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+Mulligan raises final real-task success by 10–34 percentage points; operators complete 98% of collection episodes.

papers.abstract: Finding an optimal behaviour policy within a given environment is a widely studied problem in domains as diverse as games, robotics, energy infrastructure, communication networks, and multi-agent systems. Numerous benchmarks have been developed to support such research, but the vast majority assume that the agent's embodiment (design) is fixed, focusing instead on policy learning alone. Lifting this assumption gives rise to a broader class of problems in which optimizing embodiment and policy separately is highly suboptimal. An agent's embodiment strongly shapes which control policies can be discovered, while the optimal embodiment is in turn defined by the policies it admits. To help the research community study this class of problems explicitly and systematically, we introduce Co-Design Gym - a suite of benchmark environments for jointly optimizing embodiment and policy. Our environments span domains such as robotic manipulation and locomotion, multi-robot cooperation, deformable and soft dynamics, video games, electricity grids, wireless networks, F1 racing, multi-agent warehouses, and optimal control, offering 20 environment families (domains), with over 85 distinct co-design presets in total. We further contribute a systematic evaluation of representative co-design algorithms, characterizing the current state of the art. Together, these contributions lay the groundwork for cumulative, comparable progress in co-design.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed-embodiment benchmarks, where policy-only optimization can be suboptimal.
Provides 20 environment families spanning robotics, multi-agent systems, games, infrastructure, communications, and control.
Includes more than 85 distinct embodiment-policy co-design presets.
Evaluates representative co-design algorithms to characterize current capabilities and support comparable future research.

papers.abstract: Structured policies improve efficiency, robustness, and interpretability in imitation learning by introducing task-specific inductive bias, but existing structure generation methods rely either on extensive human input or on static domain knowledge encoded in LLMs, which may be inconsistent with the expert demonstrations. We propose a closed-loop framework that iteratively refines structured policies using LLM-guided analysis of policy rollouts. By logging rollouts as semantically meaningful tabular data and prompting the LLM to generate diagnostic analysis code, our method identifies suboptimalities in the policy structure and iteratively corrects them without requiring human instruction. Experiments on car racing and door opening tasks show that our approach improves imitation learning performance by up to 15% over zero-shot LLM-generated structures and requires 75% less compute to achieve the same reinforcement learning performance. These results demonstrate that tabular rollout analysis provides an effective feedback signal to align LLM-generated policy structures with expert demonstrations, and we can utilize it to generate good policy structures automatically.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static or human-designed policy structures and expert demonstrations.
Logs policy rollouts as semantically meaningful tables and prompts an LLM to generate diagnostic analysis code.
Iteratively detects structural suboptimalities and corrects the policy.
Experiments on car racing and door opening report up to 15% better imitation-learning performance than zero-shot LLM-generated structures.
Achieves the same reinforcement-learning performance with 75% less compute, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of policy refinement. 1. Generate the initial structure by querying an LLM with the task description. 2. Update parameters through imitation learning on the demonstrations. 3. Generate analysis code based on the desired behavior of the policy and its structure topology. 4. Collect tabular trajectories, recording observations, actions, and named latent values during policy rollouts. 5. Execute analyses and revise the structure based on the analysis results. The updated program returns to parameter fitting and another refinement cycle. 6. Reinforcement learning after the structure aligns with the demonstrations to go beyond the demonstration performance.

Figure 2: A sample speed-control subgraph and its corresponding PyTorch implementation. Solid nodes distinguish observations (gray), semantic latents (blue), action outputs (green), and trainable weights (orange); dashed nodes denote operation nodes (some collapsed due to space constraints). The returned speed_error exposes the latent value for further rollout analysis.
Figure 6: Recorded slip and target-speed values before refinement (left) and after three revisions (right), with shared axis limits.

papers.abstract: Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) provide semantic cues such as depth and segmentation useful for robotic manipulation, but directly deploying them in closed-loop control is impractical due to high computational cost, temporal inconsistency, and distribution shift between static internet images and egocentric robot observations. We propose All-For-One (AFO), a two-stage distillation framework that leverages VFMs strictly as privileged information during training, using downstream robotic data. Following the privileged learning paradigm, AFO decouples semantic representation learning from inference-time policy execution. In the All stage, a teacher policy fuses RGB observations with outputs from multiple VFMs to learn a semantically enriched representation. In the For-One stage, this knowledge is distilled in-distribution into a lightweight RGB-only student policy. Evaluated on two Adroit tasks and five MetaWorld tasks in simulation, as well as three real-world manipulation tasks, AFO outperforms prior foundation-model-based approaches while using over 30x fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50x lower latency than its own teacher in simulation benchmarks, providing an efficient pathway for transferring foundation-model knowledge to robotic control.
bullets: Addresses the high cost, temporal inconsistency, and observation-distribution mismatch of deploying VFMs directly in closed-loop control.
Uses a two-stage privileged-learning framework: a teacher combines RGB with multiple VFM outputs, then transfers the learned representation to an RGB-only student.
The student performs inference without VFMs, decoupling semantic representation learning from policy execution.
Evaluated on Adroit and MetaWorld simulation tasks plus three real-world manipulation tasks.
Reports over 30× fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50× lower latency than its teacher in simulation, while outperforming prior foundation-model-based approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the All-For-One (AFO) Framework. (a) All. A teacher network employs multiple VFMs (e.g., Molmo [10], SAM 2 [46], and DAM 2 [58]) with learnable lightweight encoders (fT RGB, fT object, f T depth). The resulting representations are aggregated and used to train a policy with a BC loss. (b) For One. A student lightweight RGB encoder (fS RGB) solely learns from the teacher network via a feature distillation loss with BC loss, which benefits from the rich knowledge of large VFMs.

Figure 4. Failure Analysis of VFM-Based Teacher Policies. Directly using VFMs in the teacher introduces brittle failure modes. (a) Segmentation errors: SAM 2 misses the target or masks an irrelevant object. (b) Depth errors: DAM 2 mis-estimates geometry, e.g., predicting a shadow as a closer surface. (c) Temporal inconsistencies: depth estimates fluctuate across adjacent frames. (d) These errors substantially degrade performance: on Adroit Relocate, the teacher succeeds 87% without VFM errors, but only 45% when an error occurs.

Figure 3. Visual illustration of the simulation and real-world benchmarks. We adopt the Adroit [44] and MetaWorld [59] tasks as our simulated environments, and clutter sweep, clean toolbox, and pick-and-place as our real-world tasks. We further evaluate under visual distribution shifts, including desk mat and lighting changes and increased clutter.

Figure 1. Overcoming the Compute–Performance Tradeoff. Learning from scratch (LfS) [17] is fast but inaccurate, whereas VFM backbones [35, 37, 39, 43, 50] are accurate but slow. By distilling large-scale pretrained VFMs [10, 46, 58] into a compact student, AFO attains high success rates while remaining computationally efficient at inference.

Table 1. AFO outperforms all baselines at minimal computational cost. AFO’s student matches or surpasses VFM-based baselines on Adroit and MetaWorld while running at the lowest latency and parameter count, on par with the smallest from-scratch baseline (LfS).

Table 2. Comparison on Real-world Imitation Learning. Success rates under in-distribution (ID) and visual out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions on three real-world tasks. While all methods perform comparably in distribution, AFO degrades far less under visual shifts, surpassing both baselines by a large margin in OOD at the same cost as the lightweight ACT.

Table 5. Comprehensive Ablation Studies. Removing a teacher modality costs more than changing the distillation configuration: dropping segmentation degrades performance noticeably, whereas the loss, alignment, and λ variants all remain close to our default.

Table 3. Effect of teacher modalities on distillation. Depth and segmentation each improve the teacher, but teacher accuracy does not predict distillation quality: only the teacher with both modalities yields the best RGB-only student (2.11 ms, 2.72M).
Table 4. Comprehensive Comparison with Theia Distillation Objective. The first row is the original Theia and the last row is AFO (Student); the two middle rows vary one factor at a time.

papers.abstract: Integrating force awareness into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models involves not merely encoding wrench measurements as an additional modality, but determining when and how strongly physical interaction should influence robot action generation. Existing VLAs that use force typically inject it through a fixed pathway, without explicitly determining when it is relevant to the current action. This calls for an intermediate force relevance mechanism inside the VLA, in which visual-language context estimates the relevance of physical feedback to the current task before force enters the action pathway. FR-VLA addresses this gap with a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that uses learnable force query tokens to derive a force admission signal grounded in visual-language context, and uses this signal to modulate an external tokenized force pathway for action generation. In real-world experiments on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, FR-VLA achieves the highest mean success rate over six evaluated stages, and trajectory visualizations show that its force admission varies with the interaction phase.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed force-injection pathways in existing vision-language-action models.
Uses learnable force query tokens to infer force relevance from visual-language context.
Modulates an external tokenized force pathway according to the inferred force admission signal.
Evaluated on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, achieving the highest mean success rate over six stages.
Force admission varies across interaction phases, suggesting context-dependent physical feedback use.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FR-VLA. (a) Overall architecture: four token groups are processed by the VLM-based Implicit Force Reasoning Module, which infers contact-relevant motion phases and produces a force admission signal. Measured wrench histories are encoded by the Force Tokenizer Module and enter the Action Expert only through the admission-conditioned action-side pathway. (b) The VLM-based Implicit Force Reasoning Module grounds force query states with visual features through cross-attention and decodes them into motion phase inference, producing the admission signal that determines when force information becomes action-relevant. (c) The Force Tokenizer Module discretizes wrench histories into contact-semantic codes via a frozen VQ-Encoder and uses their Code Embeddings to FiLM-condition the force pathway.

Figure 5: Real-world success rates. Per-task/stage success rate over 20 trials for each method; FR-VLA (ours) is shown in purple. Switch Cable Connection is evaluated in two stages, covering top Ethernet cable insertion and side power connector insertion. Shaded regions denote inferred phases; admission stays positive throughout the inferred contact phase and becomes negative once the phase switches to free.

The evaluation suite spans Gear Assembly, Switch Cable Connection with a visually occluded side power connector stage, Curved Surface Cleaning, Screw Tightening, and Seat Belt Buckle Insertion, covering contact transitions, constrained insertion, sustained surface interaction, and visually limited contact reasoning.

Figure 1: (a) Two representative force-aware VLA designs either inject force into the VLM token stream or condition the action expert directly. (b) A Switch Cable Connection trajectory shows synchronized camera observations, six-dimensional wrench measurements, and the force admission signal across task stages.

papers.abstract: By learning transferable rewards, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) enables counterfactual evaluation of agents under modified environments. Such transfer places strict requirements on coverage since target environments affect agents' state occupancy. We propose a multi-task IRL method that pools data across multiple agents with different rewards in the same environment under a low-rank assumption. In addition to alleviating coverage requirements, so each task need not visit every state as long as others do, the method offers scalable evaluation of multiple tasks under new environments as computationally intensive planning scales with rank rather than the number of tasks. We provide finite sample guarantees on reward recovery and on policy learning in new environments. Experiments show our method is robust to limited coverage, recovers rewards on and off of each task's support, transfers to target environments at lower regret than baselines, with its computational advantage over per-task methods widening as tasks grow.
bullets: Addresses limited state-coverage requirements in transferable inverse reinforcement learning.
Pools demonstrations from multiple tasks in the same environment under a low-rank reward assumption.
Scales planning with the reward rank rather than the number of tasks.
Provides finite-sample guarantees for reward recovery and policy learning in new environments.
Experiments show robustness to limited coverage, off-support reward recovery, lower transfer regret than baselines, and increasing computational benefits as tasks grow.

Figure 3: Policy recovery in target perturbed environments. Error bands are ±1 s.d over ten seeds.

Figure 1: Causal test of directional coverage. Left: change in error projected onto the targeted eigendirection for treated, volume-matched control, and placebo cells. Right: treated-minus-control difference-in-differences for the targeted and remaining directions.
Figure 6: Empirical scaling in RecSim matches the theory in n and S and is more conservative in k and A.

papers.abstract: Continuous policy optimization may spread an update across many states, even when deployment permits only a few complete state-level changes. We study how much discounted return can be retained when continuous row mixtures are rounded to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. Policy-dependent visitation couples the row edits, while long horizons make global curvature bounds conservative. From $2d+2$ Bellman solves, we derive reusable envelopes that support uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. A rank-two rational representation of each exchange further permits weighted curvature integration along the realized trajectory. We prove that linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, and that exact global curvature thresholding is hard. Candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from $48.2\%$ to $74.1\%$ on the structured suite. At $γ=0.95$, local integration lowers the median bound-to-loss ratio from $402.3$ to $2.08$ on coupled instances.
bullets: Addresses sparse deployment when only a few complete state-level policy changes are allowed.
Uses $2d+2$ Bellman solves to construct reusable uniform and candidate-specific performance envelopes.
Employs a rank-two rational exchange representation and trajectory-based curvature integration for tighter certificates.
Candidate-specific bounds increase pre-rounding certification coverage from 48.2% to 74.1%.
At $\gamma=0.95$, local integration reduces the median bound-to-loss ratio from 402.3 to 2.08 on coupled instances.

Table 5: Deployment-improvement coverage on the 139 active structured cases. Direct is inferred from the existing exact-return records.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses sparse policy deployment in MDPs with Bellman-certified rounding, a technical contribution relevant to efficient robotic control and policy implementation.
papers.title: Bellman-Certified Rounding for Sparse Policy Deployment in MDPs
papers.tldr: A Bellman-based certification method safely rounds continuous policy updates into sparse binary policies while producing much tighter loss bounds.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment. Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data: existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose OopsieRecover, a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/oopsierecover for videos.
bullets: Targets the need for large amounts of corrective data and poor generalization in deployed VLA models.
Uses abduction to infer the intent behind corrective demonstrations.
Represents inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs that steer actions away from undesirable regions.
Evaluated across 6 tasks with variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks.
Reports successful recovery across broad novel situations without new corrective data for each variation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: OOPSIERECOVER: From semantic interventions to reusable VLA corrections. In OOPSIERECOVER, a human monitors VLA execution and intervenes to provide semantic corrections: a corrective trajectory and a language description for some type of correction, ci, (orange). We then synthesize the collected set of interventions for each correction type into a Semantically Grounded Gated Cost by i) parsing the sensorimotor demonstration as temporal point sets tracked on semantic scene entities, ii) generating gated costs from the motion of the point sets, and iii) verifying these costs by evaluating their capability to explain all human corrections of the same type (blue). During deployment (green), these costs determine when steering is needed and rank candidate actions using the learned corrective programs. This separates the intended correction from its demonstrated trajectory, allowing correction programs to be used in the environment where they are collected and to generalize to new situations, while the base VLA remains frozen.

Fig. 3: Simulation and real-world tasks. We evaluate a diverse set of tasks that elicit different types of corrections; avoiding collisions, improving placement precision, and correctly articulating objects.

Fig. 1: Learning reusable corrections from human interventions with OOPSIERECOVER. A human corrects a lid-closure failure and describes the intended behavior. OOPSIERECOVER grounds this feedback in semantic point sets, and uses abduction – finding a simple explanation consistent with the observed intervention – to synthesize a gated correction cost that steers a frozen VLA. (Right) The synthesized correction programs generalize: they can be reused under changed object poses and scene layouts, broadening the successful applicability of the VLA.

Fig. 5: Scaling with number of corrections. On CoffeeMug, OOPSIERECOVER rapidly reaches an 84% success rate with as few as 8 corrections, while HG-DAgger∗ achieves only 28% despite using three times as many corrections.

papers.selection_reason: VLA failure recovery from few corrective demonstrations; directly fits VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions
papers.tldr: OopsieRecover uses semantic reasoning from a few corrective demonstrations to help VLA robots recover from failures and generalize across novel objects, scenes, and task variations.

papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because policies must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise control, while reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire rich control behaviors from large-scale interaction with privileged information. We introduce \textbf{Latent RL Prior}, a two-stage framework that reuses this control knowledge for data-efficient visual policy learning. During privileged pretraining, we distill large-scale RL rollouts into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and latent task context. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images to its latent context using action supervision alone, without privileged labels or latent targets. The same decoder can further be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 in the low-data regime; on door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses full-data baselines using $10\times$ and $5\times$ fewer demonstrations, respectively. Further analysis shows that direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation performance and training stability over routing visual predictions through the pretrained state encoder. Robustness to unseen mass variation and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information in decoder representations further provide evidence of retained RL-acquired control knowledge. Project website: https://yixiaowang7.github.io/latent-rl-prior-page/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly learning visual grounding and precise dexterous control with scarce demonstrations.
Pretrains a flow-matching action decoder on privileged RL rollouts, then learns a visual-to-latent interface using action supervision alone.
The decoder can be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation.
Across three simulated tasks, it outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning baselines in low-data settings, using 10× and 5× fewer demonstrations on two tasks.
Direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation and stability; robustness to mass changes suggests retained RL control knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Latent RL Prior. (a) Privileged pretraining: a state tokenizer and Q-Former supply task context to an action decoder conditioned on flow time and single-arm proprioception. (b) Visual adaptation: an image encoder and Q-Former learn context tokens while the decoder remains frozen. For bimanual assembly, left- and right-arm queries interact within the same Q-Former; each output group conditions the shared decoder with its corresponding arm’s proprioception.

Figure 5: Target pose-alignment ablations with the action decoder frozen for both latent-transfer variants. Results show mean success rates and standard deviations over three random seeds, except for explicit transfer, which uses five seeds.

Figure 8: Generalization to increased object mass. (a) Target pose alignment at a relaxed (ϵ = 0.05 m) thresholds. (b) Door lift. The leftmost point in each plot corresponds to the reference mass used for downstream visual training, e.g., for Dvis.

Figure 7: Learning-rate ablations for (a) the image encoder with the action decoder frozen and (b) the action decoder with the image encoder frozen. Panels report strict (ϵ = 0.015 m) and relaxed (ϵ = 0.05 m) pose-alignment success. We report average success rate and standard deviation across three random seeds. Each scale multiplies the tested module’s original learning rate; zero freezes it.

Figure 9: Linear contact-force probes of the visual policies. Panels predict (a) total grasp normal force, (b) per-finger normal forces, (c) per-finger tangential forces, and (d) per-finger Cartesian force vectors from each layer of the action decoder. Colors denote visual-demonstration budgets; solid and dashed curves denote the frozen pretrained and trainable scratch action decoders. Both policies fine-tune the image encoder at 0.2× its base learning rate for 100k steps. Curves average three policy seeds on the same IID probe test episodes.

Figure 6: Training stability on target pose alignment at a relaxed (ϵ = 0.05 m) threshold. Dotted curves show individual runs for latent transfer, explicit transfer, and scratch training; shaded regions show the mean ± one standard deviation. Explicit transfer uses five random seeds, while latent transfer and scratch training use three seeds each.

Figure 2: Pretraining and downstream tasks. Left: the pretraining task of target pose alignment with varied procedural objects; the inset shows example object templates. Right: the downstream tasks of target pose alignment with a held-out brush, door lifting, and bimanual assembly (left to right). The same pretrained action decoder is reused for visual adaptation across all three downstream tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Data-efficient dexterous manipulation via latent RL priors; directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Latent RL Priors for Data-Efficient Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: Latent RL Prior transfers privileged RL control knowledge into a frozen action decoder, enabling data-efficient visual dexterous manipulation from limited demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/
bullets: Addresses the lack of physical coordination in humanoid robots trained as solitary agents.
Uses a hierarchical system with shared-token sequence modeling for reactive and anticipatory human–robot motion generation.
Combines high-level motion generation with a low-level whole-body tracking controller for robot execution.
Introduces adaptive retargeting that preserves contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale.
Builds a 260-hour Human-Humanoid Interaction benchmark from five motion-capture datasets and demonstrates coordinated behavior in simulation and the real world.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Social Humanoid Architecture. From RGB-D observations of a human partner (red), we reconstruct the human pose and localize the body in 3D using depth and estimated gravity. Relative human and humanoid states are encoded through the VQ-VAE encoders Eh and Er. The resulting latent motion tokens z∗, relative pose transforms T ∗, and canonical motion transforms ∆T ∗ are concatenated and processed by the DFoT policy, then decoded via Dh and Dr to future human behavior (blue) and socially coordinated humanoid motion (purple). SONIC executes the motion in sim or the real-world, and the robot state is updated for closed-loop interaction.

Figure 5: Retargeting Qualitative Results. Each panel shows a ground-truth human–human interaction (ego in orange, partner in dark blue) next to its retargeted counterpart. The ego is retargeted to the humanoid (tan), and the partner’s pose is morphed to preserve interaction (light blue). Across diverse interactions our Adaptive-HHI Retargeting method preserves the contacts and relative positioning between the two agents.

Figure 6: Real-world deployment. Frames run left to right in time. Top two rows: separate highfive and hand-wave trials. Bottom: a single continuous take in which the humanoid transitions directly from a handshake into a bend

Figure 7: Shadow teleoperation. The G1 shadows a human operator performing arm movements (top) and sitting down on a couch (bottom). The operator’s motion is encoded with Eh, quantized against the shared codebook C, and decoded with Dr into humanoid motion. Frames run left to right in time.

Figure 3: Shared-Codebook VQ-VAE. Human and humanoid motion sequences are independently encoded into latent features and mapped to a shared vector-quantized codebook that learns a common motion vocabulary across embodiments. Embodiment-specific decoders reconstruct the respective motions, enabling aligned, transferable motion representations between humans and humanoids.

Figure 4: Adaptive-HHI Retargeting. Our retargeting pipeline starts from two ground truth humans. In the first pass, we retarget the ego human (orange) to the humanoid using a contact-adaptive weight matrix to encourage body pose in regions close to the physical interaction to be preserved. In a second pass, we co-morph the partner’s pose towards more plausible interaction via a contactgated morphing strategy driven by the amount of physical contact present in the interaction.

Figure A.1: Cross-embodiment motion translation with a shared-codebook VQ-VAE. Human motion (red) is encoded into a discrete latent space shared between the human and humanoid embodiments, then decoded into humanoid motion (purple). Each example shows three frames of the input human motion alongside the translated humanoid motion in simulation (top row), and the same frames executed on the physical humanoid robot (bottom row).
Table 3: Retargeting comparison across three interaction datasets. Best per column in bold; ↑/↓ indicate higher/lower is better.

Table A.2: Comparison of retargeting methods. Adaptive-HHI extends OmniRetarget’s interaction-mesh SOCP base with partner co-morphing (joint optimization over the partner SMPLX) and distance-weighted, wrist-boosted adaptive Laplacian weighting for interaction and humanscale preservation.

Table A.6: Network configuration details. T is the raw sequence length and T ′ = T/ω the number of tokens after temporal compression (ω=4); P is the number of interacting agents; Din is the peragent pose dimension (Dh or Dr); Dc is the local conditioning dimension; de is the embedding dimension; and Dm = dvq + 4 × 9 × P is the unified motion token dimension tracking localized cross-agent transformations.
Table A.1: Summary statistics of our retargeted benchmark. Clip counts, frames, and durations are reported after retargeting each source dataset to the Unitree G1 with Adaptive-HHI.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
bullets: Addresses the gap between 2D vision-language pre-training and reliable 3D robotic manipulation.
Jointly trains action prediction with alignment between VLA visual features and a frozen 3D perception model.
Unifies heterogeneous robot datasets across embodiments, tasks, scenes, and geometric annotations.
Uses feature-dependent layer aggregation, partial depth/calibration, and probabilistic state dropout to improve spatial supervision and visual reliance.
Training-only auxiliary components enable direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights without changing inference.
