figures.caption: Figure 17: Multi-view RGB–LiDAR generation. Each column represents a camera or LiDAR stream. Colors denote language tokens (lavender), clean controls (green), and noisy target latents (light orange), as in Fig. 2. Each camera reads its own prompt and WSM control, while LiDAR reads all camera prompts and its HD-map control. Learned identity embeddings distinguish cameras 0, . . . , 𝑁 − 1 and LiDAR 𝑁 , retaining their identities when selecting camera subsets. Arrows connect conditioning inputs to their consumers, and the lower bidirectional links show cross-sensor attention under the temporal visibility rules. Representative views are shown, with tokenizers and optional initial observations omitted. See Sec. 7.1 to 7.3 for the model architecture, caption preparation, and training recipe.

Figure 1: From Cosmos 3 to interactive world simulation. A shared post-training recipe adapts Cosmos3Nano from the Cosmos 3 family (NVIDIA, 2026a) into three example models for camera navigation and robot manipulation, single-view video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. Each specialized model incorporates domain-specific controls tailored to its application and trained on datasets reflecting the types of interactions and physical dynamics relevant to that domain.

Figure 4: Shared post-training stages for interactive world simulation. Stages follow Causal-rCM (Zheng et al., 2026c) from top to bottom, with context and purpose alongside. Solid arrows initialize the next stage. Dashed paths supply the frozen stage-1 causal teacher for TF-dCM and the frozen stage-0 bidirectional teacher for SF-DMD. SF-DMD also uses a trainable auxiliary score model to evaluate student rollouts.

Figure 2: Autoregressive video generation with streaming controls. (a) Each generator chunk groups clean controls 𝒰𝑘 with the corresponding visual tokens. The history ℋ𝑗 comprises previously denoised chunks ̂︀𝒱𝑘 and the retained controls. The current chunk ̃︀𝒱𝜏𝑗 is progressively denoised with clean controls held constant. (b) The action-based example shows 4 individual clean action tokens per latent interval. For video transfer, aligned source latent frames form the clean control group 𝒰𝑗 for the target chunk’s interval. Source tokens entering the cache keep their conditioning role for future predictions.

Figure 5: Packed and replay-based teacher forcing. (a) The action-conditioned schematic shows 1 latent time step per chunk, with the same clean controls in both branches. Color identifies the clean-reference or noisy-target branch, while controls remain clean in both. The mask permits clean-to-clean attention, strictly earlier clean history for noisy queries, and joint reads within each noisy chunk. For larger single-view chunks, clean queries can read only their own latent interval and earlier clean intervals. (b) The replay noisy pass reads language 𝒯 , an available prefix ℋprefix from earlier segments, and strictly earlier clean chunks. (c) The clean pass supplies layerwise K/V for parallel noisy-target evaluation, with shared parameters and a single optimizer update. The dashed arrow marks the retained or recomputed gradient path through the cache.

Figure 3: Temporal-causal attention for action-conditioned video generation. Rows represent queries and columns stand for keys/values. Each generator chunk contains clean controls 𝒰𝑘 and visual tokens ̃︀𝒱𝑘, with chunk indices starting at 𝑘 = 0. When conditioning on actions, 𝒰0 is a null group and the first vision group is the clean frame 𝒱0. Language uses causal self-attention, while generator queries access reasoner keys/values, but not vice versa. Token counts are schematic only. (a) In Cosmos 3, every generator chunk can read from every other. (b) After causal conversion, reads are allowed only within the current block and to earlier ones. Video-transfer and multi-view layouts can further restrict token-role visibility.

Figure D.4: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto chunk wall time by GPU count and layout on GB200. Shipped flags, from the same-allocation ladders of Tab. D.7; bars give the median of the run medians of a configuration and whiskers their range where the configuration was repeated. Labels give the GPU layout as model ranks plus map GPUs, where map GPUs draw and encode controls on separate GPUs, so the GPU count of a configuration is their sum; blue bars are RGB and orange bars RGB + LiDAR.

Figure 6: State and dependencies in one streaming generation step. Initial context supplies language and any available observed history, while streaming inputs provide the current conditions 𝒰𝑗 . Denoising reads these inputs without modifying retained K/V. Completed latents feed the cache update and stateful decoding, which can overlap on separate GPUs. The generator refreshes clean K/V for the completed chunk and appends the retained entries before the next prediction (Eqs. (20) and (21)). For single-view action conditioning, this refresh processes latent frames in temporal order within the chunk.

Figure C.9: Object-motion errors under depth and segmentation conditioning. The depth example at 4.00 s and the segmentation example at 3.00 s show the simulator holding the target above an empty table. The prompts describe the shoe and turtle on the counter, and the generated observations place them there despite the lifted target in the source. Both examples come from 600-frame, 30-FPS VisDex rollouts using the iteration-1,500 SF-DMD checkpoint, a 30-latent-frame K/V window, and 3 sink frames.

Figure D.7: LiDAR range views under different weather prompts. The front ±90∘ of sweep 15 is shown for the same scene controls and random seed (2025). Brighter pixels indicate greater range on a shared 0–100m scale, and black pixels denote missing returns. Compared with sunny conditions, rain produces gaps in road-surface returns, while fog suppresses distant returns and preserves much of the nearby road.

Figure 23: Multi-view RGB–LiDAR generation with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto. This urban intersection under strong sun glare illustrates joint generation across eleven cameras and LiDAR. The white van retains its appearance in the rear-right and rear-fisheye views, while the forward and right-facing cameras agree on the direction of sunlight. Overlaid WSM controls align with the generated road markings and vehicle positions. The views follow the rig’s spatial layout around a central LiDAR sweep, whose height coloring distinguishes the road surface, nearby vehicles, and surrounding buildings.

Figure 24: Multi-view RGB–LiDAR generation with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto. Camera views are arranged by their viewing directions around the vehicle, with generated LiDAR shown centrally. WSM controls are overlaid on the RGB frames to highlight adherence to the supplied scene structure. Buildings, vehicles, and cyclists retain consistent geometry and appearance across overlapping views. The LiDAR point cloud is color-coded by height and captures corresponding scene geometry.

Figure C.7: Appearance inconsistency in Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer. Matched crops show inconsistent body proportions and front–rear interpretation of the generated red vehicle during a passing maneuver. The vehicle is visible in all three illustrated frames. The 121-frame, 30-FPS generation uses a 31-latent-frame K/V window and 3 sink frames.

Figure D.6: LiDAR geometry with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto and Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto. Scenes in Fig. 26 show Transfer (left) and Sim (right) at 4.9 s with matched viewpoints and a shared height scale.

Figure 25: Spatial control following in generated front-wide video. WSM overlays show correspondence with vehicles, road markings, and traffic signals at five times after conditioning. The top two rows use Cosmos3Nano-Transfer-Auto and the bottom two use Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Figure 8: Initial-state caption rewriting on an AgiBot-GEAR example. The initial frame shows the patterned slippers on the floor beside the right cabinet wall. The excerpts compare the first caption segment with its final rewrite. Pink shading marks the removed grasp and lift, while the initial location is retained. Ellipses omit other caption text. The image is shown for comparison only: the rewriter receives the first-segment text, without the video or later segments.

Figure D.2: Symmetric schematic of the complete 11-camera rig. (a) Seven standard cameras cover wideangle and telephoto views. (b) Four fisheye cameras provide wider angular coverage. Colors and numbered labels identify individual cameras, and dashed arrows indicate viewing directions.

Figure 18: Sensor-aligned structural controls. Recorded RGB, WSM, and their overlay (top) illustrate cameracontrol alignment in one data sample. A recorded LiDAR range image and its HD-map control are shown below.

Figure 10: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual camera navigation from a shared initial image. The first column shows the shared initial image. Each row then shows frames at 2.5, 5, 7.5, and 10 s from one rollout conditioned on a different camera trajectory (follow behind, crane up follow, truck left, and truck right). Insets show the supplied camera trajectory and the camera pose at the displayed frame.

Columns show frames at 0, 10, 20, 25.9, and 28 s, progressing from the initial view through base motion, tissue grasp, motion over the bin, and the final sampled view.

Figure 26: LiDAR geometry with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto. Two Transfer-I2V scenes compare ground truth (left) with generated sweeps (right), using matched viewpoints and a shared height scale. The examples reproduce the main road and roadside structure, with clear individual objects.

Figure C.5: Temporal degradation in Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer. Matched source, edge-control, and generated frames at 4.00 and 26.23 s show late-rollout ghosting around the robot arms and across the table. The recorded generation contains 788 frames at 30 FPS and uses a 198-latent-frame K/V window with 3 sink frames. These settings differ from the fixed-window VisDex runtime evaluation.

Figure 27: One-hour rollout stability of Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto. We generate two driving scenes continuously for 1 hour, cycling their WSM controls and captions with a rolling K/V cache. Video quality (DOVER), temporal consistency (ACM and TSE), and cross-view consistency (CSE-5) show no sustained degradation over the rollout. Faint curves show 4-second-window scores and bold curves show 1-minute averages.

Figure 14: Attention in Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer. Rows are queries and columns are keys/values, using the visual conventions of Fig. 3. 𝒰𝑖, 𝒱𝑖, and ̃︀𝒱𝑖 denote spatial controls, clean RGB, and noisy RGB for latent-frame chunk 𝑖. (a) The clean pass preserves causal language attention and gives control and RGB queries access to all language tokens. Control queries read controls through the current chunk and strictly earlier clean RGB, while clean RGB queries also read their own clean chunk. (b) The noisy pass reuses the clean pass’s language, control, and RGB keys and values. Each noisy RGB query reads controls through its current chunk, strictly earlier clean RGB, and noisy RGB within its own chunk. Neither controls nor noisy RGB can read the current clean RGB target. Each control or RGB chunk contains 1 latent frame and occupies one row or column, with spatial tokens aggregated into a single block. Three chunks are shown, with the optional conditioning prefix omitted.

Figure 13: Mixed manipulation and navigation rollout. Frames from a 30-second rollout are shown from top to bottom. Here, the action sequence begins with 10 seconds of manipulation, followed by 10 seconds of camera navigation and another 10 seconds of manipulation. During navigation, the camera slowly turns right and then left before returning to its original pose. The robot arms remain stationary while the camera moves, after which manipulation resumes using the accumulated visual history.

Figure 19: Camera and LiDAR sampling on a shared physical timeline. The illustrative grids share a temporal origin. Camera frames (𝑅𝑖) are sampled at 30 FPS, and the Wan2.2 tokenizer applies 4× temporal compression to produce camera latent steps (𝐶𝑗) spaced by 4/30 seconds (7.5 Hz). LiDAR sweeps and their latent steps (𝐿𝑘) retain the same 1/10-second spacing. Dashed guides and rings mark coincident camera-latent and LiDAR timestamps every 0.4 seconds, spanning three RGB latent intervals and four LiDAR intervals. Markers denote temporal positions rather than tokenizer receptive fields. Cross-sensor attention compares physical timestamps even when samples do not coincide.

Figure 22: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto per-chunk stage times of the shipped configurations on GB200. Each bar is the median run of its configuration, split into the median stage times over its steady-state chunks on the primary rank. Control preparation covers WSM drawing and encoding, or the gather of prefetched latents, plus the control-token pass that writes control K/V. The bar length uses the backend’s generation-call timer, and the gray remainder is work outside the 4 timed stages. Stage medians from a representative run need not sum to the across-run wall-time median.
Figure D.5: Cache and sink sizes for minute-long rollouts. The outlined 𝐶 = 2, 𝑆 = 1 setting achieves the best trade-off overall. Darker green is better within each panel.

Figure 21: Maskless execution of decomposed attention. Query and key/value tokens are gathered into segments for the illustrated sensor and language interactions. Variable-length attention processes each segment, and the results are scattered back to the original query order. Each attention call returns a normalized output and log-sum-exp (LSE) statistics. LSE-weighted merging recovers joint normalization when key subsets are disjoint and attention scores match, as in Eq. (D.10). Grouping must preserve the model’s temporal and conditioning restrictions. Arrows show data dependencies between logical operations.

Figure 20: Joint camera–LiDAR attention masks. Rows are queries and columns are keys/values. (a) Cosmos3Nano-Transfer-Auto with optional control-to-sensor access enabled (dashed blocks). Camera sensor and control queries read their own captions, while LiDAR queries read all camera captions (purple). Green and blue show own-control and own-sensor access. Only sensor queries read other sensors within the preceding 0.4-second window (orange). Wan2.2’s 4× temporal compression maps 30-FPS camera streams to 7.5-Hz latents, while LiDAR retains 10 Hz. Temporal indices span [0, 1.6] seconds: 13 camera latent times and 17 LiDAR times make the moving 0.4-second window visible as a narrow band. Caption lengths are illustrative. (b) Physical timestamps bound the orange band, excluding keys older than 0.4 seconds and future keys. (c) Same-sensor attention is clip-wide for Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto and block-causal for Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto, which reads the current chunk and permitted earlier clean history. Thick lines separate illustrative chunks C1–C3. For Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto, control-to-sensor access is restricted to preceding clean history. Gray cells are blocked, spatial tokens are collapsed, and caption query rows are omitted. All routes respect conditioning visibility, recording boundaries, and available context.

Figure 7: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual temporal alignment. The leftmost clean latent encodes the initial RGB frame, before any physical action. After startup, 4 per-frame actions align with each latent visual interval, and 2 latent frames form an 8-RGB-frame prediction chunk. The 16-RGB-frame pose-anchor interval spans the 4 subsequent latent frames and excludes the initial observation.

Table 16: LiDAR generation results in Transfer-T2V mode. Cosmos 3 results use 99 sweeps at 10 Hz from the joint RGB–LiDAR rollouts. LidarVerse (Che et al., 2026) is evaluated on 21- and 116-sweep rollouts. Arrows indicate the preferred score direction, while CTC ratios target 1. Scale factors in the headers multiply the displayed values; FUD denotes Fréchet Utonia distance. Bold and underlined values mark the best and second-best scores. Lighter and darker green identify the bidirectional and causal models, respectively.

Memory entries average the PyTorch allocated and reserved storage recorded at callbacks during these 597-frame generations.

CosmosTransfer2.5 denotes its multi-view variant. SG-V denotes StyleGAN-V features for FVD. Arrows indicate the preferred score direction. Bold and underlined values mark the best and second-best scores within each mode. Lighter and darker green identify the bidirectional and causal models, respectively.

Table D.7: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto chunk wall time and presented FPS on GB200, eager against the shipped optimizations. Each row compares configurations within the same GPU allocation. Chunk wall time is the median of run medians of the recorded generation call on the primary rank, with the range across repeated runs in parentheses. Bold and underlined values mark the best and second-best scores. Light and dark green distinguish the bidirectional and causal models.

papers.abstract: Controlling the shape profile of soft trunk robots extends their reach into complex regions of the workspace and enhances their use in practical applications. Recent advances in soft robot design have enabled soft trunk robots to achieve greater flexibility in conforming to complex shapes. Specifically, trunk robots whose geometries are designed as helicoids have been shown to enable extreme shape-changing capabilities. Their compliance makes them highly nonlinear, which in turn makes shape control difficult. On similar tendon-driven trunk robots, model-based controllers based on the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) have achieved high accuracy in closed-loop end-effector tracking. We extend this approach by learning an aSSM model of the full body of a trimmed-helicoid soft trunk robot from data and use this in a model predictive control (MPC) scheme to demonstrate a range of shape control tasks on hardware. On closed-loop dynamic shape regulation, our method outperforms the available linear baselines by a factor of 10. In human-in-the-loop interactive demos, our method completes section-by-section shaping and balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds, while the linear baselines fall short. A model-free reinforcement learning policy trained for 12 hours on hardware fails on the same balancing task. These results establish aSSM-based MPC as a practical route to full-body shape control on real soft hardware.
authors: Hehui Zheng, Marc Stampanoni, Roshan S. Kaundinya, Ronan Hinchet, George Haller, Robert K. Katzschmann
bullets: Soft trunk robots can reach complex regions but are difficult to control because their compliant dynamics are highly nonlinear.
The approach learns a full-body adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM) model from data and uses it within model predictive control.
Hardware experiments demonstrate dynamic shape regulation, interactive section-by-section shaping, and tennis-ball balancing.
Dynamic shape regulation outperforms available linear baselines by a factor of 10; the system balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds.
A model-free reinforcement-learning policy trained on hardware for 12 hours fails at the same balancing task.

papers.abstract: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present soccerbot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, soccerbot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.
authors: Haoyu Shao, Yunshen Wang, Jingze Zhang, Shaohang Zhu, Yong-Lu Li, Tianzhu Zhang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining locomotion, ball control, and contact-rich dynamics across continuously changing soccer behaviors.

Trains one skill-conditioned policy for moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking, including fluid transitions when switching skills.
Uses robustness-oriented simulation design to enable zero-shot transfer to the Unitree G1 humanoid.
Demonstrates agile, natural, and robust execution of the full skill repertoire in real-world conditions.

papers.abstract: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.
authors: Xuemin Hu, Kaixin Li, Qingqing Xia, Yuxin Wang, Wei Xie, Bo Tang, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses high-dimensional, coupled humanoid dynamics and differences across joint degrees of freedom.
Factorizes policies at the torque-actuated JDoF level using actuation, kinematic, and dynamic descriptors.
Co-optimizes the high-level pose planner and low-level joint executor in a closed loop using shared trajectories.
Experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym show improved locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over several baselines.
Scope: demonstrated for humanoid robot control in simulation environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. H2MARL overview. The high-level planner generates JDoF-level pose increments and converts them into absolute target poses. The low-level joint executor receives the absolute target poses combined with historical proprioception and outputs executable joint positions which are converted to torques by a PD controller. Both the high-level policy and the low-level executor are optimized by the coupling trajectories in a closed-loop.

Fig. 1. Limb- and JDoF-level multi-agent formulations for the humanoid robot. (a) Traditional limb-level formulation, where each limb is formulated as an independent homogeneous agent. (b) JDoF-level formulation, where each torque-actuated JDoF is formulated as an independent heterogeneous agent with physical attributes and functional roles.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.
authors: Shengzhe Zhang, Qi Zhang, Dazhong Shen, Chao Wang, Shaopeng Zhai, Hui Xiong
bullets: Addresses task-irrelevant visual shortcuts caused by limited perceptual supervision in action prediction.
Derives candidate target-object and robot regions from interaction-induced visual changes, then refines them offline with segmentation.
Uses attention allocation and contrastive objectives to focus visual processing on relevant regions and align them with language instructions.
Improves multiple VLA backbones across simulated and real-world benchmarks, with average success-rate gains of 6.5%–25.2%.
Scope: guidance depends on regions extracted from the manipulation process and refined offline.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning offers an effective approach to precise laboratory manipulation, yet costly real-world demonstrations and limited access to dense process rewards hinder its practical application. We present TwinBridge, a digital twin-driven framework that supplies policy initialization and dense visual rewards for real-world online learning. We construct digital twins by combining 3D Gaussian splatting with physics simulation. Here, simulator states provide task events and geometric progress under physical prerequisites and ordering constraints, yielding rewards for policy pretraining with simulated demonstrations and reinforcement learning. We distill this supervision into a visual reward model. During real-world interaction, its predictions are combined with execution history to compute dense rewards for human-in-the-loop policy refinement. Across five real-world laboratory tasks, TwinBridge achieves a final mean autonomous success rate of 98% with at most 25 minutes of real-world interaction per task. Experiments show that dense rewards improve interaction efficiency over sparse rewards, and simulation-based policy initialization further accelerates learning.
authors: Shu'ang Sun, Yibo Qiu, Haoliang Ye, Zan Huang, Ao Tian, Kan Ding, Ronald Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses costly real-world demonstrations and the difficulty of obtaining dense process rewards.
Builds digital twins with 3D Gaussian splatting and physics simulation to provide task-aware supervision.

Dense rewards improve interaction efficiency, while simulation-based initialization accelerates learning.

papers.abstract: Vortex grippers are commonly integrated into automated systems for handling objects with complex geometries in packaging, sorting, and assembling. However, their interaction with compliant objects remains difficult to predict, particularly with respect to the vortex-induced torque transmitted during grasping. This study investigates vortex-induced torque during the grasping of compliant objects and quantifies the coupled effects of supply pressure, tangential nozzle diameter, surface geometry, and curvature. The results show that increasing the tangential nozzle diameter primarily enhances the sensitivity of the generated torque to supply pressure rather than producing a uniformly higher torque. Surface geometry also strongly influences the rotational interaction, with dome-concave surfaces generally producing substantially greater torque than corresponding dome-convex surfaces, whereas the difference between cylindrical concave and convex surfaces is comparatively small. The strongest and most repeatable response was observed for a dome-concave surface exhibiting favorable object-gripper geometric matching. Among the evaluated machine-learning regression methods, Gaussian Process Regression provided the best overall predictive performance under repeated cross-validation, demonstrating that vortex-induced torque can be estimated from combined pneumatic and geometric parameters. These findings provide a basis for predicting and utilizing vortex-induced torque in the dexterous manipulation of soft objects.
authors: Roman Mykhailyshyn, Tomohiro Motoda, Ivan Virgala, Ann Majewicz Fey, Yukiyasu Domae
bullets: Increasing tangential nozzle diameter mainly increases torque sensitivity to supply pressure, rather than torque uniformly.
Dome-concave surfaces generally generate substantially more torque than dome-convex surfaces; cylindrical curvature shows little concave–convex difference.
The strongest, most repeatable torque response occurs when dome-concave object and gripper geometries match favorably.
Gaussian Process Regression achieved the best predictive performance among the evaluated regression methods under repeated cross-validation.
The findings support torque prediction and dexterous manipulation of compliant objects with vortex grippers.

papers.abstract: Ensuring safety in advanced robot control methods such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Reinforcement Learning remains an open challenge. A common approach relies on control-invariant sets, yet their exact computation for nonlinear systems is generally intractable, and numerical approximations compromise theoretical guarantees. In this work, we show that safety does not need to rely exclusively on control invariance. We introduce novel classes of safe sets, each broader than classical control-invariant sets, and analyze corresponding MPC schemes that guarantee recursive feasibility by constraining different nodes of the prediction horizon rather than only the terminal state. Furthermore, when the safe set is an inner approximation of a suitable control-invariant set, our methods can ensure safety through a safe-abort strategy, even in the absence of recursive feasibility. We validate our approaches in extensive simulations on a 6-joint robot manipulator, showing fewer constraint violations than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable tracking performance and computational efficiency. Hardware experiments further demonstrate the practicality of our schemes for real-world robotic applications.
authors: Gianni Lunardi, Elias Fontanari, Matteo Saveriano, Andrea Del Prete
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of computing exact control-invariant sets for nonlinear robots without weakening safety guarantees.
Introduces safe sets broader than classical control-invariant sets and constrains multiple prediction-horizon nodes instead of only the terminal state.
Provides recursive-feasibility guarantees and a safe-abort strategy when recursive feasibility cannot be maintained.
Simulations on a 6-joint manipulator show fewer constraint violations with comparable tracking and computational efficiency; hardware tests support practical use.

papers.abstract: Manipulating visually identical objects with different physical properties requires adapting actions based on information acquired through interaction. We address the problem of learning from demonstrations how to adapt manipulation actions, such as regrasping and changing contact locations, based on physical-property information acquired during interaction. To this end, we propose a learning-from-demonstration method that learns latent representations of physical properties needed to predict object responses and conditions a policy on online estimates of these representations. A dynamics model and object-specific latent representations are jointly learned from demonstrations that include behaviors adapting to the objects' physical properties, and the learned representations are then used to condition an imitation policy. During execution, the dynamics model and policy weights remain fixed, while the latent representation is updated based on the discrepancy between predicted and actual observations, allowing interaction with the object to inform action generation. Real-world and simulation experiments with objects whose centers of mass differ suggest that online adaptation through latent representations of physical properties can improve task success rates. However, in simulation, success rates on center-of-mass locations absent from the demonstrations remained around 30%, indicating limited adaptation to unseen physical properties. Project page: https://isri-aist.github.io/latent-dynamics-project-page/
authors: Kotaro Kajitsuka, Masaki Murooka, Fumio Kanehiro
bullets: Targets visually identical objects whose differing physical properties require actions such as regrasping or changing contact locations.

papers.abstract: In this study, we focus on service robots that retrieve and transport everyday objects based on free-form instructions that may refer to visual features and scene text. This is challenging because it requires a multimodal understanding of the visual features and spatial relationships of objects, as well as scene text embedded in the environment. To address this, we propose Scene Text-Aware multimodal Retrieval for Everyday objects (STARE), which leverages visual and textual cues in response to free-form instructions. STARE introduces Crosslingual Visual Prompt to enhance scene text interpretation, and models the complex relationships between named entities in the instructions and their corresponding objects. We evaluate STARE using two novel benchmarks, GoGetIt and TextCaps-test, both of which consist of real-world indoor/outdoor images and instructions involving object manipulation and navigation. The results show that STARE outperforms all baseline methods on standard multimodal retrieval metrics. Furthermore, in physical experiments conducted under a zero-shot transfer setting, STARE achieves an overall success rate of 80%. Our project page and code are provided in the Supplementary Materials.
authors: Kento Tokura, Ryosuke Korekata, Daichi Yashima, Kei Katsumata, Kanon Amemiya, Miyu Goko, Komei Sugiura

papers.abstract: Embodied and edge systems increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to support heterogeneous skills, yet deploying a separate task adapter for each skill while retaining a high-precision backbone creates substantial memory and management costs. We present UniCompress, a deployment-oriented framework that converts multi-task expertise into one compact, adapter-free model. Starting from a consolidated BF16 Qwen3-VL-4B teacher, UniCompress constructs an asymmetric INT2 student using GPTQ initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery. The approach jointly quantizes and recovers the projection weights in the vision encoder and language backbone, enabling aggressive compression of the complete vision-language model while preserving its multi-task behavior. We evaluate UniCompress on four heterogeneous embodied tasks: posture recognition, household-safety understanding, multimodal dialogue routing, and mobile-GUI action prediction. UniCompress reduces the approximate weight storage from 8.9 GB in BF16 to 2.1 GB in INT2, corresponding to a reduction of approximately 76%. It improves the INT2 macro task score by 34.3 percentage points over GPTQ-INT2 while remaining within 0.9 points of the consolidated BF16 teacher. These results demonstrate the potential of teacher-guided joint vision-language INT2 recovery for deploying a single multi-skill VLM on resource-constrained embodied platforms.
authors: Mingkang Liu, Peipei Jiao, Weiming Meng, Tianyuan Liu, Lichen Pang, Junyan Li

papers.abstract: Existing audio-visual segmentation methods mainly predict sound-related regions or category masks and often fail to identify the sounding instance when multiple same-class candidates coexist. Recent audio-visual instance segmentation methods address instance-level prediction but rely largely on motion and cross-frame association, which may become unreliable under sparse observations or inconspicuous motion. To this end, we introduce binaural audio, whose interaural differences encode source-direction information, to provide spatial constraints for distinguishing the sounding instance among same-class visual candidates. We propose Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation (BiSID-AVS), which progressively refines category-level candidate responses into a mask of the true sounding instance. BiSID-AVS first grounds category-consistent candidate regions through audio prompting, then projects binaural cues into an image-plane spatial response map, and finally refines the true sounding instance through dual-level spatial conditioning at the feature and decoder levels. Experiments on the binaurally extended AVS-Synthetic benchmark and Habitat-AVS dataset for robotic indoor perception show that BiSID-AVS achieves the best performance on the multi-candidate subsets, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points, respectively, while substantially reducing false activation on non-sounding same-class regions.
authors: Haoze Ma, Yidi Li, Yu Ma, Pengyuan Zhao, Yi Shi, Bin Ren, Yanwen Guo, Dimitrios Kanoulas
bullets: Targets a key weakness of audio-visual segmentation: confusing which instance is producing the sound.
Uses interaural differences in binaural audio to infer sound-source direction and constrain visual selection.
Progressively refines category-level candidates through audio prompting, image-plane spatial mapping, and dual-level spatial conditioning.
Achieves the best multi-candidate performance on AVS-Synthetic and Habitat-AVS, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points.
Reduces false activation on non-sounding regions of the same class; the method is evaluated particularly for sparse or inconspicuous-motion scenarios.

papers.abstract: Manipulating diverse objects with multi-fingered dexterous hands is challenging due to the high dimensionality and complex dynamics. Human-Object Interaction (HOI) datasets provide rich knowledge about task information and embodied interactions. Instead of solely imitating the human demonstrations, our method learns to holistically predict future hand-object states by leveraging these datasets. The predicted future states of the object can serve as a general-purpose reward term for reinforcement learning, reducing reliance on task-specific reward engineering and enhancing generalization across tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on three manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world. Our approach outperforms existing SOTA methods in both success rate and generalizability on novel objects. Furthermore, we validate the cross-embodiment compatibility of our methods by successfully deploying the skills on different robot hands.
bullets: Addresses the high-dimensional, complex dynamics of multi-fingered manipulation of diverse objects.
Predicts future hand–object states holistically rather than directly imitating human demonstrations.

Evaluated across three simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, including novel objects.

papers.abstract: Integrating six-axis tactile feedback into robotic interfaces requires compact sensors with accurate load measurement and rapid online reconstruction. This paper presents LumiTac, a low-profile, camera-free optoelectronic tactile sensor combining spatially distributed illumination with spectral encoding. Five photoemitters and five RGBW photoreceivers are mounted on opposing circuit boards coupled through translucent silicone. Load-induced interlayer motion modulates the internal light field under compression, shear, bending, and torsion. The sensing head measures 12 mm in diameter and 4.75 mm in thickness, weighs less than 2 g, and has a component cost of approximately USD 7. A compact multilayer perceptron reconstructs three force and three moment components from 20 optical channels. Independent testing yielded coefficients of determination (R-squared) of 0.9657-0.9941, with mean absolute errors of 0.054-0.190 N for forces and 0.304-1.419 mN m for moments. Online prediction achieved an average update rate of 303.57 Hz and a median software processing latency of 0.722 ms. Experiments involving combined loading, light weights, and rapid tapping evaluated load tracking, sensitivity to small forces, and transient response, respectively. Robotic demonstrations further validated its applicability to tactile-guided manipulation and physical human-robot interaction. This study paves the way for compact, high-rate optical tactile sensing in robotic manipulation and human-robot interaction.
authors: Hao Wu, Haotian Guo, Yu Feng, Yutong Wang, Jianshu Zhou

papers.abstract: Off-policy deep reinforcement learning trains on random samples from a replay buffer of past experience. In physical robot settings, that buffer is dominated by routine: thousands of near-identical transitions from normal operation, while the rare events that define the edges of the task are rarely sampled. We propose scoring every stored transition by its statistical leverage, which measures how unusual it is relative to the buffer's own data, computed from the stored numbers alone, with no labels, rewards, or value network. We draw each mini-batch from a mixture of this score and uniform sampling. First, the natural way to build the score along the directions where the data varies most turns out to be blind when actions are stored as one-hot indicators, because indicator columns always win the variance ranking; we instead select the feature columns with the heaviest tails (largest kurtosis) where small far-away populations are revealed. Second, the importance weights that prioritized replay uses to keep gradients unbiased cancel the method exactly: with full correction, training matches uniform sampling, so we drop the correction and deliberately optimize the rebalanced objective. Third, when the rare situations of a log are relational, visible only in how a stretch of behavior relates to its goal, not in any single stored coordinate-per-transition scores are blind; applying the same tail rule to short trajectory windows described relative to their goal restores the signal, and on a three-joint arm that must push an object around an obstacle it raises the rare-task success from 0.49 to 0.69 against a labeled-oracle ceiling of 0.74.
bullets: Addresses replay-buffer imbalance, where routine transitions overwhelm rare edge cases in off-policy robot learning.
Scores transitions without labels, rewards, or a value network, mixing leverage-based sampling with uniform sampling.
Uses kurtosis to select heavy-tailed features because variance-based selection is misled by one-hot action indicators.
Omits importance-weight correction because full correction cancels the prioritization effect and recovers uniform training.

papers.abstract: An ordered sequence of end-effector poses can give a redundant robot arm multiple valid joint configurations at each waypoint. Inverse kinematics (IK) computes these configurations. Choosing a configuration only for the next waypoint can leave the arm poorly placed for later waypoints. This may increase planned motion time or cause a later planning failure. This paper presents Future-Window Inverse Kinematics (FWIK), an online method that selects IK solutions by considering a small window of future waypoints. FWIK generates several IK candidates, connects them in a layered joint-space graph, and ranks candidate paths with a simple motion-time estimate. A learned model removes paths whose transitions are likely to cause self-collision. A standard MoveIt 2 planner then checks the next-waypoint IK goals from the remaining paths in ranked order, and the first goal that yields a valid trajectory is selected for execution. We evaluate FWIK in simulation on two 7-DoF manipulators, the Franka Emika Panda and the KUKA LBR iiwa. Each method-planner setting contains five repetitions of 100 sequences with 50 waypoints. Across Pilz, RRT-Connect, CHOMP, and STOMP, FWIK completes 96.8-100% of sequences and gives the shortest planned trajectory duration in all eight robot-planner settings. Its mean duration is 12.8-13.1% lower than STAMPEDE, 22.5-25.6% lower than IKLink, and 27.5-37.2% lower than retry-based TRAC-IK. The results show that a small future window can improve sequence completion and reduce planned motion time while leaving final trajectory validation to the motion planner.
authors: Jinglan Cao, Guohui Zhong, Chengwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses failures and inefficient motions caused by choosing IK solutions greedily for only the next waypoint.
Builds a layered joint-space graph of candidate IK solutions and ranks paths using estimated motion time.
Uses a learned model to filter likely self-collision transitions, then validates candidate next-waypoint goals with MoveIt 2.
In simulation on Panda and KUKA LBR iiwa arms, FWIK completed 96.8–100% of sequences and achieved the shortest planned duration across eight robot-planner settings.
Reported mean durations were 12.8–13.1% lower than STAMPEDE, 22.5–25.6% lower than IKLink, and 27.5–37.2% lower than retry-based TRAC-IK.

papers.abstract: Assessing the deployment performance of learned robot policies during training is challenging, as directly measuring task success requires costly real-world trials for each candidate checkpoint. Averaged validation loss offers a rollout-free alternative, but its checkpoint rankings can be inconsistent with deployment performance. We analyze two limitations of this criterion: it penalizes action deviations without considering whether the policy can recover from them, and gives later reference predictions equal weight even when earlier deviations may lead execution away from the reference. We propose RACE, a novel rollout-free metric for ranking checkpoints using a fixed set of held-out successful trajectories. RACE calibrates action deviations against state-conditional thresholds derived from action differences at similar states in these trajectories. We aggregate these scores through a running product, so that a substantial deviation reduces the contribution of subsequent reference predictions. Averaging the resulting cumulative scores over time and across trajectories yields the checkpoint score. In simulation, RACE outperforms baselines across validation sources, while several baselines degrade sharply when the validation set changes. On real robots, its rankings align with deployment success across the evaluated policy backbones and tasks of varying difficulty. Perturbation analyses further show that RACE distinguishes deviations with markedly different effects on task success, even when baselines respond similarly.
authors: Changyeon Kim, Yekyung Nah, Kimin Lee
bullets: Problem: Validation loss can rank policy checkpoints poorly because it ignores recovery from deviations and overweights later predictions after earlier errors.
Method: Calibrate action deviations using state-conditional thresholds from held-out successful trajectories, then combine scores with a running product.
Contribution: Produce checkpoint scores by averaging cumulative scores over time and trajectories without requiring real-world rollouts.
Results: RACE outperforms baselines in simulation, remains consistent across validation sources, and aligns with real-robot deployment success across tasks and policy backbones.
Scope: Evaluated in simulation and on real robots; the abstract does not specify broader generalization beyond these settings.

papers.abstract: We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.
authors: Yang Liu, Tong Wang, Yiming Bao, Heng Yang
bullets: Targets retargeting of human demonstrations under contact-rich robot dynamics.
GRASP-TO fits local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and uses recovered gradients to guide MCMC proposals, with Metropolis-Hastings correction.
GRASP-MPC extends the approach to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning.
Achieves 92.8% success on 1,352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations using a shared tracking objective without task-specific contact rewards.
Improves PPO tracking and transfers to dexterous and whole-body humanoid manipulation on real hardware.

papers.abstract: This paper presents Proactive Human-in-the-Loop (PHIL), a framework for proactive policy correction and preference-based post-training. PHIL enables operators to preview policy-predicted future motion and intervene before anticipated undesirable actions. During takeover, PHIL continues querying the policy and displaying its predicted trajectories in the physical workspace through an extended reality (XR) interface. PHIL pairs rejected policy predictions with corrective action chunks subsequently executed from the same physical state over the same horizon, and preference-based post-training encourages the policy to favor these corrections. This paper evaluates PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks using a diffusion policy and a pretrained vision-language-action policy. With five correction episodes per condition, PHIL increases mean success rates across the evaluated tasks and demonstration budgets from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger. Separately, policies trained with proactive corrections show fewer unnecessary recovery behaviors in successful episodes. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/PHIL-page/.
authors: Xinkai Jiang, Jing Jiang, Hongyi Zhou, Pankhuri Vanjani, Ahmad Baki, Jakub Suliga, Ge Li, Zhuoyue Li, Gerhard Neumann, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Addresses the limitation of correcting robots only after undesirable actions begin.
Uses an extended-reality interface to display predicted trajectories and enable proactive takeovers.
Pairs rejected predictions with corrective action chunks from the same state and horizon for preference-based post-training.
Evaluated on four real-world manipulation tasks with diffusion and vision-language-action policies.
Compared with HG-DAgger, mean success increased from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA.

papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant. Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions. This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives. Additional materials can be found on: https://end2end-latent-action.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of action-labeled robot data by leveraging action-free video demonstrations.
Jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder for downstream control.
Uses lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders without changing existing policy architectures or training objectives.
Outperforms prior latent-action baselines on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Scope: applies to imitation learning with video demonstrations and limited robot action labels.

papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: https://pairlab.github.io/MESA.
authors: Albert Wilcox, Frank Chang, Nhi Nguyen, Aishani Chakraborty, Jeremy A. Collins, Vaibhav Saxena, Benjamin Joffe, Siddharth Karamcheti, Animesh Garg
bullets: Evaluates in-distribution performance plus four distinct generalization axes: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition.
Uses MESA-Gen, an improved MimicGen-based pipeline, to generate tasks and demonstrations at scale.
Releases single-arm MESA and BiMESA, a large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization.
Across seven baseline methods, the strongest model reaches 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, leaving substantial room for improvement.
MESA rankings broadly agree with RoboArena scores, suggesting relevance beyond simulation.

papers.tldr: MESA is a reproducible robotics benchmark that isolates spatial, object, category, and compositional generalization, revealing substantial weaknesses in current language-conditioned policies.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion tracking has scaled to general policies that reproduce diverse human motion, but the resulting behavior is in free-space: the tracker knows where the body should be, not how it should interact with the environment. Other work makes the object part of the objective, yet abstracts that interaction to contact or geometry, which leaves the demanding cases under-explored. We argue that force is a natural command channel between motion imitation and object interaction, one that specifies not just where to make contact but how hard. We present Ctrl-F, a hierarchical motion-force framework that augments motion tracking with an explicit force command, a 3-D force at each designated contact body such as a hand or a foot. The hierarchical framework comprises: (1) A unified motion-force controller tracks the reference motion while applying the commanded force to the world. (2) A high-level force planner that issues a force command online based on object state and proprioception observations. In simulation and on hardware, Ctrl-F completes loco-manipulation that demands large, sustained interaction force and adjusts its command online as the load changes, both out of reach of a force-blind tracker. On hardware, Ctrl-F demonstrates hand-based dragging, pushing, and lifting, as well as foot-based kicking, successfully manipulating boxes weighing up to 20kg in pushing and kicking tasks where the force-blind baseline fails, while adapting online to additional loads introduced mid-task.
authors: Mengjie Zhao, Yuxin Chen, Yiyang Shao, Chuye Hong, Jiakang Chen, Koushil Sreenath, Masayoshi Tomizuka
bullets: Addresses the gap between free-space motion imitation and environment interaction requiring sustained physical force.
Uses a hierarchical framework with a unified motion-force controller and an online force planner informed by object state and proprioception.
Supports force commands at designated contact bodies, including hands and feet.
Simulation and hardware experiments show online adaptation to changing loads during dragging, pushing, lifting, and kicking.
On hardware, it manipulates boxes up to 20 kg in pushing and kicking tasks where a force-blind tracker fails.

figures.caption: Figure 9 | Weight added mid-task on hardware. Top: adapting to weight added mid-drag. In every setting the cart is loaded while the robot is already dragging the cart, whose wheels stay locked throughout (arrow marks the loading). Frames are composited at equal time intervals; the spacing between poses is therefore speed. SONIC is given the easier test, an empty cart that takes 8 kg, because it cannot start a loaded cart moving at all; even so, it stops once the weight goes in. The two variants of our method start at 8 kg and take a further 6 kg. Under a command frozen at what the high-level force planner itself issued for the initial load, the robot keeps walking but slows, its poses bunching together after the change, while the full hierarchy holds its pace. Those two share a tracker, an interface and a starting force command, and differ only in whether that command is allowed to change. Bottom: An additional 1 kg is added to a 1 kg bag hanging from the forearm. The dashed line indicates the wrist height before loading. With zero force command, the wrist drops below this line, whereas the high-level force planner adapts its command to maintain the original height.

Figure 1 | Ctrl-F on hardware, running the raise-walk-kick sequence with a 1 kg box in the hands and an 8 kg cart to kick. Raising the box is already a force task: the hands slide off a box they do not press into, and a tracker without a force command does not lift it at all.

Figure 5 | (a) Q1(b): completion and forced-body error as the replayed wrench is scaled, averaged over all twelve clips. One trace per clip is replayed identically to the four settings and scaled together with the command each is given, so the settings differ only in the command they receive. The three command variants are one policy and coincide at zero load. The scale is the fraction of the per-body command range the wrench uses, so 1.0 means the same thing on a wrist (60N) and an ankle (30N) and nothing plotted is out of distribution. Dashed line is the 90% completion level. Errors are over all active steps, a convention that flatters a setting that terminates early. (b) Commanded force through an in-episode mass change on the tethered hold and the raised box, summed over force bodies. The solid line is a moving average and the shaded band is the spread it removed, the minimum and maximum within the same window; the grey column is the mass ramp; the dashed line adds 𝑔 Δ𝑚, the change in the object’s weight, to the force before the change. A tethered box is an undamped pendulum and the commanded force oscillates with its swing, so the trend rather than the raw trace carries the reading.

Figure 2 | Ctrl-F. Stage 1 trains the motion–force tracker without objects: a force command is randomly sampled and its corresponding inverse force is applied to the robot, teaching the tracker to follow its reference while exerting the commanded load. tage 2 freezes that tracker and learns the force command itself from object and robot state, supervised by the analytical force model and refined by reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Data flywheels promise continuous improvement via insights from deployment data. Understanding how the deployed model succeeds and fails can steer subsequent data collection towards patching failures and reinforcing successes. However, robot deployments create large volumes of high-dimensional rollout data, which is challenging to understand and confidently ground data collection decisions in. To make deployment data easier to analyze and act on, we propose behavior graphs, which compress policy rollouts into a single interpretable, directed graph. We construct the graphs by learning to identify similar behavior modes across rollouts, connecting the behaviors temporally, and finally linking them to outcomes. In a user study on three real-world tasks, where participants analyzed rollouts to choose a data collection strategy, 16 of 18 preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, reaching comparable conclusions with 40.3% lower perceived temporal demand and 37.6% lower effort. Beyond interpretability for deployment data, behavior graphs are capable progress predictors: across 43 datasets, they improve the rank correlation between predicted progress and true temporal order by 22.9% and reduce mean absolute error by 53.5% relative to the strongest baseline. As the number of deployed robots grows, behavior graphs lend structure to high-dimensional policy rollouts and make deployment data easier to interpret and reason about.
authors: Erik Bauer, Jakob Thumm, Christopher Agia, Rohan Sinha, Chen Xu, Haruki Nishimura, Jeannette Bohg, Marco Pavone, Masha Itkina
bullets: Robot deployments generate high-dimensional rollout data that is difficult to interpret and use for data-collection decisions.
The method discovers similar behavior modes, connects them over time, and links them to outcomes in a directed graph.
In a user study across three real-world tasks, 16 of 18 participants preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, with lower perceived time demand and effort.
Across 43 datasets, behavior graphs improved progress-order rank correlation and reduced prediction error relative to the strongest baseline.
The approach is evaluated for deployment-data interpretation and progress prediction; its scope is limited to the studied tasks and datasets.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Behavior graph construction. Left: Each trajectory’s state-action pairs are embedded, mean-pooled over temporal windows, and assigned to behavior modes by dimensionality reduction and clustering fit on all trajectories. Consecutive windows with the same mode are collapsed into segments, and a VLM captions each mode. Right: The resulting behavior sequences from all trajectories are merged into a single directed graph from a start node to success and failure outcomes, with edges weighted by empirical transition probabilities.

Fig. 4: Tasks for the user study, in which participants analyze policy rollouts to choose which demonstrations to collect next. Keyframes of a successful rollout from left to right. (a) Set table: places a pumpkin, then a milk carton from the shelf; the training data omits the carton’s leftmost position. (b) Prepare tray: slides out a tray, places a bowl from the top or bottom shelf onto it, and grasps a fork, requiring precise grasps. (c) Cooking: a long-horizon task that clears a ladle, adds a corn, carrot, and chili to the pot, and closes the lid.

Fig. 5: Targeted data helps only when it addresses the policy’s most frequent failure mode. Estimated success rates [27] of the baseline policy and of policies retrained with 30 additional demonstrations for each candidate data-collection strategy, on three real-world DROID tasks. In Set table, only demonstrations with the milk carton on the left (the position missing from the baseline training data) improve performance. In Prepare tray, bottom-shelf bowl demonstrations improve over the baseline. In Cooking, no single-subtask strategy makes a significant difference. Violins show the Bayesian posterior over each policy’s success rate (uniform Beta prior). Dots and bars mark the posterior mean and 95% credible interval. Letters above each column [28] summarize pairwise significance tests within a task [29]: two policies that share a letter are not significantly different; policies with no letter in common are. Tests follow [29] with family-wise error rate controlled at 5%, and 60 policy rollouts to estimate each posterior. Below, histograms show the strategies participants chose with the graph and with the video browser, which are similar.

Fig. 3: Behavior graph for the cooking task of our user study (Sec. IV-A). The larger the node, the higher the visitation count. Node colors indicate success likelihood (increasing from red to green), while all terminal nodes are annotated with their likelihoods. Branches with less than 2% likelihood are pruned to simplify visualization.

Fig. 6: Behavior graphs make rollout analysis less demanding without changing the decisions users reach. Responses from 18 participants. (a) When free to choose a display for the third task, 16 of 18 participants picked the behavior graph over the video browser. (b-d) Selfreported ratings (0-100, in steps of 20) after analyzing a task with each display: the graph lowers perceived temporal demand (b) and effort (c), while confidence in the chosen data-collection strategy is unchanged (d). Boxes span the interquartile range with the median marked, whiskers span min/max values; dots are individual ratings. (e) The success rate regret (i.e., the gap between the best retrained policy in Fig. 5 and the one the participant selected) is similar for graph and videos. Arrows indicate whether higher (↑) or lower (↓) is better. Tab. I reports the corresponding effects adjusted for task, stage, and experience.

TABLE II: Progress-estimation metrics over 43 datasets spanning 4 domains. AUC is undefined for the two Robomimic datasets in which every rollout succeeds (Can-PH, Lift-PH), so the Robomimic and Average AUC entries are over 8 and 41 datasets. On average, graph-based progress estimation outperforms all baselines in the fidelity of the prediction. In AUC, which measures success classification induced by the progress estimates, Robometer outperforms on average.

TABLE III: Ablation study results for subtask segmentation. We report mean ± std over 3 datasets. Each mean row averages every dataset’s score over the three reductions, then reports the mean ± std of those averages across datasets. We report F1 at 0.75 IoU threshold and the mean IoU over matched segments. On average, policy embeddings outperform proprioception and frozen DINOv3 features. While there is no clear quantitative conclusion for reductions, UMAP performs more consistently than the others and is what we use for our other experiments.

TABLE I: Effect of the behavior graph after adjusting for task, study stage, participant experience, and individual differences in scale use. We report estimated marginal means per visualization from the mixed-effects model and their difference. papers.tldr: Behavior graphs turn complex robot rollouts into interpretable temporal graphs that help people analyze deployments and predict task progress more efficiently.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings. For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know. Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries. We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know. Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly. Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras. Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers' coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab.
bullets: Covers 30 quantitative science experiments across five disciplines and 14 simulated laboratory apparatuses.
Agents receive a goal and apparatus, choose experimental procedures, and use camera-based instrument readings to investigate resampled systems.
Evaluation scores both the knowledge acquired from recorded observations and the required resulting physical state; all tasks are verified solvable.
Six frontier models are tested with native control, enhanced perception and planning, and distilled manipulation skills.
With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; apparatus interaction causes most failures, while manipulation skills particularly help weaker agents.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of EmbodiedLab. Thirty quantitative experiments in five disciplines ask the agent to measure, predict or configure a system drawn anew per instance, by changing its state and reading the feedback on the instruments. Agents are ranked by their success rate at the lowest interface level, T0, and also evaluated at T1; the diagnostic level T2 and four capability dimensions serve the analysis.

(b) The agent acts and observes through three cameras while the environment keeps a record. (c) Success requires every gate and an error within tolerance of the hidden target.

Figure 7. Overview of the 30 experiments, grouped by primary capability dimension, as seen by one of the robot’s fixed cameras during a reference run. The tag gives the tier.

Figure 4. Interface levels. Robot, bench and camera views are the same at every level; each level supplies more between the agent and the robot. (a) T0 supplies only the camera images, the robot state, joint position targets and gripper commands. papers.abstract: Cascade world-action models (WAMs) use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, but inherit costly iterative inference from diffusion-pretrained experts. We ask what a single-step predicted future must preserve to support accurate single-step action prediction. In the evaluated WAM, resampling video noise has little effect on downstream actions, yet naively truncating both streams to one step substantially reduces task success. Video-space supervision only partially closes this gap, and a local sensitivity analysis shows that vision prediction errors have highly unequal consequences for action accuracy. These findings motivate DirectWAM, which converts pretrained video and action experts into single-step predictors without stochastic sampling through action-sufficient distillation, while retaining the explicit future-to-action cascade. After learning a one-step action model, we train the future predictor by decoding actions from its own predicted futures and backpropagating demonstration action error through the expert, with an optional future-latent reconstruction loss. The resulting objective evaluates the student-generated future through its downstream control consequences rather than relying on representation matching alone. DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success across four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same one-evaluation-per-stream budget. This advantage has also extended to three real-world tasks that we designed. Compared with the full iterative teacher, it reduces inference latency by $28.0\times$.
bullets: WAMs can lose task success when diffusion inference is naively reduced to one step, even though video-noise resampling has little effect on actions.
Vision prediction errors have unequal impacts on action accuracy, motivating action-sufficient rather than purely representation-matching distillation.
DirectWAM retains the future-to-action cascade and trains the future predictor through downstream demonstration-action error, with optional future-latent reconstruction.
It achieves 97.1% average success on four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same inference budget.
The method also extends to three designed real-world tasks and reduces latency 28.0× versus the full iterative teacher.

papers.selection_reason: Robot control via action-conditioned world-action models; directly relevant to robot policy learning and interactive world prediction.
papers.title: De-Diffusing WAMs: Action-Sufficient Direct Prediction for Robot Control
papers.tldr: DirectWAM distills cascade world-action models into fast, single-step predictors by training future representations for their downstream control value, achieving strong simulated and real-world performance with 28× lower latency than iterative inference.

papers.abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
authors: Jisoo Kim, Chaehyun Kim, Junsu Kim, Jiho Park, Seongchan Kim, Eunbeen Hong, Soowon Son, Fu-En Yang, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of disentangling action dynamics from embodiment- and appearance-specific visual variation.
Extracts latent actions from rich spatiotemporal video features and compresses each frame 300×, from 1,200 to 4 tokens.
Uses the diffusion model’s generative prior to create a shared action interface for humans and robots.
Supports any-to-any video transfer, zero-shot action transfer, and policy learning in a compact latent action space.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARY-Bench, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2{\deg} on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.
authors: Yuhan Liu, Xinqi Liu, Zixuan Dong, Keith W. Ross, Shenji Wan
