papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator's intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision-language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop. We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists. More information at https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/guild2026/
authors: Shivin Dass, Kevin Nguyen, Rohan Yelandur, Junhong Xu, Roberto Mart\'in-Mart\'in

papers.abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs \$21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus \$5 for a render contract; every further episode costs \$0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs \$107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of \$117 for teleoperation in China and below \$290 in labour alone in North America.
authors: Kewei Zhang, Juncheng Ma, Guodong Lv, Duomin Wang, Feixiang Ruan, Ruiyang Si, Chuanrui Zhang, Yuxuan Chen, Hao Chen, Yichen Liu, Yintianrun Zhang, Yufan Deng, Enze Xie, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Teleoperation is costly and must be repeated from scratch for each new task.

On five real-robot tasks, farm-only policies achieved 93/100 successes versus 84/100 for policies trained on equally many teleoperated episodes.

Under an unseen tablecloth and colored lighting, farm-trained policies achieved 87/100 successes versus 46/100 for teleoperation-trained policies; average episode cost was $0.80 after $21 task setup and a $5 render contract.

papers.abstract: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .
authors: Charles Xu, Jacob Berg, Liyiming Ke, Sergey Levine
bullets: Existing behavior-cloning regularizers overconstrain policies by preserving suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints block improvements just outside the base policy’s support.
GSBR applies zero penalty to actions within the estimated base-policy support and a smoothly increasing distance penalty outside it.
The support distance is estimated from finite samples, requiring only sample access to the base policy.
Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR increased average success from 33% for the base policy to 95%.
The method achieved the highest reported average success and throughput among compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation involves not only moving objects, but also arranging the hand around them to maintain useful contacts and enable subsequent actions. Yet many learning-based systems specify goals primarily through object poses or trajectories, leaving hand-object configurations to emerge implicitly. We introduce DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as hand-object configuration transfer: moving between feasible configurations that jointly specify hand articulation and object pose relative to the wrist. DexHOT learns a reusable relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs, without human reference motions, and composes long-horizon behaviors through closed-loop tracking of configuration subgoals. On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand, it achieves 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks. These results show that explicit hand-object goals provide an expressive and composable interface for dexterous manipulation. More details and videos are available at https://dex-hot.github.io/.
authors: Zhewei Gui, Anthony Bolton, Jiyao Zhang, Zeyuan Chen, Qiyang Yan, Tianyu Wang, Hao Dong

Achieves 80.5% success on seen objects, 69.4% on unseen objects, and 61.5% on 200 real-robot transfers.
Demonstrates 90% task success across six real-world demonstration-guided tasks.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical pipelines for humanoid loco-manipulation typically pair a task-agnostic whole-body controller (WBC) with a downstream task policy. Such WBCs are often trained through manual reward shaping, which yields visibly machine-like motions; more consequentially, they are trained without the manipulated object in the scene. Object dynamics are instead approximated through randomized end-effector force disturbances, a proxy that fails to reproduce the distributed multi-contact wrench a real payload applies across the arms and torso, with the gap becoming critical near the platform's payload limit. In this work, we train the low-level (LL) controller itself as an object-aware motion prior: a single policy trained via motion imitation on retargeted motion-capture (MoCap) references that span the core motion primitives of the downstream task, with the manipulated object physically present in the scene. This single stage inherits natural human-like coordination from the references and absorbs the realistic contact wrench at its source, while exposing the same compact task-space command interface used by command-tracking WBCs. A reference-free high-level (HL) policy is then trained on top, with its action channel anchored to the empirical envelope of the low-level training data so that it generalizes the priors to a long-horizon multi-stage task while structurally preventing queries that would push the low level off-distribution. We instantiate the framework on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place: the same deployed policy generalizes across object masses and dimensions, initial and goal poses, and reactively recovers from intentional drops mid-carry. Video: https://youtu.be/viR_ULnRDQQ.
authors: Jean-Pierre Sleiman, Bilal Hammoud, He Li, Jonathan Foster, Sylvain Bertrand, Jessica K. Hodgins, Farbod Farshidian
bullets: Addresses machine-like motions and inaccurate object modeling in conventional WBC-based humanoid loco-manipulation.

Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place across varying objects and poses.
The policy recovers reactively from intentional drops during carrying.

The frozen πLL is reused by a reference-free high-level policy πHL observing proprioception, box face centers, and a sparse goal, producing commands within the LL dataset envelope and stitching the learned priors into the full behavior for zero-shot deployment.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/
authors: Po-Yi Wu, Djengo Cyun-Jyun Fang, Dian Cheng, Tsung-Wei Ke
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of frequent scene resets and human intervention in real-world RL deployment.
Introduces a high-fidelity simulation benchmark for non-episodic VLA fine-tuning in shared-scene, multi-task settings.
Finds that naively fine-tuning pretrained policies fails under shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses.
Shows that targeted reset allocation and mitigation of pretrained-model biases improve non-episodic training.
Reports better long-horizon manipulation and generalization to unseen object configurations and task sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Forced reset of unrecoverable scenes outperforms learned reset strategies. Only methods that forcibly reset all unrecoverable scenes (HSR and HSR-only) show a sustained increase in success rate.

Figure 12: Visualization of reset-free methods. We compare five methods: (1) periodic reset (PR), which resets the scene every T = 2560 steps; (2) heuristic scene reset (HSR), which detects unrecoverable states before each task switch and resets only when necessary; (3) heuristic scene reset without periodic reset (HSR-only), which uses heuristic resets without periodic resets, avoiding unnecessary resets in recoverable states; (4) learned scene reset (LSR), which learns reset behavior as an auxiliary task within a single policy, eliminating external reset logic at the cost of interaction budget; and (5) perturbation policy (PER), which extends LSR with a second auxiliary task that perturbs the scene, with the two tasks sampled uniformly at random.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.
authors: Yihang Liu, Yiming Chen, Mingzhe Zheng
bullets: Addresses whether multimodal robot agents must repeatedly reinterpret visual observations during interaction.
Represents object-part geometry with typed, evidence-aware symbolic references grounded in calibrated RGB-D.
Provides compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after actions, while refreshing only locally observed state.
Supports offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution with visual reasoning invoked on demand.

papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
bullets: Physical-AI policy errors can compound over trajectories, causing distribution shift and task failure.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.
authors: Xingyu Wang, Yanjiang Guo, Zhijing Ding, Jiaxin Fang, Zeyu Lai, Jiayu Dong, Weikang Wan, Jianyu Chen, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the limited long-range context and high computational cost of dense short-horizon WAM prediction.
Uses sparse long-horizon and dense local-dynamics visual streams at different temporal scales.
A unified dual-DiT architecture connects the streams with structured cross-stream attention to guide actions.
Progressive inference with partial, joint, and dynamically skipped denoising achieves a reported 2.93× speedup.
Reports 93.70% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with in-domain and OOD performance on Fourier GR-3.

papers.abstract: We investigate the automated generation of executable robot reinforcement learning (RL) policies from natural-language task descriptions. Rather than using large language models (LLMs) as execution-time decision makers, we use them as designers that construct RL pipelines before deployment, including Markov decision process (MDP) formulation and simulator implementation. We identify a phase-wise structure in this problem: MDP formulation is dependency-structured and sequential, whereas simulator implementation becomes modular once the formulation is fixed. Based on this structure, we propose ARPG, a dependency-aware agentic framework that performs sequential MDP modeling, localized verification and correction, and simulator-structured implementation while externalizing intermediate artifacts. ARPG targets a key failure mode of automated policy generation: executable code may still yield non-learnable policies when state, action, reward, and termination artifacts are not semantically aligned. Experiments in Isaac Sim show that ARPG improves modeling correctness, environment executability, and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Additional demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL, and engineering-domain MDPs further suggest that the same modeling pipeline can be reused beyond the main benchmark suite.
authors: Hong Je-Gal, Jinwoo Kim, Chanbin Yi, Hyun-Suk Lee

papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.
authors: Jianye Xu, Yousef Sayed, Bassam Alrifaee

papers.abstract: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/
authors: Ju Dong, Xinyu Xiao, Yiming Zhou, Tianshuo Yang, Xuerong Liu, Lei Zhang, Jian Chen, Haocheng Zhao, Yu Fu, Yujie Wei, Diwen Zheng, Alois Christian Knoll, Angela P. Schoellig, Ping Luo, Jianwei Zhang

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable progress in AI-generated content, including images and videos. In this paper, we explore whether diffusion models can generate the parameters of policy networks in reinforcement learning (RL), and whether the generated policies exhibit generalization capabilities. To achieve this, we propose Diffusion-based Conditional Policy Network Parameter Generation (DPPG), which consists of a Transformer-based autoencoder and a task-conditioned diffusion model. The autoencoder achieves a high compression rate by patchifying network parameters, while the task-conditioned diffusion model generates corresponding parameters conditioned on different environments. Our experiments demonstrate that, with a single unified DPPG model, we can synthesize high-quality policies across a diverse set of tasks from different environment domains, including Classic Control, Atari games, and MuJoCo. Additionally, our method can generate networks with a larger number of parameters compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, we find that in previously unseen environments, DPPG can generate parameters that achieve faster convergence and reach competitive performance, showcasing the potential future applications of parameter generation via diffusion.

papers.abstract: Pretrained generative policies provide strong behavior priors for robot control, but adapting them efficiently with online reinforcement learning remains difficult. A central challenge is how to improve a frozen generative policy without destroying the structure learned from offline demonstrations. Noise-space residual methods address this by modifying the policy's input noise, but existing noise-space methods typically regulate adaptation through fixed latent feasible regions, which may exclude valuable noise edits. In contrast, action-space residual methods are more sample-efficient, but their efficiency can still be further improved. We propose Conservative Noise Directional Optimization (CNDO), a noise-space residual RL method that improves a frozen generative policy by learning state- and noise-conditioned directions around Gaussian latent samples. CNDO removes predefined latent feasible regions and instead regulates noise-space adaptation through the soft conservative constraint, which consists of conservative value estimation and gated execution. We further introduce Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization (CANDO), which adds an action-space residual, combining structured latent-space improvement with local action correction. Experiments show that, once CNDO narrows the gap between noise-space and action-space residual learning, CANDO further improves over single-space optimization, achieving 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, surpassing the best single-space results by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1% success rate. More demos and info are available on https://cando-rl.github.io/.
authors: Zeyu Gao, Chengkai Hou, Chaoyue Li, Zhuangzhe Wu, Jiaming Liu, Yao Mu, Peng Jia, Li Zhang, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting pretrained generative policies with online RL without disrupting demonstration-derived behavior.
CNDO learns state- and noise-conditioned latent directions and uses conservative value estimation plus gated execution instead of fixed latent feasible regions.
CANDO adds an action-space residual to CNDO, combining structured latent improvement with local correction.
Experiments report 76.1 NAUC and 91.4% final success, exceeding the best single-space methods by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1 percentage points.
Scope: the approach targets efficient online adaptation of frozen generative policies for robot control.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.
authors: Jaehyeong Jo, Sangwon Jang, Sihyun Yu, Seonghyeon Ye, Yekyung Nah, Hojung Jung, Kimin Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Avoids costly iterative future-video generation and reduces errors from inaccurate visual predictions.
Uses representation distillation to train a visual encoder that predicts frozen video-diffusion representations from the current observation.
An action module extracts action-relevant information to produce robot actions.
Achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs across real-world and simulated tasks, with 11Hz closed-loop control using a 14B backbone.
Supports leveraging stronger video priors, extra video data, and unannotated demonstrations—including videos from different embodiments—for learning new tasks.

papers.abstract: Natural human-robot interaction requires robots to interpret language and gestures within a 3D environment to support tasks such as pick-and-place and object retrieval. 3D Embodied Reference Understanding (3D-ERU) supports this by identifying the 3D location of a target object from a scene (point-cloud) containing a human pointing gesture and an accompanying language description. However, current 3D-ERU models lack alignment of cross-modal representations and incur high processing costs that increase with the point-cloud's size. To address this, we propose GVT3D, which employs an Embodied Fusion module that jointly models language, gesture, and vision inputs within a shared embedding space, promoting cross-modal alignment. We additionally introduce a foveation approach that selectively processes the point cloud within a coarse region around the estimated pointing direction to reduce computations. GVT3D achieves ~8% higher accuracy and foveation enables 2.95x faster execution while maintaining comparable accuracy, relative to prior 3D-ERU models.
authors: Vimarsh Shah, Dulanga Weerakoon, Ajinkya Deshpande, Saksham Agarwal, Nilesh Bhatia, Neel Kiran Naik, Parth Shah, Sravan Danda, Sanjay E. Sarma, Archan Misra, Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Sougata Sen
bullets: Targets robot understanding of object references from a 3D scene, pointing gesture, and language description.
Uses an Embodied Fusion module to jointly represent language, gesture, and vision in a shared embedding space.
Applies foveation to focus point-cloud processing on a coarse region near the estimated pointing direction.
Reports approximately 8% higher accuracy and 2.95× faster execution with comparable accuracy when foveation is used, relative to prior models.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.
authors: Junhyeong Park, Wook Jung, Taeyoung Kim, Huiwon Jang, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the costly need for target-robot demonstrations caused by the human–robot embodiment gap.
Uses geometry-anchored observation alignment and a decoupled-decoder tokenizer to bridge representation and action spaces.
Enables human demonstrations to provide behavioral supervision while preserving pretrained VLA visual, semantic, and control priors.
Improves object-transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3; skill transfer reaches 62.7.
Scope: evaluated on real-world tasks with unpaired human and robot demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy and field workflows by what their records establish. An appendix provides an evidence map of 28 workflows (26 physical, two software-boundary), characterizing validation pathways and claim confirmation requirements. We propose evaluation that separates actions, valid experiments, campaigns and confirmed claims, framing open challenges as controlled comparisons with measurable failure conditions.
authors: Wenhao Xu, Changwei Wang, Shunpeng Chen, Yukun Song, Sifan Zhou, Kaize Luo, Shibiao Xu, Yuehua Zhao, Rongtao Xu
bullets: Experiments involve latent specimen, apparatus, and measurement states, with irreversible actions and outcome-dependent missing data.
It organizes the field around operational, epistemic, and evidential closure: realizing intended experiments, updating knowledge, and supporting claims.
The Record–Diagnose–Calibrate–Confirm cycle links experiment execution, diagnosis, feedback, and evidence generation.
A taxonomy connects these closures with delegated decisions and embodiment classes, while distinguishing commanded, realized, and observed conditions.
It proposes evaluations that separately measure actions, valid experiments, campaigns, and confirmed claims, and maps validation pathways across 28 workflows.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Four terminal decisions determine the epistemic method comparison. Bayesian optimization recommends a design that requires independent verification; active learning supplies a response map assessed on a declared held-out distribution; Bayesian experimental design distinguishes decision-relevant alternatives; reinforcement learning and model-predictive control choose state-dependent action sequences. Their characteristic failures are different, so method choice and terminal loss must be tied to the scientific endpoint. Curves, maps and trajectories are conceptual illustrations with no empirical performance values.

Figure 2. Historical profile of the 48 representative systems by scientific domain and publication period. Each cell gives the number of systems; (1p) and (2p) mark arXiv preprints already included in that count. Row and column totals make the cohort size explicit. Publication status follows the records selected in the accompanying dataset: Co-Scientist uses its published Nature version, whereas π0 uses its arXiv record. The cohort contains 40 journal articles, five conference papers and three arXiv preprints. Periods are ordered categories, not an annual timeline or an estimate of field-wide growth.

Figure 3. Six delegated decisions as complementary scientific interfaces rather than an automation ladder. Each panel pairs a decision with a schematic glyph and the record it must leave; the glyphs are abstract illustrations, not measured data or depictions of particular apparatus. The bottom Shared record bar represents a unified trial ledger across all six decisions; connecting stems are schematic, and the absence of a drawn stem beneath a panel does not imply that decision omits a record. Access and Prepare primarily serve operational closure; Select serves epistemic closure; Acquire spans operational and epistemic closure; Interpret and Confirm serve evidential closure. A workflow may delegate a subset of the six decisions, and the panels are not a sequence.

Figure 4. Causal execution, observed records and specimen lineage. A decision compiles to a command and requested measurement configuration. The command acts through a latent realized condition and an updated specimen–apparatus state before observations are generated; measurement configuration may affect both state and sensing. A dashed inference link indicates that observed evidence constrains, rather than equals, the latent condition. The trial record stores commands, requested configuration, observations, metadata, audit decisions and trial status; a noisy condition estimate can be part of metadata. An interrupted transfer stays in lineage and a remade specimen receives a new identifier. Record state is distinct from claim state. Apparatus imagery is synthetic.

Figure 1. Three closures around one shared physical experiment. Each row pairs a closure with its realized state, a three-step loop with an error feedback arc, its characteristic failure and the reporting unit it counts. Operational closure compares commanded with realized conditions and recovers from tolerance violations; epistemic closure updates belief from observations and chooses the next experiment; evidential closure turns trial records into candidate claims that need fresh independent confirmation. All three loops read the shared experiment history at the base. The reporting units Nattempted, Nsel and Nconf shown here are distinct, and Nvalid (Section 8) is a further unit; no common denominator or one-to-one mapping across trial and claim units is implied. The diagram is conceptual and reports no measured data.

Figure 6. Operational stack for a physical workcell. Language protocol is an input, not a stack layer: it emits the intent trace. Five operational layers—perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policy, embodiment, and verification and recovery—emit, respectively, a state estimate, typed operation, action trace, recorded condition estimate and recovery trace into the shared trial record, from which evidence obligations are assessed. World models, teleoperation and digital twins support these layers and do not replace physical measurement. Sensing modalities include cameras, tactile gel, force–torque sensing and balance telemetry. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 10. Evidence atlas of 26 physical workflows and two software-boundary components across Access, Prepare, Select, Acquire, Interpret and Confirm. Access uses X for cross-station mobile routing, M for local manipulation, F for fixed-interface or instrument-local control, S for software-boundary components and ? for unresolved routing. For Prepare, Select, Acquire and Interpret, R denotes reported implementation, A assisted or configuration-dependent operation, P planned capability, N scoped-not-reported and ? unresolved. In Confirm, O denotes an orthogonal physical assay, F repeat or follow-up testing, OF both, with P, N and ? carrying the same reported-status meaning. The Access F code (fixed interface) and the Confirm F code (follow-up) are different vocabularies. N and ? indicate absent or unresolved reporting, not experimental failure. The cohort includes two software-boundary components, so not all 28 rows are independent physical executions. Source rechecks retained the displayed codes, including ? where the relevant step remains unreported or unresolved. Full annotations and provenance are in the supplementary machine-readable dataset (f07_evidence_map_data.json and the adjudication ledger), distributed with the audit package in manuscript_audit/supplement/.

Figure 7. Evaluation design for embodied scientific campaigns. A strict two-by-two comparison crosses a reference or adaptive selector with a baseline or improved executor under matched endpoint, information, resource boundary and acceptance criteria. Every attempt enters the physical execution gate and remains in Nattempted. The metrological and audit gate assigns v̂t and ct : valid positive, valid negative and censored records all count in Nvalid, whereas execution failures and inconclusive records remain in Nattempted but not Nvalid. Nominated claims form a separate unit with counts Nsel and Nconf; confirmation uses fresh evidence not used for nomination under prespecified criteria. rvalid, ECYG, COR and CSU use their declared denominators; DA and IRR require a privileged reference label and apply only to controlled injection benchmarks. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 8. Failure attribution and claim reassessment. A low response with qualified preparation and adequate detection can be a valid negative; valid positive, valid negative and censored records remain in the valid pool and count in Nvalid. Uncertain transfer produces an execution failure that remains in Nattempted and returns through diagnosis and recovery, while an unclear signal is inconclusive. These trial statuses ct are distinct from claim state σk. Independent confirmation of a nominated claim can retain, revise or narrow it according to prespecified evidence; narrowing is not the only permissible outcome. The apparatus is a synthetic illustrative scene.

Figure 9. Six empirical propositions grouped into three complementary research thrusts, with three cross-cutting normative invariants. P1 and P5 concern histories and realized actions; P2 and P6 concern validity-preserving recovery and matched-budget selection, diagnosis and confirmation; P3 and P4 concern endpoint-preserving transfer and qualified expansion of experimental reach. Provenance completeness, safety with human authority, and cross-site replay compliance must hold across all propositions. Grouping does not imply a temporal or causal order, predicted gains or established findings. Scientific miniatures are conceptual and apparatus imagery is synthetic.

papers.title: Embodied AI for Scientific Discovery: From Physical Action to Scientific Evidence
papers.tldr: This review frames scientific experimentation by AI and robots as one embodied-AI problem focused on turning costly, partially observed physical actions into confirmed scientific evidence.

papers.abstract: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.
authors: Shresth Grover, Andrey Kolobov, Dhruv Shah
bullets: Limited-demonstration fine-tuning can improve nominal success while harming robustness to appearance, object, and instruction variations.
RAFT uses two stages: low-rank adapter training on task-relevant reasoning annotations, followed by policy fine-tuning on action demonstrations with the adapters frozen.
On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves 75.0% out-of-distribution success versus 27.9% for plain fine-tuning.
On a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, RAFT reaches 70.0% mean success versus 36.0% for the strongest baseline.
RAFT improves performance under visual, object, and instruction shifts, while increasing attention to annotated regions and later-layer object-identity probe accuracy.

papers.abstract: Disturbances can invalidate the conditions required by a robot's next action even when much of its task program remains useful. A recovery system must therefore choose a response suited to the current state. We present DiMuRe (diagnosis-guided multilevel recovery), a framework for robot-use agents that uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA) grasping. After the original program exits, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can generate corrective code from images and execution feedback. Local verification checks the outcome of each recovery attempt. We also introduce LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for robustness and recovery under mid-execution disturbances, supporting program-based agents and VLA policies. On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local DiMuRe (program reuse and recovery skills) achieves 77.65% complete-task success, compared with 58.68% for the original program under the same physical-step allowance. Full DiMuRe achieves 81.90% with terminal replanning, an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program.

MLLM-assisted replanning (L3) starts separately after the original program exits and its entry checks pass. The planner revises corrective code using new observations and execution feedback.

papers.abstract: Object rearrangement planning in cluttered environments is often non-monotone, requiring objects to be temporarily relocated before reaching their final destinations. Although search-based planners can solve such tasks, they incur substantial computational cost and require expensive replanning when the environment changes. We propose the Visual Adaptive Rearrangement Planner (VARP), which learns non-monotone rearrangement directly from visual state representations generated from expert demonstrations. VARP predicts pick-and-place actions from the current and goal visual state representations, and incorporates an Action Refinement Strategy (ARS) to improve action feasibility and a Progress Enforcement Strategy (PES) to mitigate progress stagnation. By continuously updating actions from the latest visual state representations, VARP adapts online to disturbances without replanning from scratch or performing online combinatorial search. In challenging rearrangement benchmarks, VARP achieves a 98.3\% success rate with only 0.4 s planning time per task, 97.5\% success under execution-time disturbances, and 94.5\% under continuous severe disturbances, while generalizing effectively to unseen object counts. These results demonstrate that VARP provides a scalable and robust solution for non-monotone object rearrangement.

papers.abstract: As robot learning moves beyond the tabletop, many tasks require mobility, adjustable reach, active perception, and bimanual dexterity. Commercial platforms combining these capabilities are costly, while affordable open-source alternatives cover only a subset and require software integration. We present MABEL, an open-source anthropomorphic mobile bimanual robot with 56 degrees of freedom (DOF) and a US$8.1k parts cost. It combines two 7-DOF arms with 17-DOF hands, a pitching torso, a lift, a 3-DOF neck, and a holonomic base. Back-drivable arms and torso support compliant interaction, with fingertip reach from floor level to 2.23 m. The head and torso roughly triple modeled camera coverage relative to a torso-fixed camera. Apple Vision Pro head and hand tracking enables whole-body teleoperation without handheld controllers, with 137 ms mean glass-to-glass stereo video latency over the robot's Wi-Fi hotspot. We demonstrate an end-to-end imitation learning pipeline, from teleoperated data collection to policy deployment, using a shared command interface and whole-body controller.

papers.abstract: A mobile manipulator asked to "put the toys away in the toy box" must decide which objects are toys and which container the user means, then find base poses, grasps, and placements it can execute. Because a scene representation is built before the instruction is known, it may lack the attributes, affordances, or concepts needed to resolve the task. We present FEIJOA, a language-model agent that grounds the instruction at test time. It queries a grounding tool over a posed RGB-D scan, inspects the returned candidates, and refines its queries until they resolve the instruction. An embodiment-aware harness checks each skill's preconditions, samples base poses from which the target is reachable, and verifies the skill's effect from observations before and after execution. On 103 open-ended grounding queries, FEIJOA resolves 94.2% exactly, compared with 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation. Over 50 real-world trials on Spot, it completes 35 tasks; 17 of these successes follow recovery from a failed tool call or verification check. Of the 15 failed trials, 13 were caused by the robot's physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent's reasoning. Project website: https://williamshen-nz.github.io/feijoa/.

papers.abstract: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) aims to learn a unified policy from heterogeneous offline datasets that generalizes across tasks. However, existing offline MTRL methods often struggle with two fundamental issues: severe per-task data scarcity and limited cross-task generalization. In this paper, we propose Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer (LaMA-DT), a unified sequence-modeling framework that leverages a single large language model (LLM) for both trajectory augmentation and multi-task policy learning. LaMA-DT uses natural-language task descriptions to guide task-aligned trajectory augmentation through a set of supervised generation and alignment objectives, and incorporates a scoring-and-filtering mechanism to retain high-quality augmented trajectories. The same LLM is then repurposed as a language-conditioned Decision Transformer and fine-tuned on a mixture of real and augmented data. Experiments on Meta-World and MuJoCo multi-task benchmarks demonstrate that LaMA-DT consistently outperforms competitive baselines, particularly in low-data regimes, showing that language-guided data augmentation substantially improves cross-task generalization.

(ii) Data Preparation. Candidate trajectories are generated per task using O3, scored using aggregated multi-objective likelihoods, and the top-K trajectories are retained and merged with the original offline data. (iii) Multi-Task Policy Learning. We repurpose the LLM and shared LoRA adapter as a prompt-conditioned DT, trained on the combined real and augmented dataset, with task descriptions pi and a provenance token zprov.

papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is pivotal for computer-assisted intervention, yet demands compositional reasoning across instruments, anatomy, and workflow. Existing surgical vision-language models rely on instruction tuning with large-scale question-answer pairs, entailing laborious data curation and costly retraining. To bridge this gap, we propose SurgEye, a perception-reasoning framework that grounds reasoning in a vision foundation model without instruction tuning. Specifically, we devise Routed Multi-Task Perception (RMP) that routes the vision foundation model through task-specific pathways learned from public perception labels, producing spatial and temporal evidence. We further introduce Agentic Compositional Reasoning (ACR) that employs a frozen large language model to coordinate RMP specialists and temporal memory as callable tools, composing evidence across tasks and time into grounded answers. Moreover, we construct SurgEye-Bench spanning eight surgical procedures, pairing each question with perception labels for verifiable evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SurgEye outperforms state-of-the-arts in surgical reasoning. The source code will be available.

papers.abstract: To enable effective generalization in offline meta-RL, it is essential to accurately infer the underlying task through latent task representations, which provide a compact and transferable summary of task-specific characteristics for guiding policy generation. In this paper, we propose Contrastive Task-Aware Decision Transformer (CoTA-DT), a DT-based offline meta-RL framework that learns task representations by jointly integrating four complementary components: (i) contrastive learning from offline trajectories, (ii) alignment with natural-language task descriptions, (iii) one-step supervision via a task-conditioned world model, and (iv) long-term supervision via a task-conditioned Q function. The learned task representations are used as conditioning signals for a DT-based policy, enabling task-aware meta-policy learning. To further support generalization in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, we design a language-grounded, self-adaptive strategy that enables effective and reliable adaptation to unseen tasks. Notably, in CoTA-DT, the pretrained LLM serves as a shared backbone for language encoding, world modeling, Q-function estimation, and policy learning. This unified design facilitates parameter sharing, improving both efficiency and generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse offline meta-RL benchmarks demonstrate that CoTA-DT consistently outperforms prior methods, particularly in challenging zero-shot generalization scenarios.

papers.abstract: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.
authors: Ruijie Zhang, Jiayin Zheng, Yequan Zhao, Liyan Tan, Ziyue Liu, Zhengyang Wang, Kunpeng Song, Nathan Zhao, Jian Yao, Yin Zhang, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Problem: Downstream action models can concentrate sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of pretrained VLM representations, especially under representation–task mismatch.
Finding: Counteracting this sensitivity concentration benefits control across tested backbone–head combinations.
Method: AdaIE is a parameter-free interface mechanism that reweights pretrained representations based on evolving downstream sensitivity during training.
Results: It improves simulation success rates by up to 5.28 pp and 1.68 pp on two benchmarks, with an average 19 pp gain across five real-world manipulation tasks.
Scope: The approach also improves performance for diffusion policies and world models.

papers.abstract: One big challenge in physical AI is interacting with systems whose states are defined by implicit equilibrium. Learning in these systems is difficult because their responses can be multistable, path-dependent, and sensitive over long horizons. Adjoint learning provides an efficient way to optimize trajectories without unrolling iterative equilibrium solvers, but its gradient relies on the frozen-tangent approximation, which neglects higher-order sensitivity terms and can become inaccurate when the local equilibrium varies rapidly. In this work, we introduce Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), optimizing trajectories along which sensitivity variations are explicitly controlled. We derive a mathematical bound on the resulting gradient error and develop a practical finite-difference approximation. We validate the framework on deformable objects, which are representative of implicit equilibrium systems, ranging from simple quadratic energy models such as elastic rods to complex systems including thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures. Compared with the adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baselines, SCNC achieves faster convergence and more stable optimization by reducing switching to undesirable equilibrium branches, doubling the stable optimization rate over adjoint learning 83.3% vs. 41.7% and reducing the average loss by more than 1.5 orders of magnitude on thin-walled tubes, where sensitivity variations are pronounced.
authors: Hengyi Zhou, Haobo Fang, Xiaonan Huang, Dezhong Tong, M. Khalid Jawed
bullets: Addresses inaccurate gradients caused by the frozen-tangent approximation in rapidly varying, path-dependent equilibrium systems.
Optimizes trajectories to control sensitivity changes and uses a practical finite-difference approximation.

Evaluated on deformable objects ranging from elastic rods to thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures.

Compared with adjoint learning and gradient-free iCEM, achieves faster, more stable optimization, including an 83.3% versus 41.7% stable optimization rate and substantially lower loss on thin-walled tubes.

papers.abstract: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.

Achieves up to 6.16× speedup on LIBERO-Long with CUDA MPS and 25.04× on RoboTwin Easy across four GPUs, with unchanged reported outcomes.

papers.abstract: In robotics, shape control, or shape servoing, refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object toward a desired shape. This article is the second of a two-part tutorial on data-driven, Jacobian-based shape control, in which the deformation Jacobian, a local model of how robot motion changes the measured shape, is estimated from measurements. Part I built the shape-servoing loop and derived a local stability condition. This paper starts by using the singular value decomposition of the deformation Jacobian to identify shape changes that can be produced by small robot motions, those that require large robot motions, and those that are locally unavailable. It then analyses how the choice of shape features determines how the controller regulates the object's shape and, therefore, how much the object deforms on its way to the target. It then describes three ways in which the shape control loop can fail: loss of controllability, loss of observability, and occurrence of mechanical instabilities. It closes with shape-control extensions to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.
authors: Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco, Alessio Caporali, Miguel Aranda, Gianluca Palli, Gonzalo L\'opez-Nicol\'as, Youcef Mezouar
bullets: Uses singular value decomposition to characterize easily produced, costly, and locally unavailable shape changes.

Extends shape control to time-varying targets, secondary tasks, and three-dimensional objects.

papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

papers.abstract: Training robot policies for multi-task pick and place requires demonstrations on many objects, which handheld Universal Manipulation Interfaces (UMIs) can collect quickly and cheaply. However, existing UMIs depend on external base stations, use rigid fingers that give no signal about contact forces, or use parallel-jaw fingers that limit grip strength. We present a battery-powered handheld interface, built on YUBI, whose soft, angled fingers wrap around objects, deform visibly under load as a visual proxy for force, and match the grippers of the robot. With it, we collect a 99.7-hour dataset over 53 objects, train $\pi_{0.5}$ policies on 49 of them, and hold out the other 4 as unseen objects. We find that a top camera raises success by 13 points even when only about half of the data includes it, and that mid-training on our multi-task data raises success after fine-tuning on unseen objects from 35% to 57%. Finger design, dataset, and data processing code: https://lute-corp.github.io/soft-yubi-site/
authors: Kobi Kelemen, Tomasz Niedzia{\l}kowski, Marcin Paszczak, Victoriano Montesinos

papers.abstract: Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose MoTWorld, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, MoTWorld generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that MoTWorld achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.
authors: Fengzhi Guo, Nate Morrill, Shiqi Li, Cheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of a unified approach for 3D rigging and temporally stable 4D skeleton generation.
Generates an entire 4D sequence jointly in a single feedforward pass, while also supporting single-mesh 3D rigging.
Provides explicit control over skeleton count, uncertainty-based candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.
Uses a curriculum from large-scale 3D rigging data to mid-scale 4D mesh–skeleton data to reduce dependence on paired 4D training data.
Reports strong 3D rigging quality and high-quality, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction.

papers.abstract: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone.
bullets: Learns behavior together with spatial context by reconstructing scene geometry and estimating hand motion from each video.
Aligns geometry and hand motion at a shared scale using a 3D hand-size prior.
Uses gated residual fusion to ground a pre-trained vision-language model in geometry, while predicting future geometry and wrist/finger actions.
Generates finger motion conditioned on predicted trajectories of both wrists.
Pre-training on reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over hand-motion-only pre-training; the method also reports gains on simulated and real-world bimanual tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 5: Real-world rollouts. Fig. 1: SpatialDex reconstructs scene geometry and estimates hand motion from RGB-only human videos and aligns them at a shared video-level scale to jointly supervise policy pre-training. The policy maps RGB-D observations to bimanual dexterous actions and is adapted to specific tasks through fine-tuning on robot demonstrations. The lower panel shows the six bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks for real-world evaluation.

Fig. 3: 3D-grounded visuomotor policy. Reconstructed geometry enters the policy in two roles. As an input, depth samples from each image patch are encoded jointly in 3D and pooled back to their patches, so that the geometry grid g arrives on the same token grid as the visual features x and is fused into f through two gates and a residual whose weight warms up from zero, leaving the priors of the pre-trained VLM intact. As a target, a training-only predictor estimates future scene geometry from the shared context, which requires the representation to retain spatial structure that the action losses alone do not demand. From the same context, a wrist expert predicts both wrist trajectories and a finger expert predicts finger actions conditioned on them.

Fig. 2: Aligned scene and hand reconstruction. From an RGB-only video, SpatialDex recovers hand meshes and wrist trajectories, point clouds and camera poses up to an unknown scale. Aligning the reconstructed hand points with the estimated hand meshes across frames yields one scale shared by the whole video and a rigid transformation per frame, which places the scene geometry and the hand motion in a common frame for pre-training. The aligned reconstruction supplies the depth observations, the wrist and finger action targets, and the future geometry targets for policy pre-training.

papers.abstract: Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL) methods, while effective in settings with limited expert demonstrations, are often considered unstable. These approaches typically decompose into two components: Density Ratio (DR) estimation $\frac{\rho_E}{\rho_{\pi}}$, where a discriminator estimates the relative occupancy of state-action pairs under the policy versus the expert; and Reward Assignment (RA), where this ratio is transformed into a reward signal used to train the policy. While significant research has focused on improving density estimation, the role of reward assignment in influencing training dynamics and final policy performance has been largely overlooked. RA functions in AIL are typically derived from divergence minimization objectives, relying heavily on human design and ingenuity. In this work, we take a different approach: we investigate the discovery of data-driven RA functions, i.e, based directly on the performance of the resulting imitation policy. To this end, we leverage an LLM-guided evolutionary framework that efficiently explores the space of RA functions, yielding \emph{Discovered Adversarial Imitation Learning} (DAIL), the first meta-learnt AIL algorithm. Remarkably, DAIL generalises across unseen environments and policy optimization algorithms, outperforming the current state-of-the-art of \emph{human-designed} baselines. Finally, we analyse why DAIL leads to more stable training, offering novel insights into the role of RA functions in the stability of AIL. Code is publicly available: https://github.com/shshnkreddy/DAIL.
authors: Shashank Reddy Chirra, Jayden Teoh, Praveen Paruchuri, Pradeep Varakantham
bullets: AIL instability is studied through reward assignment (RA), a largely overlooked component alongside density-ratio estimation.
The method searches for data-driven RA functions based on the resulting imitation-policy performance.
The resulting DAIL algorithm is presented as the first meta-learned AIL algorithm.
DAIL generalizes to unseen environments and policy optimizers and outperforms human-designed baselines, according to the abstract.
The analysis provides insights into how RA functions affect AIL training stability.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained via behavior cloning are vulnerable to covariate shift, where small deviations from expert trajectories can compound into failure. Common strategies to mitigate this issue involve expanding the training distribution through human-in-the-loop corrections or synthetic data augmentation. However, these approaches are often labor-intensive, rely on strong task assumptions, or compromise the quality of imitation. We introduce Latent Policy Barrier, a framework for robust visuomotor policy learning. Inspired by Control Barrier Functions, LPB treats the latent embeddings of expert demonstrations as an implicit barrier separating safe, in-distribution states from unsafe, out-of-distribution (OOD) ones. Our approach decouples the role of precise expert imitation and OOD recovery into two separate modules: a base diffusion policy solely on expert data, and a dynamics model trained on both expert and suboptimal policy rollout data. At inference time, the dynamics model predicts future latent states and optimizes them to stay within the expert distribution. Both simulated and real-world experiments show that LPB improves both policy robustness and data efficiency, enabling reliable manipulation from limited expert data and without additional human correction or annotation.
bullets: Addresses covariate shift, where small deviations from expert trajectories can compound into failure.
Uses a base diffusion policy trained only on expert demonstrations for precise imitation.
Trains a dynamics model on expert and suboptimal rollouts to predict and optimize future latent states.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show improved robustness and data efficiency from limited expert data.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Simulation Rollouts. Left: Filtered BC baseline. Right: LPB. papers.abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel
