papers.abstract: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi
bullets: Addresses embodiment differences between human demonstrations and mobile manipulation robots.
Uses Environment-Aware Retargeting to convert scene geometry and human head/gripper trajectories into collision-aware robot joint and base targets.
Applies Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking to reduce reliance on observation views mismatched by residual retargeting errors.
Uses delay-calibrated action assignment and on-policy human corrections via DAgger to handle imperfect, contact-rich actions.
Evaluated across five challenging manipulation tasks, achieving 87.0% average task progress.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.
bullets: Addresses confirmation bias, hallucinated progress, and binary success judgments in video-based robot task evaluation.
First prompts the VLM to define task-grounded absolute success through textual scene descriptions, then scores progress against explicit rubrics.
Produces fine-grained, non-linear progress estimates that penalize failures and interpolate successful executions.
Uses only prompting, enabling generalization across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks without per-model post-training.
The resulting reward estimates support efficient downstream reinforcement learning and match or surpass post-trained reward models.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce WISE (\emph{World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation}), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0\% to 24.0\% on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1\% to 78.3\% mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision.
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible imagined futures and actions that actually succeed.
Scores sampled rollouts using action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency, and instruction-conditioned task progress.
Executes the highest-scoring candidate without updating the underlying world action model.
With four candidates, success increases from 6.0% to 24.0% on RoboLab and from 75.1% to 78.3% on LIBERO.
Task progress contributes the largest weight, while the three scoring components rank candidates differently.

The IDM maps imagined frames back to actions for comparison with the candidate’s proposed controls; the task evaluator scores progress at the final imagined frame. WISE sums the scores, executes the selected action chunk, and observes the resulting state before replanning.

papers.abstract: Open-world robotic mobile manipulation requires acting in physical environments with only partial information. While recent Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) agents show strong open-world reasoning capabilities, existing architectures that rely on direct tool calling struggle with geometric uncertainty and thus are limited to fully-observable tabletop environments. In contrast, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems can solve long-horizon tasks under partial observability but incur high computational costs and require closed worlds. We propose \textbf{TAMPAgent}, an agentic planning framework that unifies the reasoning of LVLMs with the structured constraint satisfaction of TAMP systems. We endow an LVLM agent with a belief-space planning model operating over an extensible API of perception, planning, and control tools. The agent formulates a partial task plan composed of parameterized observation and execution actions, which is subsequently completed using classical search algorithms. After extracting the plan's geometric constraints, the agent leverages its tool API to bind valid parameter values, satisfying feasibility requirements and producing an executable motion plan. Upon execution, the agent continuously updates its belief history and repeats this closed-loop process by interleaving observation and manipulation actions. Evaluated across complex household mobile manipulation tasks on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 platforms, TAMPAgent significantly outperforms direct tool-calling agentic baselines, demonstrating that integrating TAMP constraint satisfaction into agentic planning loops is essential for unstructured, partially observable environments.
bullets: Targets open-world mobile manipulation, where geometric uncertainty challenges direct tool-calling agents.
Uses an LVLM to create partial plans with parameterized observation and execution actions.
Completes plans through classical search, geometric constraint extraction, and tool-based parameter binding.
Continuously updates belief history by interleaving perception and manipulation in a closed loop.
Evaluated on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 household tasks, it outperforms direct tool-calling baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Integrating agents with planning. We compare four systems that maps a history of observations to whole body control for long-horizon mobile-manipulation tasks: (a) TAMP [14, 7] solves hand-authored problems with a task planner that orchestrates tools. (b) VLM-TAMP [9, 10] uses the agent to write the problem from open-world understanding but keeps the planning pipeline fixed. (c) CaP [3, 15, 5, 6] lets the agent write programs that orchestrate tools directly to find solutions. (d) TAMPAgent (ours) lets the agent orchestrate both the task planner and the tools to find certified solutions that satisfy the planner derived constraints.

Figure 7 | Success on the RBY1, over 20 episodes per task and method, with the tasks grouped by category. (a) Absolute success. (b) Partial success, where each episode earns the fraction of its subtasks it completes (Figure A1, Appendix C). The last group averages each over the tasks.

Figure 4 | TAMPAgent planning loop. We show how the agent orchestrates the planner and tools to solve the task “put the apple on the black table (hidden behind a toy penguin) in a bowl”. (1-3) The agent observes, hypothesizes where the apple is, and writes the problem and a plan, (4) the planner compiles the plan into a CSP, and (5) the agent writes a computation graph that calls tools to find an assignment 𝛽𝑡 satisfying the CSP. (6) The tools certify the first action’s constraints and the planner accepts 𝛽𝑡, allowing (7) the robot to execute the first action. (8) The loop repeats until (9-10) the placement is planned and the goal is achieved.
Figure 9 | Success on the threeroom tasks (Figure 6) on the RBY1, over 5 episodes per task and method.

Figure 5 | Evaluation tasks. We ask the robot to place the apple on the plate on the dining table (prompts in Table A3), starting with the robot facing away from the apple. Each task shows the whole scene with the robot at its start pose (top, walls and ceiling hidden) and a close-up of the area around the apple (bottom). The tasks fall into four categories. In the mobile manipulation (MM) tasks T1 and T2, the apple is in plain view, next to the plate or on the countertop. The MM + non-prehensile tasks add an object the robot must move first. In T4 to T6, a cup, an open drawer, or both block the direct pick, in T10, a mustard bottle stands in front of the apple, and in T8, a cracker box stands in front of the plate. The MM + occlusion tasks hide the apple, inside the fridge in T3 and behind a cracker box in T7, so the agent must hypothesize where to search. T9 is MM + non-prehensile + occlusion: the apple is inside the fridge behind a cup, which the robot must move before it can pick the apple. In the close-ups of T3 and T9, we draw the refrigerator doors translucent so that the shelf is visible. In the simulation the doors are closed.
Figure 8 | Failure attribution for RBY1 simulation experiments. Failed episodes out of 20 per task, in which an object fell or the scene was destroyed (solid), or which timed out (hatched).

Figure 3 | Hybrid beliefs over perception and manipulation variables. Left: The belief over the apple’s location moves from Unif, a uniform prior over the room, to a Lang hypothesis written by the agent, “... on the visible counter / dining table / inside the refrigerator ...”. The agent then chooses a viewpoint and calls SAM 3 to represent apple’s location as a Mask, and then as a RGBD estimate when its close enough. Right: The grasp (top) and placement (bottom) 𝑝′ requires cup’s RGBD estimate as input. The agent injects language context ℓ, such as “I must place the cup far from the apple” and calls tools to certify valid grasps and placement locations. Finally, the agent chooses a valid option based on implicitly represented planning objectives.

In T11, the robot must move a bowl from the living-room table to the kitchen table, and in T12, it must throw a used sponge from the laundry machine in the washroom into the kitchen trash can. T13 has the same goal as T11, but a chair blocks the living-room doorway. papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation benefits from tactile feedback that captures both detailed contact geometry and interaction forces. When scooping grains, contact patterns help infer spoon orientation, while resistance transmitted through the grasp guides motion. To provide these complementary sensing capabilities, we present PanoTac, a low-cost, compliant tactile fingertip designed for dense three-axis tactile sensing. Each fingertip provides a $12 \times 32 \times 3$ tactile representation, with one normal ($z$) and two shear ($x$, $y$) response components at each taxel. The sensor operates at 60 Hz and costs less than $50 per fingertip. Sensor characterization quantifies response repeatability and consistency across sensor instances and contact locations. We integrate PanoTac into a robotic system with a visuo-tactile pipeline. Across test-tube preparation, grain scooping, and salt pouring, the resulting policies outperform vision-only baselines by an average of 46.7 percentage points. Ablations show that removing either spatial contact information or shear feedback reduces overall performance across the task suite. Our project page is available at https://panotac.github.io.
bullets: Captures a 12 × 32 × 3 tactile representation: normal force plus two shear components at each taxel.
Operates at 60 Hz and costs under $50 per fingertip.
Integrated into a visuo-tactile pipeline for test-tube preparation, grain scooping, and salt pouring.
Policies outperform vision-only baselines by an average of 46.7 percentage points.
Ablations indicate both spatial contact information and shear feedback are important for performance.

papers.abstract: Conventional robot arms can be extremely heavy compared with the everyday objects they manipulate, creating a significant inertia mismatch at contact. Even a small accidental bump from a heavy arm can knock a light object out of place. Modern learning methods have nevertheless demonstrated a wide range of successful manipulation behaviors on these platforms, suggesting that even extreme inertia mismatch can be overcome with sufficient data. However, it remains unclear whether high inertia imposes a hidden cost on learning, potentially worsening scaling with data or lowering the performance ceiling of modern robot learning methods. We investigate this question through controlled simulation experiments that vary robot and object masses. We find that reinforcement learning succeeds across a broad range of mass combinations, while behavior cloning learns more reliable policies when a lighter robot manipulates a heavier object. Heavier robots require more demonstrations to attain the same performance as lighter robots. Finally, because new hardware is rarely an option, we explore ways to lower an existing arm's inertia at contact with existing hardware, either by choosing a lower-inertia workspace before collecting data or by steering the demonstrator toward lower-inertia configurations during the task. In both cases, the lower-inertia demonstrations are imitated more reliably. Project website: https://younghyopark.me/inertia-mismatch/
bullets: The study examines whether heavy robot arms create hidden costs for manipulation policy learning.

papers.abstract: Pre-touch sensing, or sensing information about an object before contact, is an attractive modality for robot hands as it can allow a robot to anticipate and respond to a contact before it happens. In this work, we introduce ToFTouch, a multimodal tactile sensor combining three multizone (4$\times$4 resolution) time-of-flight sensors with an optics-based pressure sensing array. We mount this sensor on a parallel jaw gripper and demonstrate its utility on three distinct tasks: (i) pre-grasp adjustment, (ii) item extraction from clutter, and (iii) item insertion into tight spaces. For pre-grasp adjustment, ToF feedback reduced cycle time by 7.4$\%$ by enabling anticipatory gripper closure during approach. For extraction, ToF sensing enabled successful retrieval across all tested depth offsets ($\pm$2 cm) deviating from the nominal pick point, including conditions where baseline approaches failed, with standard deviations below 0.4 cm. For insertion into dense clutter, we explore the proximity and tactile information provided from ToFTouch during an insertion trajectory. The results demonstrate the utility of multizone ToF sensing in a manipulation environment.

papers.abstract: Despite their widespread success across machine learning, the learning dynamics and generalization properties of neural networks remain poorly understood. The neural tangent kernel (NTK) provides an analytical characterization of the learning dynamics of infinitely wide neural networks and serves as a useful proxy for finite-width networks in supervised learning. In this work, we extend the NTK framework to reinforcement learning (RL) by introducing a temporal-difference (TD) flow formulation that accommodates time-varying mini-batches and TD targets, yielding a closed-form solution for value function evolution in an overparametrized setting. We also devise an optimization-based state-space exploration method that leverages the closed-form solution, coupled with constraints on the environment, to model the set of feasible states. On a deterministic grid environment, we validate that the proposed RL-based NTK formulation is indeed learning efficiently and adapting to the distribution shift in the training data distribution, and we demonstrate that the resulting exploration strategy improves sample efficiency. To our knowledge, this is the first work to extend NTK theory to characterize the learning dynamics of RL training with time-varying mini-batches and TD updates.
bullets: Formulates an NTK-based temporal-difference flow for RL with changing mini-batches and TD targets.
Derives a closed-form description of value-function evolution in the overparameterized setting.
Uses this solution with environment constraints to identify feasible states for optimization-based exploration.
On a deterministic grid environment, the method adapts to training-distribution shifts and improves sample efficiency.
Scope is validated on a deterministic grid environment; broader generalization is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Actor--critic methods rely on critic gradients to improve continuous-action policies, yet finite-sample guarantees must control both value and gradient errors and their propagation through the actor. We develop a neural actor-critic procedure that combines a regularized minimax Bellman estimator over sigmoid networks with a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient. Under uniform Bellman regularity and covered reset sampling, a positive high-order action-derivative penalty yields value and action-gradient risk bounds with classical nonparametric minimax exponents up to logarithmic factors. We propagate estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors to obtain return guarantees, with refinements for bounded multimodal potentials and strongly concave regimes. Empirical studies across controlled simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task show favorable performance relative to the considered baselines.
bullets: Targets the challenge of propagating finite-sample critic value and gradient errors into actor updates.
Estimates the Bellman critic with a regularized minimax objective over sigmoid networks and a high-order action-derivative penalty.
Uses a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient to improve continuous-action policy updates.
Derives value, action-gradient, and return guarantees accounting for estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors.
Experiments on simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task report favorable performance against the considered baselines.

papers.abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) aims to recover expert rewards that transfer across environments with differing dynamics. Prior work has shown that such transfer is possible when gathering expert demonstrations across sufficiently different dynamics. In practice, however, expert demonstrations are costly, making it critical to select the right dynamics to reduce the quantity of expert data required for learning transferable rewards. We propose a two-phase approach: we first cycle through the available dynamics to obtain a reliable reward estimate, then actively select dynamics to reduce our uncertainty about the expert reward. Crucially, this yields novel sample complexity guarantees on transfer that hold for any dynamics, with a rate independent of the number of available dynamics. Empirically, our method significantly reduces the number of expert demonstrations needed to learn a transferable reward.
bullets: Targets the high cost of collecting expert demonstrations for transferable reward learning.
First cycles through available dynamics to obtain a reliable initial reward estimate.
Then actively selects dynamics that reduce uncertainty about the expert reward.
Provides transfer sample-complexity guarantees for arbitrary dynamics, independent of their number.
Experiments show substantially fewer expert demonstrations are needed to learn transferable rewards.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires fine-grained control and complex physical interactions with the environment, posing significant challenges for robot policy learning. Vision-only policies struggle with such tasks, as contact states and interaction forces are difficult to infer from visual observations alone. Existing methods mitigate this issue by incorporating force or tactile sensing. However, they often treat these signals as auxiliary observations without fully exploiting their role in modeling future interaction dynamics. To address this, we propose ForceLDM, a force-aware latent dynamics model that learns future contact and motion dynamics to guide action generation. Rather than directly predicting future observations, which can entangle task-relevant dynamics with irrelevant sensory details, ForceLDM learns a compact representation of future dynamics through knowledge distillation. Specifically, a teacher network with privileged future force/torque and optical flow signals extracts future dynamic features, which are then distilled into a student network trained only on current observations. This enables the student model to reason about upcoming contacts and physical dynamics without relying on future sensory inputs at deployment. To improve robustness and generalization, we further introduce a curriculum-based progressive noise injection strategy to mitigate over-reliance on future features. Experiments on five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that ForceLDM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, generalizes effectively to novel objects, and remains robust to environmental perturbations. Project page and code are available at https://tpy001.github.io/ForceLDM/.
bullets: Vision-only policies struggle to infer contact states and interaction forces during manipulation.
A teacher uses future force/torque and optical-flow signals to extract dynamic features, which are distilled into a student using only current observations at deployment.
The model predicts compact future contact and motion dynamics rather than full future observations.
Progressive curriculum-based noise injection reduces reliance on privileged future features and improves robustness.
Experiments across five real-world tasks show strong performance, generalization to novel objects, and robustness to environmental perturbations.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation goals are easier to visualize than to specify numerically through explicit geometric constraints. We present VerifLM, a framework that converts image-edited goal configurations into physically verified 6-DoF object poses for planning. Using an edited image, VerifLM recovers an initial relative pose between an active object and a passive object, then prompts a vision-language model to generate axis-wise sampling constraints and a task-specific validation program. Candidate poses are evaluated in a physics simulator, and the VLM selects the most task-consistent retained candidate. To operate without predefined object meshes or physical parameters, VerifLM reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs multiple hypothetical simulations with varying physics and geometry. Parallel-world validation evaluates candidates across geometry--physics variations and ranks them by the number of worlds in which they satisfy the validation program. We evaluate VerifLM on nine manipulation tasks. VerifLM achieves the highest task success on eight of nine tasks, with the largest performance gain on goals requiring precise orientation and contact relationships.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying manipulation goals with explicit geometric constraints.
Uses a vision-language model to generate axis-wise pose constraints and task-specific validation programs from edited images.
Reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D data and tests candidate poses across simulations with varied geometry and physics.
Ranks candidates by how consistently they satisfy the validation program across parallel simulated worlds.
Evaluated on nine tasks, achieving the highest task success on eight, with the largest gains for precise orientation and contact goals.

papers.abstract: Soft robot co-design methods can jointly optimise morphology and control, but the resulting designs are often difficult to manufacture, while manufacturable approaches typically restrict actuator placement or require manual assembly. We present a simulation-based co-design framework that jointly optimises material distribution, pneumatic actuator placement and orientation, and control, while producing designs that can be fabricated monolithically using fused deposition modelling. The framework uses a differentiable 2D plane-stress Material Point Method simulator, incorporating an experimentally validated material model and an empirically derived surrogate model of a 3D-printed inflatable actuator. We demonstrate gradient-based optimisation soft robotic arms for prescribed tip trajectories. Optimised designs are transferred directly from simulation to one-shot monolithic FDM fabrication, with integrated actuators and no post-assembly. Physical experiments demonstrate that the resulting arms reproduce the behaviour predicted in simulation. This framework provides a path from task-level objectives to physically realisable soft robots while retaining substantial freedom over both morphology and actuation.
bullets: Addresses the gap between flexible co-design and manufacturable soft robots without manual assembly.
Optimises material distribution, actuator placement/orientation, and control for prescribed arm tip trajectories.
Uses a differentiable 2D plane-stress Material Point Method with validated material and actuator models.
Produces monolithic FDM-printed arms with integrated actuators, transferred directly from simulation.
Physical experiments confirm that fabricated arms behave as predicted by simulation.

papers.abstract: We release all 3,718 episodes from the ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluation (arXiv:2607.24481), which contains 600 teleoperated demonstrations and 3,118 rollouts of seven imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies on 12 tabletop tasks, recorded on low-cost SO-101 arms; 73% of the rollouts are failures. Every policy for a task was trained or fine-tuned on the same 50 demonstrations and rolled out on the same cell, so the corpus contains many policies' failures on shared tasks. An operator labelled every rollout successful, suboptimal or failure. Each episode has three camera views, joint states and actions and is available on the Hugging Face Hub in LeRobot v3.0 and a reward-model format. This note documents how the episodes were collected and the limitations that could affect their use.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained manipulation couples instruction grounding, local visual precision, and sustained execution. We present FineCraft, a framework that adapts pretrained models for fine-grained manipulation in the MetaFine Challenge. A task-routed mixture of policies selects independently adapted DINOv2-DiT or pretrained $π_{0.5}$ policies through a common observation-action interface. Local visual features help identify the instructed object parts, demonstrations and expert continuations teach the required actions, and new observations guide replanning during execution. FineCraft ranks fourth with an overall score of $0.878$, exceeding the published reference on all five tasks. Official results and local diagnostics characterize performance across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation. Code is available at https://github.com/eqcy/FineCraft

Uses a task-routed mixture of independently adapted DINOv2-DiT and pretrained π₀.₅ policies via a shared observation-action interface.
Combines local visual features, demonstrations, expert continuations, and observation-guided replanning.
Placed fourth in the MetaFine Challenge with an overall score of 0.878, outperforming the published reference on all five tasks.
Evaluates robustness across visual perturbations, instruction changes, and multi-stage manipulation.

papers.abstract: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].
bullets: Addresses the lack of accessible, standardized physical MARL benchmarks.
Uses dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors for fast, precise tabletop manipulation.
Provides open hardware designs, assembly documentation, inference software, and MARL simulation assets.
Includes an NVIDIA Isaac Lab digital twin and a learned neural actuator model for sim-to-real transfer.
Demonstrates zero-shot policy transfer with emergent adversarial behaviors.

The control stack uses PPO during training and the frozen actor network during inference. Actions pass through the learned actuator model in simulation or directly to physical motors on hardware.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.
bullets: Benchmarks latency sensitivity across tasks, object speeds, execution modes, and VLA policies.
A 100 ms latency can nearly halve success on moving-target tasks, with effects varying by task and policy.

papers.abstract: KlaskTron is an open-hardware physical platform for two-player adversarial reinforcement learning, with a learned actuator model that supports zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of trained policies. Building on this platform, we contribute KlaskTron-IL: a multi-tier imitation learning dataset (80k human demonstration timesteps collected directly on the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and synthetic expert trajectories up to 5M steps generated by the zero-shot-validated PPO policy), and diagnostic baselines that expose three characteristic failure modes of standard IL methods under contact-rich adversarial dynamics: BC's data scaling plateau, GAIL's interpretable but weak-gradient discriminator (Spearman $ρ= -1.0$ peg-ball proximity recovery, but a logit span under 0.1), and an asymmetric BC-prior x reward-density interaction. Because the policy interface used throughout this paper is the same one the actuator model bridges to hardware, a policy trained on this benchmark can run unchanged on the physical robot, as we demonstrate zero-shot for the strongest BC baseline, so long as its commands respect the actuator model's $\pm 0.2$ m/s identification range.
bullets: Uses 80k human demonstration timesteps from the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and up to 5M synthetic expert timesteps.
Benchmarks standard IL methods in two-player adversarial dynamics and identifies BC scaling plateaus, weak GAIL gradients, and asymmetric BC-prior/reward-density interactions.
GAIL’s discriminator provides interpretable peg-ball proximity recovery but produces weak logits.
The strongest BC baseline transfers zero-shot to the physical robot without policy changes.
Transfer is scoped to commands within the actuator model’s ±0.2 m/s identification range.

papers.abstract: Markerless hand-eye calibration under continuous motion requires jointly resolving camera geometry and the time offset between images and joint states. We present SyncHeC (Synchronized Hand-Eye Calibration), a dense differentiable-rendering framework that estimates both from a single robot trajectory. Continuous-time forward kinematics makes latency differentiable, metric depth complements mask contours, and an offline planner combines spatial sensitivity with temporal excitation. Alternating updates support Eye-to-Hand, Eye-in-Hand, and multi-camera calibration. On a 7-DoF arm, one $6.5$\,s motion yields $0.21$\,cm translation error against a marker-board reference, $0.34$\,cm touch-test error, and $2.7$\,ms latency error relative to an $87$\,ms reference with $95\%$ uncertainty of $\pm1.5$\,ms. Against CM-Calib on matched recordings, translation and nominal latency errors improve by $3.7\times$ and $2.3\times$. Experiments span seven arms and four depth sensors. Compensating the recovered offset during policy training and deployment increases success by $8.1$ percentage points across six families and six tasks ($1{,}800$ matched pairs; paired $95\%$ confidence interval $[6.3,9.9]$ points).
bullets: Addresses markerless hand-eye calibration when camera observations and joint states have an unknown time offset.
Uses dense differentiable rendering, continuous-time forward kinematics, metric depth, and an excitation-aware motion planner.
Supports Eye-to-Hand, Eye-in-Hand, and multi-camera calibration through alternating optimization.
On a 7-DoF arm, one 6.5-second motion achieved 0.21 cm translation error, 0.34 cm touch-test error, and 2.7 ms latency error.

papers.abstract: Contact transitions allow humanoid robots to redistribute object support across the whole body, enabling manipulation beyond hand-only grasps. Human videos provide a scalable source of such transitions for robots to learn from. However, body occlusion disrupts object pose tracking and corrupts retargeted motion. Moreover, accurately reproducing the object trajectory does not ensure that the robot applies stabilizing forces at the intended contacts, risking slips or drops in later phases. To address these challenges, we propose ReContact, which reconstructs and retargets human-object interactions through an object-centric contact plan. The plan specifies contact phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking or sliding modes. Contact priors stabilize object pose reconstruction through occlusion. A residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker is rewarded for making contact at planned anchors with forces aligned to the specified directions. In simulation, on a thigh-supported regrasp task, ReContact achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5 of episodes over three training seeds, versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline. One policy trained on 247 references re-solved for new placements raises in-workspace tube-transfer success from 20.4% (source reference only) to 97.8%. On a real Unitree G1, policies execute seven contact-rich manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.
bullets: Addresses occlusion-corrupted object tracking and the gap between matching object motion and applying stabilizing contact forces.
Uses an object-centric contact plan with phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking/sliding modes.

In simulation, the method achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5% of episodes versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline.
A policy trained on 247 references generalizes to new placements, increasing tube-transfer success from 20.4% to 97.8%; real-robot tests cover seven manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy. We augment the reward of a simulated Franka Emika Panda reaching task with a horizontal artificial potential field that penalizes proximity within a safety margin around each of two pillars (fixed nominal layout, random drift). Under hidden observation, policies trained with this term maintain a safe success rate above 88% across a radius sweep from 0.03 m to 0.055 m (30 seeds), while policies without it fall below 10% at the maximum tested radius; the term induces a minimum clearance of 47.9 mm against 9.6 mm without it and eliminates training collisions at least eight times earlier (median steps). The advantage is statistically significant at all out-of-distribution radii and holds across three reinforcement learning solvers and under full observation. Its safe success rate is comparable to that of a classical potential-field planner given the pillar positions. The margin is a fixed buffer rather than an adaptation to the radius, and it lengthens the path by about 19%.
bullets: Without clearance-aware rewards, policies skim obstacle surfaces and fail when obstacles are larger than during training.
The method adds a horizontal potential-field penalty around two pillars without revealing their size or exact position to the policy.
Across obstacle radii of 0.03–0.055 m, augmented policies maintain over 88% safe success, versus under 10% without augmentation at the largest radius.
The method increases minimum clearance to 47.9 mm from 9.6 mm and works across three reinforcement-learning solvers and full observation.
The induced margin is fixed rather than radius-adaptive and increases path length by about 19%.

papers.abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in robotics, calling for policies that address domain variations from multiple dimensions such as diverse embodiments, camera poses, and/or scene layouts. In order to approach this problem, we introduce PointPilot, a task-focused and 3D aligned manipulation framework built on a 3D space point-flow prediction. Rather than modeling the global scene, PointPilot only represents task-focused objects (robot grippers treated as objects), avoiding the prediction of potentially redundant scene parts unrelated to the manipulation tasks. Moreover, PointPilot aligns 3D spatial representation in one unified coordinate and supports closed-loop and fully automatic action execution across different manipulation modes from object point flow without a separately trained action expert, while existing works typically need an extra action head or are (semi-)automatic and single-arm mode specific. Given sensor observations and language instructions, our model jointly learns subtask planning, task-relevant object grounding, and 3D point flow prediction in an end-to-end way. By processing heterogeneous data in a shared 3D point flow space, PointPilot is able to absorb demonstrations from different embodiments. Extensive simulative and real world experiments validate our method. Notably, we demonstrate zero-shot embodiment generalization with PointPilot. A single trained policy can be deployed on previously unseen embodiments and successfully complete manipulation tasks without any additional fine-tuning.
bullets: Targets generalization across embodiments, camera poses, scene layouts, and manipulation modes.
Represents only task-relevant objects, including grippers, in a unified 3D coordinate space rather than modeling the full scene.
Jointly learns subtask planning, object grounding, and 3D point-flow prediction from sensor observations and language instructions.
Supports closed-loop, fully automatic action execution without a separately trained action expert.
Simulated and real-world experiments validate the approach, including zero-shot deployment on previously unseen embodiments without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating object acquisition, transport, and release from onboard sensing while responding to user commands and incomplete visual observations. We present ReGATE, a whole-body controller that combines egocentric depth, proprioception, and online locomotion and contact commands. Built on a teacher-student framework, ReGATE integrates interaction-state estimation through a recurrent adapter that predicts object geometry and physical contact without an external object-pose estimator. Head-wise and global gates regulate visual updates to a proprioceptive pathway. A visual-grounding and corruption curriculum trains the adapter, while phase-aware initialization increases coverage of brief contact transitions. In simulation, ReGATE achieves 85.2% success across 330 static-object acquisition trials, compared with 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol, and 85.9% across 440 moving-object acquisition trials. Deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates commanded grasp-transport-release sequences and acquisition of laterally displaced boxes. A qualitative hardware experiment further demonstrates successful box acquisition when the camera is occluded after an initial observation and before the contact command. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to extend recurrent gated fusion of onboard depth and proprioception from perceptive locomotion to humanoid loco-manipulation under interrupted visual sensing.
bullets: Addresses whole-body loco-manipulation from onboard sensing and user commands, including brief or interrupted visual observations.
Uses a teacher–student controller with a recurrent adapter that estimates object geometry and contact state without an external pose estimator.
Head-wise and global gates regulate visual information, supported by visual-grounding, corruption, and phase-aware training curricula.
Achieves 85.2% success on 330 static-object trials and 85.9% on 440 moving-object trials in simulation, versus 48.5% for VisualMimic on the static protocol.
Hardware demonstrations on a Unitree G1 show grasp–transport–release behavior, laterally displaced box acquisition, and acquisition after camera occlusion.

papers.abstract: Robust multimodal perception for soft robotic grasping is challenged by modality-dependent noise, semantic ambiguity, and limited coordinated multisensory data. We introduce Soma, a dataset containing 100 objects, 1,000 continuous grasping trajectories, and 74,914 multimodal samples grouped by software acquisition cycle, spanning remote RGB, hand RGB, depth, tactile, IMU, and structured text observations. We also collect Soma-Success, an independent grasp-outcome dataset with 1,000 trials (998 retained after quality control), to evaluate frozen-encoder transfer for post-hoc grasp outcome classification and early grasp success prediction. Built on Soma, SomaAlign learns multimodal representations in three stages: masked reconstruction estimates relative modality reliability; reliability-aware contrastive alignment uses pair-specific adaptive temperatures to adjust alignment sharpness; and conflict-aware semantic constraints improve intra-sample cross-modal consistency while preserving global feature geometry. SomaAlign achieves an average Recall@10 of 90.66% across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks. The learned representations also support physical attribute recognition, multimodal question answering, cross-modal generation, and cross-dataset transfer to grasp outcome prediction. On Soma-Success, frozen SomaAlign encoders with lightweight probes achieve 94.59% post-hoc classification accuracy and 84.07% early prediction accuracy. Together, Soma, Soma-Success, and SomaAlign provide a data and representation-learning foundation for robust and transferable multimodal perception in soft robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses modality-dependent noise, semantic ambiguity, and limited coordinated multisensory data in soft robotic grasping.
Introduces Soma, with multimodal RGB, depth, tactile, IMU, and text observations from 1,000 continuous grasping trajectories, plus the independent Soma-Success evaluation set.
Uses masked reconstruction for modality reliability, adaptive-temperature contrastive alignment, and conflict-aware semantic constraints.
Reports 90.66% average Recall@10 across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks.
Frozen encoders with lightweight probes reach 94.59% post-hoc and 84.07% early grasp-success prediction accuracy.

figures.caption: Fig. 5. Overview of the SomaAlign framework. SomaAlign follows three progressive optimization stages: (1) Reconstruction-Based Modality Reliability Estimation estimates modality reliability from normalized masked-reconstruction difficulty and constructs pairwise reliability scores; (2) Reliability-Conditioned Contrastive Alignment uses the pairwise reliability scores to adapt cross-modal contrastive temperatures and learn a shared representation; and (3) BatchAdaptive Conflict-Aware Geometry-Preserving Refinement calibrates pairwise similarities, estimates fuzzy sample-level conflict, and adaptively modulates intra-sample refinement while imposing conflict-consistency and reference-center anchoring constraints. The reference geometry constructed from Stage-II representations, including the sample-specific centers and global representation scale, is frozen and reused during Stage-III optimization. After training, only the modality-specific encoders are retained for inference.

Fig. 1. Overview of Soma, Soma-Success, and the SomaAlign framework. The soft robotic platform acquires six coordinated modalities: Remote RGB, Hand RGB, Depth, Tactile, IMU, and Text. Soma comprises 100 objects, 1,000 trajectories, and 74,914 aligned multimodal samples, while Soma-Success contains 1,000 collected grasp trials, of which 998 valid trials are retained for downstream evaluation. SomaAlign learns a unified semantic representation through Reliability Assessment, Adaptive Feature Alignment, and Conflict-aware Refinement. The learned representation supports cross-modal retrieval, physical attribute recognition, multimodal question answering, cross-modal generation, and frozen-encoder grasp success prediction.

Fig. 2. Overview of the Soma acquisition system. A unified software polling loop coordinates remote RGB-D sensing, hand-mounted RGB cameras, finger-mounted IMUs, and flexible tactile pressure arrays. Structured text descriptions are generated from experimental metadata using predefined templates. Representative sensor outputs and an example text annotation are shown on the right.

Fig. 4. Soma-Success collection protocol. The action-triggered snapshots Ta, Tb, and Tc correspond to the pre-grasp, closed-gripper, and terminal-lifting stages, respectively. The same snapshot-selection rule is applied to successful and failed trials. Representative examples are shown for the two-finger (2F) and three-finger (3F) configurations.

Fig. 9. Attribute classification accuracy retention under cross-modal generation, measured relative to the corresponding real-data baseline. (a) Single-modality probes. (b) Multi-modality probes with one generated modality replacing its real counterpart. (c) Average retention for the two strategies.
Fig. 3. Object collection in Soma. The 100 everyday objects cover diverse materials, shapes, sizes, hardness levels, colors, and functional purposes.

Fig. 6. Conceptual illustration of pair-specific distribution calibration and fuzzy membership assignment. Different modality pairs may exhibit different raw similarity distributions; therefore, the same similarity value can represent different degrees of relative inconsistency. Pair-specific ECDFs convert raw similarities into comparable conflict indicators ξi,π . The calibrated indicator is then softly assigned to overlapping ordered Gaussian fuzzy sets, allowing transitional cross-modal conflicts to partially activate multiple adjacent conflict levels.

Fig. 7. Motivation of the center-protection loss. Local cross-modal refinement may cause sample centers to deviate from the geometry established in Stage II. The center-protection constraint penalizes excessive center drift while allowing local multimodal representations to become more compact.

Fig. 8. Recall@1, Recall@5, and Recall@10 across 30 directed cross-modal retrieval tasks. Sensory-only retrieval uses paired temporal-window correspondence; text-related retrieval uses identical structured descriptions. Remote and Hand denote remote-view and hand-mounted RGB, respectively. Same-modality retrieval is excluded.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can handle noncritical stages of long-horizon manipulation yet fail during short precision-critical phases. Lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) specialists can address these failures without directly applying RL to the full VLA, but retain auxiliary controllers and switching mechanisms at deployment. We study how to transfer their capabilities into a single flow-matching VLA. Direct imitation of specialist rollouts can reproduce action jitter and leave the VLA unprepared for states encountered during its own execution. We introduce REPAIR, a value-guided distillation framework that combines offline initialization with on-policy refinement. At each critical-phase observation, REPAIR queries the corresponding specialist for multiple action candidates and weights them using its critic to construct a supervision distribution. A shared weighted flow-matching objective trains the VLA first on observations from specialist-assisted rollouts, then on observations collected through its own execution. Specialists provide supervision without taking control during on-policy collection and are removed at deployment. Across six real-robot tasks with 30 evaluation trials per task, REPAIR achieves 100% success on all six tasks, with lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.
bullets: Targets short, precision-critical phases where VLAs often fail during long-horizon manipulation.
Uses specialist critics to weight multiple candidate actions within a shared flow-matching objective.
Combines offline training on specialist-assisted rollouts with on-policy refinement on the VLA’s own observations.
Avoids reproducing action jitter and reduces distribution mismatch from direct imitation.
Achieves 100% success across six real-robot tasks and lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Training framework of REPAIR. (a) Human demonstrations initialize the base VLA π0.5. For each critical observation, the selected phase specialist generates the action candidates and its critic determines their relative weights. The VLA learns from these targets in critical phases and replayed VLA actions in noncritical phases. Only the VLA is deployed.

papers.abstract: Agentic Real2Sim2Real systems can reconstruct a scene in simulation from camera observations, but contact-rich dynamics such as friction and restitution cannot be observed without interaction. We call this the dynamics gap and present CUE, an agentic system that closes it by interacting with the environment itself. Given only a high-level instruction and no resets, the agent builds its own perception, identifies physical parameters, and targets interactions where its simulation is least accurate. On billiards, CUE reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% relative to the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics conditions in simulation, and we further deploy it on a real pool table. More details can be found on the project website: https://cue-dynamics.github.io/
bullets: Addresses unobservable contact-rich properties such as friction and restitution.
Uses agent-directed interaction to identify physical parameters and target regions where simulation is least accurate.
Operates from a high-level instruction without environment resets, while building its own perception.
On billiards, reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% versus the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics simulation conditions.
Also demonstrates deployment on a real pool table.

papers.title: Closing the Dynamics Gap through Self-Directed Robotic Interaction
papers.tldr: CUE closes the Real2Sim2Real dynamics gap by autonomously probing an environment to identify hidden contact physics and improve simulation accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic assembly requires reliable perception and action across grasping, alignment, and insertion. Vision captures global object pose and scene context, where as fingertip touch provides local contact cues that are especially useful as contact states change. We present a visuotactile diffusion policy that combines four-step histories from two camera views and two fingertip tactile images to condition action-sequence generation. A recurrent temporal representation integrates recent observations from both modalities. To encourage it to capture how contact evolves under action, an auxiliary objective predicts fingertip-image changes two steps ahead from the temporal representation and demonstrated actions. This objective is used only during training and adds no inference-time computation. Across three independent training seeds in MuJoCo assembly experiments, the full model achieves an average success rate of $59.0\% \pm 2.6\%$, improving on the visual-only baseline ($42.7\% \pm 1.5\%$) by 16.3 percentage points.
bullets: Targets reliable perception and action across grasping, alignment, and insertion, where touch provides local contact information beyond vision.
Conditions action-sequence generation on four-step histories from two camera views and two fingertip tactile images.
Uses a recurrent temporal representation to integrate multimodal observations.
Adds a training-only objective that predicts fingertip-image changes two steps ahead from the representation and demonstrated actions, with no inference-time cost.
In MuJoCo assembly experiments, it achieves 59.0% ± 2.6% success across three seeds versus 42.7% ± 1.5% for a visual-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.
bullets: Addresses failures of Markovian VLA models on tasks requiring working memory and persistent context.
Uses factorized event detection with event-triggered updates to maintain task-relevant language history.
Evaluated on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks with 56 variants, including five inter-episode tasks.
Improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and reaches 78% subtask success on compositional generalization.
Uses up to 4.5× less memory and runs 2.5× faster than a keyframe baseline at long horizons.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon dexterous manipulation remains a fundamental challenge for robot learning, requiring the composition of multiple skills, precise bimanual coordination, generalizable visual understanding, and robust skill transitions. Yet existing manipulation benchmarks largely emphasize isolated skills or support only a limited range of end-effectors, making these capabilities difficult to evaluate systematically. We introduce DexArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate learning and generalization in long-horizon bimanual dexterous manipulation. DexArena features 10 long-horizon tasks and 30 stage-level tasks spanning diverse household and industrial scenarios. Each long-horizon task is composed of explicitly defined stages with physically grounded success conditions, enabling reliable evaluation of both intermediate progress and end-to-end task completion. A unified benchmark interface and verified human-teleoperated demonstrations enable testing different policy learning algorithms, with standardized simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation. Through extensive baseline experiments, we identify substantial challenges in precise manipulation, generalization to scene variation, and skill composition. DexArena establishes a challenging and reproducible benchmark for developing robot learning methods that move toward generalizable long-horizon dexterous behavior.
bullets: Covers 10 long-horizon and 30 stage-level tasks across household and industrial scenarios.
Tasks use explicitly defined stages and physically grounded success conditions to measure both intermediate progress and end-to-end completion.
Provides a standardized interface with human-teleoperated demonstrations, simulation configurations, scene randomization, trajectory replay, and task-level evaluation.
Baseline experiments reveal persistent challenges in precise manipulation, scene-variation generalization, and composing skills.

papers.abstract: Universal humanoid motion tracking is essential for enabling humanoid robots to perform diverse tasks in human environments. To capture the wide diversity of human motions, mixture-of-experts (MoE) policies have been widely adopted, leveraging dynamic routing to enhance policy expressiveness. However, we identify that divergence between old and updated policies can be misestimated during policy-gradient updates of MoE policies, due to their dynamic routing. Because most policy-gradient algorithms regulate policy updates based on the divergence, this misestimation can lead to either overly conservative or excessively large updates, which can yield a suboptimal policy. In this paper, we propose Mixture of Experts with Alternating Policy Optimization (MAPO), which alternately optimizes the router and the experts to avoid the divergence misestimation. MAPO consistently tracks 182 motions that PPO with MoE fails to track, whereas PPO with MoE tracks only one motion that MAPO fails to track. MAPO also attains the highest tracking success rate among the compared methods and the lowest tracking error across most error metrics, demonstrating its superior performance. Videos can be found on the project website: https://mapo-corl2026.github.io/MAPO/
bullets: MoE policies can misestimate old–updated policy divergence because their routing changes dynamically.
This misestimation may cause overly conservative or excessively large policy updates, producing suboptimal policies.
MAPO alternates optimization of the router and expert policies to address this issue.
MAPO consistently tracks 182 motions that PPO with MoE fails to track, while PPO with MoE tracks only one motion MAPO fails to track.
Among the compared methods, MAPO achieves the highest tracking success rate and lowest error across most metrics.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently shown great promise in robotic control, benefiting from the future imagination capability of large-scale pretrained video models. However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at test time, incurring substantial computational overhead and latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework for real-time robotic manipulation that distills intermediate denoising representations from a video diffusion model into an action model during training, while entirely discarding the video model at test time. We hypothesize that although video latent representations are high-dimensional, a compressed low-dimensional subspace is sufficient to provide effective supervision for action generation. This makes it possible to transfer such information effectively into an action model. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate competitive success rates while significantly improving inference efficiency. On LIBERO, W2A achieves a 95.9% average success rate. More importantly, W2A achieves about 21x faster inference than the representative WAM baseline.
bullets: Existing world action models often imagine future states at test time, creating prohibitive computational overhead for real-time control.
W2A uses two-stage training to transfer intermediate denoising representations from a pretrained video diffusion model into an action model.
The approach assumes effective supervision can be compressed into a low-dimensional subspace of the video latent space.
The video model is discarded at deployment, reducing inference cost while retaining useful world priors.
W2A reports a 95.9% average success rate on LIBERO and approximately 21× faster inference than a representative WAM baseline.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents are vulnerable to perturbations of their observed state inputs. Prior works often constrain state adversaries with $L_p$-norm uncertainty sets and evaluate policy performance under the resulting perturbations. However, in continuous control tasks like robotics control, different state dimensions have distinct physical meanings and influence policy behavior to different degrees, which $L_p$-norm sets fail to capture or explain. Moreover, it is important to identify when and along which state dimensions a policy is vulnerable, independently of the algorithm used to train it. In this paper, we focus on evaluation-time attacks applied to pretrained policies. We propose \textbf{P}erformance-\textbf{D}egradation \textbf{N}on-\textbf{U}niform \textbf{U}ncertainty \textbf{S}et (\method{}), an interpretable formulation of uncertainty sets for state perturbations. \method{} is state-dependent, dimension-wise non-uniform, and can be synthesized online during policy evaluation. We first formulate an ideal constrained optimization problem for \method{} computation, then introduce a surrogate constraint to make the problem tractable. Experiments across multiple continuous-control environments, policy algorithms, and state attacks show that \method{} reveals variation in policy sensitivity across states and dimensions, while its performance degradation is moderately controlled.
bullets: Targets a limitation of uniform $L_p$-norm sets, which overlook the differing meanings and policy influence of state dimensions.
Focuses on attacks against pretrained policies during evaluation, independently of the training algorithm.
Formulates an ideal constrained optimization problem and uses a tractable surrogate to synthesize the uncertainty sets online.
Experiments across continuous-control environments, policy algorithms, and state attacks show varying sensitivity across states and dimensions with moderately controlled performance degradation.

papers.abstract: A competent learned controller already recovers from many disturbances. Improving it means learning a correction, and learning when not to apply it. Freezing a skill's parameters does not settle the second half. In a controller that routes among frozen skills, a new entry rule can redirect the states an old skill succeeded on. We therefore constrain entry instead of parameters. Each update searches for a feedback skill at a measured failure. It fits an entry rule that reads observations and rejects every state on an accumulated successful trajectory. The skill is admitted only if the composed controller reproduces the new recovery on its own and replays every protected trajectory exactly. A finite-trajectory condition states when this preserves the previous controller. One mechanism runs on four streams: two motions on each of two humanoid systems. Two updates per stream add 62 recoveries over 192 withheld perturbations, and lose none of the base controller's successes. We then price that guarantee. Removing the constraint recovers 33 more conditions but stops eight protected ones from completing at all, and excluding only what admission proves necessary recovers none of that cost.
bullets: Targets the problem of new skill-entry rules redirecting states where existing skills already succeed.
Learns a feedback recovery skill at a measured failure and an observation-based entry rule.
Admission requires reproducing the new recovery and replaying every accumulated protected trajectory exactly.
Across four humanoid motion streams, two updates per stream added 62 recoveries over 192 withheld perturbations without losing base successes.
Removing the preservation constraint recovered 33 additional conditions but caused eight protected trajectories to fail; the approach is scoped to finite recorded trajectories.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy-goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy-goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision-robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://yewr.github.io/epo
bullets: Addresses failures of fixed planner-to-policy interfaces when contacts, balance, or disturbances change faster than high-level updates.
Learns a composite energy for each modular goal-conditioned policy, where lower energy indicates greater feasibility and more accurate target realization.
Refines candidate goals and executes the lowest-energy policy–goal pair during runtime orchestration.
New policies can be added by learning separate energy models without retraining existing policies or a centralized scheduler.
Simulation shows improved precision–robustness trade-offs, with sim-to-real deployment on humanoid loco-manipulation tasks using frozen policies and energy models.
