papers.abstract: Robot policies still fail at everyday manipulation: an unfamiliar task, an object never held before, a scene that changes mid-motion, a skill that should improve with use. They fail despite pretraining on over a million trajectories, pooled from dozens of robots at great expense, while a child acquires all of these abilities within a few years of learning from a single body. This survey argues that the gap is one of design, and proposes designs for the next generation of robot models, drawn from how the nervous system solves the same problems. From the body we take compliance: the policy commands stiffness alongside position, so the controller yields where the task allows and presses where it must, which greatly lowers the demand for precise position output. From the visual system, where a fast pathway for action runs in parallel with the slow pathway for recognition, we take a dedicated fast vision system for motor behavior: it precomputes the quantities the policy needs and drives a reactive policy at camera rate. From the cerebellum we take a predictor beside the policy that forecasts the consequence of each command and recalibrates from its own error. From motor cortex we take a single model that composes action units from primitives, verifies each at a sensory boundary, practices the weakest unit with a hypothesis in mind, and reasons each attempt closer to the goal. Proven primitives are then consolidated from code into weights, so they run fluently and respond quickly the next time. Together these describe a robot that acts on its own initiative, the basis of deployment and recursive self-improvement, and we offer each proposal as a hypothesis to be tested.
bullets: Robot policies struggle with novel tasks, objects, changing scenes, and continual skill improvement despite extensive trajectory data.
It draws design principles from the body, visual system, cerebellum, and motor cortex.
Key proposals include stiffness-aware control, a fast action-oriented vision pathway, predictive models for self-calibration, and compositional primitive-based planning.
The framework emphasizes sensory verification, targeted practice, reasoning toward goals, and consolidating successful primitives into model weights.
The proposals are presented as hypotheses for future testing, with autonomous initiative and recursive self-improvement as the broader goal.

figures.caption: Figure 26: Consolidation advances a primitive from a script over many functions to an end-to-end policy. (a) At first the model writes a perception pipeline that computes the slot’s pose and the key’s geometry in the hand before calling the orient template, which runs by Cartesian control. (b) Next the model outputs both values directly from the images and supplies them to the same template, so the explicit measuring code is no longer needed. (c) In the end the template lives in the orient experts of the model’s mixture-of-experts trunk: the action head of the same model reads their latent, no number is passed, and the action stream reacts at the control rate.
Figure 3: Opposing muscles set torque and stiffness separately. The difference of flexor and extensor pull sets the net torque, and their sum sets the stiffness at the same pose.

Figure 1: A child has three abilities that current robot policies lack. Top: a boy opens an unfamiliar drawer on the first try, while a policy finds no training handle to copy. Middle: a girl catches a flying toy, while a robot is still reasoning about shape and coordinates when the toy lands. Bottom: the boy’s piano playing improves with days of practice, while a robot never trained on the piano cannot learn it or improve over time, because its learning stopped the day it was deployed.

Figure 7: Vision and touch build a single object model, and each sense fills in what the other cannot. Vision covers the visible surfaces, while touch supplies weight, texture, slipperiness, and compliance, and explores the occluded back.
Figure 4: Contact supplies the surface detail. A yielding wrist and a soft towel follow the bumps, so the controller computes fewer corrections.

Figure 6: Slowly adapting (SA) afferents report steady pressure and rapidly adapting (RA) ones report change, so the four classes split what touch carries. The traces are schematic responses to a ramp-and-hold skin indentation: SA afferents sustain firing during the hold, RA afferents respond transiently during pressing and release, and SA2 afferents also fire at a low rate before contact, driven by resting skin stretch. RA afferents can also fire during ongoing motion or vibration. Spike counts and timing are illustrative rather than measured; responses depend on the stimulus and afferent [194, 2].

Figure 13: In the prevailing model, the dorsal stream is a bank of parallel channels. The figure expands the dorsal branch of Figure 12 and draws the motion areas MT and MST, which that figure folds into the parietal box, as a separate stage. Each visual area estimates one quantity the body needs (where to look, what is moving, what is within reach, where to reach, how to turn and shape the hand, and what a tool in hand reaches) and sends it to a partner in premotor, motor, or oculomotor areas; the italic line in each visual box names the reference frame the channel works in (Section 4.2.4). Each label names an area’s dominant contribution rather than its only one [331].
Figure 9: Descending signals from cortex turn down predicted or irrelevant tactile channels and turn up the task-relevant one, so the fingertip signal arrives at high contrast.

Figure 17: Joint World Action Models let the prediction loss train the action head, while cascaded ones only pass predicted frames forward. In the cascaded design a video generator synthesizes predicted frames and a separate inverse-dynamics module reads actions off them. In the joint design a shared backbone trained under one generative objective feeds a state head that generates future frames, which some variants skip at test time, and an action head that emits the executed chunk.

Figure 27: The practice agent finds the error-prone part across attempts, corrects it during inference, and hands the corrected record to consolidation. (a) Over seven episodes of opening a lock, insert passes rarely, and the blame falls on orient’s angle, which is solved with an arbitrary offset after several model calls and fails most first attempts; it is unfamiliar and error prone and is practiced first. (b) During practice the direction to move after each attempt comes from the graded goal test, the forecast against the outcome, or the model’s reasoning; the interval halves until the goal test fires, and the angle that passed is stored. (c) Consolidation then improves the coding strategy that finds the keypoints, trains the model to output the values directly, and trains the orient experts of the trunk, so the orient primitive becomes familiar.

Figure 21: Actions attach to a vision-language backbone in one of three ways. (a) The first generation bins each action dimension and decodes actions as text tokens, one at a time. (b) The current generation keeps the backbone and attaches a small action expert that attends to its features and denoises a noisy chunk into continuous actions by diffusion or flow matching; proprioception enters the expert, as drawn, in 𝜋0 and GR00T N1, and the backbone in SmolVLA [42, 40, 354]. (c) An omni model has no head. Images, text, and actions are tokens in one sequence, so the same network predicts the next action and the next image. Purple: transformer with pretrained weights. Teal: images, text, proprioception, and the action expert. Gray: discrete action tokens and the noise the expert denoises.

Figure 20: One model composes familiar primitives into a new solution. Reach, grasp, orient, and tool use, none of them learned for this task, combine to retrieve an out-of-reach key, and the same model turns the plan into movement.
Figure 10: When an object’s properties cannot be seen, the robot should probe before it commits. Lifting, tilting, and pressing within safe bounds each test a hypothesis the camera cannot settle.
Figure 2: The slot walls supply the rod’s trajectory. The hand pushes along the slot and yields across it, so the walls shape the path and the controller has far less of the curve to compute.
Figure 11: The same ball is read twice, by the two visual streams in the brain. The ventral stream resolves its pattern and identity; the dorsal stream resolves its trajectory and guides the catch.
Figure 5: Touch alone finds the handle and opens the door. With eyes closed the hand feels its way to the handle, turns it and pushes the door open; in the dark a camera has nothing to offer.

Figure 24: Motor cortex is M1, premotor cortex, and SMA, reciprocally connected, with three cortical inputs: prefrontal goals enter through SMA and premotor cortex, the parietal state enters through premotor cortex and, from S1 and area 5, M1 directly, and ACC reaches SMA and M1 through the cingulate motor areas [364]. M1 carries most of the corticospinal tract, and SMA, premotor, and cingulate areas each add a direct projection that bypasses it [100]. Motor cortex also drives the brainstem pathways and runs loops through the basal ganglia and cerebellum [230]; reflex afferents return to the cord and touch and proprioception return to parietal cortex. Only the principal pathways are drawn.

Figure 14: A visually guided action must re-express the retinal report in the frame its effector needs. The same dumpling has different coordinates in each frame along the chain: eye, head, body, hand, tool, and object.

Figure 8: Three neurons carry a fingertip signal to primary somatosensory cortex (S1), a chain short enough to leave time for a tactile correction within about 75 ms. The first-order neuron ascends on the same side through the spinal dorsal column to the cuneate nucleus of the medulla; the second-order neuron crosses there and ascends to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamus; the third-order neuron projects to S1 on the side opposite the stimulated hand. Each line ends in a dot at its synapse, and the legend colors mark the three cell bodies. Other branches and circuits are omitted [197].

Figure 15: A second viewpoint reveals what the head camera cannot see. The mug body partly hides its far-side handle from the head camera. Moving the wrist camera of the free hand to a side viewpoint reveals more of the handle before grasping. Teal arrows mark viewing directions; the curved gray arrow marks the wrist motion.

Figure 19: The same nuclear prediction leaves by two routes. Ascending (left), it reaches cortex through the ventrolateral thalamus. Descending (right), it joins the command in flight at the brainstem and spinal cord. Both arrive within tens of milliseconds of the command, before sensory feedback could alter it through cortex.

Figure 18: The cerebellar circuit is three synapses deep, wide in the middle, and local along its length. The highlighted paths trace one local circuit: parallel fibers run only a few millimeters [315], and about forty Purkinje cells converge on one nuclear neuron [309], so coupling between body parts is local by construction. The inferior olive (amber) returns the prediction error over one climbing fiber per Purkinje cell, which adjusts the parallel-fiber synapses that were active when the faulty prediction was made. Counts are rough human figures [12, 285, 202].

Figure 16: Having tossed the ball herself, she knows from the throw where and when it will land. A copy of the tossing command is enough to forecast the ball’s arrival, so the right hand is already in place while the ball is still in the air. The faint circles show predicted positions of the same ball.

Figure 22: A robot learns mostly before it leaves the factory and afterwards executes the learned policy; a human begins with a genome rather than pretrained weights and does most of its learning after birth, through play, practice, and observation.

Figure 25: One action unit runs as a loop; the arrows show the flow of control rather than anatomical pathways. Purple marks the four stages, run clockwise, and teal what each stage reads. Solid teal arrows have direct support: the cerebellar forecast amends the unit in flight [31, 252] and sustains and times the cortical preparation of the next [122, 60]. Dashed arrows are hypotheses: whether the forecast also times the basal ganglia release is untested, and pre-SMA, which launches units and switches between them [205, 178], is proposed here to do so on the ACC verdict. Assigning one area to each stage is a simplification; each area takes part in more than one.

Figure 12: Vision for action and vision for recognition separate after V1, and a collicular route bypasses cortex entirely. The geniculate route through V1 divides into a dorsal stream through posterior parietal cortex to premotor and motor areas (vision for action) and a ventral stream through V2 and V4 into inferotemporal cortex (vision for recognition); a separate collicular route drives fast orienting of eyes and head without cortex.

Figure 23: Unlocking a door is four action units in a fixed order, reach, orient, insert, and rotate, and each ends at a sensory event: the tip reaches the slot, the key aligns, it stops at the end, the lock turns.

Table 1: No single sensor family combines fine resolution, kilohertz speed, and shear. Resolution and speed are order-of-magnitude values typical of each family, and the cited works are representative examples. A taxel (“tactile pixel”) is one sensing point on the skin.
Table 3: Discrepancies between the current robot stack and the nervous system, stage by stage, and the proposal each chapter derives from the gap.

Table 2: Four afferent classes split touch by receptive-field size and adaptation [186, 389, 194]. The pairing of SA2 afferents with Ruffini endings is disputed, since the human fingertip holds few such endings [303]. Figure 6 uses the same codes.

papers.selection_reason: Survey and proposals for robot learning inspired by neuroscience, focusing on policy design and learning.
papers.title: Neuro Inspired Robotics: What Robot Learning Can Borrow from the Sensorimotor Brain
papers.tldr: This survey proposes brain-inspired designs to make robot learning more adaptive, efficient, and capable of everyday manipulation beyond large-scale pretraining.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.
bullets: Standardizes policy serving and evaluation protocols across locally operated robots at 124 sites.
Evaluates five VLA policies and three frontier agents across four embodiments using open and fine-tuning tracks.
Frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies in open-world trials, but all systems struggle with reliable completion.
Fine-tuning changes model rankings substantially across embodiments; Open Track rankings poorly predict adapted performance.
Partial-progress metrics and active matchmaking provide more informative and trial-efficient evaluation than success rates and uniform sampling.

figures.caption: Figure 1 RoboColosseum overview. RoboColosseum connects distributed evaluation sites through shared robot interfaces, policy-serving infrastructure, and two complementary evaluation tracks. In the Fine-tune Track, policies receive the same 100 demonstrations per task and are evaluated on predefined tasks using common success and progress criteria. In the OpenTrack, policies are evaluated without additional task-specific adaptation through blinded, pairwise comparisons under matched local conditions, while tasks and environments vary across comparisons. The results shown for both tracks are based on evaluations we conducted from 17 September to 28 October 2026. The project spans SO-101, Franka in the DROID configuration, Bimanual-YAM, and Unitree G1, with participation determined by track and model compatibility. The lower panels illustrate track-specific evaluation outputs and examples of physical evaluation settings. The global network depicts the broader project vision; the scope of completed experiments is reported separately.
Figure 3 Open Track DCR ratings across embodiments. Points show posterior mean DCR ratings on an Elo-style scale, with 95% credible intervals; n is the number of evaluations involving each system.

Figure 5 Open Track performance by manipulation category. (a) Relative performance: category-specific, progress-based BTD expected comparison scores, i.e., the probability of winning plus half the probability of tying against a system of average ability, where a comparison is won by the system with higher normalized progress and 50% indicates average relative performance; bold values have 95% intervals that exclude 50%. (b) Mean normalized task progress and (c) success rate of each system’s own executions, both in percent. Values are followed by ± half the width of the 95% interval (bootstrap for (a) and (b), Wilson for (c)). n, shown in (a), is the number of evaluations involving each system and is the same in all three panels. Hatched cells have insufficient support (n < 10 or no evaluations). Relative scores in (a) compare systems under matched conditions, whereas the absolute values in (b) and (c) also reflect differences in the embodiments and tasks on which each system was evaluated.

Figure 6 Physical task performance across human-rated task difficulty. Open Track policy executions grouped by the human-rated difficulty of the task, with each pairwise evaluation contributing one execution per compared system. (a) Success rate, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals. (b) Mean normalized progress among unsuccessful executions, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. n is the number of executions in each difficulty range.

Figure 4 Task progress of frontier AI models versus VLA policies. Comparison of normalized task progress across 901 Open Track evaluations, each involving a frontier AI model and a VLA policy on the same task. (a) Percentage of comparisons in which the agent makes more progress, the VLA makes more progress, or both make equal progress. Numbers inside the bars show comparison counts. (b) Mean difference in task progress (agent minus VLA, in percentage points), with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Positive values favor the agent.

Figure 9 Cross-track ranking consistency by embodiment. Open Track and Fine-tune Track rankings of the five VLA policies on (a) SO-101, (b) DROID/Franka, and (c) Bimanual-YAM. For each embodiment, the Open Track rank is computed from the DCR rating, while the Fine-tuning rank is computed from the mean progress score (PS) across its five tasks. Rank 1 denotes the best-performing model, and the dashed diagonal indicates identical rankings across the two tracks. Each panel reports Spearman’s rank correlation and the number of model pairs with the same relative ordering in both tracks.

Figure 7 Task progress reachability. Percentage of trials satisfying at least a given fraction of task criteria, averaged over the five tasks of each embodiment with equal weight. The 100% point is the full success rate. †LingBot-VLA v2 on FT-YAM-02 was stopped after n=1 trial, and GR00T N1.7 on FT-YAM-03 was stopped after n=9 trials, for safety.
Figure 12 Per-task progress reachability on SO-101. Percentage of the 25 trials per model satisfying at least a given fraction of the task’s K progress criteria.
Figure 13 Per-task progress reachability on DROID. Percentage of the 25 trials per model satisfying at least a given fraction of the task’s K progress criteria.
Figure 15 Per-task progress reachability on Unitree G1. Percentage of the 25 trials per model satisfying at least a given fraction of the task’s K progress criteria.

Figure 8 Policy-specific failure stages after fine-tuning. We show two tasks whose progress criteria form an ordered sequence: SO-101 cube_drawer and DROID/Franka close_laptop. Each bar divides a policy’s 25 evaluation trials into full-task successes (green) and failures, shaded by the first criterion the trial did not meet (darker red indicates an earlier failure). Numbers give trial counts; segments of a single trial are unlabeled. Policies trained on the same demonstrations exhibit markedly different failure locations, revealing task- and policy-specific execution bottlenecks that are hidden by success rate alone.

Figure 2 Robot platforms and hardware configurations. From left to right: Bimanual-YAM, SO-101, Franka in the DROID configuration, and Unitree G1, shown from the front and rear. Annotations identify cameras, grippers, computing equipment, and supporting hardware. These platforms span bimanual manipulation, low-cost and researchgrade single-arm manipulation, and humanoid manipulation with locomotion. Observation and action specifications are standardized within each embodiment to support compatible policies across evaluation sites.

Figure 14 Per-task progress reachability on Bimanual-YAM. Percentage of completed trials satisfying at least a given fraction of the task’s K progress criteria. Hollow markers denote evaluations stopped early for safety, with the number of completed trials n given in the panel title; all other curves use 25 trials.

Table 4 Per-model fine-tuning hyperparameters. Peak learning rates are after linear scaling from the recipe’s batch size to the effective batch size. “Upstream default” denotes the value in the cited recipe, left unchanged.
Table 3 Fine-tuning settings shared by all models.
Table 5 Agents evaluated in the Open Track.

Table 1 Embodiments in RoboColosseum. Each embodiment has a fixed observation and action specification shared by all policies and sites. Open Track checkpoints are trained on the listed embodiment dataset; Fine-tune Track checkpoints use only the task demonstrations (Section 3.2.1). Action dimensions include one gripper dimension per arm: 5 arm joints for SO-101, 7 for the Franka, and 6 per arm for Bimanual-YAM.

Table 2 Per-task results on the Fine-tune track. Cells report normalized progress score (PS, %) and full-success rate (SR, %) as mean ± standard error (SE), using 25 trial slots per policy and task. Unexecuted trials following a safety stop are scored zero. Embodiment averages weight the five tasks equally. Best and second-best means for each metric are marked in bold and underline; ties share ranks at the displayed precision. †Evaluation stopped for safety reasons: LingBot-VLA v2 on YAM drawer after 1 trial, and GR00T N1.7 on YAM microwave after 9 trials.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict scene changes to guide robot actions, yet their RGB futures entangle state changes with appearance and lack 3D geometry. Recent WAMs add geometry as a training signal or a control interface, or build native 3D models, but decide what geometry to model rather than how the action should read it. Intuitively, control-relevant cues lie at embodiment--object interactions and their transitions, yet probing existing WAMs reveals that their action attention underweights these interactions in favor of the rest of the embodiment. To focus the action on these interactions, we present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field recording the image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. With the embodiment and objects in one field, their relative motion, which marks an interaction, can be read off. Guided by this motion and the task, Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) selects where the action reads, and Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) selects when, around grasp and release. As GeoDelta encodes surface motion rather than embodiment-specific controls, it serves as a human--robot quasi-action that links action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H, which we curate, to robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, especially under visual shifts. Project page: https://droliven.github.io/Gnomon4D.
bullets: Addresses the problem that RGB-based world-action models entangle appearance and state changes, while action attention often overlooks control-relevant interactions.
Jointly predicts future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D field of image-plane displacement and depth changes for embodiment and object points.
Uses Interaction-Salient Attention to select where to attend and Transition-Anchored Aggregation to focus around grasp and release transitions.
GeoDelta enables action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H and robot mid-training on Robot-30H by acting as a human–robot quasi-action.
Leads on RoboTwin 2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, particularly under visual shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of Gnomon4D. (a) The Video, GeoDelta, and Action experts generate their future modalities through joint attention, and an interaction readout enters the Action expert residually. (b) GeoDelta and Action share a denoising clock that finishes ahead of Video, so actions are ready before the video is refined. (c) InSAttn turns task-conditioned embodiment–object relative motion into saliency that selects interaction regions, and TransAgg aggregates the frames where this relation changes. Image tiles show RoboTwin examples.

papers.abstract: Does effective swimming with multiple underactuated soft arms require explicit coordination between arms? We hypothesize that an eight-arm swimmer can control its swimming speed and direction by independently learning each arm's actuation amplitude under a shared rhythmic drive, without prescribed inter-arm phase coupling. To test this hypothesis, we compare three reinforcement learning-based control strategies using proximal policy optimization (PPO): (1) learning arm-specific actuation amplitudes without inter-arm phase coupling, (2) learning actuation amplitudes with prescribed inter-arm phase coupling, and (3) directly learning actuator commands through end-to-end PPO without an explicit rhythmic structure. Across 200 episodes with randomized three-dimensional velocity commands, the controller without phase coupling satisfies the tracking criterion in 169 episodes, compared with 117 for the phase-coupled controller and 28 for end-to-end PPO. Straight-line swimming and commanded direction-change trials further demonstrate more accurate velocity tracking without phase coupling. These findings suggest that effective eight-arm swimming does not require prescribed inter-arm phase coupling, but can instead be achieved through learned arm-specific amplitude modulation within a rhythmic control structure.
bullets: The study tests whether explicit inter-arm coordination is necessary for swimming with underactuated soft arms.
It compares three PPO controllers: amplitude learning without phase coupling, amplitude learning with prescribed coupling, and end-to-end actuator-command learning.
Without phase coupling, the controller met the tracking criterion in 169 of 200 randomized 3D-velocity episodes, versus 117 with coupling and 28 for end-to-end PPO.
Straight-line and direction-change trials also showed more accurate velocity tracking without prescribed phase coupling.
The result is scoped to the tested eight-arm swimmer and control setup; it supports learned amplitude modulation within a rhythmic structure.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Non-coordinated PPO for an underactuated eight-arm underwater robot. (a) Idealized morphology, multibody realization, and a bent-arm schematic. The orange motor symbol marks the actuated base hinge; ten rigid links and nine passive hinges approximate arm compliance. (b) PPO learning and closedloop control. Observations from MuJoCo drive the policy, while rewards guide updates to the policy and value networks. The policy modulates a shared Hopf oscillator and the actuator mapping. (c) Nine-dimensional policy modulation consists of one common frequency f and eight arm-specific amplitude gains A1, . . . , A8. The frequency drives a single oscillator, whose common waveform is distributed to all arm channels. Each gain scales its channel before a fixed control midpoint and clipping map it to a bounded actuator input ui. The hydrodynamics inset in (b) is a conceptual illustration generated using OpenAI’s image-generation tool.

papers.abstract: Treating morphology and control as separate design problems has constrained the efficiency and adaptability of quadrupedal robots, while current co-design approaches are often constrained by restricted design spaces. We overcome this limit by introducing Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages and adjustable passive knee compliance. A two-stage framework combining reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization is developed: the morphology-conditioned control policy is trained across designs and then held fixed during task-specific design selection. The resulting designs and policies deployed zero-shot reduce the cost of transport by 18.6% and 35.7% for inspection and payload-carrying tasks. Comparisons demonstrate that full geometry-compliance co-design outperforms fixed and restricted design scopes. Cross-task tests further reveal distinct task-specific morphologies with shared mechanical trade-offs. These results provide hardware-level evidence that expanding the physical design space alongside learned control is essential to realize the full potential of task-driven morphology-control co-design in legged robotics.
bullets: Introduces Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages, and adjustable passive knee compliance.
Trains a morphology-conditioned control policy across designs, then selects task-specific designs while keeping the policy fixed.
Zero-shot deployments reduce cost of transport by 18.6% for inspection and 35.7% for payload-carrying tasks.
Full geometry–compliance co-design outperforms fixed or restricted design spaces.
Cross-task results show distinct task-specific morphologies sharing mechanical trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.
bullets: Gaussian winner-action distillation can introduce projection error and increase action variance when selected actions lie far from the policy mean.
IGP uses a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, replacing projection error with bounded discretization error.
Gumbel Top-K sampling and MPPI-style iterative refinement avoid the combinatorial cost of high-dimensional discrete search.
On DMControl and HumanoidBench, IGP reports state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency.
IGP also generates more temporally stable action sequences, supporting potential robotic deployment.

papers.abstract: RL locomotion policies trained under nominal simulation conditions may encounter distribution shifts that compromise safety. Predictive monitors could anticipate violations, but their world-model forecasts may become unreliable under shift, and ensemble disagreement is not calibrated. We evaluate predictive Signal Temporal Logic (STL) monitoring for frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies using closed-loop world-model rollouts and a three-model ensemble. Across external-force, observation-noise, and mass shifts, predicted robustness ranks HalfCheetah's future STL violations strongly, whereas disagreement does not reliably track observation prediction error or violations. Under severe noise, violations remain common ($64.2\pm24.4\%$ at $K{=}20$ across three PPO seeds), yet current-state robustness without prediction comes within $0.03$ AUROC of predictive robustness. Penalizing predicted robustness by disagreement does not consistently improve ranking. Ant provides complementary per-specification evidence, but its composite target has no positive violations and its any-violation target is single-class in most evaluated seed-condition slices. Overall, predictive robustness provides useful STL-specific ranking but little demonstrated additional ranking value over the current state; these findings caution against treating ensemble disagreement as a reliable indicator of safety uncertainty.
bullets: Studies frozen Ant-v5 and HalfCheetah-v5 policies under external-force, observation-noise, and mass distribution shifts.
Uses closed-loop world-model rollouts with a three-model ensemble to predict STL robustness and future violations.
Predictive robustness ranks HalfCheetah violations strongly, while ensemble disagreement does not reliably indicate prediction error or safety violations.
Under severe noise, violations remain frequent, but current-state robustness performs nearly as well as predictive robustness.
Results are limited for Ant because several violation targets are non-positive or single-class across evaluated slices.

papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) follows the pretrain-finetune paradigm: an agent is first pretrained on historical data and then adapted through online interaction. We study offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay, where the agent must improve using only the pretrained model and newly collected experience. A key challenge is to avoid catastrophic failure, a sharp early performance collapse during online fine-tuning, while still achieving strong asymptotic performance. Through controlled experiments, we show that removing offline replay can induce catastrophic failure, while retaining strong conservative regularization from offline RL can suppress final online performance. We also find that common stabilization strategies do not reliably prevent early collapse, and that the critic-side mechanisms we test are insufficient on their own. Motivated by these findings, we propose ANCHOR, a simple adaptation method that anchors the actor to the offline-pretrained policy early in online fine-tuning, anneals this constraint over time, and retains only a small residual conservative critic regularizer. We provide a theoretical interpretation showing that KL anchoring helps preserve critic reliability across nearby occupancy distributions, with a two-phase regret bound explaining when anchoring should be maintained or relaxed. Across FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit tasks, ANCHOR substantially reduces catastrophic failure while maintaining strong asymptotic performance. Ablations show that KL annealing and the residual conservative weight are important for balancing early stability and online adaptation, while additional analysis shows that ANCHOR is most beneficial when the pretrained policy contains useful behavior to preserve. Code is available at https://github.com/Cho-Geonwoo/ANCHOR.
bullets: Offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay can cause catastrophic early performance collapse.
Strong conservative regularization may prevent collapse but limit eventual online improvement; critic-only stabilization is insufficient.
ANCHOR anchors the actor to the pretrained policy early, anneals the KL constraint, and keeps a small residual conservative critic regularizer.
Theory links KL anchoring to critic reliability under nearby occupancy distributions and gives conditions for maintaining or relaxing the anchor.
Experiments on FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit show reduced catastrophic failure with strong asymptotic performance; benefits are greatest when pretrained behavior is useful.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ANCHOR improves both early stability and final performance. Existing methods do not consistently achieve both low catastrophic failure and strong asymptotic performance across tasks. Both metrics show task-dependent and inconsistent alignment with early performance collapse. The vertical dashed line marks the timestep at which the largest performance drop occurs.

Figure 7: Q-update volatility does not reliably predict catastrophic failure. We compare success rate and critic-update volatility across four tasks. Volatility shows weak and inconsistent correspondence with early performance collapse.

Figure 4: Benefit of ANCHOR depends on pretrained policy quality. ANCHOR reduces catastrophic failure more clearly when the offline-pretrained policy starts from a higher initial success rate. Curves with the same color correspond to the same pretrained policy. Results are averaged over three seeds.

Figure 5: Hyperparameter and architectural tweaks do not consistently mitigate catastrophic failure. From top to bottom, the plots correspond to: batch size, actor learning rate, critic learning rate, critic hidden dimension, actor hidden dimension, LayerNorm in the critic, LayerNorm in the actor, and the duration of the offline pretraining phase. Across all settings and tasks, none of these factors consistently mitigates catastrophic failure.

Here, α∗ denotes an intermediate value between 0 and αoff , where αoff is the conservative regularization weight used during offline pretraining. Increasing αKL slows the critic shift, but does not reliably prevent early performance collapse.

Figure 3: KL annealing improves early stability while preserving final performance. ANCHOR is compared with the fixed-KL and no-KL variants. The fixed-KL variant improves early stability but can limit final improvement, while the no-KL variant adapts aggressively but causes early collapse.

Figure 8: Sensitivity to batch size and UTD ratio. We vary the batch size (top) and UTD ratio (bottom) across three tasks. ANCHOR is generally robust to these choices, although larger batch size and larger UTD can increase learning instability.

Figure 12: Stronger preservation is insufficient in antmaze-ultra-diverse. Keeping both the conservative coefficient and KL coefficient fixed yields a higher mean success rate than ANCHOR during online fine-tuning, but does not significantly improve asymptotic performance.

A larger initial KL weight (β0 = 2.0) produces lower KL loss early in online fine-tuning, indicating that the KL penalty more strongly constrains deviation from the offline policy. As the KL coefficient is annealed, the gap between β0 = 0.5 and β0 = 2.0 gradually narrows.

papers.abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation is commonly formulated around explicit object pose estimation, yet reliable pose tracking is challenging under severe hand-object occlusions and often requires object-specific supervision. This dependence creates a bottleneck between perception and control that can limit robustness and scalability. We present an end-to-end visuomotor framework for dexterous in-hand reorientation that operates on RGB observations and proprioception without intermediate pose estimation. Our approach jointly learns visual representations and control policies through behavior distillation from privileged state teachers and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. Furthermore, we introduce image-goal-conditioned reorientation, allowing desired object configurations to be specified directly through images rather than canonical pose representations. We evaluate our approach across a diverse set of object geometries and instances in simulation, where it consistently outperforms pose-based methods and policies built on pretrained visual encoders. Finally, we demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer of a single image-goal-conditioned policy across five real-world objects, showing that accurate dexterous reorientation can be achieved without explicit pose estimation. For videos and code release, please refer to the project website: https://rffr.leggedrobotics.com/works/goaldex/
bullets: Addresses the brittleness and scalability limits of pose tracking under severe hand–object occlusion.
Jointly learns visual representations and control policies using privileged-state behavior distillation and auxiliary reconstruction.
Specifies target object configurations through goal images rather than canonical poses.
Outperforms pose-based methods and pretrained-encoder policies across diverse simulated object geometries and instances.
Transfers a single image-goal-conditioned policy directly to real-world reorientation across five objects.

Current RGB observations and goal images are encoded into visual representations and fused with proprioceptive inputs. A recurrent policy integrates the multimodal features over time to predict joint position targets, while auxiliary reconstruction and continuous contrastive objectives shape the latent representation using privileged simulation supervision.

papers.abstract: Learning accurate value functions is central to reinforcement learning (RL), yet remains challenging because supervision is limited and indirect: ground-truth values are unavailable, and each transition in the data only provides an immediate reward that can be used to construct bootstrapped targets as supervision. This challenge is particularly pronounced when data is limited or reward signals are sparse, as is common in real-world applications such as robotics. We argue that the key to accurate value learning in this limited data regime is extracting richer learning signals from the available data. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing, a new approach that uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and enables accurate value learning from limited data. Our key insight is that we can extract richer learning signals by enforcing Bellman consistency at every noise level. Empirically, Value Forcing improves the accuracy of estimating the return distribution, and prevents the distribution from collapsing to a single value, as occurs with prior methods. We instantiate Value Forcing with two practical value-learning algorithms: VF, an actor-critic method, and IVF, an implicit value-learning method. We evaluate both algorithms across $26$ long-horizon tasks in the offline RL setting and find that they outperform prior value-learning methods, with particularly large gains when data is limited. Our project website is available at https://chongyi-zheng.github.io/value-forcing.
bullets: Addresses inaccurate value estimation under sparse rewards and limited data, where only bootstrapped supervision is available.
Uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and applies Bellman consistency at every noise level.
Introduces two practical algorithms: VF for actor-critic learning and IVF for implicit value learning.
Across 26 long-horizon offline RL tasks, both methods outperform prior value-learning approaches, especially with limited data.
Better preserves return distributions instead of collapsing them to a single value.

figures.caption: Figure 1: We introduce Value Forcing, a new approach to learning distributional value functions with flow matching that supervises the learned return distribution at every flow noise level through Bellman consistency. Unlike prior methods that provide supervision only at selected noise levels or use inaccurate targets at others, Value Forcing provides substantially richer learning signals and enables much more accurate estimation of the return distribution, preventing it from collapsing around a single value. This in turn leads to better policy performance, especially in the limited-data regime.

Figure 2: Value Forcing learns more accurate return distributions than prior flow-based return estimators. (Left) We collect datasets to conduct policy evaluation experiments at a single state from each of the four OGBench domains. (Center) Value Forcing captures the ground-truth return distributions more accurately, while prior methods are biased and collapse their predictions into narrow peaks. (Right) Value Forcing achieves lower mean 1-Wasserstein distances than all three prior methods in all tasks.

Figure 3: Value Forcing improves offline RL performance across dataset sizes. Success rates are averaged over 20 OGBench tasks (Left) and 6 OCBench tasks (Right) at each dataset size. On OGBench, VF and IVF outperform their explicit and implicit baselines at 10% and 25% of the data, and remain competitive with more data. On OCBench, VF outperforms selected explicit methods on 25% of the dataset, while IVF leads among selected implicit methods on the full dataset. Hatched bars ( ) indicate distributional RL methods without flow matching. See Appendix C for complete results.
Figure 4: Comparisons of alternative Value Forcing instantiations for explicit methods (Left) and implicit methods (Right).

Figure 6: Similar to the results in Sec. 6.1, IVF learns more accurate return distributions than implicit distributional RL baselines. (Left) We conduct policy evaluation experiments on the same set of states from the four OGBench domains. (Center) IVF better captures the ground-truth return distributions, while Implicit C51, Implicit IQN, and DIVL produce shifted or overly concentrated predictions. (Right) IVF achieves lower mean 1-Wasserstein distances than all three baselines at the evaluated state in each of the 4 domains.
Figure 5: Reward scaling improves VF and IVF. Both VF and IVF achieve substantially higher success rates with reward scaling (w/) than without it (w/o).

Figure 8: Return flow hyperparameter ablations. We conduct ablation experiments to study the sensitivity of hyperparameters related to return flows on task 2 and task 4 of cube-triple and puzzle-4x4. For each hyperparameter, we show the success rates after aggregating over these 4 tasks.

Figure 7: Value Forcing learns return flows that better capture the spread of ground-truth returns. Following the policy evaluation experiments in Sec. 6.1, we compare the return flow paths of VF (Col 1), FlowCritic (Col 2), Value Flows (Col 3), and PCBF (Col 4) from Gaussian noise (τ = 0) to predicted returns (τ = 1). VF spreads its return paths at early noise levels (around τ = 0.25), while baselines concentrate their return paths close to the flow endpoint (around τ = 0.9).

Table 1: Comparison of Bellman constraints across flow-based value learning methods. Among the methods compared, VF and IVF model the full return distribution, while enforcing Bellman consistency at every noise level. This provides consistent supervision throughout the flow path, improving return estimation (Sec. 6.1) and offline RL performance (Sec. 6.2), particularly when data are limited.

papers.abstract: Retrieving objects from densely packed storage requires anticipating how contact disturbs surrounding objects when limited clearance prevents lifting the target over clutter. However, contact can propagate beyond the target's immediate neighbors, while accumulated prediction errors make learned dynamics unreliable over long planning horizons. We introduce DARE (Disturbance-Aware REtrieval), a geometry-aware relational dynamics framework that uses retrospective correction to improve long-horizon prediction for disturbance-aware retrieval. DARE encodes compact object descriptors and predicts action-conditioned disturbance propagation through object-level message passing. When a sparse observation becomes available, a learned corrector uses the prediction discrepancy to amend an earlier predicted state and reruns the intervening dynamics, propagating the correction through the predicted contact chain. These predictions guide a receding-horizon planner that balances retrieval progress against displacement and rotation of surrounding objects, permitting necessary contact while discouraging harmful disturbance. Experiments in planar and RoboCasa environments evaluate long-horizon prediction, generalization, and robustness for disturbance-aware retrieval in dense clutter. See our project website: https://the-back-to-the-future.github.io
bullets: Targets retrieval when limited clearance requires contacting surrounding objects.
Uses geometry-aware object descriptors and relational message passing to predict action-conditioned disturbance propagation.
Applies a learned corrector to sparse observations, amending earlier states and rerunning dynamics through predicted contact chains.
Guides receding-horizon planning that balances retrieval progress with surrounding-object displacement and rotation.
Evaluated in planar and RoboCasa environments for prediction, generalization, and robustness in dense clutter.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Pipeline Overview: Given object geometry and the current scene state, DARE propagates action-conditioned interactions over an object graph to predict scene evolution under candidate target motions. The resulting rollouts capture direct and indirect disturbances to surrounding objects, enabling the planner to select a retrieval trajectory that balances goal progress against collateral disturbance.

Fig. 1: Disturbance-aware retrieval. (a) Collision avoidance leaves the target blocked. (b) Direct retrieval topples a neighboring object. (c) Our method predicts contact-induced disturbance to plan retrieval through controlled contact, preserving stability of surrounding objects.
Fig. 6: Dynamics prediction. Terminal translation (left) and rotation (right) errors normalized by the no-motion error at each horizon. Rotation is omitted for symmetric pucks.

Fig. 8: Retrospective correction under noise. Translation (top) and rotation (bottom) RMSE over 40-step rollouts versus observation noise σ, fixed within each rollout. Shading indicates noise levels beyond the noise training range.

Fig. 4: Tabletop dynamics prediction under noise. Outlines in purple, light blue and dark blue, indicate predicted object poses in a held-out scene as the target (yellow) pushes through clutter. Uncorrected predictions drift (top), direct observation updates inherit noise (middle), and noise-trained correction maintains alignment with the objects (bottom).
Fig. 7: Effect of joint training. Terminal translation (top) and rotation (bottom) errors with shared pretrained initialization and matched additional optimization steps.

Fig. 3: Retrospective correction for long-horizon prediction. The corrector combines prior predictions with the observation mismatch at t15 (yellow) to estimate a corrected state t̃11, the first step after the last observation t10. Rerolling from it propagates the correction through the learned dynamics and initializes the next cycle, mitigating error drift.

Fig. 5: Object Retrieval Visualization Top-down views compare three planners, with target motion marked in orange. Each row shows four evenly spaced execution steps with translucent next-step poses and the executed target path in the final frame.

papers.title: Back to the Future: Predicting Long-Horizon Dynamics with Retrospective Correction for Disturbance-Aware Retrieval

papers.abstract: Data-driven sequential decision making in marketing and healthcare can benefit from observations collected in related environments, particularly when data in the environment of interest are limited. Transferring such information requires accounting for differences in rewards and transition dynamics across environments. We study knowledge transfer for offline reinforcement learning through a joint estimation framework that directly integrates source information into target value-function learning. We propose Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration (DFQI), which updates the target Q-function while simultaneously borrowing the source information through an L1 penalty that links the target coefficients to a weighted aggregate of source coefficients, with both determined jointly within each Bellman update. Using sieve approximation, we establish statistical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning in stationary discounted environments with common or heterogeneous transition kernels. Empirical studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DFQI framework in transferring source information to improve policy learning with limited target data.
bullets: Addresses offline reinforcement learning when target-environment data are scarce but related source-environment data are available.
Introduces Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration, which jointly estimates the target Q-function and a weighted source-coefficient aggregate during each Bellman update.
Uses an L1 penalty to connect target and transferred source coefficients, allowing information sharing despite differing rewards or transition dynamics.
Provides statistical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning under common or heterogeneous transition kernels.
Empirical studies show improved policy learning with limited target data; results are scoped to stationary discounted environments.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a teleoperation system for service robots that integrates human pose estimation with virtual reality (VR) to enable intuitive remote control. By using the Mediapipe framework for 2D pose detection and extending it with RGB-D data from the Intel RealSense D455 camera, a comprehensive 3D human pose estimation is achieved. This data is then mapped to the robot's kinematics, allowing the operator to control the robot's movements naturally. A VR interface was developed to provide an immersive perspective, enhancing the operator's situational awareness. Real-world experiments were conducted using the CHARMIE service robot to validate the system's effectiveness in tasks involving object manipulation. While the current system successfully demonstrates the potential of VR-based teleoperation, challenges remain in accurately capturing certain joint angles (e.g., wrist yaw) and ensuring precise mapping between human and robot movements. Future work includes the integration of inertial measurement units (IMUs) for improved rotational tracking and the implementation of more advanced control algorithms. Overall, this research contributes to the development of more intuitive and effective teleoperation systems for service robots, facilitating their deployment in complex and dynamic environments. This work further introduces a novel approach to teleoperation by combining RGB-D sensing with an innovative algorithm for real-time joint angle computation using Mediapipe, enhancing the precision of human-robot motion mapping and enabling immersive control through a VR interface. These contributions represent significant advancements in the field of human-robot interaction, particularly for service robot applications.
bullets: Combines Mediapipe 2D pose detection with Intel RealSense D455 RGB-D data to estimate 3D human pose.
Maps estimated human joint movements to the robot’s kinematics for natural control.
Provides an immersive VR interface intended to improve operator situational awareness.
Validated through real-world object-manipulation experiments with the CHARMIE service robot.
Wrist-yaw tracking and precise human–robot motion mapping remain challenging; future work includes IMUs and advanced control algorithms.

papers.abstract: Humanoid controllers need the ability to yield to external forces while retaining the capacity to resume their original tasks. However, tracking objectives penalize the deviations needed for yielding, while relaxing tracking goals persistently can make task recovery harder. Existing approaches often rely on task-specific interaction command interfaces or constructed compliant motion data and reference trajectories, limiting the direct reuse of their compliance-training mechanisms across different task interfaces. We introduce CompliantBot, a compliance-training framework for motion tracking and velocity-command locomotion. It preserves the original task inputs and requires no preconstructed compliant data or target trajectories. A state-dependent interaction force field couples applied loads to the robot's motion, enabling local articulation and whole-body movement to change the forces experienced. A complementary force-magnitude reward encourages lower interaction loads, while task rewards are downweighted during loading and restored after release to coordinate yielding and task resumption. The trained policies use task inputs and proprioceptive history without explicit external-force measurements. Across both task interfaces, CompliantBot yields farther under constant pulls and experiences lower spring interaction loads than matched baselines, while resuming task tracking after force removal. CompliantBot achieves the highest task completion among the compared methods under stronger pulls. Power evaluations further show that CompliantBot has the lowest mean joint mechanical power among the compared methods. Real-robot demonstrations further illustrate compliant responses through arm motion, stepping, and body reorientation.
bullets: Addresses the conflict between force yielding and maintaining or recovering task objectives.
Uses a state-dependent interaction force field, force-magnitude reward, and adaptive task-reward weighting during loading and release.
Supports both motion-tracking and velocity-command locomotion while preserving their original task inputs.
Outperforms matched baselines in yielding distance, spring-load reduction, strong-pull task completion, and mean joint mechanical power.
Real-robot demonstrations show compliant arm motion, stepping, and body reorientation.

papers.abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9$\times$ the success, 5.4$\times$ the generalization, and 3.9$\times$ the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8$\times$ faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.
bullets: Addresses the discontinuity of policies that predict discrete actions directly.
Uses a neural ODE to learn an action vector field and integrates actions from the previous action at deployment.
A diversity head supports multimodal behavior by randomizing the field direction.
Evaluated across visuomotor policies, VLA/WAM action heads, and model-based RL on diverse real-world robotic tasks.
Reports strong gains over flow matching in early IL training, faster action generation, smoother motion, and the highest success rate across 14 real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub.
bullets: VLA-generated actions lack guaranteed safety in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes.
Standard CBF-QP filters enforce local safety but can divert the robot from its task trajectory without providing recovery guidance.
The method detects blocked short-horizon action chunks and generates entry-exit-rejoin routes around obstacles.
These routes softly guide the CBF-QP objective, while safety constraints remain hard.
On SafeLIBERO, it improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess over AEGIS.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair. The method uses the VLA action chunk to estimate a nominal future trajectory and detect obstacle-induced blockage. When the nominal trajectory is blocked, it generates an entry-exit-rejoin route around the obstacle and adds the selected route to the CBF-QP objective as soft guidance. The CBF constraint remains hard, so the repaired action preserves safety while following a recoverable route toward task completion.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skill libraries to support complex task execution. However, determining which skills are needed remains challenging in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically select a fixed skill set before execution, implicitly assuming that a task's procedural requirements can be determined from its initial description. This assumption is restrictive for long-horizon interaction, where new requirements emerge from intermediate observations, execution outcomes, and newly revealed constraints. This motivates just-in-time skill retrieval, which dynamically selects skills as execution unfolds. Just-in-time skill retrieval is promising but challenging: the utility of a skill depends not only on the current context, but also on the evolving task state shaped by prior steps. To this end, we propose JitSkill, a state-grounded framework that addresses this challenge through continuous task-state tracking. By connecting emerging requirements with accumulated task progress, JitSkill provides procedural support throughout execution without treating each retrieval decision independently. Experiments across three agent benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness in improving long-horizon task completion. Our code is available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/JitSkill.git/.
bullets: Fixed upfront skill selection can miss requirements that emerge during execution.
JitSkill performs just-in-time retrieval based on both current needs and accumulated task progress.
Continuous state tracking links intermediate observations, outcomes, and constraints to procedural support.
Experiments on three agent benchmarks show improved long-horizon task completion.
The approach targets tasks whose procedural requirements cannot be fully inferred from the initial description.

papers.abstract: Acquiring objects in human environments is hard for humanoids: targets are partially occluded under egocentric viewpoints, and reaching them demands coordinated whole-body motion that keeps the target visible and reachable while the base stays stable. We present HuG, a framework for whole-body affordance-aware grasping with active perception that couples perception and action through a Perceive-Align-Grasp pipeline: belief-driven active perception resolves occlusion by treating viewpoint as an explicit decision variable; a point-cloud-conditioned affordance policy proposes whole-body grasps; and an affordance-aware alignment stage repositions the body to the most executable configuration. A key insight is that, on a floating base, kinematic validity is not enough: we curate training data with controller-in-the-loop dynamics simulation, rejecting 73% of kinematically valid grasps that would destabilize the deployment controller, so the policy learns kinodynamically feasible affordances. Trained entirely in simulation with zero real demonstrations, HuG attains 87.5% real-world success on a multi-level shelf task, generalizes to novel objects, and holds at least 73% success at every tested height. Beyond generalizing within its training distribution, the policy extrapolates spatially: at scale in simulation it succeeds at table heights well below any seen during training, indicating that kinodynamically filtered synthetic data grounds affordances in object geometry and whole-body feasibility rather than in memorized configurations.
bullets: Uses a Perceive–Align–Grasp pipeline that couples viewpoint selection, affordance prediction, and body repositioning.
Treats viewpoint as a decision variable to resolve occlusions and maintain target visibility and reachability.
Learns point-cloud-conditioned whole-body affordances filtered by controller-in-the-loop dynamics, not kinematics alone.
Trained without real demonstrations, HuG achieves 87.5% real-world success on a multi-level shelf task and at least 73% at each tested height.
Generalizes to novel objects and extrapolates in simulation to table heights below those seen during training.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires accurate metric depth, yet commodity RGB-D cameras often fail on non-Lambertian objects such as transparent, reflective, and translucent materials, producing holes, structured noise, and biased depth. Most restoration methods produce only a single depth map, treating noisy and reliable regions uniformly for downstream tasks while ignoring regional uncertainty. We present UA-Depth, an uncertainty-aware depth restoration framework that iteratively co-refines depth and pixel-wise uncertainty, and uses uncertainty-gated features to suppress unreliable cues for stable updates. To strengthen zero-shot behavior, UA-Depth leverages a frozen depth foundation model as a prior to initialize missing or unreliable depth, and applies two-stage MAD-weighted log-depth scale normalization to reduce outlier bias in relative-to-metric alignment. We introduce an eight-dataset zero-shot benchmark across diverse scenes, materials, and sensors. Across these benchmarks, UA-Depth achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines, with particularly strong gains on datasets dominated by transparent and reflective objects. Beyond depth metrics, we demonstrate downstream improvements in category-level 6D pose estimation and 6D grasp synthesis by exploiting the predicted uncertainty. \emph{Code, models, and data for training and evaluation will be released upon publication.}
bullets: Targets holes, structured noise, and bias in RGB-D data from transparent, reflective, and translucent objects.
Iteratively co-refines depth with pixel-wise uncertainty and gates features to suppress unreliable cues.
Uses a frozen depth foundation model for initialization and MAD-weighted log-depth normalization for relative-to-metric alignment.
Evaluated zero-shot across eight datasets spanning diverse scenes, materials, and sensors.
Achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines and improves category-level 6D pose estimation and grasp synthesis.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Detailed overview of Depth-Uncertainty Co-Refinement with Uncertainty-aware Context Feature Calibration (UCFC). We run T ConvGRU refinement steps: at step t, the ConvGRU updates the hidden state Ht and predicts residual updates that refine depth Dt and uncertainty Ut. UCFC is applied at each iteration to calibrate both RGB and depth context features using the predicted uncertainty, gating unreliable regions before they are fused into the ConvGRU update.

Fig. 7. Qualitative zero-shot comparison on in-the-wild RGB-D scenes captured with a RealSense D435. We show the raw depth and the back-projected point clouds using the same intrinsics, with insets highlighting challenging regions. Our method reduces holes and structured noise on transparent/reflective objects and better preserves fine-scale geometry and boundaries compared with baselines.

Fig. 5. Risk–coverage curves on object pixels of the DREDS test split [11] for uncertainty learned with different error proxies. Pixels are ranked by predicted uncertainty and retained from low to high uncertainty; we plot mean REL (risk) versus retained fraction (coverage). Lower AURC indicates better uncertainty ranking.

Fig. 2. Overview of UA-Depth. Given an RGB observation and a sensor depth map, we first extract RGB features with relative depth using a frozen DAV2 backbone [31]. We then derive two feature streams for refinement: an RGB context feature obtained by projecting DAV2 features through a lightweight feature transfer MLP, and a sensor-depth context feature produced by a context network (Sec. III-B). In parallel, the proposed ADF module (Sec. III-C) initializes metric depth and uncertainty by aligning the relative depth to valid sensor measurements and filling missing regions. Starting from this initialization, the Depth-Uncertainty Co-Refinement module (Sec. III-D) jointly updates depth and uncertainty over several iterations, and finally upsamples the predictions to the input resolution via convex sampling [32]. We discuss uncertainty modeling in Sec. III-E. For the mixed-dataset model, Robust-SN (Sec. III-F) replaces the scale–shift alignment in ADF with robust log-depth alignment and normalization, and is applied during both training and inference.

papers.abstract: Robots manipulating in cluttered spaces must often plan from partial views where foreground objects occlude the target, surrounding geometry, and usable free space. Reactive policies often miss these hidden constraints, while exhaustive search becomes computationally prohibitive in dense clutter. We present SCOUT, an occlusion-aware planning framework that bridges high-level deliberation with grounded physical rollouts. SCOUT leverages an object-centric scene representation to reconstruct hidden geometry and derive a relational planning state capturing blocker hierarchies and accessibility corridors. To navigate the vast action space in clutter, an LLM proposes structured action candidates which are then rigorously evaluated via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) using a learned action-conditioned world model. Evaluations on 'Reveal' and 'Placement' tasks show that SCOUT outperforms Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, embodied agents, and 3D world models, with significant gains in long-horizon tasks requiring reasoning over occluded geometry. We further validate the framework's robustness through real-world robotic manipulation in a cluttered shelf environment.
bullets: Addresses hidden geometry, blockers, and free-space constraints in cluttered, partially observed environments.
Reconstructs occluded structure into a relational planning state with blocker hierarchies and accessibility corridors.
Uses an LLM to propose structured actions, then evaluates them through MCTS with a learned action-conditioned world model.
Outperforms several policy and world-model baselines on Reveal and Placement tasks, especially for long-horizon occlusion reasoning.
Validated in real-world manipulation within a cluttered shelf environment.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SCOUT. From partial RGB-D observations, GHOST reconstructs an objectcentric hidden scene representation, which is converted into a relational planning state. (c) Hidden-scene failure: a small back-row target remains too occluded to be reconstructed from partial observations. (d) Geometric-validity failure: dense clutter leaves no feasible retrieval corridor under the current primitive set.

papers.abstract: To reduce reliance on manual design and extensive parameter tuning, a framework for the autonomous evolution of exoskeleton assistance policies through human feedback is proposed. Assistance policies are autonomously generated as executable control code by an intelligent agent and evaluated in experiments with human participants. Subjective user feedback, movement performance, and muscle activation measurements are incorporated into policy assessment. Based on these assessments, policy deficiencies are autonomously identified and the control code is revised by the agent for subsequent trials. A closed loop of policy generation, human feedback, evaluation, and autonomous refinement is thereby established. The framework is evaluated using GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi, and initial assistance performance and refinement outcomes are compared across models. Despite differences in initial performance, effective assistance is achieved with all four models after a single autonomous refinement iteration under the tested conditions. Across three tasks, biceps and triceps muscle activation levels are reduced by 29.4% and 35.2%, respectively, compared with those measured without an exoskeleton. However, limited adaptability to unexpected situations is observed, indicating that further improvements in robustness and safety are required.
bullets: Addresses the need to reduce manual policy design and extensive parameter tuning for exoskeleton control.
Generates executable control code, evaluates it with user feedback, movement performance, and muscle activation, then revises it autonomously.
Evaluates GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi; all achieved effective assistance after one refinement iteration under the tested conditions.
Across three tasks, biceps and triceps activation decreased by 29.4% and 35.2%, respectively, versus no exoskeleton.
Robustness and safety remain limited, particularly in unexpected situations.

During execution, the framework exchanges joint-state information and torque commands with the exoskeleton. EMG results, task completion, and participant feedback inform policy assessment. The feedback analysis module either proposes a revision based on a selected policy or selects an existing policy for reuse. Code revisions and policy-version selection occur between trials.
