papers.abstract: In modern robot learning, generative robot policies are first pretrained through supervised learning from demonstrations, then refined through reinforcement learning, supervised finetuning, or other forms of posttraining. Yet conventional pretraining metrics, such as validation loss and average task success, provide an incomplete account of which policies support both effective direct deployment and subsequent posttraining. In this work, we study closed-loop pass@k, which evaluates the probability that k rollouts from the same initial condition attain at least one success. Thus, pass@1 measures mean task success; large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable under repeated sampling. Across a wide range of posttraining recipes, we show that large-k pass@k reveals posttraining differences not captured by pass@1. In particular, checkpoints with similar pass@1 but different large-k pass@k have different posttraining performance. Moreover, we show pass@k peaks at different checkpoints during supervised pretraining, revealing a coverage-reliability tradeoff over the course of training. Based on these observations, we propose two practical interventions: (1) a purely offline checkpoint-selection criterion that balances coverage and reliability without closed-loop evaluation, and (2) a generative data augmentation procedure that expands supervision beyond the finite demonstration set, preserving large-k pass@k while maintaining or improving pass@1 and raising the observed coverage-reliability Pareto frontier. Together, our results motivate evaluation, checkpoint selection, and training procedures that explicitly account for posttraining. Blog post, visualizations, and code are available at https://zhanyisun.github.io/robot-policy-learning-dynamics/.
bullets: Pass@1 measures average success, while large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable through repeated sampling from the same initial state.
Policies with similar pass@1 can differ substantially in posttraining performance when their large-k pass@k differs.
During supervised pretraining, coverage and reliability peak at different checkpoints, revealing a coverage–reliability tradeoff.
The work proposes offline checkpoint selection and generative data augmentation to preserve or improve coverage and reliability.
The findings motivate evaluation and training procedures that explicitly account for downstream posttraining potential.

figures.caption: Figure 5: During pretraining, generative augmentation preserves coverage while maintaining, and in some tasks improving, reliability (pass@1). Across most MimicGen tasks and RoboCasa, Baseline DP loses pass@10 at later checkpoints. JointAug prevents this loss of coverage while maintaining or improving pass@1. PostBC also preserves pass@10 better than Baseline DP, but can do so at the cost of pass@1.

Figure 1: Later checkpoints trade large-k pass@k for mean task success; checkpoints with similar pass@1 can lead to different posttraining performance. Left: single-task BC followed by residual RL on two representative MimicGen tasks, with (a) showing pass@k during BC and (b) residual RL from different BC checkpoints. Right: multitask pretraining on RoboCasa tasks followed by SFT on target tasks, with (c) showing pass@k during pretraining and (d) downstream SFT. Across (a,c), larger-k pass@k peaks and declines earlier than pass@1, so later checkpoints increasingly favor mean task success at the expense of large-k pass@k performance. Orange marks the earlier checkpoint selected by our offline coverage–reliability criterion (Sec. 4), while blue marks the final supervised-training checkpoint; matching dashed lines in (a,c) indicate the initializations used in (b,d). Despite similar pass@1, finetuning from the orange checkpoint achieves stronger performance than finetuning from the blue checkpoint across both settings.

Figure 7: Real-robot Push-T. (a) Task setup. (b) Best-of-k validation action MSE across training epochs. (c) Quantiles of validation action error across training epochs. (d) Normalized coverage and reliability scores with the selected checkpoint at epoch 46. (e) Pass@1 and pass@5 success rates of the selected (epoch 46) and final (epoch 200) checkpoints over 20 fixed initial states.

Figure 4: Held-out action-MSE quantiles expose the coverage–reliability balance. (a) Held-out action-MSE quantiles across training, colored by percentile u from 0.05 (red) to 0.95 (blue). (b) For a held-out observation, 64 matched-noise samples from ep50 and ep800, plus the expert action, are projected with PCA; rings mark the minimum-MSE sample. ep50 is more dispersed yet has lower best-of-64 MSE, whereas ep800 contracts but its best sample lies farther from the expert. Consistent with (a), lower quantiles favor earlier checkpoints, while higher quantiles improve later. (c) We summarize the lower and upper halves as rcov|H(τ) and rrel|H(τ) and select the checkpoint minimizing max{rcov|H(τ), rrel|H(τ)}; the selected ep350 matches the closed-loop oracle.

Figure 3: Best-of-k action MSE selects earlier checkpoints than closed-loop pass@k. (a) Held-out best-of-k action MSE across training checkpoints for different k. (b) Closed-loop pass@k success rate across the same checkpoints. Matching colors and marker shapes denote the same value of k across panels; hollow markers indicate the minimum MSE in (a) and maximum pass@k in (b). As k increases, both optima shift earlier, but the best-of-k MSE minimum precedes the corresponding pass@k peak, with a larger separation at higher k.

Figure 9: Residual RL finetuning across the coverage–reliability tradeoff. We additionally finetune an earlier baseline checkpoint (ep.200/100/100 for Threading/Hammer Cleanup/Mug Cleanup) with lower pass@1 and higher coverage than the checkpoint selected by our criterion. Its performance relative to later checkpoints depends on the available online budget.

Figure 12: Observation conditioning exacerbates the deterioration in held-out denoising during late training. Relative change in held-out ϵ-prediction MSE from epoch 200 to 800 for the image-conditioned and action-only models, evaluated on the same noisy action chunks. Negative values indicate lower held-out loss at epoch 800; positive values indicate higher loss. The conditional model exhibits held-out loss deterioration at higher diffusion noise levels.

Figure 10: Flow-matching policy pretraining and OGPO finetuning. Each row shows a MimicGen task with 200 demonstrations. (a) Best-of-k validation action MSE. (b) pass@k during BC pretraining. (c) Validation error quantiles. (d) Coverage–reliability scores and selected checkpoint. (e) OGPO finetuning from the selected versus final BC checkpoint. The selected initialization generally achieves better downstream RL performance.

Figure 20: JointAug retains favorable-tail coverage while improving typical action accuracy. For four held-out Mug Cleanup states, we jointly project 64 action samples from baseline ep50, baseline ep800, and JointAug ep800 with PCA. Stars mark expert actions and rings mark the minimum-MSE sample. The baseline ep50 is dispersed with low best-of-64 but high mean MSE; baseline baseline ep800 contracts and lowers mean MSE but worsens best-of-64 MSE; JointAug ep800 achieves best of both worlds.

Figure 21: Context-Smoothed Pre-training from TMRL does not preserve coverage under prolonged training. Across five MimicGen tasks, TMRL generally underperforms JointAug in pass@10 and often loses both pass@10 and pass@1 at later checkpoints.

Figure 28: Late-training coverage loss also occurs with low-dimensional state observations. Across five tasks, baseline diffusion policies lose pass@10 at later checkpoints despite using no visual encoder. Joint (o, a) augmentation preserves substantially more pass@10.

Figure 19: JointAug is relatively robust to generator checkpoint selection. We compare the five-checkpoint mixture used in our main experiments against individual generator checkpoints from the same run . Across four tasks, single-checkpoint variants have similar pass@10 gains over the baseline, while the mixture performs similarly overall and slightly improves pass@1 on Mug Cleanup and Threading.
Figure 16: Extended training on Threading D2. The coverage–reliability dynamics persist to 1600 epochs, and the offline criterion continues to select an intermediate checkpoint.

Figure 18: JointAug enables residual RL finetuning on 3-Piece Assembly (D2). Left: JointAug substantially improves pass@1 and pass@10 during BC pretraining. Right: residual RL from the final JointAug checkpoint reaches over 0.8 success, while finetuning from the baseline checkpoint remains near zero.

Figure 6: Generative augmentation produces stronger checkpoints for posttraining. Columns correspond to Fig. 5. We compare posttraining from the baseline checkpoint selected by our coverage–reliability criterion (Sec. 4), the final Baseline DP checkpoint, and the final checkpoint from our generative augmentation run. Across MimicGen tasks, the final generative-augmentation checkpoint substantially outperforms the final baseline and often matches or exceeds the selected checkpoint. On RoboCasa, it matches the selected checkpoint on both pass@1 and pass@32.

Figure 24: The late-training coverage loss persists across denoiser widths. We vary the U-Net from 24M to 1.0B parameters while keeping the encoder, data, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and sampler fixed. All four models show a similar peak and subsequent decline in pass@10.

Figure 8: Distribution of condition-level success counts over supervised pretraining. The stacked bands show the fraction of conditions in each success-count bin; each vertical slice sums to one. Figure 13: Late-training held-out denoising loss increases more at lower diffusion noise levels and with sparser local conditioning support. Negative values indicate lower mean loss at epoch 800; positive values indicate higher mean loss. Holding p = 0.9 fixed, increasing βmax from 0.9999 to 0.99995 allows the EMA memory to continue growing later in training and further smooths the decline. Figure 26: Freezing the encoder does not prevent the late-training large k pass@k decline. From epoch 150 onward, the encoder is fixed and only the denoiser is trained. Pass@10 still decreases at later epochs. The overall training dynamics is largely the same as baseline run.

Figure 11: Later checkpoints exhibit higher held-out denoising loss near the low-noise end, and changes to the final denoising calls substantially affect pass@k profle. (b) On unseen demonstrations, later checkpoints have higher denoising loss near the low-noise end than earlier checkpoints despite lower training loss. papers.abstract: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.
bullets: Addresses the dependence on proprietary frontier models that limits further RUA training research.
Introduces a unified harness for training and evaluating open-weight robot-use agents.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing plays a crucial role in everyday human interaction. Consider inserting a plug into a tight socket, vision alone provides limited guidance during the final insertion stage, and we instead rely on both anticipated contact and realized tactile feedback to ajust the insertion motion. The same capability is equally important for robots, particularly in dexterous manipulation tasks. Yet many contemporary robot policies remain vision-dominant. This visual bias, compounded by limited tactile data and sparse contact events, can cause directly incorporated tactile signals to be ignored or even compromise the policy's pretrained capabilities, yielding degrading performance as observed in our experiments. We present $TF^2$-Steering, which refines actions via learned residual steering of the flow-matching action expert's velocity field, using a tactile mixture-of-experts architecture to integrate both tactile forecasts and real-time tactile feedback. Together with specific designed three stages training recipe, $TF^2$-Steering enables tactile signals to correct and, when necessary, redirect the flow-matching action-generation process, while building on the strong action-generation capacity of the vision-based foundation policy. Extensive experiments across six simulated and six real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of $TF^2$-Steering. It outperforms the strongest evaluated baselines by 10.7 percentage points in average simulation success rate and 9.1 percentage points in average real-world progress success rate. Project page: https://yiming-cc.github.io/tf2-steering/.
bullets: Addresses the tendency of vision-dominant policies to ignore or weaken performance when directly given sparse tactile signals.
Learns residual corrections to a flow-matching action expert’s velocity field.
Uses a tactile mixture-of-experts architecture to combine tactile forecasts with realized feedback.
A three-stage training recipe lets tactile input correct or redirect the pretrained vision policy’s actions.
Evaluated on six simulated and six real-world tasks, improving average success by 10.7 and 9.1 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: Surface cleaning requires robots to adapt both where they clean and how they interact with contamination whose response to cleaning may vary spatially and remain unobservable prior to interaction. We formulate adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process and propose a belief-aware planning framework that uses observed cleaning outcomes to update a latent local cleaning-response model and adapt subsequent cleaning motions, forces, and passes. Preliminary grid-world simulations demonstrate the resulting closed-loop planner adapting its spatial decomposition and cleaning actions as the surface evolves.
bullets: Models adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process.
Updates a latent, spatially varying cleaning-response model from observed outcomes.
Adapts cleaning motions, forces, passes, and spatial decomposition in closed loop.
Preliminary grid-world simulations show adaptation as the surface evolves.

papers.abstract: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.
bullets: Characterizes 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes spanning 1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks on H800 GPUs.
Brain contexts grow to 215k tokens; repeated long-context prefills can displace generation as robot concurrency increases.
A single VLA GPU supports one robot under a 0.25-second action deadline and at least 32 robots under a 1.0-second deadline.
Increasing sustained brain concurrency from 20 to 32 robots cuts throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/second.
A static active-episode cap restores roughly 2.24–2.25 requests/second and increases completed episodes to 5.00–5.55 per minute.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the resource constraints (KV-cache thrashing) of serving fleets of agentic robots, providing insights into system-level efficiency for embodied AI agents.
papers.title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
papers.tldr: Agentic robot fleets face competing VLA action deadlines and brain KV-cache demands, but workload-aware admission control can prevent KV thrashing and sustain much higher throughput.

papers.abstract: As learned manipulation policies become increasingly capable of solving practical manipulation tasks, assessing how well a task is performed becomes a fundamental challenge. While binary labels confirm task success, they cannot distinguish successful executions with different levels of geometric precision. To address this, we introduce SPECTRA, an object-centric framework for quantifying execution quality in manipulation of rigid objects. From a small set of oracle demonstrations generated in simulation, SPECTRA represents object interactions through progress-aligned relative poses. SPECTRA identifies which relative-pose directions are constrained and their admissible variations from demonstrations. These constraints establish a reference for evaluating robotic manipulation tasks. To score an unseen execution, deviations beyond the admissible variation are summarized by a Task Quality Index Q in [0,1]. Across seven simulated tasks, SPECTRA recovers constraints with 94% accuracy using 30 demonstrations per task. On rollouts from three learned policies, its scores achieve pooled Spearman correlations with human judgments of p=0.81 over all rollouts and p=0.61 among successful rollouts, exceeding all baselines in both subsets. Using the task reference learned in simulation, we use SPECTRA to select the highest-scoring demonstrations for training a diffusion policy on hardware. Exploratory results show higher success rate than training on randomly selected demonstrations.
bullets: Targets the problem that binary success labels cannot distinguish different levels of geometric precision.
Learns constrained relative-pose directions and allowable variation from a small set of oracle demonstrations.
Scores unseen executions with a Task Quality Index Q∈[0,1], based on deviations from the learned constraints.
Across seven simulated tasks, it recovered constraints with 94% accuracy using 30 demonstrations per task.
Its scores correlated with human judgments (Spearman p=0.81 overall; p=0.61 on successful rollouts) and supported selecting demonstrations for hardware policy training.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of SPECTRA. 1. Constraints estimation. Oracle demonstrations are segmented and aligned to shared progress samples. At each progress sample l, the task is represented by the relative poses between the reference object r, the manipulated object m, the gripper g, and the support object s. Deviations from the nominal pose T̄j,l are mapped to its tangent space, and eigen decomposition of their covariance Σj,l identifies the constrained directions Ij , whose standard deviation falls below σpin. 2. Policy evaluation. An unseen execution incurs cost only where its normalized deviation along constrained directions exceeds the tolerance z0. The average cost and a terminal gate give the Task Quality Index Q ∈ [0, 1].

papers.abstract: High-accuracy repetitive tracking is challenging for position-commanded manipulators whose low-level controllers are inaccessible, while constrained model-based iterative learning control (ILC) can require substantial manual parameter tuning. We present Differentiable Iterative Learning Control (Diff-ILC), an online bilevel framework that adapts the parameters of a constrained ILC update between physical robot executions. A closed-loop differential model is identified once from paired smooth perturbations and subsequently kept fixed. At each trial, a constrained quadratic program computes a feasible command correction, while a real-anchored next-trial prediction defines a task-level objective. Hypergradients are obtained by implicitly differentiating the locally active KKT system, enabling multiple computational parameter updates without additional robot executions. Experiments on a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and three-dimensional trajectories show substantially faster physical-trial convergence than fixed-parameter model-based ILC. Across the four primary trajectories, after only two trial-to-trial updates, Diff-ILC achieves 78.8% and 76.4% lower mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE, respectively, than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.
bullets: Addresses high-accuracy repetitive tracking when low-level robot controllers are inaccessible and ILC tuning is costly.
Identifies a closed-loop differential model once, then uses a constrained quadratic program for feasible command corrections.
Optimizes ILC parameters online with a real-anchored objective and KKT-based implicit hypergradients, without extra robot executions per update.
On a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and 3D trajectories, it converged substantially faster than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.
After two trial-to-trial updates, mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE were 78.8% and 76.4% lower, respectively, across four primary trajectories.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based vision-language-action (VLA) models cascade pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with diffusion action experts, but typically restrict the VLM to providing static conditioning. This separation limits how much pretrained perception and reasoning can guide action generation, especially in out-of-distribution settings. We introduce JADE, a Joint Action DEnoiser that enables the VLM and action expert to jointly refine actions. Our key insight is that structured action latents allow the VLM to read the current noisy action together with visual observations and language instructions. At every denoising step, the VLM contextualizes the noisy action and guides the action expert through gated cross-attention, so that its guidance evolves with the action being generated. We further supervise the VLM to recover clean action latents from noisy ones, which gives it a direct action-learning signal and couples perception with control. Additionally, joint denoising enables JADE to generate actions with fewer sampling steps, helping offset the additional cost of VLM participation. An adaptive step-size schedule further balances task performance and inference latency. On RoboDojo, JADE achieves an average success rate of 12.67%, the highest among the evaluated $π_{0.5}$-based methods, and is competitive with recent VLA and WAM foundation models pretrained at scale. It also improves performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and raises the average success rate across four real-world bimanual tasks by 20.8 percentage points compared with $π_{0.5}$.
bullets: Addresses the limited role of VLMs in diffusion-based vision-language-action models, where they usually provide only static conditioning.
Feeds noisy action latents, visual observations, and language instructions into the VLM at every denoising step.
Uses gated cross-attention to dynamically guide the action expert and supervises the VLM to recover clean action latents.
An adaptive step-size schedule balances task performance with inference latency.
Achieves the highest average success rate among evaluated π₀.₅-based methods on RoboDojo and improves results on RoboTwin 2.0 and four real-world bimanual tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Joint VLM-action denoising for VLA models; directly advances embodied action generation.
papers.title: Vision-Language Models Are Joint Denoisers in Robotic Action Generation
papers.tldr: JADE jointly denoises robotic actions with a vision-language model and action expert, improving out-of-distribution performance and reducing sampling steps.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in shared, dynamic environments must respond to rapidly approaching objects while maintaining balance. We study dodgeball as a controlled test of this capability, coupling visual threat assessment with whole-body evasion, recovery, and target reacquisition. We develop a system that integrates onboard monocular perception, temporal ball-state and threat-flag estimation, and learned whole-body control. A ball detector supplies bounding-box histories, and a temporal estimator predicts relative ball position and a binary threat flag. Separate dodge/recovery and search/track policies share this interface and are composed to support repeated encounters. A three-stage curriculum first trains control with privileged ball states, then starts estimator supervision from stable policy rollouts, and finally replaces the actor's privileged inputs with estimator outputs. Analytic projection and perception randomization provide detector-like training observations without image rendering. Across approach-angle bins in controlled simulation, dodge success ranges from 97.8--100.0% for 5.0 m launches at 6 m/s to 33.2--40.8% for 2.5 m launches at 10 m/s, with 1000 throws per speed--distance condition. On a physical Unitree G1, controlled single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials. A hardware sequence demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge. These results demonstrate an integrated onboard-monocular-vision system under highly dynamic motions.
bullets: Addresses agile reaction and balance maintenance in dynamic shared environments using dodgeball as a controlled test.
Combines ball-detection histories, temporal threat estimation, and separate learned dodge/recovery and search/track policies.
Uses a three-stage curriculum to transition from privileged ball states to vision-based control, with analytic projection and perception randomization for training.
In simulation, dodge success varies from 97.8–100.0% for slower/farther launches to 33.2–40.8% for faster/closer launches; physical single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials.
Demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting manipulation to changing garment geometry and appearance.
Uses NOCS-textured garment meshes to provide canonical surface cues to a pretrained vision-language-action model.
Fine-tunes the model on human demonstrations and corrections, then filters autonomously generated rollouts by task success.
Re-renders successful trajectories with randomized appearances for training policies that use only RGB observations.
Generated data improves RGB-policy performance over original human data across evaluated garment splits and appearances, though unseen-garment generalization remains difficult.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on skill documents, yet most retrievers rank them by description alone and ignore what earlier executions revealed, even though a relevant skill can hurt execution. We present CompSkill, which indexes skills with learned 512-d keys and compiles matched same-task comparisons into skill offsets and capped key residuals (KeyOpt), so experience changes which document the executor receives, never its text. Under a logistic outcome model with unknown task difficulty, matched comparisons cancel that difficulty and only discordant ones carry information; on support executions, predictions improve with each discordant task. An experience hypergraph keeps each comparison with its executor and document versions, recalls missed skills and grounds a cited review. Compact keys raise SkillRet NDCG@10 from 64.0 to 70.9 at one eighth of the dimension. With one document, CompSkill completes 256 and 260 of 332 ToolQA tasks with GPT-5.6-luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, more than every baseline, and stays on par with the strongest baselines on AppWorld and ALFWorld. On 332 newly generated ToolQA tasks, it completes 256 with GPT-5.6-luna, significantly more than BM25, SkillRet-8B, Tool2Vec and RankGPT; over all 844 ToolQA tasks, it completes 24 more than the strongest baseline. Selection matters beyond relevance: pairing the right guide with a same-database sibling instead of another database's guide costs 8 of 96 tasks. Code, models and support data: https://github.com/satoshinji2992/CompSkill
bullets: Motivation: Description-only retrievers ignore lessons from prior executions and may select relevant-looking but harmful skills.
Method: Learned 512-dimensional keys are updated with skill offsets and capped residuals from matched same-task comparisons; an experience hypergraph preserves executors and document versions.
Theory: Under an unknown task-difficulty model, matched comparisons remove difficulty effects, while discordant outcomes provide learning signals.
Results: SkillRet NDCG@10 rises from 64.0 to 70.9 using one-eighth-dimensional keys; CompSkill also improves ToolQA completion and remains competitive on AppWorld and ALFWorld.
Scope: The approach depends on support executions and comparison evidence; selecting the right same-database guide matters substantially.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks. Project page: https://auriga.stelledge.com/ Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Auriga
bullets: Addresses the large execution gap between high-level VLM decisions and physical robot control.
Combines explicit task beliefs, tool calls or synthesized Python programs, calibrated 3D sensing, dual-arm control, and a unified robot gateway.
Uses paused visual trajectory previews and runtime checks for tolerances and grasp bounds, enabling interruption and discrepancy-based recovery.
Achieves 57.7% success on RoboDojo and 73.2% on RoboCasa365 with a frozen, zero-shot harness.
Remains robust under scene randomization, though the abstract does not specify limitations beyond its evaluated settings.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Overview of Auriga. Top: The model maintains a task belief and an evidence record, uses observations to localize targets, and previews actions while the world is paused. Every physical motion passes through the admission gateway A, which returns a receipt and a new observation. Bottom: Closed-loop execution on hang_mugs: (1) localization, (2) grasp preview, (3) execution, and (4) placement on the rack.

Figure 1 Auriga completes manipulation tasks zero-shot within a single episode. A general-purpose model plans and acts through a shared harness, with no target-task exploration, demonstrations, or resets. The model localizes targets by multi-view triangulation, complemented by depth and point-cloud estimates (1), and reviews candidate motions before they are executed (2). The harness verifies each execution and stops when an action fails (3); the model then revises its plan and recovers from the current state (4–5) until the task succeeds (6).

Figure 5 The three nested loops of Auriga within one episode. The stage loop runs inside A and stops execution when a declared condition is violated; the model closes the action and belief loops. Deliberative calls extend the evidence record without advancing the world.

Figure 6 Preview and verification in two rounds, drawn on the head-camera image. In the first round, the previewed gripper path moves to the object, closes on it, and lifts it to a checkpoint placed by the model, where the robot pauses and the model receives a fresh wrist view (inset 1). The measured path follows the preview until a finger lands on the basket rim while the object is lowered. Once the gap exceeds the tolerance, the harness stops the arm and reports with a fresh view (inset 2), so the gripper does not open. In the second round, the model previews a revised motion from the stop that lifts clear of the rim and lowers into the basket, where the gripper opens (inset 3). The rim contact and the second round are illustrative.

Figure 2 Planning, execution, and recovery within a single tower-building episode. From left to right, the model grounds the task in visual and geometric observations, constructs a plan, and builds the tower through direct tool calls and generated programs. Action previews and execution feedback support a preview–execute–verify loop. After a failed grasp, the model inspects the scene, updates its plan, and regrasps the object to complete the tower. The harness provides measurements and execution checks; the model selects actions and recovery strategies. The scene is never reset.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses embodied manipulation using a task-agnostic agent harness that integrates vision-language models with robot control, closing the planning-execution gap.
papers.title: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: Auriga is a task-agnostic robot-control harness that substantially narrows the gap between vision-language planning and reliable zero-shot manipulation.

papers.abstract: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
bullets: Uses Navigation, Action, and Planning agents connected by a shared internal language and training factory in a closed-loop workflow.
Applies symbolic verification before consequential actions execute, with validated physics serving as the safety basis rather than learned models.
Improved unseen-aircraft CFD convergence from under 1% to 74% across 100 single-attempt cases; also demonstrated live Mach 6 cases on three facilities.
Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters increased ParaView control success from 55% to 75%; validated world modeling achieved the best conjunction-risk score among five methods.
Demonstrations span space-domain awareness, reactor anomaly detection, debris avoidance, large simulated aircraft teams, and a control-grade microreactor digital twin.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Data Factory outputs feed multiple automated-machine-learning frameworks trained in parallel. Candidate models are evaluated, compared, and ranked under Monte Carlo cross-validation, and the best predictor for each target is registered for downstream use in the workflow.

Figure 1: The GURU hierarchy. The Planning layer performs long-horizon forecasting and planning with JEPA world models and model predictive control. The Action layer turns plans into bounded decisions through optimization, parameter prediction, and anomaly detection. The Navigation layer executes and monitors operations across software and physical systems. Feedback flows bidirectionally, so plans constrain low-level action while observations update the planner. The middle layer, labeled Discrete actions in the figure, is the Action layer.

Figure 8: Knowledge-graph construction pipeline. Heterogeneous software sources are converted into a common, provenance-preserving observation representation, using vision-language models and automatic speech recognition (ASR) for video and deterministic or vision-language extraction for PDF documents, before being transformed into candidate claims and merged into a canonical knowledge graph. The shared intermediate schema allows document and video evidence to contribute to the same reusable representation.

Figure 21: The horizon-aware forecaster that produces the forward tracks. The extended model takes a look-ahead interval, up to 72 hours (at most 7 days), from as much as 28 days of history, and predicts the embedding of the whole future trajectory rather than a single point. Sweeping the look-ahead forward and backward turns the same model into a scanner across the historical archive for behavior staggered in time to avoid notice. The forecaster is a joint-embedding predictive architecture (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023).

Figure 17: Software-control architecture and knowledge-learning loop for ParaView. The Planning agent decomposes a user goal into structured actions; the Grounding agent maps each action and the current application state to executable code or GUI operations; and the Execution agent applies the selected operation and returns the resulting state. Tutorials, documents, and interaction trajectories provide knowledge for retrieval and role-specific training.

Figure 2: The GURU platform. The Learning Engine trains Navigation, Action, and Planning agents. The rules engine validates schemas, ontologies, constraints, and execution state. The agent society coordinates specialized agents through message pools and a shared workspace for auditable execution. Inputs span sensor streams, simulation outputs, documents, and direct user interaction, and the same platform drives applications in digital engineering, space operations, and reactor operations.

Figure 4: The Common Internal Language unifies agents through a shared semantic substrate for concepts, values, rules, and procedures, a uniform message format for the global workspace, and hierarchical task structures ready for planning and execution. Inset: a natural-language and geometry request is translated into typed, unit-aware attribute records with explicit provenance and uncertainty fields.

Figure 3: Lightweight clients capture multimodal input and workflow intent. Structured representations and high-dimensional embeddings are routed to backend services for reasoning, orchestration, and execution across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments. Remote applications can be driven and viewed through a streamed display.

Figure 45: CFD simulation outcomes by grid generator and parameter selection. Stacked outcome shares for the earlier Pentagrow pipeline with predicted parameters, the extrusion-based generator with random parameters, and the extrusion-based generator with learned parameter selection. Outcomes are failed grid generation, failed initial solve, failed during adaptation, not finished, not converged, and converged. The rightmost configuration is the headline result in the text: 100 cases, one attempt each, of which 92 completed and 74 converged.

Figure 6: Current and target states are encoded into latent embeddings. The predictor learns action-conditioned transitions in that latent space, which lets agents forecast the behavior of an interface or environment without reconstructing raw observations.

Figure 7: Multimodal sources for software-knowledge acquisition. Document and video tutorials provide procedural demonstrations and application knowledge, while autonomous ParaView exploration produces state-action-outcome trajectories. The exploration examples show before-and-after application states; several attempts did not achieve the requested goal, which is why execution without an error is never treated as achievement. Both sources are transformed into reusable observations for knowledge extraction and agent training.

Figure 49: Quantitative comparison of anomaly-detection methods and JEPA scoring rules. (Top left) Balanced accuracy at the warning threshold by method. (Top right) Correct-classification rate per fault group. (Bottom left) Temporal anomaly scores for four JEPA scoring variants. (Bottom right) Balanced accuracy and average precision for each scoring rule. Embedding kNN gives the best and most consistent balance across fault families.

Figure 46: Frozen JEPA matches or exceeds configuration-matched baselines on conjunction risk, with seed-stable performance. Mean binary F1-score over 10 seeds on the shared test split, with every method trained under the same budget (batch size 96, 1,000 training steps); labels show mean ± standard deviation. The frozen JEPA encoder with a small MLP head scores highest, and its low seed-to-seed variance shows the result does not depend on a lucky seed, even though none of its backbone weights are trained.

Figure 11: GURU CFD Suite workflow for high-speed aerial vehicles. The figure shows one representative airframe from the live run described above, the Fury: from a natural-language prompt, GURU configured an aerodynamic sweep at Mach 2 to 4, 40 to 50 km, plus or minus 5 degrees angle of attack, about 1M cells, and autonomously submitted it to HPC. Post-processed output for the Fury airframe shows Mach contours and surface pressure-coefficient distribution, the computational mesh, converged residual histories, and axial surface pressure and heat-flux profiles. Video: https://youtu.be/GQIJjjVolNY

Figure 13: The generation model maps image embeddings and augmented renderings into meshable vehicle geometries. Representative outputs span 11 aerial vehicle classes, from fixed-wing subsonic and transonic to supersonic and hypersonic, eVTOL, flying-wing and blended-wing-body, delta-wing and canard, high-lift, rotorcraft, lighter-than-air, and unconventional configurations, with 673 geometries reaching successful volume-grid generation.

Figure 36: Historical traffic replay with modeled hazard bands and candidate reroutes. The dashboard combines recorded aircraft tracks, event evidence, illustrative debris bands, and proposed route alternatives. The evidence panel distinguishes published predictions, event confirmation, and traffic records; the decision panel summarizes modeled intersections and rerouting costs. The displayed alternatives are simulation outputs, not aircraft actions that occurred during the event. Also identified in the dashboard - limits on route completion, cost estimation, and multi-aircraft conflict assessment. Video: https://youtu.be/Jtyf78QsXlE

Figure 20: Two-phase design. In pre-training, the world model learns from context and target windows split from up to 28 days of state-vector history, with a slow exponential-moving-average target encoder and a Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer optimized under an MSE objective in embedding space. In the conjunction stage, the frozen encoder produces embeddings for the history of two objects, which are combined into a symmetric pair representation and read by a conjunction head trained on public conjunction-message labels to output a collision risk score.

Figure 43: OpenMC drum-angle runs are fit to a smooth reactivity model used by the point-kinetics controller. The MPC then chooses drum rotations to track a scheduled power target or to maximize power while holding a fuel-temperature cap.

Figure 18: Ablation of context, retrieval, and learned adaptation for ParaView software control (successful attempts out of 150 per configuration). Explicit program state, API information, and capability catalogs improve base-model performance, while graph retrieval is most valuable when supplied context is limited. Under full context (state, API inventory, and catalogs), the role-specific Planning and Grounding adapters provide additional gains, with retrieval and adaptation showing complementary effects in some configurations.

Figure 9: Knowledge-graph snapshot for ParaView by semantic family. The graph contains 105,125 nodes and 106,202 edges from 64 source packages (42 PDF, 19 video, two API, and one exploration package), including 1,552 exact API definitions, of which 1,478 carry nonempty signatures. The panels count nodes in the ten semantic families; the remaining nodes include procedure steps and transitions, which are stored as supporting control-flow records. These are corpus-wide counts, not counts of facts relevant to any single goal. Automatic semantic matching between documentation and exploration was disabled in this release, so shared storage should not be read as complete automatic linkage.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing plays an important role in imitation learning for contact-rich manipulation by providing direct observations of physical contact with objects. Recently, several tactile foundation models (TFMs) have been proposed to learn general-purpose tactile representations through pretraining on large-scale tactile datasets. However, how these pretrained tactile representations should be leveraged for end-to-end imitation learning remains insufficiently explored. In this work, we integrate multiple TFMs into Diffusion Policy and systematically evaluate their effectiveness for contact-rich manipulation under common experimental settings. We further investigate adaptation strategies, including encoder fine-tuning and task-specific mid-training, to understand how pretrained tactile representations can be effectively used for downstream imitation learning. Through extensive evaluation across diverse manipulation tasks in both real-world and simulation environments, including more than 5,000 real-world policy rollouts, we provide empirical insights into the use of TFMs for end-to-end imitation learning. Project page: https://mmurooka.github.io/tfm4il-project-page/

papers.abstract: Fine-grained robotic manipulation requires instruction grounding, robust perception, and precise contact control. We describe our submission to the MetaFine Open Competition at CoRL 2026. Five independently trained models use a common architecture with frozen DINOv2 and CLIP encoders, trainable language-conditioned feature modulation, and task-specific action heads. We improve demonstrations through contact-aware grasp filtering, instruction-matched data, and expert correction of insertion failures. At inference, task-dependent strategies include photometric test-time augmentation, stochastic action averaging, and uncertainty-triggered replanning. Our submission achieves an official overall score of 0.914 and ranks third among 15 teams. We analyze the models and their task-specific behavior.

papers.abstract: We test whether Koopman structure helps a differentiable world model used to train a simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tracking policy by backpropagation through imagined rollouts, replacing the MLP world model of an otherwise unchanged pipeline. It does not: return is at best equal (0.823 versus 0.830), one-step error on identical data is 1.3 to 1.6 times the MLP's, and training is about 15% slower. Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; of the schemes tested, re-lifting at every imagined step trains best. Re-lifting never uses the lifted linear dynamics and leaves a model affine in the action, with state-dependent offset and slope; an action-affine MLP also predicts worse, so the accuracy cost belongs to this class. At a fixed state, the dynamics' curvature in the action explains only part of it. Across states, the policy's actions span a curved region, so an affine model fits policy data only as the tangent at the policy's action, the operating point: on G1, the MLP's tangent there is as accurate as the MLP; at the mean action, 31 times worse. The offset must encode, from the state alone, where the policy acts, whereas an MLP reads the action. Supplying the policy's action removes most of the remaining gap on G1, Ant and Humanoid. The only tested online repair approaching the MLP feeds the action into the nonlinear lift, abandoning the structure. For this use, the MLP world model remains the better choice.
bullets: Replacing the MLP with Koopman-based models yields comparable-or-worse return, higher one-step error, and roughly 15% slower training.
Lifted rollouts diverge or fail to train policies; re-lifting each imagined step performs best but does not use lifted linear dynamics.
The resulting action-affine structure poorly represents the curved state-dependent action regions visited by the policy.
Providing the policy action to the model recovers most of the accuracy gap across G1, Ant, and Humanoid; nonlinear action lifting largely abandons the intended structure.
For this setting, the standard MLP world model remains preferable.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires policies to act on information that is no longer visible. Modified objects may leave the field of view, while completed subtasks continue to constrain future actions. Existing approaches extend temporal context through recurrent state updates, test-time training, or storage and retrieval of past observations. As horizons grow, these mechanisms can still leave the policy to infer task state from long, redundant, and viewpoint-dependent visual experience. We argue that long-horizon agents benefit not merely from remembering more, but from remembering task-relevant state changes and progress. We propose Memory of Object States and Task Progress (MOST), a policy-internal memory framework that compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens. Historical and predictive future tokens are explicitly supervised with object states and subtask progress, structuring memory around what has changed in the world and what has already been accomplished. The resulting memory directly conditions action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage. We further introduce RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Across RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and real-world robot experiments, MOST consistently outperforms Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), the previous state-of-the-art model. It raises average success from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. MOST also outperforms a matched visual-history memory variant, showing that effective long-horizon memory depends not only on how much experience is retained, but on whether it preserves decision-relevant progress and world-state changes.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of acting on modified objects and completed subtasks that are no longer visible.

papers.abstract: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.
bullets: Addresses the need to retain motion history and earlier visual evidence missing from current observations.
Trains memory with temporal supervision from predicted future visual features.
At execution, uses spatially normalized prediction discrepancies to selectively update the visual state.
Improves success from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO and 14.4% to 83.8% on RMBench M(1).
Also improves general manipulation and spatial-perturbation robustness, with 7.7 ms mean inference overhead on an NVIDIA H800.

papers.abstract: The MetaFine Open Competition (RoboFineMani workshop, CoRL 2026) evaluates fine-grained manipulation beyond binary success. Its five simulated tasks, from grasping a bottle by an instructed part to inserting letter-shaped pegs with 4 mm clearance, are scored on perception under lighting and camera changes, instruction understanding, and behavior. This report presents Team Friday's solution, which got second place with an overall score of 0.947, more than twice the $π_0$ baseline. Instead of fine-tuning a large vision-language-action (VLA) model, we train one 19M-parameter policy per task with a separate instruction classifier and focus on the data, all generated in the simulator by a privileged scripted teacher, including its corrections of the student's mistakes. By analyzing failed episodes, we find that a teacher that almost always succeeds can still teach a memoryless student badly: its pauses become stalls, its fixed habits become shortcuts, and it never shows the errors the student makes. Making the teacher \emph{imitable} raised the official score on letter insertion, the hardest task, from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32\% more data and the same architecture, and finally to 0.88. We summarize practical lessons on demonstration data and evaluation, which we hope will help in imitation learning for precise manipulation.
bullets: The challenge evaluates fine-grained manipulation under visual changes, language instructions, and behavioral precision across five simulated tasks.
The solution uses one 19M-parameter policy per task, a separate instruction classifier, and simulator-generated demonstrations from a privileged scripted teacher.
Failure analysis showed that near-perfect teachers can teach memoryless students poorly through pauses, fixed habits, and missing recovery examples.
Making demonstrations more imitable improved letter insertion from 0.44 to 0.82 with 32% more data, and ultimately to 0.88 using the same architecture.
The team’s overall score was 0.947, earning second place and motivating practical lessons about demonstration design and evaluation.

papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $π_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $π_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit https://doubleblind-sae-pi05.github.io for video rollouts.
bullets: Per-token goal-word edits steer π₀.₅-LIBERO without changing the instruction text.
At layer 0, BatchTopK swaps redirected up to 20/20 rollouts in one scene, while random-feature swaps redirected none; results varied across scenes and layers.
Word-selected Matryoshka edits generally did not outperform random swaps, and SAEs were not necessary: a scaled difference-in-means vector also redirected behavior.
Edits remained effective through layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity; patching camera tokens extended effectiveness to layer 13.
The study is a simulated proof of existence and an initial characterization of the depth limits of goal-redirection edits.

papers.tldr: Swapping SAE features for a single goal word can redirect π₀.₅’s simulated robot behavior toward an alternative task, with effectiveness depending on feature type, layer, and token coverage.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to adapt pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs). We investigate the problem of behavioral steering: adapting a VLA's execution style to preferences such as carrying objects higher. To investigate how little trainable capacity such steering requires and how much pretrained capability can be retained, we freeze an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and optimize TinyLoRA adapters with 8 to 384 trainable parameters using either policy-gradient RL (GRPO) or evolutionary search (CMA-ES). With just 256 trainable parameters, we raise carry height by 120 mm on trained tasks at 92% success and by 74 mm on a held-out task at 80% success. By rescaling the learned update, we can tune the trade-off between style gains and capability retention without retraining. Increasing adapter capacity generally improves this trade-off, retaining more pretrained capability at comparable style gains. The choice of optimizer also depends on capacity, with CMA-ES being competitive at low parameter counts, while GRPO offers better trade-offs as capacity grows. These findings show that extremely low-dimensional updates can steer pretrained VLA behavior, with adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling offering practical control over adaptation and retention.
bullets: Studies behavioral steering, such as making a robot carry objects higher, without updating the full policy.
Freezes an OpenVLA-OFT 7B policy and trains TinyLoRA adapters with 8–384 parameters using GRPO or CMA-ES.
With 256 parameters, carry height increases by 120 mm on trained tasks and 74 mm on a held-out task, with 92% and 80% success respectively.
Adapter capacity, optimizer choice, and update scaling control the trade-off between behavioral change and capability retention.
CMA-ES is competitive at very low capacities, while GRPO provides better trade-offs as capacity increases.

papers.abstract: Most agentic robotic systems use vision-language models (VLMs) either to orchestrate predefined skills or to directly generate actions, constraints, and control programs. The former is limited by the available skill library, while the latter requires VLMs to reason about precise geometry and contact. In this paper, we propose WorldSketch, a new paradigm for agentic robotics in which a VLM constructs a world model rather than generating robot actions. The VLM acts as an agent that actively queries perception tools to build and visually validate a minimal kinematic world model, capturing only task-relevant objects, their interaction geometry, and possible motions. A geometric planner then jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion on the resulting model. Moreover, the world model is self-improving: execution feedback verifies outcomes, updates uncertain hypotheses, and enables the agent to revise the model when its predictions are contradicted. We demonstrate the generality of this paradigm across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, achieving zero-shot success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively. On RoboCasa, WorldSketch outperforms the next-best zero-shot agent baseline by 58 percentage points while using 10 times fewer VLM input tokens; on LIBERO-PRO, it exceeds CaP-X by 82 percentage points. In navigation, it matches the success rate of step-by-step VLM agents while using 6 times fewer input tokens.
bullets: Addresses the limits of skill-library orchestration and the difficulty of precise geometric reasoning by VLMs.
The VLM actively queries perception tools to construct and visually validate minimal kinematic models of relevant objects, interactions, and motions.
A geometric planner jointly optimizes contact and whole-body motion using the constructed model.
Execution feedback verifies results, updates uncertain hypotheses, and supports model revision when predictions fail.
Demonstrated across RoboCasa, LIBERO-PRO, and R2R-CE navigation, with success rates of 91%, 97%, and 76%, respectively, while using substantially fewer VLM input tokens than comparable approaches.

papers.selection_reason: VLM constructs a kinematic world model for zero-shot mobile manipulation and navigation, directly relevant to embodied AI and world-model representations.
papers.title: WorldSketch: Sketching World Models for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: WorldSketch enables zero-shot mobile manipulation by having a VLM build and refine task-specific geometric world models for a planner instead of directly generating robot actions.

papers.abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition - reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored - with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website - https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-only methods and language-based planners that lack spatial beliefs.
Combines VLM object-likelihood scores with geometric occupancy evidence using Bayesian log-odds filtering.
Uses high-belief voxel regions to choose viewpoints, explore unseen areas, or interact with closed cabinets.
Evaluated end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid, outperforming geometry-only and LLM-based search methods.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct observations of contact physics, local geometry, and interaction dynamics, making it a vital source of feedback for contact-rich manipulation. However, existing tactile manipulation studies are often developed and evaluated within specific task settings, making it difficult to systematically compare how tactile information contributes under different interaction conditions. In this work, we develop a benchmark in simulation comprising 128 tasks organized around three complementary evaluation regimes: Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic. The benchmark further includes controlled static and dynamic task variants and 12 perturbation settings for evaluating robustness under changes in visual and physical conditions. These settings motivate studying tactile information as a temporally evolving interaction representation rather than only as an instantaneous observation. We therefore propose an action-conditioned latent predictive world model that integrates tactile history and learns a tactile state through prediction of future tactile latents. Building on this representation, we design a model that conditions action generation on the learned tactile state and uses predicted future tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the evaluated regimes. Project Page: https://tacmind-bench.github.io/
bullets: Covers Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic evaluation regimes with static and dynamic variants.
Includes 12 perturbation settings to test robustness to visual and physical changes.
Learns a temporally evolving tactile state by predicting future tactile latents from tactile history and actions.
Uses predicted tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection.
Experiments show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the benchmark regimes.

papers.abstract: Before foraging, desert ants perform learning walks (LWs) to acquire visual memories around their nest. With experience, these walks expand, become straighter, and contain fewer visual scans. We previously proposed a model in which these behaviours emerge from the angular mismatch between path integration (PI) and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass (VC). Here, we test whether this mechanism can generate learning walks on a physical robot, despite the sensory and motor noise inherent to real-world conditions. We implement the model on a four-wheeled robot equipped with a panoramic camera, an IMU and wheel encoders providing compass and stride information for PI, and test it outdoors using a replicated desert-ant experimental setup. The PI--VC mismatch regulates walking speed, turning, pirouettes, and returns to the nest, while PI provides a teaching signal for visual learning. The robot autonomously decides when to acquire visual memories, while its behaviour gradually shifts from exploration towards foraging as visual learning progresses. The robot reproduces desert-ant LW features, including expanding and straightening trajectories, decreasing pirouette frequency, and improved visual homing. These results demonstrate that a simple error-driven mechanism can generate key features of learning walks under real-world conditions, supporting its plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants. More broadly, this work illustrates how physical robots can be used to test biological models.
bullets: Learning walks emerge from angular mismatch between path integration and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass.
The mechanism controls speed, turning, pirouettes, nest returns, and visual-memory acquisition.
Implemented on an outdoor four-wheeled robot with a panoramic camera, IMU, and wheel encoders despite real-world noise.
The robot reproduced expanding and straightening paths, fewer pirouettes, and improved visual homing as learning progressed.
Results support the mechanism’s plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants and demonstrate physical robots as tools for testing biological models.

Mean centroid error increased monotonically with circular variance, from 20.42◦ in the lowest-variance bin (0–0.1) to 83.32◦ in the highest-variance bin (0.9–1.0). Prediction variance was positively correlated with centroid error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.358, p < 0.001), with a linear R2 = 0.167 and mutual information of 0.113 nats. (B) Frequency distribution across all the one-second prediction samples across circular-variance bins. Low-variance samples were more frequent. Unlike the visual familiarity or novelty signals commonly derived from MBON activation in visual-compass models [1, 34, 41, 48], this signal would reflect the consistency of successive directional predictions rather than the familiarity of the visual input itself.

papers.abstract: Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b) abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost. Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.
bullets: Addresses the need for intuitive, adaptable cobot programming as shop-floor tasks and environments change.
Uses a three-stage pipeline: teach workflows, abstract them into skills, then apply those skills to new situations.
Evaluated on a collaborative structure-building task with open- and closed-model agents in self-play and cross-model setups.
Skill abstraction improved task success rates and reduced interaction cost.
A preliminary human-in-the-loop study indicates the approach can also handle human instructions.

papers.abstract: Held-out validation loss is the standard offline signal for choosing checkpoints and comparing models, but its relation to closed-loop success on a real robot is rarely measured. We measure it for ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ (action expert only), trained on nested subsets of 12 to 200 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. We score 82 checkpoints on 25 held-out demonstrations, with each policy's training loss and with the error of the actions it outputs, and compare the scores with 930 bench rollouts. We also score all 700 intermediate checkpoints of 70 training runs, and recover the ball positions of every training, held-out and bench episode from the front camera. Within each policy, hold-out action error correlates with bench success (Spearman $ρ$ from -0.23 to -0.88), but no more strongly than the number of training episodes alone, and not at all among seeds trained on the same data. Across policies the ranking is inverted ($ρ$ = +0.90 at 200 episodes): the policy with the lowest hold-out error succeeded in 3 of 110 rollouts. The most common failure, the arm never leaving its rest pose, ended 96% of rollouts for Diffusion Policy trained on untrimmed demonstrations and 47% for SmolVLA, and cannot occur in a hold-out set made of demonstrations. Among rollouts in which the arm moved, SmolVLA's hold-out action error predicts success well ($ρ$ = -0.81). For the diffusion and flow-matching policies, hold-out loss rises two- to five-fold during training while hold-out action error falls by up to 29%. Held-out metrics are a sound diagnostic of learning but no substitute for evaluation on the robot, and we recommend reporting initiation failure and success among started rollouts as separate bench outcomes.
bullets: Evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π₀.₅ on a pick-and-place task using 82 checkpoints, 70 training runs, and 930 real-robot rollouts.
Within individual policies, held-out action error often correlated with bench success, but not reliably across random seeds trained on the same data.
Across policies, lower held-out error could correspond to worse robot performance; one policy with the best error succeeded in only 3 of 110 rollouts.
A frequent failure— the arm never leaving its rest pose—cannot appear in demonstration-based hold-out metrics and accounted for many failed rollouts.
The authors recommend real-robot evaluation and reporting initiation failures separately from success conditional on the arm starting.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.
bullets: Supports one to five Shadow Hands in a unified family of scalable piano-playing tasks.
Covers task performance, robustness to configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation.
Provides at least 912 task settings, 36 baseline algorithms, and LLM-based agents for broader evaluation.
Experiments show that current RL methods and frontier LLM agents still struggle with challenging piano tasks, even in standard RL settings.
