papers.abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves $23/36$ successful trials (63.9\%), compared with $19/36$ (52.8\%) with memory alone and $2/36$ (5.6\%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from $7/9$ to $4/9$, while removing retained experience reduces it to $3/9$. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.
authors: Antonio Terpin, Francesco Banelli, Alan Bonomi, Raffaello D'Andrea
bullets: PIV performance depends on expert choices in preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing, which may fail as conditions change.

Experiments in a water-channel fluidic pinball demonstrate adaptive estimator and region-of-interest selection, including physical-world reinforcement-learning control.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed as heterogeneous fleets with diverse kinematic and actuation capabilities. While graph control barrier function (GCBF) methods provide a scalable framework for decentralized safe control, existing approaches typically assume homogeneous robot dynamics. Methods that directly encode robot classes can distinguish known types, but do not represent state-dependent motion capabilities or naturally transfer to unseen robot models. To address this challenge, we propose the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point operational space. This formulation provides a common geometric representation of safety across heterogeneous robots while retaining their model-specific dynamics and admissible control constraints. To enable zero-shot transfer, we introduce the Radial Capability Field (RCF), a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of each robot's state-dependent finite-horizon reachable velocity set. Conditioning the shared graph barrier and decentralized policy on the RCF enables them to adapt to changes in robot state, kinematic constraints, and control limits without relying on predefined robot identities. We jointly train the barrier and policy using proactive safety labeling and neural CBF-QP supervision, and evaluate them on mixed teams containing both seen and unseen robot models. Experiments demonstrate scalable safe coordination and zero-shot transfer to robot models and capability variations withheld during training. Physical-robot experiments further demonstrate zero-shot deployment to unseen kinematic models without retraining.

papers.abstract: Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator's natural dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI), a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces. The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment. CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action representations, improving mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand-task pairs on LEAP and Wuji. Hardware designs and software are publicly available.

Uses a hierarchical policy with a contact-surface trajectory planner and a wrist–finger coordination controller.
Improves mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand–task pairs on LEAP and Wuji.
Hardware and software designs are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.
authors: Paul Lutkus, Lars Lindemann, Stephen Tu
bullets: Targets feedback control from learned latent dynamics while preserving stability of the original system.
For linear time-invariant systems, jointly learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with sufficiently long multi-step backward losses recovers stabilization-relevant structure.
A minimum H∞-norm controller designed in latent space can stabilize the original system through the learned encoder when the latent dimension is sufficient.
Forward prediction-only losses may discard unstable modes, and single-step reconstruction may produce controllers that fail to stabilize the original system.
Experiments on a nonlinear flexible-arm system demonstrate practical implications for nonlinear autoencoders and latent dynamics.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
authors: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
bullets: Evaluated 281 policies from seven families across about 1,700 trials of RJ45 grasping and insertion with a five-fingered hand.

Absolute actions improved vision-language-action insertion success by up to 70 percentage points; decomposition, multi-view sensing, and recovery data appeared beneficial but were not isolated.
Only five of 67 offline metrics correlated reliably with success, and only within one policy family, so real-robot evaluation remains necessary.

papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

papers.abstract: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.
authors: Jun Cen, Yubo Guo, Hao Li, Liangkai Li, Yaoxu Lyu, Meng Wei, Zeqi Xiao, Sizhe Yang, Yuqiang Yang, Yifan Ye, Shanghang Zhang, Duo Zheng

The model uses two-scale visual memory, action forcing, and a unified pipeline for heterogeneous robot and egocentric supervision.
It reports strong performance across manipulation benchmarks, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1.
The study emphasizes complementary roles for visual prediction and action grounding in task generalization.

papers.abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.
bullets: Provides a prompt-driven pipeline for generating diverse drawing trajectories in simulation and on real robots.
Evaluates five VLA models using 28,200 simulated demonstrations across 282 drawing tasks.
Enables analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, action generation, and multimodal drawing behavior.
Finds that some models benefit from increased task diversity and demonstration scale and can generalize to new compositions of familiar objects.
Demonstrates reactive drawing with a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm under human intervention.

papers.abstract: A dexterous hand can change an object's pose without setting it down. This survey covers 113 learning-based methods that attempt it, the hands they run on, the simulators they train in, and how they report results. The field has largely converged on one recipe: reinforcement learning on privileged state in a GPU simulator, distilled into a vision-only student for transfer to hardware. Almost half the corpus trains that way, nearly all of it in one simulator, whose own successors are barely used. A second and faster-growing branch learns from teleoperated demonstration instead, through vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, and systems whose contribution is the collection rig itself. Published work has tripled since 2022. Grasping remains the largest task family and bimanual coordination the fastest-rising, and almost every experiment runs on one of four hands. What the survey adds comes from reading released code and vendor specifications beside the papers. Eight hands that can be bought or built from published designs appear in no method paper here. Where the depth a hand sinks into the object it holds is reported at all, it is not measured in the physics that produced the motion. Section VII proposes a protocol for the unreported quantities; the body gives the counts behind every claim above.
bullets: Reviews the hands, simulators, training paradigms, tasks, and evaluation practices used in 113 methods.
The prevailing pipeline trains reinforcement learning on privileged state in a GPU simulator, then distills it into a vision-only policy for hardware transfer.
A faster-growing alternative learns from teleoperated demonstrations using vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, or specialized data-collection rigs.
Research output has tripled since 2022; grasping is the largest task family, while bimanual coordination is growing fastest, and most studies use one of four hands.
The survey identifies underused available hands and missing physical measurements, including object penetration depth, and proposes a reporting protocol.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce \textbf{RoboCasa-Shift}, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0$ despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera $L_2$ and Gaussian blur $L_1$ both yield $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0.188$, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark with controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean–perturbed rollouts, and simulator-grounded stage-aware failure analysis.
Evaluates GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks across four perturbation factors and three severity levels, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts.
Robustness varies across tasks and perturbations, and greater severity does not always cause monotonic performance degradation.
Perturbations with identical end-to-end success degradation can produce different failure-depth profiles, revealing where execution breaks down.
Motivates reporting outcome degradation, paired-outcome sensitivity, and failure progression jointly; code is publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of RoboCasa-Shift. RoboCasa-Shift evaluates VLA robustness on selected long-horizon RoboCasa tasks under controlled single-factor distribution shifts with multiple frozen severity levels. Strictly matched clean-perturbed rollouts enable counterfactual comparison under shared task conditions, while robustness is characterized jointly through end-to-end task outcomes and stage-aware semantic execution diagnostics. Representative findings illustrate that aggregate success rates can mask substantial episode-level outcome changes, similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to different failure locations, and severe visual corruption can shift failures toward earlier stages of task execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of StageTracker. (a) A long-horizon task is represented as an ordered sequence of semantic subgoals, each associated with a simulator-state predicate. (b) During rollout, StageTracker evaluates the current predicate, records the completion step when it is first satisfied, and advances to the next subgoal. Completed subgoals are latched, allowing the tracker to report the deepest semantic progress reached and the first incomplete subgoal for failure localization.

Fig. 2: Pipeline of RoboCasa-Shift. (a) Task Suite. Candidate RoboCasa tasks are filtered through clean-competence screening to construct the formal evaluation suite. (b) Controlled Shifts. Selected tasks are evaluated under four singlefactor distribution shifts with calibrated and frozen severity levels. (c) Counterfactual Pairing. Clean and perturbed rollouts share the underlying task conditions and policy seed and differ only in the target shift. (d) Diagnosis. RoboCasa’s official task outcome is complemented by stage-aware semantic diagnostics of execution progress, first incomplete subgoal, and subgoal reach.

Fig. 8: Representative severity calibration examples. Rows correspond to the four perturbation factors, and columns show the clean condition (L0) and three calibrated severity levels (L1–L3). Illumination progressively darkens the scene, camera orientation changes the third-person viewpoint, robot base initialization perturbs the initial base position and yaw orientation, and Gaussian blur progressively reduces visual sharpness. For base initialization, the inset provides a schematic top-down view, where the black and orange markers represent the nominal and perturbed base poses, respectively, while the straight and curved arrows indicate planar displacement and yaw rotation. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor and are not assumed to be physically equivalent across factors.

Fig. 9: Task-wise distributions of first incomplete semantic milestones among perturbation-induced failures. Each subplot corresponds to one formal task. For each perturbation factor and severity level, the stacked bar shows the distribution of first incomplete milestones g1, . . . , gK among strictly matched S→F transitions, where K depends on the task. Trackercomplete official failures, in which all tracked milestones are reached but RoboCasa’s official task-success criterion remains unsatisfied, are reported separately without assigning a first incomplete milestone. The proportions are calculated over all S→F transitions in the corresponding task and condition. The annotation above each bar indicates the number of transitions n; conditions without such transitions are marked as n = 0.

Fig. 7: Representative matched replays at different semantic failure depths. Each case compares a strictly matched clean– perturbed rollout pair that shares the same task instance, initial simulator state, episode metadata, and episode-level policy seed, while differing only in the target perturbation. The two rows show the clean and perturbed executions, respectively, and the columns present selected frames spanning the execution process. Checkmarks and crosses indicate whether the corresponding tracked semantic subgoals are completed, while the final annotation reports the official task outcome. These examples provide a qualitative view of how perturbations can change execution depth and failure location, complementing the aggregate stage-aware statistics in Figure 6.

Fig. 5: Task-level robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Each cell reports the paired success-rate degradation ∆SR for one task and perturbation condition, computed from 20 matched episode pairs. Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition, while negative values indicate a higher success rate under the shifted condition for the corresponding finite paired sample. The task-level breakdown reveals heterogeneous severity responses that can be obscured by macro aggregation.

Fig. 10: Representative counterfactual outcome transitions under camera orientation at L1. Case A (StackBowlsCabinet) shows a success-to-failure (S→F) transition, whereas Case B (PreSoakPan) shows a failure-to-success (F→S) transition. Within each case, the clean and perturbed rollouts share the same task instance, initial simulator state, and episode-level policy seed, differing only in the target camera-orientation perturbation. Columns show selected frames from the initial, intermediate, and final stages of execution, with the final outcomes determined by RoboCasa’s official task-success criterion. These examples illustrate opposite episode-level outcome changes under the same perturbation condition, despite zero aggregate success-rate degradation at L1.

Fig. 4: End-to-end robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Macro-averaged paired success-rate degradation ∆SR is shown for the four distribution-shift factors, with each factor evaluated at three frozen severity levels (L1– L3). Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals obtained from paired bootstrap resampling. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor, and equal level indices across different factors do not imply physically equivalent perturbation magnitudes.

Fig. 6: Stage-aware execution depth of perturbationinduced failures. Each marker summarizes strictly matched clean-success-to-perturbed-failure (S→ F) transitions under one perturbation factor and severity level. The vertical position indicates the mean normalized subgoal progress of the corresponding S→F cohort, marker size represents the number of transition events, and marker color denotes the fraction of failures occurring before the first tracked semantic milestone. The annotated n gives the number of transitions in each condition. Gray lines connect L1–L3 within the same perturbation factor only to visualize the within-factor severity trend and do not encode an additional quantity. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor and are not assumed to be physically equivalent across factors.

The left half summarizes the GR00T policy and evaluation settings, while the right half reports the software and hardware environment. Runtime package versions are reported separately from the underlying container configuration.

Positive ∆SR indicates degradation relative to the matched clean condition. Confidence intervals are obtained from paired bootstrap resampling.

TABLE IX: Complete counterfactual outcome transitions across all perturbation conditions. Each row contains 80 strictly matched clean–perturbed episode pairs, categorized into four mutually exclusive outcomes: success-to-success (S→S), success-to-failure (S→F), failure-to-success (F→ S), and failure-to-failure (F→F).

TABLE VI: Task-specific semantic subgoal specifications. Each gk denotes a task-specific diagnostic milestone. The criteria were frozen before formal perturbation evaluation. For WashLettuce, thresholds refer to the simulator washed time counter.

TABLE XII: Clean-competence screening on the frozen four-task suite. GR00T N1.5 results are from the secondround final clean screening (N = 20 per task), whereas SmolVLA and π0 results are from the third-round initial screen (N = 10 per task). Neither additional policy reached the clean-screen extension threshold on any task.

TABLE II: Validation of the counterfactual pairing protocol. Environment-side pairing is verified through the initial-state fingerprint. The policy-side comparison shows that uncontrolled inference randomness breaks repeatability, whereas sharing the episode-level policy seed restores consistent action sequences.

TABLE V: Pairing integrity validation. Environment-side checks verify consistency of the simulator configuration before perturbation injection, while policy-side checks control stochastic variation during paired execution.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces stage-aware robustness evaluation for VLA policies in long-horizon manipulation; directly targets vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation
papers.tldr: RoboCasa-Shift shows that VLA robustness in long-horizon manipulation is multi-dimensional and cannot be captured by aggregate task success alone.

papers.abstract: For practical motion generation, it is essential to handle multimodality (multiple actions can be correct for the same observation) while maintaining low inference cost and strong generalization from limited demonstrations. We introduce an attentive mixture-density policy trained with the Energy Score that represents future visuomotor trajectories as explicit probability distributions with a single forward pass. Concretely, we output Gaussian mixture parameters for joint commands (and optionally attention points) and optimize them with the Energy Score (computed as a sum of 1D CRPS under a diagonal covariance assumption) instead of the negative log-likelihood (NLL) to avoid MDN singularities and gradient-scale instabilities. Our architecture couples explicit spatial attention with mixture-density outputs, enabling robust multimodal behavior selection under visual noise and small-data regimes. On an 8-DOF manipulator, the method generates distinct avoidance trajectories and stabilizes learning in obstacle avoidance. Moreover, in a randomized moving-object grasping task, where spatiotemporal multimodality and fast timing decisions are required, the proposed model outperforms Diffusion Policy by 15-25% under several unseen conditions, demonstrating superior generalization and real-time feasibility.
bullets: Represents future visuomotor trajectories as explicit Gaussian-mixture distributions in a single forward pass.
Uses Energy Score, implemented via 1D CRPS under diagonal covariance, instead of NLL to reduce MDN singularities and gradient-scale instability.
Combines spatial attention with mixture-density outputs for robust behavior selection under visual noise and limited demonstrations.
Produces distinct obstacle-avoidance trajectories and outperforms Diffusion Policy by 15–25% in several unseen moving-object grasping conditions.
Demonstrates real-time feasibility on an 8-DOF manipulator, with scope focused on the evaluated manipulation tasks and assumptions.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Architecture of the proposed model. The output layer (green box) represents the multimodality of future predictions by outputting joint angles and attention points as GMM parameters (π,µ,σ). The Energy Score (CRPS) is adopted as the loss function. The yellow box indicates the reconstruction process optimized for the modified prediction format.

Fig. 3: Comparison of Exp. 1 results. The left panel shows the success rate, and the right panel shows the failure rate and its breakdown. The left graph confirms that the proposed model achieves success rates equivalent to or higher than representative conventional models such as ACT and DP. In the right graph, the area enclosed by the crimson frame indicates the proportion of ”mode averaging” generated; it can be seen that this proportion is significantly reduced in the proposed model compared to SARNN without GMM.

papers.abstract: It has been difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to quickly create and iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io
bullets: Targets the difficulty of modeling contact mechanics, coupled dynamics, deformation, stiffness, and friction in robot-object interactions.
Lets users explicitly edit the solver, contact model, and physical parameters while iteratively matching observed behavior.
Built using the open Newton physics simulation system.
Evaluated through human-guided real2sim with visual assessment, force feedback, and agentic Real2Sim2Real.
The abstract does not report quantitative results or specific limitations.

papers.abstract: Latent safety filters certify safety on a learned low-dimensional representation of the state, enabling constraints that resist analytic description. Because the encoder is lossy, a filter can report safe while the physical state is unsafe, with no detectable model error. Existing transfer conditions leave the effect of discarded safety information implicit. We ask when a lossy encoder admits a safety certificate that transfers to the physical system, and show the answer is governed by the detectability of the discarded safety-relevant dynamics. We construct a system whose latent model is exact and whose latent signals always report safe, while the physical state becomes arbitrarily unsafe. For this system no certificate exists and no monitor downstream of the encoder can detect the failure. When the discarded dynamics contract, a latent barrier certifies true safety up to two explicit margins, one for the latent-model error and one for the variation of safety across states the encoder cannot distinguish. In the linear case and under boundedness and non-degeneracy conditions, every calibrated barrier transfers with a finite margin when the safety-relevant subspace is detectable, and none does otherwise. On learned cartpole encoders, the model error does not indicate for which representations the estimated bound is non-vacuous, while the second margin does.
bullets: Lossy encoders can report safety while the physical state is arbitrarily unsafe, even when the latent model is exact.
No downstream monitor can detect failures hidden by the encoder when discarded dynamics are undetectable.
Contractive discarded dynamics yield latent safety certificates with separate margins for latent-model error and encoder-induced safety variation.
For linear systems, calibrated barriers transfer with finite margins exactly under detectability of the safety-relevant subspace; otherwise they do not.
In learned cartpole encoders, encoder-induced safety variation—not model error—indicates when the transfer bound is non-vacuous.

papers.selection_reason: Formal transfer guarantees for safety certificates on learned latent state representations for physical control systems.
papers.title: Latent Safety Filters: When a Lossy Encoder Admits a Transferable Certificate
papers.tldr: A lossy latent safety filter transfers to the physical system only when discarded safety-relevant dynamics are detectable and sufficiently contractive.

papers.abstract: Rare but consequential failures can persist in learned locomotion policies for legged robots even when average task performance is high, in part because standard curricula primarily adapt task difficulty rather than the distribution of safety-critical experience. We introduce Predictive Safety Curricula (PSC), a framework for allocating locomotion training experience using learned predictions of future safety cost. PSC trains a distributional safety critic from policy rollouts and uses its predictions to prioritize both terrain contexts and previously encountered randomized events. The resulting curriculum modifies the training distribution while leaving the task reward and policy-optimization loss unchanged. We evaluate PSC in controlled rough-terrain locomotion and in production locomotion systems. PSC improves reliability relative to standard terrain progression, advantage-based replay, and learning-progress curricula, with the largest gains on difficult terrain and under degraded observations. The same allocation principle transfers to two production locomotion stacks. On ANYmal-D hardware, PSC reduces shank-collision incidence by $63\%$ relative to the learning-progress curriculum across three matched training seeds, with a reduction in every seed. On a production stair-climbing platform, PSC eliminates observed shank collisions in the evaluated hardware trials. These results show that learned predictions of future safety cost can provide an effective signal for allocating training experience toward rare failure modes and improving locomotion reliability.
bullets: Targets rare, consequential failures that standard task-difficulty curricula may overlook.
Trains a distributional safety critic from rollouts to prioritize terrain contexts and previously seen randomized events.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid skills from videos typically requires a successful human demonstration, which often demands custom data collection. Although failures have traditionally been treated only as negative examples in robot learning, they can still reveal a usable trajectory prefix before the task fails, as well as the intended outcome. To leverage this information from a failed-attempt video, we propose TRACC, a pipeline that imitates the useful portion of the motion trajectory and then completes the task based on the inferred task outcome. The usable motion prefix serves as prior knowledge until the failure occurs, after which the task-completion reward guides the policy to learn the intended task goal without requiring a successful task trajectory. We evaluate our method on six in-the-wild failed human tasks from the Oops! dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for learning from failed attempts when no successful demonstration is available. Thus, these findings establish failed human videos as a viable source of supervision for humanoid skill learning.
bullets: Failed demonstrations provide both a usable trajectory prefix and clues about the intended outcome.
TRACC imitates the motion before failure, then uses task-completion rewards to learn the remaining behavior.
The method targets settings without any successful task demonstration.
Evaluated on six in-the-wild failed human tasks from the Oops! dataset.
Results support failed human videos as a viable supervision source for humanoid skill learning.

papers.abstract: Recently, LLM-based autonomous agents have shown strong capabilities in iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining executable solutions. In robotic manipulation, Code-as-Policy lets these agents search over modular and editable robot programs. However, effective program search requires physical understanding: agents must understand how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why interactions succeed or fail. Existing methods rely mainly on execution feedback for program refinement, often leaving these physical questions unresolved. We introduce RoboAuto, a framework for robot program search that explicitly organizes physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through three components. First, a hierarchical knowledge base combines executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, learned from embodied data and online task solving. Second, scene grounding connects this knowledge to the current environment by identifying relevant objects and resolving action-critical quantities. Third, multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments checks whether each stage produces its expected physical effects and actively tests competing hypotheses to resolve physical uncertainties. RoboAuto achieves superior performance across five benchmark families, attaining an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than twice the mean success rate of ASPIRE on LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus. It also outperforms ASPIRE and $π_{0.5}$ on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. We further show that the knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments, and that program search performance scales with its size. Project page: https://roboauto-ai.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the limitation of refining robot programs from execution feedback without resolving underlying physical uncertainties.
Uses a hierarchical knowledge base covering executable skills, object affordances, spatial relations, and action effects.
Grounds this knowledge in the current scene by identifying relevant objects and action-critical quantities.
Employs multi-stage planning and self-designed experiments to verify expected effects and distinguish competing hypotheses.

Reports strong results across simulated and real-robot benchmarks, including an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and improved long-horizon performance; knowledge transfers across simulators and embodiments.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RoboAuto. The Hierarchical Knowledge Base (left) stores object-centric physical knowledge, comprising affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, together with executable skills. Physical Scene Grounding (middle) binds the entries relevant to a task to quantities measured in the current scene. Search and Exploration (right) plans the task as stages that end in verified state changes and designs experiments that separate competing physical hypotheses. Interaction evidence updates the knowledge, and verified programs return to the knowledge base as new skills. RoboAuto is evaluated across five benchmark families, LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-PRO Long, LIBERO-Plus, Robosuite, and RoboTwin 2.0, where RoboTwin 2.0 tests transfer to a new simulator and embodiment.

Figure 13. Search and Exploration. The coder decomposes the task into stages with intended object states and executable verifiers (1), and the environment executes these stages sequentially (2). When an execution fails, an independent auditor evaluates the stage outcomes from synchronized videos and may reject a state that the program verifier accepted (3). The earliest incomplete stage is returned to the coder (4), which revises the stage or replans the task before executing the next candidate program (5). If the cause remains uncertain, the coder branches into a separately implemented experiment that collects targeted physical evidence before revision continues. Programs verified across the search pool contribute reusable executable skills.

papers.abstract: Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios. Although egocentric human demonstrations provide a complementary source of task experience, differences in visual embodiment and missing robot proprioception complicate transfer to humanoid policies. To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs pre-trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, HuGe employs three existing representative VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller, together with hand-control signals. Based on this, we introduce a three-stage training pipeline that combines egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning. To facilitate transfer across embodiments, we construct pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulation playback during pre-training and modify arm appearance in egocentric observations through re-rendering during downstream fine-tuning. With this pipeline, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art on simulation benchmark HumanoidArena. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 indicate that augmenting robot demonstrations with visually adapted egocentric demonstrations significantly increases success on a pick-and-drop task.
bullets: Addresses costly, limited humanoid demonstrations and the mismatch between human egocentric video and robot embodiment.
Uses VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller plus hand-control signals.
Trains in three stages: egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning.
Bridges embodiment gaps with simulated pseudo-proprioception and re-rendered arm appearances.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on HumanoidArena; adapted egocentric data improves real-world Unitree G1 pick-and-drop success.

papers.abstract: Motivated by ten years of Learning-Based Control Invited Sessions at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), this tutorial paper reviews key advances at the intersection of machine learning and control. We focus on methods that combine the flexibility of machine learning techniques with the structure and theoretical foundations of control to design autonomous systems that are capable, reliable, and safe. We first introduce core notions for establishing stability and safety guarantees, then review approaches that learn dynamics models to improve control under uncertainty, and finally discuss data-driven methods that directly synthesize or learn policies, including reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and Bayesian optimization. We further discuss representative applications and open challenges. The goal is to provide an accessible entry point to the field and to support continued progress toward reliable learning-based control in real-world systems. To support learning and practical exploration, we share implementations and illustrative examples along with our discussion, together with additional resources on our website: https://learning-based-control.github.io/tutorial/.
bullets: Reviews a decade of learning-based control research presented at IEEE CDC.
Introduces stability and safety concepts for providing formal guarantees.
Covers learned dynamics models for control under uncertainty.
Discusses policy synthesis through reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and Bayesian optimization.
Includes representative applications, open challenges, implementations, examples, and additional resources.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Scope of the tutorial paper. We review learning-based control methods that combine machine learning with control-theoretic structure to improve system capabilities while preserving desired closed-loop properties. The paper first introduces foundations for stability and safety guarantees (green), then covers methodological paradigms ranging from structured model-based learning to increasingly data-driven policy learning (orange), and finally discusses representative application domains (grey).

Fig. 5: Illustration of the stability and safety notions of this section. (a) Nominal stability: a Lyapunov function V decreases along closed-loop trajectories (level sets in grey) and the state converges to the equilibrium x̄. (b) Robust and stochastic stability: under disturbances w, the state converges to a neighbourhood of x̄ (grey), whose size depends on the disturbance bound or the noise covariance. (c) Safety: constraint satisfaction at one time instant does not imply safety (red dashed arrow); safety is guaranteed by an invariant set S (blue) contained in the constraint set (white). (d)–(f) Safety filters: the desired input udes,k would violate the constraint and is modified to u⋆ k to stay inside of the constraint set (white). HJ reachability computes the maximal safe set S offline, the largest invariant set within the constraint set. A CBF certifies invariance of {b(x) ≥ 0} by the one-step condition on b(xk+1). A PSF does not compute the safe set but certifies safety by a backup trajectory (dotted) into a smaller terminal set Sf .

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model's current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses. We introduce Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI), a technique designed to elicit successful trajectories beyond the policy's intrinsic exploration capacity. RTI operates by leveraging reward-side evidence (i.e., evaluation rubrics) during rollout to convert erroneous trajectories into successful ones, providing effective learning signals for tasks that the policy rarely solves on its own. Although intervention trajectories are inherently off-policy, we find that they can effectively guide policy optimization when trajectories with excessive distributional shifts are filtered out. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines, enabling the post-trained policy to approach the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs and, more importantly, transcend its original capability boundary. The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr.
bullets: Addresses sparse successful trajectories and training collapse when tasks exceed an agent’s current abilities.
Intervenes during rollout using evaluation rubrics to correct erroneous trajectories.
Filters interventions with excessive distributional shifts so off-policy data can still guide policy optimization.
Across five benchmarks, RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines and approaches the performance of stronger LLMs.
Scope: effectiveness depends on reward-side evidence and controlling distributional shift in intervention trajectories.

papers.abstract: Multimodal imitation learning requires diverse executable futures under the same observation and consistent behavior across replanning cycles. We present Conditional Trajectory Peaks (CTP), a single-pass policy framework that jointly predicts complete action-chunk candidates, probability masses, and trajectory scales. Distribution-Aware Peak Specialization (DAPS) specializes trajectory peaks using trajectory-level posterior responsibilities and mass- and scale-modulated overlap constraints. Evidence-Gated Trajectory Belief Transport (ETBT) maintains cross-chunk consistency through geometric correspondence between exchangeable candidate sets, while allowing current policy evidence to override historical constraints. CTP achieves a coverage score of 91.40% on Push-T; success rates of 100.0%, 79.72%, and 84.44% on D3IL Avoiding, Aligning, and Sorting-2, respectively. On LIBERO, CTP achieves an average success rate of 97.25%. In real-world dual-arm experiments, CTP preserves both placement modes in a two-plate task, succeeding in all 50 trials. On bottle uprighting and pen placement into a holder, it maintains success rates comparable to $π_{0.5}$ while reducing policy inference latency from 218.24 ms to 75.80 ms. These results demonstrate that single-pass trajectory modeling can combine multimodal behavior, closed-loop consistency, and efficient inference.
bullets: Jointly predicts complete action-chunk candidates, their probability masses, and trajectory scales.
Uses DAPS to specialize trajectory peaks through posterior responsibilities and mass- and scale-aware overlap constraints.
Uses ETBT to transport trajectory beliefs across chunks while allowing current evidence to override past constraints.
Reports strong simulated and real-world performance, including 97.25% average success on LIBERO and 50/50 success in a two-plate task.
Reduces inference latency from 218.24 ms to 75.80 ms while retaining comparable success to π₀.₅ on bottle uprighting and pen placement.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of CTP. (b) Inference: ETBT propagates historical behavioral beliefs through geometric correspondences between candidate trajectories in successive replanning cycles. Current policy evidence determines whether historical constraints are retained or released.

papers.tldr: CTP is a single-pass multimodal imitation-learning policy that predicts diverse action chunks while maintaining consistency across replanning cycles with efficient inference.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) offer visual foresight for robotic manipulation, but pixel-space models repeatedly reconstruct entire future scenes, incurring high computational cost and spatio-temporal redundancy. In physical manipulation, consecutive frames often share most of their visual context; the changes between them are what an action policy needs to anticipate. We introduce DeltaWAM, a change-centric WAM that makes a compact delta token the unit of future prediction. Each token is a single vector encoding changes between consecutive dense DINO feature maps. DeltaWAM builds on DeltaWorld, a latent world model pretrained on large-scale videos, to autoregressively predict one delta token per future frame. A flow-matching action expert then conditions on the predicted transitions and current DINO features, which serve as spatial anchors, to generate action chunks. Trained for 256 GPU hours on two H100 GPUs, DeltaWAM has 0.725B parameters and achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO. It also shows robust generalization under procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro. Inference takes 142.1 ms per action chunk with 3.86 GB peak memory.
bullets: Addresses the redundancy and computational expense of reconstructing entire future scenes in visual foresight.
Represents each frame transition as a single delta token derived from consecutive dense DINO feature maps.
Uses DeltaWorld for autoregressive delta prediction and a flow-matching action expert conditioned on predicted changes and current visual anchors.
Achieves 92.8% average success on LIBERO and robust generalization to procedural perturbations on LIBERO-Pro.
Runs at 142.1 ms per action chunk with 3.86 GB peak memory; scope is demonstrated on robotic manipulation benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: DeltaWAM overview. (a) Existing policies represent an imagined future as a single subgoal or a sequence of dense frames or latent states, whereas DeltaWAM predicts one compact transition token per future step. (b) DeltaWAM couples a latent transition-centric world model DeltaWorld with an Action DiT, preserving efficient test-time visual foresight. (c) DeltaWAM is lightweight and has low latency compared with representative World-Action models.

Figure 2: Detailed DeltaWAM architecture. DeltaWAM couples the change-centric DeltaWorld with a flow-matching Action DiT. The pretrained DeltaWorld is first finetuned on demonstrations; then Action DiT is trained on robot data with the finetuned DeltaWorld frozen. DeltaWorld first rolls out predicted delta tokens autoregressively. Afterwards, both current DINO latents (the spatial anchor) and predicted delta tokens (the dynamic subgoal) are fed to Action DiT.

Figure 11: Task structure in predicted delta tokens across standard LIBERO suites. Each point concatenates synchronized agent-view and wrist-view tokens at one future step, yielding one joint embedding per step. Samples come from middle-phase windows of collected rollouts.

Figure 12: Action DiT attention to predicted future delta tokens. Native cross-attention probabilities are averaged across Action DiT layers. Rows denote action positions within a generated chunk, columns denote predicted future steps, and agent and wrist tokens are shown separately. Probabilities remain normalized over the complete conditioning context, not only the displayed future tokens.

Figure 5: Delta-token structure under LIBERO-Pro task variations. The two t-SNE projections compare predicted delta tokens from a perturbed task (green triangles) with tokens from its nominal original task (blue) and an original task whose task requirements match the perturbation (orange).

Figure 4: DeltaWAM training and inference. During the second training stage, Action DiT learns from oracle-selected or randomly sampled future trajectories produced by frozen DeltaWorld. At inference, one sampled future trajectory conditions action generation.

Figure 6: Training and Test Ablations. (a) Success rates of three models across the four task suites on LIBERO. Current DINO only, decoded future DINO, and delta tokens use 2,048, 14,336, and 2,060 visual tokens in total for one action chunk, respectively. (b) Comparison of success rates on LIBERO as the number of predicted future steps per camera view varies. Each step contributes one delta token per view, and the dashed line marks the default six-step horizon.
Figure 8: Delta-token structure under LIBERO-Plus lighting variation. LIBERO-Goal task embeddings under original light (circles) and a changed light condition (triangles).

Table 5: LIBERO success rates (%) with six versus eight future steps.

Table 2: Success rate (%) under the LIBERO-Pro task perturbation, broken down by the four standard task suites. Official benchmark baselines follow Zhou et al. [57]. We evaluated the results for Fast-WAM and Lingbot-VA ourselves.
Table 3: Training Hyperparameters.

papers.title: DeltaWAM: Change-Centric Visual Foresight via Delta Tokens for an Efficient World-Action Model
papers.tldr: DeltaWAM predicts compact visual changes rather than full future frames, enabling efficient robotic action generation with strong LIBERO performance and low inference cost.

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors (VBTS) provide rich contact information for robotic manipulation, but existing designs can be hard to simplify and adapt to the size and constraints of humanoid fingertips. We introduce \textbf{GlowTact}, a pressure-responsive vision-based tactile sensing mechanism that directly visualizes contact pressure. \textbf{GlowTact} requires only single-color, non-directional illumination, and the raw tactile image directly represents the pressure distribution without explicit geometry reconstruction. This simple sensing principle enables compact, customizable tactile sensors while preserving high sensitivity and rich spatial detail. We demonstrate gram-scale contact detection, accurate normal-force estimation, and reconstruction of fine contact geometry, including M1 screw threads. These results establish \textbf{GlowTact} as a practical new sensing technology for compact humanoid fingertips, combining a durable nitrile membrane and simple optical design with sensitive and information-rich tactile perception.
bullets: Targets the complexity and size constraints of tactile sensors for humanoid fingertips.
Uses a pressure-responsive mechanism with non-directional, single-color illumination.
Produces raw tactile images that directly encode pressure distributions without geometry reconstruction.
Demonstrates gram-scale contact detection, normal-force estimation, and fine contact-geometry reconstruction, including M1 screw threads.
Combines a durable nitrile membrane with a simple optical design for compact, information-rich sensing.

figures.caption: Fig. 8. 3D reconstruction of GlowTact, compared against 9DTact [8]. Top row: representative test objects. GlowTact is evaluated using an M5 Phillips screw head, threaded screws (M3, M2.5, M2, M1.5, and M1), and a steel-ball array. Representative 9DTact results [8] are included for reference, with set screws (M4, M6, and M8) and a steel-ball array. Middle row: corresponding tactile images. Bottom row: reconstructed contact geometries. Despite relying on a fundamentally different sensing mechanism, GlowTact retains sufficient spatial information to recover the overall contact geometry.

Fig. 9. Comparison of low-load contact sensitivity between GlowTact (left) and GelSight Mini (right). Lightweight objects are gently placed on each sensor under their own weight without additional loading. For each object, the raw tactile image, the difference image, and a 3× contrast-enhanced difference image are shown. GlowTact produces clear contact responses for all tested objects, whereas GelSight Mini exhibits weaker image changes under the same passive loading conditions.

Fig. 10. Force sensitivity comparison between GlowTact and GelSight Mini. (a) Mean tactile response as a function of normal force. (b) Signalto-noise ratio (SNR) versus force; the dashed line denotes the detection threshold (SNR = 3). (c) Minimum detectable force for each probe geometry. GlowTact produces stronger low-force responses, higher SNR, and consistently lower detection thresholds than GelSight Mini.

Fig. 2. Working principles of representative vision-based tactile sensors. (A) GelSight uses directional illumination and an opaque reflective membrane to encode surface geometry through shading. (B) 9DTact uses light attenuation in a translucent gel beneath a black membrane to encode local gel thickness in image intensity.

Fig. 3. GlowTact sensing principle. In the unloaded state (A), a thin air gap separates the black membrane from the gel’s micro-textured surface, so light within the gel is diffusely reflected at the gel–air interface, and the camera sees a uniform light gray. When an indenter presses the membrane into optical contact with the gel (B), the reflective interface is eliminated and light is instead absorbed by the black membrane, darkening the contact region as pressure increases.

Fig. 1. GlowTact is a pressure-responsive vision-based tactile sensing mechanism. A GlowTact-equipped LEAP hand grasps a screw (left), while the tactile images (right) directly visualize contact pressure and fine thread geometry. GlowTact combines sensitive low-force response with rich spatial detail using only single-color illumination.

Fig. 6. Exploded view of the Omnidirectional GlowTact fingertip sensor. A black membrane cut from a nitrile glove is stretched across the surface of the textured silicone, which coats a clear epoxy skeleton. A singlecolor LED ring and fisheye camera sit at the base of the sensor.

Fig. 4. Exploded view of the Flat GlowTact sensor. A black membrane cut from a nitrile glove is stretched across the textured silicone gel pad, which is supported by the gel holder, forming the pressure-sensitive optical interface. A perimeter LED strip illuminates the interface through an acrylic plate, while a fisheye camera mounted in the camera holder observes it from within the sensor shell.

Fig. 7. Humanoid GlowTact fingertip sensor. (a) Main components of the sensor: wide-angle camera, U-shaped LED strip, finger housing, and curved gel sensing body. (b) Assembled fingertip without and with the black nitrile contact membrane. (c) Raw tactile image produced by pressing a U.S. quarter against the sensor; dark regions indicate increased local pressure, while the coin edge and raised lettering remain visible.

Fig. 5. Response of flat GlowTact sensor. Fingerprint images demonstrate high sensitivity and high resolution, shown for normal loads of 0.3 N, 1.0 N, and 2.0 N. Increasing force results in progressively stronger optical coupling and a larger contact area while preserving fine ridge patterns.

papers.abstract: This abstract addresses the incorporation of human motion prediction into proactive and dynamic human-aware motion planning, with the goal of enabling safe collaboration between humans and robots. A deep learning, graph-based model is used to forecast human motion and is integrated into a planning framework. This framework employs a static roadmap along with a time-variant A* algorithm to modify the trajectory of a UR5e manipulator. This method greatly improves human-robot interaction and enables proactive collision avoidance by combining precise motion forecasts with adaptive trajectory planning.
bullets: Targets safe, dynamic human–robot collaboration through proactive motion planning.
Uses a deep learning, graph-based model to forecast human motion.
Integrates predictions with a static roadmap and time-variant A* planning.
Adapts UR5e manipulator trajectories for proactive collision avoidance.
The abstract reports greatly improved human–robot interaction, without specifying quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45. Project website: https://anonymousprojects-dev.github.io/LLM-guided-LocoManipulation-Quadrupeds/
bullets: Addresses navigation tasks where movable obstacles require physical interaction rather than collision-free motion alone.
Jointly selects the skill, relevant object, and geometric target, producing variable-length parameterized action sequences from language and structured scene representations.
Uses a LoRA-fine-tuned language-conditioned planner with low-level reinforcement-learning policies, including an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy.
The pushing policy achieves 93.3% simulation success versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline and reduces completion time by over 60%.
On hardware, the planner composes the correct skills in 44/45 trials, with end-to-end success in 34/45.
