The Metabolic policy was deployed and tested without retraining in eight healthy adults walking at 1.25 m/s, using indirect calorimetry. Results: In simulation, the Metabolic policy reduced modeled muscle metabolic power by 13.8% relative to no-device walking, versus 8.8% for Metabolic + Power. On hardware, MARL-Exo reduced net metabolic rate by 18.3 $\pm$ 6.6% relative to Passive in all eight participants. Relative to No-Exo, the mean reduction was 7.4 $\pm$ 10.0%; six participants more than offset the 13.1% device-wearing penalty, walking up to 24.2% below their No-Exo cost. Conclusion: A metabolically informed policy co-adapted in simulation transferred to users without per-user tuning and consistently reduced the metabolic cost of walking with the device, while explicit power shaping reduced the simulated benefit. Significance: Unlike per-user human-in-the-loop optimization, this approach yields a single population-level controller and allows assistance objectives to be screened in simulation before human testing.
authors: Yifei Yuan, Jakob Wolf, Ghaith Androwis, Xianlian Zhou
bullets: Trains human and exoskeleton agents concurrently using a muscle-metabolic-energy reward, with randomized anatomy, gait, and speed.
The controller uses delayed hip kinematics and past commands; adding mechanical-power shaping reduced simulated metabolic benefit.
In simulation, the metabolic-only policy reduced modeled muscle metabolic power by 13.8% versus no-device walking.
In hardware tests with eight adults, it reduced net metabolic rate by 18.3% versus passive use and 7.4% versus no exoskeleton on average.
Six participants overcame the 13.1% device-wearing penalty, with reductions of up to 24.2% versus no exoskeleton.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent RL for co-adaptive hip-exoskeleton control directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Co-Adaptive Hip Exoskeleton Control (MARL-Exo) for Metabolic Energy Reduction
papers.tldr: MARL-Exo learns a single hip-exoskeleton controller with a simulated co-adapting human model and reduces walking metabolic cost in users without per-user tuning.

papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.
authors: Sinjae Kang, Dong Kyu Shin, Jaehong Kim, Kamin Lee, Hyoeun Kim, Kaixin Wang, Li Zhao, Seonghyeon Ye, Kimin Lee
bullets: Addresses the limitation of binary success signals by incorporating controllable attributes such as speed and motion smoothness.
Introduces Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP) for controlling individual quality attributes and their combinations at inference time.
Uses iterative hindsight relabeling: collect rollouts under target qualities, retain successful trajectories, relabel them by measured quality, and fine-tune.
Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval show improved execution quality and success rates across iterations, including beyond the initial demonstrations.
Real-world tasks demonstrate practical benefits for conveyor throughput and stable transport of wine glasses.
papers.selection_reason: Robot policies with inference-time quality control and iterative hindsight relabeling, directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling
papers.tldr: QCP enables inference-time control of robot execution quality, with iterative hindsight relabeling expanding controllable behaviors and improving task performance in simulation and real-world manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
authors: Hanqing Wang, Zhaotian Cai, Ruichuan An, Bohan Zeng, Tao Zhang, Yilin Chen, Xu Jiang, Kaiquan Chen, Chongyang Wu, Haoran Li, Fan Yang, Mingan Lin, Wentao Zhang, Zenan Zhou, Youzheng Wu
bullets: Addresses limited physical-dynamics understanding in VLA models and the latency of video-based world-model control.
Uses a Physical Dynamics Module to extract physical tokens from vision-language features and condition action generation.
Learns by predicting future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision from a frozen video world model.
Trains entirely on publicly available data augmented with human-to-robot synthesis, subtask labels, and embodied chain-of-thought annotations.
Reports success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv; ablations assess supervision and conditioning choices.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action model with physical dynamics representations and future feature prediction directly fits embodied AI and is closely tied to world-model prediction.
papers.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations
papers.tldr: PDRVLA enhances vision-language-action control with lightweight physical-dynamics representations, avoiding costly online video generation while achieving strong performance across four simulation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate high-level reasoning with low-level action execution for end-to-end robotic control. However, most VLA models target static manipulation in unconstrained environments, overlooking spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles. Fine-tuning VLAs on obstacle-avoidance data is a straightforward solution, but collecting such data is costly, especially for dynamic scenarios, and may degrade their original task capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose VLA-Stem, a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA systems. Without fine-tuning the underlying VLA policy, VLA-Stem converts its action chunks into motion references and uses trajectory-level guidance to preserve their spatial intent while allowing flexible motion and timing adjustments. Conditioned on these references, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information, the Stem policy adaptively modifies execution at inference time, preserving the original task intent while enabling responsive adaptation to spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles. For robust and sample-efficient training, we combine teacher-student distillation with curriculum learning. We evaluate VLA-Stem on reference following, static spatial constraints, and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Across six constrained simulation settings, VLA-Stem achieves 52.8% average collision-free task success versus 23.7% for the strongest safety baseline, while preserving base-policy performance in obstacle-free settings; real-world experiments further show consistent collision reductions under static and dynamic obstacles. These results demonstrate that VLA-Stem couples high-level VLA task intent with rapid, reflex-like responses to immediate physical risks, providing a brainstem-inspired mechanism for robust robot execution.
authors: Bojun Zou, Wenhao Yu, Jiaohao Li, Jiaxuan Lin, Guanting Ye, Haohan Geng, Weihao Yu, Yanyong Zhang, Jianmin Ji
bullets: Addresses VLA limitations in spatially constrained environments and dynamic-obstacle scenarios, where safety data collection is costly.
Converts VLA action chunks into motion references and adaptively modifies execution using proprioception and local obstacle information.
Trains the safety policy with teacher-student distillation and curriculum learning for robust, sample-efficient adaptation.
Achieves 52.8% average collision-free task success across six constrained simulation settings, compared with 23.7% for the strongest safety baseline.
Preserves base-policy performance in obstacle-free settings and reduces collisions in real-world static and dynamic-obstacle experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Safety mechanism for VLA models via RL; fits VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: VLA-Stem: A Lightweight Safety Mechanism for Vision-Language-Action Models via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: VLA-Stem adds lightweight, inference-time safety control to VLA robots, enabling obstacle avoidance without fine-tuning the underlying policy or sacrificing task intent.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a promising paradigm for scalable robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on success-only behavioral cloning leaves them brittle; lacking corrective training signals, minor execution errors rapidly compound into unrecoverable, out-of-distribution failures. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Failure-Informed Learning (AFIL), an end-to-end framework that leverages failure trajectories as adaptive negative guidance for diffusion- and flow-based VLA policies. AFIL uses a pretrained VLA to generate failure rollouts online, avoiding the need for handcrafted failure-mode design or human-in-the-loop recovery. It then jointly trains Dual Action Generators (DAGs) for successful and failed behaviors while sharing a common vision-language backbone, enabling efficient failure-aware policy learning with limited parameter overhead. During sampling, the failure generator adaptively steers action generation away from failure-prone regions and toward more reliable success modes, with guidance strength determined by the per-diffusion-step distance between success and failure distributions. Experiments across in-domain and out-of-domain robotic manipulation tasks, covering both short- and long-horizon settings, show that AFIL consistently improves task success rates and robustness over existing VLA baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness, efficiency, and generality.
authors: Hanwen Ren, Meng Zheng, Wenzhe Cui, Benjamin Planche, Zhongpai Gao, Anwesa Choudhuri, Terrence Chen, Ziyan Wu
bullets: Addresses brittle success-only behavioral cloning, where small execution errors can compound into unrecoverable failures.
Uses a pretrained VLA to generate failure rollouts online, avoiding handcrafted failure modes and human-in-the-loop recovery.
Jointly trains success and failure action generators with a shared vision-language backbone and limited parameter overhead.
Adaptively guides diffusion or flow-based action sampling using the distance between success and failure distributions at each step.
Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain, short- and long-horizon manipulation tasks show improved success and robustness over VLA baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-informed VLA policy learning for manipulation; fits VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Tokens of Motion: Primitive Motion Learning for Human-Humanoid Skill Transfer
papers.tldr: AFIL improves the robustness of vision-language-action policies by learning from online-generated failure trajectories and steering action generation away from failure-prone behaviors.

papers.abstract: The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely. We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families. The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones. Project Page: https://y0uroy.github.io/JAM
authors: Yonghao Yu, Lang Huang, Runyi Li, Toshihiko Yamasaki
bullets: The paper disentangles three factors often conflated in VLA–WAM comparisons: backbone initialization, future-observation objectives, and inference-time future-loss machinery.
JAM combines a pretrained visual backbone, an action expert, an action loss, and a foresight loss predicting frozen future-observation encodings.
Its foresight prediction head is discarded after training, avoiding visual generation during both training and inference while allowing flexible backbones.
JAM outperforms matched FastWAM and ImageWAM policies on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and matches or slightly exceeds them on RoboTwin.
Cached foresight targets reduce estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% versus FastWAM.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified action-model framework with action and foresight losses for control policies, directly relevant to vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models
papers.tldr: Just Action Models separate backbone choice, action learning, and future-observation supervision to improve robot control without visual generation at inference.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies demonstrate remarkable semantic generalization, yet remain highly vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) visual shifts during execution. While existing test-time methods attempt to suppress spurious visual cues, they fundamentally overlook the rich, uncorrupted kinematic priors embedded in the policy's own training experience. We introduce Retrieve to Act (R2A), a test-time scaling framework that formulates OOD robustness purely as a geometric motion primitive retrieval problem. R2A bypasses fragile visual features by structuring successful training demonstrations into an offline spatiotemporal motion primitive graph. During inference, a query-dependent Graph Neural Network dynamically localizes the robot's ongoing execution within this graph, retrieving structurally compatible future motion primitives. These retrieved geometric priors are then seamlessly harmonized with the frozen VLA's predicted actions via a learned, dimension-wise gating mechanism, adaptively rectifying erroneous spatial trajectories while preserving the policy's local reactivity. Extensive experiments across three state-of-the-art VLA architectures, GR00T N1.7, $\pi_{0.5}$, and StableVLA, demonstrate that R2A consistently and significantly enhances robustness against diverse contextual perturbations. R2A achieves absolute success rate improvements of up to +12% in simulation benchmarks (LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin2.0-Plus) and +40% in real-world deployments, without requiring any finetuning of the base policies. Project page: https://retrieve2act.github.io/r2a/
authors: Pham Tri Quang, Bao-Ngoc Dao, Minh Duc Nguyen, Duc-Duy Nguyen, Hung T. Ho, Linh Dang Le, Trong-Bao Ho, Thien-Loc Ha, Tan Q. Nguyen, Tuan Dam, Vu N. Duong, Daniel Sonntag, Ngan Le, Khoa D. Doan, Jan Peters, An Thai Le, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Vien Anh Ngo
bullets: Targets VLA vulnerability to out-of-distribution visual perturbations while preserving local action reactivity.
Builds an offline spatiotemporal graph of successful training motion primitives.
Uses a query-dependent GNN to localize execution and retrieve structurally compatible future primitives.
Combines retrieved motion priors with frozen VLA predictions through learned dimension-wise gating.
Improves success rates by up to 12% in simulation and 40% in real-world deployments across three VLA architectures, without base-policy finetuning.
papers.selection_reason: Retrieval-based motion primitive graph improves OOD robustness of VLA policies; directly in vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Retrieve to Act: Motion Primitive Graph Retrieval for Robust VLA Execution
papers.tldr: R2A improves VLA robustness to visual distribution shifts by retrieving compatible geometric motion primitives from training demonstrations and blending them with the policy’s actions at test time.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies on feedback from sequences of interactions, making credit assignment to individual actions difficult. Existing methods such as GiGPO compare actions at shared states to compute relative advantages, but estimate each action's value from a single sampled continuation. The resulting local credit remains sensitive to decisions made later in the trajectory. To address this problem, we propose ConCal (Continuation Calibration), a recursive continuation-value estimator that incorporates continuation evidence already present in a rollout batch. ConCal matches visits from the same task by their incoming state-action-state transitions, combines shared continuation evidence with each visit's own transition estimate, and propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates. This reduces dependence on individual sampled continuations and mitigates local credit distortions without additional rollouts. Held-out return diagnostics show lower error in within-group value differences and higher agreement with reference action orderings than estimates based on individual continuations. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, ConCal improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 and 5.86 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yingjian-Chen/ConCal.
authors: Yingjian Chen, Lang Zhou, Zixin Zhao, Pingfan Li, Weishi Zheng, Zhilin Zhao
bullets: Targets local credit distortion caused by estimating each action from only one sampled continuation.
Matches same-task visits through shared incoming state-action-state transitions to reuse continuation evidence.
Recursively propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates.
Held-out diagnostics show lower within-group value-difference error and better agreement with reference action orderings.
Improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 percentage points on ALFWorld and 5.86 points on WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: Action-value calibration for long-horizon RL is a general credit-assignment technique transferable to embodied robot policy learning.
papers.title: Action-Value Calibration via Continuation Sharing for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ConCal improves long-horizon reinforcement-learning credit assignment by sharing and recursively calibrating continuation values across matching transitions, yielding better value estimates and higher task success without extra rollouts.

papers.abstract: We trained four widely used imitation-learning policies, ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$, on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100 and 200 teleoperated demonstrations of one pick-and-place task with distractor objects, using one fixed training recipe per policy. Every trained model was then run on a physical SO-101 arm on a fixed set of object placements: 1,340 scored episodes in 126 blocks. ACT, trained from scratch, rose from 1 success in 40 episodes at 12 demonstrations to 37 in 40 at 100. $\pi_{0.5}$ with its action expert fine-tuned was the best policy when data was scarce (16 of 40 at 12 demonstrations, 28 of 40 at 25) and then stayed near 70%; from 100 demonstrations ACT was ahead, by a margin this study does not fully resolve. SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked near 50%, and both were affected by a failure to start: SmolVLA's arm never started moving in 47% of episodes, and Diffusion Policy hardly ever started until an idle lead-in was trimmed from the demonstrations. For $\pi_{0.5}$ the fine-tuning recipe mattered more than the amount of data: low-rank adaptation succeeded in 4 of 110 episodes, against 130 of 200 for action-expert fine-tuning. From the joint and camera recordings we place every episode on a four-stage ladder (started, reached the ball, carried it, delivered it) and show that for ACT more data moves failures from reaching, to grasping, to none, while the failures $\pi_{0.5}$ retains are in grasping. We also measure how weak a ten-episode block is as a measurement (the same checkpoint tested twice differs by 2 successes in 10 on average), separate seed-to-seed variation from that noise, and audit the human scoring against the recordings. Training length was fixed within each recipe, so the amount of data and the number of times it was seen change together; we state which conclusions survive that confound and which do not.
bullets: The study compares ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π₀.₅ using 12–200 demonstrations for one distractor-heavy pick-and-place task.
π₀.₅ performs best with 12–25 demonstrations, whereas ACT improves sharply with more data and reaches 37/40 successes at 100 demonstrations.
SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peak near 50%; startup failures substantially limit both, especially SmolVLA.
For π₀.₅, action-expert fine-tuning is far more effective than low-rank adaptation under the tested recipes.
A four-stage failure analysis shows ACT’s errors shift from reaching toward grasping as data increases, while π₀.₅ mainly retains grasping failures.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical scaling study of imitation-learning policies on a physical robot; directly relevant to robot manipulation and policy learning.
papers.title: From 12 to 200 Demonstrations: How ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ Scale on a Low-Cost Arm
papers.tldr: On a low-cost arm, imitation policies scale very differently with demonstrations: π₀.₅ leads with scarce data, while ACT becomes strongest from 100 demonstrations onward, with evaluation noise and training confounds limiting some conclusions.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) incorporate the prediction of future observations into robot policy learning. However, most WAMs build on billion-parameter vision-language or video-generation backbones, which incur high training cost and inference latency. In this letter, we present GAWM (Geometry-Aware World Model), a compact multi-task WAM that predicts future observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. GAWM compresses the features of each camera view into a small set of tokens. A lightweight predictor, conditioned on the task rather than on actions, forecasts these tokens at two future horizons. The forecast is supervised with the dense patch features of future frames, which requires it to encode the spatial layout of the future scene. An action decoder directly regresses a chunk of future actions from the current and predicted tokens. With fewer than 100M parameters and no robot or video pretraining, GAWM outperforms billion-parameter WAMs on RoboTwin 2.0 and performs comparably to billion-parameter VLAs on LIBERO. On a dual-arm robot, it achieves lower action-prediction error on held-out demonstrations than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA, with substantially lower inference latency. Ablation studies show that the latent world model substantially improves performance when training data or training time is limited. Code is available at https://github.com/gaoxiang12/ga-wm.
authors: Yang Liu, Xiaoli Liu, Liuzhao Li, Yuduo Song, Muyuan Liu, Xiang Gao
bullets: Addresses the high training cost and inference latency of large world-action and vision-language models.
Predicts future multi-view observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder using compact tokens.
Forecasts task-conditioned future tokens at two horizons and uses dense future-frame patch features to preserve scene geometry.
Directly predicts chunks of future robot actions from current and predicted latent tokens.

Uses fewer than 100M parameters, requires no robot or video pretraining, and performs strongly across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and a dual-arm robot; benefits are especially pronounced with limited data or training time.
papers.selection_reason: Compact latent world-action model for multi-task manipulation; directly combines robot action learning with future visual prediction.
papers.title: GAWM: A Compact Latent World-Action Model for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: GAWM is a compact, geometry-aware latent world-action model that enables effective multi-task robot manipulation with lower computational cost and latency than billion-parameter alternatives.

papers.abstract: Maintaining contact in non-prehensile manipulation requires more than nominal friction cone feasibility: a force barely inside the cone and one well inside it are both feasible, but they provide different margins against slip and contact loss. This paper uses signed friction distance to measure friction margin in force space and derives a task-adaptive margin from the force correction needed to balance pivot moment deviations in bimanual tilting. The resulting contact margins are embedded in a sequence of second-order cone programs (SOCPs), each giving a globally optimal contact force solution at a tilt angle. The optimizer balances the object about an environmental pivot while keeping robot and pivot contact forces away from the nominal friction boundary. Optimizer-level results show interpretable force redistribution and adaptation to object property changes. Real-world experiments demonstrate successful execution under object property variations and model mismatch, while fixed margin and no-margin comparisons illustrate the importance of adapting the margin to task demand. These results support signed friction distance margins as a force planning mechanism for maintaining contact in bimanual non-prehensile manipulation. Project page: https://keeping-contact.github.io/
authors: Qian Ying Lee, Lin Yang, Domenico Campolo
bullets: Signed friction distance distinguishes barely feasible contact forces from forces with greater slip and contact-loss margin.
The margin is adapted to the force correction required to balance pivot-moment deviations during tilting.
A sequence of SOCPs computes globally optimal contact forces while balancing the object about an environmental pivot.
Results show interpretable force redistribution and adaptation to object-property changes.
Real-world experiments succeed under property variation and model mismatch; fixed- and no-margin comparisons highlight the value of adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Contact-aware force planning for bimanual non-prehensile manipulation; directly relevant to robotic manipulation and physical interaction.
papers.title: Keeping Contact: Task-Adaptive Friction Margins for Bimanual Non-Prehensile Manipulation
papers.tldr: A task-adaptive friction-margin planner uses SOCPs to maintain robust contact during bimanual non-prehensile tilting despite changing object properties and model mismatch.

papers.abstract: Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) enables structured world representations for planning, interpretability, and safe execution. Most existing approaches rely on passive perception, which creates real2sim gaps due to imperfect observation. Inspired by how humans perceive actively through actions, we propose ActiveAlign, a framework that leverages active perception to align the Real2Sim2Real gap from interactions. ActiveAlign introduces two complementary modules: (i) ActiveAlign-Waving, which performs hand-eye calibration by exploiting active hand motions and differentiable rendering, and (ii) ActiveAlign-Touching, which refines object alignment through tactile feedback to achieve millimeter-level precision. Together, these capabilities enable strong real2sim alignment. We demonstrate that ActiveAlign-Waving can be used to curate simulation environments for open-sourced uncalibrated robot manipulation datasets, and demonstrate on a real Unitree G1 robot that ActiveAlign enables fine manipulation of millimeter-scale objects such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.
authors: Ri-Zhao Qiu, Bowen Wen, Yifeng Jiang, Chen Tessler, Eric Heiden, Xue Bin Peng, Xiaolong Wang, Stan Birchfield, Erwin Coumans
bullets: Addresses misalignment caused by passive perception in Real2Sim2Real systems.
ActiveAlign-Waving performs hand–eye calibration from active hand motions using differentiable rendering.
ActiveAlign-Touching refines object alignment with tactile feedback to millimeter-level precision.
Demonstrations include curating simulation environments from uncalibrated manipulation datasets and fine manipulation on a real Unitree G1 robot.
The system handles millimeter-scale tasks such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.
papers.selection_reason: Active perception and tactile alignment for real-to-sim robot manipulation, fitting learned manipulation and control.
papers.title: ActiveAlign: Aligning Egocentric Manipulation via Active Perception
papers.tldr: ActiveAlign uses action-driven visual and tactile perception to close Real2Sim2Real gaps for precise egocentric robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
authors: Marc Ziegler, Batu \"Ozen, Sami Mentes, Thomas Waschulzik, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses sensor corruption when the robot policy is frozen or inaccessible.
Separates periodic gait dynamics from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair.
On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis improved success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reached 382/640.
Produced no false triggers across 64 held-out fault-free episodes; a matched boosted-tree surrogate showed no repair benefit.
Separate surrogate fits helped Go1 and ANYmal C, while phase-aware gradients performed better.
papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses sensor failure in robot foundation models by proposing a transparent surrogate for online diagnosis and repair of inputs to a frozen locomotion policy. This falls under robot learning (surrogate modeling) and test-time learning (online adaptation).
papers.title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
papers.tldr: A transparent, phase-aware surrogate can diagnose and repair sensor faults around a frozen robot policy, improving simulated locomotion but with limited validation.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
authors: Xu Hu, Changjie Wu, Linzhe Shi, Hang Zhang, Chen Yang, Lingjun Zhang, Guowen Zhang, Mu Xu, Junran Peng, Qing Li, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Targets a key mismatch in WAMs: whole-scene video prediction may underemphasize robot-object interaction dynamics.
Adds auxiliary supervision for temporal point correspondence, image-plane displacement, and depth change.
Uses a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer architecture for video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation.
Keeps the action policy conditioned only on current visual observations, requiring one visual pass followed by action denoising.
Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus show strong in-distribution performance and improved generalization, especially with limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Robot manipulation policy learning augmented with future 3D motion prediction; directly fits embodied robot learning and world-action models.
papers.title: Trace-WAM: Learning to Act via 3D Motion Prediction for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Trace-WAM improves robot manipulation policies by adding future 3D motion prediction to video-action learning while preserving efficient action inference.

papers.abstract: Humanoid parkour requires robots to reason about future footholds and whole-body motions over highly discontinuous terrain. We revisit the information asymmetry in asymmetric actor-critic learning for perceptive humanoid locomotion: the critic exploits privileged simulator signals during training, whereas the deployable actor operates solely from onboard perception. We argue that the key is not exposing privileged information to the actor, but learning a deployable approximation of it to narrow the information gap between training and deployment. We present HC2Robot, a deployable perceptive humanoid parkour framework consisting of a Predicted Foresight Module (PFM) and a Hyper-Connection (HC) Transformer. PFM predicts from deployable observations the policy-conditioned timing, location, and support quality of each foot's next touchdown event, converting privileged supervision into a deployable latent representation that provides the actor with predicted touchdown information without privileged runtime sensing. The HC Transformer further enhances temporal reasoning through learnable multi-stream routing, while a future motion prediction head provides short-horizon motion priors for regularization. Across stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes, HC2Robot achieves a mean simulated traversal success rate of 97.60% and consistently higher safe foothold rates than strong perceptive locomotion baselines, supporting improved traversal performance and geometric foothold support under deployable sensing.
authors: Wenhao Xu, Yanheng Mai, Yifei Fu, Nan Zheng, Yanbo Zhou, Zirui Huang, Mingsheng Ling, Xinjue Wang, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses the training–deployment information gap in asymmetric actor–critic learning without giving privileged runtime signals to the actor.
Uses a Predicted Foresight Module to estimate each foot’s next touchdown timing, location, and support quality.
Employs a Hyper-Connection Transformer for multi-stream temporal reasoning and a future-motion head for short-horizon regularization.
Across stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes, reports a 97.60% mean simulated traversal success rate and higher safe foothold rates than perceptive locomotion baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Deployable perceptive humanoid parkour framework with predicted foresight, fitting robot learning and control.
papers.title: HC2Robot: Hyper-Connection Transformers with Predicted Foresight for Multi-Terrain Humanoid Parkour
papers.tldr: HC2Robot enables deployable humanoid parkour by predicting future footholds from onboard observations and using them to improve temporal whole-body control.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model's latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at https://tapestry-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy A. Collins, Seungjae Lee, Rachanon Wachakorn, Krishnan Srinivasan, Animesh Garg, Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini, Paarth Shah
bullets: Avoids costly video generation at test time and avoids training a separate action head from scratch.
Maps each action timestep into the pretrained VAE’s patch space, then processes actions with the shared video patchifier and transformer backbone.
Jointly trains video diffusion, video–action diffusion, and action-only diffusion objectives to combine visual dynamics priors with robot demonstrations.
Generates smooth action chunks in one DDIM step, achieving 84 ms per chunk on consumer hardware.
Shows strong results in simulation and real-robot experiments with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video–action policies.
papers.selection_reason: Repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a visuomotor robot policy, fitting learned manipulation.
papers.title: TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control
papers.tldr: TAPESTRY turns a pretrained video diffusion transformer into an efficient robot-control policy by representing actions as video-like latent patches.

papers.abstract: We fine-tuned a separate $\pi_{0.5}$ policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.
authors: Lifan Zheng, Guotao Chen, Zhenyang Li, Shujie Cui, Qiang Huang, Fan Liu
bullets: Trained a separate π₀.₅ policy for each of the five competition tasks.
Used task-specific training mixtures and action counts per prediction.
Diagnosed grasping, pushing, and insertion failures through local evaluation.
Revised demonstrations and added expert continuations from policy-reached states while retaining original demonstrations.
Ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action policy fine-tuning and demonstration refinement for robotic manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Evaluation-Guided Demonstration Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies: The Winning Entry in the MetaFine Open Competition
papers.tldr: MAI won the MetaFine Open Competition by iteratively refining demonstrations and selecting checkpoints with instruction-level evaluation for task-specific vision-language-action policies.

papers.abstract: Flow-based policies for language-conditioned multi-task manipulation commonly share a single $\textit{Gaussian}$ source prior and a common linear transport path across tasks. However, reliably executing multiple tasks with distinct motion requirements remains challenging for a shared policy. We introduce $\textbf{TOPS}$ ($\textbf{T}$ask-$\textbf{O}$riented $\textbf{P}$riors and $\textbf{S}$chedules), which adapts the flow source prior and interpolation schedule to each task without modifying the network architecture. TOPS first constructs multimodal task sources from reverse-mapped expert action sequences, allowing language instructions to select where generation begins. Guided by source-target covariance mismatch, it then slows the transition toward expert actions early in denoising and accelerates it later along directions requiring expansion. Under a $\textit{Gaussian}$ endpoint model, our analysis shows that this schedule adjustment can lower an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN demonstrate improved performance across in-distribution, perturbation and cross-environment settings, alongside better data efficiency. Using one integration step, TOPS raises LIBERO-10 success from $53.44\%$ to $69.67\%$ compared with ten-step Standard Flow Matching (FM), while reducing inference time to approximately one-sixth of the baseline. TOPS also yields consistent gains when transferred to the large-scale flow-based $\pi_{0.5}$ policy across all four evaluated settings. Real-world experiments further demonstrate improved task success, including an increase from $20\%$ with standard FM to $80\%$ with TOPS on the upper-drawer opening task.
authors: Tuo An, Chuhao Zhou, Jiahua Dong, Jingliang Li, Jiaqi Bai, Jindou Jia, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Shared Gaussian priors and transport paths struggle with tasks requiring distinct motion patterns.
TOPS builds multimodal, task-specific source priors from reverse-mapped expert actions, selected through language instructions.
It adapts denoising schedules using source–target covariance mismatch, slowing early transitions and accelerating later expansion directions.
The method improves performance across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, transfer to π0.5, and real-world manipulation settings.
On LIBERO-10, one-step TOPS reaches 69.67% success versus 53.44% for ten-step Standard Flow Matching, with roughly one-sixth the inference time.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces TOPS, a method for adapting flow-based policies in multi-task robot manipulation by reshaping source priors and transport schedules, directly addressing robot control and manipulation efficiency.
papers.title: TOPS: Reshaping Flow Source and Transport for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: TOPS improves language-conditioned multi-task robot manipulation by tailoring both the flow prior and transport schedule to each task, enabling faster and more reliable execution.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference. To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations, proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages. We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11x that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. Project page: https://huahungy.github.io/RoboSTD/
authors: Hongyu Wu, Chong Liu, Shaoxuan Xie, Shaqi Luo, Hanyu Feng, Shihan Wu, Guocai Yao
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations and the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination, and arm-side preferences.
Mirrors observations, proprioception, and actions across the sagittal plane to create executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations.
Uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal constraints for reconstructing pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages.
Evaluated in RoboTwin simulation and on a real AgileX ALOHA platform.
In cup collection, it collects 2.11× as many cups as the single-arm baseline without additional bimanual demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes zero-shot data construction for bimanual robot policy learning, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: RoboSTD: Zero-Shot Single-to-Dual Transfer via Sagittal Mirroring for Bimanual Learning
papers.tldr: RoboSTD enables zero-shot transfer from single-arm data to bimanual robot learning by combining sagittal mirroring with LLM-generated coordination constraints.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video generative models for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual observations and actions. The visual prediction objective plays a key role in adapting pretrained video representations to the target robot domain. Yet standard visual prediction inherited from video pretraining treats all visual regions uniformly, despite their differing relevance to robotic control. We therefore investigate the spatial allocation of visual supervision in WAMs and show that focusing supervision on dynamic regions can substantially improve policy performance. Building on this finding, we introduce Motion-Guided Asymmetric Prediction (MoGAP), which augments WAM training with motion-focused visual prediction. MoGAP allocates noise asymmetrically across regions, training the model to reconstruct more heavily corrupted dynamic regions using less corrupted static regions as context. MoGAP is trained alongside standard video-action prediction through a training-only auxiliary prediction path within the shared video diffusion backbone. It uses motion cues derived directly from training videos, requiring neither an external teacher nor additional modalities. Across robot manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP consistently improves policy performance, increasing success rates on the GR-1 tabletop benchmark from 38.8% to 47.5% for Fast-WAM (Wan2.2-5B) and from 52.3% to 62.3% for Cosmos3-Nano.
authors: Taeyoung Kim, Junyoung Sung, Heeseung Kwon, Minseop Kim, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: WAMs benefit from allocating more visual supervision to regions that move and matter for control.
MoGAP applies asymmetric noise: dynamic regions are more corrupted, while static regions provide context for reconstruction.
It adds a training-only auxiliary prediction path alongside standard video-action prediction, using motion cues from training videos without extra modalities or teachers.
Across manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP improves success rates, including GR-1 gains from 38.8% to 47.5% and 52.3% to 62.3%.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts video world models for robot control with motion-guided prediction.
papers.title: Adapting Video Models for Robot Control via Motion-guided Asymmetric Prediction
papers.tldr: MoGAP improves video-based robot control by focusing visual prediction on dynamic regions rather than treating all pixels equally.

papers.abstract: Enabling a humanoid to interact naturally with human partners requires preserving not only individual motions but also the spatial, semantic, and contact relationships underlying the interaction (i.e., hugging, dancing, hand-shaking, etc.). Furthermore, a practical solution should generalize across various humanoid embodiments with distinct morphologies and kinematic constraints. To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically plausible human-humanoid interactions. HumiTransfer first reconstructs 3D human motion with consistent foot-ground contact, then transfers one participant to a target humanoid embodiment via interaction modeling, using weighted joint-relative directions and anatomical offsets to prioritize interaction-critical inter-body relationships, while post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings.
authors: Nghia Le (Hann), Khang Nguyen (Hann), Ba Long Tran (Hann), Thi Quynh Nhu Pham (Hann), Binh Nguyen (Hann), Tuong Do (Hann), Erman Tjiputra (Hann), Hoan Nguyen (Hann), Tung D. Ta (Hann), Baoru Huang (Hann), Hai-Nguyen (Hann), Nguyen (Hann), Anh Nguyen
bullets: Addresses natural human-humanoid interaction across robots with different morphologies and kinematic constraints.
Reconstructs 3D human motion with foot-ground contact, then retargets one participant using interaction-aware joint directions and anatomical offsets.
Post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance.
Generates the HumiMimic dataset from 1,200 videos, covering about 500,000 frames for two humanoid platforms.
Experiments and real-robot deployments show improved motion fidelity, inter-body relationship preservation, contact accuracy, and physical executability over baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Transfers human-human interaction from in-the-wild videos to humanoid embodiments, directly relevant to learning from human video and robot learning.
papers.title: Mimetic Embodiment Transfer of Human-Humanoid Interaction from In-the-Wild Videos
papers.tldr: HumiTransfer converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically executable interactions for humanoid robots while preserving key spatial and contact relationships.

papers.abstract: Handheld data-collection interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) allow manipulation demonstrations to be gathered in the wild without a robot in the loop, but the quality of the resulting action labels is bounded by the accuracy of vision-based localization. Existing systems recover end-effector pose from monocular visual-inertial odometry, which is subject to scale ambiguity and drift, or delegate tracking to closed-source modules and external infrastructure that reintroduce cost and setup burden. We present OpenJaws, a fully open hardware and software framework for sensorized UMI that improves localization and simplifies deployment across robot platforms. OpenJaws pairs a modular, 3D-printed gripper exposing a standardized ISO adapter with a low-cost stereo camera to recover metric camera trajectories. We further introduce UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, a benchmark quantifying real-world localization accuracy for handheld data-collection devices, and show that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives. Finally, we demonstrate that policies trained on data collected with OpenJaws can be deployed on a real robot across multiple tasks. Hardware, software, and data are released under a commercially permissive license. Code, data, and videos are available at https://open-jaws.github.io/
authors: Adithyavairavan Murali, Yash Oza, Karanbir Chahal, Neel Jawale, Silas De Vries, Hesam Rabeti, Erwin Coumans, Balakumar Sundaralingam, Stan Birchfield
bullets: Addresses scale ambiguity and drift in monocular UMI localization, while avoiding closed-source tracking systems and external infrastructure.
Combines a modular 3D-printed gripper with a standardized ISO adapter and a low-cost stereo camera.
Introduces UMI-Loc-Bench-v1 for evaluating real-world localization accuracy of handheld data-collection devices.
Reports that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives.
Demonstrates robot policies trained with OpenJaws-collected data across multiple real-world tasks; hardware, software, and data are openly released.
papers.selection_reason: Open hardware UMI framework with stereo localization for collecting manipulation demonstrations; supports imitation learning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: OpenJaws: An Open Hardware UMI Framework with Stereo Localization for Generalist Manipulation
papers.tldr: OpenJaws is an open, low-cost stereo-tracked UMI framework that improves metric localization for collecting robot manipulation demonstrations and supports deployment across multiple tasks.

papers.abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.
authors: Chengxuan Pei, Ziyao Wang, Teng Mei, Zhe Li
bullets: Addresses the interface gap between generative language models and decision models that require explicit candidate lists.
Trains a formalizer on offline teacher-generated lists to construct validated alternatives from task context, while keeping the decision model frozen.
In CALVIN-D evaluations, formalization improved reported task success from 11.8% to 52.6% in a privileged-state setting.
A motivating comparison reported 46.5% success with pose candidates versus 11% with generic motions.
End-to-end latency was 2.09 s, compared with 3.67 s for Qwen3.5-27B under the stated experimental setting.
papers.selection_reason: Formalizer plus frozen decision model selects pose candidates for embodied tasks, evaluated on CALVIN-D task success.
papers.title: Learning to Formalize: Bridging Open-Ended Workloads and Fast Decision Models
papers.tldr: A small candidate-formalization model converts open-ended tasks into validated alternatives that a fast decision model can select, substantially improving success while maintaining low latency.

papers.abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand--contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on $43$--$78\%$ of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on $<10\%$ and $22.5\%$ of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12\% to 32\% on GRAB dataset. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
authors: Cunxi Dai, Botao He, Francois R Hogan, Wei Pan, Rao Fu, Wen-Han Hsieh, Ruoshi Liu, Jitendra Malik, Guanya Shi, Akash Sharma
bullets: Addresses the failure of kinematics-only retargeting to preserve the contact dynamics needed for successful manipulation.
Uses a shared hand–contact representation for video, motion capture, and tactile-glove data, generating both robot actions and contact-force targets.
Introduces Vid-HACO for inferring contacts from video and a tactile tracking controller for hardware open-loop replay.
Maintains contact on 43–78% of contact frames, compared with under 10% for kinematic and 22.5% for object-aware retargeting.
Improves strict task success on GRAB from 12% to 32% when integrated with physics-based retargeting; hardware results show tactile tracking is essential for reproducing forces.
papers.selection_reason: Contact-anchored retargeting of human demonstrations to dexterous manipulation, including video-to-contact model; strongly relevant to robot manipulation and learning from human video.
papers.title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: CARD retargets human dexterous manipulation to robots by preserving contact forces—not just hand kinematics—across multiple demonstration modalities.

papers.abstract: We present CPG-ENN, a trainable quadruped locomotion framework that combines explicit neural coordination with learned motion realization. A symmetry-based eight-neuron central pattern generator (CPG) supplies gait rhythms, while a pretrained, leg-shared execution neural network (ENN) maps rhythmic signals and trajectory parameters to joint-angle references without online inverse kinematics. A single feedback policy modulates six physically interpretable trajectory variables. The controller tracks planar velocity and yaw-rate commands across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk without gait-specific learned controllers or transitionspecific rewards. Simulation yields 99.39% transition success across all 20 directed gait pairs and all source-target speed combinations from {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} m/s. Ablations show high cross-gait transition feasibility without transition exposure; exposure mainly refines gait acquisition and velocity transients. Comparisons with AllGaits and Walk These Ways demonstrate accurate gait-speed regulation, and Unitree Go2 experiments validate five gaits and their transitions.
authors: Xiyan Liu, Yide Liu, Guoyong Mao, Shaoxing Qu
bullets: Targets robust velocity and yaw-rate control across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk.
Uses an eight-neuron CPG for gait rhythms and a pretrained leg-shared ENN to generate joint-angle references.
A feedback policy adjusts six physically interpretable trajectory variables.
Simulation achieved 99.39% transition success across 20 directed gait pairs and tested speed combinations.
Experiments on a Unitree Go2 validated all five gaits and their transitions; transition exposure mainly improved gait acquisition and velocity transients.
papers.selection_reason: Trainable CPG framework for quadruped locomotion with learned execution network; directly relevant to legged robot control.
papers.title: A Trainable CPG Framework for Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: CPG-ENN combines a symmetry-based CPG, shared neural motion execution, and feedback control to produce and transition among five quadruped gaits without gait-specific transition training or online inverse kinematics.

papers.abstract: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.
authors: Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang, Yiheng He, XinJun Liu, Senhao Hou, Huichan Zhao, Xiaoqiang Tang
bullets: Addresses policy reuse challenges caused by differences in musculoskeletal morphology.
Combines individualized model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation.
Achieves 99.24% completion across 31 held-out models and reduces tracking error by 22.60% versus an unconditioned MLP.
Generalizes to single-image-based models and models with unilateral lower-limb shortening.
Simulations agree with measured ground-reaction forces and show channel-dependent agreement with electromyography.
papers.selection_reason: Morphology-conditioned generalist policy for muscle-driven control; transferable learning-based control across embodied models.
papers.title: A generalist policy for muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models
papers.tldr: MyoAcross enables one muscle-driven control policy to track reference movements across diverse individual musculoskeletal models without per-model fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.
authors: Liang Li, Guoyao Zhang, Xingyu Chen, Sikai Wu, Qianyang Wu, Yuhang Lin, Renjing Xu, Mingliang Zhou, Diyun Xiang
bullets: Targets missing terrain adaptation in flat-ground-trained behavior foundation models, especially foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing.
Adds a terrain-conditioned residual adapter that modifies only lower-body execution targets while preserving the frozen tracker and reference interface.
Trains with task and foot-geometry rewards, suppresses unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distills privileged terrain information to onboard depth.
Evaluated on four frozen trackers across stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation.
Demonstrated real-world terrain traversal on a Unitree G1 using the adapted SONIC tracker, onboard depth, and unmodified references.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware residual adaptation for frozen humanoid behavior trackers; learned terrain-conditioned control relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
papers.tldr: GRAFT adapts frozen humanoid behavior trackers to uneven terrain by learning lightweight, geometry-aware lower-body corrections from depth without retraining the underlying tracker.

papers.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.
bullets: Targets low-cost SO-101 arms, addressing the lack of accessible benchmarks for spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks.
Provides four tasks across five evaluation families, 138 objects, seen/unseen splits, 916 episodes, and simulated demonstrations in an Isaac Lab digital twin.
Policy rankings in simulation exactly matched physical-robot rankings for five policies tested, though simulation overestimated success.
Best learned policies achieved about 61%, while an LLM code-writing agent paired with a learned grasping policy reached 83.2%.
Spatial placement, unseen object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain open challenges.
papers.selection_reason: Simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation on low-cost arms, evaluating VLAs and LLM agents; directly embodied manipulation and VLA.
papers.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
papers.tldr: SO-101 Bench is a simulated, language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark whose digital twin reliably ranks policies but exposes substantial challenges in generalization, planning, and spatial placement.

papers.abstract: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
authors: Fanqi Yu, Matteo Tiezzi, Cigdem Beyan, Tommaso Apicella, Vittorio Murino
bullets: Targets sequential learning from multimodal demonstrations without storing or revisiting past data.
Uses hierarchical dual attention to separate instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement.
Adds key-level geometric regularization to align representations within tasks and separate them across tasks.
Supports an expandable expert set for continual adaptation and reliable expert selection.
On LIBERO suites, including heterogeneous and paraphrased tasks, it improves AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting; gains are stronger under interference and language variation.
papers.selection_reason: Replay-free lifelong imitation learning for robot manipulation with expert routing and continual adaptation.
papers.title: HIDRA: Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention for Replay-Free Lifelong Imitation Learning
papers.tldr: HIDRA enables replay-free lifelong imitation learning by stabilizing expert routing under continual representation drift.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP). While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified. We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL. We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation $\sigma$ has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques. We observe a significant effect of $\sigma$ on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments. Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
authors: Andrea Vasco Grieco, Evelyn D'Elia, Edoardo Caldarelli, Raffaello Camoriano
bullets: Analyzes loss of plasticity (LoP), where RL agents become less able to learn from new data.
Studies PPO with isotropic Gaussian policies and examines how policy standard deviation σ relates to LoP.
Provides theoretical and experimental evidence that σ substantially affects the extent of LoP.
Connects the findings to why commonly used LoP mitigation techniques may be effective.
Validates the analysis on LoP benchmarks and through deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes loss of plasticity in on-policy RL with robotic-arm deployment; relevant to robot learning and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Bridging Exploration and Loss of Plasticity in On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: The study identifies policy standard deviation in PPO’s isotropic Gaussian policies as a key factor influencing loss of plasticity in continuous-control reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.
authors: Simone Manni, Annika Wollschl\"ager, Dario Bellicoso, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter, Simon Le Cleac'h, Jan Br\"udigam
bullets: Targets long-horizon tasks combining maneuvers such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion.
Uses a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated rewards, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to structure exploration.
Employs decoupled hierarchical control, separating low-level balance from high-level phase execution.
Demonstrates multi-stage skills on Unitree G1 and Boston Dynamics Spot with a manipulator arm.
Ablation studies validate the proposed design choices.
papers.selection_reason: Learns multi-phase loco-manipulation policies with phase-conditioned PPO, directly relevant to Embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: A phase-aware PPO framework learns complex multi-stage loco-manipulation directly from environment interaction across different robot platforms.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction.
