Separate recurrent modules infer torso inertial changes and task-relevant history from proprioception, while a height-map teacher is distilled into a depth-based student. We extensively evaluate LOAD and its variants in simulation and on hardware across beam widths and payload configurations. The results show that implicit dynamics features accelerate training, while explicit inertial estimation further improves traversal success; combining both enables LOAD to approach the performance of a privileged policy supplied with ground-truth inertial parameters. Hardware experiments demonstrate traversal with unilateral payloads of 6 kg on a 10 cm beam and 9 kg on a 15 cm beam, and an evenly distributed 11 kg payload on a 15 cm beam. These results support combining physical estimates and history features for precision locomotion under unknown loads.
authors: Kunzhao Ren, Zhishuo Zhu, Xiaobin Xiong
bullets: Targets precision footholds when payload changes make robot dynamics uncertain.
Uses recurrent proprioceptive modules for explicit inertial estimation and implicit task-history features.
Distills a height-map teacher into a depth-based student for perceptive locomotion.
Combining both feature types approaches a privileged policy with ground-truth inertial parameters.
Hardware tests demonstrate loaded traversal on narrow beams, including unilateral and distributed payloads.
papers.selection_reason: Learned perceptive locomotion with online dynamics awareness for precision footholds, relevant to robot navigation and learning.
papers.title: Locomotion with Online Awareness of Dynamics for Precision Footholds
papers.tldr: LOAD combines estimated inertial changes and learned dynamics history to help robots traverse narrow beams precisely under unknown payloads.

papers.abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.
bullets: Multivariate distributional RL needs joint return distributions, but categorical critics scale exponentially and quantiles lack a canonical multivariate form.
The critic represents returns with Stein particles transported by Stein variational gradient descent along a learned score field.
Bootstrapped denoising score matching and a Bellman consistency loss learn and stabilize the score field across recursion.
A reverse-diffusion sampler supports tail-risk queries below the resolution of the particle set, with Wasserstein evaluation guarantees for bounded, possibly multimodal returns.
SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than equal-particle critics and performs comparably on MuJoCo continuous control.
papers.selection_reason: Distributional RL with Stein particles for multivariate returns, evaluated on MuJoCo continuous control; relevant to robot learning.
papers.title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
papers.tldr: SVDRL uses learned score fields to transport return particles and sample multivariate return distributions, improving rare-event estimation beyond the particle resolution.

papers.abstract: Can an AI agent turn high-level user intent into a functioning robot and teach it how to behave? We study this question from two complementary aspects: embodiment and behavior creation. For embodiment creation, we investigate how well current multimodal models capture mechanical requirements, and introduce computational metrics for evaluating generated designs before fabrication. For behavior creation, we present Roboforge, an agentic framework that turns task specifications into executable policies through motion generation, policy learning, and execution-grounded revision. Given a robot embodiment and task, the agent generates a reference motion, configures the learning objective, and trains a policy. Crucially, motion remains in the loop: rollout feedback can revise the reference motion, reward, or both. We evaluate a generated embodiment across multiple MLLMs and behavior creation across four diverse robots against reward-refinement and one-shot motion baselines. Our computational metrics expose recurring mechanical failures in generated designs, while behavior experiments show that execution-grounded refinement improves task-level behavior and execution quality. Finally, we fabricate an agent-generated Gorilla and directly deploy learned behaviors on the physical robot.
authors: Xuebing Li, Yibo He, Sitong Liu, Ran Ji, Jiayuan Gu
bullets: Studies both mechanical embodiment creation and behavior creation from high-level task specifications.
Introduces computational metrics to detect mechanical failures in generated robot designs before fabrication.
Presents Roboforge, which generates motions, configures learning objectives, trains policies, and revises them using rollout feedback.
Evaluations across multiple multimodal models and four robots show improved task behavior and execution quality over the reported baselines.
Fabricates an agent-generated Gorilla robot and deploys learned behaviors on it.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic framework generating, verifying, and revising robot embodiments and learned behaviors, directly relevant to robot learning and embodied AI.
papers.title: Agentic Robot Creation through Generation, Verification, and Revision
papers.tldr: The paper presents an agentic pipeline that generates robot embodiments and learns behaviors through execution-grounded verification and revision.

papers.abstract: Proactive dynamic grasping requires robots to predict the future state at which physical contact will occur, rather than reacting to the currently observed object pose. But what future must the robot predict, and at what level of abstraction? We argue that contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) is a compact task-sufficient abstraction for this problem: it directly determines where and when the robot should establish contact, without requiring visually complete future scenes. This insight leads to a lightweight object-centric forecast-then-select framework that predicts future rigid-body trajectories from short pose histories and uses a reachability-aware interception selector to choose feasible contact states under kinematic and timing constraints. Trained with randomized physics simulation over primitive shapes, the forecaster transfers to real objects once their metric geometry and SE(3) state histories are recovered. Experiments across simulation and real-world dynamic grasping tasks show that our framework improves the average success rate from \(24.5\%\) to \(62.0\%\) in simulation, and from \(15.3\%\) to \(67.3\%\) in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable interception. The SE(3) forecaster runs in \(15\,\mathrm{ms}\), orders of magnitude faster than dense visual future prediction, enabling real-time contact decision making. Our results suggest that effective proactive grasping does not require imagining the entire future scene. Instead, predicting the compact physical future that determines contact provides an effective and practical abstraction for real-time dynamic grasping.
authors: Yirui Zhou, Hongli Xu, Ying Zheng, Yi Wang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Frames contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) as a task-sufficient abstraction for predicting when and where contact should occur.
Forecasts future object trajectories from short pose histories, then selects reachable interception states under kinematic and timing constraints.
Trained in randomized physics simulation on primitive shapes and transferred to real objects using metric geometry and SE(3) histories.
Improves average success from 24.5% to 62.0% in simulation and from 15.3% to 67.3% in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable tasks.
Runs in 15 ms, supporting real-time contact decisions while avoiding dense visual future prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Object-centric SE(3) forecasting for proactive dynamic grasping, directly relevant to robot manipulation.
papers.title: Physics-Aware Object-Centric SE(3) Forecasting for Real-Time Proactive Dynamic Grasping
papers.tldr: A lightweight object-centric SE(3) forecasting and interception framework enables real-time proactive dynamic grasping without predicting entire future scenes.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation has traditionally relied on end-effector-centric interactions. In contrast, humans routinely exploit whole-arm contacts to improve efficiency, robustness, and adaptability, especially when the hands are occupied or when precise grasping is unnecessary. Enabling similar capabilities in robots remains challenging: the robot must select where on its arm to make contact, generate effective non-prehensile interactions, and satisfy task-specific pose or safety constraints on the end-effector. We propose Whole-Arm Contact Learning (WACL), a hierarchical framework that describes each whole-arm contact task with three robot-agnostic representations and hands them to a quasi-static surface-contact optimizer: semantic keypoints that summarize the scene, a reference contact trajectory that specifies where and how the arm presses on the object, and safety-aware path constraints that a vision-language model generates from the task description to protect the end-effector's task. The robot's kinematic chain enters only in this optimizer, which grounds these representations onto the arm by jointly searching over which link makes contact, where on that link, and the joint configuration that realizes it. This decomposition lets WACL learn the contact trajectory from 10 bare-hand human demonstrations per task collected without teleoperation, while new end-effector constraints change only the optimizer's input rather than any trained component. Real-world experiments on a 7-DoF arm across four whole-arm tasks show that WACL sustains contact under end-effector constraints where a strong link-pose baseline fails (78% vs. 33% success) and generalizes to new constraints without retraining. Website: https://wacl-robot.github.io
authors: Bo-Ruei Huang, Daniel Seita, Erdem B{\i}y{\i}k
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing arm-contact locations while preserving task-specific end-effector pose and safety constraints.
Uses three robot-agnostic representations: semantic scene keypoints, a reference contact trajectory, and vision-language-model-generated safety-aware path constraints.
A quasi-static surface-contact optimizer grounds these representations onto a robot by jointly selecting the contacting link, contact location, and joint configuration.
On a 7-DoF arm across four tasks, WACL achieved 78% success under end-effector constraints versus 33% for a link-pose baseline.
Demonstrations use bare hands rather than teleoperation; the method’s scope is whole-arm, non-prehensile contact tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Whole-arm contact manipulation learned from human demonstrations with VLM-generated constraints and contact optimization.
papers.title: Beyond the End-Effector: Learning Whole-Arm Contact Manipulation from Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: WACL learns whole-arm contact manipulation from just 10 human demonstrations per task and adapts to new end-effector constraints without retraining.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables driving policies to adapt to changing deployment conditions, but requires safe exploration throughout training. Safety filtering alone does not ensure stable policy improvement or reduced dependence on corrections. We propose Safe Online Adaptive Refinement (SOAR-Flow), a framework for safe and stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized Flow-based driving policies. A control barrier function (CBF)--model predictive control (MPC) filter corrects potentially unsafe actions before execution. To support stable policy updates, we introduce Gaussian-return-aware value calibration based on calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL), using recorded behavior returns and predicted return variability to smooth conservative critic updates and mitigate policy degradation. Paired corrective learning teaches feasible action adjustments, while an intervention-to-go predictor encourages decisions requiring fewer future corrections. Its predictions also regulate guidance strength, allowing recovery supervision to weaken as predicted dependence decreases. Together with gradually reduced calibration regularization, this supports continued task improvement while preserving hard execution constraints. We analyze conditions for safe execution at control steps and diminishing auxiliary learning influences. We evaluate SOAR-Flow in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV). The results demonstrate improved driving performance and reduced reliance on safety corrections during protected online fine-tuning. The demonstration video and project overview are available at https://lzqw.github.io/SOAR-Flow/.
authors: Zeqiao Li, Yijing Wang, Haoyu Wang, Zheng Li, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Addresses unstable policy improvement and persistent safety-correction dependence during online RL for autonomous driving.
Combines a CBF–MPC safety filter with Gaussian-return-aware value calibration to enforce safe actions and mitigate policy degradation.
Uses paired corrective learning and an intervention-to-go predictor to guide feasible actions and adaptively reduce recovery supervision.
Evaluated in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle, showing improved driving performance and fewer safety corrections during protected fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Safe online RL fine-tuning of driving policies with CBF-MPC filtering, relevant to learned navigation and robot RL.
papers.title: Beyond Safe Execution: Safe Online Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving with Value Calibration and Adaptive Guidance
papers.tldr: SOAR-Flow enables safer, more stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized driving policies while reducing reliance on corrective interventions.

papers.abstract: A long-horizon manipulation task consists of primitive skills and the transitions connecting them. Learning skills that can be executed in sequence requires supervision for both, which is costly to collect on a robot. Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations, but transferring them to robots requires extracting robot-compatible observations and actions together with their skill structure. We present DexStitch, a framework that cuts long-horizon human videos into skills and transitions, converts them into aligned robot observation-action-skill data, and stitches the learned skills into a requested sequence. A skill classifier first segments the videos into manipulation skills and transitions. DexStitch then converts the human demonstrations into robot observations and actions while retaining their corresponding skill labels. During conversion, per-finger human-object contacts guide dexterous hand retargeting and robotic inpainting, preserving contact geometry and finger-object occlusion ordering. To stitch the learned skills into a sequence, a shared skill-conditioned policy is pretrained on the resulting synthetic data and finetuned on a mixture of synthetic data and a small set of single-skill teleoperation episodes. Conditioning on the current and next skills guides each transition toward the following skill, while predicted skill progression enables closed-loop switching. On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.

papers.abstract: Robotic assistance for human mobility could benefit care recipients and reduce caregiver burden during physically demanding tasks such as Sit-to-Stand (STS) and Lift-and-Transfer (L&T). Learning robot policies for these whole-body assistive tasks is challenging: real-world data collection for human-robot interaction is costly and safety-critical, making simulation an attractive alternative. Prior work, however, typically treats the human as static or minimally responsive and thus fails to capture the cooperative nature of mobility assistance. We present a simulation-based framework for learning whole-body assistive robot policies. At its core is a human policy trained with an adversarial motion prior that produces realistic care-recipient motion in response to the robot's actions. A human-adaptive scripted controller interacts with this policy to collect diverse robot demonstrations at scale. From these demonstrations, we train 3D diffusion policies that map segmented human point clouds and robot joint positions to whole-body actions for a mobile manipulator, without relying on privileged human state at deployment. The resulting robot policies successfully perform both STS and L&T assistance in simulation. Preliminary experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer for STS after fine-tuning on a small amount of real-world data. Videos are available on our project page: https://rchi-lab.github.io/human-gen-mobility-assistance/

papers.abstract: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks. Under this protocol, I3L improves autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and achieves at least 90% success on every task, outperforming demonstration-only training by 35.6 percentage points on average with the same number of training trajectories. Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation. Videos, visualizations, and appendix are at https://i-3l.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/
authors: Yusuf Umut Ciftci, Joonwon Kang, Ajay Suresha Sathya, Somil Bansal
bullets: Uniform behavior cloning overlooks that some states are critical while others are recoverable.

papers.title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning

papers.abstract: Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity. We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps. These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .
bullets: Addresses the need for action likelihoods in RL while preserving the flexibility of diffusion and Flow Matching policies.
Uses Jacobian-Tractable Transformers to make each sampling step invertible and efficiently compute its density.
Trains finite sampling steps with Conditional Euler-step Training, which theoretically aligns with fitting Flow Matching Euler updates under stated assumptions.
Reaches 96% success on Robomimic Lift and OGBench Cube-Triple, and supports SAC-style actor-critic training.

papers.title: PrT-Flow: Probability-Tractable Flow Matching for Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: PrT-Flow enables multimodal, multi-step robot action generation with tractable action probabilities for reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.
authors: Yiwei Zhang, Yantai Yang, Jin Gao, Jin Lou, Andong Chen, Yufei Liu, Boyang Xing, Yuchen Zhu, Weiming Hu, Zhipeng Zhang

papers.title: Acting Through Registers

papers.abstract: Estimating simulation-ready material parameters from visual observations is crucial for deformable-object manipulation but challenging because material properties are only indirectly revealed through physical responses. We introduce physical-field-bridged material inference, a single-pass framework that uses dense physical responses to connect multi-view RGB deformation videos with constitutive-type classification and continuous parameter regression. Unlike inverse-physics methods requiring per-scene reconstruction, online tuning, or simulation-in-the-loop optimization, our model predicts force/contact masks, projected motion-flow fields, and projected stress-response maps, then conditions material inference on these fields to reduce reliance on appearance or category shortcuts. We construct DeformFieldBench, a 3DGS MPM learning environment comprising 5,000 simulations across 100 object shapes and five mechanically informative loading modes, with dense pixel-aligned physical supervision. Our method achieves the best median errors on all four continuous parameters, improves stress-hotspot recall from 0.0762 to 0.5121, and attains 0.8676 SSIM/36.82 dB PSNR in same-simulator replay on unseen objects. Under a protocol-matched GSO evaluation, inference and future-state prediction take approximately 30 seconds, compared with 15-120 minutes for per-scene optimization. The method also yields measurable replay agreement on five real-world sequences. These results support dense physical fields as an effective bridge for fast material inference, while cross-simulator and real-world tests reveal remaining domain and identifiability gaps.
authors: Linrui Shou, Jie Li, Yu Liu, Tao Huang

papers.abstract: Tracking object motion within a gripper provides essential feedback for robotic manipulation. However, limited contact coverage and uneven deformation make tactile estimation challenging. In this study, we present TacSpin, a method that tracks in-gripper object rotation on SO(3) using only two vision-based tactile sensors. The key idea is to estimate the axis and magnitude of the rotation response separately, rather than fitting a rigid-body model by least squares. Each finger's response is further refined with contact-boundary cues. The two fingers are then fused according to their agreement. On standard objects, TacSpin achieves lower mean checkpoint errors. Qualitative demonstrations on real-world objects, using calibration transferred from a standard sphere, illustrate tracking under different contact geometries.

Fuses the two tactile estimates according to their agreement.
Achieves lower mean checkpoint errors on standard objects.

papers.title: TacSpin: Tactile Tracking of In-Gripper Object Rotation on SO(3) via Axis-Magnitude Estimation
papers.tldr: TacSpin tracks in-gripper object rotation on SO(3) using two vision-based tactile sensors by separately estimating rotation axis and magnitude.

papers.abstract: While expert demonstrations on real robots are difficult to collect, human ego-centric videos are easy to collect and abundant on the internet. However, learning dexterous manipulation policies from human videos remains challenging---one of the most important challenges being the difficulty of reconstructing physically grounded robot trajectories due to the large embodiment gap. In this paper, we propose EgoCPT, a novel paradigm for learning high-quality retargeted dexterous hand trajectories directly from an ego-centric video, which can then be deployed directly on real robots. The only inputs to our method are an ego-centric RGB video and a reference hand pose trajectory, which can be easily obtained through off-the-shelf software or specialized cameras during recording. Our method is particularly robust to noisy hand poses attributed to our novel contact-aware optimization framework, which iteratively optimizes the contact points between the robot hands and objects. Across five manipulation tasks, our method achieves overall success rates of 67.3% on noisy EgoDex hand-pose reconstructions and 92.0% on high-quality TACO reconstructions collected using motion-capture hardware, outperforming multiple baselines on both benchmarks.
authors: Zhixin Sun, Kairui Shi, Tianao Ren, Ming Yang, Mark Cutkosky, James Jingxi Xu

papers.tldr: EgoCPT turns a single human ego-centric video and reference hand poses into contact-aware, robot-deployable dexterous manipulation trajectories.

papers.abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
authors: Jack Lu, Yurong You, Boyi Li, Yulong Cao, Thomas Tian, Chaowei Xiao, Xiangyu Chen, Wenjie Luo, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone, Yan Wang

For long-horizon tasks, reasoning can be generated during execution and used as episodic memory rather than delaying action.
Across four manipulation and driving benchmarks, TacitVLA matches explicit-reasoning performance with up to 3.4× lower latency.
It matches the latency of non-reasoning training while achieving up to 17.1% higher success.

papers.title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency
papers.tldr: TacitVLA preserves the benefits of reasoning in vision-language-action models while avoiding reasoning-induced action latency.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions. We show that box trajectory prediction substantially reduces com- putational cost while improving action prediction performance, suggesting that object-centric compact states can serve as an efficient alternative to video-based world action modeling for robotic manipulation. Result videos can be found on https://box-wam.github.io
authors: Qinxi Yu, Wenzhou Ding, Gloria X. Wang, Albert J. Zhai, Shenlong Wang

Represents task-relevant object motion with object-centric oriented bounding-box trajectories.

Focuses on robotic manipulation; the abstract does not specify datasets or numeric results.

papers.title: Box-WAM: Box Trajectories as Compact State Representations for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Box-WAM uses oriented bounding-box trajectories instead of future video frames to make world action models more efficient while improving action prediction for robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. In particular, policies relying on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras (e.g., YUBI handheld gripper data) are heavily exposed to visual artifacts (holes, floaters) in wide-angle views, directly degrading task performance. To address this, we present YUBI-Real2Sim, a unified framework for 3DGS-based scene reconstruction and real-to-sim policy evaluation under dual fisheye wrist views. We develop an integrated pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye camera capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and MuJoCo-based physical simulation, reproducing the observed real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons. Using this framework, we construct a benchmark across two bimanual robot platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and dual pi0.5-based policies. This systematically measures real-to-sim rank agreement and evaluates policy sensitivity against counterfactual 3DGS artifacts (ceiling holes, floaters, warping) and capture disturbances. We further analyze whether novel-view quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability under a scene-held-out evaluation protocol. The results show task-dependent performance and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction, highlighting the need to assess reconstruction quality when using Real2Sim for policy evaluation. These results do not yet establish a generally reliable scene-acceptance rule. Project Page: https://yubi-real2sim.airoa.io.
authors: Hiroki Nishizawa, Takehiko Ohkawa, Nicola Scianca, Tatsuya Matsushima, Shigeo Morishima, Kei Ota

Tests policy sensitivity to ceiling holes, floaters, warping, and capture disturbances, and examines whether novel-view quality predicts ranking reliability.

papers.title: YUBI-Real2Sim: 3DGS Scene Verification for Reliable Policy Evaluation

papers.abstract: Precise control of movement across various robotic embodiments is a longstanding challenge. Modeling complex robotic structures requires significant time, dedicated sensors, and manual labeling. Recent advancements in 4D representation learning offer an interesting alternative: can we leverage 4D features lifted from 2D observations to densely map a robot's spatial movement based on the action signal? To this end, we propose Act4R, a framework that builds on 3D foundation model to predict a robot's 3D scene flow with any given action. Act4R introduces a Spatial-Action Encoder, which encodes the current 2D robot state and its action signals into embeddings that represent future robot state in 3D. Then, both the current and future spatial embeddings are decoded into point maps to estimate action-conditioned scene flow. To effectively learn the mapping between action and future state, Act4R introduces spatial-action fusion in its transformer-based encoder, and a spatial alignment loss that guides the encoder for future flow prediction. After training on some samples of a given embodiment, Act4R can perform inverse control by optimizing the signal to achieve the desired scene flow. We evaluate Act4R on a public real-world dataset and synthetic data collected in simulator. Experiments on various robotic platforms show that Act4R outperforms the previous SoTA in scene flow prediction. Our method also performs better in inverse control, both on the action accuracy metric and in closed-loop control in simulation.
authors: Zhaoliang Zhang, Chenhao Yu, Zhimin Shao, Xijun Liu, Cheng Peng
bullets: Addresses the costly modeling, sensing, and labeling required for precise control across robot embodiments.
Uses a 3D foundation model with a Spatial-Action Encoder to combine 2D robot observations and actions into future 3D spatial embeddings.
Decodes current and future embeddings into point maps and estimates action-conditioned 3D scene flow.
Introduces spatial-action fusion and a spatial alignment loss to improve future-flow prediction.
Outperforms prior state of the art in scene-flow prediction and improves inverse control on real-world and simulated data.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Act4R, a 3D foundation model framework that predicts action-conditioned 3D scene flow from 2D observations, effectively bridging world models and robot control.
papers.title: Act4R: Action-conditioned 4D reconstruction for kinematics-free control
papers.tldr: Act4R predicts 3D robot motion from action signals and enables inverse control without explicit kinematics models or dedicated sensing.

papers.abstract: Trajectory smoothness has been proposed as a cheap, training-free signal for curating imitation-learning demonstrations, most recently by rinse, which introduces Spectral Arc Length (SAL) and a contact-aware Trajectory-Envelope Distance (TED). We test whether these published metrics survive episode-length controls on real robomimic data. On can/mh, SAL separates better from worse operators with AUROC 0.952, but episode length alone achieves 0.957, and inside a duration-matched band SAL falls to 0.628 while raw mean jerk, the baseline rinse argues against, rises to 0.896. The confound replicates on square/mh. On can/mg, where every episode is exactly 150 steps, SAL is at chance (0.454) and TED is inverted (0.376) against task success, while jerk reaches 0.706. Training GMM behavior-cloning policies on each metric's curated subset (10 seeds), curating by TED costs roughly a third of downstream success relative to random selection of the same size (0.240 vs. 0.360, p=0.0001, surviving Bonferroni correction), while SAL and jerk are indistinguishable from not curating. Under a diffusion policy TED still ranks worst, though its deficit is not resolvable at five seeds, and jerk becomes significantly better than both baselines, so the curation decision does not transfer unchanged across the two policy configurations we tested. Inspecting trajectories shows why TED inverts: successful manipulation requires sustained high-deviation motion through contact, while failure is low-amplitude hovering that a smoothed envelope follows closely.
bullets: On can/mh, episode length alone slightly outperformed SAL; duration matching reduced SAL’s AUROC from 0.952 to 0.628, while mean jerk reached 0.896.
The confound replicated on square/mh; on fixed-length can/mg, SAL was near chance and TED was inversely associated with success, whereas jerk reached 0.706.
TED-curated data produced substantially worse GMM behavior-cloning performance than random selection, while SAL and jerk were not different from random curation.
Under diffusion policies, TED still ranked worst, but jerk became significantly better than both baselines, indicating policy-dependent curation effects.
Trajectory inspection suggests TED fails because successful contact requires sustained high-deviation motion, whereas unsuccessful hovering remains close to a smoothed envelope.
papers.selection_reason: Audits trajectory-smoothness curation metrics for imitation-learning demonstrations and evaluates downstream behavior-cloning performance, fitting robot learning.
papers.title: Smoothness Ranks Skill, Not Success: An Audit of Published Trajectory-Smoothness Curation Metrics Under Episode-Length Controls
papers.tldr: Episode length can make trajectory-smoothness metrics appear skill-sensitive, while contact-aware TED may favor unsuccessful hovering over successful manipulation.

papers.abstract: Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation-action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. MIRROR couples these transformations through adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples, while explicit group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of the group-operation axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61% reduction in compatibility error (which measures consistency under transformation composition) relative to an adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using the learned transformations in frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks, increasing average success from 80.48% to 85.12%, with per-task gains up to 9.66 percentage points. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a real Kinova GEN3 arm. Project page: https://pomdp-mirror.github.io.
authors: Shiqi Liu, Yihang Yao, Peide Huang, Mengdi Xu, Ding Zhao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying viewpoint-dependent image transformations for symmetry-aware robot learning.
Learns observation–action transformations in POMDPs using adversarial matching of one-step transition tuples.
Enforces group-operation consistency with explicit regularization.
On four Robosuite tasks, achieves the best aggregate performance on three of four symmetry metrics and reduces compatibility error by 61% versus an adapted LaLiGAN baseline.

Using the learned transformations with frame-averaged BC raises mean success from 80.48% to 85.12%; a policy trained with heightmaps and segmentation masks transfers zero-shot to a real Kinova GEN3 arm.
papers.selection_reason: Learns symmetry transformations for robot policy learning from offline interaction data, directly relevant to imitation and manipulation learning.
papers.title: MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data
papers.tldr: MIRROR learns symmetry transformations jointly for pixel observations and actions from offline robot interaction data, improving symmetry quality and behavior-cloning success.

papers.abstract: We use a frozen frontier vision-language model, GPT-6-Astra, directly as the robot policy on RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 memory-dependent manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. The model keeps the whole episode in context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command, with no RoboMME-specific training. On the 800 test episodes it succeeds in 92.1%, above the previously reported human score of 90.5%, which was obtained with an oracle skill interface, and far ahead of the best leaderboard entry (60.8%) and of a hierarchical system that pairs the same model with a RoboMME-trained policy (79.1%). It matches or exceeds the human score on 13 of the 16 tasks. Its 63 failures concentrate in two tasks and are mostly premature completions and mistimed or unintended button presses. These results blur the usual division between long-horizon planning, memory and end-effector control, and raise the question of how much of this stack a single general-purpose model can take over in embodied systems. Project website: https://embodied-astra.github.io. Code, prompts and all episode logs: https://github.com/jackbjed/embodied-astra-robomme.
authors: Jack B. Jedlicki, Amish Sethi, Heng Yang
bullets: Evaluated on 800 RoboMME test episodes covering 16 tasks requiring temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory.
The model processes the full episode context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command directly.
Its 92.1% success exceeds the reported human score of 90.5% (with an oracle skill interface) and the best leaderboard result of 60.8%.
It matches or surpasses the human score on 13 of 16 tasks; 63 failures are concentrated in two tasks.
Most failures involve premature completion or mistimed/unintended button presses.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a frozen frontier VLM directly as a robot policy for memory-dependent manipulation, strongly fitting vision-language-action and manipulation.
papers.title: Can a Frontier VLM Serve as a Robot Policy for Memory-Dependent Manipulation?
papers.tldr: A frozen frontier vision-language model can directly control robots on memory-dependent manipulation, achieving 92.1% success without task-specific training.

papers.abstract: In this work, we explore the idea of expert intervention delays in human-supervised robotic systems for imitation learning system. Previous works in imitation learning have primarily examined the impact of suboptimal experts, where the expert policy makes mistakes, but assumed expert interventions occur immediately after errors are made. Although delayed expert intervention can be viewed as a form of noise that might improve policy robustness, our results show that learning from delayed expert interventions is overall less effective than learning from non-delayed expert interventions; delayed expert interventions are less effective at demonstrating error avoidance behaviors. To address this, we propose Learning from Delayed Intervention (LfDI), which learns a cost function based on where and when the expert intervenes, combined with limited information about the extent of intervention delays provided by the expert. This cost function is then used to infer additional supervision for states without expert data, guiding the policy to avoid states that would likely trigger interventions. We evaluate our method, Learning from Delayed Intervention (LfDI), on simulated environments and show that it outperforms other methods that do not account for intervention delays.
authors: Xiru Zhu, David Meger, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Delayed interventions are less effective than immediate interventions at teaching error-avoidance behavior.
LfDI learns a cost function from where and when experts intervene, using limited delay information.
The inferred costs provide supervision for states lacking expert demonstrations.
In simulated environments, LfDI outperforms methods that ignore intervention delays.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses imitation learning from delayed expert interventions in human-supervised robotic systems, directly fitting robot policy learning.
papers.title: Improving Policy Learning from Delayed Interventions
papers.tldr: Delayed expert interventions weaken imitation learning, so LfDI uses intervention timing and location to infer extra supervision and improve policy learning.

papers.abstract: SE(3)-equivariance provides a useful geometric inductive bias for visuomotor policies, encoding that actions covary with rigid transformations of the observation. However, existing SE(3)-equivariant visuomotor policies build this bias on a global equivariance assumption that treats the entire observation as governed by a single rigid transformation, which breaks down in real-world manipulation tasks where the task-relevant region changes across different objects. We address this by learning a phase-conditioned affordance field (PAF) over the observed point cloud, a per-point score that the SE(3)-equivariant policy uses in two complementary ways. Its score-weighted centroid serves as a learned, phase-conditioned anchor that canonicalizes the observation and the action around the active region, replacing the fixed gripper-frame reference, and the score itself is appended as a per-point feature. This introduces a local geometric inductive bias, while preserving the policy's global SE(3) equivariance. We validate on multiple MimicGen tasks under varying spatial randomization, and PAF consistently improves the success rate of the underlying policy. On multi-object real-robot tasks, PAF outperforms baselines and keeps its lead under lighting variations.
authors: Xinzhe Chen, Liqi Huang, Sihua Ren, Haowen Sun, Mingyang Li, Zeyang Liu, Xingyu Chen, Xuguang Lan
bullets: Global SE(3) equivariance can fail when the task-relevant object or region changes during manipulation.
The method learns a per-point, phase-conditioned affordance score over observed point clouds.
The score-weighted centroid anchors and canonicalizes observations and actions around the active region, while scores are also used as point features.
Experiments on MimicGen and multi-object real-robot tasks show consistently higher success, including under spatial randomization and lighting variation.
papers.selection_reason: SE(3)-equivariant visuomotor policy with phase-conditioned affordance fields for manipulation.
papers.title: Phase-Conditioned Affordance Fields for SE(3)-Equivariant Visuomotor Policies
papers.tldr: Phase-conditioned affordance fields add a learned, local geometric reference to SE(3)-equivariant visuomotor policies, improving manipulation robustness across changing active regions and visual conditions.

papers.abstract: Learning symmetries through data augmentation offers an alternative to architectural equivariance, but does not guarantee that a network respects those symmetries. Measuring learned equivariance is especially difficult for intermediate representations, whose group actions are not specified. In a finite discrete setting, we show that equivariance requires representations of original and transformed inputs to determine one another exactly, yielding a test based on normalized mutual information (NMI). For high-dimensional activations, we use centered kernel alignment (CKA) as a scalable test, with an exact guarantee for orthogonal feature transformations. Across architectures and tasks, augmentation usually increases transformation consistency, showing that learned equivariance can be probed directly from representations without recovering the hidden transformation rules that relate them.
authors: Claire Schlesinger, Wolfgang Gatterbauer, Robin Walters
bullets: Data augmentation can encourage, but does not guarantee, equivariant behavior.
For finite discrete representations, equivariance requires original and transformed representations to determine each other exactly.
Normalized mutual information (NMI) provides a test for this exact recoverability.
Centered kernel alignment (CKA) offers a scalable test for high-dimensional activations, with guarantees for orthogonal feature transformations.
Across architectures and tasks, augmentation generally increases transformation consistency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a general method to measure learned equivariance in representations, transferable to evaluating equivariant visuomotor and robot policies.
papers.title: Measuring Learned Equivariance: An Information Theoretic Approach
papers.tldr: The paper introduces information-theoretic tests for measuring whether learned representations respect symmetries without explicitly recovering their hidden transformation rules.

papers.abstract: Search-based policy learning, such as Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), offers the flexibility to trade runtime computation for data efficiency and adaptation to novel environments. For robot learning, however, applying search requires discretizing the continuous action space and associated dynamics, typically through action quantization. While reconstruction-based quantization is sufficient for representing the continuous action space alone, policy learning additionally requires the quantized actions to preserve their effects on future states and values. We show that such requirement is not necessarily captured by action reconstruction error. Instead, we prove that the error in the value function resulting from action quantization is tightly bounded by the reconstruction error of state reachability under the quantized actions. Based on these results, we propose value-preserving action quantization (VAQ), which quantizes actions by preserving state reachability. We further combine VAQ with MCTS (VAQ-MCTS) as a value-preserving, search-based policy learning framework for behavioral cloning. Using a wide range of object pushing tasks as a controlled benchmark, we evaluate VAQ-MCTS against state-of-the-art behavioral cloning methods. VAQ-MCTS matches or exceeds their performance under standard settings, while substantially improving data efficiency and robustness to heterogeneous demonstrations, while enabling zero-shot adaptation to novel environments. Hardware experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of VAQ-MCTS, completing all 30 real-world object pushing trials with only 10 minutes of demonstration data.
authors: Max Muchen Sun, Jueun Kwon, Benjamin Riviere, Todd Murphey
bullets: Action reconstruction error alone may not preserve the values relevant to policy learning.
Theoretical analysis bounds value-function error by state-reachability reconstruction error under quantized actions.
VAQ quantizes actions to preserve state reachability and is integrated with MCTS in VAQ-MCTS.
On object-pushing benchmarks, VAQ-MCTS matches or exceeds behavioral cloning baselines while improving data efficiency, robustness to heterogeneous demonstrations, and zero-shot adaptation.
Hardware trials completed all 30 real-world object-pushing tasks using 10 minutes of demonstration data.
papers.selection_reason: Value-preserving action quantization for search-based robot policy learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Value-Preserving Action Quantization
papers.tldr: Value-Preserving Action Quantization discretizes robot actions by preserving their effects on future states, enabling more data-efficient and adaptable search-based policy learning.

papers.abstract: What information does a reinforcement learning policy omit? At each state, a standard policy stores one probability per action. It has no place to record how actions relate to each other, such as which pairs go together and which conflict. We ask when this missing structure matters, and we give exact answers. We store the policy at each state as a density matrix, a positive semidefinite, unit-trace matrix borrowed from quantum information theory. We use it here as a purely classical data structure, computed on ordinary classical hardware. The diagonal holds the usual action probabilities. The off-diagonal entries, called coherences, are new parameters. This gives density-matrix reinforcement learning (DMRL). Coherences change outcomes in two settings. First, suppose a policy is regularized toward a coherent reference policy using matrix relative entropy. The optimum then has coherences that no diagonal reference policy produces, and its action probabilities can depend on the reference policy's coherences. This is relevant to fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) with a Kullback--Leibler penalty. Second, suppose the agent chooses a unit-vector action and the reward is a quadratic function of that vector. This could arise when an LLM judge scores a weighted consolidation of reasoning paths, or when coupled robotic sensors each respond to a mix of actions. Then some coherent policies earn strictly more expected reward than every classical policy with the same action probabilities, and we give the margin in closed form. In a two-action example, both policies assign probability $0.5$ to each action, yet the classical one earns expected reward $0$ while the coherent one earns $1$, the maximum. Outside these two settings, DMRL matches or transfers the classical results. This is a theory paper. All results are proved, and we report no empirical evaluation.
bullets: Standard policies record action probabilities but not relationships such as action compatibility or conflict.
DMRL represents each state policy as a positive semidefinite, unit-trace density matrix; its diagonal gives probabilities and off-diagonal terms encode coherences.
With matrix-relative-entropy regularization, coherent reference policies can induce optimal coherences and alter action probabilities, including in LLM fine-tuning with a KL penalty.
For unit-vector actions with quadratic rewards, coherent policies can outperform every classical policy sharing the same action probabilities; a two-action example reaches reward 1 versus 0.
The paper is theoretical: it proves the results and reports no empirical evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Novel RL policy representation with coherent action structure; transferable to robot learning and LLM fine-tuning settings.
papers.title: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning augments action probabilities with coherence terms, enabling provable benefits in regularized policies and quadratic-reward settings while recovering classical RL otherwise.

papers.abstract: Cutting a piece of food looks effortless in human hands. For a robot, however, every cut is a high-contact interaction with a deformable, elasto-plastic object whose behavior changes with pose, contact mode, and cutting stage. Collecting real-world data is expensive and wasteful: each trial typically contaminates or damages the food, so obtaining scalable real world data for dexterous cutting is expensive and difficult. Simulation is an appealing alternative, but a large sim-to-real gap exists in both physics and perception. This gap is especially severe for topology-changing interactions like cutting, where small errors in contact, friction, or material and elasticity responses quickly compound. We propose \textsc{DexNinja}, a real2sim2real framework that turns a handful of real demonstrations into a dense and realistic training distribution. \textsc{DexNinja} (i) reconstructs object instances from real captures, (ii) randomizes physically meaningful parameters under category-level constraints, and (iii) produces augmented dexterous manipulation episodes using a custom differentiable simulator that couples robot dynamics, tactile contact, and deformable cutting. We evaluate \textsc{DexNinja} on a dexterous food-slicing task and show that (1) with tens of real demonstrations and hundreds of augmented simulator data, the success rate could reach more than 60\%. (2) the augmented data consistently improves success rates when only using real data with more than 20\% via sim-to-real, and (3) the resulting policies generalize to out-of-distribution objects with varying shapes and sizes.
authors: Haozhe Lou, Runyi Yang, Wanqi Zhong, Caiyun Liu, Yicheng Liu, Wenhao Liu, Wenlong Ma, Jiawei Xia, Kanzhi Wu, Danda Pani Paudel, Luc Van Gool, Hang Zhao, Yiming Li
bullets: Dexterous cutting is difficult because it involves high-contact interactions with deformable objects and changing contact dynamics.

The framework reconstructs objects from real captures, randomizes physically meaningful parameters, and generates episodes in a differentiable simulator coupling robot, tactile, and deformable-cutting dynamics.
Using tens of real demonstrations plus hundreds of simulated episodes, the evaluated policy achieved over 60% success on food slicing.
Simulation augmentation improved success by more than 20% compared with using real data alone.
Policies generalized to unseen objects with different shapes and sizes.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a real2sim2real data engine for dexterous cutting, handling deformable objects and sim-to-real transfer for robotic manipulation.
papers.title: DexNinja: Learning Robust Dexterous Cutting Policy with a Real-to-Sim-to-Real Data Engine
papers.tldr: DexNinja uses a real-to-sim-to-real pipeline to train robust dexterous food-cutting policies from limited demonstrations and augmented simulation data.

papers.abstract: Achieving complex, long-horizon robot behavior remains challenging because successful execution depends on skills grounded in a robot's physical affordances. Existing training-task distributions are often handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs), relying on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility. This mismatch can produce curricula that are too difficult, redundant, or blind to non-obvious but learnable behaviors. We propose Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (FOSA), a framework for discovering embodiment-specific capabilities by learning a grounded task generator. FOSA parameterizes an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons. Each skeleton is compiled into a simulation environment, where low-level policy-learning performance provides the reward signal for the abstract policy. Across heterogeneous robot platforms, FOSA discovers diverse and executable tasks near the robot's empirical capability frontier. After distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy, FOSA improves performance on unseen complex and long-horizon tasks. The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/fosa.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between semantically plausible task curricula and tasks that are feasible for a robot’s physical embodiment.
Builds symbolic task skeletons with a Generative Flow Network and compiles them into simulation environments.
Uses low-level policy-learning performance as the reward for discovering tasks near each robot’s empirical capability frontier.
Works across heterogeneous robot platforms and finds diverse, executable behaviors.
Distilling the discovered policies into one language-conditioned policy improves performance on unseen complex, long-horizon tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Generative flow network for embodiment-specific task discovery and robot skill learning.
papers.title: Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions for Embodiment Capability Discovery
papers.tldr: FOSA discovers robot-specific, executable training tasks by using low-level learning performance to guide a Generative Flow Network over symbolic task structures.

papers.abstract: Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot learning. Dexterous manipulation, however, requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces. Operators can specify motion, but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of human manipulation without feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce Force-Modulated Dexterity (FOMO-Dex), a unified compliance formulation for contact-rich manipulation. FOMO-Dex expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure. It applies force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly, FOMO-Dex reduces excessive contact forces compared with stiff control. A user study shows that operators collect more successful demonstration data per hour after brief practice. For policy learning, imitating the corrected actions improves card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands. Policies trained on FOMO-Dex demonstrations also achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving than those trained on demonstrations collected with the stiff controller. Videos are shown on https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .
authors: Ying Yuan, David Held, Jitendra Malik, Haozhi Qi
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reproducing subtle force adjustments during teleoperated dexterous manipulation.
Represents actions using task geometry and contact structure, then applies force-driven corrections only along selected directions.
Reduces excessive contact forces across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly compared with stiff control.
Helps operators collect more successful demonstrations per hour after brief practice.
Learning from corrected demonstrations improves card-picking success and rotational performance in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving.
papers.selection_reason: Force-modulated teleoperation for contact-rich dexterous manipulation and improved policy learning.
papers.title: Force-Modulated Dexterity: Unified Compliance for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.tldr: FOMO-Dex enables dexterous teleoperation by automatically adjusting motion in response to contact forces, improving demonstrations and contact-rich manipulation.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the opacity and lack of direct correction in implicit robot world models.
Uses a Sense–Plan–Act architecture where perception builds an executable scene twin and planning searches for actions in simulation.
Revises object states and physical parameters after each action chunk, accepting updates only when replayed measurements remain within residual tolerances.
Frames information-seeking actions as dual control, balancing task progress with exposing and correcting model errors.
Demonstrates real-to-sim-to-real operation on dual-arm towel and toaster tasks, including local corrections that avoid full scene reconstruction.
papers.selection_reason: Explicit world-language-action model with digital-twin self-improvement for robot manipulation and planning.
papers.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
papers.tldr: D-World enables robots to improve an explicit, inspectable digital twin through measurement-grounded planning and execution, without updating the underlying LLM.

papers.abstract: Generative policies such as diffusion models provide expressive data-driven priors for robot behavior, yet the situations a robot faces at execution time rarely match its training data and impose constraints and objectives the policy never learned. Existing inference-time guidance methods either rely on gradients that can push samples away from the learned prior, or on sampling procedures that can be inefficient, collapse modes, or average them into out-of-distribution predictions. We introduce MOSAIC, a mode- and support-aware framework for gradient-free inference-time control of robotic diffusion models. MOSAIC treats the initial noise and all stochastic reverse-step perturbations as a joint input to the pretrained denoising process and adapts a distribution over this input using importance weights computed from fully denoised outputs. Physical feasibility and consistency with the learned support are balanced using adaptive penalties, while mode-wise importance-weighted updates preserve modes and avoid destructive averaging. The same formulation can jointly steer multiple independently trained diffusion models through shared coupling costs, enabling coordinated behavior without requiring a joint model. We evaluate MOSAIC on navigation, dexterous grasping, motion planning with unseen geometry, and collaborative box manipulation with independently trained robot priors. Across these settings, MOSAIC adapts and composes frozen diffusion priors under new deployment constraints without retraining.
authors: Sabrina Bodmer, Rahel Rickenbach, Ren\'e Zurbr\"ugg, Melanie N. Zeilinger, Colin Jones
bullets: Addresses deployment constraints and objectives not represented during diffusion-policy training.
Adapts the joint distribution of initial noise and reverse-process perturbations using importance weights on fully denoised outputs.
Balances physical feasibility with support consistency through adaptive penalties and preserves modes with mode-wise updates.
Can coordinate independently trained diffusion models using shared coupling costs, without a joint model or retraining.
Evaluated across navigation, dexterous grasping, unseen-geometry planning, and collaborative manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Gradient-free inference-time control of robot diffusion models with mode preservation, directly advancing robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: MOSAIC: Mode- and Support-Aware Inference-Time Control of Robot Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: MOSAIC enables gradient-free, inference-time adaptation and coordination of frozen robot diffusion policies while preserving feasible, in-distribution behavior and multiple modes.

papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn effective policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction. Although generative models such as diffusion and flow matching enhance policy expressiveness, they typically start from uninformative Gaussian noise and generate actions through multi-step iteration, leading to high computational costs and failing to effectively leverage suboptimal trajectories in datasets. We propose MeanFlow2Better (MF2B), which reformulates offline RL as generative decision chunk optimization from current performance status to better performance status in a high-level latent decision space. MF2B maps trajectory chunks to high-level latent decision representations through an encoder, placing generation starting points within a structured decision space sculpted by behavioral data. The model learns a shared conditional mean velocity field in this space, constructing two flow mappings: from Gaussian-Induced Decision Sources toward positive behavioral decision regions, and from suboptimal decisions toward high-value decision regions. Both flow mappings complete decision refinement through one-step ODE integration over the unit time interval $\Delta t=1$, requiring neither multi-step iterative sampling nor backpropagation through time. Furthermore, we propose hierarchical chunk-level advantage to guide the flow direction toward high-return regions, where the high-level decisions cover multiple low-level actions, leading to sequence length compression from $T$ to $K \approx T/H$ and significantly lower computational overhead. On the D4RL Gym-MuJoCo benchmark, MF2B achieves an average score of 90.91, matching or surpassing strong baselines.
authors: Shenghua Lu, Zixuan Yang, Rongxu Zhao, Bohao Qu, Jifeng Hu, Hechang Chen
bullets: Targets the cost and weak use of suboptimal trajectories in multi-step generative offline RL.
Encodes trajectory chunks into a structured high-level latent decision space shaped by behavioral data.
Learns shared flow mappings from Gaussian-induced or suboptimal decisions toward positive and high-value decision regions.
Uses hierarchical chunk-level advantages to guide refinement while compressing sequences from T to approximately T/H.
Achieves an average score of 90.91 on D4RL Gym-MuJoCo, matching or surpassing strong baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Offline RL policy learning with latent flow generation for robotic control benchmarks; relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: From Suboptimal to Optimal: One-Step Latent Flow Policies for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: MF2B learns one-step latent flow policies that refine suboptimal behavioral chunks into higher-value decisions for efficient offline RL.

papers.abstract: Physical AI is commonly formulated around an explicitly specified task: given a goal or instruction, a system perceives, reasons, and acts. In many real-world settings, however, important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before a person explicitly formulates them. We study this complementary problem as Proactive Physical AI, where an AI system continuously observes the physical world, identifies situations that warrant intervention, and initiates appropriate actions at the right time. We develop ProAgent, an end-to-end system built around two components: a Jev-style proactive timing model (dubbed StreamingJev) that determines whether and when intervention is needed, and a Response Model that generates responses for people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution. To support learning at scale, we develop an automated data pipeline that converts videos into supervision for proactive timing. Experiments demonstrate strong proactive performance under both explicit objectives and standing roles, combining more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate ProAgent's ability to identify emerging needs and translate them into appropriate physical actions.
authors: Zhenhua Yang, Jiafeng Liang, Xingyu Zhou, Yi Jiang, Xiayu Cao, Zui Chen, Luqi Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yufei Xiang, Chang Li, Rongchuan Mu, Bowen Chi, Zihe Tong, Mingyu Li, Huijie Ma, Yiqiao Yang, Baoqi Ren, Zhiming Ma, Zhihao Zhu, Jiahao Ji, Zhuoyao Wang, Qianyu Wang, Xiangyu Liu, Wang Zixiang, Shunliang Zhang, Ming Liu, Xiaocheng Feng, Duyu Tang, Bing Qin
bullets: Addresses proactive intervention in changing physical environments, where tasks arise before users specify them.
Combines StreamingJev for deciding whether and when to intervene with a Response Model for generating human or device actions.
Uses an automated video-to-supervision pipeline to support scalable learning of proactive timing.
Experiments show more accurate timing and fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline across explicit objectives and standing roles.
Real-robot evaluations demonstrate detection of emerging needs followed by appropriate physical actions.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an embodied system that continuously observes the physical world, identifies intervention needs, and executes physical actions; includes real-robot evaluation.
papers.title: Proactive Physical AI through Continuous Observation and Timely Intervention
papers.tldr: ProAgent enables Physical AI to continuously detect emerging needs and intervene at the appropriate time without waiting for explicit instructions.

papers.abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.
authors: Wenjing Bian, Ranran Huang, Andreas Geiger
bullets: Predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters from RGB, aligned segmentation, and depth, with optional additional images or video.
Represents joint geometry in gravity-aligned, view-relative coordinates without requiring category-specific canonical orientations.
Adapts a pretrained vision–language model for inference in seconds, without observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation.
Outperforms evaluated baselines and transfers to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos.
Predicted joints support simulated robot manipulation trajectory generation; training is task-specific and exclusively synthetic.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts part articulation and connectivity from images/depth and demonstrates utility for generating robot motion trajectories; view-grounded spatial representation is transferable to embodied manipulation and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: ViewStruct: View-Grounded Articulation and Connectivity Inference
papers.tldr: ViewStruct infers object part connectivity and articulation from visual inputs using a view-grounded representation that transfers beyond synthetic training categories and assets.

papers.abstract: Video-to-robot pipelines for quadrupedal imitation insert a learned lifting stage, either a monocular depth model or a per-clip 3D reconstruction, to recover the one axis a side-view camera cannot see. We present CopyQuad, which omits that stage and pins the missing axis to the robot's own stance width instead. The setting is side-view footage of sagittally dominated motion, where limb motion is almost entirely in the image plane.
