Experiments on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and real robots report speedups up to 24.84×, with success rates close to multi-step baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Speeds up World Action Models for robotic action generation via one-step denoising; relevant to robot learning and inference efficiency.
papers.title: 1Step-WAM: Your World Action Model but Faster using 1-Step Action Generation
papers.tldr: 1Step-WAM converts multi-step WAM action denoising into a single calibrated forward pass, substantially accelerating inference while largely preserving task success.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs), often built upon pretrained video-generation world models, have emerged as a promising framework for general-purpose and open-ended robot control. However, their real-world deployment often suffers from discontinuous and jerky execution. Existing methods typically address this issue by either improving inference efficiency or enhancing action continuity across prediction chunks, without jointly addressing both challenges. To bridge this gap, we propose StreamingWAM, a streaming-diffusion framework for WAM-based robot control. StreamingWAM combines a noise ladder for chunk-wise action prediction, a prefix rollout module for cross-chunk continuity, and dense video-history memory for temporally consistent conditioning. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that StreamingWAM improves action continuity across static and dynamic settings, achieving competitive performance while reducing steady-state replanning latency to 72.9 ms in simulation and 57.3 ms on the real robot. The method also produces smoother action transitions, while the streaming staircase reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
authors: Shaojie Ren, Jingwen Sun, Zezhi Liu, Hongjin Chen, Xin Jin, Wei Zou, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses jerky, discontinuous execution in World Action Model-based robot control.
Uses chunk-wise staircase flow matching with a noise ladder for streaming action prediction.
Combines prefix rollouts and dense video-history memory for cross-chunk temporal consistency.
Evaluated in simulation and real-world tasks, with steady-state replanning latency of 72.9 ms and 57.3 ms, respectively.
Produces smoother transitions and reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming world action model for robot control.
papers.title: StreamingWAM: Streaming World Action Modeling via Chunk-Wise Staircase Flow Matching
papers.tldr: StreamingWAM enables smoother, lower-latency robot control by jointly improving streaming inference and continuity between action chunks.

papers.abstract: Open-world mobile manipulation requires a robot to find an object, approach it, and move it to a target receptacle from a language instruction. Training vision-language model (VLM) agents for these tasks requires demonstrations of both action selection and active vision. Existing pipelines often convert planned trajectories into high-level action labels, but shortest-path progress provides limited supervision for deciding where to look. We introduce Agent-Interface Data Alignment (AIDA), a data collection pipeline in which a teacher directly selects and executes actions through the deployed agent's skill interface. For mobile manipulation, we design teachers that maintain target visibility, recover lost targets, and approach for picking or placing. We add template-based spatial reasoning supervision and use a shared harness to organize observations, history, and outputs during training and inference. The resulting agent, AIDA-OWMM, achieves 71.76% full-task success on 170 held-out OWMM episodes. Teacher sensitivity analysis shows that active-vision demonstrations improve student success. The simulation-trained agent achieves 38% end-to-end success on a real mobile robot without additional training. Applying AIDA to a navigation subset of EmbodiedBench further demonstrates the pipeline's utility for navigation tasks.
authors: Ronghe Qiu, Teli Ma, Jiaming Zhou, Zeying Gong, Yiting He, Qiang Huang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Targets open-world tasks requiring object search, approach, pickup, and placement from language instructions.
Collects teacher demonstrations through the agent’s actual skill interface, including maintaining and recovering target visibility.
Adds template-based spatial-reasoning supervision and a shared harness for organizing observations, history, and outputs.
AIDA-OWMM reaches 71.76% full-task success on 170 held-out simulation episodes; active-vision demonstrations improve performance.
The simulation-trained agent achieves 38% end-to-end success on a real mobile robot without additional training.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based open-world mobile manipulation with aligned supervision.
papers.title: Look Before You Move: Agent-Interface-Aligned Supervision for Open-World Mobile Manipulation
papers.tldr: AIDA trains mobile-manipulation VLM agents with demonstrations aligned to their deployed action and active-vision interfaces, achieving strong simulated and real-robot task completion.

papers.abstract: Visual self-modelling lets robots learn body models from observations, but such models usually encode kinematics implicitly rather than exposing metric joint parameters for computation and control. Moreover, a good fit to images does not by itself establish accurate kinematics. Here we present an explicit analytic robot self-model that requires neither deformation networks nor URDF/CAD templates. Multi-view images and joint readings establish Gaussian appearance and provide motion evidence for rigid link assignments, whereas sparse end-effector poses independently identify metric screw axes. The resulting closed-form forward kinematics and analytic Jacobian can be evaluated beyond the fitting ranges. We validate the model on a simulated seven-axis arm, a simulated twelve-joint quadruped and a real six-axis arm. In simulation, it achieves millimetre-level reaching and pick-and-place, as well as closed-loop quadruped walking. On the real arm, it renders held-out configurations, predicts end-effector positions with a median error of 6.4 mm, compared with 11.7 mm for a calibrated nominal model, and supports reaching with external marker feedback. A controlled comparison shows that image fit alone is not enough: two Panda models differing only in their joint axes are 0.54 dB apart in PSNR, yet their end-effector prediction errors differ 13.7-fold.
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible self-models and kinematic models with computable metric joint parameters.
Combines multi-view appearance and joint-motion evidence with sparse end-effector poses to identify rigid links and screw axes.
Produces closed-form forward kinematics and an analytic Jacobian that extrapolate beyond the fitting ranges.
Validated on simulated seven-axis and quadruped robots plus a real six-axis arm, supporting reaching, pick-and-place, and walking.
Shows that image fit alone is insufficient: similar PSNR can hide substantially different end-effector prediction accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Learned analytic robot self-model for control.
papers.title: Analytic Robot Self-Model: Learning Screw-Axis Kinematics for Rendering and Model-Based Control
papers.tldr: An explicit analytic robot self-model learns metric screw-axis kinematics from images, joint readings, and sparse poses, enabling accurate rendering and model-based control without CAD or URDF templates.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly generate robot actions token by token through Large Language Model (LLM) decoders, causing inference latency to grow with action sequence length and limiting closed-loop control frequency. We present Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces autoregressive decoders with a lightweight latent control loop. A shared vision encoder and a frozen text encoder embed observations, goal images, and instructions; a neuro-symbolic selector chooses a discrete skill; a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor forecasts the next latent state; and a flow-matching solver generates an entire action chunk in a few integration steps, so that sequential network evaluations per decision step do not depend on the action horizon. We analyze inference complexity, regularization against representation collapse, and conditions under which latent sub-goal thresholding limits error accumulation across task phases. As an initial proof of concept, we evaluated VPA on the LIBERO-10 suite. The trainable model has under 20M parameters (checkpoint under 75 MB, excluding a frozen 63.4M-parameter CLIP text encoder); a decision step of a single-camera reference configuration takes 10-14 ms on an Apple M4; and trained only on LIBERO-10 demonstrations in under three hours on a single GPU, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes. These preliminary results from a single training run suggest the approach is workable. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/ylee-sling/Vision-Predictor-Action and https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/vpa-libero10, and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960920.
bullets: Addresses inference latency that grows with action-sequence length in autoregressive VLA models.
Uses shared vision and frozen text encoders, discrete skill selection, a JEPA latent-state predictor, and flow matching for action-chunk generation.
Analyzes representation-collapse regularization and latent sub-goal thresholding to limit error accumulation across task phases.
On LIBERO-10, a two-camera policy achieved 40.0% success over 200 episodes in a preliminary single-run evaluation.
The model has under 20M trainable parameters; a single-camera decision step took 10–14 ms on an Apple M4.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model replacing autoregressive action decoding with latent predictor and flow-matching action chunks; directly fits embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: Vision-Predictor-Action: Towards Efficient Embodied AI via Neuro-Symbolic JEPA Predictors
papers.tldr: VPA replaces slow autoregressive VLA action decoding with a lightweight neuro-symbolic latent predictor that generates full action chunks efficiently for closed-loop robot control.

papers.abstract: Quadruped robots deployed for inspection and field missions must cross heterogeneous terrain, from stairs, slopes, and gaps to high platforms, stepping stones, and balance beams, where safe support is sparse or see-through. Existing methods interpose a terrain map or a depth image between sensing and control. Maps are costly to maintain, corrupted by odometry drift and outliers, and misled by see-through gratings, while depth cameras degrade with lighting and surface material. In this paper, we present PointWalker, a mapless framework whose single reinforcement learning policy directly consumes raw point clouds from four light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors. Voxelized points are encoded by linear self-attention and fused with proprioception through cross-attention, so terrain geometry reaches the policy without maps or foothold estimation. One proximal policy optimization (PPO) run, with terrain-aware rewards and dual-channel simulation of see-through gratings, yields one policy for all seven terrain classes with a 90.1% mean success rate in simulation. Deployed zero-shot on a Deep Robotics X30 at 50 Hz onboard, it crosses 0.8-m gaps, climbs 0.8-m platforms and 45{\deg} steel-grating stairs, carries a 50-kg payload, and completes a 2.5-km mountain route.
authors: Sicen Li, Zhen Chu, Chao Li, Jun Zheng, Qiuguo Zhu, Jun Wu
bullets: Addresses map maintenance, odometry errors, see-through surfaces, and depth-camera limitations in field locomotion.
Uses one reinforcement-learning policy that combines voxelized LiDAR features via self-attention with proprioception via cross-attention.
Trains with PPO, terrain-aware rewards, and dual-channel simulation of see-through gratings across seven terrain classes.
Achieves a 90.1% mean simulation success rate and transfers zero-shot to a quadruped at 50 Hz.
Demonstrates traversal of gaps, high platforms, steel-grating stairs, mountain terrain, and a 50-kg payload.
papers.selection_reason: RL policy for mapless quadruped locomotion from LiDAR.
papers.title: PointWalker: Mapless Quadruped Locomotion Directly From Raw LiDAR Point Clouds
papers.tldr: PointWalker enables a quadruped to traverse diverse and challenging terrain directly from raw LiDAR point clouds, without maps or foothold estimation.

papers.abstract: Active debris removal requires a servicer spacecraft to approach a non-cooperative tumbling object, capture it, and arrest its rotation. This sequence is conventionally divided among phase-specific controllers, each depending on knowledge of the target's inertia, a dedicated grappling fixture, or a hand-designed switch at the contact-rich seam where such pipelines are most fragile. We show that a single constrained reinforcement learning policy can execute the entire mission, driving a dual-arm free-flying servicer from free-space closing through friction-based fixture-free capture to full detumbling of a target whose mass and inertia are unknown and whose state is observed only through noisy estimates. The enabling mechanism is a smooth proximity gate applied at three loci of a constrained Markov decision process. In the reward it induces the phase structure rather than imposing it; in the action space it forecloses a degenerate grab-and-pull exploit as a hard guarantee; and in the constraint set it resolves a normalization failure of constraint-based learning, in which a constraint spanning phases that load it unequally is rendered nearly inert in the phase where precision matters most. Both the failure mode and the remedy apply to any multi-phase problem of this kind. Over 1000 randomized trials the policy succeeds in 99.5% while holding its contact-force, actuator, base-reaction and collision limits throughout, transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries and centre-of-mass offsets, and extrapolates across a tenfold range of target mass.
authors: \'Alvaro Belmonte-Baeza, Celia Redondo-Verd\'u, Jos\'e L. Ram\'on, Miguel Cazorla, Leonard Felicetti, Jorge Pomares
bullets: Addresses fragile handoffs between separate approach, capture, and detumbling controllers for non-cooperative targets.
Uses a smooth proximity gate in the reward, action space, and constraints to structure phases, prevent grab-and-pull exploits, and balance constraint enforcement.
Controls a dual-arm free-flying servicer using noisy state estimates despite unknown target mass and inertia.
Achieves 99.5% success over 1000 randomized trials while respecting contact-force, actuator, base-reaction, and collision limits.
Transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries and center-of-mass offsets and across a tenfold target-mass range.
papers.selection_reason: Constrained RL for multi-phase robotic capture and detumbling.
papers.title: Phase-Gated Constrained Reinforcement Learning for End-to-End Capture and Detumbling of Non-Cooperative Targets
papers.tldr: A single phase-gated constrained reinforcement-learning policy robustly performs end-to-end capture and detumbling of unknown, tumbling targets without phase-specific controllers or dedicated fixtures.

papers.abstract: Robotic systems for lunar surface operations must act autonomously and preserve their own integrity in an environment where failures are unrecoverable and continuous supervision is impossible. This paper presents a Constrained Reinforcement Learning framework for quadrupedal mobile manipulators that learns a single whole-body policy for tracking a 6D end-effector pose specified in task space, with operational limits enforced during learning through a constrained learning mechanism. We introduce a reward formulation in which the transition between locomotion and manipulation emerges from the reward geometry rather than from an explicit gating mechanism, a stability term derived from the Gravito-Inertial Inclination Margin and motivated by the reduced-gravity dynamics of the lunar surface, and a design rule for reward regularization that follows from the multiplicative structure of the termination-based objective. The framework is evaluated in a lunar-analog simulation spanning three terrain morphologies at five difficulty levels under lunar gravity, with regolith contact properties calibrated to the JSC-1a simulant and varied from loose to dense. The learned policy attains mean position and orientation errors of 3.22 cm and 6.83 deg. under nominal conditions, retains this precision across regolith densities and over the operationally representative range of terrain difficulty, and reduces soft-constraint violation time by up to an order of magnitude relative to an unconstrained baseline while incurring no hard-constraint violations.
authors: Alvaro Belmonte-Baeza, Miguel Cazorla, Gabriel J. Garc\'ia, Carlos J. P\'erez-Del-Pulgar, Jorge Pomares
bullets: Targets autonomous 6D end-effector pose tracking while enforcing operational safety limits during learning.
Uses a single whole-body policy, with locomotion–manipulation transitions emerging from reward design rather than explicit gating.
Introduces lunar-specific stability shaping based on the Gravito-Inertial Inclination Margin and a reward-regularization rule for termination-based objectives.
In lunar-analog simulation across terrain types, difficulty levels, and regolith densities, it achieves 3.22 cm position and 6.83° orientation error under nominal conditions.
Reduces soft-constraint violation time by up to an order of magnitude versus an unconstrained baseline, with no hard-constraint violations.
papers.selection_reason: Constrained RL for whole-body loco-manipulation.
papers.title: Learning Safety-Constrained Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation for Lunar Surface Operations
papers.tldr: A constrained reinforcement-learning framework learns safe, unified locomotion and manipulation for quadrupedal robots operating on varied lunar terrain.

papers.abstract: Context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning (COMRL) has advanced almost entirely through better task representations, which separate task identity from artifacts of the behavior policy so that the latent reflects the task alone. The implicit expectation has been that a clean representation will transfer to out-of-support (parameter-extrapolation) tasks. On such a task, however, the encoder produces a latent outside the training support, where the policy has never been trained. We address this gap with Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization (PLATO), which exposes the policy to off-support latents during training. PLATO assumes a mild manifold hypothesis: task latents lie on a low-dimensional manifold, and out-of-support tasks lie farther from the training centroid. It exploits this geometry by perturbing inferred latents outward from the centroid to synthesize counterfactual tasks. A learned decoder ensemble then rolls out short trajectories at each perturbed latent, and the policy is updated on the imagined transitions under a pessimism weight that down-weights steps on which the ensemble disagrees. We prove that the perturbation leaves the training support by a controllable margin and that the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by the same perturbation reach, and we give explicit conditions, verified empirically, under which the epistemic disagreement at the perturbed latent stays bounded away from zero. On eight MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, PLATO consistently improves out-of-support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive on in-distribution tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/deephoony/plato.
authors: Chang-Hoon Jeong, Kisung Shin, Hanwool Sul, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Problem: Clean task representations may encode out-of-support latents where the policy has not been trained, limiting extrapolation to unseen tasks.
Method: Perturb inferred task latents outward from the training centroid to create counterfactual tasks under a low-dimensional manifold assumption.
A learned decoder ensemble generates short imagined trajectories, while ensemble disagreement down-weights uncertain policy updates.
Theory: The perturbation exits the training support by a controllable margin, and the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by this reach.
Results: Across eight MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, PLATO improves out-of-support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive in-distribution.
papers.selection_reason: Offline meta-reinforcement learning with pessimistic latent task-aware optimization for robust control.
papers.title: Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization for Robust Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: PLATO improves robust offline meta-reinforcement learning on unseen task parameters by training policies on pessimistically weighted, synthesized off-support task latents.

papers.abstract: In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long-horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long-horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long-horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post-training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot-reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks. Code: https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/RoboCombine.
authors: Xupeng Zhang, Yantai Yang, Chang Guo, Zhaokai Yin, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Full-instruction training appears to memorize seen sequence templates: 40.0% success on covered combinations versus 7.7% on recombinations.
HSE diagnoses failures across planning, triggering, and policy execution through a shared modular interface.
RoboCombine evaluates skill recombination without combined-skill training trajectories using ordered-success and transition-conversion metrics.
Failures cluster at subtask boundaries, revealing a start state gap between canonical starts and handoff states.
PRTI broadens atomic-task initialization and reaches 18.16% ordered success under oracle-timed HSE, outperforming the reported perturbation and reset baselines.
papers.selection_reason: VLA skill recombination and manipulation generalization.
papers.title: Exploring the Limits of Combinatorial Generalization in Embodied Manipulation
papers.tldr: Atomic skill competence does not guarantee long-horizon recombination; robust execution requires skills that handle noncanonical handoff states.

papers.abstract: VLMs provide promising solutions to embodied reward design. Most current methods that train VLMs as reward regressors not only require extensive annotations but are also primarily designed for finetuning pretrained policies, and perform less well in the more challenging from-scratch RL setting. This issue stems from a fundamental mismatch: regressing precise rewards is misaligned with what VLMs naturally excel at. We posit that it is more aligned with VLMs' inherent multi-modal VQA capabilities for the models to function as success detectors, and propose VLM success reward via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating (VLMeg) to well harness VLM for embodied reward design. As the core of VLMeg, the proposed exploration-augmented key-observation gating first determines whether the current RL episode is judgment-worthy based on its similarity to a generated success trajectory. Then, the key observation with the lowest confusion from the judgment-worthy episode will be selected for VLM evaluation as episodic reward. This gating mechanism not only avoids redundant calls but also enables higher detection accuracy of VLM. Considering the sparsity of judgment-worthy episodes, the advanced exploration incentives based on the generated trajectory are introduced, enabling more efficient exploration toward judgment-worthy trajectories for more VLM reward triggers and thus gaining higher RL efficiency. Extensive experiments in MetaWorld demonstrate VLMeg achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL, outperforming advanced VLM-based baselines on 12 challenging reward-free tasks. Furthermore, VLMeg also enables effective RL without any ground-truth reward in 3 challenging real-world experiments. Code will be open after acceptance at https://github.com/Raina915/VLMeg.
authors: Xin Liu, Yutong Jiang, Jian Su, Ziheng Wang, Chuang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the annotation burden and poor from-scratch performance of VLM reward regressors.
Uses exploration-augmented key-observation gating to identify judgment-worthy episodes and select a low-confusion observation for VLM evaluation.
Adds trajectory-based exploration incentives to reach more VLM reward-triggering episodes efficiently.
Achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL on 12 challenging MetaWorld reward-free tasks and works in 3 real-world experiments without ground-truth rewards.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-based reward design for from-scratch embodied reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Harnessing VLM in Embodied RL: From Reward Regressor to Success Detector via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating
papers.tldr: VLMeg improves from-scratch embodied RL by using VLMs as selective success detectors rather than precise reward regressors.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).
authors: Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma, Chuhao Zhou, Jingliang Li, Stefano V. Albrecht, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Uses a trained message channel and per-arm diffusion action heads on frozen VLA backbones with decentralised execution.
Communication is valuable mainly under partial observability, such as an occluded handover where only one agent sees the box marker.
With shared overhead-camera views, disabling messages has little effect on two- and three-arm handover performance.
On a wrist-only variant, messages improve success from 64.3% to 74.8%; on the occluded tray task, success is 76.0% with messages versus 1.3% when removed during training.
CoLA generalises across VLA backbones and matches a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline while using fewer trainable parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces coordination among multiple Vision-Language-Action models via learned adapters, directly fitting VLA and robot learning topics.
papers.title: CoLA: Multi-VLA Coordination via Learned Adapters
papers.tldr: CoLA adds lightweight learned communication to frozen VLA agents, enabling coordination when crucial information is privately observed while remaining unnecessary under shared visibility.

papers.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative and within-chunk future action flexibility,. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.
authors: Wenbo Yu, Jifan Li, Wenke Xia, Yuchen Li, Yizhuo Zhang, Pei Ren, Zhengping Che, Di hu
bullets: Addresses boundary misalignment between predicted action chunks and the committed execution stream.
Uses a lightweight Control Barrier Function-inspired constraint between consecutive chunks.
Computes corrections in closed form, avoiding backpropagation through the VLA action head.
Progressively tightens consistency during generation while preserving early and within-chunk action flexibility.
Improves success rates by 10%–15% on average and reduces per-chunk inference latency by over 45% versus RTC across simulated and real robotic settings.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free alignment of asynchronous VLA action chunks; directly relevant to vision-language-action execution.
papers.title: Barrier-Constrained Guidance For Real-time Asynchronous VLA Execution
papers.tldr: FreeBar is a training-free, low-overhead plugin that improves real-time asynchronous VLA execution by correcting action-chunk misalignment with barrier-guided constraints.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Abu Hanif Muhammad Syarubany, Hwanhee Kim, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets the high training and inference costs of diffusion-based offline RL policies caused by iterative denoising and backpropagation through time.
Uses average-velocity modeling with a compositional formulation to learn a direct noise-to-action mapping across scales.
Combines the generative policy with behavior-regularized actor–critic learning using one policy network, without distillation, multi-stage training, or Jacobian computations.
Generates actions in one forward pass, with optional value-guided candidate selection for refinement.
Experiments on offline RL benchmarks and robotic manipulation tasks show performance comparable to or better than diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing training and inference time.
papers.selection_reason: Single-step flow-matching policy for offline RL, evaluated on robotic manipulation, fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Compositional Average Velocity Modeling for Efficient Diffusion Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: InsQL enables efficient offline RL by replacing multi-step diffusion-policy sampling with a single-step, compositional average-velocity policy that avoids BPTT and reduces computation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.
authors: Shutong Ding, Zhaoyang Liu, Yimiao Zhou, Jingya Wang, Jiayuan Gu, Ye Shi
bullets: Addresses reduced exploration diversity and capability loss when fine-tuning diffusion policies with RL.
Combines two policies’ score or velocity fields during sampling to control exploration–exploitation trade-offs.
Supports online RL with a frozen exploration branch and offline-to-online RL with a frozen pretrained exploitation branch.
Integrates with QSM, QVPO, and Flow-SDE+PPO across MuJoCo and RoboTwin manipulation tasks.
Provides a unified, plug-and-play framework without changing the underlying RL objectives.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion policy framework for RL in robotic control and manipulation, directly fitting embodied AI subtopics.
papers.title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
papers.tldr: CFG-Policy uses classifier-free guidance to combine separate exploration and exploitation diffusion policies, improving RL adaptation while preserving behavioral diversity and pretrained capabilities.

papers.abstract: Multi-finger hands contact objects at different times, so a global close command can overload early-contact fingers while others are still moving. Dense tactile arrays address this problem but add hardware, calibration, bandwidth, and computation. We present an edge-native pipeline that uses only built-in joint-angle and pre-use-calibrated actuator-load feedback to recognize the grasped object and predict an independent Stop event for each finger. Four samples and their first differences form a 4-by-20 contact-evolution window. At its core is a heterogeneous dual-expert architecture, termed DualExpert, that assigns complementary tasks to a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and a Finger Graph Filter Network (FGFN). The TCN models short-term contact evolution and supplies all five Stop probabilities, while the FGFN encodes finger topology and contributes only to object classification. Fixed 0.7/0.3 class-probability fusion reaches 93.78\% trajectory-level classification accuracy on 225 held-out trials, improving the standalone TCN and FGFN by 4.00 and 2.22 percentage points, respectively. The TCN Stop path attains 95.25\% F1. The dataset contains 1,500 automatically collected trajectories from five object instances. In Flash deployment, mixed accelerator execution retains 93.78\% classification accuracy and 94.84\% Stop F1 with 2.890~ms mean inference time and 9.172~ms mean sample-to-stop latency. Across 50 physical trials, the system achieves 96.00\% recognition and 98.00\% grasp success while the complete embedded board draws approximately 0.80~W.
authors: Jiajian Zheng, Bin Zhang, Wen Fan, Yanan Liu
bullets: Addresses asynchronous multi-finger contact without dense tactile hardware, using pre-calibrated actuator-load and joint-angle signals.
Builds a 4×20 contact-evolution window from four samples and first differences.
DualExpert combines a TCN for temporal contact evolution and per-finger Stop prediction with an FGFN for finger-topology-aware object classification.
Fixed probability fusion achieves 93.78% trajectory-level classification accuracy and the TCN Stop path achieves 95.25% F1 on held-out trials.
Flash deployment maintains 93.78% classification accuracy and 94.84% Stop F1 with 2.890 ms inference, 9.172 ms sample-to-stop latency, and approximately 0.80 W board power.
papers.selection_reason: Learned dexterous grasp classification and per-finger stopping from joint/load feedback; relevant to robot manipulation.
papers.title: Edge-Native Temporal--Graph Dual-Expert Inference for Dexterous Grasp Classification
papers.tldr: An edge-deployable dual-expert model uses joint-angle and actuator-load feedback to classify grasped objects and independently stop each finger, achieving high accuracy with low latency and power.

papers.abstract: Robust motion planning and control for manipulators is the problem of guaranteeing safe execution and collision-free motion under disturbances. The Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF) is a recently proposed planner that comes with robustness guarantees and is particularly attractive for collision-free control as it guarantees closed-loop evolution inside a funnel, i.e., a collision-free region around a nominal trajectory. Despite its attractive theoretical properties, the current approach for computing funnels is computationally demanding, which limits its expressiveness and performance. We address its current limitations by proposing a novel funnel planning and control solution. Our key tool to enable this is a neural Signed Configuration Distance Function (nSCDF) which allows us to estimate collision-free balls and gradients in a computationally efficient way. We use the nSCDF in our planner to compute a nominal trajectory, where path length and clearance are balanced. To track the trajectory with collision-avoidance guarantees, we design a funnel controller that exploits the geometric information from the nSCDF. From numerical experiments, we observe that our planner produces nominal paths $2$ times faster, while at the same time obtaining $20 \%$ shorter path length and $5$ times the clearance. Finally, we also observe improved motion performance and robustness properties when using the nSCDF for funnel control.
authors: Bernhard Wullt, Christos K. Verginis, Per Mattsson, Mikael Norrl\"of, Thomas B. Sch\"on
bullets: Targets the computational cost and limited expressiveness of Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF).
Uses an nSCDF to efficiently estimate collision-free balls and gradients for planning and control.
Plans nominal trajectories that balance path length and obstacle clearance, then tracks them with a geometry-aware funnel controller.
Numerical experiments report paths computed 2× faster, with 20% shorter length and 5× greater clearance.
The approach also improves motion performance and robustness when the nSCDF is used for funnel control.
papers.selection_reason: Neural signed configuration distance functions for manipulator motion planning and control; relevant to learned robot control.
papers.title: Funnel planning and control for manipulators using neural Signed Configuration Distance Functions
papers.tldr: A neural Signed Configuration Distance Function makes funnel-based manipulator planning and control more efficient while preserving collision-avoidance guarantees.

papers.abstract: Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.
authors: Buzhen Huang, Xingchen Wu, Yuanwang Yang, Chenyi Xie, Kun Li
bullets: Targets collaborative manipulation tasks involving sequential actions, role specialization, and multiple agents.
A commander performs joint semantic and geometric planning, then decomposes tasks into role-specific subtasks and shared object-centric plans.
Executors use local observations and the commander’s strategy to learn physics-based coordination through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum.
Experiments across varied manipulation tasks show long-horizon collaboration and scaling from two agents to multiple agents.
The method reports higher success rates than state-of-the-art methods, though specific quantitative results are not provided.
papers.selection_reason: Learned hierarchical control for multi-human cooperative manipulation.
papers.title: Scalable Multi-Human Cooperative Manipulation via Commander-Executor Coordination
papers.tldr: A hierarchical commander–executor framework enables scalable, role-dependent, long-horizon multi-human cooperative manipulation.

papers.abstract: Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones. We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion. TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation. Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.
authors: Weiji Xie, Junsong Wu, Zibo Zhou, Yueru Chen, Xingyi Wang, Zhenhua Xiong, Weinan Zhang, Chenjia Bai
bullets: Addresses the command-execution gap that limits whole-body accuracy in downstream loco-manipulation.
Introduces TTCO, which uses sampling-based optimization over closed-loop BFM and robot-dynamics simulations to adapt input commands.
Across three BFMs on AMASS, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79–84% in simulation.
Derives an approximate compute-optimal scaling strategy to preserve gains with larger test-time budgets.
Generates BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories, validated in simulation and on a real robot for high-level policy training.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time command optimization improves humanoid behavior foundation model execution; relevant to robot learning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Test-Time Compute for Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Test-time command optimization substantially improves humanoid behavior foundation model execution accuracy without retraining, while enabling compute scaling and reuse of demonstrations across models.

papers.abstract: Bilateral teleoperation with force feedback is becoming increasingly important, and the quality of external-torque estimation is critical to this process. However, manufacturer-provided disturbance-torque estimates on commercial robotic arms are often inaccurate, while the use of end-effector force/torque sensors adds cost and payload. We propose LETS, a physics-guided learning approach that assigns rigid-body dynamics to recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics and reserves learning for only the robot-specific residual. LETS uses only the robot's URDF model and joint feedback, deliberately excluding control commands and thereby decoupling external-torque estimation from control-command inputs. It trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute, without requiring a dedicated end-effector six-axis force/torque sensor. In bilateral teleoperation, LETS achieves real-time external-torque estimation that enables stable force feedback. Its free-space error is 69% lower than the manufacturer-provided estimate, substantially reducing coupled oscillations between leader and follower; its contact error is 28% lower, yielding more accurate haptic feedback.
authors: Zonghao Guo, Dongchen Guan, Yubo Wang, Peng Yang
bullets: Addresses inaccurate manufacturer disturbance-torque estimates and the cost and payload of end-effector force/torque sensors.
Combines recursive Newton–Euler rigid-body dynamics with learning of only the robot-specific residual.
Uses only the URDF model and joint feedback, excluding control commands to decouple estimation from inputs.
Trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute without a dedicated six-axis force/torque sensor.
Reduces free-space error by 69% and contact error by 28%, improving haptic feedback and reducing coupled oscillations.
papers.selection_reason: Physics-guided residual learning for external-torque sensing in teleoperation, relevant to robot physical interaction and manipulation.
papers.title: LETS: Low-Overhead External-Torque Sensing for Force-Feedback Bilateral Teleoperation
papers.tldr: LETS enables low-overhead, real-time external-torque estimation for bilateral teleoperation using robot feedback and a physics-guided residual learner, improving force-feedback accuracy and stability.

papers.abstract: Action chunking improves temporal coherence in visuomotor imitation learning by jointly predicting sequences of future actions. However, many existing policies regenerate entire action chunks even when errors are localized, potentially replacing otherwise valid predictions. We introduce Contextual Masked Action Policy (CMAP), a visuomotor policy that refines continuous action chunks through history-conditioned local regeneration. Specifically, CMAP introduces a history-conditioned action tape that combines executed commands with masked future positions to produce coarse action predictions and per-step uncertainty scores. An uncertainty-guided span regeneration mechanism then selects a high-uncertainty contiguous span and reconstructs it using the executed history and retained future predictions as context. By jointly reconstructing neighboring actions, CMAP models local temporal dependencies while preserving all predictions outside the selected span. Extensive experiments on nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that CMAP achieves superior overall performance over several competitive baselines. Ablation studies validate the complementary contributions of its key components, while held-out trajectory analysis shows that local regeneration reduces prediction errors within selected spans.
authors: Chenyang Wang, Yuntian Wang, Jiaying Tang, Chunzheng Li, Yang Liu, Siao Liu
bullets: Addresses the problem of full action-chunk regeneration replacing valid predictions when errors are localized.
Uses a history-conditioned action tape combining executed commands with masked future actions to predict coarse action chunks and per-step uncertainty.
Selects a contiguous high-uncertainty span for local action regeneration using executed history and retained future predictions as context.
Experiments across nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks show superior overall performance over several baselines.
Ablations and held-out trajectory analysis support the complementary components and reduced errors within regenerated spans.
papers.selection_reason: History-conditioned action regeneration for visuomotor imitation learning; fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Predict in Chunks, Revise in Spans: History-conditioned Action Regeneration for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: CMAP improves robotic manipulation by regenerating only uncertain action spans while preserving reliable predictions elsewhere.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a stage-dependent sensory conflict: vision and proprioception are essential for localization and approach, when force is largely uninformative and potentially distracting, whereas force becomes critical after contact, when irrelevant visual details and correlated robot states may become shortcuts. We propose DEFT-VLA (Dual-Expert Force-specialized Training for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation), which retains the task-adapted base expert for vision-dominated non-contact behavior and introduces a force-aware contact expert for critical contact stages, localizing force-conditioned adaptation to where it is needed. We further introduce a contact-localized force-attending curriculum that applies force-attending post-training only to the contact expert, progressively restoring vision and masking state tokens to suppress shortcuts. Real-robot experiments on pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping show that DEFT-VLA effectively exploits force feedback to improve contact-stage performance while maintaining strong non-contact behavior and robustness to held-out grasp heights. It improves overall task success by 20-40 percentage points over the strongest baseline on each task.
authors: Zan Huang, Yibo Qiu, Kan Ding, Xuanping Zhang, Ao Tian, Ronald X Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the conflict between vision/proprioception before contact and force sensing during contact.
Uses separate experts: a base vision-dominated expert for non-contact behavior and a force-aware expert for contact stages.
Applies a contact-localized curriculum that progressively restores vision and masks state tokens to reduce shortcut learning.
Real-robot tests cover pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping.
Reports 20–40 percentage-point overall success gains over the strongest baseline on each task, while retaining non-contact performance and robustness to held-out grasp heights.
papers.selection_reason: Force-specialized VLA for contact-rich manipulation; fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: DEFT-VLA: Stage-Localized Force Specialization for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: DEFT-VLA improves contact-rich manipulation by using force feedback only during contact stages while preserving vision-led behavior during approach and localization.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing believable 4D hand-object grasping sequences is important for character animation, extended reality, and embodied agents. Grasping requires a hand to approach, contact, and lift or manipulate an object coherently. Existing synthesis methods often model only the final static grasp or rely on additional conditions, such as language, target grasps, or object trajectories, to specify the interaction. We instead study the underconstrained problem of generating a complete grasping motion from a single initial hand-object state. Our framework decouples hand-motion generation from object-motion recovery. Given an object point cloud in the initial wrist frame and the initial parameterized hand configuration, conditional flow matching predicts a sequence-level contact map and a hand pose at each normalized sequence time. This time-indexed formulation avoids the error accumulation of autoregressive rollout while representing the complete motion. We then infer an attachment frame and recover rigid-object motion through training-free, contact-guided weighted registration. We evaluate on held-out DexYCB objects and unseen object geometries reconstructed from in-the-wild videos by Open-CHOIR. Compared with LatentHOI, our method produces smoother hand and object motion in every setting, matches or improves on its contact and penetration metrics in the wild under a shared initialization, and is about 30x faster per generated frame. In a 15-participant study, our motions were preferred in roughly two thirds of (forced-choice pairwise) comparisons. Precise contact closure on novel geometry, however, remains a key open challenge.
authors: Nga Kiu Kelly Ho, Yilin Liu, Hao Xu, Niloy J. Mitra
bullets: Addresses underconstrained grasp synthesis without language, target grasps, or object trajectories.
Predicts a time-indexed contact map and hand poses using conditional flow matching, avoiding autoregressive error accumulation.
Recovers rigid object motion via training-free, contact-guided weighted registration after estimating an attachment frame.
On held-out and in-the-wild objects, motion is smoother than LatentHOI, about 30× faster per frame, and preferred in roughly two thirds of user comparisons.
Precise contact closure on novel geometry remains an open challenge.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based 4D hand-object grasping synthesis; relevant to embodied manipulation and physical interaction.
papers.title: Learning Dynamic Grasping
papers.tldr: A conditional flow-matching framework generates complete, smooth hand-object grasping motions from only an initial hand-object state, with faster inference and strong perceptual quality but imperfect contact closure on novel objects.

papers.abstract: We present a learning-based framework that enables a full-scale bipedal humanoid to sprint at over 7 m/s with motion-prior-guided gait and perform aggressive cornering at high speed with a pronounced trunk lean of up to $25^\circ$. Achieving this combination is challenging: above approximately 4 m/s, periodic foot impacts induce severe, high-frequency yaw-rate oscillations intrinsic to high-speed gaits. This high-frequency temporal structure corrupts the history of proprioceptive feedback that flat-MLP policies rely on, while rendering conventional yaw-rate tracking rewards counterproductive, as they fight against the robot's natural oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, a single style prior shared across skills cannot tell which skill is commanded and inherently compromises the low-speed skill fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we adopt a causal multi-head attention (MHA) module to explicitly model the high-frequency temporal feedback. In place of the oscillatory yaw rate, we design a heading-direction reward that supervises only the low-frequency velocity direction, allowing agile turning at high speed without suppressing natural gait oscillations. We further introduce skill-conditioned multi-adversarial-motion-prior (MAMP) discriminators that condition the style reward on the commanded skill. Ablation experiments confirm that each mechanism is essential: replacing structured temporal encoding with a flat-history MLP caps the top speed; reverting to yaw-rate tracking prevents high-speed turning; and a single shared discriminator makes in-place turning collapse into a quasi-static stance. Our framework bridges the gap between raw sprinting speed and reference-motion fidelity, demonstrating stable high-speed sprinting and aggressive cornering in both simulation and real-robot deployment.
authors: Huaxing Huang, Ruidong Li, Jinchao Han, Ziyang Dong, Wenhao Cui
bullets: High-speed foot impacts create yaw-rate oscillations that disrupt flat-history policies and make direct yaw-rate tracking counterproductive.
Causal multi-head attention captures high-frequency proprioceptive dynamics in the policy.
A heading-direction reward encourages turning while preserving natural gait oscillations.
Skill-conditioned multi-adversarial motion priors maintain distinct motion styles across sprinting and turning.
Ablations and simulation-to-real deployment demonstrate stable sprinting and aggressive cornering, including trunk lean up to 25°.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based high-speed humanoid locomotion with structured temporal feedback; fits embodied robot control.
papers.title: Push the Limit: Learning High-Speed Sprinting and Aggressive Cornering on a Full-Scale Humanoid
papers.tldr: A learning framework enables a full-scale humanoid to sprint above 7 m/s and execute aggressive, high-speed cornering by modeling temporal feedback and conditioning motion style on the commanded skill.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation under uncertain object dynamics and geometry remains a core challenge in real-world robotics. Policies trained under fixed assumptions often degrade when object mass, friction, scale, or shape vary. Embedding-based adaptation methods such as Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) address this by conditioning actions on latent representations of environment dynamics inferred from interaction history. We investigate whether this paradigm scales from single arm settings to coordinated bimanual manipulation, where higher dimensional control, coupled contacts, and shared object forces introduce additional complexity. We evaluate bimanual RMA on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties. Bimanual RMA, using observation-action history and dual wrist depth images, retains privileged policy performance on bimanual picking and lifting, while an otherwise matched stationary PPO policy without latent conditioning achieves low success; all methods remain limited on long-horizon stacking. We further demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer on a dual Franka lifting task without real-world finetuning. Together, these results suggest that latent conditioning provides useful structure for scaling robust control to coordinated bimanual systems, while longer horizon tasks require additional temporal structure.
authors: Seung-Bin Joo, Alessandro Albini, Luca Wiehe, Perla Maiolino, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Jo\~ao F. Henriques
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by uncertain object mass, friction, scale, and shape.
Extends Rapid Motor Adaptation to bimanual control using observation-action histories and dual wrist depth images.
Evaluated on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties.
Retained privileged-policy performance for bimanual picking and lifting, while stationary PPO without latent conditioning had low success.
Demonstrated sim-to-real transfer on dual Franka lifting without real-world fine-tuning; stacking remained challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Scales latent motor adaptation to bimanual manipulation; fits robot learning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Scaling Latent Motor Adaptation to Coordinated Bimanual Manipulation
papers.tldr: Latent adaptation enables robust coordinated bimanual manipulation under varied object properties and transfers directly from simulation to real hardware, but struggles with long-horizon stacking.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. Relative to Fast-WAM, BridgeWAM reduces single-sample inference FLOPs by 28.72% in simulation profiling and real-robot latency to 77.1 ms (a 2.47-fold speedup). Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.
authors: Jiaxin Fang, Ruitong Liu, Zeyu Lai, Xingyu Wang, Mingyuan Jia, Pingyue Sheng, Weikang Wan, Mengdi Xu, Yuxiang Gao
bullets: Replaces dense layer-wise video–action coupling with 32 Latent Bridge Queries that aggregate visual, language, and proprioceptive information.
Joint video–action supervision adapts visual representations for action prediction, while cross-attention retrieves task-relevant features.
Decouples expert depths and reuses bridge queries, enabling a deep 30-layer Video Expert with an ultralight two-layer Action Expert.
Achieves 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus; reduces simulated single-sample FLOPs by 28.72% and reaches 77.1 ms real-robot latency.
Qualitative results suggest preferential attention to target objects and destinations under perturbations.
papers.selection_reason: VLA-style world action model with latent bridge queries for robot action prediction and real-robot execution.
papers.title: BridgeWAM: Bridging Video and Action Experts via Latent Bridge Queries
papers.tldr: BridgeWAM uses latent bridge queries to selectively connect video and action experts, improving robot-task performance while reducing inference cost and latency.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.
authors: Peizheng Guo, Cheng Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: WAMs can misjudge actions when predicted futures mix action-induced and environment-driven changes.
An SCM uses intervention and backdoor adjustment to isolate each candidate action’s future change.
CAG-WAM compares action-conditioned and environment-only futures to compute causal action gain (CAG).
CAG guides GRPO-based policy learning and supports inference-time action revision.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Causal action-gain world action model for robot manipulation; fits robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: CAG-WAM: Causal Action-Gain World Action Models for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: CAG-WAM uses causal modeling to separate action-driven effects from environmental changes, improving action evaluation and policy learning for robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with a diffusion or flow-matching action expert has become the mainstream vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm for embodied policies, yet they remain unreliable once a task demands precise manipulation, e.g., submillimeter cable insertion. We attribute this weakness to a training objective that averages flow-matching errors across contexts and flow times, allocating little supervision to the few decisive moments determining task success. Along the generative path, inference integrates a locally supervised velocity field, so equally penalized errors at different flow times can affect the executed action unequally. Consequently, precision-task performance deteriorates as physical tolerance tightens by orders of magnitude. We call this supervision imbalance across contexts and flow times Flow-Time Starvation. The remedy is to jointly align supervision allocation and representation learning with context-dependent precision demand, enabling the policy to recognize when greater precision is needed. We instantiate this precision-forcing strategy as Precision-aware Reweighting and Internalization for Skilled Manipulation (PRISM), which scores precision demand offline, strengthens flow supervision where errors are consequential and action signals are visible, and internalizes that demand in the VLM condition representation. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that PRISM preserves or improves general-task performance while raising mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% across drive connector insertion, bimanual connector mating, and screw tightening, substantially extending the precision boundary of existing embodied policies without new sensors or observation modalities.
authors: Chenghao Yue, Peiyan Li, Hao Wang, Lei Lv, Jiahao Chen, Huaping Liu, Yu Luo, Yuanlong Zhang
bullets: Identifies “Flow-Time Starvation”: standard flow-matching objectives under-supervise decisive moments in precise tasks.
Uses offline precision-demand scores to reweight flow supervision toward consequential, observable action signals.
Internalizes precision demand in the VLM representation so the policy can recognize when finer control is needed.
Simulation and real-robot experiments cover connector insertion, bimanual mating, and screw tightening.
Raises mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% while preserving or improving general-task performance, without new sensors or modalities.
papers.selection_reason: Precision-forcing strategy for generalist VLA policies, improving precise manipulation, fitting vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: PRISM: Precision Forcing for Generalist Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: PRISM improves the precision of vision-language-action policies by focusing training on context and flow times where small errors critically affect manipulation success.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Zihan Gao, Yuhong Zhang, Mengzhe Wang, Kaisheng Liu, Shengpeng Li, Siyao Xiao, Runqing Cheng, Xiao Lin, Zhifang Liu, Haoqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the need for expensive, manually teleoperated demonstrations in dexterous imitation learning.
Uses joint 3D hand-object interaction reconstructions from monocular RGB-D videos as learning input.
Introduces the DexHand Motion Perception Module to encode inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies.
Conditions a diffusion policy on these compact motion representations to generate future robot actions.
Real-world experiments show strong performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Learns dexterous robot control from human videos, fitting robot learning and human video learning.
papers.title: DexCast: Learning Real-World Dexterous Control from Human Videos
papers.tldr: DexCast learns dexterous robot control directly from monocular RGB-D human videos, avoiding costly teleoperation through joint HOI reconstruction and diffusion-based action generation.

papers.abstract: Test-time sampling promises to turn one action prediction into a set of distinct executable candidates that a verifier can choose among. Downstream fine-tuning works against that promise. A vision-language-action model trained to solve one task distribution concentrates its flow-matching decoder around the dominant demonstrated action, so repeated samples differ only marginally and the verifier receives many copies of one decision. We call this proposal contraction and identify it as a key constraint on test-time scaling: repeated samples can remain highly redundant as the candidate budget grows. Action Dynamic Sampling (ADS) alleviates the constraint on the proposal side, during training. At each training step, ADS integrates $K$ additional trajectories from the current policy under fresh base noise, scores each by the flow support along its path with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and corrects the policy's local action distribution toward this weighted set through a detached finite-set KL term. Training cost rises; deployment cost is unchanged. Across simulation and four physical-robot tasks, ADS raises proposal spread without the success penalty that Gaussian perturbation incurs, lifts oracle best-of-8 success on RoboCasa from 57.6% to 63.0%, improves fixed verifiers by 2.4 to 4.9 points in simulation, and raises TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on real-world manipulation.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Haitao Shen, Guanlin Li, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Problem: Fine-tuned VLA flow-matching policies contract around dominant demonstrated actions, producing redundant test-time candidates.
Method: Sample additional policy trajectories, weight them by flow support estimated with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and apply a detached finite-set KL correction.
Contribution: A training-time proposal-diversification method that increases candidate spread while avoiding the success degradation of Gaussian perturbations.
Results: Oracle best-of-8 RoboCasa success rises from 57.6% to 63.0%; fixed verifiers improve by 2.4–4.9 points in simulation and TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on physical-robot tasks.
Scope: ADS increases training cost, while deployment cost remains unchanged.
papers.selection_reason: Improves test-time verified VLA policies for manipulation; directly relevant to vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Flow-Support-Weighted Proposals for Test-Time Verified VLA Policies
papers.tldr: Action Dynamic Sampling reduces redundant action proposals during training, improving verifier-based test-time scaling for VLA policies without increasing deployment cost.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning has shown superior sample efficiency by leveraging the learned latent dynamics either in the form of derivative-free planning/imagined rollout training or dynamics gradient-based policy updates. While these approaches achieve comparatively fast learning, they all suffer, to varying degrees, from issues of recurrent compounding errors, high inference-time latency, and instability in backward propagation through time (BPTT). In this work, we propose a model-based RL approach that uses the chunk world model as a differentiable training-time evaluator to optimize the chunk actor without recurrent model invocation. Through the collaborative chunk-wise prediction of the world model and policy, we can generate H-step hypothetical rollouts in a single forward pass and directly optimize value expansion, avoiding the costly and unstable BPTT. We evaluate our method on 19 challenging high-dimensional humanoid tasks from HumanoidBench and deploy our method to the real-world for quadruped bipedal walking. Project Website: https://song-wx.github.io/cmpo.github.io/
authors: Weixi Song, Donglin Wang, Yong-Lu Li
bullets: Targets compounding model errors, inference-time latency, and instability from backpropagation through time in model-based RL.
Uses collaborative chunk-wise prediction between the world model and policy to generate H-step hypothetical rollouts in a single forward pass.
Directly optimizes value expansion through the chunk world model during training, without recurrent model invocation.
Evaluated on 19 challenging high-dimensional humanoid tasks in HumanoidBench and deployed for real-world quadruped bipedal walking.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative results or comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Model-based RL with chunk world model for humanoid and quadruped control, fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Chunk-wise Model-based Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: Chunk-wise Model-based Policy Optimization improves model-based RL by using a differentiable chunk world model to optimize multi-step actions in one forward pass, avoiding recurrent rollouts and BPTT.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches rely on video or motion-capture data for reinforcement learning (RL) training; however, all of these methods require an upper-level module to generate reference trajectories in real time. In object carrying tasks, the humanoid can only lift objects from designated locations along the reference trajectory, resulting in poor spatial generalization. Moreover, existing policies can only be evaluated inside a motion-capture studio. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MOVER}, a multi-stage, Teacher-Assistant-Student, RL training framework for humanoid object carrying. We first collect data from videos and employ GENMO and GMR to retarget the video data, combining this with data augmentation techniques to generalize the data across objects of varying shapes and sizes.
