papers.selection_reason: World action model for robotic manipulation with implicit tactile dynamics, fitting interactive world models and robot learning.
papers.title: TacDyn-WAM: Learning Implicit Tactile Dynamics in a Heterogeneous Visuo-Tactile World Action Model
papers.tldr: TacDyn-WAM improves visuo-tactile robot manipulation by predicting robust, implicit tactile dynamics instead of reconstructing future tactile images.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies often see only one or a few recent frames, which makes it difficult to evaluate how they use information that disappears during a task. We introduce MIKASA-Robo-VLA, a benchmark of 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks. All but 10 hide the cue an action depends on. Those 10 are reactive controls. MIKASA-Robo, the suite it rebuilds, has 32 tasks and uses language only in a representative VLA subset. Here every task provides an instruction, while memory-dependent tasks hide a task-relevant cue and reactive controls keep it available. For 70 tasks, environment phase timings specify an information gap, and for 28 of them the gap exceeds the 16-frame window of the widest fixed-context VLA we survey. The gap counts only the interval the cue is provably absent, not the full duration a policy must retain it, so every memory-dependent task still requires memory by construction, including the ones whose measured gap is short. We release 22,500 oracle trajectories across 10 memory types in RLDS and LeRobotDataset v3. A reference $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline with current images and proprioception, but no observation history or explicit memory module, is fine-tuned on 14 tasks and achieves 0.211 $\pm$ 0.044 mean task success. Its lower success on the evaluated Long-split tasks is confounded by open-loop chunking and the memory types represented in that subset. Project page: https://mikasarobo.github.io/
authors: Egor Cherepanov, Nikita Kachaev, Aleksandr I. Panov, Alexey K. Kovalev
bullets: Introduces 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks, including 80 memory-dependent tasks and 10 reactive controls.
Memory tasks hide an action-relevant cue, while controls keep the cue observable; 70 tasks define explicit information-gap timings.
For 28 tasks, the cue gap exceeds the 16-frame context of the widest surveyed fixed-context VLA.
Releases 22,500 oracle trajectories covering 10 memory types in RLDS and LeRobotDataset v3.

A reference π₀.₅ model without observation history or an explicit memory module reaches 0.211 ± 0.044 mean task success on 14 fine-tuned tasks; Long-split performance is confounded by chunking and subset composition.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks memory in VLA models for long-horizon manipulation, directly relevant to embodied VLA, robot learning, and embodied memory.
papers.title: MIKASA-Robo-VLA: Benchmarking Memory in VLA Models for Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.tldr: MIKASA-Robo-VLA benchmarks whether vision-language-action policies can retain hidden task cues during long-horizon manipulation.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-enabled VLA policies expose chain-of-thought (CoT) traces that appear to explain and guide their actions, creating a potential interface for runtime safety through reasoning monitoring and correction. In this work, we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for assessing when this interface can improve embodied behavior: correctability, which measures whether unreliable reasoning can be detected and improved during generation, and actionability, which measures whether reasoning corrections produce behaviorally meaningful changes in the intended direction. To enable correctability, we introduce Token-level Reward for Utility-Steered Chain-of-Thought (TRUST), an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial prefixes and uses these estimates to monitor and selectively steer reasoning generation in frozen VLA policies. On the Alpamayo 1.5 driving VLA, TRUST monitors correctness with 88.9% accuracy and improves reasoning correctness from 75.9% to 90.0%. On a baseline-defined challenging subset in AlpaSim, TRUST reduces collision rate by 30.4% and maximum trajectory error by 11.5% relative to the unsteered policy, outperforming a compute-matched Best-of-4 baseline. On the DeepThinkVLA manipulation VLA, TRUST improves the correctness of grasp-state claims from 69.3% to 90.2% and action-choice claims from 68.8% to 85.9%, yet closed-loop task performance on LIBERO-Plus remains largely unchanged. Empirical analysis reveals intent-consistent behavioral effects in Alpamayo 1.5 but limited effects in DeepThinkVLA, helping interpret these different task-level outcomes. Together, our results show that gains in reasoning correctness do not automatically imply gains in embodied performance, motivating evaluation of correctability and actionability when using CoT as a runtime safety interface.
authors: Sathwik Karnik, Joseph JR. Lee, Aryaman Gupta, Somil Bansal
bullets: The paper evaluates two properties of CoT-based runtime safety: correctability (detecting and improving flawed reasoning) and actionability (causing intended behavioral changes).
TRUST is an offline-trained value model that predicts reasoning correctness from partial CoT prefixes and selectively steers generation.
In Alpamayo 1.5 driving, TRUST raises reasoning correctness from 75.9% to 90.0% and reduces collision rate and trajectory error on a challenging AlpaSim subset.
In DeepThinkVLA manipulation, TRUST improves grasp-state and action-choice claim correctness, but produces little change in closed-loop LIBERO-Plus performance.
Results indicate that improved reasoning correctness does not necessarily improve embodied behavior; task-level gains depend on whether corrections affect actions consistently.
papers.selection_reason: Studies monitoring and steering chain-of-thought in VLA policies for driving and manipulation, directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: When Reasoning Helps Action: Monitoring and Steering Chain-of-Thought in Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: TRUST monitors and steers chain-of-thought in frozen vision-language-action policies, improving reasoning correctness but translating to safer behavior only when reasoning is actionable.

papers.abstract: Continual imitation learning evaluates whether a robot can learn new knowledge without forgetting previously learned skills. However, retaining task performance does not ensure the behavior remains grounded in language because policies may rely on scene cues, object associations, or memorized task structure. We introduce a benchmark protocol to study how language-guided behavior changes as robotic policies learn successive tasks. We construct meaning-preserving and meaning-changing instruction variants for the Goal, Spatial, Object, and Long suites of LIBERO. Policy experiments focus on LIBERO-Goal, evaluating Original and Paraphrase instructions after each continual-learning stage. We compare representative continual imitation learning methods under their original assumptions while separating task competence from language sensitivity. The proposed diagnostics complement standard learning and forgetting metrics by measuring semantic robustness, goal adaptation, and language sensitivity. Results show that strong continual-learning performance does not always translate to reliable language grounding, and our diagnostics help determine whether retained skills remain correctly guided by their instructions. Additional materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/stillgrounded
authors: Siddeshwar Raghavan, Ziqin Yuan, Fengqing Zhu, Byung-Cheol Min
bullets: Motivation: Retaining robotic skills does not guarantee that behavior remains guided by instruction meaning.
Method: Introduces meaning-preserving and meaning-changing instruction variants across LIBERO’s Goal, Spatial, Object, and Long suites.
Evaluation: Tests representative continual imitation learning methods, focusing on Original and Paraphrase instructions in LIBERO-Goal across learning stages.
Contribution: Adds diagnostics for semantic robustness, goal adaptation, and language sensitivity alongside standard learning and forgetting metrics.
Finding: Strong continual-learning performance does not consistently imply reliable language grounding.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for language grounding in continual imitation learning for robots; fits embodied robot learning and continual learning.
papers.title: Does Continual Imitation Learning Remain Grounded? A Language-Perturbed Benchmark for Robotic Task Retention
papers.tldr: The benchmark reveals that continual imitation learning can preserve task performance while losing reliable language grounding.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often struggle to generalize to skill combinations absent from their fine-tuning demonstrations, even when every constituent skill has been demonstrated. We focus on a vision shortcut as one failure mode: during fine-tuning, visual observations can serve as a proxy for the instruction, so a policy may execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations rather than the instructed combination. This motivates training with counterfactual pairs formed by holding a demonstration observation fixed while changing the instruction to specify an undemonstrated combination. These pairs, however, lack corresponding demonstrated action targets. Crucially, the currently required skill has already been demonstrated, but actions from those executions cannot serve as direct targets because the same skill can require different actions across observations. We propose CRAFT, which transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to counterfactual pairs using skill representations that can be reused across executions of the same skill. Across three VLA models and two simulation benchmarks, CRAFT improves success on undemonstrated combinations while maintaining high success on demonstrated ones; it also improves compositional generalization on a real robot. Project website: https://taegeunyang.github.io/craft/
authors: Taegeun Yang, Youngju Na, Yoonki Cho, Sung-Eui Yoon
bullets: VLAs may rely on visual shortcuts, executing familiar skill combinations instead of following instructions for unseen combinations.
CRAFT holds an observation fixed while replacing its instruction with an undemonstrated skill combination.
It transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill using reusable skill representations, despite differing action targets across observations.
Across three VLA models and two simulation benchmarks, CRAFT improves unseen-combination success while preserving demonstrated-combination performance, and also helps on a real robot.
papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual skill alignment improves compositional generalization in vision-language-action policies.
papers.title: Same Scene, Different Task: Skill Alignment for Compositional Generalization in VLAs
papers.tldr: CRAFT improves VLA compositional generalization by aligning skill supervision across counterfactual instruction–observation pairs.

papers.abstract: Autonomously constructing physically realizable 3D structures remains a significant challenge due to combinatorial action spaces, interchangeable components, equifinal assembly sequences, and strict stability requirements during construction. State-of-the-art methods fine-tune large language models for text-based generative construction. However, these approaches do not allow for Multimodal (text, image, sketch) conditioning, overlook the practical role of scaffolding for stabilizing intermediate structures, and suffer from slow inference speeds. Therefore, we formulate construction as a probabilistic next-block generation task with multiple potential assembly actions and multiple potential task conditioning modalities. Concurrently, we explicitly consider the utility of scaffolding by introducing an auxiliary scaffold block token. We present Scaffold Multimodal Monte Carlo (ScaffoldM3C), a multimodal, lightweight, auto-regressive model for stable block-based construction, that proposes a set of next-step candidate blocks. Leveraging these candidates, we utilize Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to maintain a population of possible assembly sequences, allowing us to consider multiple, potentially different, assembly directions simultaneously. We train our multimodal architecture by extending the StableText2Brick dataset to contain image conditioning prompts and scaffold-stabilized build sequences. ScaffoldM3C is 4x smaller than competing baselines, yielding a 5x to 20x speedup during inference, while achieving comparable construction quality to state-of-the-art methods and higher overall stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and real-world robot assembly demonstrations.
